The court below, after finding that the non-party, who was the Plaintiffs’ person exercising parental authority and the representative director of the non-party Geojin Textile Co., Ltd., while operating the non-party company, for the purpose of raising operating funds, as stated in its reasoning, entered into mortgage creation contracts with the Defendants, designating the non-party company as the debtor, in his capacity as the legal representative of the minor Plaintiffs and in his own capacity, with respect to each of the real properties in this case jointly owned by the non-party and the Plaintiffs, and then completed the registration thereof, further held that, even taking into account the circumstance that the non-party, as the representative director of the non-party company, was a major shareholder owning approximately 66% of its shares, and that the act of establishing mortgages on each of the real properties in this case was for securing the debts of the non-party company and would bring only disadvantage to the minor Plaintiffs, the aforementioned act of establishing mortgages, by its objective nature, was for securing the debts of the non-party company, and could not be deemed an act in conflict of interests for which there is a risk of a conflict of interests arising between the non-party, who was the legal representative of the Plaintiffs as the person exercising parental authority, and the Plaintiffs who were his children; such holding is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, as alleged, in the misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning an act in conflict of interests prescribed in Article 921 of the Civil Act. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, all appeals are dismissed and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the unsuccessful Plaintiffs, and the Justices participating in the case having reached unanimity, judgment is rendered as stated in the dispositive part."}

question: A and B entered into a partnership agreement under the Civil Act to conduct a business related to artificial intelligence. Due to personal circumstances, B withdrew from the partnership. Which of the following statements concerning this are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) A partner’s voluntary withdrawal is a kind of termination of the partnership agreement and must be effected by a manifestation of intention to the other partners; however, such manifestation of intention may also be made impliedly. (b) Because B withdrew, the partnership relationship terminated, and as a result the partnership is naturally dissolved or liquidated. (c) Partnership property belonging to the joint ownership of A and B, after B’s withdrawal, belongs to A’s sole ownership. (d) B may demand from A an accounting of the partnership property due to withdrawal, and such accounting must be based on the condition of the partnership property at the time of B’s withdrawal. (e) Unless there are special circumstances, such as a separate agreement regarding the method of calculating the share, when calculating B’s share, A bears the burden of proving the condition of the partnership property.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2019DA207851]": "We determine the grounds of appeal (as to the petitions submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal, to the extent that they supplement the grounds).\\n\\n1. Claim for damages and claim for return of investment funds (Grounds of Appeal, Points 1 and 2)\\n\\nThe court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim for damages and claim for return of investment funds on the ground that it is difficult to find that the Defendant deceived the Plaintiff and received the investment funds, or that the Defendant agreed to return the investment funds to the Plaintiff.\\n\\nUpon examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, there is no error in the judgment of the court below, such as, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, failing to conduct the necessary hearing, deviating from the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by acting against the rules of logic and experience, or misconstruing the legal principles concerning the interpretation of declarations of intent.\\n\\n2. Claim for settlement amount arising from withdrawal from a partnership (Grounds of Appeal, Point 3)\\n\\na. The accounting between a withdrawn partner and the other partners shall be made according to the status of the partnership property at the time of withdrawal (Civil Act Article 719(1)).\\n\\nIn a partnership composed of two persons, if one person withdraws, the partnership relationship terminates; however, unless there are special circumstances, the partnership is neither dissolved nor liquidated. Rather, the partnership property held in joint ownership by the partners belongs exclusively to the remaining partner, and an accounting for the withdrawal must be made between the withdrawn partner and the remaining partner (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2018. 12. 13., 2015DA72385).\\n\\nA withdrawn partner may recover his or her share if, as a result of calculating the partnership property at the time of withdrawal, the financial condition of the partnership is not in deficit. Therefore, when calculating the share of a withdrawn partner, unless there are special circumstances such as a separate agreement on the method of calculating the share, the burden of proving the condition of the partnership property rests on the person asserting recovery of the share.\\n\\nb. The court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim for a settlement amount arising from withdrawal from the partnership for the following reasons.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff and the Defendant agreed to carry on a business relating to Cambodia together, and this agreement constitutes a partnership contract under the Civil Act. The Plaintiff withdrew from the partnership by filing the action in this case. In order for the Plaintiff to seek from the Defendant the return of the Plaintiff’s share in the partnership property on the ground of withdrawal, the financial condition of the partnership at the time of withdrawal must first be established, and the Plaintiff bears the burden of proving this. Based on the evidence submitted by the Plaintiff alone, the size or details of the partnership property at the time of withdrawal cannot be identified; therefore, it cannot be found that the Defendant bears an obligation to settle the Plaintiff’s investment funds of 170,000,000 won with the Plaintiff.\\n\\nc. Although there are improper parts in the reasons of the judgment of the court below, when the reasons of the judgment of the court below are examined in light of the legal principles stated above, the conclusion that the Defendant does not bear an obligation to settle the Plaintiff’s share upon withdrawal from the partnership is proper. There is no error in the judgment of the court below, such as, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, failing to conduct the necessary hearing, deviating from the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by acting against the rules of logic and experience, or misconstruing the legal principles concerning the burden of proof.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed as it is without merit, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

question: B, having been granted authority by A to sell X land owned by A, entered into a sales contract with C concerning X land. Which of the following explanations is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies)
A: If C demanded performance of the obligation from A, but A argues that because he had not granted agency authority to B, he is under no obligation to perform, C must prove that B had authority to sell X land.
B: If B received the balance from the buyer C, then, absent special circumstances, C’s obligation to pay the balance is extinguished even if B did not remit the balance to A.
C: If C was deceived by D, a third party, and entered into the sales contract with B, C may rescind the sales contract on the ground of a manifestation of intent induced by fraud only when B learned of D’s fraudulent conduct.
D: If A argues that the above sales contract was concluded at a price markedly lower than market value and is void as an unfair legal act, the distress requirement is determined based on A, and the rashness/inexperience requirement is determined based on B.
E: Even if adult guardianship is commenced for A after A granted authority to B, B’s agency authority does not terminate.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA38927]": "The part of the lower court judgment against the Defendant is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Seoul District Court, Main Office."}

{"[93DA39379]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 1\\n\\n1. In light of the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below’s factual findings are acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in violation of the rules of evidence evaluation.\\n\\n2. The evidence indicated in the argument, namely Exhibit B No. 3-2, 3 (receipt, copy of the register), Exhibit B No. 4 (witness examination record), and Exhibit B No. 17-1 through 4 (supplemental statement of grounds for appeal, statement, lease agreement, receipt), may serve as evidence of indirect facts that would lead to the inference that the nonparty was the Defendants’ duly authorized agent, but they cannot be said to be inconsistent with the facts found by the court below or with the fact that the said nonparty was the Defendants’ agent; accordingly, it cannot be said to be unlawful for the court below not to have made an evidentiary determination as to the above evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below’s action in comprehensively considering the various evidence submitted and finding that the said nonparty was the Defendants’ duly authorized agent is acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any violation of the rules of evidence evaluation or any illegality in omission of determination as argued, nor can it be said that the court below’s determination conflicts with the view of this Court’s precedents. The precedents of this Court cited by the argument concern cases with factual circumstances different from those of this case, and are not appropriate.\\n\\n3. The argument is nothing more than an attack on the court below’s judgment on the premise of facts different from those lawfully found by the court below through its discretionary selection and evaluation of evidence, which falls within its exclusive province, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAccordingly, the argument is without merit.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 2\\n\\n1. In voluntary agency, the scope of the agent’s authority is determined by the act of authorization (the act of granting agency authority); therefore, whether a certain act falls within the scope of agency authority is to be determined by the contents of the individual act of authorization or its interpretation. However, generally speaking, voluntary agency authority as the ordinary content of an act of authorization should be regarded as including, within the extent necessary incidental to such authority, the so-called authority to receive declarations of intent from the counterparty.\\n\\nAlso, an agent who has been granted authority by the owner of real property to conclude a sales contract should, absent special circumstances, be regarded as also having authority to receive the intermediate payment or balance under that sales contract (see, inter alia, this Court’s Decisions rendered on 1991. 1. 29., 90DA9247; and on 1992. 4. 14., 91DA43107). In this case, where there are no special circumstances warranting a finding that the said nonparty had only authority to conclude the sales contract but no authority to receive the purchase price, the court below’s action recognizing the said nonparty’s authority to receive the balance of the purchase price is correct and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the legal principles concerning authority to receive the balance of the purchase price.\\n\\n2. The argument contends that, because there were circumstances that should have caused suspicion as to the said nonparty’s agency authority, such as the fact that the said nonparty did not possess material indicia such as the Defendants’ power of attorney or seal affixed to a stamp, the Plaintiff should have paid the purchase price directly to the Defendants or should have paid it after confirming with the Defendants, and should have notified the Defendants of the payment even after payment; nevertheless, the Plaintiff paid the purchase price to the said nonparty without taking such measures, and therefore the legal effect of the payment of the purchase price cannot be attributed to the Defendants, who are the principals, but this cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. The argument also disputes the factual findings that are within the exclusive province of the court below, and, premised on factual circumstances different from those found by the court below, asserts that the court below’s judgment contains an illegality in misapprehending the legal principles concerning authority to receive the balance of the purchase price; accordingly, it is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[93DA42047]": "We consider the first point of the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below recognized that Non-party 1, who is the Plaintiff’s wife, as stated in the judgment, on 1991. 8. 13. issued to the Defendant one promissory note for KRW 30,000,000 in face value, with Non-party 1 and the Plaintiff as makers and with the issue date as 1991. 8. 13., and that on that same day she requested the attorney in charge belonging to the law firm authorized for notarization to prepare, together with the Defendant and in the capacity of both herself and the Plaintiff’s agent, a notarial deed stating that there would be no objection even if immediate compulsory execution were taken in the event of delay in payment of the amount of the above promissory note, thereby having a notarial deed as stated in the main text of the judgment of the court below prepared and delivered to her; and the court below further held that, according to the contents of Defendant’s Exhibit No. 1 (original of the notarial deed), Defendant’s Exhibits No. 2-1 and 2 (certificate of seal impression, power of attorney), and the testimony of Witness 1 at the first instance, it could be recognized that at the time the notarial deed as stated in the judgment was prepared, Non-party 1 was in possession of the Plaintiff’s seal and one copy of the Plaintiff’s certificate of seal impression for notarization, which was shown as having been issued upon delegation from the Plaintiff, but that these recognized facts alone were insufficient to find that the Plaintiff had granted Non-party 1 authority to act as agent with respect to the issuance of the above note and the preparation of the notarial deed, and that there was no other evidence to recognize this.\\n\\nUpon comparison with the record, the power of attorney for issuance of a certificate of seal impression in the Plaintiff’s name and the certificate of seal impression alleged by the theory of appeal are nothing more than one set of materials from which authority may be recognized, and by such materials it is not naturally recognized that Non-party 1 had authority to issue the promissory note in this case on behalf of the Plaintiff or to request the preparation of the notarial deed as stated in the judgment of the court below with respect to this note, and the burden of proving the existence of such authority lies with the Defendant who asserts the effect thereof; accordingly, the court below’s finding and determination to that effect are proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the allocation of the burden of proof or the effect of dispositive documents as alleged by the theory of appeal.\\n\\nMoreover, although the authenticity of the portion directly prepared by the notary of Defendant’s Exhibit No. 1 (certified copy of the notarial deed) alleged by the theory of appeal is presumed, the fact that may be recognized thereby is only that Non-party 1 made the request for the above notarial deed as the Plaintiff’s agent, and it does not naturally follow that Non-party 1 had lawful authority to act as agent.\\n\\n2. The statement of acceptance of compulsory execution, which enables a notarial deed to have enforceability as an instrument evidencing an obligation, is a litigation act against the notary, and as to such a litigation act, the provisions on apparent agency under the Civil Act cannot be applied or applied mutatis mutandis.\\n\\nThe court below’s action in rejecting the Defendant’s assertion of apparent agency by reasoning to this effect is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of legal principles as alleged by the theory of appeal.\\n\\nAll arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved as stated in the main text."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning acquisitive prescription of possession are correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, it follows case law) (a) If X land is in a co-ownership relationship of sectional ownership between B and C, A, who has completed acquisitive prescription with respect to B’s specific sectional ownership portion, may demand performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of completion of acquisitive prescription not only against B but also against C, who is unrelated to B’s specific sectional ownership portion, with respect to each co-ownership share in that land portion. (b) Where a person who has lawfully and validly registered and acquired ownership of real property possesses his own real property, unless special circumstances exist, such possession cannot be said to be possession that forms the basis of acquisitive prescription. (c) If A, who has created an assignment by way of security over X land, has possessed X land peacefully and openly with intent to own for 20 years, since acquisition of ownership by acquisitive prescription is an original acquisition, A may seek cancellation of the ownership transfer registration made for security purposes on the ground of acquisitive prescription of possession. (d) If A, the prescriptive acquirer of X land, assigns to C the right to claim registration of transfer of ownership arising from completion of acquisitive prescription, notification by A to B, the registered title holder, of that assignment gives rise to opposability against B.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2014DA21649]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to Grounds of Appeal 1 and 2\\n\\nWhere, in relation to a debt, it is agreed that ownership of real property owned by the debtor shall be transferred to the creditor, the issue of whether such transfer was made as a dation in payment in lieu of performance of the prior debt, or whether it was made for the security of the prior debt while reserving a subsequent liquidation procedure, is a matter of interpretation of the parties’ intent at the time of the agreement. Where there is no clear proof on this point, whether it was for security purposes must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances, such as the amount of the debt at the time of the agreement and the value of the real property at that time, the circumstances under which the relevant debt was incurred and the subsequent process, the circumstances at the time of the agreement, and the later control and disposition of the relevant real property (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA11648, decided January 16, 2013).\\n\\nIn light of the facts and circumstances as stated in the judgment below and recognized by the evidence admitted by the court below, the court below determined that Non-party 2, around April 18, 1941, while borrowing money from Non-party 3, transferred ownership of the 1st, 3rd, and 4th parcels of land stated in the attached list of real property in the name of Non-party 3 as so-called security assignment for the purpose of securing the claim.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the court below’s such determination is proper, and there is no illegality in that it violated the rules of logic and experience, exceeded the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or erred in the law concerning violation of the adversarial principle or failure to exercise the right to clarify.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground of Appeal 3\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, premised that the security assignee, Non-party 3, only acquired, in trust, ownership of the 1st, 3rd, and 4th parcels of land stated in the attached list of real property, within the scope of the purpose of security, and that Non-party 2, as the security assignor, had possessed and used the above parcels with intent to own as the substantive owner; accordingly, it held that the Plaintiff, who inherited such possession as an heir of Non-party 2, had also possessed the above parcels with intent to own, and then determined that the Plaintiff had acquired by prescription, as of August 22, 2010, which was 20 years after August 22, 1990, when the Plaintiff inherited possession from Non-party 2, the (Sa) portion of the first parcel of land in this case and the 3rd and 4th parcels of land, and thus granted in full the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendants, who are the heirs of Non-party 3, for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of acquisitive prescription by possession.\\n\\nb. The portion of the court below’s decision that held that, because the security assignor had possessed the real property subject to security assignment peacefully and openly with intent to own for 20 years, a claim for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of acquisitive prescription may be brought against the security assignee, cannot be accepted as it stands for the following reasons.\\n\\nSince acquisitive prescription of possession of real property constitutes original acquisition, unless there are special circumstances, it results in the acquisition of ownership in full content, unaffected by various restrictions imposed on the ownership of the original owner (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA31463, decided September 24, 2004). However, where a debtor or a person who provided real property as security for another’s debt, who was not the true right holder, after having completed registration of establishment of a mortgage on the real property in favor of the creditor for the purpose of securing a debt, acquires the real property by prescription, because the debtor or the third-party guarantor is a person who is obligated or liable to perform payment of the secured claim and has already possessed the property while accepting the existence of the mortgage, the mortgagee’s right does not extinguish by the acquisitive prescription acquisition of the mortgaged property. This legal principle applies equally to cases of real-property security assignment; therefore, even if the security assignor has possessed the real property subject to security assignment peacefully and openly with intent to own for 20 years, apart from the issue of seeking cancellation of the ownership transfer registration made for security purposes by asserting extinguishment by prescription of the secured claim against the security assignee, the security assignor cannot seek cancellation of the ownership transfer registration made for security purposes on the ground of acquisitive prescription by possession, nor can the security assignor seek an ownership transfer registration in the name of the security assignor that has such effect.\\n\\nExamining the factual relations recognized by the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles, as the heir of Non-party 2, who was the security assignor, the Plaintiff may seek, against the Defendants, who are the heirs of Non-party 3, who was the security assignee, cancellation of the ownership transfer registration made for security purposes while asserting extinguishment by prescription of the secured claim; however, apart from that, the Plaintiff cannot seek an ownership transfer registration on the ground of acquisitive prescription by possession. Nevertheless, the court below granted the Plaintiff’s claim solely for the reasons stated in its judgment; thus, the court below’s determination contains an error of law concerning real-property security assignment and the person entitled to invoke acquisitive prescription by possession, and the ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe portions of the judgment below concerning the Defendants with respect to the 1st parcel of land stated in the attached list of real property and the portions concerning the 3rd and 4th parcels of land stated in the attached list of real property are all reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and a new determination on those portions, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating.\\n\\n[Appendix] List of Real Property: Omitted"}

{"[2015DA36167]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Examination of the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. With respect to the grounds for appeal concerning Defendant 2 and Defendant 12\\n\\n(1) Even if the trial was conducted by service by public notice as to the Defendant at the court of first instance and the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant was dismissed, this does not mean that the Defendant can be deemed to have disputed the Plaintiff’s cause of action; therefore, where, in the appellate trial appealed by the Plaintiff, the Defendant was served by a means other than service by public notice but did not dispute the claim, a deemed admission under Article 150 of the Civil Procedure Act is established (see Supreme Court Decision rendered 2011DA104079 on 2013. 10. 31.).\\n\\n(2) According to the record, it can be ascertained that the court of first instance conducted the trial by service by public notice as to Defendant 2 and Defendant 12 and then dismissed in full the Plaintiff’s claims against the above Defendants; and that, after the Plaintiff appealed, the lower court served a duplicate of the petition of appeal, a notice of hearing date, and the like on the above Defendants by a means other than service by public notice, but the above Defendants did not dispute the Plaintiff’s allegations.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, with respect to Defendant 2 and Defendant 12, a deemed admission under Article 150 of the Civil Procedure Act should be considered to have been established; nevertheless, the lower court dismissed the Plaintiff’s claims against the above Defendants on the ground that there was no evidence to recognize the Plaintiff’s assertions. The lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning deemed admission.\\n\\nB. With respect to the grounds for appeal concerning the remaining Defendants among the Defendants listed in Attachment 1, excluding Defendant 2 and Defendant 12\\n\\nThe lower court rejected the claims, on the grounds stated in its holding, that the presumption of possession in one’s own right by the non-party with respect to the land in this case was rebutted, and therefore a claim right to registration of transfer of ownership based on completion of the acquisitive prescription by possession was not recognized, and accordingly the Plaintiff’s claim that he had successively acquired from the non-party a claim right to registration of transfer of ownership arising from completion of the acquisitive prescription by possession could not be recognized either.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper, and there is no error therein, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning possession in one’s own right, inadequate deliberation, or omission to decide.\\n\\n2. Examination of the grounds for appeal by the Defendants listed in Attachment 2\\n\\nIn a real estate sale and purchase contract, the seller and the buyer bear certain obligations that are in a concurrent-performance relationship with each other, so a relationship of trust accompanies the performance process. In particular, from the seller’s standpoint, there is room to consider differently whether to maintain the contract depending on who the buyer is, such as the buyer’s financial ability or credit for payment of the purchase price.\\n\\nFor this reason, the assignment of a claim right to registration of transfer of ownership arising from a sale is, absent special circumstances, restricted, and the debtor’s consent or approval is required for such assignment; accordingly, unlike ordinary assignment of claims, mere notice by the assignor to the debtor does not produce opposability against the debtor, and opposability arises only upon obtaining the debtor’s consent or approval (see Supreme Court Decision rendered 2000DA51216 on 2001. 10. 9.).\\n\\nHowever, a claim right to registration of transfer of ownership arising from completion of the acquisitive prescription contains no contractual relationship or relationship of trust whatsoever between the creditor and the debtor, and, accordingly, there is no obligation that the creditor must bear as counterperformance to the debtor.\\n\\nTherefore, in the case of the assignment of a claim right to registration of transfer of ownership arising from completion of the acquisitive prescription, the legal doctrine of restriction on assignment concerning a claim right to registration of transfer of ownership arising from sale should not be applied.\\n\\nIf that is so, since the Plaintiff alleged all of the requisite facts regarding assignment of claims, and the effect of deemed admission under Article 150 of the Civil Procedure Act has arisen with respect thereto, the legal effect of acquisition by assignment of the claim right to registration of transfer of ownership should be recognized.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no error therein, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning restriction on assignment of the claim right to registration of transfer of ownership, the subject matter or effect of admission, or the burden of proof.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the lower judgment concerning the claims against Defendant 2 and Defendant 12 is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; all appeals by the Plaintiff against the remaining Defendants among the Defendants listed in Attachment 1, excluding Defendant 2 and Defendant 12, and all appeals by the Defendants listed in Attachment 2 are dismissed; and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating.\\n\\n[[Attachment 1] List of Defendants: omitted]\\n[[Attachment 2] List of Defendants: omitted]"}

{"[2017DA204629]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (supplementary briefs on the grounds of appeal, etc., filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal, only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Whether the Plaintiff’s provisional attachment is extinguished upon completion of acquisitive prescription\\n\\na. Facts\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\nOn November 25, 1985, Non-party 1 granted Non-party 2 a provisional registration of the right to claim transfer of ownership, based on a pre-sale agreement, with respect to the real property at issue owned by Non-party 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the provisional registration at issue”). The Plaintiff, a creditor of Non-party 1, made a provisional attachment registration with respect to the real property at issue on August 29, 2005. Non-party 2 made the principal registration based on the provisional registration at issue on September 15, 2005, and commenced possession around that time, and, as a result, the provisional attachment registration at issue was erased ex officio on October 24, 2005. The Defendants purchased the real property at issue from Non-party 2 and, on July 3, 2015, made registrations of transfer of ownership with respect to the real property at issue, in shares of 1/2 each, based on sale.\\n\\nb. The judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe provisional registration at issue became ineffective because the right to complete the pre-sale agreement was extinguished upon the lapse of the peremptive period; however, thereafter Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 agreed to the utilization of the provisional registration and, accordingly, the principal registration in the name of Non-party 2 was completed, so the registrations of transfer of ownership in the names of the Defendants based thereon are valid. However, the ex officio erasure of the provisional attachment registration at issue arising from the provisional registration at issue was made without legal cause and is therefore void, and the Defendants, as third parties with an interest in the registration concerning the real property at issue, have a duty to express their intention of consent to the procedure for restoration registration of the provisional attachment registration at issue.\\n\\nThe Defendants argue that they acquired ownership of the real property at issue free from any restrictions because acquisitive prescription based on the registry was completed with respect to the real property at issue; however, even if the Defendants acquired ownership of the real property at issue upon completion of acquisitive prescription based on the registry, the retroactive effect thereof does not affect the provisional attachment registration at issue completed before the date on which Non-party 2 commenced possession, and therefore the Defendants’ argument is without merit.\\n\\nc. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n(1) The reason for the existence of the system of acquisitive prescription for real property is that, where the state of possession of real property has continued for a long time, the factual state bearing the appearance of a right is respected and elevated into a true legal relationship so as to protect it, thereby promoting the stability of the legal order, and that, in view of the fact that a factual state continuing for a long period has a high probability of corresponding to the true legal relationship, it is intended to relieve the possessor’s difficulty of proof when a dispute arises concerning the legal relationship.\\n\\nWhere a person who has acquired ownership by making a lawful and valid registration with respect to real property possesses his or her own real property, absent special circumstances, such possession cannot be said to be possession forming the basis of acquisitive prescription. In such a case, there is no need to elevate and protect the factual state into a legal relationship, and because the registered owner of the real property is presumed to lawfully hold ownership of the real property, there is also no need to relieve the difficulty of proving ownership (see Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA26574, Sept. 26, 1989, Supreme Court Decision 2016DA224596, Oct. 27, 2016, etc.). However, even a person who possesses real property based on ownership may, in exceptional cases where, because he or she has not registered title, it is difficult to prove his or her own ownership or he or she cannot assert ownership against a third party, and where there is a need to elevate and protect the factual state of possession into a legal relationship and to relieve the difficulty of proof, have possession of his or her own real property regarded as possession forming the basis for recognizing acquisitive prescription.\\n\\n(2) We examine this case in light of the foregoing legal principles. Since the real property at issue is owned by the Defendants, who have also completed lawful and valid registrations of transfer of ownership, their possession cannot be possession forming the basis of acquisitive prescription. The Defendants’ defense premised on completion of acquisitive prescription with respect to the real property at issue cannot be accepted without need for further examination. Although there is an improper part in the reasons of the judgment below, the conclusion of the court below rejecting the Defendants’ defense is proper, and there is no error of misapprehending the legal principles as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Whether there was a violation of the principle of good faith or an abuse of rights\\n\\nThe court below determined that the Plaintiff’s alternative claim is not so manifestly unjust as to be deemed unreasonable, and that requiring the opposing party to bear it is clearly contrary to fairness and therefore does not rise to a degree that cannot be tolerated in social life.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the judgment below in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of good faith or abuse of rights, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendants’ appeal is without merit and is dismissed in its entirety, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[97DA1730]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below found, based on the evidence it presented, that Nonparty 1 built one house on the 89.10 square meters of the portion marked ㉮ in the diagram attached as an appendix to the judgment below among the land at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the portion of the land at issue”) on an unknown date around May 1960, occupied the portion of the land at issue as the site of that house and resided there, and then, around April 1966, gratuitously lent the house to his wife’s brother-in-law, Nonparty 2, so that he resided in the house until 1995, thereby continuously occupying the portion of the land at issue through the said Nonparty 2; that, as of May 31, 1980, the Defendants owned the land at issue in co-ownership in the proportions of Defendant 1’s 68.8/445 share and Defendant 2’s 30.75/445 share; and that Nonparty 1 died on November 15, 1993, and the Plaintiffs became the co-heirs of his estate. The court below then held that, according to the above facts found, Nonparty 1 had occupied the portion of the land at issue directly or through the said Nonparty 2 for more than 20 years from an unknown date around May 1960, and such possession is presumed to have been peaceful and open with the intent to own; therefore, Nonparty 1 acquired, as of May 31, 1980, when 20 years had elapsed since he began occupying the portion of the land at issue, a right to claim registration of transfer of ownership, based on completion of acquisitive prescription, against the Defendants, who were the co-owners of the portion of the land at issue, with respect to their respective shares in ownership, and accordingly, the Defendants are under a duty to implement the registration procedure for transfer of ownership, based on completion of acquisitive prescription, to the Plaintiffs, who are the heirs of the deceased, according to each of their respective inheritance shares, with respect to each of their respective co-owned shares in the portion of the land at issue. The court below further rejected the Defendants’ argument that, since the land at issue is owned exclusively by specific portions according to the respective co-ownership shares by the Defendants and several others, and the portion of the land at issue is a portion exclusively owned by Nonparty 3, the Defendants, who have no relation to the portion of the land at issue, cannot comply with the Plaintiffs’ claim for registration of transfer of ownership in this case, on the ground that even if a property relationship such as the one asserted by the Defendants has been formed among the co-owners of the land at issue, including the Defendants, such relationship cannot be asserted against the Plaintiffs, who are third parties, and therefore the Defendants’ above argument lacks merit in itself.\\n\\nExamining this in comparison with the record, the court below’s factual findings and determination appear to be correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in the misapprehension of law concerning acquisitive prescription and the Real Estate Registration Act regarding real property subject to a co-ownership relationship for sectional ownership, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nFurther, even if the Plaintiffs lost the action for delivery brought by Nonparty 3 and thereafter were subjected to execution of delivery and thereby lost possession of the portion of the land at issue, unless such circumstances can be regarded as a waiver of the benefit of prescription, the already acquired right to claim registration of transfer of ownership would not be extinguished (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 93DA47745 rendered on March 28, 1995); therefore, the ground of appeal asserting this point cannot be accepted either.\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning the ancillary clauses of a juristic act is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to case law)
A: Even if there is an intent to make the arising or extinguishment of the effect of a juristic act depend on whether an uncertain future fact occurs, if such intent is not externally manifested, it cannot constitute a condition as an ancillary clause of the juristic act.
B: The burden of proving that a certain juristic act falls under a juristic act subject to a suspensive condition lies with the person who seeks to assert that the legal effect arising from that juristic act has not occurred.
C: The phrase “when the fulfillment of a condition has been hindered” refers to a case in which, in light of social common sense, the condition would have been fulfilled had there been no hindering act by one party, but it was not fulfilled because of the hindering act; this includes even cases in which the possibility of fulfillment of the condition was markedly low even if there had been no such hindering act.
D: If, after completing the registration of a transfer of ownership of real property due to a gift subject to a resolutory condition, the resolutory condition is fulfilled, ownership reverts to the donor. In such a case, acts of disposition made by the donee before the fulfillment of the condition are void to the extent that they limit the effect of the fulfillment of the condition; however, if that condition has not been registered, the donee may not assert such voidness against a third party who acquired rights through the disposition act.
E: If the parties have designated the time when an uncertain fact occurs as the time for performance, then the time for performance should be deemed to have arrived not only when that fact occurs, but also when the occurrence of that fact has become impossible.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2015DA219504]": "We examine the grounds for appeal (the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds for appeal filed after the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal has expired, only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. A novation agreement is a dispositive act that extinguishes the old obligation and creates a new obligation; because the extinguishment of the old obligation depends on the creation of the new obligation, if the new obligation arising from the novation is not created or is rescinded due to illegality of the cause or for a reason unknown to the parties, the old obligation is not extinguished (Civil Act Article 504), and in the so-called conditional novation, in which a condition is attached to the novation agreement, the extinguishment of the old obligation and the very creation of the new obligation depend on whether the condition is fulfilled (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2007. 11. 15., 2005DA31316).\\nHowever, a condition is an accessory clause of a juridical act that makes the arising or extinction of the legal effect of the juridical act depend on the occurrence or non-occurrence of a future uncertain fact, and therefore forms an integral part of the declaration of intent constituting the relevant juridical act. Accordingly, under the general principle governing declarations of intent, an intent to attach a condition, namely a conditional intent, and its manifestation are required; and even if there is a conditional intent, if it is not externally manifested, it is merely a motive for the juridical act and does not by itself become a condition as an accessory clause of the juridical act (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2003. 5. 13., 2003DA10797, and others).\\n\\n2. The court below found that: (1) ① on 2005. 1. 21., the Plaintiff, Sone Son Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Sone Son”), and a third party entered into an agreement to jointly carry out the apartment housing construction project stated in the judgment below (hereinafter “the subject project”) on the 35 parcels of land in Geoje-si, Sinhae-eup, Sangdong-ri, including the parcels of land listed in the attached Schedule to the judgment below (hereinafter “the subject lands”); ② accordingly, on 2005. 1. 26., Sone Son, designating the purchaser as “Sone Son and one other person,” entered into each sale and purchase contract with the Defendants, who were the owners of the subject lands, to purchase the subject lands (hereinafter collectively “the First Contract in this case”); ③ Buseong Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Buseong Industrial Development”) entered into a contract with Sone Son on 2005. 8. 4. to acquire all rights to the subject project site, and on 2006. 6. 27. entered into a business rights transfer and assignment agreement (hereinafter “the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case”) to acquire the rights to the subject project; ④ upon acquiring the rights to the subject project site, Buseong Industrial Development, around 2005. 8., entered into each sale and purchase contract with the Defendants to repurchase the subject lands from the Defendants (hereinafter collectively “the Second Contract in this case”), while stating in the contract the date thereof as 2005. 1. 26., the same as the First Contract in this case; and the like. Then, (2) it found that the Second Contract in this case, newly concluded by Buseong Industrial Development with the Defendants in substitution for the First Contract in this case, constituted a novation that extinguished the obligations under the First Contract in this case, which correspond to the old obligation, and created a new obligation; meanwhile, (3) because the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case, which was the cause of the above novation, was void for failure to undergo a special resolution of the shareholders’ meeting of Sone Son, it ultimately held that the obligations under the Second Contract in this case between Buseong Industrial Development and the Defendants, which correspond to the new obligation, were not created, and therefore the obligations under the First Contract in this case, which correspond to the old obligation, were not extinguished, and thus Sone Son, as the purchaser under the First Contract in this case, could still seek performance of the First Contract in this case against the Defendants.\\n\\n3. However, the court below’s conclusion that the new obligation under the Second Contract in this case was not created and that the old obligation under the First Contract in this case was not extinguished is difficult to uphold for the following reasons.\\n\\n(a) Since the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case concluded between Sone Son and Buseong Industrial Development is a separate contract creating obligations from the Second Contract in this case, it is difficult to view the effect of the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case as naturally affecting the obligational relationship created under the Second Contract in this case.\\n\\n(b) Even if, as the court below found, the purpose or intent in entering into the Second Contract in this case, which changed the purchaser under the First Contract in this case from Sone Son to Buseong Industrial Development, lay in Buseong Industrial Development’s desire to carry out the subject project by acquiring from Sone Son the rights to the subject project site and the subject project, or even if Buseong Industrial Development intended to render the Second Contract in this case ineffective in the event it failed to validly acquire the rights to the subject project, in order for Sone Son and Buseong Industrial Development to link the future uncertain fact of valid acquisition of the rights to the subject project to whether the Second Contract in this case becomes ineffective or whether the obligational relationship thereunder is created, a condition to that effect must constitute part of the content of the juridical act by the parties’ intent. Thus, the intent to attach such condition must be externally manifested, for example by making the failure to acquire the rights to the subject project a resolutive condition or a condition of lapse of the Second Contract in this case with the Defendants; and if such conditional intent was not manifested, it is merely a motive for the juridical act, and the mere circumstance that the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case between Sone Son and Buseong Industrial Development is void does not permit the conclusion that the claims and obligations under the Second Contract in this case concluded with the Defendants were not created.\\n\\n(c) However, even upon review of the record, no material can be found showing that Buseong Industrial Development and the Defendants, who are the parties to the Second Contract in this case, attached the above condition to the Second Contract in this case, and there is otherwise no material sufficient to recognize that the above conditional intent was manifested. Therefore, absent other circumstances, it must be deemed that the fact that the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case is void does not allow denial of the creation of Buseong Industrial Development’s and the Defendants’ obligations under the Second Contract in this case.\\n\\n4. Nevertheless, the court below, while recognizing that the Second Contract in this case constituted a novation extinguishing the obligations under the First Contract in this case, erroneously held that the obligations under the Second Contract in this case were not created solely because the Business Rights Transfer and Assignment Agreement in this case was void, and thus held that Sone Son could seek performance of the First Contract in this case from the Defendants. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the creation of a new obligation and the extinguishment of an old obligation by novation, and the effect of an unmanifested conditional intent. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n5. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, the judgment of the court below shall be reversed, and the case shall be remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination. It is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DA266645]": "We decide the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. The Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “Defendant Company”) is a corporation established on 2006. 2. 7., which promoted a business of developing and selling electronic products, such as portable internet terminals and ultra-small internet terminals, using patents related to input devices for electronic products.\\n\\nb. On 2007. 1. 30., the Plaintiff invested KRW 10,000,000 in the Defendant Company and entered into an investment agreement (hereinafter referred to as the “investment agreement at issue”) containing the following term: “The Defendant Company shall reimburse to the Plaintiff, from the profits out of each occurrence of sales through intellectual property rights, 10% of the profits until the amount reaches five times the Plaintiff’s principal investment amount.”\\n\\nc. Meanwhile, the representative director of the Defendant Company, Nonparty, was prosecuted on charges of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (fraud), etc., on the ground that “from around May 2009 to around August 2010, at product presentations, etc. of the Defendant Company, he deceived a number of owners of distribution outlets by lying, such as, ‘our products are scheduled to be released soon, and we will supply products only to those who have entered into distribution outlet contracts. The Defendant Company will soon become a company with sales of KRW 1 trillion, so all owners of distribution outlets will make a big profit,’ and thereby obtained distribution outlet contract application fees, product advance payments, etc. from them,” and a guilty judgment became final and conclusive (Daejeon District Court, Judgment of February 21, 2018, 2017GOHAP167; Daejeon High Court, Judgment of August 17, 2018, 2018NO131; Supreme Court, Judgment of December 13, 2018, 2018DO13845).\\n\\n2. The court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, held that the Defendant Company had no intention from the outset to achieve the condition for payment of the investment repayment amount, namely, “the occurrence of sales through the intellectual property rights held by the Defendant Company” (hereinafter referred to as the “condition at issue”), by mass-producing and selling electronic products, etc., but deceived the Plaintiff in order to receive the investment funds and thereby entered into the investment agreement at issue; therefore, pursuant to Article 150(1) of the Civil Act, fulfillment of the condition at issue is deemed to have occurred, and accordingly, it upheld part of the Plaintiff’s claim for the agreed amount.\\n\\n3. However, the judgment of the court below is not acceptable for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Article 150(1) of the Civil Act provides that, when the party who would suffer disadvantage due to the fulfillment of a condition has prevented the fulfillment of the condition in violation of good faith and fair dealing, the other party may assert that the condition has been fulfilled, thereby establishing a rule to protect, from the unjust intervention of one party, the state that should originally exist if the condition had been fulfilled. This provision reflects the fundamental principle of the legal order that the exercise of rights and the performance of obligations shall be done faithfully in accordance with good faith (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DA2757, decided May 14, 2015), and embodies the idea that no one should obtain benefits through conduct contrary to good faith and fair dealing (see Supreme Court Decision 2018DA223054, decided January 14, 2021).\\n\\nHowever, it cannot be immediately concluded that, merely because there was obstructive conduct, etc. by one party in violation of good faith and fair dealing, the result that the other party hoped would occur is deemed to have occurred under Article 150(1) of the Civil Act. Thus, the phrase “when [a party] has prevented the fulfillment of the condition” means a situation where, in light of social norms, the condition would have been fulfilled but for the obstructive conduct of one party, yet the condition failed to be fulfilled due to such obstructive conduct; it does not include cases where, even absent such obstructive conduct, the possibility of fulfillment of the condition was extremely low. If fulfillment of the condition were deemed even in such cases, then the legal effect arising from fulfillment of the condition would be recognized immediately merely because there was unjust intervention by one party, and this could result in the other party obtaining an unjust gain beyond a fair and reasonable result.\\n\\nMeanwhile, whether one party prevented the fulfillment of a condition in violation of good faith and fair dealing must be determined individually and specifically by considering various circumstances, such as the circumstances and intent under which the parties engaged in the conditional juristic act, the purpose and content of the conditional juristic act, the manner of the obstructive conduct, the likelihood of fulfillment of the relevant condition and the effect of the obstructive conduct on fulfillment of the condition, and whether there exist other factors affecting fulfillment of the condition.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles, considering the following circumstances that may be ascertained from the facts and record set forth above, it is difficult to view the Defendant Company as having prevented the fulfillment of the condition at issue, namely, “occurrence of sales related to intellectual property rights,” as stipulated in the investment agreement at issue.\\n\\n(1) As the court below held, if the Defendant Company merely received investment funds from the Plaintiff without any intent or ability to actually mass-produce and sell the relevant electronic products and thereby generate sales, there may be room to evaluate such conduct as contrary to good faith and fair dealing in relation to the Plaintiff, who was the counterparty to the investment agreement at issue.\\n\\n(2) However, the investment agreement at issue was entered into at the preparatory stage or early stage of the business of developing and selling relevant electronic products by utilizing the intellectual property rights held by the Defendant Company, and at that time it appears to have been difficult to predict the success of the business, as it was not known whether the Defendant Company would be able to develop and mass-produce the products, or further whether such products would in fact be sold to purchasers, etc.\\n\\n(3) The Plaintiff also proceeded with the investment despite the existence of substantial risks, such as failure of the Defendant Company’s business, and in return agreed to receive repayment equal to five times the investment amount if sales occurred, regardless of the scale of sales. In light of the contents of such investment agreement, the Plaintiff also appears to have recognized that the occurrence of sales as the condition at issue would not be easy to achieve. In addition, considering that, as noted above, the representative director of the Defendant Company, Nonparty, was criminally punished on charges of obtaining product advance payments, etc. from a number of owners of distribution outlets despite lacking the ability to develop and mass-produce the relevant products and thereby generate sales, there is room to view the likelihood of fulfillment of the condition at issue as being extremely low even if there had been no obstructive conduct by the Defendant Company.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, even if the Plaintiff trusted at the time that the Defendant Company’s business of developing and selling electronic products would succeed, or invested in expectation thereof, if the possibility itself of generating sales from the sale of the electronic products to be developed by the Defendant Company was extremely low, it is insufficient to evaluate the Defendant Company as having prevented fulfillment of the condition of generating sales merely because the Defendant Company did not make sincere efforts to proceed with the above business or, from the outset, had no such intent.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the judgment of the court below, which found otherwise, erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning prevention of fulfillment of a suspensive condition and by failing to conduct the necessary deliberation, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the part of the judgment of the court below against the Defendant is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[88DAKA10579]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below found that the Defendants entered into a lease agreement with the Plaintiff on 1986.7.26. whereby they agreed to lease to the Plaintiff the store premises referred to in the original judgment, and on that day received from the Plaintiff a down payment of KRW 4,000,000 and, on 9.12. of the same year, an intermediate payment of KRW 4,000,000, for a total of KRW 8,000,000; that the Defendants, on 1986.10.6., by agreement, rescinded the above lease agreement with the Plaintiff and agreed to return to the Plaintiff the aggregate amount of KRW 8,000,000 received from the Plaintiff as the down payment and intermediate payment when the store premises in this case should be sold or leased to another person; and, after finding that there was no evidence to find that the Defendants had leased the above store premises to another person, but rather that it was only recognized that the non-party, who sold footwear in the store next door, was using the above store premises to display his merchandise, shoes, the court below held that, in the end, the due date for performance of the Defendants’ obligation to pay KRW 8,000,000, which they agreed to return to the Plaintiff, had not arrived by the conclusion of oral argument in this case because the above store premises had not yet been sold or leased to another person.\\n\\nHowever, where the parties designate as the due date for performance the time when an uncertain fact occurs, the due date for performance must be deemed to have arrived not only when that fact occurs, but also when the occurrence of that fact has become impossible.\\n\\nAs found by the court below, if the Defendants did not sell or lease the store premises referred to in the original judgment to another person but allowed the non-party to use it, and as of the time of the conclusion of oral argument in the court below, more than 1 year and 5 months after 1986.10.5., when the Defendants agreed to return the amount stated in the judgment, the said non-party was still occupying and using the above store premises, then, absent special circumstances, it must be deemed that the occurrence of the fact that the above store premises would be sold or leased to another person has become impossible, and the due date for performance of the Defendants’ obligation to pay the amount stated in the original judgment, which they agreed to return to the Plaintiff, must be deemed to have arrived.\\n\\nThe court below’s holding that the due date for performance of the obligation to pay the amount at issue had not arrived as above constitutes an illegality due to misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the arrival of an uncertain due date; thus, the argument on this point is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges sitting on the case."}

{"[92DA5584]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the Plaintiff’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nEven if the registration of transfer of ownership of real property arising from a gift subject to a condition subsequent has been completed, if that condition subsequent is fulfilled, ownership shall revert to the donor; and in such case, unless there is a separate manifestation of intent between the parties, the effect of fulfillment of the condition shall not be retroactive, but the act of disposition made by the donee before fulfillment of the condition shall be void to the extent that it restricts the effect of fulfillment of the condition; provided, however, that unless that condition has been registered, such invalidity may not be asserted against a third party who acquired rights by reason of the act of disposition.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below found that the Plaintiff, on 1980.5.7., gifted a forest land of 908 square meters in (address omitted), Dongjak-gu, Seoul (the first land in this case), to Nonparty 1, subject to the condition subsequent that, when the Seoul Metropolitan Government carried out road construction work for that portion, the said Nonparty side would not gratuitously donate it to the Seoul Metropolitan Government; that on 1981.7.10., the said Nonparty had a provisional registration preserving the right to claim transfer of ownership, as stated in the judgment, completed in the name of the Defendant (respondent), with respect to the said real property; and that thereafter, by not gratuitously donating the said real property to the Seoul Metropolitan Government that carried out road construction work on the said land, the said condition subsequent had been fulfilled at least by 1987.4.30., and, as to the Plaintiff’s argument that the provisional registration became void upon fulfillment of the said condition subsequent, the court held that a legal act subject to a condition subsequent loses its effect from the time the condition is fulfilled unless there are special circumstances, and therefore, since there was no allegation or proof by the Plaintiff that the parties had agreed to make the effect of fulfillment of the said condition subsequent retroactive to a time before such fulfillment, namely, to a time before the completion of the said provisional registration, or that such agreement satisfied the requirements for asserting it against the said Defendant, a third party, the Plaintiff could not assert the fulfillment of the said condition subsequent against the said Defendant, a third party, and dismissed the argument.\\n\\nThe above determination of the court below can be said to have erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the effect of the act of disposition made by the donee before fulfillment of the condition in a gift subject to a condition subsequent; however, there being no evidence whatsoever to establish that the condition subsequent in this gift was registered (see Exhibit A No. 1), the Plaintiff cannot assert the fulfillment of the said condition subsequent against the said Defendant, the holder of the provisional registration, so the determination of the court below is proper in result, and therefore such error does not affect the judgment.\\n\\nMoreover, it cannot be said that, because the heirs of the said Nonparty, by reason of fulfillment of the condition subsequent, bear the obligation toward the Plaintiff to register transfer of ownership with respect to the said land, it became impossible to complete the principal registration of transfer of ownership based on the provisional registration in the name of the said Defendant, thereby rendering the said provisional registration nugatory. The determination of the court below to the same effect is also proper, and the argument criticizing it is without merit.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds for final appeal of Defendant 1 (Appellant), Defendant 2 (Appellant), and Defendant 3 (Appellant)\\n\\nEven upon review of the record, the factual finding of the court below that there is no evidence to establish that the Dongnae Jeongssi Imdanggongpa Jongchinhoe and the Plaintiff clan are the same clan group is persuasive, and the mere fact that the same person once concurrently served as representative of both clan groups does not mean that they should be regarded as the same clan group. The argument that the judgment below erred in violating the rules governing the weighing of evidence is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and each appeal cost shall be borne by each losing party, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a physician’s duty to explain are incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents) (a) A physician’s duty to explain, for the purpose of obtaining the patient’s consent to surgery, etc., cannot be exempted solely on the ground that the likelihood of adverse sequelae or side effects accompanying the medical act is slight; if such sequelae or side effects are risks that typically arise from the relevant treatment act or are serious and irreversible, they are subject to explanation notwithstanding the slightness of the likelihood of their occurrence. (b) The burden of proof as to a physician’s breach of the duty to explain lies with the patient side, absent special circumstances. (c) A physician’s duty to explain must be performed with sufficient temporal margin before the medical act is carried out. (d) Even if a patient is a minor and has decision-making capacity, it is difficult to regard the patient as having a right of self-determination even with respect to medical acts that expose the patient’s own body to risk; accordingly, in principle, a physician does not bear a duty to explain medical acts to a minor patient.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA48443]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAs a general rule, where a physician performs a medical act that involves subjecting a patient to an invasive procedure such as surgery, and thereafter there is a likelihood of adverse consequences, or where the physician performs a medical act in which serious consequences such as death are foreseeable, in the case of an emergency patient or absent any special circumstances, as a prerequisite to obtaining consent for such invasion, etc. under the medical treatment contract, the physician has a duty to explain to the patient concerned or his or her legal representative matters concerning the symptoms of the disease, the content and necessity of the treatment method, and the risks anticipated to arise, to the extent deemed reasonable in light of the medical standards then prevailing, so that the patient concerned may sufficiently compare the necessity and risks and choose whether to undergo the medical act. Such duty of explanation by a physician cannot be exempted merely because the possibility of risk occurrence, such as sequelae or side effects accompanying the medical act, is slight; and where the sequelae or side effects are risks that ordinarily occur in the relevant treatment act or are serious and irreversible, they must be deemed subject to explanation notwithstanding the slight possibility of their occurrence. In a case where, after a physician violates the duty of explanation and performs surgery, etc., and serious consequences such as inflicting unexpected harm upon the patient occur, if a claim is made for all damages resulting from such consequences, there must be a proximate causal relation between the serious consequences and the physician’s violation of the duty of explanation, or mistake in the process of obtaining consent. In such case, the physician’s violation of the duty of explanation must be of such a degree as to be equated with a physician’s breach of the duty of care required in the course of a medical invasion upon the patient’s life and body, in light of the fact that it is intended to protect the patient’s right of self-determination and opportunity to choose the treatment act. However, where only compensation for emotional distress is claimed on the basis that the patient’s side lost the opportunity to choose and became unable to exercise the right of self-determination, it suffices to prove only the fact that the opportunity to choose was lost due to the physician’s lack or insufficiency of explanation; it is unnecessary to prove further the relation that, had an explanation been given, no result such as death would have occurred (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA3421, decided on 1995. 1. 20.).\\n\\nAnd the term “medical act” means acts of prevention or treatment of disease carried out by diagnosis, examination, prescription, medication, or surgical procedures based on experience and skill grounded in medical expertise, and any other acts that, if not performed by a medical practitioner, are likely to cause harm in terms of public health and hygiene (see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 74DO1114, decided on 1974. 11. 26.; Supreme Court Decision 91DO3219, decided on 1992. 5. 22.; Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2002DO807, decided on 2002. 6. 20., etc.), and since plastic surgery is also clearly a medical act falling within the category of treatment of disease (see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 74DO1114, decided on 1974. 11. 26.), the same legal principle concerning the duty of explanation stated above likewise applies to cases where a physician subjects a patient to an invasion in the course of such plastic surgery.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the following facts: around 1993. 10. 7., the Plaintiff came to the hospital operated by the Defendant and, saying that she wanted to enter a beauty contest and have her forehead and chin raised and undergo eyelid surgery, consulted about plastic surgery; on 1993. 11. 17., she paid the Defendant 6,000,000 and received surgery to insert silicone implants into the chin and forehead areas, as well as eyelid surgery; thereafter, the Plaintiff participated as the Korean representative in an international beauty contest and engaged in activities without any particular hindrance, and then requested reoperation from the Defendant and around 1994. 12. 13. underwent additional corrective surgery to slightly reduce the size of the double eyelids and replace the implants inserted into the forehead and chin with thinner ones; however, from around 1997. 12., the silicone inserted in the Plaintiff’s chin area began to move diagonally, and by around 1998. 10., part of the silicone implant protruded into the oral cavity, and part of the hair had not regenerated in the 5 cm scar on the head area caused by the insertion of the silicone. On that basis, the court below determined that, in the case of plastic surgery, by its nature it is not urgent, and even if plastic surgery is performed, only some improvement in appearance can be expected, and there may be cases where the post-surgery condition differs from the patient’s subjective expectations; therefore, the physician has a duty to make a specific explanation to the patient regarding the method and necessity of treatment, the state of improvement after treatment, and side effects, etc., so that the patient may choose whether to undergo the medical act. However, there was no evidence sufficient to find that the Defendant gave the Plaintiff an explanation of the above degree and that the Plaintiff decided to undergo the surgery; rather, according to the result of the examination of the Defendant as a party in the court below, etc., the Defendant, at the time of the above plastic surgery, explained to the Plaintiff only that, as side effects of the above surgery, bleeding and inflammation may occur, that the size of the implant may not be what the Plaintiff desired, and that the incision site on the head may heal as hair grows and that there may be some minute portions where hair does not grow, but did not sufficiently explain that the above implant could move. On the basis of such finding, the court below held that the Defendant, in performing the above surgery, violated the duty of explanation and thereby infringed the Plaintiff’s right to decide whether to undergo surgery, and that the Defendant is liable to compensate for the mental harm thereby caused to the Plaintiff.\\n\\nUpon comparing the judgment of the court below with the record, the above factual findings and determination by the court below are in accordance with the foregoing legal principles and are proper, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence, no error in fact-finding, no omission of judgment, no failure to exercise the right of elucidation, or error of law concerning causation in the physician’s duty of explanation, as alleged.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

{"[2005DA5867]": "We adjudicate the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Concerning the Plaintiff’s first ground of appeal\\n\\nMedical practice is an area requiring highly specialized knowledge, and, as a special characteristic, it is extremely difficult for laypersons who are not experts to determine whether there was a breach of the Duty of Care in the course of a physician’s medical practice or whether there is a causal relation between such breach of the Duty of Care and the occurrence of damage;
