Thereafter, with respect to the Defendant’s argument that the Plaintiffs’ requested subcontract construction prices should be deducted by the construction costs for the unperformed portions and the defect repair costs arising from defective construction, the court below rejected the Defendant’s argument on the ground that, merely because the Defendant agreed to pay the subcontract construction prices directly to the Plaintiffs as stated in the holding, it cannot be deemed that the Plaintiffs and the Defendant became parties to the contract for the construction work at issue, nor can it be deemed that the Plaintiffs, based on the contract for work between the Defendant and Bangwon General Construction, directly assumed liability for defect repair or construction liability for the unperformed portions toward the Defendant; and that there is no other evidence to find that the Plaintiffs bear such obligations toward the Defendant.\\n\\n2. However, the court below’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. Interpretation of a juristic act is to clearly ascertain the objective meaning that the parties attributed to their expression, and while it is not bound by the literal wording, it must, regardless of the parties’ subjective intent, reasonably interpret the objective meaning that the parties attributed to their expression based on the content of the wording; and where the objective meaning is not clearly revealed by the wording expressed by the parties, it must be reasonably interpreted in accordance with logic and the rules of experience, and the common sense of society and commercial practice, so as to conform to the ideals of social justice and equity, by comprehensively considering the content of the wording, the motive and circumstances in which the juristic act was made, the purpose and true intent the parties sought to achieve through the juristic act, and the customs of transactions (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DA40858, rendered on March 23, 2001).\\n\\nAccording to the facts lawfully found by the court below or as shown by the record, Bangwon General Construction, due to a shortage of funds, failed to properly pay the Plaintiffs the subcontract construction prices, and when the Plaintiffs, in or around June 2004, suspended the works each subcontracted to them by Bangwon General Construction, thereby placing the construction work at issue in danger of being suspended, Bangwon General Construction and the Defendant, on July 1, 2004, delegated to the non-party site manager at the construction site of the construction work at issue the authority to use and execute the expected income related to the construction work at issue (interim and final payments for the apartments and commercial units, physical assets of unsold apartments, and additional loans from members); and thereafter, on July 8, 2004, the Defendant promised to bear responsibility for paying the respective subcontract construction prices to the Plaintiffs, and each prepared for the Plaintiffs a “Construction Cost Payment Confirmation” stating, “With respect to the Mokhwa, Bugang Reconstruction Project (Sinwol-dong 19-1 and 5 other parcels), it is confirmed that unpaid construction costs (outsourcing, services, deliveries, etc.) as of the present time shall be paid, based on the monthly-end unpaid rate (%) against the total construction cost, when income arises from the general occupants’ move-in final payments and disposition of in-kind assets[(commercial unit 3rd floor sale price 90%), (apartment units 102, 1101, 1108 sale price 30%)] after approval for use of the construction is obtained. Proviso 1: Amounts arising from non-move-in and unsold units shall be paid with delay until move-in or sale. Proviso 2: Site operating expenses, entrusted construction costs, defect repair costs, civil petition handling costs, design fees, and supervision fees shall be used at discretion,” and the Plaintiffs on the same day prepared and gave to the Defendant each an “Undertaking of Responsible Construction” stating, “The Plaintiffs, as subcontractors who received a promise of payment of construction costs in connection with the construction work at issue, undertake to enable the pre-move-in inspection by occupants from July 8, 2004, and to apply for approval for use by August 5, 2004, so that the moving-in of association members and general occupants will not be impeded.”\\n\\nAs shown in the above facts found, in light of the circumstances under which the “Construction Cost Payment Confirmation” and the “Undertaking of Responsible Construction” were exchanged between the Plaintiffs and the Defendant, as well as the titles and contents of the respective documents, it is reasonable to view that, on July 8, 2004, the Plaintiffs and the Defendant agreed that the Defendant, as the employer, would directly pay the unpaid subcontract construction prices to the Plaintiffs, who are subcontractors, while the Plaintiffs also directly promised the Defendant the defect-free completion of the works each had subcontracted within the construction work at issue.\\n\\nTherefore, with respect to the Defendant’s argument to the effect that the construction costs for the unperformed portions and the defect repair costs arising from defective construction should be deducted from or set off against the subcontract construction prices sought by the Plaintiffs, the court below should have further examined whether, in relation to the performance of the works each subcontracted by the Plaintiffs, there existed unperformed portions or defects in the construction portions, and then reached its conclusion.\\n\\nB. In addition, under a contract for work, where the completed subject matter has defects, the employer may demand repair of the defects from the contractor and may claim damages in lieu of such repair or together with such repair; and these claims, absent special circumstances, are in a concurrent performance relationship with the contractor’s claim for the construction price (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 96DA7250, 7267, rendered on July 12, 1996). Therefore, the employer who has assumed the subcontract construction price debt owed by the contractor to the subcontractor may, absent special circumstances, resist the subcontractor by means of a defense of concurrent performance based on the contractor’s claim for repair of defects or damages in lieu of defects, which is in a concurrent performance relationship under the subcontract between the contractor and the subcontractor. According to the record, the Defendant argues that, although the Plaintiffs had unperformed portions or performed defective construction, it would be unjust for them to receive the entire construction price without fully performing their obligations, and thus the Defendant should be reimbursed by the Plaintiffs in the amount asserted by the Defendant arising from the construction of the unperformed portions and the repair of defects caused by defective construction. Accordingly, the Defendant’s argument appears to include not only the contention that defect repair costs, etc. should be deducted from or set off against the construction price sought by the Plaintiffs, but also the contention that the Defendant cannot comply with the Plaintiffs’ claim until the Plaintiffs perform the debt of damages in lieu of defect repair for the construction of the unperformed portions and defective construction.\\n\\nTherefore, even assuming, as the court below did, only that the Defendant assumed Bangwon General Construction’s debt for the subcontract construction price owed to the Plaintiffs, the court below should have determined the Defendant’s defense of concurrent performance based on the claim for repair of defects or the claim for damages, which is in a concurrent performance relationship under the subcontract between Bangwon General Construction and the Plaintiffs.\\n\\nC. Nevertheless, the court below rejected the Defendant’s argument for the reasons stated in its holding, and thus the judgment below contains an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interpretation of juristic acts or the defense of concurrent performance by an employer who has assumed the debt for the subcontract construction price, and by failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2018DA242727]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. The judgment of the lower court  \\nWith respect to the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery of the leased premises on the ground of expiration of the lease term, the Defendants raised a defense of simultaneous performance, asserting that they could not deliver the leased premises until the Plaintiff performed the obligation to compensate for damages caused by interference with recovery of premium. In response, the lower court rejected the Defendants’ defense by determining as follows.\\n\\na. 1) Since the entire lease term of the lease agreement in this case exceeds 5 years, the Defendants cannot demand renewal of the contract from the Plaintiff, and thus the Plaintiff does not bear the duty to protect the opportunity to recover premium under Article 10-4(1) of the Commercial Building Lease Protection Act; and 2) even if the Plaintiff’s duty of protection were recognized, there is no evidence to establish that the Defendants had arranged a new tenant for the Plaintiff, or had engaged in acts of interfering with recovery of premium, such as refusing without justifiable cause to conclude a lease agreement with a person seeking to become the new tenant arranged by the Defendants; therefore, in the end, the Plaintiff does not bear liability for damages to the Defendants arising from interference with recovery of premium.\\n\\nb. Even if the Plaintiff were liable for damages arising from interference with recovery of premium, because there is no interrelationship in performance between the landlord’s obligation to compensate for damages arising from interference with recovery of premium and the tenant’s obligation to return the leased premises, the Defendants’ defense of simultaneous performance is without merit.\\n\\n2. The Defendants’ arguments on the grounds of appeal  \\nThe Defendants argue that the lower court judgment, which did not recognize the Plaintiff’s liability for damages, contains errors such as an erroneous interpretation of law concerning Article 10-4(1) of the Commercial Building Lease Protection Act and a violation of the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence regarding whether an act of interfering with recovery of premium was recognized.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination  \\na. The right to assert a defense of simultaneous performance is a system that, based on the notion of fairness and the principle of good faith, recognizes an interrelationship in performance when the obligations borne by each party are mutually reciprocal in nature, thereby allowing one party to refuse performance of its own obligation when the other party demands performance of that party’s obligation without having performed, or without having tendered performance, of the other party’s obligation. In light of the purpose of this system, even where the respective obligations borne by the parties are not obligations in an inherent quid pro quo relationship in a bilateral contract, the right to assert a defense of simultaneous performance may be recognized if both obligations arise from the same legal requirements and have reciprocal significance, or if, from the standpoint of fairness, they ought to be performed in an interrelated manner (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2017DA291593 rendered on July 24, 2018).\\n\\nHowever, the tenant’s obligation to return the leased premises arises upon termination of the lease agreement, whereas the landlord’s obligation to compensate for damages arising from interference with recovery of premium is based on a violation of the duty to protect the opportunity to recover premium prescribed by the Commercial Building Lease Protection Act; thus, the two obligations arise not from the same legal requirements but from separate causes, and even from the standpoint of fairness, it is difficult to recognize an interrelationship in performance between them. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination rejecting the Defendants’ defense of simultaneous performance is proper.\\n\\nb. Although the lower court judgment held that, in cases where a tenant cannot exercise the right to demand renewal against the landlord, the landlord does not bear the duty to protect the opportunity to recover premium, thereby erring by misinterpreting the law concerning the requirements for the occurrence of the landlord’s duty to protect the opportunity to recover premium prescribed in Article 10-4(1) of the Commercial Building Lease Protection Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2017DA225312, 225329 rendered on May 16, 2019), insofar as the Defendants cannot assert the right to a defense of simultaneous performance, the above error in the lower court does not affect the judgment. In addition, even if the lower court judgment concerning whether an act of interfering with recovery of premium was recognized contains an error such as a violation of the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, as argued in the grounds for appeal, since the Defendants’ defense of simultaneous performance ultimately cannot be accepted, it is clear that such error likewise cannot have any effect on the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties; and it is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[84DAKA781]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the statement of reasons in the judgment of the court below, the court below, after collecting the evidence cited therein, found that as of 1983.7.1., the Plaintiff’s debt secured by the provisional registration in this case still had principal in the amount of KRW 1,213,809 outstanding, and that on 1983.7.1. the Plaintiff made an offer of performance for the purpose of satisfying the above loan debt owed to the Defendant, but the Defendant refused to accept it, and therefore the Plaintiff deposited KRW 510,000; on that basis, the court determined that the amount of KRW 730,746, obtained by deducting the above KRW 510,000 from KRW 1,240,746, which is the sum of the above KRW 1,213,809 and delay damages calculated at the annual rate of 5 percent prescribed by the Civil Code for the period from 1983.1.21. to 1983.7.1., is the secured claim secured by the provisional registration in this case, and held that the Defendant is obligated, against receipt from the Plaintiff of the above KRW 730,746 and delay damages thereon calculated at the annual rate of 5 percent, which is the interest rate prescribed by the Civil Code, from 1983.7.2. until full payment, to carry out the procedure for cancellation registration of the provisional registration preserving the right to claim ownership transfer registration concerning the real property in this case.\\n\\nHowever, an offer of partial performance of an obligation cannot be said to be an offer of performance in accordance with the true nature of the obligation, and therefore its effect cannot arise. Even according to the text of the judgment below itself, it is not at all made clear how much, when, and in what manner the Plaintiff’s offer of performance, which the Defendant refused to accept, was made, and on this basis it is stated that KRW 510,000 was deposited in performance; this amounts to no more than partial performance of the obligation, and cannot be said to be performance in accordance with the true nature of the obligation, so the effect of payment cannot arise either. Moreover, where a transfer registration in the name of the creditor or a provisional registration preserving the right to claim such transfer has been completed for the purpose of securing an obligation, in order to seek cancellation of such transfer registration or provisional registration, the obligation must first be performed, and cancellation cannot be sought in exchange for performance of the secured obligation. Therefore, the court below’s order directing the Defendant to carry out the procedure for cancellation registration of the provisional registration in this case against receipt of payment of KRW 730,746 contains illegality in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the discharge of an obligation and provisional registration, and failed to state reasons or contained contradictions in the reasons of the judgment; thus, the grounds of appeal are well-founded.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the Seoul High Court. The conclusion is unanimously reached by the judges participating in the decision, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition."}

question: A had, with his de facto spouse B, an adult child C whom A had acknowledged, and C has a child D born during marriage. A, after being treated for a chronic illness for a long time, died on 2022. 10. 1. At the time of death, A had a loan claim against A, real property X, and a debt for the price of goods to B. Which of the following is incorrect with respect to this? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, the case law applies)
A: Even if B cared for A during A’s illness to the extent of special support beyond the primary duty of support required between spouses, B cannot claim a contributory share under Article 1008-2(1) of the Civil Act.
B: If C filed a declaration renouncing inheritance on 2022. 10. 20, and before being notified of the judicial decision accepting the renunciation declaration C collects and receives payment from A of the above loan claim, it is deemed a simple acceptance.
C: If C filed a declaration renouncing inheritance on 2022. 10. 20, then from that time until before being notified of the judicial decision accepting the renunciation declaration, C bears the duty to manage real property X with the care of a good manager.
D: If B obtained an order of provisional seizure against C regarding real property X on 2022. 10. 12, and as execution thereof a provisional seizure registration was completed on the 13th of the same month, and thereafter C was notified of the judicial decision accepting the renunciation declaration on 2022. 10. 24, B may receive a distribution as a provisional seizure creditor in an auction proceeding for real property X lawfully conducted thereafter.
E: If A had a lawful spouse E who had been living separately for a long time, and after A’s death C filed with the Family Court a declaration renouncing inheritance that satisfied the legal requirements, then E becomes the sole heir.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2013DA73520]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 1026, item 1, of the Civil Act provides that where an heir has performed an act of disposition over inherited property, the heir shall be deemed to have accepted the inheritance unconditionally. However, after the effect of qualified acceptance or renunciation of inheritance has arisen, there is no longer room to regard the heir as having unconditionally accepted the inheritance; accordingly, this provision should be construed as applying only where the inherited property was disposed of before the effect of qualified acceptance or renunciation arose (see Supreme Court Decision of March 12, 2004, 2003DA63586). Meanwhile, qualified acceptance or renunciation of inheritance does not become effective merely by the heir’s declaration of intent, but only when the heir files a report with the Family Court and receives the Family Court’s adjudication, and such adjudication becomes effective upon notice thereof to the party concerned (see Supreme Court Decision of June 25, 2004, 2004DA20401). This is intended to clarify the existence of the declaration of intent for qualified acceptance or renunciation, thereby ensuring that legal relations arising from inheritance are uniformly handled, and thereby protecting the trust of third parties such as coheirs, next-order heirs, inheritance creditors, and counterparties to dispositions of inherited property who have an interest in the inherited property, and promoting legal stability. Therefore, even if an heir filed a report of renunciation of inheritance with the Family Court, if the heir disposed of the inherited property before the adjudication of the Family Court accepting such report was notified, this falls under an act of disposition performed before the effect of renunciation of inheritance arose, and the heir should be deemed to have unconditionally accepted the inheritance pursuant to Article 1026, item 1, of the Civil Act.\\n\\n2. The court below recognized that, ① upon the death of the deceased Non-Party 1 on December 27, 2011, the heirs, including the Defendant, filed a report of renunciation of inheritance with the Suwon District Court on January 26, 2012, stating that they renounced inheritance of the deceased Non-Party 1’s property, and that said court rendered an adjudication accepting that report on March 14, 2012; and ② the Defendant caused Non-Party 2, the representative director of Cheonwoo Transport Co., Ltd., the company to which six cargo vehicles formerly owned by the deceased Non-Party 1 had been entrusted, to have those six cargo vehicles scrapped or sold to another person on January 30, 2012, which was before the date of the above adjudication accepting renunciation of inheritance, and thereafter received the proceeds of KRW 27.3 million from Non-Party 2 on February 6, 2012. Furthermore, on the premise that Article 1026, item 1, of the Civil Act does not apply even if an heir disposed of inherited property before the adjudication accepting the report of renunciation of inheritance is rendered, the court below determined that, since the time when the Defendant caused Non-Party 2 to scrap or sell the above cargo vehicles and received the proceeds was after the Defendant filed the report of renunciation of inheritance, this did not constitute a case in which the Defendant is deemed to have unconditionally accepted the inheritance.\\n\\n3. However, if the above factual relationship is examined in light of the legal principle set forth above, the Defendant, after filing the report of renunciation of inheritance, caused Non-Party 2 to scrap or sell the above cargo vehicles and received the proceeds, thereby disposing of the inherited property before the court’s adjudication accepting the Defendant’s report of renunciation of inheritance was notified; accordingly, pursuant to Article 1026, item 1, of the Civil Act, the Defendant, as an heir, should be deemed to have unconditionally accepted the inheritance.\\n\\n4. Nevertheless, the court below held that Article 1026, item 1, of the Civil Act did not apply solely because the time when the Defendant disposed of the inherited property was after the filing of the report of renunciation of inheritance; in doing so, it erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the statutory grounds for deemed simple acceptance under Article 1026, item 1, of the Civil Act and the time when the effect of renunciation of inheritance arises, thereby affecting the judgment. The allegation in the grounds of appeal pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\n5. Therefore, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, the judgment of the court below is reversed without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, and the case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged as ordered."}

{"[2014DA39824]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 1001 of the Civil Act provides, with respect to succession by representation, that where a lineal descendant or sibling who is to become an heir dies or becomes disqualified before the commencement of inheritance and has lineal descendants, those lineal descendants (hereinafter referred to as “successors by representation”) shall become heirs in the order of the person who died or became disqualified (hereinafter referred to as the “represented person”). In such a case, the spouse of the person who died or became disqualified before the commencement of inheritance becomes a co-heir in the same order as the heir under Article 1001 pursuant to Article 1003(2) of the Civil Act.\\n\\nUpon the death of the decedent, all property rights and obligations of the decedent are comprehensively succeeded to by the heirs as a matter of law (Article 1005 of the Civil Act), and the system established to protect heirs in consideration of their intent is the disclaimer of inheritance system.\\n\\nA disclaimer of inheritance is an act that causes the loss of the legal status concerning inheritance, and it has a significant effect on other co-heirs, the decedent, the creditors of the heir, and the like. The Civil Act, in order to clarify the existence of the declaration of intent and to handle legal relations uniformly, limits the period for disclaimer of inheritance to 3 months from the day on which the commencement of inheritance became known (the main clause of Article 1019(1) of the Civil Act), deems an heir who does not make a qualified acceptance or a disclaimer within that period to have made a simple acceptance (Article 1026(2) of the Civil Act), and does not permit revocation of a disclaimer of inheritance (Article 1024(1) of the Civil Act). In addition, the form of disclaimer of inheritance is strictly limited so that a notice of disclaimer is filed with the Family Court within the above period (Article 1041 of the Civil Act). The Family Litigation Act and its Rules prescribe the procedure and form for disclaimer of inheritance: heirs, etc. must file a notice with the Family Court by a written document stating certain matters such as the decedent’s name and last address, the relationship with the decedent, and the like, and signed or affixed with name and seal (Article 36(3) of the Family Litigation Act; Article 75(1) and (2) of the Family Litigation Rules), and when the Family Court accepts a notice of disclaimer of inheritance, it must necessarily go through adjudication proceedings and prepare a written adjudication (Article 75(3) of the Family Litigation Rules).\\n\\nThe above provisions of the Civil Act prescribing the period, form, and procedure for disclaimer of inheritance are mandatory provisions, and if they are violated and a disclaimer is made before inheritance has commenced, or if the prescribed form and procedure are not followed, the disclaimer of inheritance is without effect (the Supreme Court Decision of Oct. 14, 1994, 94DA8334, and the Supreme Court Decision of July 24, 1998, 98DA9021, likewise held to the same effect).\\n\\nIf, after inheritance has commenced upon the death of the decedent, an heir disclaims the inheritance, the effect arises retroactively as of the time inheritance commenced (Article 1042 of the Civil Act). Accordingly, if the spouse and children who are first-order heirs disclaim the inheritance, the person in the second order becomes the heir (see, e.g., the Supreme Court Decision of Apr. 7, 1995, 94DA11835). The effect of such disclaimer of inheritance extends only to the inheritance that commenced upon the death of the decedent, and does not extend to succession by representation that later commences with the decedent as the represented person. This is because succession by representation arises from a cause separate from inheritance, and because it is not permitted to disclaim it before succession by representation commences. The same applies even where, by the prior disclaimer of inheritance by an heir, a lineal ascendant of the represented person inherited from the represented person. In addition, there is no basis to distinguish depending on whether, at the time of death of the lineal ascendant of the represented person, that person owned own property, whether assets or liabilities, other than the property inherited from the represented person.\\n\\nTherefore, where, after the death of the decedent, inheritance debts exceeded the inherited estate and the heirs, namely the spouse and children, disclaimed the inheritance, but thereafter the decedent’s lineal ascendant died and succession by representation commenced pursuant to Articles 1001 and 1003(2) of the Civil Act, if the successor by representation does not make a qualified acceptance or disclaimer of inheritance in accordance with the procedure and form prescribed by the Civil Act, simple acceptance shall be deemed to have been made. In such a case, although it may be deemed that the spouse and children of the already deceased decedent intended also to disclaim succession by representation arising from the death of the decedent’s lineal ascendant, the effect does not arise unless they disclaim the inheritance with respect to the decedent’s lineal ascendant in accordance with the procedure and form for disclaimer of inheritance. On the other hand, if the effect of disclaimer of succession by representation were recognized on the basis of the disclaimer of inheritance with respect to the decedent, there would be a risk that the disclaimer of inheritance system, which seeks legal stability by clarifying the intent to disclaim inheritance and handling legal relations uniformly, would be circumvented.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 1019(3) of the Civil Act provides the so-called special qualified acceptance system by stating that where the spouse and children who are heirs, without gross negligence, do not learn within 3 months from the day on which they became aware of the commencement of inheritance of the fact that inheritance debts arising from the death of their lineal ascendant exceed the inherited estate, and make simple acceptance (including cases where they are deemed to have made simple acceptance pursuant to Article 1026(1) and (2) of the Civil Act), they may make qualified acceptance within 3 months from the day on which they learned of that fact. Accordingly, even in the case of succession by representation, the successor by representation may be protected under the above provision, so it is not improper even if the Civil Act provisions concerning the procedure, form, and effect of disclaimer of inheritance are applied to succession by representation.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. On April 28, 1993, the Plaintiff entered into a small-loan guarantee insurance contract with Nonparties 1 and 2, designating Daehan Education Insurance Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Daehan Education Insurance”) as the insured, and Nonparty 3 jointly and severally guaranteed the reimbursement debt owed by Nonparties 1 and 2 to the Plaintiff under the above contract (hereinafter referred to as “the reimbursement debt at issue”).\\n\\nb. Because Nonparties 1 and 2 defaulted on payment of the principal and interest on the loan to Daehan Education Insurance, the Plaintiff, on July 25, 1995, made a payment by subrogation to Daehan Education Insurance in the total amount of 21,653,352 won, 10,826,676 won each.\\n\\nc. Nonparty 3 died on November 24, 2000, and the surviving family members were Defendant 1, his spouse, Defendants 2, 3, and 4, his children, and Nonparty 4. The Defendants and Nonparty 4 disclaimed the inheritance, and Nonparty 5, the mother of Nonparty 3, inherited Nonparty 3’s property solely.\\n\\nAt that time, the Defendants and Nonparty 4 submitted to the Changwon District Court, on February 3, 2001, a petition for adjudication disclaiming the property inheritance of the deceased Nonparty 3, and accordingly, on February 22, 2001, that court rendered an adjudication in Case No. 2001NEUDAN50HO reading, “The notices filed by the petitioners on February 3, 2001 disclaiming the inheritance of the estate of the decedent, the deceased Nonparty 3, are accepted.”\\n\\nd. Thereafter, Nonparty 5 died on February 10, 2004, and her children were the deceased Nonparty 3, Nonparties 6 and 7, the deceased Nonparty 8 (died on August 20, 1995), and Nonparty 9.\\n\\n3. In light of the above factual relations and the legal principles discussed above, it is clear that the disclaimer of inheritance by the Defendants and Nonparty 4 had only the effect of disclaiming inheritance from the decedent Nonparty 3. Therefore, the reimbursement debt at issue owed by Nonparty 3 was inherited solely by Nonparty 5, the second-order heir, pursuant to the Defendants’ and Nonparty 4’s disclaimer of inheritance after Nonparty 3’s death, and thereafter, upon Nonparty 5’s death, was jointly inherited by her children, Nonparties 6, 7, and 9, the Defendants and Nonparty 4 as successors by representation of Nonparty 3, and the successors by representation of Nonparty 8. Even if the Defendants disclaimed the inheritance after the death of Nonparty 3, this was merely a disclaimer of inheritance with respect to Nonparty 3, and its effect cannot be deemed to extend to succession by representation arising upon the death of Nonparty 5, the mother of Nonparty 3. If the Defendants, after succession by representation with Nonparty 3 as the represented person had commenced upon the death of Nonparty 5, intended to exclude the effect of inheritance, they should, separate from the disclaimer of inheritance with respect to Nonparty 3, have again disclaimed the inheritance with Nonparty 5 as the decedent in accordance with the form and procedure for disclaimer of inheritance within the period prescribed by the Civil Act.\\n\\nThe court below, relying on the incidental circumstance that Nonparty 5 had no own property at the time of her death other than the property inherited from Nonparty 3, held that the effect of the Defendants’ disclaimer of inheritance with respect to Nonparty 3 extended even to the succession by representation arising upon Nonparty 5’s death, and consequently that the Defendants ended up disclaiming the succession by representation of Nonparty 5’s reimbursement debt at issue to the Plaintiff. However, the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning disclaimer of inheritance and succession by representation discussed above. The ground of final appeal pointing out this point is meritorious.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a rehearing and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2021DA224446]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. An heir succeeds, from the time the inheritance opens, to the decedent’s comprehensive rights and obligations concerning the decedent’s property (main clause of Article 1005 of the Civil Act). However, an heir may make an unconditional acceptance, a qualified acceptance, or renunciation within 3 months from the day he or she became aware that the inheritance had opened (main clause of Article 1019(1) of the Civil Act), and renunciation of inheritance takes effect retroactively to the time the inheritance opened (Article 1042 of the Civil Act).\\nAn heir shall manage inherited property with the same care as in managing his or her own property until renouncing the inheritance (Article 1022 of the Civil Act). When an heir renounces the inheritance, he or she shall file a notice of renunciation with the Family Court within the period under Article 1019(1) of the Civil Act (Article 1041 of the Civil Act), and because renunciation of inheritance becomes effective when the Family Court renders a ruling accepting the heir’s notice of renunciation and notifies the parties thereof (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA20401, decided June 25, 2004; Supreme Court Decision 2013DA73520, decided December 29, 2016), the heir bears the duty to manage the inherited property under Article 1022 of the Civil Act until being notified of the Family Court’s ruling accepting the notice of renunciation of inheritance.\\nAs such, because an heir has the duty, even while the inheritance relationship has not yet been finalized by acceptance of inheritance, renunciation, or the like, to provisionally acquire the decedent’s property by operation of law and to manage the inherited property, an inheritance creditor may, during that period, obtain a decision of provisional attachment concerning the inherited property against the heir and enforce it. Even if the heir thereafter loses his or her status as heir retroactively by renunciation of inheritance, this does not affect the already arisen effect of the provisional attachment. Therefore, the above inheritance creditor may lawfully receive distribution as a provisional attachment creditor in an auction procedure concerning the inherited property with the person who ultimately became the heir or the administrator of inherited property appointed pursuant to Article 1053 of the Civil Act as the debtor.\\n\\n2. Upon examining the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\na. The decedent died on 2013. 7. 16., and Non-Party 1, etc., who were the first-ranking heirs of the decedent, filed a renunciation of inheritance concerning the decedent’s property with the Pyeongtaek Branch of Suwon District Court on 2013. 10. 15. and received a ruling on 2014. 2. 4. accepting the above filing.\\nb. After the decedent’s death, on 2013. 12. 26., the Defendant filed, against Non-Party 1, etc., with the Seosan Branch of Daejeon District Court, an application for provisional attachment of real property concerning the real properties No. 2 through No. 7 in this case, which were inherited property of the decedent, by taking a claim for 293,639,978 won against the decedent as the claim to be preserved, and received the provisional attachment order in this case on 2014. 1. 28., and the registration of provisional attachment was completed around that time.\\nc. Thereafter, as all of the decedent’s other heirs also renounced the inheritance, the Defendant petitioned the Pyeongtaek Branch of Suwon District Court for the appointment of an administrator of the decedent’s inherited property, and the said court appointed Attorney Non-Party 2 as the administrator of the decedent’s inherited property on 2015. 3. 27.\\nd. Meanwhile, upon another creditor’s application for a voluntary auction of the decedent, the auction sale proceedings in this case were commenced with respect to each of the real properties in this case, and the auction court in this case prepared the first distribution schedule on 2016. 8. 5.\\ne. After acquiring from a creditor of the decedent a claim against the decedent, the Plaintiff, using an enforceable authenticated copy of a payment order received against the administrator of the decedent’s inherited property as the title of execution, applied for seizure and assignment of claim with respect to the amount up to 896,561,129 won among the claim for receipt of surplus money that the administrator of the decedent’s inherited property would receive from the Republic of Korea in the distribution procedure of the auction in this case, and received the order of seizure and assignment of claim on 2016. 8. 8.\\nf. The auction court in this case, as the provisional attachment order of some provisional attachment creditors among the creditors listed in the first distribution schedule was canceled, proceeded with the additional distribution procedure and prepared the additional distribution schedule on 2019. 5. 16., and the Plaintiff appeared at the additional distribution date and objected to the entirety of the 151,379,651 won that the Defendant had received as additional distribution as the provisional attachment creditor in this case.\\n\\n3. We examine these facts in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\nThe provisional attachment order in this case is valid because it was made concerning the inherited property with Non-Party 1, etc., who were then heirs bearing the duty to manage the inherited property, as the debtors. Even though the ruling accepting Non-Party 1, etc.’s notice of renunciation of inheritance was subsequently notified and Non-Party 1, etc. thereby retroactively lost their status as heirs, this does not affect the already arisen effect of the provisional attachment order in this case, and it is lawful that the auction court distributed to the Defendant, who is the creditor of the provisional attachment order in this case.\\nNevertheless, the lower court determined that, because Non-Party 1, etc. retroactively lost standing as execution debtors by renunciation of inheritance after the provisional attachment order in this case, the provisional attachment order in this case is void, and that the distribution to the Defendant, who is the provisional attachment creditor, lacks legal cause. In this determination of the lower court, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of a provisional attachment order against an heir before the renunciation of inheritance takes effect.\\n4. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment against the Defendant is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as set forth in the Disposition."}

{"[2021DA224446]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. An heir succeeds to the comprehensive rights and obligations concerning the decedent’s property from the time the inheritance opens (main clause of Article 1005 of the Civil Act). However, an heir may make a simple acceptance, a qualified acceptance, or a renunciation within 3 months from the day he or she became aware that the inheritance has opened (main clause of paragraph 1 of Article 1019 of the Civil Act), and renunciation of inheritance has retroactive effect as of the time the inheritance opened (Article 1042 of the Civil Act).\\n\\nAn heir must manage the inherited property with the same degree of care as for his or her own property until renunciation of inheritance is made (Article 1022 of the Civil Act). When an heir renounces the inheritance, he or she must file a notice of renunciation with the Family Court within the period under paragraph 1 of Article 1019 of the Civil Act (Article 1041 of the Civil Act), and since renunciation of inheritance becomes effective when the Family Court renders a ruling accepting the heir’s notice of renunciation and notifies the parties thereof (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA20401, rendered on June 25, 2004; Supreme Court Decision 2013DA73520, rendered on December 29, 2016), the heir bears the duty to manage the inherited property under Article 1022 of the Civil Act until notified of the Family Court’s ruling accepting the notice of renunciation of inheritance.\\n\\nAs such, since an heir, even before the inheritance relationship is finally determined by acceptance or renunciation, provisionally acquires the decedent’s property and has the duty to manage the inherited property, an inheritance creditor may, during that period, obtain a provisional attachment order concerning the inherited property against the heir and execute it. Even if the heir thereafter retroactively loses the status of heir due to renunciation of inheritance, this does not affect the effect of the provisional attachment that has already arisen. Therefore, the above inheritance creditor may lawfully receive distribution as a provisional attachment creditor in the auction proceedings concerning the inherited property against the person who ultimately became the heir or the estate administrator appointed pursuant to Article 1053 of the Civil Act.\\n\\n2. Examining the reasoning of the lower judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The decedent died on 2013. 7. 16., and Non-party 1, etc., who are the first-priority heirs of the decedent, filed a renunciation of inheritance concerning the decedent’s property with the Pyeongtaek Branch of the Suwon District Court on 2013. 10. 15., and received a ruling accepting the above filing on 2014. 2. 4.\\n\\nb. After the decedent’s death, on 2013. 12. 26., the Defendant filed an application for a provisional attachment of real property concerning the real properties Nos. 2 through 7 in this case, which are inherited property of the decedent, with the Seosan Branch of the Daejeon District Court, against Non-party 1, et al., based on a claim of 293,639,978 won against the decedent as the right to be preserved, and received the provisional attachment order in this case on 2014. 1. 28., and around that time the provisional attachment registration was completed.\\n\\nc. Thereafter, as all of the decedent’s other heirs also renounced the inheritance, the Defendant petitioned the Pyeongtaek Branch of the Suwon District Court for the appointment of an estate administrator for the decedent, and the said court appointed Non-party 2, an attorney, as the estate administrator for the decedent on 2015. 3. 27.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, upon an application for involuntary auction by another creditor of the decedent, the auction proceedings in this case were commenced with respect to each real property in this case, and the auction court in this case prepared the first distribution schedule on 2016. 8. 5.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff, after acquiring the claim against the decedent from a creditor of the decedent, used as the title of execution a certified copy of an enforceable payment order obtained against the decedent’s estate administrator, and applied for seizure of claim and assignment order for the amount up to 896,561,129 won out of the claim to receive the surplus that the decedent’s estate administrator would receive from the Republic of Korea in the distribution proceedings of the auction in this case, and received seizure of claim and assignment order on 2016. 8. 8.\\n\\nf. As the provisional attachment order of some of the provisional attachment creditors listed among the creditors in the first distribution schedule was cancelled, the auction court in this case proceeded with supplementary distribution proceedings and prepared a supplementary distribution schedule on 2019. 5. 16., and the Plaintiff appeared on the supplementary distribution date and objected to the entire 151,379,651 won that the Defendant received in supplementary distribution as the provisional attachment creditor in this case.\\n\\n3. The above factual relationship is examined according to the legal principles previously stated.\\n\\nThe provisional attachment order in this case was validly made concerning the inherited property, with Non-party 1, etc., who were then heirs and bore the duty to manage the inherited property, as the debtors. Even if Non-party 1, etc. later retroactively lost their status as heirs by the Family Court’s ruling accepting their notices of renunciation of inheritance, this does not affect the effect of the provisional attachment order in this case that has already arisen, and it is lawful for the auction court to have distributed to the Defendant, the creditor under the provisional attachment order in this case.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court determined that, because Non-party 1, etc. retroactively lost their eligibility as execution debtors through renunciation of inheritance after the provisional attachment order in this case, the provisional attachment order in this case was invalid, and the distribution to the Defendant, the provisional attachment creditor, lacked a legal ground. In this determination by the lower court, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of a provisional attachment order over inherited property against an heir before the renunciation of inheritance becomes effective.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the part of the lower judgment against the Defendant is reversed, and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination on this part, and it is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the disposition."}

question: A and B jointly own Building X in shares of 1/2 each. Building X was constructed on Land Y owned by C. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, the answer is based on precedents)
A: Absent special circumstances, A may claim damages or restitution of unjust enrichment only against the unlawful possessor of Building X, within the extent of A’s share.
B: Even if A exclusively uses Building X, B cannot demand delivery of Building X from A.
C: If Building X was constructed without authorization on Land Y, C may claim demolition of Building X against A, who is exclusively in possession of Building X, within the extent of A’s share, but may not claim that A vacate Building X.
D: If A and B agreed to use Building X alternately for one week at a time, absent special circumstances, that agreement is succeeded to by the specific successor C who acquired B’s share.
E: If A concluded a repair construction contract with D and E for the repair of Building X, and A does not pay the construction price, D and E may claim against B restitution of the construction price as unjust enrichment within the extent of B’s share.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA49307]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Plaintiffs’ grounds of appeal\\n   a. According to the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence it adopted and considered in its entirety, found that the land and building at issue are their jointly owned property, inherited in co-ownership by the Plaintiffs and the Defendant (Counterclaim Plaintiff, hereinafter referred to only as the “Defendant”), each holding a 1/3 share, and that the Defendant has resided in the building at issue since before the commencement of the succession and has occupied the entire building, while the land at issue has been used as the site thereof. The court below then held that, insofar as the portion of the benefit arising from the possession and use of the building at issue corresponds to the Plaintiffs’ co-ownership shares, the Defendant has an obligation to return such portion to the Plaintiffs as unjust enrichment; however, with respect to the land at issue, even if only some of the co-owners of the building are occupying that building, absent special circumstances, the site of the building is to be regarded as being jointly possessed by all co-owners for the ownership of the building, and therefore the Defendant cannot be said to be exclusively occupying the land at issue; on that basis, the court rejected the Plaintiffs’ claim for restitution of unjust enrichment concerning that portion.\\n\\n   b. However, the court below’s determination cannot be accepted as it stands.\\n      As a matter of social convention, a building cannot exist apart from its site, so land that serves as the site of a building is to be regarded as being possessed by the owner of that building, as the court below stated (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 84NU763 dated July 8, 1986). However, in restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that a party has benefited without legal cause, “benefit” refers to a substantial advantage, and thus is distinct from the possession of real property and the use and profit of real property, which constitute the premise for restitution of unjust enrichment (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 63DA235 dated July 11, 1963). On the other hand, a co-owner may use and derive profits from the entirety of the co-owned property in proportion to his or her share, and matters concerning the management of co-owned property are determined by a majority of the shares of the co-owners. Therefore, with respect to the specific method of use and profit of co-owned property, if one co-owner exclusively possesses and uses it without an agreement by co-owners representing a majority of the shares, that co-owner is obtaining unjust enrichment corresponding to the shares of the other co-owners (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA13948 dated December 11, 2001).\\n\\n      In this case, the Defendant, while being one of the co-heirs together with the Plaintiffs, did not merely possess the building and land at issue, but by residing in the building at issue, he exclusively uses and derives profits from the building and land at issue. Accordingly, absent special circumstances such as that such use and profit were based on a resolution by a majority of the co-ownership shares, the Defendant would be obligated to return to the Plaintiffs as unjust enrichment the portion corresponding to the Plaintiffs’ co-ownership shares among the benefits arising from his exclusive use and profit not only of the building at issue but also of the land.\\n\\n   c. Nevertheless, the court below, proceeding from a different premise, rejected the Plaintiffs’ claim for restitution of unjust enrichment concerning the land at issue, and thus the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising from exclusive use and profit of co-owned property among co-owners. The argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is well taken.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n   Examining the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below properly rejected, for the reasons stated in its opinion, both the Defendant’s assertion that he purchased the land and building at issue from the deceased non-party around December 31, 1983, and the Defendant’s assertion that he delivered KRW 14,000,000 to Plaintiff 1 in or around 1983. There is no error, such as incomplete trial or error in fact-finding due to violation of the rules on the assessment of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the part of the judgment below that ruled against the Plaintiffs with respect to the principal claim is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination of that part. Since the Defendant’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed. Accordingly, it is so adjudged unanimously by the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2010DA108210]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (each supplemental ground submitted after the expiration of the period shall be considered to the extent that it supplements the same).\\n\\n1. Where the sectional owners of one building jointly own the land appurtenant to the building in proportion to the ratio of their respective co-ownership shares in the land at the time they originally purchased the building, then, absent special circumstances, such sectional owners have a lawful title to use the entire land appurtenant to the building according to its purpose, regardless of the ratio of their co-ownership shares in the land, and therefore, as between such sectional owners, a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment cannot be made on the ground of a difference in the ratio of co-ownership shares in the land (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA60144, rendered on March 14, 1995; Supreme Court Decision 2009DA76522, 2009DA76539, rendered on July 14, 2011, etc.), but where a person other than a sectional owner of the building acquires only a co-ownership share in the land through auction proceedings, etc., and thus has a co-ownership share in the land but is wholly unable to use or derive profits from the land, it may be said that, absent other special circumstances, such person may bring a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment based on the co-ownership share right in the land.\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence it admitted, acknowledged the facts as found in its opinion, namely, that the non-party purchased the land 1,514 square meters in size at (lot number omitted), Hannam-dong, Yongsan-gu, Seoul, on June 29, 1983 (hereinafter referred to as “the land in this case”), and thereafter, on December 7, 1984, constructed on the land an aggregate building with 3 basement floors and 5 above-ground floors; that, beginning on December 29, 1984, in selling the newly constructed building, because at the time of sale the Act on the Ownership and Management of Aggregate Buildings had not yet entered into force, the non-party had the purchasers register transfer of the co-ownership share rights in part of the land in this case, together with each corresponding exclusive section (the total of such shares being 1,182.5290/1,514), and retained the remaining co-ownership share (331.47/1,514) for the purpose of future extension of the building or use as his own building site; that, on December 29, 1984, for the purpose of securing debts owed to Seoul Trust Bank Co., Ltd., he established a mortgage right over his co-ownership share, with the maximum secured amount set at KRW 750,000,000; that, upon the petition of Inno Seoul First Asset Securitization Special Purpose Company, LLC, which acquired the mortgage right and the claim secured thereby from the said bank, auction proceedings based on the said mortgage right were commenced, and in those auction proceedings, the Plaintiffs and the co-plaintiff in the court below purchased the co-ownership share of the said non-party inherited by Jeong Bok-su and acquired ownership thereof by paying the entire sale price on April 13, 2007; and that the Defendants each acquired, together with their respective sectional-owned buildings, a co-ownership share in the land in this case prior to April 13, 2007. On that basis, the court below held that the Defendants, regardless of the ratio of their co-ownership shares in the land in this case, which serves as the site of the aggregate building, have lawful title to use the entire land according to its purpose, and thus the Defendants’ exclusive possession and use of the portion of the land in this case corresponding to the Plaintiffs’ co-ownership shares cannot be regarded as infringing the Plaintiffs’ co-ownership shares without legal cause, and therefore dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claim in this case for restitution of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the foregoing legal principles and the factual findings made by the court below, the Plaintiffs, who acquired the 331.47/1,514 share in the land in this case through auction proceedings but are wholly unable to use or derive profits from the land, should be regarded as being able to bring a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising therefrom against the Defendants, who exclusively possess and use the land in this case.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claim in this case for restitution of unjust enrichment solely for the reasons stated in its opinion; such disposition by the court below contains an error of law by misapprehending the legal principles concerning possession, etc. of commonly owned property, and the grounds of appeal pointing this out are well founded.\\n\\n2. Matters concerning the management of commonly owned property shall be determined by a majority of the co-owners’ shares, and a special agreement between co-owners concerning the use, benefit, and management of commonly owned property shall also be succeeded to by the specific successor, but where such a special agreement concerning commonly owned property infringes an essential part of the co-ownership share right, such as by in effect waiving the right to use and derive profits as a holder of the share, it cannot be deemed to be automatically succeeded to by the specific successor, absent special circumstances such as the specific successor’s acquisition of the co-ownership share while knowing of such facts (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA54294, rendered on December 10, 2009).\\n\\nThe court below additionally found, based on the evidence it admitted, the facts as found in its opinion, and then held that, although the non-party, in constructing and selling the aggregate building, transferred to the purchasers only the land share corresponding to the portion where the aggregate building is located, together with the exclusive section, and retained the remaining land share for future extension, etc., the non-party implicitly granted the Defendants authority to use the remaining land share free of charge in accordance with the usage of the aggregate building; that the Plaintiffs, too, when acquiring the remaining co-ownership share through auction proceedings, were fully aware through the sale notice (including the specification of the property to be sold and the real estate status investigation report) and the certified copy of the register that an aggregate building existed on the co-owned land; and that since it cannot be said that the Plaintiffs failed to acquire a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to ground rent or rent against the Defendants, the essential part of the right to use and derive profits from the land was not infringed, the Plaintiffs succeeded to the obligation to allow the Defendants to possess and use their land share free of charge.\\n\\nHowever, such determination by the court below is also difficult to accept.\\n\\nEven if, where a person who sold an aggregate building had registered transfer of ownership only with respect to part of the land shares among the land appurtenant to the building and retained the remaining shares himself, it may be construed that he granted the sectional owners authority to use his retained shares free of charge in accordance with the usage of the aggregate building (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA16965, rendered on December 27, 2002), such an agreement amounts to a waiver, until the building is demolished, of the use and benefit based on the co-ownership share right, so it is difficult to regard it as automatically succeeded to by the Plaintiffs, and the circumstances cited by the court below, as found in its opinion, are not enough to conclude that the Plaintiffs acquired the co-ownership share in this case while knowing that such an agreement existed.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below concluded that the Plaintiffs succeeded, as against the Defendants, to the obligation to allow the land shares they owned to be possessed and used free of charge; thus, this determination by the court below is also unlawful and cannot stand as is, and the grounds of appeal pointing this out are well founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DA287522]": "We adjudicate the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case and the issue\\nThe Plaintiff, as a so-called minority share-right holder who owns a 1/2 share in the land at issue, brought claims against the Defendant, who has planted pine trees on the land and exclusively possessed it, seeking removal of the above-ground objects such as the pine trees and delivery of the possessed land, among other relief. The court of second instance held that, as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, the Plaintiff could seek removal of obstruction and delivery with respect to the co-owned land, and therefore granted all of the Plaintiff’s claims.\\nThe main issue in this case is whether, when the Defendant, who is a minority share-right holder in the co-owned land, exclusively occupies all or part of the co-owned land without consulting the other co-owner(s), the Plaintiff, another minority share-right holder, may seek removal of obstruction and delivery as an act of preservation of the co-owned property.\\n\\n2. Whether a minority share-right holder of co-owned property may seek removal of obstruction and delivery against another minority share-right holder who exclusively occupies the co-owned property\\nA. Existing Supreme Court precedents\\nWhere both the Plaintiff and the Defendant are minority share-right holders and there is no agreement among the co-owners concerning the management of the co-owned property or any decision by a majority of shares, the question arises whether the Plaintiff may seek, against the Defendant, removal of obstruction and delivery concerning the co-owned property as an act of preservation. Existing Supreme Court precedents have held that, because a co-owner may not exclusively possess and use, collect fruits from the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s), another co-owner, even if only a minority share-right holder, may seek removal of obstruction and delivery against the possessing co-owner as an act of preservation of the co-owned property (see Supreme Court Decision 73DA381 rendered on June 11, 1974, en banc Supreme Court Decision 93DA9392, 9408 rendered on March 22, 1994, and Supreme Court Decision 2012DA43324 rendered on May 16, 2014, among others).\\n\\nB. Whether a minority share-right holder may seek delivery of co-owned property against another minority share-right holder who exclusively occupies the co-owned property\\nIt should be understood that, where the Defendant, who is a minority share-right holder of the co-owned property, exclusively occupies all or part of the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s), the Plaintiff, also a minority share-right holder, cannot seek delivery of the co-owned property against the Defendant. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Article 265 of the Civil Act provides: “Matters concerning the management of co-owned property shall be determined by a majority of the shares of the co-owners: Provided, That each co-owner may perform an act of preservation.” Here, an act of preservation means factual and legal acts performed to prevent loss or damage to the co-owned property and to maintain its present condition. The purpose of allowing a co-owner to perform such an act of preservation alone, without consulting the other co-owner(s), is that acts of preservation often require urgency and ordinarily benefit the other co-owner(s) as well (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA54736 rendered on April 7, 1995, among others). However, where the Defendant, one of the co-owners, exclusively possesses the co-owned property and the Plaintiff, another co-owner, seeks delivery of the co-owned property against the Defendant, such an act conflicts with the interests of the Defendant, who possesses the co-owned property. Considering that the reason an act of preservation may originally be performed unilaterally by one of the co-owners is that it also benefits the other co-owner(s), such an act cannot readily be deemed an act of preservation under the proviso to Article 265 of the Civil Act.\\n\\n(2) All co-owners may use and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property in proportion to their shares (Article 263 of the Civil Act). The same applies even when there is no agreement among the co-owners or decision by a majority of shares concerning the management of the co-owned property (main clause of Article 265 of the Civil Act). A co-ownership share right that a co-owner holds in the co-owned property is a quantitative part of ownership, but because it has the same nature as independent ownership, the co-owner has the right to use and collect fruits, which belongs to the powers of ownership. Article 263 of the Civil Act means that such rights of use and profit constitute the content of the co-ownership share right as ownership, while implying that, because one ownership right is divided and vested in several co-owners, certain restrictions apply to the exercise of ownership. Therefore, even if the Defendant, a minority share-right holder, exclusively possesses and uses the co-owned property for gain, this is different from a third party, who is not a co-owner, unlawfully possessing the co-owned property. Although the Defendant’s exclusive possession of the co-owned property while excluding the other co-owner(s), as if the Defendant were the sole owner, is unlawful, the Defendant is at least entitled to possess, use, and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property within the scope of the Defendant’s own share, so the Defendant’s possession should be deemed unlawful only to the extent exceeding that share ratio. Even if physical division of possession over a thing according to shares is impossible, whether such possession is legally worthy of protection within the scope of the share remains a separate question.\\n\\nTherefore, if the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery were allowed on the pretext of correcting the unlawful condition in which the Defendant exclusively possesses the co-owned property, it would entirely exclude the Defendant’s possession and, as a result, would unjustifiably deprive the Defendant of the “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio,” which the Defendant lawfully holds, as described above.\\n\\n(3) In general, “delivery” of a thing means completely transferring actual and factual dominion over the thing. Under the Civil Execution Act, execution of a claim for delivery is carried out by a court execution officer taking possession of the thing away from the debtor and delivering it to the creditor (Articles 257 and 258 of the Civil Execution Act). Therefore, if the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery is allowed, the Plaintiff, through compulsory execution, will take possession away from the Defendant, who has been possessing the co-owned property, and will possess it exclusively.\\n\\nFor the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery of the thing against the Defendant to be recognized, a legal basis entitling the Plaintiff to demand delivery must first be recognized. If the Plaintiff has no such legal basis, the Plaintiff’s claim cannot be granted even if the Defendant’s possession is unlawful. Yet, in this case, since the Plaintiff, like the Defendant, is merely a minority share-right holder, the Plaintiff has no legal basis to demand that the Defendant, a co-owner, be entirely excluded and that the property be delivered so that only the Plaintiff may exclusively possess the co-owned property.\\n\\nExisting Supreme Court precedents have held that the Plaintiff may seek delivery of the entire co-owned property against the co-owner Defendant as an act of preservation. The theory of an act of preservation may provide a basis for the Plaintiff to make a certain claim concerning the entirety of the co-owned property beyond the Plaintiff’s own share ratio, but it cannot serve as a basis for the Plaintiff, as a co-owner, to demand from another co-owner not merely that the Defendant’s condition of exclusive occupation of the co-owned property be removed, as discussed in subparagraph C below, but that the co-owned property be “delivered to the Plaintiff.” The Plaintiff may demand return of the co-owned property from a third party who has no right to possess it, namely, from the perspective of the owner, or more precisely, from the perspective of the holder of a share right in the co-owned property, who has legal title to possess it. However, as against the co-owner Defendant, the Plaintiff is merely a minority share-right holder and has no legal basis to exclusively possess the co-owned property. Since the Plaintiff, like the Defendant, merely has mutually limited authority according to a minority share, and there is no determination regarding the management of the co-owned property, there is no basis for the Plaintiff to assert that the property be delivered to the Plaintiff so that only the Plaintiff may possess it.\\n\\n(4) The result of a judgment for delivery of the co-owned property and the execution thereunder is not different from the unlawful state before delivery, where “some minority share-right holder exclusively possesses the co-owned property while excluding the other co-owner(s),” in that the Plaintiff becomes able to exclusively possess and use and collect fruits from the co-owned property. This would produce the result of creating yet another unlawful state in order to correct the unlawful state. As a result, unless the Plaintiff, after receiving delivery of the co-owned property, voluntarily permits the Defendant to jointly use the co-owned property, the Defendant is placed in the position of having to file a suit against the Plaintiff again in order to exercise the Defendant’s rights in the co-owned property. The result of execution pursuant to a judgment should be to place the co-owned property in a lawful state of possession. However, the above result cannot be said to be the lawful state that a judgment and execution should achieve for the final resolution of the dispute.\\n\\nThe supplementary opinion to the majority opinion in en banc Supreme Court Decision 93DA9392, 9408 rendered on March 22, 1994 states that delivery of a thing means excluding the former possessor and causing the recipient to actually control the thing, but that this is a matter separate from use and profit, and therefore there may be cases where one receives delivery and actually controls the thing but does not use or profit from it, such as where the thing is merely kept for the co-owners, and that a claim for delivery based on an act of preservation of co-owned property is permitted only within the scope of the latter purpose. However, as noted above in (3), execution of a claim for delivery under the Civil Execution Act is carried out by a court execution officer taking possession of the thing away from the debtor and delivering it to the creditor (Articles 257 and 258 of the Civil Execution Act). The execution officer completes the execution procedure by excluding the debtor and causing the creditor to acquire actual possession of the thing, and thereafter the creditor is not subject to any procedural restriction on using and collecting fruits from the delivered thing. The above supplementary opinion is incorrect in that it overlooks the fact that, through execution of delivery, the creditor acquires unrestricted possession of the thing exclusively, and it interprets the meaning of delivery by reducing it merely to the sense of “removal of interference” that eliminates only the debtor’s exclusive possession.\\n\\n(5) It may be said that existing Supreme Court precedents permitted claims for delivery of co-owned property between co-owners as an act of preservation because delivery claims were viewed as the most effective means of relief in order to remedy the unlawful state in which a minority share-right holder arbitrarily and exclusively possesses the co-owned property (see the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion in the above en banc Supreme Court Decision 93DA9392, 9408). However, as discussed in subparagraph C below, the Plaintiff can sufficiently remedy such unlawful state by exercising the right to claim removal of interference based on the share right against the Defendant, who exclusively possesses the co-owned property and infringes the Plaintiff’s co-ownership share right. Therefore, even without using the conventional method of taking possession of the co-owned property away from the Defendant and delivering it to the Plaintiff, that is, substituting the Defendant’s possession with the Plaintiff’s possession, the Plaintiff may remove the Defendant’s unlawful exclusive possession and interference and ensure that the co-owned property is made available for the joint use and enjoyment of all co-owners in accordance with its intended purpose.\\n\\nC. Whether a minority share-right holder may seek removal of interference against another minority share-right holder who exclusively occupies the co-owned property\\n(1) All co-owners may use and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property in proportion to their shares (Article 263 of the Civil Act). How the co-owned property is specifically to be used and profited from, for example whether to use the co-owned land alternately or by dividing the area, or to allow a particular person to use the entirety and receive compensation therefor, is in principle determined by the co-owners by a majority of their shares (Article 265 of the Civil Act). In the absence of such determination, no individual co-owner may exclusively use and collect fruits from the co-owned property (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA13948 rendered on December 11, 2001, among others).\\n\\nMeanwhile, as owners of the co-owned property, the co-owners have the right to use and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property (Article 263 of the Civil Act), and as noted above, this remains the same even when there is no decision among the co-owners concerning the management of the co-owned property. The fact that there are certain restrictions on the manner of use and profit, such as that the co-owned property cannot be exclusively used even in part, does not mean that the co-owners’ right to use and collect fruits is merely abstract or conceptual, or that it is a right that cannot be concretely realized in the absence of a decision regarding the management of the co-owned property.\\n\\nThe essence of a co-ownership share right lies in ownership, and ownership is a real right whose content consists in direct control over a thing. The power to use and collect fruits from a thing belongs to the most fundamental and core powers of ownership, which is a real right (Article 211 of the Civil Act). Article 263 of the Civil Act merely means that such powers of ownership equally exist in a co-ownership share right, but in a co-ownership relationship, because one ownership right is divided and vested in several co-owners, each co-owner is subject to the restriction that he or she must not infringe the other co-owners’ rights of use and profit. Therefore, where there is no decision among the co-owners concerning the management of the co-owned property, it is unlawful and impermissible for a co-owner to exclude the other co-owner(s) and exclusively possess and use the co-owned property; however, using and possessing the entirety of the co-owned property together with the other co-owner(s), in a non-exclusive manner that does not infringe the other co-owners’ rights of use and profit, is lawful as an exercise of the co-owner’s own share right.\\n\\n(2) If some co-owners exclusively possess all or part of the co-owned property, this infringes the rights of use and profit based on the other co-owner(s)’ share right.
