A co-owner may exercise the right to claim removal of interference under Article 214 of the Civil Act against acts interfering with the exercise of the co-owner’s own share right, and since the share right in the co-owned property belongs to each individual co-owner, each co-owner may exercise such claim.\\nAs a concrete form of a claim for removal of interference concerning co-owned property, where there exist above-ground objects such as buildings, trees, etc. that were unlawfully constructed or planted by the Defendant on the co-owned land, the above-ground objects, by their very existence, interfere with the other co-owner’s possession and use of the co-owned land, and thus the Plaintiff may seek removal or collection of the above-ground objects (this is executed by way of substitute execution). Once the above-ground objects are removed, the co-owned land becomes bare land, and unless the Defendant again commits active interference, the Plaintiff can enter and use the land on the Plaintiff’s own. Thus, in ordinary cases where the Defendant’s above-ground objects exist on the co-owned land, removal of the above-ground objects alone can eliminate the exclusive possession of the co-owned land. If, even after removal of the above-ground objects, the Defendant acts in a manner that interferes with the Plaintiff’s joint possession, or such conduct is anticipated, the Plaintiff may seek against the Defendant an injunction against such interference, for example, an injunction against interfering with the Plaintiff’s entry onto or passage over the co-owned land.\\n\\nIn addition, taking into account the type of co-owned property (land, building, movable property, etc.), its use, condition (the current status of the co-owned property before and after the Defendant’s exclusive possession), and the relationship of the parties, the Plaintiff may formulate the claim by specifying in detail the Defendant’s acts and interference-causing objects that interfere with or are likely to interfere with the Plaintiff’s joint possession, and seek prohibition, removal, or prevention of such interference (performance of affirmative or negative obligations). The court may grant such claim if it is necessary to remove the Defendant’s state of interference and if the state the Plaintiff seeks to achieve accords with the joint possession status of the co-owners. Such ancillary affirmative and negative obligations, including injunctions against interference with entry, may be effectively enforced by means of indirect compulsion under the Civil Execution Act.\\n\\nThus, even without using the conventional method of taking possession of the co-owned property away from the Defendant and delivering it to the Plaintiff in order to remove the Defendant’s state of exclusive possession, by recognizing a claim for removal of interference based on the co-ownership share right, the Plaintiff can achieve a lawful state that removes the Defendant’s unlawful exclusive possession and interference and ensures that the co-owned property is made available for use and profit by all co-owners in accordance with its original purpose.\\n\\nD. Change of precedent\\nAccordingly, where a minority share-right holder of co-owned property exclusively possesses or uses all or part of the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s), the other minority share-right holder cannot seek delivery as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, but may only seek removal of the interference with the co-owned property or injunctions against acts interfering with joint possession, based on the minority share-right holder’s own share right.\\n\\nIn contrast, Supreme Court Decision 65DA2033 rendered on April 19, 1966; Supreme Court Decision 71DA1040 rendered on July 20, 1971; Supreme Court Decision 73DA381 rendered on June 11, 1974; Supreme Court Decision 75DA2104 rendered on June 8, 1976; Supreme Court Decision 77DA1157 rendered on May 23, 1978; Supreme Court Decision 79DA647 rendered on June 12, 1979; Supreme Court Decision 80DA1280, 1281 rendered on February 22, 1983; Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA19002, 19019 rendered on January 15, 1991; en banc Supreme Court Decision 93DA9392, 9408 rendered on March 22, 1994; Supreme Court Decision 95DA33290, 33306 rendered on June 14, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 95DA48308 rendered on December 23, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 98DA12317 rendered on August 21, 1998; Supreme Court Decision 2002DA57935 rendered on November 13, 2003; Supreme Court Decision 2005DA688, 695 rendered on April 13, 2007; Supreme Court Decision 2006DA40980 rendered on August 24, 2007; Supreme Court Decision 2006DA40997, 41006 rendered on August 24, 2007; Supreme Court Decision 2012DA104458, 104465 rendered on March 28, 2013; Supreme Court Decision 2012DA43324 rendered on May 16, 2014; Supreme Court Decision 2012DA109804 rendered on May 29, 2014; Supreme Court Decision 2014DA58719 rendered on December 24, 2014; and the like, which held that where a minority share-right holder of co-owned property exclusively possesses all or part of the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s), another minority share-right holder may seek delivery as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, shall be changed to the extent that they are inconsistent with the view of this judgment.\\n\\nE. Determination in this case\\n(1) According to the reasoning of the judgment of the court of second instance, the following facts may be found.\\nNon-party 1 and Non-party 2 died while each co-owned a 1/2 share in the land at issue. The Plaintiff, as the heir of Non-party 2, completed registration of transfer of ownership on November 28, 1992, with respect to the entirety of Non-party 2’s share in the land at issue. The Defendant, as the eldest son of Non-party 1, jointly inherited Non-party 1’s property with his siblings upon Non-party 1’s death around 1995.\\nFrom around 2011 to the present, the Defendant has planted pine trees on part of the land at issue and exclusively possesses that part of the land (hereinafter, the “land portion on which pine trees were planted”).\\n(2) Examining the above facts in light of the legal principles discussed above, the Plaintiff, as a minority share-right holder of the land at issue, cannot seek delivery of the land against the Defendant, who is another minority share-right holder exclusively possessing the land portion on which pine trees were planted. However, the Plaintiff may seek removal of the above-ground objects such as the pine trees planted on the co-owned land as a removal of interference based on the share right.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court of second instance held that the Plaintiff could seek delivery of the land portion on which pine trees were planted against the Defendant as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, granted this part of the Plaintiff’s claim, and, on the premise that the Defendant had a duty to deliver the land, granted the Plaintiff’s claim for return of unjust enrichment calculated at KRW 194,750 per month from January 1, 2012 until completion of delivery of the land.\\nThe court of second instance erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning acts of preservation of co-owned property, thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment, in granting the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery of the land. Since the portion of the judgment below concerning the claim for delivery of the land must be reversed, the portion ordering payment of money from the day after the date of closing of oral argument in the court below, namely September 21, 2018, until completion of delivery of the land, among the Plaintiff’s claim for return of unjust enrichment that had not yet definitively accrued, must also be reversed.\\nMeanwhile, although the court of second instance’s view that the Plaintiff’s claim for removal of above-ground objects is permitted as an act of preservation of the co-owned property is not appropriate, the conclusion granting the Plaintiff’s claim for removal of above-ground objects is proper as noted above, and therefore there is no error affecting the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\n3. Whether there was an agreement concerning the land at issue\\nIn the grounds for appeal, the Defendant argues that the Plaintiff and the Defendant agreed, on two occasions around 2006 and 2008, to use and profit from the co-owned land at issue and the land in Paju-si (lot number omitted) alternately, and that the Defendant lawfully possesses the land at issue pursuant to such agreement. However, this ground for appeal merely disputes the selection and appraisal of evidence and the factual findings, which belong to the exclusive prerogative of the court below as the trier of fact, and thus does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. Furthermore, even upon review of the record, there is no error in the court below’s factual findings that violated the rules of logic and experience or exceeded the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the claim for delivery of the land and the claim for payment of money calculated at the rate of KRW 194,750 per month from September 21, 2018 until completion of delivery of the land is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; the remaining appeal is dismissed; and judgment is rendered as stated in the order. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, Lee Dong-won, Kim Sang-hwan, and Noh Tae-ak concerning the claim for delivery, and Justice Lee Ki-taek’s dissenting opinion concerning the claim for removal of interference, the opinions of the Justices participating in this case were unanimous, and there are the supplementary opinions of Justices Kim Jae-hyung and Ahn Cheol-sang to the majority opinion, as well as Justice Lee Ki-taek’s supplementary opinion concerning the claim for delivery among the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Dissenting opinion of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, Lee Dong-won, Kim Sang-hwan, and Noh Tae-ak concerning the claim for delivery of co-owned property\\nThe majority opinion is that, where the Defendant, a minority share-right holder of co-owned property, exclusively possesses or uses all or part of the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s), the Plaintiff, another minority share-right holder, cannot seek delivery of the co-owned property to the Plaintiff as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, but may only seek removal of the interference with the co-owned property or injunctions against acts interfering with the Plaintiff’s joint possession and use, based on the Plaintiff’s own co-ownership share right; and, accordingly, the existing Supreme Court precedents that affirmed the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery should be changed.\\n\\nHowever, in a co-ownership relationship where the Defendant, as a minority share-right holder, has arbitrarily created and maintained an unlawful state by exclusively possessing the co-owned property, the other minority share-right holder, namely the Plaintiff, should be able to seek delivery of the co-owned property as an act of preservation in order to restore the unlawful state to a lawful one. The existing Supreme Court precedents affirming the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery are valid and should be maintained, and we cannot agree with the majority opinion that seeks to change them. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA. Established legal principles of existing Supreme Court precedents on the issue\\nSupreme Court Decision 65DA2033 rendered on April 19, 1966 held that a co-owner of land may not arbitrarily use it exclusively, even in part, and that, unless such use is based on a resolution by a majority of the co-ownership shares, it is unlawful, so another co-owner may seek delivery of the co-owned property as an act of preservation. Supreme Court Decision 73DA381 rendered on June 11, 1974 clearly held, in a case where the Plaintiff was a minority share-right holder, that even if a co-owner of land is merely a minority share-right holder falling short of a majority, the co-owner may, as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, seek delivery of the land and removal of the above-ground building against a co-owner who unlawfully possesses the co-owned land without a resolution by a majority of the shares. These holdings were also cited in Supreme Court Decision 79DA647 rendered on June 12, 1979 and Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA19002, 19019 rendered on January 15, 1991. Thereafter, through en banc Supreme Court Decision 93DA9392, 9408 rendered on March 22, 1994, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the validity of that legal principle, and even the more recent Supreme Court decisions, including Supreme Court Decision 2012DA43324 rendered on May 16, 2014 and Supreme Court Decision 2012DA109804 rendered on May 29, 2014, follow the same principle.\\n\\nThus, the legal principle of the existing Supreme Court precedents on the issue has been established over a long period of time, enabling another minority share-right holder to effectively remedy, by way of a claim for delivery, the unlawful state caused by a minority share-right holder’s arbitrary and exclusive possession of co-owned property, which frequently arises in co-ownership relationships. Since the Supreme Court established this legal principle in the 1994 en banc decision, judicial practice has also been operating stably. In such circumstances, it is not appropriate for the Supreme Court to overturn the existing established legal principle on the resolution of disputes in co-ownership relationships among minority share-right holders without presenting a clear alternative.\\n\\nB. Validity of the legal principle of the existing precedents\\nIt is legally sound for the existing Supreme Court precedents to have permitted a minority share-right holder’s claim for delivery. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) A co-owner may use and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property in proportion to the shares (Article 263 of the Civil Act). Therefore, even if the Defendant, a minority share-right holder, possesses the entirety of the co-owned property, if such possession can be recognized as use and profit corresponding to the Defendant’s share ratio, it may be viewed as lawful possession based on the co-ownership share right. However, if, without any agreement or decision among the co-owners regarding the management of the co-owned property, the Defendant exclusively possesses the entirety or part of the co-owned property while excluding the other co-owner(s), such possession infringes the other co-owner(s)’ right of use and profit and is therefore unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA13948 rendered on December 11, 2001, among others).\\n\\nPossession means factual control over a thing, and therefore, by its nature, it cannot be divided quantitatively. Accordingly, while one may possess a specific part of a thing, possession of a fraction of a share cannot be conceived (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA72469 rendered on January 25, 2017). As noted above, because the Defendant, who is merely a minority share-right holder, has no right vis-à-vis the other co-owners to exclusively possess all or part of the co-owned property, the Defendant’s exclusive possession must be deemed unlawful as a whole. In light of the factual and indivisible nature of possession, it is not possible, as the majority opinion does, to divide the Defendant’s possession into a lawful portion within the Defendant’s share and an unlawful portion exceeding it. If the “right to use and collect fruits” that the Defendant may exercise were concretely formed by agreement or decision among the co-owners, one might consider that the unlawful state could be removed while leaving that partial right intact. However, if there is no agreement or decision among the co-owners, and the “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio” held by the Defendant has not been concretely specified in any content, then the use and profit right asserted by the Defendant is merely conceptual, and therefore even if the Defendant is ordered to deliver the entirety of the co-owned property, this cannot be regarded as infringing the Defendant’s rights.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion’s position that the Plaintiff, being merely a minority share-right holder, has no legal basis to seek delivery of the entirety of the co-owned property is not valid. The reason the conventional precedents recognized that a Plaintiff, as a minority share-right holder, may seek delivery of the entirety of the co-owned property is that such claim was regarded as an act of preservation of co-owned property that each co-owner may perform under the proviso to Article 265 of the Civil Act. In other words, where one co-owner exclusively possesses the co-owned property, removing the interference or recovering the co-owned property for the purpose of correcting such unlawful state and restoring the status of the co-owned property to a state in which all co-owners may use and collect fruits therefrom constitutes an act for the preservation of the co-owned property. In ordinary circumstances, the Plaintiff cannot seek delivery of the entirety of the co-owned property to the Plaintiff solely on the basis of the Plaintiff’s minority share. However, if it falls within the act of preservation under the proviso to Article 265 of the Civil Act, it is appropriate to view the Plaintiff as entitled to seek delivery of the entirety of the co-owned property, not limited to the Plaintiff’s own share. Under other legal principles established by the Supreme Court as well, it is permitted for a rights holder, in order to effectively preserve his or her rights, to claim delivery or payment of a thing or money beyond the scope of his or her own rights. By way of example, there is the legal principle that where a creditor exercises subrogation over the debtor’s monetary claim in order to preserve the creditor’s own monetary claim, the creditor may seek performance directly to the subrogated creditor himself or herself by the third-party obligor (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA236547 rendered on August 29, 2016, among others), and the legal principle that restoration following rescission of a fraudulent act may be sought directly by the cancelling creditor to be performed to himself or herself, irrespective of whether restitution in kind or compensation by value is involved (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA23468, 23475 rendered on August 24, 1999; Supreme Court Decision 2007DA84352 rendered on April 24, 2008, among others).\\n\\nThe majority opinion cites Supreme Court Decision 93DA54736 rendered on April 7, 1995, which held that when one co-owner exercises a right of preservation and the result of such exercise conflicts with another co-owner’s interests, that exercise cannot be regarded as an act of preservation. On that basis, the majority opinion says that if the Plaintiff’s claim is made against another co-owner, it conflicts with that co-owner’s interests and therefore cannot be an act of preservation. However, the “interests of another co-owner” referred to in that decision cannot be said to include the benefit that the Defendant, who is both the opposing party to the claim and the party who committed the unlawful act, enjoys while maintaining the unlawful state. The Defendant has not only infringed the rights of the other co-owner(s) without authority, but also, so long as the Defendant’s exclusive possession of the entirety of the co-owned property continues, the unlawful state continues. Even if, in the process of correcting such unlawful state, the Defendant can no longer obtain the benefit enjoyed under the prior unlawful state, that cannot be considered a factor to be taken into account when determining whether the act is one of preservation. If such a factor is considered, then whenever the party to the unlawful act also has the status of a co-owner, acts of preservation for the benefit of the other co-owners would always be impossible.\\n\\nIf the claim by the Plaintiff, a minority share-right holder, contravenes the interests of the other co-owner(s) apart from the Defendant, who is the opposing party, or is contrary to their will, then such an act of preservation may not be permitted and may be possible only as an act of management of the co-owned property determined by a majority of shares (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA208252 rendered on September 26, 2019, among others). However, in such case, the burden of asserting and proving that the Plaintiff’s claim is contrary to the interests or will of the other co-owner(s) lies with the party asserting it. The above Supreme Court Decision 93DA54736 cited by the majority opinion involved a case in which the Plaintiff, one of the co-owners, sought cancellation of a registration of transfer of ownership made in favor of the Defendant, another co-owner, to the extent exceeding the Defendant’s original share, and some of the other co-owners had clearly expressed during the litigation that they regarded the Defendant’s registration of transfer of ownership as valid. By contrast, in this case, the will of the other co-owner(s) apart from the Defendant has never been manifested in the litigation, so allowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery cannot be said to be contrary to the purport of that Supreme Court decision.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion states that if the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery is allowed, it will produce the unjust result of causing the Plaintiff, another minority share-right holder, to exclusively possess and use the co-owned property, which is not materially different from the existing unlawful state in which a minority share-right holder exclusively possesses the co-owned property. However, this criticism is based on a misunderstanding of the purpose of permitting the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery, by presupposing that the nature of the possession acquired by the Plaintiff through the delivery judgment is the same as the Defendant’s prior exclusive possession, and is therefore not valid. Since the Plaintiff receives delivery of the co-owned property as an act of preservation not solely for the Plaintiff’s own benefit but for the benefit of all co-owners, the possession acquired by the Plaintiff should be regarded as for all co-owners, and such possession cannot be said to be the same as the Defendant’s prior possession, which unlawfully and exclusively occupied the co-owned property. Allowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery is not intended to enable the Plaintiff alone to acquire possession, but to exclude the Defendant’s unlawful exclusive possession, and the exclusion of the co-owner Defendant in the process of execution of delivery is merely a temporary phenomenon for the purpose of eliminating the unlawful state. Pursuant to the purpose of the act of preservation, the Plaintiff must not exclusively possess or use the delivered co-owned property, but must faithfully preserve the co-owned property so that the original form of a normal co-ownership relationship may be realized. The Plaintiff must make the co-owned property available for joint use by all co-owners, and after the act of preservation is completed, the Defendant, the former possessor, also stands in a position to use and collect fruits from the co-owned property jointly, just like the other co-owners. Accordingly, merely allowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery as an act of preservation cannot be said to deprive the Defendant of the right to use and collect fruits according to the share.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that where a third party who is not a co-owner unlawfully possesses the co-owned property, the Plaintiff may seek delivery of the co-owned property even as a minority share-right holder, but as against the co-owner Defendant, the Plaintiff has no legal basis to exclusively possess the co-owned property and therefore cannot seek delivery. However, if, as the majority opinion views it, the possession acquired by the Plaintiff is characterized as exclusive possession, then one may question whether a minority share-right holder, the Plaintiff, has a legal basis to receive delivery of the co-owned property from a third party and possess it exclusively, beyond merely removing the third party’s possession by removal of interference. The result of that execution of delivery also leads to the unlawful state in which the minority share-right holder, the Plaintiff, exclusively possesses the co-owned property without authority. Ultimately, the majority opinion cannot avoid the criticism that it differently characterizes, without sufficient basis, the nature of the possession acquired by a minority share-right holder through delivery from a third party and from another co-owner.\\n\\nAllowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery does not, of course, justify or guarantee the Plaintiff’s exclusive possession and use of the co-owned property. If the Plaintiff, having received delivery of the co-owned property as an act of preservation, exclusively possesses and uses it without consulting the other co-owner(s), this is contrary to the purpose for which the Plaintiff’s claim was originally permitted as an act of preservation, so the other co-owners, including the Defendant, may thereafter again seek removal of interference and delivery against the Plaintiff. In such case, through the reasons of the prior delivery judgment, it can be seen that the Plaintiff’s prior claim for delivery was made as an act of preservation of the co-owned property; therefore, even if the Defendant later again seeks removal of interference and delivery against the Plaintiff, this should be deemed not to contravene the res judicata of the prior delivery judgment.\\n\\nAs is well known, the “res judicata” prescribed in Articles 216 and 218 of the Civil Procedure Act operates to prohibit a later suit on the same subject matter as the suit in the earlier final judgment having res judicata effect, and at the same time, even if the subject matter of the later suit is not the same as that of the earlier suit, when the determination regarding the subject matter of the earlier suit becomes a preliminary issue in the later suit or is in a contradictory relationship with it, it prevents assertions different from the determination in the earlier judgment from being made in the later suit. In particular, although Article 216(1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides that a final judgment has res judicata only with respect to matters included in the operative part, this is true as to the objective scope of res judicata, as indicated by the title of that provision, and in determining whether the preclusion effect by reason of the temporal scope of res judicata applies, one must examine the reasons of the final judgment together with the operative part in an integrated manner. A right relationship established at the time of closing of oral argument at the standard time in the fact-finding court, by virtue of the res judicata of a final judgment, may thereafter change, and therefore, as to a cause arising after the standard time, the preclusion effect by res judicata does not apply, so that a party may file a new action by asserting a new cause that the factual relationship changed after the standard time (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA46817 rendered on September 29, 1995; Supreme Court Decision 98DA7001 rendered on July 10, 1998, among others), because whether the matter asserted by the party constitutes a cause arising after the standard time can be clearly ascertained only by comparing it with the reasons of the final judgment in the prior suit.\\n\\nTherefore, where a judgment granting the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery as an act of preservation becomes final and the Plaintiff thereafter receives delivery of the co-owned property and comes to exclusively possess and use it without consulting the other co-owner(s), this should be regarded as a new cause arising after the standard time of the final judgment, to which the res judicata of the prior suit does not extend.\\n\\nFurthermore, as noted above, considering the position of the Plaintiff who receives delivery of the co-owned property as an act of preservation, it cannot be said that allowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery necessarily entails the problem of circular litigation whereby the Defendant would again sue the Plaintiff for delivery. The situation in which the Defendant in the prior suit brings a claim for delivery of the co-owned property against the Plaintiff does not arise from the point when the Plaintiff’s prior claim for delivery was granted and execution of delivery was completed, but only when, after completing execution of delivery, the Plaintiff exclusively possesses and uses the co-owned property contrary to the original purpose. The reason cases of circular litigation are not easily found in practice is also that the Plaintiff, who exercised the right of preservation, does not exclusively possess and use the co-owned property in accordance with the purport of the prior delivery judgment, but instead either reaches an agreement among the co-owners regarding the management of the co-owned property so that the co-ownership relationship operates normally, or, if that is difficult, resolves the co-ownership relationship through partition of the co-owned property.\\n\\n(4) Although the result of allowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery is that the former possessor, the Defendant, is temporarily excluded from possession, this may be regarded as inevitable because it is a reflex result of measures taken to dissolve the Defendant’s exclusive possession and correct the unlawful state. As noted above, after completing execution of delivery, the Plaintiff who exercised the right of preservation must, in the position of a diligent custodian, make the co-owned property available for joint use by the co-owners; and the Defendant, who was temporarily excluded in the course of the act of preservation, may at that time jointly use and collect fruits from the co-owned property together with the other co-owners.\\n\\nSince, as above, the Defendant is in a position to jointly use and collect fruits from the co-owned property after execution of delivery, which is an act of preservation, is completed, it may in theory be simpler to merely dissolve the Defendant’s exclusive possession and immediately enable all co-owners, including the Plaintiff and the Defendant, to possess the property. However, in our litigation and execution practice, there is no precedent for, nor legal basis permitting, execution in the manner of a claim for establishment of joint possession, such as “the Defendant shall establish joint possession for the Plaintiff with respect to the co-owned property,” as in Germany, or execution replacing the Defendant’s possession with the joint possession of the Plaintiff and the Defendant. Therefore, as a fallback measure to realize the act of preservation under the proviso to Article 265 of the Civil Act, it is unavoidable for the Plaintiff, one of the co-owners, first to dissolve the Defendant’s possession and then make the property available for joint use by the co-owners.\\n\\n(5) The majority opinion, while denying the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery, holds that claims for removal of above-ground objects against the Defendant and injunctions against interference with joint possession and use are possible, and takes the position that through these, the unlawful state in which the Defendant exclusively possesses the co-owned property can be sufficiently remedied. However, where there is a dispute between the Plaintiff and the Defendant concerning the method of using the co-owned land and neither obtains the consent of a majority of shares, “joint use of co-owned property in a non-exclusive manner” is extremely limited in practice and difficult to conceive except in very limited cases, such as passage over land. In most cases, use of economically valuable co-owned property will, even if only temporarily, involve exclusive possession.\\n\\nFurthermore, the majority opinion anticipates that the Plaintiff may formulate the claim in the form of seeking prohibition, removal, or prevention of interference by specifically identifying the Defendant’s acts and interference-causing objects that interfere with or are likely to interfere with the Plaintiff’s joint possession, taking into account the type, use, condition, and the parties’ relationship, and that the court may grant such claim. However, the prospect that such claims for injunction against interference will establish themselves as a new means to remedy the rights of minority share-right holders does not appear as bright as the majority opinion expects. Not only is there a question of whether the interference act the Plaintiff seeks to prohibit is properly specified and whether it falls within the scope of the claim for removal of interference under Article 214 of the Civil Act, but also the scope and limits are unclear as to whether the form of joint possession the Plaintiff seeks to achieve through such claims for injunction against interference constitutes an act of management requiring a decision among the co-owners under the main clause of Article 265 of the Civil Act. For that reason, it is difficult to say categorically that the court can subsume such claims under the “right to claim removal of interference,” which can be exercised unilaterally by one co-owner, and grant them.\\n\\nMoreover, if the claim for injunction against interference sought by the Plaintiff is deemed to go beyond removal of interference and to constitute an act of management of the co-owned property, the court hearing the case would have no choice but to dismiss the Plaintiff’s claim because the requirements of the main clause of Article 265 of the Civil Act were not satisfied. Otherwise, the court would have to exercise its right to clarify in order to make the claim correspond to a “claim for removal of interference.” However, there has not been sufficient discussion or review as to whether the exercise of the right to clarify in such a manner complies with the limits of the adversarial principle, and the majority opinion has not presented any view on this point. One may think of a method of having the other co-owners apart from the Plaintiff participate in the litigation and then deciding after reflecting their opinions, but the current Civil Procedure Act does not separately provide any institutional mechanism by which other co-owners may be brought into the litigation. In this respect, it is difficult to regard the majority opinion, which seeks to change the legal principle of existing Supreme Court precedents that have operated stably in practice without any particular problem, on the basis of exploratory and abstract discourse without presenting any clear alternative for resolving co-ownership disputes among minority share-right holders, as valid.\\n\\nAlso, both the majority opinion and the existing Supreme Court precedents may be said to share the goal that above-ground objects such as buildings, which were arbitrarily built on co-owned land, must be removed and that no one may exclusively use the co-owned property without an agreement or decision among the co-owners regarding the management of the co-owned property. However, there is merely a difference between the two as to the means of realizing this goal. If delivery is allowed, as in the existing Supreme Court precedents, the Plaintiff can exclude the Defendant’s unlawful possession at once by means of direct execution (Article 258 of the Civil Procedure Act), whereas under the majority opinion, claims for injunction against interference can only be executed by indirect compulsion (Article 261 of the Civil Procedure Act). The latter method indirectly compels the Defendant’s conduct (cessation of exclusive possession) through monetary pressure, and the execution procedure, including indirect compulsion orders, issuance of a writ of execution through proof of the violating act, and execution procedures for collection of the indirect compulsion amount, is much more complicated, making it difficult to correct the unlawful state caused by the Defendant’s exclusive possession.\\n\\nThese negative aspects are even greater in light of the limitations inherent in indirect compulsion under the current Civil Execution Act. For example, if the profit the Defendant can obtain by exclusively possessing the co-owned property is far greater than the compensation amount imposed by indirect compulsion, the method of indirect compulsion can hardly be regarded as an effective means of dissolving the Defendant’s exclusive possession. In addition, if the Defendant does not comply with the court’s compensation order, the only remaining path is to pressure the Defendant’s property through monetary execution based on the compensation order as the title of execution. If at that time the Defendant is insolvent and monetary execution ends in failure, indirect compulsion will not function properly as a means of pressure, and the attempt to change the condition in which the Defendant exclusively possesses the co-owned property will ultimately come to nothing.\\n\\n(6) On the other hand, according to the majority opinion, contradictory conclusions arise where a minority share-right holder leases the co-owned property to a third party (the same applies to a loan for use). Since leasing the co-owned property to another is an act of management of the co-owned property and must be decided by a majority of the co-ownership shares, and since a lease by a co-owner not based on such decision is ineffective against the other co-owners, the consistent position of the Supreme Court is that the other co-owners may seek delivery of the co-owned property against a tenant who leased it from a minority share-right holder (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA569 rendered on May 27, 2010, among others), and it is understood that the majority opinion would not view this point differently either. Yet under the majority opinion, contradictory results arise: where the Defendant exclusively possesses the co-owned property by the Defendant’s own possession or through an auxiliary possessor, the Plaintiff cannot seek delivery, whereas if the Defendant maintains the status of an indirect possessor by leasing it to a third party, etc., then delivery may be sought against the third party, who is the direct possessor. Since how the co-owned property is to be possessed in concrete terms can be freely chosen by the Defendant in practice, it is difficult in itself to understand, let alone find any fundamental reason to justify, treating the former and latter situations entirely differently.\\n\\nThe problems with the majority opinion become even clearer when the Plaintiff, a minority share-right holder, seeks delivery by naming both the Defendant and a third party who leased the co-owned property from the Defendant as co-defendants. According to the majority opinion, in such a case, unless the action is treated as a necessary joinder suit requiring a unified determination of the legal relationship, it would ordinarily be a joint action, and the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery against the Defendant, who is an indirect possessor, would be dismissed, whereas the claim against the third party, who is the direct possessor, would be granted. However, even if the Plaintiff thereafter seeks to execute the final judgment in the Plaintiff’s favor against the third party, the Defendant could easily render execution impossible by filing a third-party objection action on the ground that the Defendant is both a minority share-right holder and a possessor and by applying for a stay of compulsory execution, or by converting possession in relation to the third party from indirect possession to direct possession, or by changing the third party from an indirect possessor to an auxiliary possessor, and so on. Before changing the existing Supreme Court precedents, as the majority opinion suggests, sufficient review is needed regarding the ripple effects and influence on other legal principles.\\n\\n(7) The majority opinion states that, if the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery is allowed under the pretext of correcting the unlawful state in which the Defendant exclusively possesses the co-owned property, it would result in the unjust deprivation, without basis, of the “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio” that the Defendant lawfully holds. Yet it arrives at the conclusion that the Plaintiff’s claim for removal of interference is permissible because it does not infringe the Defendant’s “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio.” However, while the majority opinion treats the Defendant’s “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio” as so significant in relation to the former delivery claim that it would deny the Plaintiff’s exercise of the right of preservation, it is not clear how, in relation to the latter claim for removal of interference, the Defendant’s “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio” is not infringed and yet the claim for removal of interference may be granted, or how the two can be reconciled. If the logic applied by the majority opinion to delivery claims is applied in the same way to claims for removal of interference, then, for example, where above-ground objects such as buildings or trees unlawfully constructed or planted by the Defendant exist on the co-owned land, the Defendant would be deemed to be using and collecting fruits from the co-owned land by leaving the above-ground objects in place, and further, the Defendant can be said to have rights in proportion to the Defendant’s share regarding such use and profit. Therefore, if, as the Plaintiff seeks through exercise of the right to claim removal of interference, removal of the entire above-ground object is granted, the result would be an infringement of the “right to use and collect fruits according to the share” that the Defendant held while the above-ground object existed on the co-owned land. Consequently, the exercise of the right to claim removal of interference should also not be permitted, just as with delivery claims. Nevertheless, the majority opinion treats delivery claims and claims for removal of interference entirely differently when determining whether the Plaintiff, a minority share-right holder, is exercising a right of preservation. Such majority opinion is either logically inconsistent or, at a minimum, difficult to defend against the criticism that different standards are being applied to the two types of claims.\\n\\nC. Conclusion in this case\\nThe court below held that, although the Plaintiff is a co-owner of the land at issue and its ownership share does not amount to a majority, the Plaintiff may seek, as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, removal of the above-ground objects on the land at issue and delivery of the possessed portion against the Defendant, who is a minority share-right holder exclusively occupying part of the land at issue, and accordingly granted the Plaintiff’s claim.\\n\\nThat determination by the court below follows the existing Supreme Court precedents and is proper, and the court below did not err in a way that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning acts of preservation of co-owned property.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we state that we cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek concerning the claim for removal of interference\\nA. The majority opinion states that where the Defendant, a minority share-right holder of co-owned property, exclusively possesses or uses all or part of the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s), the Plaintiff, another minority share-right holder, cannot seek delivery of the co-owned property to the Plaintiff as an act of preservation of the co-owned property, but may seek removal of the above-ground objects, collection thereof, and injunctions against acts interfering with the Plaintiff’s joint possession and use, based on the co-ownership share right.\\n\\nHowever, since the right of use and profit in co-owned property based on Article 263 of the Civil Act is merely a general and abstract right whose content is not determined by statute, where there is no determination among the co-owners by a majority of shares concerning the method of use and profit from the co-owned property, no co-owner can be said to have the right to use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in the way he or she asserts, regardless of its content. The existing Supreme Court decisions should all be changed, including not only the minority share-right holder’s claim for delivery but also the part recognizing the claim for removal of interference, and we cannot agree with the majority opinion’s denial of the minority share-right holder’s claim for delivery while affirming the claim for removal of interference. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) In a co-ownership relationship, because one ownership right is divided and vested in several persons, co-owners, unlike a sole owner, are subject to certain restrictions in exercising ownership over the co-owned property. A co-owner may freely dispose of his or her co-ownership share (Article 263 of the Civil Act), but to dispose of the co-owned property itself, the consent of the other co-owner(s) is required (Article 264 of the Civil Act). With respect to use and profit from co-owned property, the co-owners may only use and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property in proportion to their shares (Article 263 of the Civil Act). The Civil Act does not provide any more detailed rule as to what “use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in proportion to the shares” means.\\n\\nThere are diverse ways to use and collect fruits from a thing, and even more diverse ways for co-owners to use and collect fruits from a single thing together. For example, land may be left as bare land, paved and used as a passage or parking lot, planted with crops or trees, or used for construction of a building, and it may also be leased to another, or a servitude or superficies may be established over it. When co-owners use land together, they may designate its use, such as a parking lot, paddy field, or building site, or use it by dividing into areas without designating a use, or use it by alternating periods of use. It may also be used collectively, as with landscaped space or a parking lot in a residential complex. Moreover, it is possible for only one co-owner to use the thing while compensating the others, or to lease it to another person and distribute the rent received.\\n\\nSince the methods by which a thing may be used and collected fruits from are so varied that they are difficult to enumerate, co-owners must, in order to use and collect fruits from a single co-owned property together, make decisions among themselves in some manner. The main clause of Article 265 of the Civil Act provides that “matters concerning the management of co-owned property shall be determined by a majority of the shares of the co-owners,” and precedents hold that determining the specific method by which co-owners use and profit from the co-owned property constitutes a “matter concerning the management of co-owned property” within the meaning of that provision and must be determined by a majority of the co-ownership shares (see Supreme Court Decision 92MA290 rendered on June 13, 1992; Supreme Court Decision 2002DA9738 rendered on May 14, 2002, among others). Therefore, co-owners must consult on how to use and collect fruits from the co-owned property, and if no consensus is reached among the co-owners, the method may be determined by a majority of the shares. In that case, “using and collecting fruits from the co-owned property in proportion to the shares” may be understood to mean that co-owners may decide the method of use and profit from the co-owned property by exercising voting power in proportion to their own shares.\\n\\nFurthermore, where, pursuant to a decision by majority shares, one co-owner exclusively uses and collects fruits from the co-owned property or leases it to another and receives rent, the co-owners who hold shares but do not use or collect fruits from the co-owned property at all may claim return of unjust enrichment in an amount equivalent to their share of the rent (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA9738 rendered on May 14, 2002, among others). In that case, “using and collecting fruits from the co-owned property in proportion to the shares” may also be understood to mean that co-owners may acquire economic benefits arising from the co-owned property, in proportion to their shares, including natural fruits and statutory fruits such as rent.\\n\\nHowever, where no decision based on a majority of shares has been made among the co-owners, there may be cases where the co-owners do not agree on the method of use and profit from the co-owned property and no one obtains the consent of a majority of shares, for example where A, who holds a 1/2 share in co-owned land, wishes to build a structure on the land, while B, who holds the other 1/2 share, wishes to leave it as bare land and use it as a parking lot. In such cases, the Civil Act contains no provision as to how the co-owners may use and collect fruits from the co-owned property. This is distinct from situations in which, for partition of co-owned property, division of property upon divorce, or contribution shares, the parties may autonomously determine the matter by agreement, but if no agreement is reached, the court may be requested to decide it and may make a discretionary, formative determination thereon (Articles 269, 839-2, and 1008-2 of the Civil Act, etc.). In the above example, the respective methods desired by A and B are both one form of use of co-owned property under the Civil Act, but neither A nor B may request the court to allow the land to be used and profited from in the specific manner he or she desires, absent a decision based on a majority of shares. Since the court is also provided with no substantive or procedural basis to determine, in place of the co-owners, the specific method of use and profit from the co-owned property, it cannot determine which of A’s or B’s methods is lawful. Precedents have held that, in the absence of a determination of the method of use and profit from co-owned property, no co-owner may exclusively use and collect fruits from even part of the co-owned property, and that even if the area used by the co-owner is less than the area corresponding to the co-owner’s share, the co-owner still bears a duty to return unjust enrichment in proportion to the shares to the other co-owner(s) (see Supreme Court Decision 72DA1814 rendered on December 12, 1972; Supreme Court Decision 2000DA13948 rendered on December 11, 2001, among others). This presupposes that, in the absence of a determination regarding the method of use and profit from the co-owned property, the co-owners cannot use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in any specific manner, whether exclusive or non-exclusive.\\n\\nUltimately, where no decision has been made among the co-owners concerning the method of use and profit from the co-owned property, the “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio” held by the co-owners is merely a general and abstract right and cannot be considered a concrete right that can be asserted through an action. For the co-owners to bring a lawsuit premised on the use and profit of the co-owned property in a specific manner, it is required that the right to use and collect fruits be concretely formed through a decision by majority shares. In the absence of such a decision, it cannot be permitted for the co-owners simply to invoke the “right to use and collect fruits according to the share ratio” provided by law and, under the pretext of realizing such right, claim a specific form of removal of interference or delivery.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion says that even if there is no decision concerning the method of use and profit from the co-owned property, the co-owners may jointly use and collect fruits from the entirety of the co-owned property in a non-exclusive manner, i.e., in a manner that does not infringe the other co-owner’s rights of use and profit, and that to realize such a state, the Plaintiff may seek removal of interference against the Defendant who exclusively occupies the co-owned property. However, this reasoning of the majority opinion overlooks the point that “joint use and profit” of co-owned property is also impossible without a specific decision concerning the method of use and profit from the co-owned property.\\n\\nCo-ownership, unlike joint ownership in which several persons form an association and own a thing as members of that association, or a partnership ownership relationship in which partners own a thing in order to operate a joint business, has no rules, such as articles of incorporation, resolutions of a general meeting, or partnership agreements, that minimally determine the method of use and profit from the co-owned property or impose collective restrictions among the co-owners. Each co-owner’s power to control the co-owned property is independent and free vis-à-vis the others, and is merely subject to restriction because the object is the same. One must ask how it is realistically possible for co-owners who lack even the minimum agreement or common understanding required for joint use of a thing to jointly use a single thing without any decision for joint use.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that the Plaintiff may, by specifically identifying the Defendant’s acts and interference-causing objects that interfere with the Plaintiff’s joint possession, seek against the Defendant injunctions against interference, removal, and prevention (performance of affirmative and negative obligations). As noted above, there are many possible ways for several persons to use a single thing together, and in the absence of a decision concerning the method of use and profit, the co-owners cannot assert that they will use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in a specific manner of their choosing. Therefore, there is no reason why the Defendant should bear affirmative or negative obligations in order for the Plaintiff to use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in the manner the Plaintiff desires. This presupposes that the court has non-contentious discretion to determine the specific method of use and profit from co-owned property, which, as noted above, has no basis in law.\\n\\nThe majority opinion cites, as an example of a non-exclusive joint use and profit method, the use of co-owned land for passage. It is true that “co-owners using the co-owned land as a passageway” is one method of joint use of the co-owned land, but, as noted above, the methods of joint use of co-owned land are very diverse, and among those methods there is no basis for the Plaintiff to claim that it will be used as a “passageway.” If the Plaintiff claims use as a passageway and the Defendant claims another method of use, such as a parking lot, the absence of any substantive or procedural basis for the court to order the Defendant to perform affirmative or negative obligations on the premise that the land be used in the manner asserted by the Plaintiff remains as noted above.\\n\\nUltimately, the legal relationship concerning the use of co-owned property by co-owners results in one of the following two situations: either the co-owners use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in a specific manner determined as the management method, or, absent such determination, they confront each other by asserting that they will use the property in their own preferred manner. The third category described by the majority opinion—where co-owners jointly possess and use a thing in a specific manner without any determination concerning the management of the co-owned property—does not exist as a matter of law.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, it is difficult to think of a method by which a thing may be “jointly used and enjoyed in a non-exclusive manner” without decision among co-owners. In most cases, using a thing presupposes exclusive possession, even if only temporarily. For example, if one co-owner places objects on co-owned land or takes and uses a movable co-owned thing, this may be said to constitute exclusive possession of the thing during that period, regardless of the length of time, and thus does not amount to non-exclusive use. Even in the case of cohabiting in a co-owned house or jointly conducting business in a co-owned store, if the area is divided for use, that ultimately amounts to exclusive possession over part of the co-owned property, and it is difficult to conceive that co-owners with no personal relationship such as divided ownership or partnership would live or conduct business together in the same space without dividing it. Even the simple use of co-owned land for passage requires at least minimal rules regarding the number and manner of passages; otherwise, conflict arises among the co-owners and joint use becomes impossible.\\n\\nUltimately, the “state in which co-owners jointly use and enjoy the co-owned property in a non-exclusive manner without any decision” described by the majority opinion is merely a conceptual assumption and is difficult to conceive realistically. The majority opinion recognizes removal of interference in the name of achieving an impossible state.\\n\\n(4) As noted above, in the absence of a decision by majority shares, the minority share-right holder has no concrete right to use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in a specific form. Therefore, where the Defendant, a minority share-right holder, uses and collects fruits from the co-owned property in a specific manner without such decision, this is unlawful, whether exclusive or non-exclusive. However, no matter how unlawful the Defendant’s possession may be, if the Plaintiff has no legal basis to demand removal of that unlawful state, the Plaintiff’s claim cannot be granted; this is a fundamental principle of civil adjudication.\\n\\nA claim for removal of structures on land and a claim for delivery of land based on land ownership are separate claims, and the landowner need not necessarily bring both; he or she may bring only one. However, since the landowner’s claim for removal of structures is intended to effectively restore possession of the land on which the structures exist, if the landowner has no right to seek delivery of the land, then a claim for removal of structures to realize that purpose is also impossible.\\n\\nSince the Plaintiff is also merely a minority share-right holder and has no concrete right to use and collect fruits from the co-owned property in a specific form without a decision by majority shares, it is impossible for the Plaintiff to seek a change in the current state of use and profit from the co-owned property in order to realize that right, namely, not only delivery of the land but also an injunction against interference for joint possession and use of the land. Ultimately, the Defendant’s possession is unlawful, but because the Plaintiff cannot demand its removal, the current state must be maintained, and even if the Defendant possesses the co-owned land through ownership of above-ground objects, this is merely one form of the Defendant’s possession of the co-owned land, so the Plaintiff must be understood to be unable to seek collection or removal thereof.\\n\\nWhere, as above, one co-owner exclusively or non-exclusively possesses and uses the co-owned property and no one can obtain the consent of a majority of shares, the other co-owner(s) may receive the benefits arising from such use and profit by way of damages or return of unjust enrichment. Furthermore, because a co-owner dissatisfied with such monetary compensation may at any time seek partition of the co-owned property and thereby dissolve the co-ownership relationship, this conclusion cannot be said to unduly restrict the co-owners’ rights of use and profit.\\n\\nB. The court below, notwithstanding the absence of any decision by majority shares among the co-owners regarding the land at issue, held that the Plaintiff, who owns a 1/2 share in the land at issue, may seek removal of the above-ground objects on the land at issue as an act of preservation of the co-owned property against the Defendant, who exclusively possesses part of the land at issue, and granted the Plaintiff’s claim for removal of above-ground objects. In light of the legal principles discussed above, the court below erred in granting the Plaintiff’s claim for removal of above-ground objects by misapprehending the legal principles concerning acts of preservation of co-owned property and the co-owner’s right to use and collect fruits from co-owned property, thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment. Therefore, the portion of the judgment below concerning the claim for removal of above-ground objects must also be reversed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we state that we cannot agree with the majority opinion concerning the claim for removal of interference.\\n\\n7. Supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung and Ahn Cheol-sang to the majority opinion\\nThe two dissenting opinions concerning the majority opinion take completely opposite positions. One says that both the claim for delivery of co-owned property and the claim for removal of interference should be recognized, while the other says that neither should be recognized. These dissenting opinions raise, in new fashion, some issues not found in prior discussions. We think this will help develop the legal principles concerning co-ownership, and therefore here we offer our views to reinforce the majority opinion (hereinafter, the dissenting opinion of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, Lee Dong-won, Kim Sang-hwan, and Noh Tae-ak is referred to as “Dissent 1,” and the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek as “Dissent 2”).\\n\\nA. Are the co-owners’ rights of use and profit in co-owned property general and abstract rights, becoming individual and concrete rights only after a decision concerning management of the co-owned property has been made?\\n(1) Dissent 2 says that where there is no decision concerning management of the co-owned property, the co-owner’s right of use and profit in the co-owned property is merely a general and abstract right and therefore cannot be the subject of a procedural claim, and that even if the Defendant exclusively possesses the co-owned property, the Plaintiff cannot seek delivery of the co-owned property or removal of interference in order to realize the Plaintiff’s right of use and profit.\\n\\nThe majority opinion has already noted that the essence of a co-ownership share right lies in ownership as a type of real right and that it includes the power of use and profit. In particular, Article 263 of the Civil Act expressly provides that co-owners also have the right to use and collect fruits according to their shares. Because co-owners are subject to restrictions arising from the co-ownership relationship, if the method of managing the co-owned property is determined by a majority of the co-ownership shares, they must comply with it (main clause of Article 265 of the Civil Act). However, this does not mean that in the absence of such determination, no one may use and collect fruits from the thing.\\n\\nDissent 2 unduly narrows the powers of the co-ownership share right, contrary to the essence of the share right as a real right and to the language of Article 263 of the Civil Act. Moreover, if a minority share-right holder unlawfully exclusively possesses the co-owned property, the other co-owner(s) would be unable to possess or use the thing except to receive monetary compensation, which is contrary to common legal sentiment and results in downgrading the real right of co-ownership share into a mere right to receive rent. Due to the restrictions inherent in the co-ownership relationship, each co-owner cannot exclusively possess the co-owned property like a sole owner, but should be understood to be able to actually use and collect fruits from the co-owned property together with the other co-owner(s), in a non-exclusive manner that does not infringe the other co-owners’ rights of use and profit.\\n\\nThere is no basis in the Civil Act, especially in the part concerning real rights, for regarding rights or powers as conceptual rights or general and abstract rights. The logic that the co-owners’ rights of use and profit in co-owned property are merely general and abstract rights and become individual and concrete rights only after a decision concerning management of the co-owned property has been made would instead unnecessarily confuse legal relations. Regardless of whether there is a decision concerning management of the co-owned property, the co-owners may claim against the person possessing and using the co-owned property return of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent or damages based on tort. The basis for such claims based on unjust enrichment or tort can also be said to be the right of use and profit in the co-owned property, and that right cannot be called general and abstract.\\n\\n(2) Dissent 1 says that if no decision concerning management of the co-owned property has been made among the co-owners, the Defendant’s right to use and profit according to share ratio is merely conceptual, so ordering the Defendant to deliver the entirety of the co-owned property does not infringe the Defendant’s rights. This, like Dissent 2, presupposes that no co-owner has a concrete right to use and profit from the co-owned property unless the method of management of the co-owned property has been determined. Meanwhile, Dissent 1 says that the Plaintiff, a minority share-right holder, after receiving delivery of the co-owned property, must provide the property to all co-owners so that all may use it jointly. However, if no co-owner has a concrete right of use and profit from the co-owned property where the method of management has not been determined, then even if the Defendant exclusively possesses the property, it would lead to the unreasonable conclusion that neither the Plaintiff nor the other co-owner(s)’ rights of use and profit are infringed. Moreover, if the co-owner’s right of use and profit is merely conceptual, there would likewise be no reason for the Plaintiff to provide the property again for joint use with the other co-owner(s).\\n\\nThus, Dissent 1 takes a contradictory position on whether a minority share-right holder may use and profit from the co-owned property where there is no determination on management. If the co-owners’ right of use and profit is understood to be nothing more than a conceptual right, then it is more logical, as in Dissent 2, to hold that no co-owner may seek removal of interference or delivery until a decision concerning management of the co-owned property is made.\\n\\nB. Is it necessary to permit a claim for delivery in order to exclude the Defendant’s unlawful possession?\\n(1) There is no disagreement between the majority opinion and Dissent 1 that it is unlawful for the Defendant, a minority share-right holder, to exclusively possess the co-owned property without consulting the other co-owner(s). The same is true regarding the fact that the Plaintiff may seek removal of interference in order to exclude the Defendant’s unlawful possession of the co-owned property. The issue here is whether the Plaintiff may further seek to exclude the Defendant’s possession and claim that the co-owned property be “delivered to the Plaintiff.” Dissent 1 says that the Plaintiff may seek delivery to the Plaintiff on the ground that it is an “act of preservation of the co-owned property,” that delivery is indispensable to effectively exclude the Defendant’s unlawful possession, and that the majority opinion, which permits claims for removal of interference while denying claims for delivery, is either logically inconsistent or applies different standards to the two claims.\\n\\n(2) A claim for delivery based on ownership is a proprietary claim under Article 213 of the Civil Act, which requires that the Plaintiff be the owner and that the Defendant possess the thing, with the exception of cases where the Defendant has the right to possess. A claim for removal of interference based on ownership is a proprietary claim under Article 214 of the Civil Act and requires that the Plaintiff be the owner and that the Defendant unlawfully interfere with ownership. Typical examples are a landowner’s claim for removal of above-ground structures or for cancellation of a registration made without underlying cause.\\n\\nThus, claims for delivery and claims for removal of interference differ in their legal basis, requirements, and operation, so they need not logically reach the same conclusion. If the Defendant has the right to possess the thing but possesses it in an unlawful manner, the Plaintiff may only seek removal of the interference. For example, where a tenant who leased land for cultivation uses part of the land for raising livestock, in some cases the lessor may terminate the lease and seek collection of the livestock and delivery of the land; but where the breach does not rise to a ground for termination of the lease, the lessor may seek only collection of the livestock.\\n\\nIn this case, the Defendant planted trees on the co-owned land and exclusively possesses the land. This is an unlawful interference with the Plaintiff’s share right, so the Plaintiff may seek collection of the trees, and generally, once the trees are removed, the Defendant’s state of interference may be regarded as removed. If the Plaintiff further seeks to have the land delivered to the Plaintiff, what is required is that “the Defendant have no legal basis to possess.” Since the Defendant, as a co-owner, does have authority to possess and use the co-owned property jointly, it is not the case that the Defendant has no legal basis at all to possess the land. In a situation where the tangible object causing the exclusive possession can be removed through removal of interference, such as removal of above-ground objects, there is no need for the Plaintiff to take away all of the Defendant’s possession; rather, it is sufficient to prohibit the Defendant’s conduct exceeding the shared possession authorized to the Defendant, namely, conduct that interferes with the Plaintiff’s joint possession and that exclusively possesses the co-owned property. That is sufficient to achieve the state in which all co-owners can jointly use the co-owned property.\\n\\n(3) Dissent 1 states that allowing the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery is not intended to enable the Plaintiff alone to acquire possession, but to exclude the Defendant’s unlawful exclusive possession, and that the Plaintiff must make the delivered co-owned property available for joint use by the co-owners, including the Defendant. This, in the sense that the final objective is a state in which the co-owners jointly possess the co-owned property, is no different from the majority opinion, which seeks to achieve joint possession by excluding only the Defendant’s exclusive possession through a claim for removal of interference. The difference is that Dissent 1 proposes to realize a legal state beyond the right actually held by the Plaintiff (joint possession), namely the Plaintiff’s exclusive possession, and then to return the excess to the Defendant voluntarily in order to achieve the originally to-be-realized state (joint possession), whereas the majority opinion aims to achieve the state of joint possession directly, without the intermediate process of the Plaintiff’s exclusive possession.\\n\\nThe result of a delivery judgment and execution ends with realizing the Plaintiff’s exclusive possession, and there is no guarantee, as Dissent 1 expects, that the Plaintiff will then provide it to the other co-owners and thereby lead to joint possession. The Plaintiff is not an execution agency, and therefore there is no way to compel, as part of execution, the Plaintiff first to receive delivery of the co-owned property and then provide it to all co-owners.\\n\\nThere is no reason to create a state exceeding what is necessary when the unlawful current state (the Defendant’s exclusive possession) can be directly transformed into the lawful state that should ultimately be achieved (joint possession) through claims for injunction against interference. Dissent 1 says this is necessary to exclude the Defendant’s exclusive possession. This means permitting removal of interference not by requiring the Plaintiff to specify and seek prohibition of concrete acts interfering with joint possession and use, but by allowing removal of interference through a method that takes away from the Defendant any possession or use of the co-owned property. However, it is clear that this exceeds the scope of lawful removal of interference and infringes the Defendant’s possessory authority.\\n\\n(4) Dissent 1 criticizes indirect compulsion, the method of enforcing a claim for injunction against interference, as being less effective than direct execution. However, a claim may not be granted beyond the right recognized to the rights holder merely for convenience in compulsory execution. Even though the Defendant’s exclusive possession can be dissolved and a state in which the Plaintiff and Defendant can jointly possess and use the land can be created through an injunction against interference, the land cannot be delivered to the Plaintiff merely for the Plaintiff’s convenience in execution.\\n\\nMeanwhile, as noted above, there are many cases where merely removing above-ground objects interfering with the Plaintiff’s joint possession, which can be executed by substitute execution, is enough to dissolve the Defendant’s exclusive possession. Considering that the court can set an appropriate amount as indirect compulsion money to compel the Defendant’s performance of obligations in connection with claims for injunction against interference, and can impose repeated monetary obligations for each violation if the Defendant’s breach continues, indirect compulsion cannot be said to be less effective than direct execution.\\n\\nRather, in the case of direct execution, even after delivery has been executed, the Defendant may again invade the Plaintiff’s possession, but since the enforceability of the delivery judgment has already ended with the completion of compulsory execution, in such a case the Plaintiff cannot again receive delivery of the co-owned property on the basis of that delivery judgment.\\n\\nC. What is the basis for a minority share-right holder to seek delivery of the co-owned property against a third party who is not a co-owner?\\nDissent 1 says that the majority opinion is contradictory because, while it holds that the Plaintiff may bring both a claim for removal of interference and a claim for delivery against a third party who is not a co-owner, it says that as against a co-owner only a claim for removal of interference may be brought and no claim for delivery may be brought.\\n\\nWhere a third party unlawfully possesses the co-owned property, the Plaintiff is the owner, more precisely the co-ownership share-right holder, and because the Plaintiff’s share right extends to the entirety of the co-owned property, the Plaintiff may bring a claim for delivery to exclude the third party and possess the property himself or herself. The third party has no legal basis to possess the thing and therefore cannot refuse the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery.\\n\\nHowever, the case is different where the Defendant possesses a thing co-owned by the Plaintiff and the Defendant. In that case, absent a decision concerning the management of the co-owned property, the Plaintiff has no legal basis to demand against the Defendant that the Defendant be excluded and that only the Plaintiff possess the thing. Because the Defendant, like the Plaintiff, has legal basis as a co-owner to possess the thing, the Defendant may refuse the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery. Ultimately, in litigation between co-owners, only a claim in the form of removing the Defendant’s exclusive possession and allowing the Plaintiff and the Defendant to jointly possess the co-owned property is possible, and as discussed above, removal of above-ground objects and claims for injunction against interference fall within such claims. Therefore, the criticism in Dissent 1 that there is no basis for treating claims for delivery against third parties differently from claims against co-owners is not valid.\\n\\nD. What is the basis for the Plaintiff’s claim for injunction against interference, and what is its concrete form?\\n(1) Dissent 1 and Dissent 2 say that the claim for injunction against interference described by the majority opinion has no precedent in our litigation and execution practice and no legal basis, and is therefore impossible. However, since both the Plaintiff and the Defendant have the right to jointly use and collect fruits from the co-owned property, the Plaintiff may seek removal of interference or an injunction against interference in order to place the co-owned property in a state of joint possession with the Defendant. Such an interpretation can sufficiently be derived, as noted above, from the essence of the co-ownership share right, the basic legal principles of the co-ownership relationship, and the provisions governing the co-owners’ rights of use and profit in the co-owned property (Article 263 of the Civil Act). This conclusion is also justified in view of the substantive-law nature of the right of use and profit in co-owned property and the need to operate it so that it can be realized.\\n\\nIn our practice, the aspect of compelling execution by seeking performance of affirmative and negative obligations, such as prohibition of interference and removal of the result of a violating act, is easily found. Precedents have recognized claims for injunction against interference and their compulsory execution where necessary to preserve rights, such as injunction against interference with passage based on a right of way, injunction against infringement based on copyright, and injunction against construction on the ground of interference with daily life. The reason there had been no practical examples of such claims being granted between co-owners was that the existing precedents allowed claims for delivery between co-owners, so the Plaintiff had no need to bring a claim in this form.\\n\\n(2) We will examine claims for injunction against interference between co-owners in somewhat more concrete terms. Since the manner in which the Defendant exclusively possesses and uses the co-owned property differs from case to case and is diverse, the content of the acts whose prohibition the Plaintiff seeks must also differ accordingly. In the complaint, the Plaintiff must specifically identify the Defendant’s actual interfering acts (including acts likely to be committed by the Defendant) and seek prohibition of such acts, or, if there are results caused by such interfering acts, specifically identify those results and seek their removal.
