The title trustor may, by subrogating the seller, exercise the claim for substitute performance concerning the proceeds from disposition or compensation against the title trustee, and may also exercise the seller’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment. Depending on the degree of negligence of the title trustor or the seller, the compensation for loss may not be sufficient; however, this is in part attributable to the title trustor’s own conduct and cannot necessarily be regarded as unjust. In this respect, the majority opinion, which proceeds on the premise that the title trustor cannot seek return of the purchase price from the seller or claim damages arising from the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership, but must instead receive the full amount of the proceeds from disposition or compensation, etc. from the title trustee, is not free from the criticism that it excessively protects the title trustor.\\n\\n6) It is contrary to the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act to conclude that the seller bears no fault.\\nA) The majority opinion states that if the seller transferred the registration title to the title trustee at the title trustor’s request, it is difficult to find fault on the part of the seller regarding the conclusion or performance of the sales contract, or even if the seller is at fault, the title trustor cannot seek return of the purchase price from the seller or claim damages arising from impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership; based on this premise, it says that the title trustor and title trustee must directly adjust their interests through restitution of unjust enrichment. The cited Supreme Court Decision 2001DA61654 also held, in a title trust relationship created before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, that in a case where the title trustor, by subrogating the seller, claimed damages equal to the proceeds from disposition against the title trustee, “because there is no fault on the part of the seller in the impossibility of performance, and the title trustor cannot, in good faith, seek return of the purchase price from the seller or require the seller to complete transfer registration of ownership in the title trustor’s name, the seller’s claim for damages against the title trustee is not recognized,” thereby ruling that the seller bears no responsibility.\\n\\nB) However, such reasoning can no longer be applied after the Real Name Registration Act, which treats the title trust agreement as void ab initio. As noted by the majority opinion, the Real Name Registration Act is a statute enacted for the purpose of ensuring that registration is made in the name of the actual right holder so as to conform to the substantive rights relationship regarding changes in real rights, including ownership of real estate. This Act was enacted on 1995. 3. 30. and has been in force for approximately 25 years; during that time it has become widely known that if real estate is not registered in the name of the actual right holder, the registration is void and title trust relationships violating the Act are not legally protected and are subject to criminal punishment, as well as penalty surcharges and enforcement fines. In such a situation, the act of a seller who, at the request of the title trustor, cooperates with or acquiesces in the title trust relationship of the title trustor and transfers the registration title to the title trustee is to disregard the Real Name Registration Act and assist the title trustor’s unlawful conduct. Even so, to hold that the seller bears no fault or no liability for impossibility of performance merely because the seller complied with the title trustor’s request is to render the Real Name Registration Act powerless and is an interpretation of law that departs from the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act to effect registration in the name of the actual right holder.\\n\\n7) Recognizing a direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment by the title trustor against the title trustee when there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc. is also contrary to the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act.\\nWhere, in a three-party registered title trust, ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., it is definitively established, pursuant to the third-party protection provision in Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act, that the title trustor cannot receive a transfer of ownership of the real estate. This third-party protection provision has the aspect of limiting the achievement of the Real Name Registration Act’s purpose, namely to have registration made in the name of the actual right holder, for the protection of third parties who relied on the appearance formed by the title trust agreement and for the safety of transactions. Meanwhile, the Real Name Registration Act contains no provision for adjusting the interests among the title trustor, title trustee, and seller where, as above, the trust real estate has been transferred to a third party and registration in the name of the actual right holder has become impossible; thus, it is necessary to realize the purpose and intent of the Act through interpretation of law. However, if, as the majority opinion holds, the title trustor may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, it creates an effect as if the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee were valid, enabling the title trustor to easily recover the purchase price that he/she invested once transfer of registration in his/her own name has become impossible. This is an interpretation that, although the purpose of the law is to have the title trustor register ownership in his/her own name as the actual right holder, at the same time does not allow a direct transfer of ownership registration concerning the real estate from the title trustee to the title trustor, yet when that is violated, allows direct recovery of the resulting loss; it directly contradicts the position of the Real Name Registration Act, which renders the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights void.\\n\\n8) The majority opinion primarily relies on the view that recognizing a direct restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustee who obtained the unjust benefit and the title trustor who suffered property loss conforms to the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests. However, this perspective of the majority opinion risks obscuring the requirements for the establishment of a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment and excessively expanding the scope in which such a claim may be recognized.\\nA) The ideals of fairness and justice, which are cited as the purpose of the unjust enrichment restitution system, are highly abstract concepts. A claim for restitution of unjust enrichment is not a claim whose effect arises according to a particular juristic act; it is a statutory claim that arises according to the requirements prescribed by law. The requirements of “benefit without legal cause” and “loss resulting therefrom” under Article 741 of the Civil Act are not univocal concepts, and therefore it is not easy in individual cases to determine whether the requirements for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment are satisfied. If a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment is recognized merely because recognizing a restitution relationship between the person who suffered property loss and the person who obtained the benefit conforms to the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests, then it becomes difficult to determine in which cases a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment may be recognized.\\nB) Let us assume a case where A enters into a contract to purchase a movable owned by B from B, pays the full purchase price to B, but has not taken delivery, and C, who incidentally acquires possession of B’s movable, sells it to D and transfers possession as well, so that D acquires the movable from B in good faith. In such a case, A may rescind the sales contract and demand return of the purchase price from B by way of restoration, and B may demand from C the return as unjust enrichment of the consideration for the disposition of the movable owned by B. However, if one were to consider that a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment may be recognized on the ground that it accords with the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests, then A’s direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against C would also become possible. Yet in practice, such a direct claim by A against C is rarely granted, because this is regarded merely as an infringement of a claim right and not an infringement of an exclusive real right.\\nAs another example, suppose contracts are separately concluded whereby A sells real estate owned by A to B, and B resells it to C, with the purchase price paid sequentially from C to B and from B to A, but before the transfer registration of ownership is made, A sells the real estate to D and completes transfer registration of ownership in D’s name. In such a case, because the obligation to register transfer of ownership under the contract between A and B and under the contract between B and C becomes impossible to perform, B and C, who are creditors under each respective contract, will rescind the respective sales contracts and seek restoration from A and B, who are the other parties to those contracts, for the respective purchase prices. Even in such a case, if one were to consider that a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment may be recognized on the ground that it accords with the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests, then C could also directly seek from A restitution of unjust enrichment equal to the consideration for A’s disposition of the real estate, disregarding the concrete contractual relationships between A and B and between B and C. Yet even in such a case, it is rare in practice for C’s claim to be granted.\\nC) In order to recognize a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment in a particular case, the underlying substantive legal relationship between the restitution creditor and the restitution obligor, namely the existence of performance without legal cause, expenditure of costs, or exclusive infringement of rights, must be premised. The same applies even where there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a three-party registered title trust. A restitution relationship of unjust enrichment should be recognized between the seller, whose ownership has been infringed, and the title trustee, who thereby obtained a benefit such as proceeds from disposition or compensation; it cannot be recognized between the title trustor and the title trustee, who have no direct legal relationship, merely on the abstract ground that doing so conforms to the ideals of fairness and justice or simplifies the adjustment of interests.\\nD) The Supreme Court has, in cases involving the intertwined acquisition of benefits and loss of rights among multiple parties, denied restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that the parties are not direct parties to the contract or not parties to the return of performance, etc. Supreme Court Decision of 2005. 7. 22., 2005DA7566, 7573 held that where a contract constituting the legal relationship between the promisor and the stipulator in a contract for the benefit of a third party (the so-called basic relationship) is rescinded, the settlement of that contractual relationship must be made between the promisor and the stipulator, who are the parties to the contract; therefore, absent special circumstances, even if the promisor has already performed to the third party, the promisor cannot seek return from the third party by relying on rescission or unjust enrichment. Supreme Court Decision of 2003. 12. 26., 2001DA46730 held that where one party to a contract, at the direction of the counterparty, etc., shortens the performance process and directly performs to a third party who has another contractual relationship with the counterparty, the performance not only constitutes performance by the contractual party to the counterparty but also constitutes performance by the counterparty to the third party, and therefore the one party to the contract cannot, against the third party, claim restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that the third party received performance without legal cause. According to such precedents, restitution of unjust enrichment should also be denied in this case.\\n\\n9) With the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act and the resulting invalidity of title trust agreements, the Supreme Court has, in a line of decisions, sequentially changed prior holdings based on legal relationships formed between the title trustor and the title trustee as substantive owner in title trusts created before the Real Name Registration Act in a manner consistent with the legal principles of the Real Name Registration Act. Specifically, the title trustor cannot, against the title trustee, (1) demand transfer registration of ownership concerning the real estate itself on the ground of restitution of unjust enrichment (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2008. 11. 27., 2008DA55290, 55306, etc.); (2) demand transfer registration of ownership on the ground of termination of the title trust (see Supreme Court Decisions of 1999. 1. 26., 98DA1027; 2008. 10. 23., 2008DA43693, etc.); or (3) demand return of the real estate or cancellation of the transfer registration of ownership on the ground of an agreement to return the real estate (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2006. 11. 9., 2006DA35117; 2015. 9. 10., 2013DA55300, etc.). Further, in a three-party registered title trust, because the title trustor is not the owner of the real estate and there is no relationship of entrustment and trust between the title trustor and the title trustee, the title trustee cannot be said to be in custody of the title trustor’s property, and therefore even if the title trustee disposes of the real estate without authorization, embezzlement is not established in relation to the title trustor (see Supreme Court Decision of 2016. 5. 19., 2014DO6992, en banc, etc.).\\nThese legal principles should be applied consistently to the adjustment of interests among the title trustor, title trustee, and seller arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and accordingly the prior decisions cited by the majority opinion should be changed.\\n\\nb. The case where the title trustee has established a mortgage over the real estate\\nIn a three-party registered title trust, when the title trustee establishes a mortgage over the trust real estate, the legal relationship among the title trustor, title trustee, and seller is basically the same as the case noted above where ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\nIf the title trustee establishes a mortgage over the real estate in favor of a third party, that third party validly acquires the mortgage (Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act). Even if the seller regains title by transfer registration of ownership based on restoration of the true title concerning the real estate, the seller obtains ownership burdened with the mortgage. Thus, the act of the title trustee, who is merely a person holding the title to ownership without having any right in the real estate, in establishing a mortgage in favor of a third party over the real estate constitutes an infringement of the seller’s ownership, and the title trustee bears an obligation to return the benefit obtained through the establishment of the mortgage to the seller as unjust enrichment through infringement or an obligation to compensate damages arising from tort.\\nOrdinarily, in a sales contract, the seller bears the obligation to effect transfer registration of complete ownership free from restrictions or burdens on the subject matter of sale (see Supreme Court Decision of 2000. 11. 28., 2000DA8533, etc.). The same applies in the relationship between the title trustor and the seller in a three-party registered title trust. The fact that the title trustee has established a mortgage over the real estate does not alter this. As a rule, the seller bears toward the title trustor the obligation to transfer ownership of the trust real estate free of any security. If the seller transferred ownership of the real estate to the title trustor without cancelling the mortgage established by the title trustee, this constitutes non-performance of the obligation under the sales contract and renders the seller liable to the title trustor for damages. However, the extent to which the seller may be held liable for breach of contract may vary depending on the individual case.\\nFurthermore, because the title trustor, in relation to the seller, is merely in the position of holding a claim for transfer registration of ownership concerning the real estate under the sales contract and does not own the real estate, the title trustor’s rights are not infringed by the title trustee’s act of establishing a mortgage over the real estate.\\nTherefore, the title trustee bears an obligation to the seller to return unjust enrichment or compensate damages, and does not bear an obligation to return unjust enrichment to the title trustor.\\n\\nc. Conclusion in this case\\nThe court below did not accept the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to the amount of the secured debt of the mortgage at issue, on the ground that the loss arising from the establishment of the mortgage at issue belongs to the Non-party, the seller of the real estate at issue, and that the Plaintiff suffers no loss. The court below’s determination is correct. The court below’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, of violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence without fully examining the necessary matters, or misapprehending the law on unjust enrichment or violating the duty to explain, thereby affecting the judgment. The Plaintiff’s appeal on this point should be dismissed.\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I cannot concur with the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplementary opinion of Justice Jo Jae-yeon concurring with the majority opinion\\na. The purpose of the Real Name Registration Act\\nThe Real Name Registration Act regulates title trust agreements and changes in real rights thereunder on the premise that ownership of real estate is attributed to the actual right holder (see Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2019. 6. 20., 2013DA218156).\\nThat is, the Real Name Registration Act provides that title trust agreements and changes in real rights thereunder are void (Article 4(1) and (2)), while imposing penalty surcharges on the title trustor as a sanction for violation and obligating the title trustor to register the real rights concerning the title-trusted real estate under his/her own name without delay, and providing that if this is violated, enforcement fines may be imposed in addition to penalty surcharges (Article 5(1)(1), Article 6). Because the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights are void, the real rights in the real estate remain with the previous registered title holder regardless of the registration; therefore, the title trustor may exercise rights such as restoration of the registration based on a legal relationship other than the title trust agreement, and further bears the obligation to eliminate the discrepancy between the registration title of the real estate and the substantive rights relationship.\\nIn this way, while the Real Name Registration Act renders void the changes in real rights made through a title trust agreement and the resulting registration, it does not prohibit the title trustor from exercising rights such as restoration of the registration based on another legal relationship; rather, it merely imposes administrative sanctions or criminal penalties on the title trustor to indirectly compel the elimination of the discrepancy between the registration title and the substantive rights relationship and thereby eliminate the unlawful state and secure the effectiveness of the Real Name Registration Act (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2003. 11. 27., 2003DA41722; 2016. 6. 28., 2014DU6456; 2019. 6. 20., 2013DA218156, en banc, etc.). It does not contain any provision that causes the title trustor to lose rights concerning the title-trusted real estate and thereby deprive the title trustor of property benefits therefrom or allow the title trustee to retain property benefits related to the title-trusted real estate. Meanwhile, although the Real Name Registration Act imposes administrative sanctions and criminal penalties on the title trustor and title trustee, it does not directly impose administrative sanctions on the seller, who is the previous registered title holder, save for the separate question of general criminal liability such as aiding and abetting a violation of the Real Name Registration Act.\\n\\nb. The meaning of the restitution system of unjust enrichment\\nThe restitution system of unjust enrichment is a system that, where the property benefit of the beneficiary lacks legal cause, imposes on the beneficiary an obligation of return based on the ideals of fairness and justice (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2008. 3. 13., 2006DA53733, 53740, etc.). It is a system that resolves the inconsistency arising where, in a particular relationship between parties, a certain change in property value occurs and appears generally and formally to be proper, but, from a relative and substantive perspective, the change in property value among the parties conflicts with the ideal of fairness, another ideal of law, by ordering return of the value from the acquirer of the property value (see Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2015. 6. 25., 2014DA5531). In adjusting such improper changes in property value, categorizing unjust enrichment according to substance and determining whether unjust enrichment has been established may be a useful tool for concretely and clearly grasping the legal relationships concerning unjust enrichment. However, in real legal relationships, unjust enrichment may manifest in various forms based on diverse causes, and among them there may be cases that do not fall within a certain category of unjust enrichment or for which it is not appropriate to apply the standards for determining categories of unjust enrichment as they are. Therefore, ultimately, whether unjust enrichment is established and the rights and duties regarding restitution of unjust enrichment must be determined according to the ideals of justice and fairness in the concrete case, and it is not the case that issues of unjust enrichment should be resolved only within the framework of categorized unjust enrichment.\\n\\nc. Supplement to the majority opinion and rebuttal of the dissenting opinion\\n1) A restitution relationship of unjust enrichment may also arise between the title trustor and the title trustee.\\nA) Where, after the Real Name Registration Act came into force, a title trust agreement and registration pursuant thereto are effected, it may be said that, under Article 4(1) and (2) of the Real Name Registration Act, the changes in real rights made by the title trust agreement and the registration pursuant thereto are void, and therefore no legal relationship regarding the trust real estate exists between the title trustor and the title trustee. However, even in such a case, the title trustor may realize transfer registration of ownership in his/her own name concerning the trust real estate through the valid sales contract. Yet if the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs, then, in conjunction with Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act, a third party validly acquires the real rights concerning the trust real estate, and consequently the registration in the name of the actual right holder, which the Real Name Registration Act aims to achieve, cannot be realized or becomes restricted. Before the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title trustor could realize his/her registration title through the seller, but once the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs, a “new event” arises in relation to the ownership attribution of the trust real estate, namely the third party’s acquisition of ownership. Due to such “new event,” the purpose of the Real Name Registration Act to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder through the seller can no longer be achieved, and the rights and obligations existing before the occurrence of that event necessarily change. Since this change in legal relationships stems from the title trust agreement entered into between the title trustor and the title trustee, a legal relationship also arises between the title trustor and the title trustee that requires adjustment of the transfer of property value.\\nBecause the Real Name Registration Act aims to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder of real estate, and not to deprive the title trustor of property rights, once realization of registration in the name of the actual right holder becomes impossible due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act, recognizing a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee cannot be equated with treating as valid the title trust agreement and the registration arising therefrom, which are void under the Real Name Registration Act. Even after reaching the stage where the purpose of the Real Name Registration Act can no longer be achieved, there is no need to deny, on the ground of the invalidity of the title trust agreement, the legal relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee that has emerged through the occurrence of the “new event.”\\nB) Precedents hold that, where due to the third-party protection provision a person without title disposes of property and the original right holder loses the right, the benefit obtained by the person without title must be returned to the original right holder as unjust enrichment through infringement. This legal principle was declared in a case where the original right holder received no consideration in the process by which the person without title became able to dispose of the real estate at issue. It should not be mechanically applied to cases such as a three-party registered title trust, where the original owner, namely the seller, loses ownership due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. but, through the sales contract with the title trustor, receives and retains the purchase price, and where, among multiple parties, acquisition of benefit and loss of rights are closely intertwined. As noted above, while categorization of unjust enrichment can be useful in concretely and clearly grasping the rights relationships surrounding restitution of unjust enrichment, considering the purpose of the restitution system and the diverse factual relationships of real life, it is not appropriate to grasp the establishment of unjust enrichment and the rights relationships regarding restitution only within a fixed category.\\nC) The dissenting opinion says that because the requirements for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment are abstract concepts and it is not easy to determine in individual cases whether such requirements are met, in order to recognize a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment there must be, as a premise, a substantive rights relationship serving as the basis between the restitution creditor and the restitution obligor, namely performance without legal cause, expenditure of costs, or exclusive infringement of rights, and the same applies even when there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a three-party registered title trust. However, the cases cited by the dissenting opinion as examples in this part concern situations unrelated to each other, namely a buyer who purchased a thing from the original owner and a person who infringed the original owner’s ownership, and the prior precedents cited by the dissenting opinion concern cases where performance was made to a third party under a contract for the benefit of a third party or by instruction to make a shortened performance. By contrast, a three-party registered title trust case is one in which, due to the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee and the registration pursuant thereto, a legal relationship concerning the registration title of the trust real estate has been formed among the title trustor, title trustee, and seller, and that relationship changes due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.; thus it differs from the examples cited in the dissenting opinion and is not the same as the cases cited by the dissenting opinion. Therefore, it cannot be said that because there is a similarity merely in the existence of a legal relationship among multiple parties concerning a certain object or performance, the conclusion concerning the establishment of restitution of unjust enrichment must also be the same. The change in legal relationships arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a three-party registered title trust is more complex than that arising merely from a person without title’s disposition act; and because it stems from a title trust agreement and registration that are legally void, the relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee that caused such a situation cannot be ignored.\\n\\n2) Where there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title trustee’s benefit without legal cause and the resulting loss to the title trustor are recognized, and the requirements for the establishment of the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment are satisfied.\\nA) Due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act, the title trustee, though not the owner, obtains a benefit without legal cause, such as the proceeds from disposition or compensation.\\nB) Before the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs, the seller, as the owner of the trust real estate, may demand restoration of the title from the title trustee; however, where the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs, the seller loses ownership of the trust real estate. Yet at the same time, the seller is released from the obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate, and further, while retaining the purchase price received under the sales contract, either does not bear liability for damages arising from impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership or, at the very least, the title trustor cannot, in good faith, seek return of the purchase price from the seller or demand performance of the transfer registration of ownership. The reasons are as follows.\\n(1) The seller bears toward the title trustor the obligation to register transfer of ownership under the sales contract, but where the obligation to register transfer of ownership becomes impossible to perform due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., absent special circumstances, it is difficult to find fault on the part of the seller for such impossibility. This is because, in the sequence of the conclusion of the sales contract between the seller and the title trustor, the transfer registration of ownership in the title trustee’s name at the title trustor’s request, and the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller cannot be said to have breached the duty of care owed under the sales contract to the buyer, namely the “title trustor.”\\nMeanwhile, the title trustor, who is the counterparty to the duty to register transfer of ownership, actively intended the title trust agreement and registration thereunder prohibited by the Real Name Registration Act, arranged the title trustee, entered into the sales contract with the seller, and caused the seller and the title trustee to produce a registration that did not conform to the substantive relationship; furthermore, even after that, the title trustor could have avoided the impossibility of performance resulting from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. by subrogating the seller, cancelling the transfer registration of ownership in the title trustee’s name and transferring ownership registration into the title trustor’s own name, but neglected to do so.\\n(2) As above, since the seller cannot be found at fault for the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership, and this may be regarded as a case in which performance became impossible due to a cause attributable to the creditor, namely the title trustor, the seller may retain the purchase price under Article 538(1) of the Civil Act and does not bear liability to the title trustor for damages arising from impossibility of performance. Even if the seller’s cooperation in violating the Real Name Registration Act is viewed as negligence in relation to the impossibility of performance, the title trustor’s negligence regarding the impossibility of performance, as noted above, is substantially heavier and greater in content and degree of breach of duty of care than that of the seller; therefore, it is not permissible in good faith for the title trustor to argue that the seller also bears fault for the impossibility of performance and seek return of the purchase price or claim damages arising from the impossibility of performance.\\nSupreme Court Decisions of 2011. 9. 8., 2009DA49193, 49209, by recognizing the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, held that the trial court’s reasoning—that the title trustor could demand from the title trustee payment of compensation concerning the trust real estate in order to preserve the right that arose due to the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership toward the seller—was not proper, thereby deciding on the premise that the title trustor does not have any right against the seller arising from the impossibility of performance of the transfer registration of ownership. Supreme Court Decisions of 2015. 9. 10., 2015DA207235, and 2019. 7. 25., 2019DA203811, 203828, concerning cases where a title trust agreement and registration pursuant thereto were made after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, may be seen as having repeatedly confirmed that the title trustor cannot exercise any right against the seller for impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership by holding that the legal principle of Supreme Court Decisions 2009DA49193, 49209 likewise applies to cases where, after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, a three-party title trust agreement is made and registration pursuant thereto is completed.\\n\\nC) Even though the seller received the purchase price from the title trustor, if due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title trustor becomes impossible to perform, the seller may refuse return of the purchase price and does not bear liability for damages arising from impossibility of performance; therefore, the seller cannot be said to suffer economic loss due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. Further, the title trustor, although paying the purchase price to the seller on the basis of the sales contract, becomes unable to receive transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and also cannot obtain relief by claiming return of the purchase price or damages against the seller for the impossibility of performance; therefore, the title trustor can be said to have suffered direct loss due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n\\nD) In this way, because the title trustee, due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act, obtained a benefit equivalent to the consideration for disposition of the real estate and thereby caused the title trustor to lose the right to acquire ownership of the real estate, the requirements for the establishment of the title trustee’s restitution obligation for unjust enrichment toward the title trustor are satisfied where there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc. The claim for restitution of unjust enrichment concerning the benefit obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. belongs to the title trustor.\\n\\n3) Recognizing the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee accords with the principle of self-responsibility, which imposes on the title trustor responsibility for his/her own decision-making, and is also a solution that does not contravene the principle of fairness in the process of adjusting interests.\\nA) The title trustor should bear responsibility for his/her own decision-making, because the title trustor proceeded, by his/her own decision, with arranging the title trustee, concluding the title trust agreement, entering into the sales contract with the seller, and transferring the registration pursuant to the title trust agreement.\\nHowever, if, as in the dissenting opinion, the seller exercises a claim for damages or restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, and the title trustor obtains relief by exercising the right of rescission against the seller and claiming return of the purchase price by way of restoration or damages arising from breach of contract, then the risk arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and even the risk of the title trustee’s insolvency is imposed on the seller, thereby shifting to the seller the risk that should be borne by the title trustor, who took the lead in creating the state of violation of the Real Name Registration Act.\\n\\nB) Where there are multiple parties surrounding a benefit without legal cause, in determining how to allocate the rights and obligations of restitution of unjust enrichment among the parties, the legal defenses and degree of risk borne by the parties in the original legal relationship should not differ, and one should not allow them to retain more benefits than before or to be deprived of rights.\\nIn adjusting the interests arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a three-party registered title trust, even if the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is recognized, the legal defenses recognized in the prior legal relationship before the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. are not deprived from the title trustor, title trustee, or seller, nor is additional risk imposed on them.\\nBy contrast, if the title trustor claims damages for breach of contract against the seller, it may be assumed that, due to contributory negligence or other reasons, the amount the title trustor can receive from the seller becomes less than the purchase price retained by the seller. This would allow the seller to retain an unexpected benefit due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., while depriving the title trustor of economic benefit, which is not consistent with the ideals of fairness or the purpose of the Real Name Registration Act.\\n\\nd. Subconclusion\\nRecognizing the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, as the majority opinion does, is by no means intended to protect the title trustor in a three-party registered title trust relationship. The Real Name Registration Act renders void the changes in real rights concerning real estate made through a title trust agreement and the registration pursuant thereto, while, where there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc., it provides a third-party protection provision so that changes in real rights concerning real estate are validly effected. Nevertheless, because the Real Name Registration Act does not provide any rule regarding the changes in rights and obligations arising therefrom, the problem of adjusting interests arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. ultimately must be resolved according to the legal principles of restitution of unjust enrichment. Since the Real Name Registration Act did not permit the title trustee to retain the proceeds from disposition of the trust real estate, the question of return of that benefit is most directly and reasonably resolved between the parties to the title trust agreement, which was the original cause of the improper change in property value between the parties. Moreover, as noted above, the requirements for the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee are satisfied, so there is no need to draw the seller, who acquired the purchase price and performed obligations under the sales contract, back into the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment.\\nFor these reasons, I supplement the grounds of the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplementary opinion of Justices Park Jeong-hwa and No Tae-ak to the dissenting opinion\\na. Can a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment be recognized between the title trustor and the title trustee in a title trust agreement rendered void by the Real Name Registration Act?\\n1) The majority opinion and the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion state that the Real Name Registration Act aims at realizing registration in the name of the actual right holder of the trust real estate, and while rendering void changes in real rights made through a title trust agreement and the registration pursuant thereto, does not prohibit the title trustor from exercising rights such as restoration of the registration based on another legal relationship, and does not deprive the title trustor of property benefits by extinguishing the title trustor’s rights concerning the trust real estate.\\nThe dissenting opinion also has no reason to object to the proposition that the Real Name Registration Act, while treating the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights as void, does not prohibit the title trustor from exercising rights such as restoration of the registration based on another legal relationship, and does not deprive the title trustor of property benefits.\\nHowever, the dissenting opinion differs from the majority opinion in how to adjust the title trustor’s restoration of the registration as the actual right holder and the corresponding property interests. That is, the dissenting opinion views the “other legal relationship” that enables the title trustor’s exercise of rights such as restoration of the registration, as stated in the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion, as the “sales contract between the title trustor and the seller,” and insists that, based on the legal effects arising therefrom, all matters—whether restoration of rights in the name of the actual right holder or adjustment of interests in respect of the transformed object—must be handled consistently and uniformly.\\nBy contrast, the majority opinion states that the legal effects based on the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller apply only where the trust real estate remains in the title trustee’s name, and that when the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. causes a third party to acquire the trust real estate, interests may be adjusted not according to the effects of that contract but according to the restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee.\\n\\n2) Since the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller is valid, it must continue until that contract terminates. There is only a difference in the legal effects depending on whether performance of the obligation is possible or impossible; the occurrence of a cause making performance impossible in a valid sales contract does not convert it into a juristic act void for lack of cause. Yet the majority opinion, upon the occurrence of a cause of impossibility of performance while the sales contract remains in force, seeks to resolve the matter by bringing in, while leaving unchanged the legal relationship based on the still-valid sales contract, the separate title trust agreement that is void under the Real Name Registration Act and excluding the seller, who is a party to the sales contract, thereby framing the matter as a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee.\\n\\n3) From the perspective of the dissenting opinion, the third party’s acquisition of ownership due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., namely the “new event” mentioned in the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion, is merely a cause of impossibility of performance in the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller, and therefore is not an element affecting the legal relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee under the title trust agreement, which has been void from the outset.\\nThe dissenting opinion views the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller as not yet terminated until the seller has fully performed his/her obligations, and that, even if a cause of impossibility of performance arises in the process, the parties must resolve the issue according to the original sales contract. In other words, whether performance of the debt is possible or impossible, the legal interpretation must consistently treat the seller as the party.\\n\\nb. From this perspective, I will specifically rebut the majority opinion and its supplementary opinion and supplement the grounds of the dissenting opinion.\\n1) The title trustor is not a person entitled to a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment.\\nThe title trustor does not have a legitimate right to claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee. The title trustor is not a person who acquired ownership, a real right, but merely holds against the seller a claim for transfer registration of ownership arising from the sale, and this right of the title trustor does not change merely because a third party acquires the trust real estate and the seller’s performance of its debt becomes impossible.\\nSupreme Court Decisions of 2008. 11. 27., 2008DA55290, 55306, cited in the dissenting opinion, held that in a three-party registered title trust the title trustor cannot directly seek transfer registration against the title trustee, the nominal holder of a void registration, and cannot seek transfer registration of ownership on the ground of restitution of unjust enrichment, citing as the basis that the title trustor is not the owner but merely has a claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller. In light of that reasoning, even when a third party acquires ownership due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title trustor is not the owner and therefore should not be able to seek against the title trustee restitution of the proceeds from disposition of the real estate, etc. as unjust enrichment.\\n\\n2) The majority opinion is no different from recognizing the title trust agreement as valid.\\nA) The supplementary opinion to the majority opinion states that, in a three-party registered title trust, when the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee can be recognized because in a three-party registered title trust acquisition of benefit and loss of rights are closely related among the parties, and that this situation presents special circumstances different from other cases of disposition by a person without title, etc. In the end, it says that the relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee cannot be considered apart from one another.\\nHowever, Article 4(1) and the main text of Article 4(2) of the Real Name Registration Act clearly state that title trust agreements and the resulting changes in real rights are void, and precedents also hold, in light of the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act, that the delegation agreement for sale of real estate incidental to a title trust agreement, and the agreement to return title-trusted real estate and its proceeds from disposition premised on a title trust agreement, are also void (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2006. 11. 9., 2006DA35117; 2015. 9. 10., 2013DA55300, etc.). Even in a three-party registered title trust, the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee is void, and the legal relationship should be analyzed on the premise that no legal relationship exists between them; only then does the result conform to the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act. The fact that precedents do not allow the title trustor, in a three-party registered title trust, to directly claim transfer registration of ownership concerning the real estate against the title trustee, but instead require the title trustor to subrogate the seller and claim cancellation of the transfer registration of ownership against the title trustee or transfer registration of ownership based on restoration of the true title registration, and that they hold that embezzlement is not established in relation to the title trustor even if the title trustee disposes of the real estate without authorization, all stem from the premise that the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee is void and that there is no legal relationship between them.\\n\\nB) So long as the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee is void, the legal relationship between the title trustor and the seller and the legal relationship between the seller and the title trustee are each independent and separate legal relationships and cannot affect each other. Where the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., that affects only, separately, the legal relationship between the title trustor and the seller, and the legal relationship between the seller and the title trustee. Accordingly, between the title trustee and the seller, the issue of restitution of unjust enrichment arises from the title trustee’s infringement of the seller’s ownership, and between the title trustor and the seller, the issue of contractual non-performance arises from the seller’s inability to perform the obligations under the sales contract. Therefore, in a case where the title trustee disposes of the real estate in a three-party registered title trust, the structure is the same as the case addressed in Supreme Court Decision of 2011. 6. 10., 2010DA40239, where a person without title disposed of another’s right to a third party and the original right holder lost the right due to the protection provision for a good-faith third party. Just as a person without title who must return the right to the true right holder must return to the true right holder the consideration for the disposition as unjust enrichment when the right is lost by disposing of the right to a third party, so too the title trustee bears responsibility to return to the seller, the true owner of the real estate, the consideration for the disposition, etc.\\n\\nC) Recognizing a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment merely because the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a three-party registered title trust causes the real estate to be transferred to a third party, as the majority opinion does, is tantamount to creating a new legal relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee. And the basis for such recognition must ultimately be understood as the existence of a valid title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee, that is, the validity of the title trust agreement.\\nHowever, precedents after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act have maintained an attitude of denying the premise that a title trust agreement is valid or that legal relationships are formed on that basis. Recognizing the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, as in the majority opinion, not only contradicts this consistent line of precedents but also leads to a result that violates the Real Name Registration Act.\\nD) The supplementary opinion to the majority opinion says that one should not view the restitution relationship of unjust enrichment only within a categorized framework, but should determine it according to the ideals of fairness in the concrete case. There are many cases other than three-party registered title trusts involving intertwined acquisition of benefits and loss of rights among multiple parties, where the question is whether a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment may be recognized. However, in the Supreme Court Decisions of 2003. 12. 26., 2001DA46730; 2005. 7. 22., 2005DA7566, 7573, etc., as noted in the dissenting opinion, restitution of unjust enrichment cannot be recognized merely on the ground that the legal relationship among the multiple parties can be simply resolved or that it may conform to the principles of justice and fairness. Rather, where there is no substantive rights relationship, such as a contract, between the parties that would ground a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment, direct restitution of unjust enrichment is not recognized. Even so, the majority opinion’s attempt to recognize a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee in a three-party registered title trust can only be explained as arising from the view that the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee was valid, despite the denial in the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n3) The majority opinion’s rationale for denying that it is permissible in good faith for the title trustor to seek return of the purchase price from the seller or to demand performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership lacks rational persuasiveness.\\nA) Precedents state, regarding the principle of good faith under the Civil Act, that “the parties to a legal relationship must not exercise rights or perform obligations in a manner that is inequitable or betrays trust in consideration of the other party’s interests; as an abstract norm, in order to deny the exercise of a right on the ground of violation of the principle of good faith, the other party must have conferred trust or, objectively viewed, be in a position where it is justifiable to have trust, and the exercise of the right contrary to that trust must reach a degree that cannot be tolerated in light of the concept of justice; moreover, absent special circumstances, a person who entered into the juristic act while knowing that it violated a statute and was void cannot be said to violate the principle of good faith or the principle of estoppel, or to constitute an abuse of rights, merely because he/she later asserts invalidity on the ground of violation of a mandatory provision” (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2001. 5. 15., 99DA53490, etc.).\\nB) Before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, title trust agreements and the resulting changes in real rights were deemed valid, so if at that time the seller, at the title trustor’s request, transferred the title of ownership to the title trustee, the seller would have trusted that he/she had thereby completed performance of the obligations under the sales contract, and such reliance would have been justified. However, if, after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, one were to say that the title trustor may again demand performance of the obligations under the sales contract from the seller, such as a claim for transfer registration of ownership or return of the purchase price, on the ground that the title trustor failed to regain registration title, then this would undermine the trust already formed in the seller. Accordingly, before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, there was a need to protect the seller’s reliance when the seller transferred the title of ownership to the title trustee pursuant to the title trust agreement. For this reason, Supreme Court Decision of 2002. 3. 15., 2001DA61654 held that if, before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, the seller transferred the title of ownership to the title trustee at the title trustor’s request, it is not permissible in good faith for the title trustor, on account of the failure to register under his/her real name after the statutory grace period had elapsed due to the title trustor’s own fault, to seek return of the purchase price from the seller or to require the seller to complete transfer registration of ownership again in the title trustor’s name.\\nHowever, such legal principle cannot be applied as is after the Real Name Registration Act came into force. After the Real Name Registration Act came into force, it is clear to both the title trustor and the seller that the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights are void. Even if the seller, at the title trustor’s request, transfers the title of ownership to the title trustee, this is void, so ownership of the real estate still remains with the seller, and because the sales contract with the title trustor is valid, the seller should be understood to know that he/she still bears toward the title trustor the obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate. For the same reason, it cannot be said that the seller formed a reliance that all his/her obligations under the sales contract were fully performed by the transfer of title to the title trustee and that he/she will no longer be subjected to claims for performance under the sales contract from the title trustor. Even if the seller had such reliance, it would be contrary to the mandatory provisions of the Real Name Registration Act and cannot be regarded as a justified reliance protected by the principle of good faith under the Civil Act. Therefore, even though there is no circumstance showing that the seller had justified reliance, the title trustor’s claims against the seller under the sales contract cannot be limited on the ground that they violate the principle of good faith.\\n\\nC) Whether the seller has a justified reliance worthy of protection in a three-party registered title trust can be seen more clearly when compared with the seller’s position in a so-called contract title trust. The proviso to Article 4(2) of the Real Name Registration Act provides that where, in a contract to acquire a real right concerning real estate, the title trustee becomes one of the parties and the counterparty does not know that there is a title trust agreement, the changes in real rights pursuant to the title trust agreement are not void. In a contract title trust, an innocent seller would have transferred the title of ownership to the title trustee believing the sales contract to be valid, and this would have formed reliance that he/she had fully performed all obligations under the sales contract. Therefore, the Real Name Registration Act also does not regard those changes in real rights as void in order to protect such reliance of the seller. By contrast, the Real Name Registration Act does not provide, for the seller in a three-party registered title trust, a rule protecting reliance comparable to that for an innocent seller in a contract title trust; rather, there remains the possibility of criminal liability for aiding and abetting a violation of the Real Name Registration Act. This supports the conclusion that a seller who knew of and cooperated with a void title trust agreement has no reliance to protect.\\n\\nD) To conclude, as the majority opinion does, that, based on the principle of good faith, the title trustor’s claim against the seller for return of the purchase price or damages arising from impossibility of performance is uniformly disallowed, not only deprives the title trustor of rights under the sales contract from the outset but may also create legal confusion when resolving concrete cases in the future.\\nThe supplementary opinion to the majority opinion gives as grounds for saying that the title trustor’s claim against the seller for return of the purchase price or damages arising from impossibility of performance is not permissible in good faith the circumstance that the seller bears no fault for the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership caused by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., or, even if the seller is at fault, that the title trustor’s fault in bringing about the three-party registered title trust is substantially heavier than the seller’s.\\nHowever, it is questionable whether, in all three-party registered title trust cases, it can be uniformly concluded that the seller bears no fault or that the title trustor’s fault is much heavier than the seller’s. Let us consider an example. A seller may, to a buyer who hesitates to purchase real estate at a high price because of tax burdens and other expenses, recommend a title trust registration by telling the buyer that costs can be reduced thereby, and may sell the real estate at the desired price. Also, a seller who urgently wishes to sell real estate and cannot find a prospective buyer may, after finding a suitable buyer, if the buyer cannot have ownership transferred into his/her own name or if the title trustor faces difficulty in acquiring ownership due to public-law restrictions on the trust real estate, step in and inform the title trustor of the method of the title trust agreement or actively arrange a title trustee and then recommend that the buyer entrust the registration title to the arranged title trustee. In such cases, can it truly be said that the title trustor is the principal responsible party for actively creating a three-party registered title trust that does not conform to the substantive relationship, and that the seller bears no fault or is substantially less at fault than the title trustor? There can be various circumstances in which a three-party registered title trust relationship is formed. Without examining the concrete circumstances, as the majority opinion does, to conclude that the seller bears no fault or that the title trustor’s fault is much heavier than the seller’s and then to deprive the title trustor of the claim against the seller for return of the purchase price or damages arising from impossibility of performance from the outset cannot be the proper solution in all three-party registered title trust cases, nor can it readily lead to a sound conclusion in specific cases.\\n\\nE) In general, three-party registered title trust cases arise at the title trustor’s request for the title trustor’s benefit, and in many cases the title trustor’s fault will be heavier than the seller’s. However, even in such cases, the title trustor’s contractual status against the seller should not be uniformly stripped away on the basis of good faith and the like asserted by the majority opinion. As in the dissenting opinion, the title trustor’s contractual rights should be permitted or limited according to the general principles such as Article 390 of the Civil Act, and the concrete circumstances of the title trustor and the seller should be reflected within that framework. Let us examine this a bit more concretely. There may be cases where, in a situation where the seller’s duty to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate has become impossible to perform, the title trustor is deemed to bear substantial fault. In such cases, the provisions on comparative negligence under Article 396 of the Civil Act would apply, and the seller’s liability for damages arising from breach of contract would be limited. Also, considering the circumstances of the entire contract, there may be cases where the title trustor’s fault is substantially heavier than the seller’s, or where the fault is so light that the seller cannot be held responsible, such that it can be evaluated that the impossibility of performance did not arise from a cause attributable to the seller. In such cases, the seller would not be recognized as bearing a duty to compensate under Article 390 of the Civil Act, nor would the title trustor be recognized as having a right of rescission under Article 546 of the Civil Act. Conversely, there may be cases where the three-party registered title trust was created at the initiative of the seller and the seller bears much heavier responsibility than the title trustor. In such cases, the title trustor would be recognized as having a claim for damages under Article 390 of the Civil Act or rights of rescission and restitution under Articles 546 and 548 of the Civil Act.\\nThe supplementary opinion to the majority opinion probably presumes that, once a direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is recognized, the seller’s responsibility cannot again be recognized and thus the seller’s responsibility is denied wholesale. However, this can only be described as an inversion of the proper order of analysis.\\n\\n4) Denying the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee does not produce a result contrary to the ideals of fairness.\\nA) The supplementary opinion to the majority opinion states that if the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is denied, then the seller must bear the risk that should have been assumed by the title trustor, or the seller will retain the benefit that should have been retained by the title trustor, which is contrary to the principle of fairness.\\nHowever, when the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and the seller’s duty to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate becomes impossible to perform, the legal effects arise according to the separate legal relationships between the title trustor and the seller and between the seller and the title trustee. The dissenting opinion does not say that the legal relationship arising from the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller should, regardless of whether performance is possible, always be resolved by the sales contract between those parties, but rather that the risk should not be shifted to the seller. Rather than having to consider even the insolvency risk of the title trustee and the seller in performing the sales contract, greater fidelity should be paid to the legislative purpose of the Real Name Registration Act. If, as the majority opinion does, one must consider even the insolvency risk of the contractual party or the title trustee, then the matter should be resolved more by the ordinary method under the sales contract, not by the law of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nThe supplementary opinion to the majority opinion found it contrary to the principle of fairness to deny the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee because, once the ultimate objective of acquiring ownership of the trust real estate becomes impossible, the interests should be adjusted so that the purchase price invested by the title trustor can be returned to the title trustor in line with the purpose of the title trust agreement. However, such interpretation premised on the title trust agreement can no longer be accepted after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act.\\n\\nB) Even if the title trustor’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is denied, there is still a way for the title trustor to recover the purchase price paid.\\nAlthough the Civil Act does not separately provide for a claim for substitute performance as an effect of impossibility of performance apart from the creditor’s claim for damages and right of rescission, precedents recognize such a claim by interpretation (see Supreme Court Decisions of 1992. 5. 12., 92DA4581, 4598, etc.). If the seller’s duty to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate becomes impossible to perform, the title trustor may recover the purchase price by exercising a claim for substitute performance against the seller. If, because the real estate has been transferred to a third party by expropriation, etc., compensation arises, or if the title trustee disposes of the real estate to a third party and proceeds from the disposition arise, and such compensation or proceeds are transferred to the seller, the title trustor may, by exercising a claim for substitute performance, seek return of the compensation or proceeds from the seller. If the compensation or proceeds have not been transferred to the seller but remain with the title trustee, the title trustor may also seek, by exercising a claim for substitute performance, that the seller assign his/her claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee (see Supreme Court Decisions of 1996. 10. 29., 95DA56910, etc.). A claim for substitute performance does not ask whether the debtor or creditor is responsible for the cause. Therefore, if the seller’s duty to register transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate becomes impossible to perform, the title trustor may, without inquiring into fault, exercise the above claim for substitute performance against the seller and receive compensation for the loss incurred by paying the purchase price.\\nSince it is not the case that all means of recovering the purchase price paid by the title trustor are fundamentally excluded, it is not proper to recognize a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee, who have no legal relationship.\\n\\n5) Rather, recognizing a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment by the title trustor against the title trustee leads to a result contrary to the principle of self-responsibility and the ideals of fairness, and is therefore improper.\\nIf, in a three-party registered title trust, the title trustor paid the entire purchase price to the seller while creating an uncertain legal relationship by making a void title trust registration concerning the real estate purchased for his/her own benefit, then it is consistent with the principle of self-responsibility for the title trustor to bear the risk that may arise therefrom. However, if a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee is recognized, the title trustor can resolve the problem by seeking restitution of unjust enrichment from the title trustee, who is not even a party to the sales contract, without bearing the risk he/she created. This shifts contractual risk, which the title trustor entered into and performed according to self-responsibility, onto the third-party title trustee, contrary to the basic principles of contract law.\\n\\nc. After the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment cannot be recognized between the title trustor and the title trustee under a void title trust agreement.\\n1) Precedents take the position that if there is no substantive rights relationship between the two parties, a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment is not recognized. Where the debtor under a contract can be required to perform, relief is afforded through the debtor, and a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against a third party is denied (Supreme Court Decisions of 2002. 8. 23., 99DA66564, 66571). Also, in a contract for the benefit of a third party, even if performance is rendered to the third party, if that performance has meaning as performance in the legal relationship between the promisor and the stipulator, restitution of unjust enrichment exists only between the promisor and the stipulator, and the promisor cannot seek restitution of unjust enrichment from the third party (Supreme Court Decision of 2005. 7. 22., 2005DA7566, 7573). Furthermore, a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment arising from infringement of rights is recognized between the right holder and the person who infringed the right (Supreme Court Decision of 2011. 6. 10., 2010DA40239).\\nNevertheless, prior precedents recognize a direct restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee, who have no substantive rights relationship, in a three-party registered title trust. This is because prior precedents judged the legal relationship on the premise that a valid title trust agreement had been formed between the title trustor and the title trustee. If the title trust agreement and changes in real rights occurred before the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, the stance of the prior precedents can be understood. At that time, because the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights were valid, legal relationships could be constructed on that premise.\\nHowever, cases where the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights occurred after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act are different. Because it is clear that the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights are void, the legal relationship in a three-party registered title trust must be determined on the premise that no valid title trust agreement exists between the title trustor and the title trustee. There exists no legal relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee, and only separate legal relationships exist between the title trustor and the seller and between the seller and the title trustee; the title trustor has no legal basis whatsoever to exercise a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, who is a party to a separate legal relationship.\\nUltimately, recognizing a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee is a repetition of the prior precedents premised on the validity of the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee, and is not suitable to the situation after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act.\\n2) Even after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, the practice of real estate title trust did not disappear; however, due to various regulations and the like, the transaction environment surrounding real estate title trust changed, and it became widely known that real estate title trust agreements are void and hard to protect legally, so the public’s legal sentiment toward such agreements also changed greatly. As noted in the dissenting opinion, the Supreme Court has changed its legal principles on many issues in accordance with the purpose of the provisions of the Real Name Registration Act. The same legal principles should also apply in the case of a three-party registered title trust, and prior precedents based on pre-Real Name Registration Act logic should not be repeated in a way that causes confusion in the interpretation of the Real Name Registration Act.\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I supplement the grounds of the dissenting opinion and express my views on the majority opinion and the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2020DA208997]": "The grounds of appeal are determined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case  \\nAccording to the reasons of the lower judgment, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff purchased each of the parcels of land at issue from C, and it was agreed that the registration would be made in the Defendant’s name; pursuant to that agreement, C completed registration of transfer of ownership in the Defendant’s name with respect to each of the parcels of land at issue, thereby effecting a three-party registered title trust.\\n\\nb. Without the Plaintiff’s consent, the Defendant sold each of the parcels of land at issue to D on April 7, 2014, for KRW 1.4 billion, and, among the purchase price, KRW 980 million was structured under a sales contract whereby D would assume the debt secured by the mortgage over each of the parcels of land at issue; on April 11, 2014, the Defendant registered transfer of ownership in D’s name with respect to each of the parcels of land at issue on the basis of the above sale.\\n\\nc. The Plaintiff filed this lawsuit seeking payment from the Defendant of KRW 420 million (= KRW 1.4 billion - KRW 980 million) and delay damages thereon, by asserting that the Defendant’s disposition of each of the parcels of land at issue without the Plaintiff’s consent constitutes a tort or that the Defendant obtained unjust enrichment without legal cause, and seeking damages or restitution of unjust enrichment.\\n\\n2. Claim for Damages Arising from Tort (Ground for Appeal 3)\\n\\na. Even if the act by which the title trustee, by disposing at his own discretion of real property for which registration of transfer of ownership was received from the seller pursuant to a three-party registered title trust, is not punished as the criminal offense of embezzlement, such act infringes the title trustor’s claim right to demand registration of transfer of ownership, and therefore may constitute a tort under Article 750 of the Civil Act, so that the title trustee may incur liability for damages to the title trustor. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Where, in violation of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name (hereinafter referred to as the “Real Estate Real-Name Act”), the title trustor, with respect to real property purchased by the title trustor, effected what is known as a three-party registered title trust by entering into a title trust agreement with the title trustee and completing registration of transfer of ownership directly from the seller to the title trustee, the issue is whether the title trustee’s arbitrary disposition of the real property constitutes embezzlement. In its en banc Decision 2014DO6992 rendered on May 19, 2016, the Supreme Court changed its prior precedents and held that, in such a case, since the title trustor is not the owner of the real property and a fiduciary relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee cannot be recognized, the title trustee cannot be said to be a person who keeps custody of the title trustor’s property, and therefore, even if the title trustee arbitrarily disposes of the trust real property, embezzlement is not constituted in relation to the title trustor.\\n\\n(2) Civil liability and criminal liability are governed by different principles in terms of the guiding ideology, the burden of proof, and the degree of proof required.
