The majority opinion explains that the traditional ancestral rite system aims, based on patriarchal lineage ideology, at the maintenance and succession of the family centered on the patrilineal bloodline through ancestor worship; that succession to the “property for ancestral rites” stipulated in Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act accompanies such traditional inheritance of ancestral rites and primarily aims at preserving the tradition of ancestor worship and performance of ancestral rites through maintenance and preservation of property for ancestral rites, which has the special meaning of securing continuity of ancestral rites for one’s ancestors and symbolizing the family lineage and serving as a medium for clan unity; that there is no statutory provision concerning the determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites who becomes the successor to the property for ancestral rites provided in Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act; and that, since the force of the traditional custom or case law has partly become invalid, the matter must be determined according to reason by comprehensively considering the legislative purpose, the general principles of the Civil Act, and the historical and social meaning of ancestral rites. On that premise, the majority opinion concludes that the person who presides over the ancestral rites should be first determined by consultation among the co-heirs, and if no such consultation is reached, then the eldest son of the deceased (or, if the eldest son has already died, the eldest son’s son, namely the eldest grandson), and where there is no son among the co-heirs, the deceased’s eldest daughter, should become the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and bases this on the point that this better accords with relative legitimacy in current custom and social common sense and simplifies the legal relationship concerning succession to property for ancestral rites.\\n\\nHowever, the logic and conclusion developed by the majority opinion ultimately amount to nothing more than a declaration that, in determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites who becomes the successor to the property for ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, it will continue to maintain, as the guiding principle, the eldest-son-first rule based on the traditional patriarchal lineage ideology and the idea of a family centered on the patrilineal bloodline, except that the distinction between legitimate and illegitimate status is eliminated and the eldest daughter’s priority is recognized in families with only daughters.\\n\\nYet, as properly pointed out in the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan and Jeon Soo-an (hereinafter referred to as the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc.), this not only contradicts the purpose of the 1990 amendment to the Civil Act, which sought to separate property for ancestral rites from the privilege of the family head heir, but also disregards the facts that the Civil Act has repeatedly been amended to equalize inheritance shares among siblings, that succession to property for ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act intrinsically bears the character of property inheritance, the changed nature of ancestral rites themselves as remembrance for the deceased rather than family succession, the weakening of members of society’s legal conviction concerning the traditional custom relating to the heir to ancestral rites, and the gradual yet consistent changes in our society’s legal order and perception concerning kinship inheritance, such as the strengthening of gender equality and the abolition of the family head system. Therefore, it is difficult to say that this interpretation accords with current custom and social legitimacy.\\n\\nFurthermore, even from the standpoint of simplifying the legal relationship concerning succession to property for ancestral rites, the majority opinion, instead of consistently adhering to the eldest son, etc. first principle, gives priority to consultation among co-heirs that is not publicly announced to third parties, and even where consultation fails, admits an exception that the eldest son, etc. cannot become the person who presides over the ancestral rites where there are special circumstances preventing the maintenance of that status. Therefore, in most disputes where the question arises as to whether the eldest son, etc. can be recognized as the person who presides over the ancestral rites among co-heirs, the complexity and uncertainty of the legal relationship surrounding the matter remain. Thus, this also does not appear to be a persuasive and sufficient basis for the majority opinion’s preference for the eldest son, etc.\\n\\nI fully sympathize with the awareness of the problem raised by the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc. on this point, but I am not readily able to agree with the interpretive theory that, as an alternative, the principle of majority vote should be adopted as the criterion for determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nThis is because, in interpreting Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act and related provisions, although the question of whether one falls within the category of the person who presides over the ancestral rites includes many status-law elements, applying a uniform standard that simply takes majority vote as a property-law general theory may exclude elements that should in fact be considered important depending on the case in the various matters where the determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites is in question. This makes it difficult to achieve harmonious realization of the various ideologies and values, and the reality, spanning tradition and modernity, that may conflict with one another, and may lead to conclusions lacking concrete appropriateness.\\n\\nTherefore, while accepting as is the interpretive premise that the person who presides over the ancestral rites is to be determined based on reason as a basic principle for deciding the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, and that as an initial method of determination, consultation among co-heirs should be prioritized, I believe that, as a supplementary method where such consultation is not reached, one should not, as the majority opinion suggests, follow the order of “the eldest son, etc.” reflecting mainly the will and interests of a family centered on the patrilineal bloodline based on patriarchal lineage ideology, nor, as the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc. suggest, use “majority rule” as the de facto absolute, preferential, and uniform standard for determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites. Rather, through a new interpretation more faithful to the legislative purpose of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act and the text of that provision, a rational standard consistent with reason should be presented.\\n\\nB. As seen above, the establishment of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act reflects the legislature’s intent to separate succession to property for ancestral rites from the family head system, and in the same vein, the subject of such succession was replaced from the former “family head heir” to the value-neutral and open-ended indeterminate concept of “the person who presides over the ancestral rites.”\\n\\nThis fundamentally reflects the reality that the ancestral inheritance system belongs to the category of morals and customs, and that since the family head system, which had previously served as the standard, has lost its value as a guiding principle, one has no choice but to explore valid dominant norms, customs, perceptions, etc. in society and their changes, and seek a solution with concrete appropriateness.\\n\\nIf so, where no consultation is reached or consultation is impossible as to who among the co-heirs should be the person who presides over the ancestral rites, rather than judging on the basis of only one circumstance suggested by the majority opinion or the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc.—such as the “traditional custom favoring the eldest son, etc.” or “whether there is a co-heir supported by more members among the co-heirs”—it is, in my view, most desirable, in light of the purpose of the establishment of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, to determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites by comprehensively, in parallel, and integrally considering on the same plane such circumstances, including objective factors such as the lifetime family relationship and pattern of life between the decedent and the co-heirs, religion, the support relationship of the surviving spouse, the circumstances in which consultation among the co-heirs failed, the kind and scope of ancestral rites to be presided over, the living conditions and places of residence of the co-heirs, the content of the inherited property and its division, and the economic value of the property for ancestral rites to be succeeded, together with subjective factors such as the decedent’s lifetime intent or wishes, and the intentions of the surviving spouse and the co-heirs. I believe that by doing so, one can also derive a foreseeable conclusion that is as far as possible not disconnected from the universal norms and concrete sentiments of society.\\n\\nIn this sense, “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” in Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, newly established on 1990. 1. 13., is no different from providing that it means “the co-heir most suitable to succeed to property for ancestral rites and preside over the ancestral rites,” and determining which co-heir among the co-heirs corresponds to such a person will ultimately be the most in accord with the reason of our society today if the various factors above are comprehensively considered.\\n\\nC. The majority opinion, which treats reason as the basic principle for determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act and, through value judgment as to whether a specific person has special circumstances precluding maintenance of the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites, presents as the concrete method of determination whether there is a defect in qualification for the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites; and the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc., which present as their concrete method that, by majority vote, and if majority vote is irrational then by comprehensive consideration of various circumstances in cases where majority vote cannot be used, including where there is an equal split of votes for and against, the court must decide who will be the person who presides over the ancestral rites, both recognize room for the court to make normative judgment from a guardianship-like standpoint in interpreting and applying the above provision. In that respect, they do not differ from the legal theory presented in the interpretive view set forth in B above; rather, they are understood to differ only as to the concrete standards of value assessment regarding whose qualification as the more suitable person who presides over the ancestral rites better accords with reason.\\n\\nHowever, as seen above, when Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act provides that “property for ancestral rites shall be succeeded to by the person most suitable among co-heirs to succeed to property for ancestral rites and preside over the ancestral rites” (where consultation among co-heirs is not reached or consultation is impossible), the question of who is most suitable as the person who presides over the ancestral rites under the above provision is a matter entrusted to the court by the text itself, and such guardianship-like role of the court is ordinarily incidental to the purposive interpretation of statutory provisions containing blank clauses or indeterminate concepts scattered throughout the Civil Act. Moreover, according to various provisions belonging to the family and succession part of the Civil Act, in disputes concerning domestic cases, if no agreement is reached among the parties, the court’s guardianship-like role is adopted as the principle, without exception, as an immediate solution. I think this can serve as a useful reference even in interpreting the legal concept of the person who presides over the ancestral rites (for precisely this reason, the view that “the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act means the person among the heirs most suitable to preside over the ancestral rites, selected by the various judgment criteria noted above, is what best accords with reason” is undeniably a possible interpretive theory of the legal concept itself, and as also noted in the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion below, it should not be dismissed as a mere legislative theory; I emphasize this once again).\\n\\nMoreover, the Family Litigation Act, after listing in Article 2(1) the family cases falling under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Family Court, provides in Article 2(2) that “the Family Court shall also hear and adjudicate matters that are vested in the authority of the Family Court under other statutes or Supreme Court Rules.” Therefore, by codifying in the Family Litigation Rules, which are Supreme Court Rules, the interpretive theory set forth in B above, it would be entirely possible to pursue a simple and rational settlement of disputes through domestic non-contentious procedures, etc.\\n\\nD. In conclusion, the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act means the co-heir most suitable, in light of reason, to succeed to property for ancestral rites and preside over the ancestral rites; and in determining which co-heir is most suitable, I do not endorse, as a supplementary standard where no consultation among co-heirs is reached, either the eldest-son-first principle based on patriarchal lineage ideology suggested by the majority opinion or the majority rule suggested by the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc. Rather, as an alternative, where a dispute arises as to the status of the person who presides over the ancestral rites, the matter should be determined by hearing and adjudicating, in each individual case, the merits of the parties’ assertions, while faithfully interpreting the text of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act and its legislative purpose, and comprehensively considering the ideology of litigation concerning domestic matters, which is based on human dignity and equality of men and women and seeks to maintain and promote family peace and the good custom of mutual assistance among relatives, as well as the various related factors noted above.\\n\\nFor a different purpose, the Supreme Court decisions that, even after the forced family head inheritance system was abolished by the 1990 amendment to the Civil Act and the heir to ancestral rites was changed from family head heir to the person who presides over the ancestral rites, the eldest descendant of the main line still becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, should be changed to the extent that they imply recognition of the eldest descendant of the main line as the person who presides over the ancestral rites solely because of that status, regardless of concrete circumstances, rather than because the eldest descendant of the main line is the most suitable person among other co-heirs to preside over the ancestral rites in the particular case.\\n\\nE. Examining this case in light of the above interpretive theory, in a case like this one where in fact no consultation among the co-heirs was reached and a dispute arose, it is not proper, as the majority opinion does, to conclude that the eldest son becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites merely because he is the eldest son, while disregarding, without weighty consideration, circumstances that should be considered seriously, such as the deceased’s lifetime intent or wishes, the lifetime family relationship between the deceased and the co-heirs such as the Plaintiff and Defendants, the support relationship, and the circumstances in which consultation among the co-heirs failed, unless there are special circumstances such that the eldest son himself cannot maintain the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites. As stated in the reasons for the judgment below, where the deceased lived for about 44 years separated from the Plaintiff’s side, who is the eldest son, and established and maintained a household together with the Defendants, who are his half-siblings, and, along that line, after the deceased’s death, the Defendants are enshrining and managing the deceased in a park cemetery, in order to determine whether the Plaintiff can be regarded as having the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites sufficient to take from the grave of the deceased, who was the common decedent of the Plaintiff and Defendants, the deceased’s remains and bones against the Defendants’ intent, one would have to specifically examine the various considerations that can serve as judgment criteria, as noted above.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, concerning the determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, did not investigate or examine the various circumstances necessary to determine among the co-heirs, including the Plaintiff and Defendants, who was most suitable as the person who presides over the ancestral rites of the deceased in this case where no consultation among co-heirs had been reached, but merely gave the Plaintiff, the eldest son, preferential recognition of the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites and thus held that the Plaintiff had rights to the deceased’s remains and bones, thereby granting the Plaintiff’s claim. Thus, the judgment below contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites and by failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\nF. Therefore, the judgment below should be reversed and the case remanded to the court below for further trial and determination.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion of Justices Lee Hong-hoon and Kim Neung-hwan on the Majority Opinion\\n\\nA. As to the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites\\n\\n(1) As stated in the majority opinion, former Civil Act Article 996 before amendment by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13. provided that the family head heir succeeded to property for ancestral rites and, in Article 984 et seq. of the same Act, in detail regulated who becomes the family head heir. However, the former Civil Act amended by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13. changed the successor to property for ancestral rites from “family head heir” to “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” and provided this in Article 1008-3, but it did not provide any rule as to who becomes “the person who presides over the ancestral rites.” Here, “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” means not the “person who in fact presides over the ancestral rites,” but the “person who should preside over the ancestral rites,” so it is necessary to determine who that is, and the problem cannot be resolved merely by interpreting the meaning of “the person who presides over the ancestral rites.”\\n\\nAccordingly, the Civil Act’s failure to determine who “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” is constitutes a statutory gap, so under Article 1 of the Civil Act it should be determined by customary law. However, as the majority opinion holds, since the force of the prior custom or customary law and Supreme Court decisions concerning this matter can no longer be maintained, it has no choice but to be determined by reason. Therefore, the view expressed in the dissenting opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo (hereinafter referred to as the “dissenting opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, etc.”) to the effect that resolving the issue of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites by interpretive theory of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act is sufficient cannot be said to be proper.\\n\\nAlso, the reason why the majority opinion believes the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites must be decided by reason is not because it considers that the content of the prior custom or customary law has changed into something else, but because the traditional custom that the eldest descendant of the main line, i.e., the legitimate eldest son, becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites regardless of consultation among heirs is no longer consistent in principle with the changed family system based on individual dignity and equality, and thus can no longer maintain its force as custom or customary law. Nevertheless, the supplementary opinion of Justice Ahn Dae-hee regarding the dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, etc., to the effect that the content of the new custom concerning the person who presides over the ancestral rites must be examined and fixed and used as the adjudicative norm, cannot be proper, because it is no different from refusing to adjudicate.\\n\\n(2) The dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran and Kim Ji-hyung (hereinafter referred to as the “dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, etc.”) argues that where consultation among co-heirs is not reached, the court should determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites by hearing and adjudicating the merits of the parties’ assertions in each individual case. However, this cannot be adopted as an interpretation of our current Civil Act, even if left open as a legislative theory.\\n\\nArticle 1008-3 of the Civil Act concerning succession to property for ancestral rites is the provision introduced in the 1990 amendment to the former Civil Act (amended by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13.) that changed the successor to property for ancestral rites from “family head heir” to “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” while converting the compulsory family head inheritance system into a discretionary family head succession system; at the time of that amendment, the legislature did not adopt a system allowing the court to determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nMoreover, a court’s determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites should, by its nature, be regarded as a domestic litigation or domestic non-contentious case. However, Article 2(1) of the Family Litigation Act enumerates in a limited manner the family litigation or domestic non-contentious cases falling within the jurisdiction of the Family Court, and Article 2(2) thereof provides that the Family Court may also hear and adjudicate matters vested in its authority under other statutes or Supreme Court Rules. Yet a determination to set the person who presides over the ancestral rites belongs to neither of these categories, so the Family Court cannot hear and adjudicate it. Therefore, for the court to determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites in individual cases should be possible only after Article 2(1) of the Family Litigation Act or other statutes or the Family Litigation Rules are amended to provide for this.\\n\\nUltimately, the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, etc. is no different from raising another problem rather than answering the issue of how to determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(3) The dissenting opinion of Justices Park Si-hwan and Jeon Soo-an (hereinafter referred to as the “dissenting opinion of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc.”) argues that where consultation among co-heirs is not reached, determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites by majority vote is the most appropriate.\\n\\nHowever, as also pointed out in the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, etc., determining by majority vote a matter that includes not only the area of simple property relations but also many matters in the realm of family relations and status relations cannot be said to be appropriate, and it does not accord with the general sentiment of the members of our society today. In addition, this could provoke unnecessary disputes concerning property for ancestral rites among co-heirs, thereby undermining the stability of family relations and harming fraternal harmony among family members.\\n\\nMoreover, because the dissenting opinion of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc. states that if the person who presides over the ancestral rites cannot be decided by majority vote, such as where the votes are evenly split, the court must decide by comprehensively considering all circumstances, the problems noted above in relation to the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, etc. can likewise be directly pointed out to that extent.\\n\\nTherefore, I cannot agree with the dissenting opinion of Justices Park Si-hwan, etc. either.\\n\\nB. As to the effect of the method of disposal of the remains and bones or designation of the burial place\\n\\n(1) As to succession to the remains and bones\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, etc. is to the effect that, since the manner of ancestral rites and funerals has diversified, and since it has become common not to perform ancestral rites at all or not to establish a grave, the attribution of rights regarding a grave and the attribution of rights regarding the remains and bones should be separately determined; thus, the majority opinion’s view that the attribution of the remains and bones should be related to the attribution of the grave and that the person who presides over the ancestral rites succeeds by analogy to succession of graves, etc. is inappropriate.\\n\\nHowever, as seen in the majority opinion, since there can be no grave without remains and bones, succession under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act presupposes that the grave subject to succession contains remains and bones; accordingly, where remains and bones are buried and a grave is established, the attribution of rights regarding the remains and bones and the attribution of the right of protection and management over the grave cannot be separated from each other. Moreover, in this case the deceased’s remains have already been interred in the grave and have become the object of ancestral rites by the bereaved family; the majority opinion develops its legal theory concerning succession to property for ancestral rites and to the remains and bones on that premise, and discussion detached from such premise is inappropriate.\\n\\n(2) As to the deceased’s personality rights and the effect of the deceased’s expression of intent based thereon\\n\\n(a) The dissenting opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, Jeon Soo-an, Ahn Dae-hee, and Yang Chang-soo are to the effect that, based on the deceased’s personality rights, the deceased’s expression of intent during life concerning the method of disposal of his or her own remains and bones or designation of the burial place (hereinafter referred to as “the method of disposal of the remains and bones, etc.”) has legal binding force upon the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\n(b) Today, with the development of science and technology, the growth of various mass media, and the spread of the internet, the risk of infringement on a person’s personality value has increased, and accordingly the need to protect personality rights has grown. The Copyright Act and the Press Arbitration and Remedies Act contain protective provisions against infringement of the deceased’s moral rights in authorship or the deceased’s personality rights caused by media reporting. However, that does not mean that, even where positive law does not contain protective provisions concerning the deceased’s personality rights, general recognition of the deceased’s personality rights can be readily accepted. I think a cautious approach is needed.\\n\\nA person becomes the subject of rights and duties only while living (Civil Act Article 3), and thus cannot be such a subject after death. Also, because personality rights are highly personal rights inseparable from the personality of their subject and cannot be separated from that subject, unlike property rights they cannot be transferred or inherited, and thus, absent special statutory provision, they should be deemed extinguished upon the death of the person to whom they belonged.\\n\\nAn argument may be made that, because our Civil Act recognizes limited legal capacity for an unborn fetus (Articles 762, 1000(3), 1064), such recognition may also be possible for the deceased. However, in the case of a fetus, special provisions are established because the fetus is expected to become a natural person and acquire legal capacity in the near future. By contrast, in the case of the deceased, legal capacity conclusively extinguishes upon death, so the fetus cannot serve as an appropriate comparative subject.\\n\\nIf the deceased’s personality rights were generally recognized absent a positive law provision, questions would arise as to who is the subject to whom such rights belong (i.e., whether the personality rights of a deceased person can belong to the deceased person), who would exercise them (i.e., whether the deceased person can exercise his or her own personality rights), and if the bereaved family is deemed able to exercise them on behalf of the deceased, what the legal basis is, or what happens if there is no bereaved family. It would be difficult, in my view, to hastily recognize the deceased’s personality rights generally without the grounds therefor and their validity having been verified.\\n\\nTherefore, unless the law provides for the method of exercising the deceased’s personality rights, etc., recognition of the deceased’s personality rights should be approached cautiously; rather, by indirectly protecting the deceased’s personality rights through protection of the bereaved family’s own personality rights, the above problems could be resolved.\\n\\n(c) Meanwhile, recognizing the deceased’s personality rights and whether the person who presides over the ancestral rites is legally bound by the deceased’s lifetime expression of intent regarding the method of disposal of his or her own remains and bones, etc., are separate matters. Even if the deceased’s personality rights are recognized, it is obvious that the bereaved family’s own personality rights, such as feelings of respect and remembrance for the deceased, should also be protected separately.\\n\\nHere, we should note that, if one readily recognizes the personality rights of a person whose legal capacity has already extinguished by death and seeks to resolve matters that appear to belong to the moral sphere through personality rights, this may instead result in infringement of the personality rights of the bereaved family members, including the person who presides over the ancestral rites, who are living rights holders. The Organ Transplant Act Article 2(2) provides that the voluntary intent expressed by a person who wishes to donate organs should be respected, but Article 18(3)1 of the same Act provides that, even if the person consented to organ removal before death, if the family or bereaved family expressly refuses the organ removal, then the organs may not be removed, thereby recognizing legal binding force in the bereaved family’s intent contrary to the deceased’s intent and simultaneously making Article 2(2) a declaratory provision. This can be understood as intended to protect the bereaved family’s own personality rights, such as their feelings of respect and remembrance for the deceased.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act is a mandatory provision enacted for the purpose of preserving our tradition of ancestor worship and performance of ancestral rites by allowing the person who presides over the ancestral rites to succeed to property for ancestral rites, preventing dispersal and dilution of property for ancestral rites, and simplifying the legal relationship concerning succession thereto. If the person who presides over the ancestral rites is legally bound by the deceased’s expression of intent concerning the method of disposal of the remains and bones, etc., then that may conflict with the above legislative purpose, and this must also be considered.\\n\\nFurthermore, where the deceased’s remains and bones are disposed of or buried in a specific place according to the deceased’s intent, there may be cases where the person who presides over the ancestral rites, etc. cannot arbitrarily seek delivery of the remains and bones. However, this should be limited to special circumstances such as where there was the lawful successor’s, i.e., the person who presides over the ancestral rites’, prior consent or subsequent approval regarding the disposal of the remains and bones, etc.; it cannot be so interpreted even where the disposal was carried out unlawfully against the will of the person who presides over the ancestral rites or by excluding that person. If interpreted otherwise, it would encourage the attitude of first disposing of or burying the remains and bones by some means or other by invoking the deceased’s intent, which could foster further disputes and illegality among the bereaved family over the deceased’s remains and bones.\\n\\n(d) In conclusion, a deceased person’s lifetime expression of intent concerning the method of disposal of his or her own remains and bones, etc. should of course be respected, but this is a moral duty and cannot be regarded as a legal duty. It is proper to think that the choice of the disposal or burial place of the remains and bones should ultimately be made according to the will of the person who presides over the ancestral rites, who is the right holder to the deceased’s remains and bones, so long as it does not violate good morals or other social order.\\n\\n8. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Ahn Dae-hee to the Dissenting Opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo\\n\\nA. As to determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites by reason\\n\\n(1) First, in this case, as pointed out in the dissenting opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo above, I once again state that it is unnecessary to discuss who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and supplement the following views.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion interprets that, on the premise that the traditional custom or case law concerning the person who presides over the ancestral rites can no longer maintain its force, the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites must be determined by reason; it then concludes that the person who presides over the ancestral rites should first be determined by consultation among co-heirs, and if consultation is not reached, then, regardless of legitimate or illegitimate status, the eldest son or eldest grandson, and where there is no son among the co-heirs, the eldest daughter, should become the person who presides over the ancestral rites, on the ground that this is relatively more legitimate in social common sense and can be said to secure foreseeability to some extent, and thus is most consistent with reason.\\n\\nI agree with the majority opinion that today, because our people’s perception of ancestral rites and social custom has changed, the prior interpretation that the person who presides over the ancestral rites is the eldest descendant of the main line can no longer be maintained. However, I cannot avoid questioning whether it is proper to interpret the person who presides over the ancestral rites by reason, and further whether the reason articulated by the majority opinion is truly proper.\\n\\n(3) First, ancestral rites are a traditional custom for honoring and remembering our ancestors and are based on Confucian thought. As to who presides over such ancestral rites, it should basically be determined by “custom or customary law generated by repeated practice in society,” not by reason. The Supreme Court has traditionally recognized the custom that the eldest descendant of the main line is the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and if such custom no longer conforms to the constitutional ideology or has changed with social developments, one should identify the new “repeated practice in society” and interpret accordingly.\\n\\nIn other words, because ancestral rites are carried out according to traditional custom and the determination of the person who presides over ancestral rites is generally also determined according to custom, the person who presides over ancestral rites should be determined according to a socially accepted custom, not by theoretical normativity. If one says that the eldest son or eldest daughter becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites in accordance with reason, then one must ask what should be answered with respect to the custom of societies that in practice conduct ancestral rites differently. If the eldest son refuses ancestral rites on religious grounds and the second son is performing ancestral rites in the traditional manner, it would be difficult to explain whether in such a case the eldest son still becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites and whether that can truly be reason.\\n\\nReason originally refers to the nature of things or the general principles of law approved by society. As the principle for determining the person who presides over ancestral rites based on traditional custom, it is not appropriate. Even the content the majority opinion sets forth as the basis of reason appears, in substance, to mean custom, saying that “the perception that the eldest son or eldest grandson becomes the person who presides over ancestral rites, and if there is no son, the daughter becomes the person who presides over ancestral rites, appears to be widely accepted, ... and giving priority to elders is our traditional good custom and general social common sense.” Therefore, it is questionable whether this really is a reason grounded in the general principles of law approved by society or in justice. In other words, the majority opinion, abandoning any effort to recognize changed custom, is merely packaging what it thinks remains part of custom as reason. Therefore, the Supreme Court should continue examining what our society members’ notion of ancestral rites is and who they regard as the person who presides over such rites, recognize the changed custom, and determine accordingly, rather than simply declaring that, because custom has changed, the person who presides over ancestral rites should be determined by reason as a categorical imperative of the court.\\n\\n(4) Next, I cannot agree with the content of the person who presides over the ancestral rites as determined by reason set forth by the majority opinion. The majority opinion attempts a general interpretation of the person who presides over the ancestral rites beyond the scope of resolving this case, which is a dispute between the eldest son and the second son; I cannot help pointing out that this contains theoretical contradictions and risks.\\n\\nIn the current legal system where the family head succession system has been abolished, a strong view has emerged that, concerning the determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites, it is reasonable first to reflect the decedent’s intent. The reason articulated by the majority opinion says nothing about that point and, disregarding the decedent’s intent, determines the person who presides over the ancestral rites, so one cannot help but question whether it is truly the reason, i.e., the general principle of law.\\n\\nMoreover, while the majority opinion states that prior precedents cannot be maintained in light of Article 36(1) of the Constitution, which provides for gender equality, it nevertheless distinguishes men and women in substance. In particular, under the majority opinion, if there is a daughter who is the eldest daughter and a son younger than her, the son is recognized as having the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites. I think it is dangerous to call that reason, the general principle of law. This is ultimately a modified application of prior precedents, violating the gender equality principle set forth in the Constitution, and if such a principle is especially labeled reason, the Supreme Court will face criticism that it is rendering decisions based on male-dominance ideology.\\n\\nIn addition, while the majority opinion determines the general person who presides over the ancestral rites, it makes no clear statement as to who is the person who presides over ancestral rites for a grandfather or above, not the immediate preceding generation. That is, where the eldest son’s descendants consist only of daughters and the second son’s descendants include a son, who presides over the grandfather’s ancestral rites? Under the majority opinion, it seems that the son among the second son’s descendants becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites. And considering that there are today a considerable number of people who, for religious reasons, refuse traditional ancestral rites, it is also unanswered whether in such cases the eldest son or eldest daughter must unconditionally become the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\n(5) Reason, as a supplementary legal source, should be used only when there is no statute or customary law. In the present situation where custom or customary law cannot be said to be absent because ancestral rites based on traditional custom continue to be performed among members of society even though the custom or customary law has changed, the approach of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites by reason appears to err in trying to impose, as a theoretical ought, a problem of recognizing a real existence. And although reason is generally recognized through precedent as a general principle of law, it presupposes approval by society grounded in universally valid values. A judge should not immediately treat his or her own rational thought as reason to be recognized as such (that may even be criticized as judicial arrogance). Especially in a case like this, where a considerable number of Supreme Court Justices have expressed dissenting opinions, such views can no longer be said to have social approval and are insufficient to be called reason.\\n\\nTherefore, if there is truly a necessity to discuss who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites in this case, that should be determined only after clearly recognizing, through broad investigation and examination, what the customs of ancestral rites today are and what the custom is for determining the person who presides over ancestral rites in light of social change.\\n\\nB. As to the constitutional rights of the deceased\\n\\n(1) Our legal system maintains a unified legal order with the Constitution, the highest norm, at its apex. Since all legal norms of the social community realize the values and content of the Constitution, systematic unity must be maintained within the boundaries of the Constitution. Therefore, the Constitution serves as both the foundation and the limit in interpreting and applying all legal norms, including public and private law norms, and becomes the principle supplementing statutory gaps.\\n\\nArticle 10 of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall be assured of human dignity and value and have the right to pursue happiness. It shall be the duty of the State to confirm and guarantee the inviolable basic human rights of individuals.” This provision on human dignity is a fundamental norm among constitutional norms, supplying criteria for the purposes and value judgments of all state action and serving as the standard for interpreting the validity and content of all legal norms, as well as the primary principle for supplementing statutory gaps.\\n\\nArticle 10 of the Constitution is not a merely declaratory provision, but guarantees the individual’s personality rights and the right to pursue happiness, which are the essence and unique value of human beings. These personality rights and the right to pursue happiness presuppose the individual’s right to self-determination (fate self-determination) (Constitutional Court Decision 89HEONMA82 dated 1990. 9. 10.), and this right of self-determination guarantees all autonomous decisions made by a human being as a personal being, including the right of self-determination over one’s body, and in particular, after death, the freedom to donate or dispose of one’s organs or remains and bones, and the freedom to decide the method of burial or the burial place of remains and bones.\\n\\n(2) Since the subject of rights and duties in law is limited to living persons, and the same holds true as the subject of constitutional fundamental rights, there may be a question as to whether the deceased can be the subject of personality rights. However, the State’s duty to protect human dignity continues even after death. And if a person’s personality is degraded after death, human dignity and value are impaired, and the guarantee of human dignity even during life cannot be maintained. This cannot be accepted as consistent with the basic spirit of our Constitution grounded in human dignity and with the ideology of guaranteeing individual personality rights under Article 10 of the Constitution.\\n\\nIf so, regardless of whether there is an express provision in positive law, general personality rights such as honor must be guaranteed even after death, and to that extent the deceased also becomes the subject of personality rights. In other words, although the deceased’s rights cannot be recognized simply as a corpse after death, the honor, personality, and expressions of intent established during the deceased’s lifetime must naturally be protected under the Constitution. However, the deceased’s personality rights are not protected forever; as memory of the deceased fades and time passes, the need for such protection diminishes accordingly.\\n\\n(3) Since deciding the method of disposal of one’s remains and bones, or the method or place of burial, after death is part of the right of self-determination over one’s body derived from the individual’s personality rights under Article 10 of the Constitution, in interpreting and applying our Civil Act or supplementing its gaps, the deceased’s personality rights should not be infringed.\\n\\nAlthough our Civil Act does not regulate the specific content or limits of the person who presides over the ancestral rites’ rights, nor does it define disposal of one’s remains or decision on burial place as a statutory testamentary matter, if the deceased, during life, determined the method of disposal of his or her own remains or the method or place of burial, that has legal effect within the scope of the deceased’s personality rights.\\n\\nThe supplementary opinion of Justices Lee Hong-hoon and Kim Neung-hwan to the majority opinion states to the effect that one cannot recognize a deceased person’s personality rights lacking legal basis. This view says that no right can be recognized unless an individual statute specifically and explicitly provides otherwise. Yet the constitutional provisions on basic rights are open and comprehensive, and it is the judiciary that, through interpretation, concretizes the content of rights. That is precisely the authority and duty conferred on the Supreme Court by the Constitution. In particular, when a constitutional right has been infringed, interpretation to remedy the infringement or prevent its occurrence must be even more active, and constitutional fundamental rights cannot be denied merely because no individual statute expressly provides for them.\\n\\nAs noted above, this interpretation maintains a unified legal order in our legal system with the Constitution, the highest norm, at its apex, because the Constitution serves as the standard for interpreting all legal norms, including judicial law, while simultaneously supplementing gaps in law.\\n\\nAs with the majority opinion, interpreting the right of the person who presides over the ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act to include, even against the deceased’s intent, authority to dispose of the deceased’s remains or move the grave would ignore the decisions made by the deceased during life as a personal being and damage human dignity, thereby violating Article 10 of the Constitution. Moreover, it does not accord with the essence of ancestral rites or the legislative purpose of the system of inheritance of ancestral rites, given that the person who presides over the ancestral rites is the person who presides over respect and remembrance for the deceased, and it also runs counter to our traditional thinking.\\n\\nI state the above supplementary opinion to the dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo.\\n\\n9. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Kim Young-ran to the Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran and Kim Ji-hyung\\n\\nA. The majority opinion states that the traditional custom that the legitimate eldest son should succeed first to ancestral rites regardless of consultation among co-heirs ignored the autonomous will of the co-heirs, who are family members, and discriminated between legitimate and illegitimate status, and therefore no longer conformed in principle to the changed family system based on individual dignity and equality and thus could no longer maintain its force as custom or customary law. However, it further states that the system of ancestral rites and the succession of property for ancestral rites is based on the past patrilineal family succession through ancestor worship, and although the character of ancestral rites has changed significantly today, it cannot yet be said to have completely escaped the character of family succession; that the perception that, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son or eldest grandson becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites and, if there is no son, the daughter becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, appears to be widely accepted; that among people in equal conditions and status, giving priority to the elder is our traditional good custom and general social common sense; and that the perceptions or traditions of the members of our society above do not appear to contradict the present entire legal order. Therefore, it concludes that where consultation among co-heirs is not reached, the eldest son of the deceased (or, if the eldest son has already died, the eldest son’s son, namely the eldest grandson) should become the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and where there is no son among the co-heirs, the deceased’s eldest daughter should become the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nB. As pointed out in the dissenting opinions, the majority opinion is, except for eliminating the distinction between legitimate and illegitimate status in the determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites, which is the successor to property for ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, and recognizing the priority of the eldest daughter in a family with only daughters, no different from a declaration that it will continue to maintain as guiding principle the eldest-son-first rule based on the traditional patriarchal lineage ideology and the family-centered-on-patrilineal-bloodline concept.\\n\\nAs the majority opinion points out, our society, since the 1970s, has, through rapid economic growth, become a highly industrialized and urbanized society; the extended family system has changed into a nuclear family system; within the family, the will of each family member has been respected; discrimination between legitimate and illegitimate status has disappeared; and with the decline of son preference, the proportion of families with only daughters has increased. Accordingly, Article 34(1) of the Constitution, fully amended by Constitutional Amendment No. 9 on 1980. 10. 27., proclaimed that “marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and gender equality,” and this has been maintained as Article 36(1) of the current Constitution. Thereafter, institutions were improved in the direction of realizing equality among family members in all areas of society; through several amendments to the Civil Act, the inheritance shares of siblings became equal; the family head system was abolished and the family centered on the family head was reorganized into a new family system centered on the individual and spouse; and even the family register system was eventually replaced by the new family relationship registration system on 2008. 1. 1. However, the principle of eldest-son priority based on the traditional patriarchal lineage ideology and the family-centered-on-patrilineal-bloodline concept, which the majority opinion treats as the guiding principle, clearly discriminates among co-heirs on the basis of sex and age, which cannot be a rational standard in modern society, and thus runs counter to the above changes in social life and institutions. Therefore, the majority opinion falls into a contradiction in that it fails to satisfy even the premise it itself posits, and it also runs counter to our Civil Act and the long-standing efforts of the Supreme Court to substantially realize the constitutional principle of equality within family relations.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that because the traditional custom or case law concerning the person who presides over the ancestral rites can no longer maintain its force, the method of determining that person should be determined by reason, and further that according to reason, where no consultation among co-heirs is reached, the eldest son of the deceased, and if there is no son, the deceased’s eldest daughter, should become the person who presides over the ancestral rites unless there are special circumstances. Inasmuch as the majority opinion wholly excludes the force of the traditional custom or customary law on the ground that it disregards the result of consultation formed by the autonomous will of co-heirs and discriminates between legitimate and illegitimate status, and inasmuch as it says that, through consultation, etc., sons other than the deceased’s eldest son or daughters may also become the person who presides over the ancestral rites, it is clear that the majority opinion presupposes freedom from the traditional custom, etc. Nevertheless, it is internally inconsistent for the majority opinion to reintroduce the very custom it has excluded by saying that where consultation is not reached, one should return to the traditional custom and case law on the ground of patrilineal family succession centered on the patrilineal bloodline. There is no need even to point out that sons other than the eldest son and daughters are also patrilineal blood relatives.\\n\\nC. By Supreme Court en banc Decision 2002DA1178 dated 2005. 7. 21., the Supreme Court held that, with respect to the traditional custom limiting the qualification of clan members to adult males and denying women the qualification of clan members, the legal conviction of members of our society has been substantially shaken or weakened, and above all, our entire legal order, with the Constitution as the highest norm, guarantees family life based on individual dignity and gender equality and does not discriminate between men and women in substantive rights and duties within the family. It has changed in the direction of eliminating discrimination against women in all areas including politics, economy, society, and culture and realizing gender equality, and this principle of gender equality will further strengthen in the future. A clan association is a kinship group formed for the purposes of protecting the grave of the common ancestor and performing ancestral rites and promoting camaraderie among clan members, and although it naturally comes into existence by the descendants of the common ancestor upon the common ancestor’s death, the traditional custom that only adult male descendants among the descendants of the common ancestor may be members and women cannot be members of the clan association is one that inherently grants or fundamentally deprives the opportunity to participate in the protection of the common ancestor’s grave and performance of ancestral rites, based solely on sex arising from birth; such custom does not accord with our changed entire legal order, lacks legitimacy and rationality, and thus the traditional customary law limiting clan-member qualification to adult males can no longer have legal effect.\\n\\nHowever, by reasons such as “it is relatively legitimate in social common sense” or “it is caused by the non-formation of consultation among co-heirs,” the majority opinion uniformly determines the person who presides over the ancestral rites by sex arising from birth where no consultation among co-heirs is reached, thereby effectively depriving daughters of the opportunity to become the person who presides over the ancestral rites even where the deceased has a son. This is clearly contrary not only to our entire legal order, which guarantees family life based on individual dignity and gender equality and does not discriminate between men and women in substantive rights and duties within the family, but also to the spirit of the above en banc decision.\\n\\nD. Even if the nature of the person who presides over the ancestral rites necessarily requires the designation of a specific single person among the heirs, thereby inevitably resulting in discrimination among heirs, discrimination based on rational differences does not violate the constitutional principle of equality. Therefore, the court may secure the legitimacy of such discrimination by guardianship-like intervention in the determination of the person who presides over the ancestral rites and by considering the various circumstances presented in the dissenting opinions. Moreover, I point out that the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, etc. is proper in that, in a rapidly changing modern society, it can appropriately reflect changes in our society members’ perceptions regarding the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and I state the supplementary opinion to that dissenting opinion."}

{"[2020DA267620]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case and Issues\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Non-party 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the Decedent”) married Non-party 2 and had five children with her, including Non-party 3 and the Plaintiffs. The Decedent divorced Non-party 2 on May 25, 2013, and died on October 29, 2015.\\n\\n(2) Non-party 3 died earlier than the Decedent on June 28, 2011. Defendant 1, who was Non-party 3’s wife, and Defendant 2, who was his son, filed a report of renunciation of inheritance with respect to the Decedent on December 7, 2015, and received an adjudication accepting said report on January 4, 2016 (Daejeon Family Court, Seosan Branch 2015NEUDAN479).\\n\\n(3) The Plaintiffs filed this action seeking return of the forced share against the Defendants, who are Non-party 3’s substitute heirs, on the ground that Non-party 3 had received gifts of real estate and cash from the Decedent (hereinafter referred to as “the gifts at issue”), resulting in a deficiency in the Plaintiffs’ forced shares.\\n\\nb. The principal issue in this case is the scope of inter vivos gifts to be included in the basic estate for calculating the forced share where the represented heir received a special benefit from the Decedent by inter vivos gift before the occurrence of the cause for substitute inheritance, but the substitute heir renounces substitute inheritance against the Decedent.\\n\\n2. Scope of inter vivos gifts to be included in the basic estate for calculating the forced share where the substitute heir has renounced substitute inheritance\\n\\na. Civil Act Article 1008 is intended, where among the coheirs there is a special-benefit recipient who received a gift or testamentary gift of property from the Decedent, to treat the property received as an advance payment of the inheritance share and to have it taken into account when calculating the concrete inheritance share, in order to ensure fairness among the coheirs (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 95DA17885, decided February 9, 1996). If the concrete inheritance share of the substitute heir were calculated without taking into account the special benefit of the represented heir, on the premise that substitute inheritance has commenced, even though the represented heir received a special benefit from the Decedent during his or her lifetime, the substitute heir would acquire benefits exceeding those that the represented heir could have acquired. This would not only impair fairness among coheirs, but also run counter to the purport of substitute inheritance. Therefore, where the represented heir received a special benefit from the Decedent by inter vivos gift before the occurrence of the cause for substitute inheritance, it is reasonable to regard such inter vivos gift as the substitute heir’s special benefit.\\n\\nb. Since Civil Act Article 1118 concerning the forced share applies Civil Act Article 1008 mutatis mutandis, if among the coheirs there is a person who received the special benefit under Civil Act Article 1008 by inter vivos gift of property from the Decedent, Civil Act Article 1114 does not apply, and the gifted property is included in the basic estate for calculating the forced share, regardless of whether the gift was made within one year before the commencement of inheritance or whether both parties knew that they would thereby cause damage to the person entitled to the forced share (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 95DA17885, decided February 9, 1996).\\n\\nHowever, where a coheir who received an inter vivos gift constituting a special benefit from the Decedent renounces the inheritance, Civil Act Article 1114 applies, and thus such gift should be included in the basic estate for calculating the forced share only if it was made within one year before the commencement of inheritance or if both parties made it knowing that it would cause damage to the person entitled to the forced share. The calculation of a concrete inheritance share pursuant to Civil Act Article 1008 is limited to cases where the heir actually received a special benefit from the Decedent (see Supreme Court Decision 2011SEU191, 192, April 16, 2012), and because renunciation of inheritance has retroactive effect to the time when the inheritance commences (Civil Act Article 1042), and the renouncing heir is deemed never to have been an heir from the beginning (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DA29307, decided June 9, 2011), there is no room for Civil Act Article 1008 to apply to a renouncing heir.\\n\\nThe foregoing legal principle applies equally where the represented heir received a special benefit from the Decedent by inter vivos gift before the occurrence of the cause for substitute inheritance, and thereafter the substitute heir renounces substitute inheritance against the Decedent.\\n\\n3. Determination on This Case\\n\\na. The lower court, on the premise that Civil Act Article 1114 applies because the Defendants, who are substitute heirs, renounced inheritance from the Decedent, dismissed all of the Plaintiffs’ claims for return of the forced share in this case for the following reasons. Even according to the Plaintiffs’ assertion, the gifts at issue were ultimately made on February 9, 2011, which was more than one year before the date of commencement of inheritance. In light of the timing and details of the gifts at issue and the circumstances thereof, whether inter vivos gifts were made to the Plaintiffs and the details thereof, and the status and value of the property held by the Decedent at the time of the gifts at issue, it is difficult to conclude that the Decedent and Non-party 3 knew, at the time of the gifts at issue, that they would cause damage to the Plaintiffs.\\n\\nb. Examining the reasons for the lower court judgment in light of the legal principles and the record set forth above, the lower court’s determination is proper, and there is no error that affected the judgment, such as an error of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or a departure from the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged unanimously by the Justices participating, as set forth in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding the right to claim the substitute? (In case of dispute, according to case law) (a) If, due to expropriation of the object of sale, the seller's duty to register the transfer of ownership has become impossible to perform, the statute of limitations for the right to claim the substitute runs from the time performance became impossible, even if the method and procedure for claiming compensation due to the expropriation were not established until after a considerable period had elapsed thereafter. (b) A obtained a final judgment in a lawsuit against B seeking revocation of a fraudulent act and, by return of the original property, cancellation of the registration of creation of a mortgage. Thereafter, the relevant real property was sold to a third party at auction, thereby making impossible B's duty, under the final judgment, to cancel the registration of creation of the mortgage. In this case, A may exercise the right to claim the substitute and demand the return of the dividends received by B on the basis of the above mortgage. (c) Where the object of sale is expropriated before registration of the transfer of ownership under the sale, a purchaser's claim against the seller seeking a declaration that the right to claim expropriation compensation belongs to the purchaser is a claim concerning the attribution of a claim, in which two or more persons assert that they are creditors with respect to one claim, and thus there is a legal interest in seeking such a declaration.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DA71431]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (a supplemental statement of grounds of appeal filed after expiration of the filing period for the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds of appeal).\\n\\nAlthough our Civil Act does not separately provide, as an effect of impossibility of performance, for the creditor’s claim for substitute performance in addition to the creditor’s claim for compensatory damages and the right to rescind the contract, there is no reason to deny a claim for the substitute by interpretation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DA4581, 92DA4598, decided May 12, 1992).\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the facts as stated in its opinion and then held: ① the date of conclusion of oral argument in the prior lawsuit was March 27, 2009, and the real property in this case was sold in the related auction case on July 17, 2009 by voluntary auction, thereby making it impossible to cancel the registration of the mortgage creation in this case, which the Plaintiff sought by return in kind in the prior lawsuit against the Defendant; ② although a registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Non-party 1 had been completed with respect to the real property in this case after the registration of mortgage creation in this case, the Plaintiff was also seeking cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Non-party 1 on the ground of fraudulent conveyance, so it could not be said that, as of the conclusion of oral argument in the prior lawsuit, return in kind was impossible or markedly difficult merely because the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Non-party 1 had been completed, and even if the related auction case was pending as of the conclusion of oral argument in the prior lawsuit, it could not be said that return in kind had become impossible or markedly difficult thereby, so that the Plaintiff could not even seek compensation in value as of the conclusion of oral argument in the prior lawsuit; ③ even if the related auction case was pending, since the Plaintiff could not claim compensation in value as of the conclusion of oral argument in the prior lawsuit, it cannot be said that, in the prior lawsuit, the Plaintiff should have waited for the progress of the related auction case and changed the purport of the claim accordingly, and to say that the Plaintiff cannot exercise the right to claim compensation in value because he did not do so would excessively restrict the creditor’s avoidance claim for restoration to the original state and confer an unfair benefit upon the beneficiary; ④ considering that a creditor who exercises the creditor’s right of revocation receiving preferential satisfaction in substance through compensation in value is a result generally occurring in cases of compensation in value, the present action cannot be deemed contrary to the res judicata of the final judgment in the prior lawsuit or lacking a protectable legal interest; therefore, the court granted the Plaintiff’s claim in this case on the ground that the Defendant, who received a distribution based on the mortgage that had been revoked as a fraudulent act, is obligated to return to the Plaintiff the amount distributed as compensation in value.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle and the facts of this case, where, as in this case, the real property was sold to a third party through the non-judicial auction procedure, thereby rendering impossible the Defendant’s duty to complete the registration procedure for cancellation of the mortgage creation registration based on the final judgment in the prior decision, the Plaintiff should be deemed able, as an exercise of the claim to the substitute, to claim the return of the distribution money received by the Defendant as the mortgagee based on the registration of mortgage creation to be cancelled. According to the record, the Plaintiff, in the complaint, argued that “the contract for the creation of the mortgage in this case had already been revoked by a final judgment as a fraudulent act, and since the Defendant’s registration of mortgage creation in this case has been converted into a right to claim distribution money due to the progress of the non-judicial auction, we seek a declaration of intent against the Defendant, such as assigning the above right to claim distribution money to Non-party 2 as a means of restoration to the original state,” and then, when the Defendant received a distribution as the mortgagee in the non-judicial auction procedure concerning the real property in this case, it can be seen that the Plaintiff, by submitting an application for change of the purport and cause of claim on October 9, 2009, changed the purport and cause of the claim to “seeking payment of an amount equivalent to the distribution money received by the Defendant as restoration to the original state”; thus, it is appropriate to view the Plaintiff’s above argument as seeking not only compensation in value but also a claim to the substitute.\\n\\nIf so, although the court below was somewhat unclear and inappropriate in its explanation, the conclusion granting the Plaintiff’s claim is acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as an error in the legal principles regarding the subject matter of litigation in a creditor’s revocation action, as argued in the grounds of appeal; therefore, the Defendant’s grounds of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, it is so adjudged as per the Disposition."}

{"[95DA56910]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 1\\n\\nWhere real property that is the subject matter of an obligation to register a transfer of ownership has been expropriated by a third party, such obligation to register a transfer of ownership should be deemed to have become impossible to perform; therefore, the court below’s determination, which rejected all of the Plaintiff’s registration claims in this case on that basis, is proper, and the Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 8, 1994, 93DA42016 cited in the argument concerns a case where the obligation to register had become impossible to perform but the obligor thereafter recovered ownership, so that case is different, and its purport is not, as contended, that a transfer registration of ownership should be ordered even while the obligation to register ownership is impossible to perform.\\n\\nAccordingly, it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains, as contended, an error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning the impossibility of performance of a claim for transfer registration of ownership, and the argument disputing this point lacks merit.\\n\\nWith respect to Points 2 and 5\\n\\nEven according to the Plaintiff’s own assertions, the Plaintiff’s registration claim in this case is without merit, so there is no need to further examine whether there was an agreement for intermediate omitted registration or whether acquisition by prescription was completed; accordingly, the argument that criticizes the court below for not recognizing the alleged agreement for intermediate omitted registration or the facts of acquisition by prescription lacks merit without further examination, and moreover, the court below did not even determine whether acquisition by prescription existed.\\n\\nIn addition, a review of the statement of the relief sought and the reasoning in the judgment of the court below makes it clear that the court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim seeking performance of the procedure for direct registration of transfer of ownership to the Plaintiff, so the assertion that it omitted a determination thereon also lacks merit.\\n\\nAccordingly, since it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains, as contended, any illegality, all of the arguments lack merit.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 3\\n\\nEven if the existence of a registration claim such as that asserted by the Plaintiff is recognized, the holder of the obligation to register can only, by exercising the right to claim the substitute object, seek return of the expropriation compensation received by the obligor or seek assignment of the claim to expropriation compensation, and it cannot be said that the claim to expropriation compensation itself vests in the holder of the registration claim; furthermore, the Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 9, 1994, 94DA25025 cited in the argument concerns a case where the obligor actually received the expropriation compensation, and is not appropriate to this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains, as contended, an error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning the right to claim the substitute object or an error of law concerning the attribution of rights to the deposited expropriation compensation, nor any violation of the rules of evidence; thus, the argument disputing this point also lacks merit.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 4\\n\\nWhere two or more persons each claim to be the creditor with respect to one claim, a claim by one party seeking against the other party a confirmation as to the attribution of the claim that such claim belongs to himself has a legal interest in confirmation (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 27, 1988, 87DAKA2269); therefore, it was erroneous for the court below to deny legal interest in confirmation based on the reasons stated in the opinion, but even according to the factual allegations asserted by the Plaintiff, it is clear that the claim that the claim to expropriation compensation belongs to the Plaintiff is without merit, and meanwhile, because the court below dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal against the first-instance judgment that dismissed the claim for confirmation, it cannot be said that the above illegality by the court below affected the result of the judgment. Ultimately, the argument lacks merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the deliberation, and it is so adjudged as stated in the Order."}

question: A entered into a contract with B on 2023. 2. 1. to sell B real property X owned by A for KRW 100,000,000, and received KRW 10,000,000 as a down payment from B on the day of the contract. Under the written contract, the due date for payment of the intermediate payment of KRW 30,000,000 is 2023. 5. 1., and the due date for payment of the balance of KRW 60,000,000 is 2023. 8. 1., each set as follows, and the contract includes the following content. Article △△ (Rescission of Contract) If the buyer fails to pay the intermediate payment on the agreed date, the contract is automatically rescinded. In this case, the buyer may not claim return of the down payment paid. If, due to the seller's intentional act or negligence, the buyer is unable to acquire ownership of real property X and the buyer rescinds the contract, the seller shall return the money received from the buyer by adding interest at 10% per annum from the date of receipt until the time of rescission. Which of the following statements are all correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is dispute, case law shall govern) (a) If B failed to pay the intermediate payment to A by 2023. 5. 1., then unless special circumstances exist, the contract is rescinded without a separate demand or expression of intent to rescind, and B may not claim return of the down payment paid. (b) Even if the above contract was rescinded pursuant to Article △△, Paragraph 1, if A and B continued discussions on the premise that the contract remained valid and A urged performance according to the contract without asserting the legal effects of rescission, then unless special circumstances exist, it is appropriate to regard that there was an agreement between A and B to revive the rescinded contract. (c) If B rescinded the above contract pursuant to Article △△, Paragraph 2, and claimed return of the money paid to A and payment of interest thereon, and A delayed performance thereof, then unless special circumstances exist, the delay damages therefrom must be calculated at the rate of 10% per annum. (d) If A and B agreed to rescind the contract irrespective of the above contractual clause, and there was no separate agreement on interest to be added to the money to be returned due to the consensual rescission, then the money paid by B must be returned with interest at 10% per annum from the date of payment.
label: D
