supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA9123]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\nThe court below, after determining that the real estate sale contract at issue between the Plaintiffs and the Defendant was lawfully rescinded by the Plaintiffs’ exercise of their contractual right of rescission, granted the Plaintiffs’ claim seeking the return of the principal amount of the purchase price as a restitution measure following rescission of the contract. However, with respect to the claim seeking payment at the rates of 5 percent per annum from 1997. 10. 30., the due date for payment of the balance of the purchase price, until service of a duplicate copy of the complaint in this case, and 25 percent per annum from the following day until the date of full payment, it dismissed that part of the Plaintiffs’ claim on the ground that, on the premise that the nature of the amount claimed in this part was to seek delay damages for delay in returning the purchase price in this case, the Defendant’s duty to return the purchase price in this case was in a concurrent performance relationship with the Plaintiffs’ duty to cancel the registration of transfer of ownership concerning the real estate at issue, which had been completed as performance of the real estate sale contract in this case, and therefore, until the Plaintiffs performed the above obligation, the Defendant could refuse to return the purchase price, so that the Defendant could not be deemed liable for delay in performance.\\n\\nHowever, in the case of the exercise of a statutory right of rescission, the requirement that, in returning the money received, one party add statutory interest from the time of receipt is as prescribed by Article 548(2) of the Civil Act; this falls within the scope of restitution to the original status, has the nature of a kind of restitution of unjust enrichment, and is not attributable to delay in performance of the duty to return. Accordingly, where a real estate sale contract is rescinded, regardless of whether the seller’s duty to return the purchase price and the buyer’s duty to perform the procedure for cancellation registration of the registration of transfer of ownership are in a concurrent performance relationship, the seller must, with respect to the purchase price to be returned, pay statutory interest at the statutory rate of 5 percent per annum prescribed by the Civil Act from the date of receipt (see Supreme Court Decisions 94Da47728 delivered on 1995. 3. 24. and 95Da28892 delivered on 1996. 4. 12., among others), and such legal principle would not be different merely because the contractual right of rescission is exercised.\\n\\nAccording to the record, however, it is unclear whether the nature of the amount the Plaintiffs seek to have paid in this part of their claim is a request for payment of statutory interest on the purchase price following rescission of the real estate sale contract at issue, or a request for payment of delay damages due to delay in returning the purchase price in this case. If so, the court below should have exercised its authority to clarify matters and, after making clear the purport of the Plaintiffs’ allegation regarding the nature of the amount sought in payment in this part of their claim, determined this part of the claim. Nevertheless, without taking such measures, the court below, as noted above, rashly concluded that this part of the claim was solely a request for delay damages and made the above determination. Thus, the court below’s measures in this regard misapprehended the legal principle concerning the scope of the duty of restitution upon rescission of a contract and, moreover, failed to exercise its authority to clarify and conducted an incomplete examination, thereby affecting the outcome of the judgment. The grounds for appeal asserting this point are well founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the court below’s judgment that granted the claim seeking payment at the rate of 5 percent per annum from 1997. 10. 30. until service of a duplicate copy of the complaint, and at the rate of 25 percent per annum from the following day until the date of full payment, with respect to the purchase price at issue, is reversed, and the case on that part is remanded to the court below. It is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2011DA50509]": "The grounds of appeal are determined (the statements in the supplemental grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the petition for final appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. The appellate court’s determination on interest and delay damages added to restitution\\n\\na. The court below, based on a comprehensive review of the evidence it admitted, found the following facts: Article 2, paragraph 3, main sentence, of the sales contract for this case provides, “Where the purchaser is unable to take occupancy within 3 months from the scheduled occupancy date due to reasons attributable to the Defendant, the purchaser may rescind this contract.” Article 3, paragraph 2, of the sales contract for this case provides, “Where this contract is rescinded for reasons falling under Article 2, paragraph 3, the Defendant shall pay the purchaser 10% of the total supply price as liquidated damages.” Paragraph 3 thereof provides, “In the cases of paragraphs 1 and 2, the Defendant shall refund to the purchaser the amount already paid (provided, in the case of paragraph 1, the liquidated damages shall be deducted therefrom), with interest added thereon at an annual rate of 3% from the date each amount was received until the date of refund.” It also found that the Plaintiff (Selected Party) and the selected persons, who were the purchasers under the sales contract for this case (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the Plaintiffs etc.”), became unable to take occupancy within 3 months from around December 2008, the scheduled occupancy date under the sales contract for this case, due to delays in construction caused by the Defendant’s financial difficulties, etc.\\n\\nb. Furthermore, based on the above factual findings, the court below held that the Plaintiffs etc. filed this action seeking rescission of the sales contract for this case on the ground of the delay in occupancy caused by reasons attributable to the Defendant, and seeking return of the already paid sale price and payment of liquidated damages, and that since a copy of the complaint in this case was served on the Defendant on March 25, 2009, the sales contract for this case was validly rescinded around April 1, 2009, three months after the scheduled occupancy date for the apartment in this case, and that, as the corresponding duty of restitution, the Defendant was obligated to return the sale price received and to pay liquidated damages. As to interest or delay damages on the above duty to return the sale price and the duty to pay liquidated damages, the court below partially granted and partially dismissed the claims asserted by the Plaintiffs etc. as set forth in (1) below, as set forth in (2) below.\\n\\n(1) Claims: ① With respect to the duty to return the sale price, the Plaintiffs etc. sought payment of the amount calculated at the agreed annual rate of 3% under Article 3, paragraph 3, of the sales contract for this case from each date of payment of the sale price until the date of service of a copy of the complaint in this case (March 25, 2009), and the amount calculated at the rate of 20% per annum under the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, Etc. of Legal Proceedings (hereinafter “the Special Cases Act”) from the following day until the date of full payment. ② With respect to liquidated damages, they sought payment of the amount calculated at the rate of 20% per annum under the said Special Cases Act from the day following service of a copy of the complaint in this case until the date of full payment.\\n\\n(2) Amounts granted by the court below: ① With respect to the duty to return the sale price, the court below granted the amount calculated at 3% per annum from each date of payment of the sale price until the date of the judgment of the court below (May 20, 2011), and at the rate of 20% per annum from the following day until the date of full payment; ② with respect to liquidated damages, the court below granted the amount calculated at 5% per annum from the date of rescission (April 1, 2009) until the date of the judgment of the court below, and at the rate of 20% per annum from the following day until the date of full payment.\\n\\n2. Regarding the distinction, etc. between interest and delay damages to be added upon restitution due to rescission of contract\\n\\na. When one party rescinds a contract, each party has a duty of restitution against the other party, and in such case, the money to be returned must be paid with interest added from the date it was received. The interest added here falls within the scope of restitution and has, as a kind, the nature of return of unjust enrichment; it is not delay damages arising from delay in performance of the duty to return (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DA9123, rendered on June 9, 2000). Accordingly, if there is a special agreement between the parties concerning such interest, the agreed interest rate applies first; if there is no agreed interest rate, the civil or commercial statutory interest rate applies. On the other hand, for the period after the duty of restitution falls into delay in performance, delay damages on the duty to return arise rather than interest as return of unjust enrichment, so the rate for delay damages must be applied there. As to the rate for such delay damages, if there is a separate agreement between the parties, it must be followed, and the same applies even if it is lower than the statutory interest rate (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA26797, rendered on October 12, 1995).\\n\\nMeanwhile, where there is an agreement between the parties concerning the interest to be added to money to be returned upon rescission of a contract, it accords with the parties’ intent, absent special circumstances, to view delay damages arising from delay in performance as also being governed by the agreed interest rate (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA14363, rendered on April 24, 2008). Provided, however, that if the agreed interest rate is lower than the statutory interest rate, it is appropriate to hold that delay damages may be claimed not at the agreed rate but at the statutory rate. This is because, even where there is an agreement exempting the obligation to pay interest to be added from the date of receipt on money to be returned upon restitution due to rescission of a contract, it is consistent with logic and equity to allow a claim for delay damages at the statutory rate when the monetary return obligation falls into delay in performance (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA85342, rendered on December 24, 2009).\\n\\nb. Examining the determination made by the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles, there is a part that is partially erroneous with respect to the Defendant’s duty to return the sale price in this case (that is, excluding the part concerning the duty to pay liquidated damages).\\n\\n(1) First, the interest accruing during the period from each date the Plaintiffs etc. paid the sale price until April 1, 2009, when the duty to return the sale price arose due to rescission of the sales contract for this case, should be governed by the agreed annual rate of 3% under Article 3, paragraph 3, of the sales contract for this case. The conclusion of the court below is the same as to the above period, and thus there is no illegality in its reasoning, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning interest to be added to money to be returned as restitution due to rescission of contract, as argued in the grounds of final appeal.\\n\\n(2) However, the determination of the court below regarding the rate of delay damages for the period after the Plaintiffs etc. demanded return of the above sale price and the Defendant fell into delay in performance cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\nFirst, in light of the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, examining whether there was a separate agreement between the Plaintiffs etc. and the Defendant concerning the rate of delay damages applicable in case of delay in performance, Article 3, paragraph 3, of the sales contract for this case sets the interest rate to be added to the sale price to be returned by the Defendant upon rescission of the contract at 3% per annum, and uses only the terms “interest” or “refund,” without using terms such as “delay damages” or “compensation,” and does not mention “delay in performance” at all. If the Defendant had intended to apply, not only to restitution but also in the case of delay in performance, a rate of delay damages lower than the statutory interest rate, it would have provided likewise for the liquidated damages to be paid to the purchaser together with the sale price if the sales contract were rescinded for reasons attributable to the Defendant, but there is no provision at all concerning liquidated damages as to the interest to be added. In light of these points, Article 3, paragraph 3, of the sales contract for this case cannot be regarded as an agreement concerning delay damages after falling into delay in performance, but only as a provision concerning the scope of restitution that sets the interest to be added to the sale price to be returned by the Defendant upon rescission of the sales contract for this case, as a special agreement under Article 548, paragraph 2, of the Civil Act. Moreover, because the agreed interest rate is lower than the statutory interest rate, it is appropriate to view that from the time the Defendant began to delay in performing the duty to return the sale price, the statutory interest rate, rather than the agreed rate, applies.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to the factual findings of the court below as seen above, a copy of the complaint in this case by which the Plaintiffs etc. rescinded the sales contract for this case and sought payment of the sale price, etc. was served on the Defendant on March 25, 2009, and accordingly, the sales contract for this case was rescinded around April 1, 2009, three months after the scheduled occupancy date of the apartment in this case, so that the Defendant fell into delay in performing its duty to return the sale price, etc. to the Plaintiffs etc. from the following day, April 2, 2009.\\n\\nTherefore, with respect to the sale price to be returned to the Plaintiffs etc., the Defendant has the obligation to add and pay delay damages at the civil statutory interest rate of 5% per annum, as requested by the Plaintiffs etc., from April 2, 2009, when liability for delay in performance arose, until the time it is deemed reasonable that the Defendant contested the existence and scope of its duty of performance.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, held that even after the Defendant’s duty to return the sale price fell into delay in performance, the agreed annual rate of 3% under Article 3, paragraph 3, of the sales contract for this case continued to apply to delay damages on the sale price, and accordingly added delay damages by applying the agreed annual rate of 3% to the sale price from April 2, 2009, the date on which liability for delay in performance arose, until the time it is deemed reasonable that the Defendant contested the existence and scope of its duty of performance.\\n\\nSuch determination by the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interpretation of an interest agreement lower than the statutory interest rate and the rate of delay damages to be added after delay in performance. The grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well taken within the above scope of recognition.\\n\\n3. Regarding the interpretation and application of Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Special Cases Act\\n\\na. The phrase in Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Special Cases Act, “when it is deemed reasonable for the debtor to contest the existence or scope of the duty of performance,” is construed to mean a case where there is substantial basis for the debtor’s assertion contesting the existence or scope of the duty of performance; therefore, the question of whether such contest is reasonable or not concerns the court’s factual findings and evaluation in the case at hand (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 99DA20155, rendered on February 25, 2000, and 2004DA39092, rendered on November 25, 2005). However, where the appellate court maintains unchanged the amount of the claim granted by the first-instance court, absent special circumstances, it cannot be regarded as reasonable for the Defendant to have contested the existence and scope of the duty of performance in the appellate proceedings as to the amount so granted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2002DA34581, rendered on September 10, 2002).\\n\\nb. The court below, after citing the reasons of the first-instance judgment, rejected among the additional arguments submitted by the Defendant at the court below the argument that, at the time of rescission of the sales contract for this case, the Plaintiffs etc. were obligated to pay interim installments and the balance to the Defendant but exercised the right of rescission without tendering performance, and thus such rescission was unlawful, on the ground that the exercise of the right of rescission was an exercise of the contractual right of rescission under Article 2, paragraph 3, of the sales contract for this case, so such tender of performance was unnecessary, and moreover, at the time of rescission of the sales contract for this case, the time for performance of the obligation to pay the interim installments and the balance had not yet arrived, so such obligation could not be said to exist. It also held, with respect to the Defendant’s argument that setting liquidated damages at 10% of the total supply price was unjustifiably excessive and should be reduced, that this too was without merit, considering, among other things, that setting an amount equivalent to 10% of the total purchase price as liquidated damages is a general commercial practice. As a result, the court below maintained as is the amount granted by the first-instance court for the Plaintiffs etc.’s claims against the Defendant for the sale price and liquidated damages.\\n\\nExamining this in light of the legal principles stated above and the reasons of the first-instance and court below judgments and the record, as to the Plaintiffs etc.’s claims for the sale price and liquidated damages in this case, it can be deemed reasonable for the Defendant to have contested the existence or scope of its duty of payment until the date of the first-instance judgment, but from the following day onward, the Defendant merely advanced arguments without reasonable basis concerning the existence and scope of its duty of performance after appeal and was rejected; therefore, it cannot be deemed reasonable to contest thereon, and there are no special circumstances that would lead to a contrary conclusion. Accordingly, as to the sale price and liquidated damages for which the court below maintained the amount granted by the first-instance court, delay damages calculated at the rate of 20% per annum prescribed by the Special Cases Act shall be added from January 30, 2010, the day following the date of the first-instance judgment, until the date of full payment.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, held that even during the period from the day following the date of the first-instance judgment to the date of the judgment of the court below, it was reasonable for the Defendant to contest the existence and scope of its duty of performance with respect to the sale price and liquidated damages, and thus added delay damages at the above rate of 20% per annum from May 21, 2011, the day following the date of the judgment of the court below.\\n\\nSuch determination by the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interpretation and application of Article 3 of the Special Cases Act. The grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well taken within the above scope of recognition.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal by the Plaintiff (Selected Party) is partially granted, and among the judgment of the court below, the portion against the Plaintiffs etc. corresponding to the amounts the Defendant must additionally pay is reversed as follows; and, as this Court is sufficiently able to adjudicate directly on the reversed portion, it shall render its own judgment thereon and order payment accordingly.\\n\\nThat is, the Defendant is obligated to pay to the Plaintiffs etc., with respect to each corresponding sale price listed in the attached schedule, delay damages calculated at 2% per annum (5% per annum minus 3% per annum) from April 2, 2009, the date on which liability for delay in performance arose, until January 29, 2010, the date of the first-instance judgment, and at 17% per annum (20% per annum minus 3% per annum) from the following day until May 20, 2011, the date of the judgment of the court below, and, with respect to each corresponding liquidated damages amount listed in the attached schedule, delay damages calculated at 15% per annum (20% per annum minus 5% per annum) from January 30, 2010, the day following the date of the first-instance judgment, until May 20, 2011, the date of the judgment of the court below.\\n\\nThe remainder of the appeal by the Plaintiff (Selected Party) is dismissed, and the total costs of litigation shall be borne by the Defendant. The judgment is rendered unanimously by the Justices who participated, as set forth in the operative part.\\n\\n[[Appendix 1] List of selected persons: omitted]\\n[[Appendix 2] List: omitted]"}

{"[2019DA216817]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. In a case where, upon entering into a bilateral contract, the parties agreed that if either party failed to perform its obligation by a certain deadline, the contract would be automatically rescinded, if one party failed to perform its obligation, the contract must be deemed to have been automatically rescinded by that nonperformance itself without requiring a separate demand for performance or a manifestation of intent to rescind. However, if the parties continued their discussions on the premise that the contract remained valid and, without asserting the legal effects arising from rescission, urged performance in accordance with the contract terms, or if the other party who had not received full performance accepted part of the performance without any particular objection, then, absent special circumstances, it is reasonable to regard this as an agreement between the parties to the contract to deprive the automatic rescission clause of effect and to revive the contract that had been automatically rescinded. In such a case, the party that has not received performance of the obligation may not exercise the right of rescission immediately without a fresh demand for performance (see Supreme Court Decision of October 27, 1992, 91DA483; Supreme Court Decision of January 24, 2003, 2000DA5336, 5343, etc.).\\n\\n2. a. The court below, based on the evidence it admitted, found the following facts.\\n1) On October 19, 2015, the Plaintiff entered into a business rights transfer agreement with Defendant 2, acting on behalf of Defendant 1, to the effect that “the Plaintiff transfers to Defendant 1 the entire business rights to ○○ grill plates and all rights to patents and design registrations for a transfer price of 180,000,000 won” (hereinafter referred to as “the first contract at issue”).\\n2) On October 22, 2015, the Plaintiff completed registration of the full transfer of all rights to the patents and design registrations subject to transfer under the first contract at issue in favor of Defendant 1. However, Defendant 1 paid only 42,500,000 won of the contract deposit stipulated in the first contract at issue to the Plaintiff and did not pay the remaining amount.\\n3) Accordingly, on July 10, 2016, the Plaintiff entered into a renewal contract with Defendant 1 for the smooth payment of the price stipulated in the first contract at issue, to the effect that “Defendant 1 shall pay the Plaintiff a total of 137,500,000 won, and shall pay it in seven installments between July 30, 2016 and April 30, 2020” (hereinafter referred to as “the second contract at issue”), and Defendant 2 guaranteed Defendant 1’s obligation to the Plaintiff under the second contract at issue.\\nArticle 6 of the second contract at issue provided: “In the event of default, Defendant 1 shall transfer to the Plaintiff the patent rights and all rights pending application that had been transferred from the Plaintiff, and if Defendant 1 fails to comply, Defendant 1 shall be liable to compensate all damages suffered by the Plaintiff arising from delay in the transfer of patents, etc. (paragraph (1)).” “In the event of default, Defendant 1 shall lose ownership of all patents transferred by the Plaintiff and all business rights related thereto (paragraph (2)).”\\n4) Pursuant to the second contract at issue, Defendant 1 paid to the Plaintiff 6,000,000 won out of the first installment of 7,500,000 won to be paid by July 30, 2016, by paying 6,000,000 won on July 27, 2016, 1,000,000 won on August 20, 2016, and the remaining 500,000 won on August 31, 2016. And of the second installment of 10,000,000 won to be paid by September 30, 2016, Defendant 1 paid 1,000,000 won on September 30, 2016, 2,000,000 won on October 6, 2016, and 1,000,000 won on October 20, 2016, but did not pay the remaining 6,000,000 won.\\n5) On January 2, 2017, the Plaintiff sent Defendant 1 a text message to the effect that, “I have waited for three months. It is no longer possible, and as promised, please complete the patent transfer by January 4, 2017,” and on January 4, 2017, a text message to the effect that, “The patent transfer must be completed by today,” respectively.\\n\\nb. Then, with respect to the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendants for payment of the remaining amount of 126,000,000 won under the second contract at issue and delay damages thereon, the court below construed Article 6 of the second contract at issue as an automatic rescission clause to the effect that the second contract at issue would be automatically rescinded if Defendant 1 failed to perform its obligation, and, because Defendant 1 failed to pay 6,000,000 won out of the second installment of 10,000,000 won that was to be paid by September 30, 2016, the above automatic rescission clause was triggered and the second contract at issue was rescinded around that time, the court below dismissed all of the Plaintiff’s claims against the Defendants on the ground that the Plaintiff could no longer seek payment of the price on the premise that the second contract at issue remained valid.\\n\\n3. However, the court below’s determination is difficult to uphold for the following reasons.\\n\\na. As found by the court below, even if Defendant 1 failed to timely perform the payment obligation stipulated in the second contract at issue and Article 6 of the second contract at issue, which is an automatic rescission clause, was triggered, the Plaintiff appears to have thereafter, without asserting the legal effects of automatic rescission, waited for Defendant 1’s payment of the price for a considerable period on the premise that the second contract at issue remained valid.\\n\\nb. Originally, the Defendant had already fallen into delay in performance at that point, because he had failed to complete repayment of the first installment (7,500,000 won) even after the initial due date for payment under the second contract at issue, July 30, 2016, had passed. Nevertheless, on the premise that the second contract at issue remained valid, the Defendant paid part of the installment amount to the Plaintiff several times until October 20, 2016, and the Plaintiff also received the money paid by the Defendant without any particular objection.\\n\\nc. Therefore, in light of the legal principle stated above, it may be deemed that there was an agreement between the Plaintiff and Defendant 1 to deprive the automatic rescission clause of effect and revive the second contract at issue, and thereafter it would no longer be possible to assert the former legal effects arising from the triggering of the automatic rescission clause, nor would it be possible to exercise the right of rescission immediately without a new demand for performance.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below, without specifically examining these circumstances, dismissed all of the Plaintiff’s claims against the Defendants solely for the reasons stated in its opinion, by deeming that the second contract at issue had immediately lost effect pursuant to Article 6, which is the automatic rescission clause. There is error in the court below’s determination that affected the judgment, in that it misapprehended the law concerning the effect, etc. of the automatic rescission clause and failed to conduct the necessary examination. The ground of appeal asserting this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and in order to have the case retried and decided, the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[92DA46905]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence cited, found as follows: while the Plaintiff entered into the contract set forth in the judgment with the Defendant Company, the Plaintiff prepared a memorandum of agreement concerning the operation of a commission consignment sales store, stipulating a penal clause to the effect that, if the tenant failed to enter and deposit sales proceeds by omitting any sales amount, the tenant would pay the landlord, as a penalty amount, an amount equivalent to 10 times the omitted amount, and that such amount would be deducted from the merchandise payment that the landlord closes at the end of each month and pays to the tenant; and in a commission consignment sales store contract, because the landlord does not receive a deposit, monthly rent, management fees, and the like from the tenant but instead collects a certain percentage of the sales amount, the landlord needs to secure the tenant’s accurate reporting of sales in order to secure a legitimate interest, and as the means to that end, the foregoing penal clause was agreed upon. The court further found that thereafter, pursuant to the above contract, while the Plaintiff was operating a commission consignment sales store in which the Plaintiff’s dispatched salesperson directly sold clothing products of the Kolon line at Store No. 2118, Kolon Mad, at the Manmosu Department Store of the Defendant Company, and the Defendant Company’s cash-handling employee directly received the sales proceeds, the Plaintiff failed to register and omitted sales proceeds in the amount of KRW 2,545,500 on the cash register managed by the Defendant Company’s cash-handling employee, and upon learning this, the Defendant Company, pursuant to the above penal clause, deducted from the merchandise payment to be paid to the Plaintiff an amount of KRW 25,455,000, being 10 times the omitted amount, and paid only the remaining amount. The court then rejected the Plaintiff’s argument that the above memorandum of agreement was signed and sealed without even reading its text because the Defendant Company unilaterally put out in advance a printed form for the memorandum of agreement and compelled the Plaintiff to sign and seal it only on the condition that the commission consignment sales store contract would be concluded thereby; and that the above penal clause, by setting the penalty amount at 10 times the amount of omitted sales reporting, which is 100 times the sales commission, thereby permitting the Defendant Company to obtain excessive unjust enrichment, is contrary to public order and good morals and therefore void, or, by analogy applying Article 398(2) of the Civil Act, which provides for liquidated damages, the amount of such compensation should be reduced within a reasonable range. The court held that the evidence cited alone was insufficient to find that the above memorandum of agreement had been prepared under coercion by the Defendant Company, and that there was no other evidence to support such finding; further, that a penal clause is determined to secure the performance of an obligation and differs in content from liquidated damages, and therefore Article 398(2) of the Civil Act concerning liquidated damages cannot be applied by analogy so as to reduce the amount; and that only where the agreed penalty is excessively heavy compared to the creditor’s interest obtained by compelling the performance of the obligation, all or part of it becomes void as contrary to public policy and good morals. As to whether the above penal clause can be evaluated as void contrary to public policy and good morals, the court held that the testimony of the cited witnesses alone was insufficient to so evaluate it, and that there was no other evidence on this point; rather, considering all circumstances revealed in the pleadings, including that the above penal clause is the only means, in a commission consignment sales store contract, to secure the tenant’s faithful reporting of sales in order to secure the landlord’s legitimate interest, and therefore the multiple of the compensation amount must be such as to ensure the maintenance of order in the commission sales store, and that it is in fact difficult for the landlord to identify all omitted sales reported by the tenant, the court ruled that the mere circumstance that the compensation multiple of the above penal clause corresponds to 100 times the sales commission does not mean that the above penal clause is wholly or partly void as contrary to public policy and good morals, and accordingly rejected the Plaintiff’s above argument.\\n\\nUpon review of the record, the above factual findings and determinations of the court below are all acceptable as they stand, and there is no illegality alleged in the theory of the case, such as an error in the interpretation of law concerning liquidated damages or an agreement on a penal clause. In addition, even though, at the fifth oral argument date in the court below, the Plaintiff was urged to assert and prove the basic facts for evaluating the above agreement as void, the Plaintiff failed to do so through to the later oral argument dates that were repeatedly continued and ultimately concluded; therefore, it cannot be said that the court below’s action in not accepting the Plaintiff’s argument for reduction, as alleged, involved any illegality such as failure to exercise the right to clarify or insufficiency of deliberation. All arguments are without merit.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal are to be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the judges involved."}

{"[95DA16011]": "1. We determine the grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant’s litigation representative (the supplemental grounds of appeal stated in the supplemental appellate brief filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\na. Regarding the first point of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to Article 38 of the Act on Industrial Location and Development and Articles 39 and 40 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, even if the project implementer is subject to certain public-law regulations, such as being required to prepare an allotment plan concerning the qualification requirements of eligible allotment recipients, the timing, method, and conditions of allotment, and the determination of the allotment price, and to submit it to the approving authority and the authority having jurisdiction over the industrial complex, and then to allot factory sites in accordance with that plan, the project implementer’s factory-site allotment contract under said Act is no different from an ordinary sale between private persons.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 30(1) of the Act on the Regulation of Terms and Conditions (hereinafter referred to as the Terms and Conditions Regulation Act) provides that “this Act shall not apply where terms and conditions relate to contracts falling within Book III of the Commercial Act, the Labor Standards Act, or other fields of nonprofit business prescribed by Presidential Decree,” and paragraph (3) thereof provides that “where there is a special provision in another Act with respect to terms and conditions in a particular field of transactions, such special provision shall prevail over the provisions of this Act.” However, the Enforcement Decree of the same Act has not yet prescribed the fields of nonprofit business to which the above Act is excluded from application, and no provision governing terms and conditions concerning factory-site allotment contracts under the Act on Industrial Location and Development can be found in the Act on Industrial Location and Development, etc.; therefore, it cannot be said that the Terms and Conditions Regulation Act is excluded from applying to terms and conditions concerning factory-site allotment contracts under the Act on Industrial Location and Development.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and since it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains the illegality alleged in the grounds of appeal, this argument is without merit.\\n\\nb. Regarding the third point of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nThe argument is premised on the proposition that the factory-site allotment contract at issue was rescinded by agreement, but according to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, it cannot be said that the court below held that the factory-site allotment contract at issue was rescinded by agreement; therefore, this argument is also without merit.\\n\\nc. Regarding the fourth point of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held that although the Plaintiff argued that the rescission was due to the Defendant’s fault or that it was rescinded by agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, the effect of rescission of a contract is the same whether it is rescinded due to the fault of one party or rescinded by agreement of both parties, and since the Plaintiff’s claim in this case is premised on the fact that the above sales contracts were rescinded, it would not go further into this point. It then held that the clause in the first sentence of the latter part of the second sentence of Article 16(5) of the factory-site allotment contract in this case, stating that “no interest shall be added to the amount returned by the Defendant to the Plaintiff,” is invalid; therefore, the Defendant is obligated, pursuant to Article 548(2) of the Civil Act, to pay to the Plaintiff interest at the statutory civil rate from the date of receipt on the amount of 2,212,091,890 won received from the Plaintiff as part of the duty of restoration to the original state.\\n\\nHowever, where a contract is rescinded by the unilateral manifestation of intent of the party having the right of rescission, the effect of the contract retroactively ceases, and the performance already rendered pursuant to the obligations under that contract must be returned as unjust enrichment for restitution to the original state. Since this duty of restoration to the original state is naturally borne not only by the other party to the rescission but also by the party who effected the rescission, if the agreement between the parties has been lawfully rescinded, then regardless of whether the rescission was due to the fault of one party, the party must, in returning money already received under that agreement, add interest from the date of receipt pursuant to Article 548(2) of the Civil Act. By contrast, a rescission by agreement or a rescission contract is, irrespective of whether a right of rescission exists, a new contract whose content is that both parties to the contract, by agreement, extinguish the effect of the existing contract and restore the parties to the state as if no contract had been concluded from the outset; its effect is determined by the content of that agreement, and the provisions of Article 548(2) of the Civil Act concerning rescission do not apply thereto. Accordingly, unless otherwise agreed between the parties, it cannot be said that there is an obligation to add interest from the date of receipt to money to be returned due to rescission by agreement (see Supreme Court Decision dated October 30, 1979, 79DA1455).\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, solely for the reasons stated in its decision, held that the Defendant is obligated, pursuant to Article 548(2) of the Civil Act, to pay interest on the above received amount to the Plaintiff; thus, the judgment of the court below contains an error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine on rescission of contracts and in failing to state the reasons for the judgment.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, the Plaintiff not only failed to pay the remaining balance by the due date for payment of the remaining balance under the factory-site allotment contract at issue, which had passed on December 31, 1992, but also, on December 29, 1992, unilaterally notified the Defendant that if it was impossible to extend the due date for payment of the remaining balance to December 31, 1993, it would rescind the allotment contract at issue; and in response, the Defendant, on February 8, 1993, gave notice that it would not comply with the Plaintiff’s request and would rescind the allotment contract at issue. If the facts are as such, the allotment contract at issue was lawfully rescinded by the Defendant’s manifestation of intent to rescind on the ground of the Plaintiff’s fault; accordingly, the Defendant is obligated, pursuant to Article 548(2) of the Civil Act, to return the money received with interest. Therefore, the above illegality in the judgment of the court below has no effect on the outcome of the judgment. This argument is also without merit.\\n\\nd. Regarding the second point of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the relevant provisions of the Terms and Conditions Regulation Act, a term and condition clause that is contrary to the principle of good faith and unfairly loses fairness is void (Article 6(1)); a clause that is unfairly disadvantageous to the customer is presumed to lack fairness (Article 6(2) item 1); and a clause that unfairly reduces the business operator’s duty of restoration to the original state or duty to compensate for damages arising from rescission or termination of the contract is void (Article 9 item 4). In light of the fact that, under the discretionary provision of Article 548(2) of the Civil Act, if a contract is rescinded, interest must be added to the money to be returned; and in light of the fact, as shown in the record, that Article 19(1) and (2) of the Ordinance on the Creation and Sale of Local Industrial Complexes in Jeollabuk-do, which the Defendant is enforcing, provides that when the Defendant rescinds an industrial land allotment contract due to the fault of the contracting counterparty, the amount paid, excluding the contract deposit paid, shall be returned with statutory interest added during the period; the part of the provisions of Article 16(5) of the factory-site allotment contract in this case that excludes payment of interest on the money to be returned is a clause that unfairly reduces the business operator’s duty of restoration to the original state and is therefore void for violating Article 9 item 4 of the Terms and Conditions Regulation Act.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and since it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains the illegality alleged in the grounds of appeal, this argument is without merit.\\n\\ne. Regarding the fifth point of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nUpon review of the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, it cannot be said that the court below held on the validity or invalidity of the provisions of Article 19(2) of the Ordinance on the Creation and Sale of Local Industrial Complexes in Jeollabuk-do, which the Defendant is enforcing; therefore, this argument is also without merit.\\n\\n2. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party. The participating Justices have unanimously agreed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning monetary claims and liability for delay thereon is correct? (In the event of any dispute, in accordance with case law)
A: If the creditor of a loan for consumption, through intent or negligence, receives interest exceeding the maximum interest rate under the Interest Limitation Act, and if, after the excess portion is appropriated to the principal, there remains an amount even after the principal has been fully extinguished, then, absent special circumstances, tort liability arises for the creditor with respect to that portion.
B: If an order of assignment for all of a part of a monetary claim becomes final and conclusive, a set-off by a third-party debtor, who holds a counterclaim against the debtor subject to seizure with respect to that claim, must be exercised in accordance with the respective proportions of the amount of the claim assigned in full and the amount of the claim not assigned in full, relative to the total amount of the claim.
C: Unless there is a separate agreement concerning the overdue interest rate on a surety obligation, the overdue interest rate agreed upon for the principal obligation applies to the surety obligation.
D: Where the time for performance is set as an uncertain due date, the debtor becomes liable for delay in performance from the time the due date arrives.
E: If damage arises due to the tort of the person guaranteed, the identity guarantor bears liability for delay with respect to the identity guarantee obligation from the time of the person guaranteed’s tort.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DA35152]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. Ground of appeal No. 1\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Defendant’s preparatory brief dated September 1, 2006 states: “In addition to borrowing KRW 350,000,000 from Plus Mutual Savings Bank Co., Ltd. by using the apartment site at issue owned by the Defendant as security with the maximum amount of the secured claim set at KRW 455,000,000, KP General Construction Co., Ltd. had debts such as other credit loan debts, and the Defendant suffered damages exceeding KRW 100,000,000 even after deducting the loan principal and interest debts of KRW 350,000,000 offset from the construction price at issue discussed above by subrogating and paying KRW 455,000,000, which is the above maximum amount of the secured claim, to the above bank.” It can be known that the Defendant stated the above preparatory brief at the first hearing date of the first instance court at which the Plaintiff’s litigation representative was present.\\n\\nIt is sufficiently understood that the Defendant’s argument includes the purport that, because the Defendant subrogated and paid the above loan principal of KRW 350,000,000 and the overdue interest thereon, it acquired a claim for reimbursement, and, using that reimbursement claim as the automatic claim, it offsets against the Plaintiff, who seized and received assignment of KP General Construction Co., Ltd.’s construction price claim against the Defendant.\\n\\nAlthough there are some inadequacies in the reasoning of the judgment below, the judgment below, which reached the same conclusion, is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law in violation of the adversarial principle, as alleged by the Plaintiff as a ground for appeal.\\n\\nb. Ground of appeal No. 2\\n\\n(1) Where there is an attachment and assignment order with respect to a monetary claim, the attached claim is transferred from the debtor subject to attachment to the attaching creditor while maintaining its identity, and since the third-party obligor may assert against the attaching creditor any ground that could have been asserted against the debtor subject to attachment before the claim was attached, if the third-party obligor’s automatic claim against the debtor subject to attachment is in a relationship of simultaneous performance with the attached claim, the third-party obligor may assert the defense of simultaneous performance even if the automatic claim arose after the attachment order was served on the third-party obligor and the effect of attachment arose. In such case, since the cause on which the automatic claim is based had already arisen and existed before the attached claim was attached, it is proper to view that the automatic claim does not fall under “a claim acquired thereafter by a third-party obligor who has received an order prohibiting payment” as prescribed in Article 498 of the Civil Act, and the third-party obligor may assert against the attaching creditor a set-off based on that automatic claim (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 28, 1993, 92DA55794; Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 10, 2005, 2004DA37676, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, even if the obligations borne by both parties are not obligations under a bilateral contract having an inherent reciprocal relationship, the defense of simultaneous performance must be recognized where, in a specific contractual relationship, there is a reciprocal meaning between the obligations borne by both parties and there are circumstances under which a correlative relationship in performance should be recognized. Also, where one contract, or an agreement added to that contract, comprehensively includes two or more typical contracts under the Civil Act or civil-law obligational rights-and-duty relationships under the Civil Act (hereinafter referred to as “typical contracts under the Civil Act, etc.”), and the various rights and duties between the parties under such arrangement are closely connected with one another for the same economic purpose, they should not be separated into parts corresponding to the typical contracts under the Civil Act, etc., and only the obligations in reciprocal relationship within the scope of each such typical contract, etc., should be deemed to be in a relationship of simultaneous performance; rather, insofar as the various obligations of one party and the various obligations of the other party are recognized as having a reciprocal relationship in a comprehensive manner, those various obligations of one party and those of the other party should be deemed to be in a relationship of simultaneous performance (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 22, 1995, 95DA1521; Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 26, 2001, 99DA47501, etc.).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasoning of the judgment below, it is ascertainable that the Defendant and Nonparty 1, the representative director of KP General Construction, concluded a partnership contract on July 30, 2003, under which the Defendant was to be the builder, provide the site for the villa at issue owned by the Defendant, and KP General Construction was to be the constructor, build the villa at issue on the site for the villa at issue, and share the profits from sales; that thereafter, the Defendant and KP General Construction agreed to change the contract from a partnership method to a contracting method, and on February 5, 2004, concluded a construction contract for building works (hereinafter referred to as “the construction contract at issue”) under which the Defendant was to contract out the construction of the villa at issue to KP General Construction for a construction price of KRW 1,152,800,000 and a completion date of June 29, 2004; that the Defendant, on September 24, 2004, established a mortgage on the site for the villa at issue, with Plus Mutual Savings Bank Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Plus Mutual Savings Bank”) as the mortgagee and with the maximum amount of the secured claim set at KRW 455,000,000, and KP General Construction, as debtor, borrowed KRW 350,000,000 from Plus Mutual Savings Bank and used it as the construction price for the villa at issue; that KP General Construction defaulted around April 2005; and that, even after the date of approval for use of the villa at issue, May 24, 2005, had passed without KP General Construction repaying the above loan, the Defendant, on June 23, 2005, subrogated KP General Construction and repaid the loan principal of KRW 350,000,000 from Plus Mutual Savings Bank and overdue interest of KRW 36,857,459; that the Plaintiff, in order to preserve a contractual payment claim of KRW 551,588,000 against KP General Construction, obtained a provisional seizure order on January 12, 2005, with respect to the construction price claim for the villa at issue, and thereafter, on July 3, 2006, obtained an assignment order converting the provisional seizure at issue into a principal attachment with respect to the said contractual payment of KRW 551,588,000, attaching the construction price claim at issue with respect to delay damages of KRW 76,768,960, and assigning to the Plaintiff the construction price claim at issue corresponding to the total attached amount of KRW 628,356,960, and that a certified copy of the decision was served on the Defendant on July 5, 2006 and became final and conclusive on August 26, 2006.\\n\\n(3) This is examined in light of the legal principles stated above. The Defendant provided the site for the villa at issue owned by the Defendant as security in order to support construction funds so that KP General Construction could smoothly carry out the construction at issue, thereby enabling KP General Construction to establish a mortgage thereon, borrow funds, and expend construction costs. Thus, the Defendant’s fund support through the provision of security substantially functions as an advance payment of the construction price under the construction contract at issue, and it is proper to view that the rights and duties concerning the establishment of the above mortgage between the Defendant and KP General Construction are closely related to the rights and duties concerning the construction price under the construction contract at issue for the same economic purpose. Therefore, when KP General Construction asserts the construction price claim, which legally has not been extinguished on the ground that it was itself the principal debtor for the loan debt and thus the construction price claim equivalent to the above loan amount has not been extinguished, despite the fact that funding support was effectively made in the manner of advance payment through such funding support, it is consistent with the economic substance of the transaction between the parties and the parties’ reasonable intentions to consider not only the obligation to build the villa at issue and deliver it to the Defendant, but also the correlative relationship with the obligation to cause the above mortgage to be cancelled and restore the position to that existing before the funding support (hereinafter referred to as the “obligation to cancel the mortgage”). If, contrary to this, the Defendant were unconditionally required to comply with KP General Construction’s claim for the construction price, there is a risk that, after performance of the construction price debt, the Defendant may be exposed to the risk of double payment, such as having to repay the loan on its own in order to prevent enforcement of the above mortgage if KP General Construction fails to perform the obligation to cancel the mortgage.\\n\\nTaking all such circumstances together and comprehensively considering them, KP General Construction’s obligation to cancel the mortgage is not, like the obligation to deliver the villa at issue, an obligation that has an inherent reciprocal relationship with the Defendant’s construction price debt under the construction contract; however, in light of the course and purpose of the provision of security, the use of the loan proceeds, the effect of fund support akin to a practical advance payment of the construction price, and the resulting risk of double payment that the Defendant would face, it is proper to recognize a correlative relationship in performance with the specific contractual relationship in question. Therefore, the two obligations are in a relationship of simultaneous performance. Furthermore, the reimbursement debt incurred by KP General Construction as a result of the Defendant’s subrogated payment of the above loan principal and overdue interest because KP General Construction failed to perform the obligation to cancel the mortgage should also be viewed as a modified form of the obligation to cancel the mortgage and, within the extent of the equal amount, as being in a relationship of simultaneous performance with the Defendant’s construction price debt.\\n\\nIf so, even though the reimbursement claim acquired by the Defendant upon subrogated payment of the above loan arose only after the provisional seizure order and attachment order concerning the construction price claim at issue were served on the Defendant and the effects of the provisional seizure and attachment arose, it shall be deemed that the Defendant may assert against the Plaintiff, who is the attaching and assignee creditor of the construction price claim at issue, a set-off based on the reimbursement claim as the automatic claim.\\n\\nThe judgment below to the same effect is understandable as proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law regarding the relationship of simultaneous performance or set-off, as alleged by the Plaintiff in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nc. Ground of appeal No. 3\\n\\n(1) If an assignment order becomes final and conclusive regarding a part of a divisible monetary claim, then, absent special circumstances, independent divided claims are established separately for the portion of the claim assigned and the portion not assigned, retroactively from the time the assignment order is served on the third-party obligor. Therefore, a third-party obligor who intends to set off such claim against a counterclaim against the debtor subject to attachment may designate either the assignee creditor or the debtor subject to attachment as the counterparty to the set-off and make the set-off or assert it as a defense. The assignee creditor who receives such notice of the third-party obligor’s declaration of intent to set off may not object on the ground that the claim portion remaining with the debtor subject to attachment must first be set off or that the set-off must be made in proportion to the ratio of each divided claim amount to the total claim amount (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 8, 2002, 2000DA50596).\\n\\n(2) Examining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the above legal principles, the determination of the court below that the Defendant may assert against the Plaintiff, who received assignment of the portion of KRW 628,356,960, which is part of KP General Construction’s construction price claim against the Defendant, a set-off using the entire amount of the reimbursement claim acquired by the Defendant by subrogated payment on June 23, 2005 of the above loan principal of KRW 350,000,000 and overdue interest of KRW 36,857,459 as the automatic claim, is in accordance with the above legal principles and is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law regarding the scope of claims extinguished by set-off upon assignment of a part of a claim, as alleged in Ground of Appeal No. 3.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. Grounds of appeal Nos. 1 and 2\\n\\n(1) According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below rejected the Defendant’s assertion that, on October 25, 2004, the Defendant settled the remaining construction price with KP General Construction at KRW 432,000,000, and, by agreement with KP General Construction, fully paid the construction price at issue by means of performance in lieu of payment, by selling and transferring three units of the villa at issue (Units 201, 301, and 401) for the remaining construction price at KRW 144,000,000 per unit, totaling KRW 432,000,000, on the ground that there was no evidence to support such assertion, citing the circumstances as set forth in the judgment.\\n\\nIn light of the evidence lawfully admitted by the court below, it cannot be said that the court below, in this regard, selected and weighed the evidence in a manner contrary to the rules of logic and experience or exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence. Accordingly, the Defendant’s grounds for appeal disputing this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAnd to the extent as viewed above, the Defendant’s grounds for appeal, to the effect that the Plaintiff’s provisional seizure at issue and the attachment and assignment order were invalid because they were directed at a construction price claim that had already been extinguished and did not exist by reason of performance in lieu of payment, as alleged by the Defendant, or that the provisional seizure at issue and the attachment and assignment order were invalid because, by the agreement on performance in lieu of payment as alleged by the Defendant, the Defendant’s construction price debt to KP General Construction was changed into and extinguished by a villa sales debt, yet they were nevertheless directed at the construction price claim, also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) According to the reasoning of the judgment below, with respect to the Defendant’s assertion that Nonparty 1, the representative director of KP General Construction, defaulted and disappeared without completing the construction at issue, and that the Defendant caused KP General Construction’s subcontractors to carry out the above window and door work, etc. on the condition that the Defendant directly pay the construction costs, thereby suffering a loss equivalent to KRW 377,000,000 by performance in lieu of payment, the court below determined that although the fact of performance in lieu of payment as alleged was recognized, there was no evidence to support the assertion that the Defendant directly concluded subcontracting contracts with the subcontractors and had them perform the work, and rather, in light of the circumstances set forth in the judgment, the subcontractors carried out the subcontracted work pursuant to subcontracting contracts with KP General Construction, so KP General Construction bore the obligation to pay the subcontracted construction price, and it is proper to view the Defendant, as the employer, as having directly made performance in lieu of payment to Nonparty 2, etc. in lieu of paying KP General Construction the construction price.\\n\\nIn light of the evidence lawfully admitted by the court below, it cannot be said that the court below, in this connection, selected and weighed the evidence in a manner contrary to the rules of logic and experience or exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence. Accordingly, the grounds for appeal disputing this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAnd to the extent as viewed above, the court below properly determined that the execution of the subcontractors’ subcontracted work should be regarded as KP General Construction’s performance of its construction obligations as the contractor to the Defendant, and that the subject to whom the relevant construction price claim belongs should therefore be deemed to be KP General Construction. There is no illegality such as an error of law regarding the requirements for the creation of a construction price claim, as alleged by the Defendant as a ground for appeal.\\n\\nb. Ground of appeal No. 3\\n\\n(1) According to the record, while asserting that the Defendant subrogated and paid a total of KRW 455,000,000 in various debts of KP General Construction to Plus Mutual Savings Bank, the Defendant submitted objective third-party evidence, including the confirmation of subrogated payment by Plus Mutual Savings Bank, which acknowledges the fact of subrogated payment in that amount (Exhibit No. 13), and a statement certification by Nonparty 3 consistent with the Defendant’s assertion of such subrogated payment (Exhibit No. 14), and the Plaintiff has not submitted any special counterevidence thereto. Moreover, the court below itself adopted the contents of the above confirmation of subrogated payment as evidence and recognized that the Defendant, on June 23, 2005, subrogated KP General Construction and repaid to Plus Mutual Savings Bank the loan amount of KRW 350,000,000 related to the construction at issue and overdue interest of KRW 36,857,459. Taking these factors together, it is consistent with the rules of experience to view that the Defendant, on June 23, 2005, subrogated KP General Construction and repaid to Plus Mutual Savings Bank KRW 455,000,000 in excess of the total of the above loan principal of KRW 350,000,000 and overdue interest, thereby also subrogating and repaying the other loan debt of KP General Construction to Plus Mutual Savings Bank (hereinafter referred to as “the other loan debt”), in addition to the principal and interest of the above loan.\\n\\nContrary to the above, the determination of the court below that the contents of the above confirmation of subrogated payment alone were insufficient to recognize the fact that the Defendant subrogated and paid the other loan debt, and that there was no other evidence to recognize it, is flawed in that it failed to conduct a necessary examination or, in selecting and weighing the evidence, exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence, thereby affecting the judgment. The Defendant’s grounds for appeal pointing this out are well taken.\\n\\n(2) And if, as above, the Defendant on June 23, 2005 subrogated KP General Construction and repaid the other loan debt to Plus Mutual Savings Bank, then the Defendant would have acquired a reimbursement claim against KP General Construction in the amount of such subrogated payment (although the Defendant asserted that this was a damages claim, in light of the Defendant’s assertion that the Defendant acquired a reimbursement claim against KP General Construction by subrogated payment of the construction-related loan principal of KRW 350,000,000 and overdue interest thereon, the above assertion may also be construed as an assertion that the Defendant acquired a reimbursement claim).\\n\\nHowever, the above reimbursement claim arose only on June 23, 2005, after the provisional seizure decision regarding the portion of KRW 551,588,000 out of the construction price claim at issue was served on the Defendant on January 12, 2005; unlike the above subrogated payment of the loan principal of KRW 350,000,000 discussed above, there is no material to conclude that KP General Construction’s other loan debt had an inherent reciprocal relationship under the construction contract with respect to the construction price debt at issue, or that it had a relationship of simultaneous performance with the construction price debt at issue; and even if a mortgage whose secured claim is the loan debt had been established before service of the attachment order, the Defendant cannot assert it against the attaching creditor by extinguishment through such repayment. Therefore, with respect to the portion of the construction price claim amounting to KRW 551,588,000, for which an attachment and assignment order converting the provisional seizure into a principal attachment was made, the Defendant cannot assert against the Plaintiff a set-off based on the reimbursement claim acquired by subrogated payment of the other loan debt as the automatic claim.\\n\\nHowever, as noted above in 1. a. (2), the portion of KRW 76,768,960 in delay damages among the construction price claim at issue, for which the Plaintiff received the attachment and assignment order, was not converted from the above provisional seizure into a principal attachment, but was additionally attached on July 3, 2006, after the Defendant had acquired the reimbursement claim against KP General Construction by subrogating and paying the other loan debt on June 23, 2005, and the assignment order was issued, and a certified copy of the decision was served on the Defendant on July 5 of the same year. Therefore, with respect to the portion of the construction price claim of KRW 76,768,960 that was additionally assigned, the Defendant may assert against the Plaintiff a set-off, using as the automatic claim the reimbursement claim acquired by subrogated payment of the other loan debt before service of the attachment order.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below determined that because the time when the reimbursement claim acquired by the Defendant by subrogated payment of the other loan debt arose was after the provisional seizure decision, which formed the basis of the Plaintiff’s assignment order, had been served on the Defendant, and because that claim was not in a relationship of simultaneous performance with the construction price at issue, the Defendant could not assert against the Plaintiff a set-off based on that claim as the automatic claim. In so determining, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the time when an assignment order takes effect and concerning set-off upon attachment and assignment of a claim, and such error affected the judgment. The Defendant’s grounds for appeal pointing this out are well taken to the extent recognized above.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the judgment below against the Defendant is reversed insofar as it concerns KRW 76,768,960 and the delay damages thereon, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination on that part; the Plaintiff’s appeal and the remainder of the Defendant’s appeal are all dismissed, and it is so adjudged with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2009DA59671]": "1. Judgment on the Grounds of Appeal Concerning the Calculation of the Amount of Liability for Suretyship\\n\\nArticle 6 of the former Suretyship Act (prior to its full amendment by Act No. 6592 of January 14, 2002) provides that “in determining the surety’s liability for damages and the amount thereof, the court shall consider whether the employer was negligent in supervising the employee, the reason why the surety undertook the suretyship and the degree of care exercised in doing so, changes in the employee’s duties or identity, and all other circumstances.” In light of the legislative purpose of the said Act, which aims to reduce the burden on the surety to the extent that does not impair the social function of the suretyship system, the court, pursuant to the said provision, must necessarily consider all circumstances under the said provision in determining the surety’s liability for damages and the amount thereof.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since the surety’s liability must be determined based on the amount of damages that the guaranteed person is liable to compensate, by considering all circumstances before and after the occurrence of the cause giving rise to such liability, if part of the amount of the guaranteed person’s liability for compensation has already been paid and payment of the balance is claimed against the surety, then the existence and scope of the surety’s liability must be determined on the basis of the balance, taking into account the circumstances of such payment as well (see Supreme Court Decision 80DA3057, Decided December 28, 1982; Supreme Court Decision 92DA23049, Decided September 14, 1992, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, in Busan District Court Case No. 99GAHAP17596, a damages (tort) case between the Plaintiff and the Non-Party, who is the guaranteed person, there was a decision in lieu of conciliation setting the amount of the Non-Party’s liability for compensation to the Plaintiff at KRW 150,000,000, and that decision became final and conclusive on February 17, 2001; part of the above amount of liability for compensation was then repaid through foreclosure proceedings involving real property owned by the Non-Party; the Plaintiff is claiming KRW 100,000,000 from the Defendant, who is the surety of the Non-Party, asserting that it is part of the above balance; and there are circumstances that may be considered under Article 6 of the former Suretyship Act, such as whether the Plaintiff was negligent in supervising the Non-Party, the reason why the Defendant undertook the suretyship and the degree of care exercised in doing so, whether part of the Non-Party’s liability for compensation was repaid, and the Defendant’s financial circumstances.\\n\\nIf so, the court below should have determined the amount of the Defendant’s surety liability by considering all circumstances prescribed in Article 6 of the former Suretyship Act on the basis of the remaining balance of the Non-Party’s liability for compensation, and then examined and determined whether that amount exceeded the KRW 100,000,000 claimed by the Plaintiff.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, confusing the legal principles on limitation of a general surety’s liability with those on limitation of a surety’s liability under the suretyship system, accepted the Plaintiff’s claim as is without considering any of the circumstances under Article 6 of the former Suretyship Act; in light of the foregoing legal principles, such determination by the court below contains an error of law in misapprehending Article 6 of the former Suretyship Act and a violation resulting from failure to conduct sufficient review.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the Grounds of Appeal Concerning Delay Damages\\n\\nThe obligation of a surety is not the damages liability itself arising from the guaranteed person’s tort, but an obligation arising from the suretyship contract, and as it is an obligation with no fixed time for performance, no liability for delay arises unless a demand for performance is made by the creditor.\\n\\nNevertheless, without making any review as to whether the Plaintiff had demanded performance of the credit guarantee obligation from the Defendant, the court below determined that the Defendant must also pay the delay damages obligation arising from the delay in performance of the Non-Party’s damages obligation; such determination by the court below contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal principles on delay in performance of the suretyship obligation and a violation resulting from failure to conduct sufficient review.\\n\\n3. Judgment on the Remaining Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, there is no error in the part of the court below’s judgment pointed out by the remaining grounds of appeal, such as misapprehension of legal principles, violation of the rules of evidence, or failure to conduct sufficient review, as alleged.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. The opinion of all participating Justices is unanimous, and judgment is rendered as stated in the order."}

{"[2013DA205693]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal\\n\\na. Since the appellate court may determine only the propriety of the first-instance judgment within the limits of the parties’ application for review, even if the Defendant’s appeal is well-founded, the appellate court must, within the extent in which the Defendant objected to the first-instance judgment and sought its reversal, reverse it and dismiss the Plaintiff’s claim as to that part; it cannot, beyond that extent, reverse the first-instance judgment or dismiss the Plaintiff’s claim as to any part for which the Defendant did not seek reversal (see Supreme Court Decisions 86DAKA829 dated July 22, 1986, 95MEU1192, 1208 dated December 23, 1996, etc.).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the first instance rendered a judgment stating, “The Defendant shall pay to the Plaintiff 61,890,000 Japanese yen and, with respect thereto, the amount calculated at the rate of 19% per annum from May 1, 2010 through May 17, 2011, and at the rate of 20% per annum from the following day until the day of payment”; that the Defendant appealed to the effect that delay damages from May 1, 2010 through July 14, 2011 should be calculated according to the agreed interest rate under the facility-fund loan agreement between the Plaintiff and the non-party, which was the principal obligation; and that, however, the lower court, without any particular reason, did not recognize any of the delay damages from May 1, 2010 through November 4, 2010, and rendered a judgment ordering payment only of delay damages from November 5, 2010.\\nAccording to the legal principle stated above, the lower court should have reversed the first-instance judgment only within the extent in which the Defendant objected to the first-instance judgment and sought its reversal, and dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim as to that part; however, although the Defendant acknowledged liability to pay delay damages at the agreed interest rate from May 1, 2010 through November 4, 2010 with respect to 61,890,000 Japanese yen, the lower court, beyond the scope of the Defendant’s objection, reversed the first-instance judgment in full as to the delay damages for the above period and dismissed the claim as to that part. This constitutes an erroneous determination resulting from a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the scope of adjudication in appellate proceedings. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s argument pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nBecause a guarantee obligation is a debt separate from the principal obligation, delay damages arising from delay in the performance of the guarantee obligation itself are separate from the guarantee limit amount;
