The offense of quasi-rape (Article 299) is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist; the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302), is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse by deceit or force against a minor or a person with diminished mental capacity; and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305) is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse with a person under 13 years of age. The offense of quasi-rape differs from the rape offense, which is the basic constituent element of offenses under Chapter 32 of the Criminal Act, in its objective constituent elements, in that its special mode of conduct is taking advantage of a person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist; the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302), in that its object is a minor or a person with diminished mental capacity and its special mode of conduct is the use of deceit or force; and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305), in that its object is a person under 13 years of age and that it is established even if violence or intimidation, deceit or force are not used as the means of the offense. However, like the offense of rape, they all share the protected legal interest of infringement of sexual self-determination, that is, they all require the occurrence of the constitutive result of sexual intercourse.\\n\\nb. Article 27 of the Criminal Act (Impossible Offense) provides, “A person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger. However, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted.” The “impossible offense” referred to in the heading of this provision means a case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of the occurrence of the result or of infringement of the protected legal interest (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO2313, decided October 23, 1998; Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687, decided July 26, 2007). Here, a “mistake as to the means of execution” means a case in which execution has been commenced, but, although the means chosen by the actor cannot, by its nature, actually cause the intended result to occur, the actor, due to ignorance or error, assumes the possibility of consummation of the relevant constituent act. And a mistake as to the object means a case in which the actor, although due to the nature of the object of conduct chosen by the actor the object is defective or placed in a state in which it cannot be infringed and thus cannot actually cause the intended result to occur, assumes the possibility of consummation of the relevant constituent act due to ignorance or error. Meanwhile, in Article 27 of the Criminal Act, “impossibility of occurrence of the result” is a concept that includes not only the impossibility of completion of the offense but also the impossibility of realization of the offense. If judgment is made at the ex post facto point after the act has been completed, all forms of attempted offense prescribed in the Criminal Act can be seen as situations in which the result did not occur; thus, if one does not distinguish between “non-occurrence of the result,” that is, the fact that the result did not actually occur, and “impossibility of occurrence of the result,” that is, the impossibility of realizing the offense, a thwarted attempt and an impossible attempt cannot be distinguished. In other words, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act is a concept strictly distinguishable from “non-occurrence of the result,” which is revealed at the stage of factual determination.\\n\\nAlthough the heading of this provision is “impossible offense,” its content concerns the punishable impossible offense, namely “impossible attempt.” Impossible attempt means a case in which, by the nature of the act, there is no possibility in any case that the constituent elements will be realized, but punishment is imposed as an attempt offense because of “danger.” The precedents take the position that, as the standard for determining impossible attempt, danger should be assessed by considering, from an objective standpoint, whether there was a possibility of the occurrence of the result based on the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 77DO4049, decided March 28, 1978; Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided December 8, 2005). On this basis, the Supreme Court held, ① in a case where the Defendant tried to kill the Victim by making her drink decoction mixed with pesticide made from “chowpuri” or “bujja,” that the Defendant’s act fell under a case in which the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the means of execution, but that punishment as attempted murder was proper because there was danger (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687), and ② in a case in which an indictment was brought for attempted quasi-forcible indecent assault after nighttime intrusion into a residence, that because the Victim had already died when the Defendant intruded into the Victim’s residence, the Defendant’s act fell under a case in which the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the object, but that, because there was danger, the lower court properly found the Defendant guilty of impossible attempt of quasi-forcible indecent assault after intrusion into a residence (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DO5355, decided July 11, 2013).\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of Article 27 of the Criminal Act is that, because realization of the constituent elements in the manner intended by the actor was objectively impossible from the outset, the actor would in principle not be subject to punishment even as an attempt offender; however, in exceptional cases that satisfy the danger requirement from a normative perspective, the actor should be treated as an attempt offender and made subject to criminal punishment. For this reason, whether the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Criminal Act must be judged not by the actor who mistook the means or object of execution, but by whether there is a probability of the occurrence of the result under any condition, when the meaning of the act itself is viewed from the standpoint of an insightful ordinary person. Accordingly, where there is a probability of the occurrence of the result under certain conditions but, because of the circumstances at the time of the act, the result did not occur, it is not an impossible attempt but only a thwarted attempt.\\n\\nc. 1) First, we examine the course of this case. The gist of the original charge in this case is that “the Defendant, at around 02:00 on April 18, 2017, at the master bedroom of his home, touched the Victim’s breasts while she was lying down, blocked the Victim’s mouth, took off her pants and panties, and had sexual intercourse once, thereby raping her.” In response, the Defendant denied the offense at the first instance trial, arguing that although it was true that the Victim was intoxicated at the time of the offense as stated in the indictment, the sexual intercourse was consensual. The Military Prosecutor then added an alternative charge alleging that “at the date, time, and place above, the Defendant touched the Victim’s breasts while she was intoxicated and lying down, took off her pants and panties, and had sexual intercourse once, thereby raping her by taking advantage of her inability to resist.” The court of first instance found the principal charge not guilty in the reasoning on the ground that there was no proof of the criminal facts concerning violence or intimidation, and found the alternative charge of quasi-rape guilty.\\n\\nOnly the Defendant appealed the first instance judgment, and defense counsel filed a statement of reasons for appeal, disputing that there was no proof of the crime with respect to the allegation that the Defendant took advantage of the Victim’s inability to resist. The Military Prosecutor then additionally cited, in the alternative, Articles 300, 299, and 297 of the Criminal Act, which are the applicable provisions for the offense of attempted quasi-rape, with respect to the offense of quasi-rape found guilty in the first instance. This means that, even if the Victim was not in a state of inability to resist as the Defendant alleged, the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape, and thus the offense of attempted quasi-rape (impossible attempt) could be established. The lower court accepted the Military Prosecutor’s argument and held that, although there was insufficient evidence to recognize that the Victim was, at the time of this case, in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and therefore this fell under a case in which the proof of the criminal facts was lacking, so long as the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape, it constituted impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape.\\n\\n2) The Defendant was indicted for the offense of rape and the offense of quasi-rape among the “offenses of rape and indecent acts” prescribed in Chapter 32 of Part II of the Criminal Act. Rape and quasi-rape are result offenses that require the occurrence of a constitutive result, and also offenses of infringement that require actual infringement of the protected legal interest. Therefore, whether the constitutive result of rape or quasi-rape occurred must be determined based on whether sexual intercourse took place, that is, whether the protected legal interest, the individual’s sexual self-determination, was infringed. In this case, both the court of first instance and the lower court recognized that sexual intercourse, which is the constitutive result of the offenses of rape and quasi-rape, took place. However, the court of first instance only found that there was no evidence that the special mode of conduct of rape, namely “violence or intimidation,” had been used, and the lower court only found that there was no evidence that sexual intercourse had been committed by the special mode of conduct of quasi-rape, namely “taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” As to the point that the Victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by the sexual intercourse, there is no doubt. Then, does this case truly correspond to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Criminal Act, that is, a “case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of the occurrence of the result or of infringement of the protected legal interest” (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687)? It should be answered in the negative. This case is not a matter to be discussed in the domain of attempts.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that where the Defendant believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, had sexual intercourse with the Victim, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, then, due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape was impossible and the result corresponding to the constituent elements of quasi-rape did not actually occur, but because, from the standpoint of an ordinary person objectively considering the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act, there was a risk of the result of quasi-rape occurring, impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. However, because the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is a person, there is no mistake as to the object in the sense that the object could not be the subject of realization of the constituent elements from the outset in this case. Further, there was no mistake as to the identity of the object in the Defendant’s selection of the Victim as the object of sexual intercourse. Although the majority opinion states as if the Defendant also had a “mistake as to the means of execution,” it gives no explanation as to in what respect there was a mistake as to the means of execution in this case. It is erroneous for the majority opinion to hold that this case falls under a case in which the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape, namely infringement of the Victim’s sexual self-determination by sexual intercourse, was impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution.\\n\\nThe majority opinion views the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape as a “person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” However, Article 299 of the Criminal Act provides that “A person who commits sexual intercourse or indecent conduct by taking advantage of another’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist shall be punished in accordance with Articles 297, 297-2, and 298,” and thus punishes “committing sexual intercourse or indecent conduct” against a “person” by “taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” That is, taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist corresponds to the special mode of conduct of the constituent elements as a method of offense, and the object of the constituent act is a person. This point becomes clearer when compared with Article 297 of the Criminal Act, which provides, “A person who rapes another by violence or intimidation shall be punished by imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 3 years.” The part in Article 297 corresponding to “by violence or intimidation” in Article 299 is the part “by taking advantage of another’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” It is the same for both rape and quasi-rape that the sexual intercourse, which is the constituent act and also the constitutive result, occurs when the victim is placed in a state in which resistance is impossible. The difference is only that rape makes resistance impossible by “violence or intimidation,” whereas quasi-rape “takes advantage of” an already existing state of inability to resist. The view of the majority opinion is an interpretation that goes beyond the text of the penal provision.\\n\\nThe majority opinion holds that, because it was ex post facto confirmed that the Victim was not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist at the time the Defendant attempted the offense, it was impossible for the Defendant to take advantage of the Victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and therefore the occurrence of the result of the offense of quasi-rape was impossible from the outset. However, does this case truly correspond to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible, as prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act, that is, a case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of the occurrence of the result or of infringement of the protected legal interest? The majority opinion’s concern and legal construction are worth hearing, but an affirmative answer cannot readily be given. As seen above, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act is a concept that includes not only the impossibility of completion of the offense but also the impossibility of realization of the offense, and thus is different from the concept of “non-occurrence of the result,” meaning that the result did not actually occur. In this case, the court of first instance found the offense of quasi-rape guilty. The lower court found that the evidence was insufficient to recognize the offense of quasi-rape as guilty. The Military Prosecutor additionally cited, in the alternative, at least impossible attempt of quasi-rape in case the offense of quasi-rape was found not guilty. It has already been observed that the legislative purpose of Article 27 of the Criminal Act was not intended for such a case. This case is merely a matter of whether the evidence is sufficient with respect to the special mode of conduct that constitutes the constituent elements of the offense of quasi-rape for which the Military Prosecutor seeks application.\\n\\n3) In conclusion, the majority opinion confuses the issue of conformity to the constituent elements or satisfaction of the constituent elements with the meaning of impossibility of occurrence of the result under Article 27 of the Criminal Act. If one follows the majority opinion, it would amount to saying that if the Defendant’s conduct fails to satisfy the constituent elements of the offense charged by the prosecutor, that corresponds to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible, and it would lead to the conclusion that even where the prosecutor fails to prove the facts constituting the elements of the offense prescribed in the applicable provision stated in the indictment, as in this case, the Defendant may be punished as an impossible attempt offender. Such a theory of interpretation cannot be accepted because it would completely hollow out the principle of legality in criminal law, the fundamental principle of modern criminal law.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the lower court, unlike this, held that attempted quasi-rape, which was charged as an alternative count, was established based solely on the circumstances stated in its opinion. This lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state my dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Concurring Opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Park Jeong-hwa, and Kim Seon-su on the Majority Opinion\\n\\nI would supplement the majority opinion’s grounds and offer several views regarding the criticism in the dissenting opinion.\\n\\na. 1) Penal statutes must be strictly construed and applied according to their text, and no analogical interpretation may be made arbitrarily in a manner unfavorable to the Defendant. However, even in construing penal statutes, teleological interpretation taking into account the legislative purpose and objective of the statute, and its legislative history, is not excluded so long as it does not go beyond the ordinary meaning of the statutory text (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DO2162, decided June 14, 2007; Supreme Court Decision 2009DO13332, decided May 13, 2010). Furthermore, examining the legislative purpose of a penal statute, its overall content, and structure, and finding a reasonable interpretive standard that shapes or limits the type of conduct corresponding to the constituent elements by the understanding and judgment of an ordinary person properly equipped with the ability to distinguish things, is also an act of interpreting and applying the law and does not violate the principle of legality in criminal law (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2001DO3531, decided November 13, 2001).\\n\\n2) The majority opinion distinguishes impossible attempt from thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt based on whether there is “impossibility of occurrence of the result” as prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act, and distinguishes impossible attempt from non-punishable impossible offense based on whether there is “danger.”\\n\\na) The forms of crime that the Criminal Act fundamentally regulates are those satisfying the objective constituent elements and the subjective constituent elements, and among them the objective constituent elements involve the performance of a certain act or the occurrence, as a result of that act, of a certain infringement upon the legal interest that the Criminal Act seeks to protect, and that a normative causal relation and objective attribution between such act and result are recognized. Therefore, an attempted offense under the Criminal Act, like a completed offense, has intent as to the realization of a specific constituent element as a subjective constituent element, but it may be regarded as a reduced form of offense in which the objective constituent elements are not completed and the requirements for the establishment of the offense are reduced.\\n\\nb) Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides, “When a person has commenced the execution of a crime but has failed to complete the act or the result has not occurred, the person shall be punished as an attempt,” thereby providing for a thwarted attempt, and Article 26 provides, “When an offender voluntarily ceases the act commenced for execution or prevents the occurrence of the result caused by such act, the punishment shall be mitigated or remitted,” thereby providing for an abandoned attempt. An act that has commenced execution is punished as a thwarted attempt or an abandoned attempt because, although the constitutive result of actual infringement or endangerment of the protected legal interest has not occurred, there was commencement of execution and a possibility that the result would occur. Accordingly, a thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt may be said to be an attempt offense in which realization of the constituent elements was possible, that is, the occurrence of the result was possible, but the offense did not reach completion.\\n\\nc) Originally, an impossible offense means a case in which the actor has criminal intent and has engaged in conduct that appears externally to be commencement of execution, but, by the nature of the act, the occurrence of the result is impossible, that is, a case in which, because there is no possibility of realization of the constituent elements, the offense in principle is not established. However, as a legislative decision on whether to subject impossible offenses to criminal punishment, Article 27 of the Criminal Act, under the heading of impossible offense, provides, “A person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger. However, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted,” thereby exceptionally punishing impossible attempts that involve danger. The “impossibility of occurrence of the result” prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act is an essential marker of impossible attempt, and the content of the constitutive result does not change depending on whether it is an impossible attempt or a thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt. Therefore, there is no basis for interpreting the “occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act differently from the “occurrence of the result” in Articles 25(1) and 26 of the Criminal Act, and because an impossible attempt is also a type of attempt offense, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act must be interpreted to mean that the offense could not reach completion because there was no possibility from the outset that the constituent elements would be satisfied.\\n\\nd) The Supreme Court held, in a case where the Defendant, intending to kill his husband, mixed pesticide into cabbage soup and made him drink it, but the Victim spat out the soup, that, although the Defendant’s act fell under a case in which the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the means of execution, it was proper to punish it as attempted murder because there was danger, and that the lower court’s failure to examine whether the Defendant’s act fell under either case was unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 83DO2967, decided February 14, 1984). The Supreme Court also held that, in a case where the Defendant, believing that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity, inserted his finger into the Victim’s genitalia, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity, the Defendant’s act made the occurrence of the result of attempted quasi-forcible quasi-rape impossible due to a mistake as to the object, and danger was recognized, so there is a high likelihood that impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO7343, decided August 13, 2015).\\n\\nThrough such decisions, the Supreme Court made clear that thwarted attempt and impossible attempt are distinguished, and that impossible attempt is established, from the outset of commencement of execution, when fulfillment of the constituent elements is ultimately impossible but danger exists.\\n\\nb. The dissenting opinion states that, because the offense of quasi-rape is a result offense that requires the occurrence of a constitutive result and an offense of infringement that requires actual infringement of the protected legal interest, whether the constitutive result occurred must be determined based on whether sexual intercourse took place, that is, whether the protected legal interest, the individual’s sexual self-determination, was infringed; therefore, since the Victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by sexual intercourse, which is the constitutive result of the offense of quasi-rape, there is no room for impossible attempt. Furthermore, it states that the majority opinion confuses the issue of conformity to the constituent elements or satisfaction of the constituent elements with cases in which the occurrence of the result is impossible. However, the above criticism in the dissenting opinion is not proper for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) The offense of quasi-rape under Article 299 of the Criminal Act is consummated when a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist is sexually intercourse with by taking advantage of such state. Sexual intercourse with a person who is not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist is neither the object nor the constitutive act of the offense of quasi-rape; therefore, even if sexual intercourse has occurred, it cannot be said that the offense of quasi-rape has reached completion. If the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the Victim with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, but the Victim was in fact not in such a state, then, at the time of commencement of execution, because of a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the constituent elements could not be satisfied, and thus the offense of quasi-rape could not be completed; accordingly, the issue is whether impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. Once the Defendant has commenced execution with intent for quasi-rape, it is in principle obvious, given the logic of criminal theory, that the conduct becomes subject to criminal evaluation.\\n\\n2) The dissenting opinion contends that “sexual intercourse” itself is the constitutive result of the offenses of rape and quasi-rape, but this is contrary to the Criminal Act’s system of separately prescribing rape and quasi-rape as distinct constituent elements. In rape and quasi-rape, the result of infringement of sexual self-determination, which is the protected legal interest, is not produced by the sexual intercourse itself alone, but only when combined with a separate act of the perpetrator or the victim’s state, etc., that infringes the victim’s right of self-determination. Therefore, the dissenting opinion appears to confuse “act,” which corresponds to one of the objective constituent elements, with “consummation,” which means the occurrence of the constitutive result.\\n\\nc. The dissenting opinion states that, because the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is “a person,” it cannot be said that there was a mistake as to the object in this case, and that the majority opinion, which interprets the object of the act as “a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist,” goes beyond the textual scope of the penal provision. It also states that the majority opinion did not explain in what respect there was a mistake as to the means of execution.\\n\\n1) The Criminal Act provides in Chapter 32 of Part II the “Offenses of Rape and Indecent Acts,” explicitly prescribing as the object of the act in the offense of rape (Article 297) “a person,” as the object of the act in the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302) “a minor or a person with diminished mental capacity,” and as the object of the act in the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305) “a person under 13 years of age.” By contrast, the offense of quasi-rape prescribed in Article 299 of the Criminal Act is an offense of sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and “by taking advantage of” means that the actor recognizes a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and that, because of such state, sexual intercourse became easier. Therefore, the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape must be understood as “a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” Because one must take advantage of “another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist,” the object of the act can only be interpreted as a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist. This is because one does not take advantage of another person other than the sexual partner’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist. Since the majority opinion systematically and logically interprets Article 299 of the Criminal Act within the ordinary meaning and scope of such wording, we cannot agree with the dissenting opinion that the majority opinion goes beyond the wording of the penal provision.\\n\\n2) The “mistake as to the means of execution” prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act refers to the impossibility or unsuitability of means, meaning that, by the method of conduct attempted by the actor, the occurrence of the result is impossible from the outset. A “mistake as to the object” refers to the impossibility or unsuitability of the object, meaning that the object of the conduct attempted by the actor cannot be the object that satisfies the constituent elements. As seen above, the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is “a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist,” and the act corresponding to the constituent elements is “committing sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” In the offense of quasi-rape, that the Victim is in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist is not only a characteristic of the object but also a premise of the means of execution. If the Defendant believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and had sexual intercourse with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, but the Victim was in fact not in such a state, then this corresponds to a case in which, because of the impossibility or unsuitability of the method of conduct or the object of conduct attempted by the Defendant, there was no possibility from the outset that the offense of quasi-rape could reach completion. Since, as above, the mistake as to the means of execution and the mistake as to the object cannot be clearly distinguished, and distinguishing whether the case is a mistake as to the means or a mistake as to the object does not affect the conclusion that “the occurrence of the result is impossible,” there is no practical benefit in making the distinction. Therefore, the dissenting opinion’s criticism that the majority opinion does not explain in what respect the Defendant had a mistake as to the means of execution, or that the Defendant had no mistake as to the object on the premise that the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is simply “a person,” is incorrect.\\n\\nd. The dissenting opinion states that, according to the majority opinion, the conclusion would be reached that any conduct that does not satisfy the constituent elements of a crime is always an impossible offense and may be punished as an attempt offense if there is danger, and that this theory of interpretation would completely hollow out the principle of legality in criminal law. However, the above criticism in the dissenting opinion is not proper for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) The majority opinion does not mean that impossible attempt is established for all acts not satisfying the constituent elements; it means that the punishability of impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Criminal Act must be determined only where the constituent elements cannot be satisfied from the outset because of a mistake as to the means or object of execution.\\n\\n2) An impossible attempt under criminal law, like other attempt offenses, also requires intent for realization of a specific constituent element as a subjective constituent element, and conditional intent suffices. Such subjective constituent element forms part of the criminal facts and requires strict proof beyond a reasonable doubt; if the prosecutor’s proof does not reach the level that creates such conviction, the matter must be decided in the Defendant’s favor (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO231, decided June 28, 2012; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO12649, decided December 22, 2017). Therefore, if the Defendant’s intent, which is a subjective constituent element, cannot be recognized, there is no need to consider whether impossible attempt was established in the first place.\\n\\n3) Article 27 of the Criminal Act provides that a person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger, thereby exceptionally recognizing the establishment of a punishable impossible attempt. The majority opinion merely means that impossible attempt can be established only in cases where such requirements for impossible attempt are satisfied, and does not purport to extend impossible attempt to cases where the occurrence of the result is impossible for reasons other than a mistake as to the means or object of execution, or to cases where there is no danger.\\n\\n4) Article 29 of the Criminal Act provides, “The crimes punishable as attempts shall be prescribed in each relevant article,” meaning that an attempt is punished only where there is a punishment provision, and impossible attempt is punished only where there is danger, as provided in Article 27 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\n5) Accordingly, it cannot be said that the majority opinion’s logic hollow out the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\ne. Article 13 of the Criminal Act provides, “An act that does not recognize the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished,” and the majority opinion and the dissenting opinion agree that the “facts constituting an element of a crime” means the objective constituent elements, which are external indicia in the constituent elements of offenses prescribed in the Criminal Act, namely, the actor, object, act, result, etc.\\n\\nHowever, the dissenting opinion concludes that, in this case, impossible attempt is not in issue because it is not a case of “mistake as to the means or object” under impossible attempt, and that the Defendant is simply not guilty. If the meaning of “impossibility of occurrence of the result due to a mistake as to the means or object,” which is a requirement of impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Criminal Act as assumed by the dissenting opinion, is limited to cases in which the actor thought the object was a person but it was actually not a person, then in a case where the Defendant saw the Victim lying down, believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and had sexual intercourse with the Victim with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, but the Victim had already died at the time of commencement of execution, impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape would be established, whereas if the Victim was alive but in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, the conclusion would be not guilty. Such a conclusion is difficult to accept for the following reasons. First, once the Defendant has commenced conduct of having sexual intercourse with the Victim with intent for quasi-rape, whether the Victim was dead at that time or alive but not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist cannot be a reason affecting intent for quasi-rape. Second, from the standpoint of objectively existing facts at the time of commencement of execution, the circumstance that the Victim was dead and the circumstance that the Victim was alive but not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist are the same in that there was no possibility of realizing the constituent elements of the offense of quasi-rape and therefore consummation could not be reached; yet there is no rational reason to treat them differently by recognizing impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape only in the former case. Third, if a not-guilty verdict were rendered on the ground that the Victim was not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and therefore there was no conformity to the constituent elements, that would amount to protecting the sexual self-determination of a deceased victim more strongly than that of a living victim, which is unreasonable.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state the concurring opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Concurring Opinion by Justices Min Yu-sook and No Jeong-hee on the Majority Opinion\\n\\na. This case concerns a situation in which only the Defendant filed a final appeal against the lower court’s recognition of impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape. Therefore, whether the offense of quasi-rape is consummated is not subject to review in the final appeal, and only the issue of whether impossible attempt is established is in dispute. With respect to the distinction between thwarted attempt and impossible attempt, and between impossible offense and impossible attempt, and the relationship between the problem of satisfaction of the constituent elements and impossibility of occurrence of the result, I proceed on the premise of what the previous concurring opinion on the majority opinion discussed, and below I will supplement only the elements of the offense of quasi-rape to the extent necessary to show that the establishment of an attempted offense of quasi-rape in this case is clear.\\n\\nb. Regarding intent for quasi-rape and commencement of execution\\n\\n1) Impossible attempt is a form of attempt offense, and the establishment of an attempt offense requires intent and commencement of execution, while also requiring incompletion of the offense.\\n\\n2) Article 299 of the Criminal Act provides that a “person who commits sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist” shall be punished for quasi-rape. “Mental incapacity” means a state in which a person cannot make a judgment regarding sexual conduct because of mental disorder or impaired consciousness, and “inability to resist” means a state in which psychological or physical resistance is impossible or markedly difficult due to reasons other than mental incapacity. “Taking advantage of” means recognizing that the victim is in such a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and using it as a means to facilitate sexual intercourse. Therefore, intent for quasi-rape is recognized where the Defendant has commenced execution with a definite intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, having recognized such state, or with conditional intent to the effect that it does not matter even if sexual intercourse is committed by taking advantage of such state.\\n\\n3) Commencement of execution of a crime is recognized when conduct that corresponds to the constituent elements or conduct closely linked to such conduct is begun. In the case of the offense of quasi-rape, for example, if the Defendant undresses a sleeping Victim, lowers his own pants, and touches the Victim’s genitalia, then at that point he has begun conduct that can be regarded as a means of sexual intercourse, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s inability to resist, and commencement of execution of the offense of quasi-rape can be recognized (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO5187, decided January 14, 2000). The Supreme Court has held in such a case that even if the Victim woke up because the Defendant performed the above acts, there is no obstacle to the establishment of attempted quasi-rape.\\n\\n4) As the majority opinion has examined, the Defendant’s ground of appeal that there was no intent for quasi-rape in this case lacks merit. Also, in light of the factual circumstances found by the lower court based on evidence lawfully admitted, it can be sufficiently recognized that the Defendant engaged in conduct that can be regarded as commencement of execution of quasi-rape. Although the dissenting opinion does not expressly state so, it appears to assume this. If so, the Defendant’s conduct must be regarded as an attempted offense of quasi-rape unless it constitutes a non-punishable impossible offense.\\n\\nc. Regarding whether sexual intercourse and the establishment of an attempted offense are mutually exclusive\\n\\n1) Nevertheless, I think the reason the dissenting opinion questions the establishment of the attempt offense itself is largely because sexual intercourse occurred in this case. A summary of the dissenting opinion’s argument on this point is as follows. In this case, the constitutive result of sexual intercourse occurred, and the Victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by the sexual intercourse. Therefore, this does not correspond to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Criminal Act, and it is not a matter to be discussed within the domain of attempts.\\n\\nIn this way, the dissenting opinion says that, while the constitutive result occurred, neither the completed offense nor even an attempt offense is established, and while stating that impossible attempt is not established, it remains silent on whether a thwarted attempt is established. To point out the logical inconsistency of the dissenting opinion, we first examine the relationship between sexual intercourse and the completion of the offense or consummation.\\n\\n2) A Korean dictionary explains the meaning of “sexual intercourse” as “illicit sexual relations” or “sexual relations, usually with someone other than one’s spouse.” As can be seen from this, although the term “sexual intercourse” contains a negative connotation, it is generally understood not to include the meaning of coercive elements or sexual relations against the other party’s express or implied will. Therefore, directly linking sexual intercourse with infringement of sexual self-determination creates confusion between the act or the factual result of the act and infringement of the protected legal interest, and thus they need to be used distinctly. On this premise, reconsidering the constituent elements of rape and quasi-rape, rape and quasi-rape do not punish sexual intercourse itself, but instead define and punish as crimes sexual intercourse when it is carried out by a method that infringes the victim’s sexual self-determination, such as suppressing the victim’s will to refuse by violence or intimidation. Therefore, even if sexual intercourse took place as the Defendant intended or desired, rape or quasi-rape cannot be said to have been consummated unless the sexual intercourse was committed by violence or intimidation or by taking advantage of the victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.\\n\\nThis sort of case, in which the completion of the offense is denied due to lack of causation even though what the Defendant aimed for or desired was realized, is often discussed in the context of extortion and fraud. In the case of extortion, if the Defendant used violence or intimidation with extortionate intent but the Victim was not actually frightened and instead disposed of property for another reason, then the Defendant obtained the intended result of acquiring property, but extortion is not evaluated as consummated. The same is true in the case of fraud, where the Defendant engaged in deceptive conduct with intent to obtain property but the Victim, without falling into error, delivered property for another reason. This is because causation between the Defendant’s violence or intimidation, etc. and the Victim’s act of disposal is denied. In rape and quasi-rape as well, even if the result intended or desired by the Defendant occurred, an attempted offense can be established due to lack of causation. Incompleteness of the offense means that the constitutive result did not occur, and it is not determined by whether the actor achieved his purpose.\\n\\n3) Further, one may ask whether, unless sexual intercourse is committed by the Defendant’s violence or intimidation or by conduct taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, there is no infringement or danger of infringement of the Victim’s sexual self-determination, and thus even an attempt offense cannot be established. However, we must consider whether this question is perhaps based on a prejudice that forcing sexual intercourse on a victim is impossible unless there is violence or intimidation sufficient to render resistance impossible or markedly difficult, or unless such a state is used.\\n\\nIn the offense of quasi-rape, interpreting “a state of inability to resist” as a state in which resistance is absolutely impossible or markedly difficult is influenced by the need to balance with the position of the narrowest interpretation, which most strictly requires a degree of violence or intimidation in establishing rape (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO2001, decided April 23, 2009). One of the long-standing grounds for limiting violence or intimidation to the narrowest scope in rape is the notion that, unless the degree is such that resistance is impossible or markedly difficult, rape against the victim’s will is impossible. However, this is not very different from a leap to the conclusion that, if the victim did not resist with all possible effort, the victim consented to sexual intercourse and therefore there was no infringement of the victim’s sexual self-determination, by arbitrarily interpreting the victim’s will. There is a wide gap between the two situations. In everyday life, too, we often fail to respond properly to unexpected attacks, unlike what we would rationally imagine in ordinary circumstances. Even if an act of attack is minor when viewed objectively and ex post facto, the specific circumstances at the time may cause serious fear or psychological or physical paralysis or confusion. Moreover, one must not make the mistake of demanding only the victim to make a rational and desirable choice in an absurd and abnormal criminal situation and then blaming the victim for failing to do so. In other words, even sexual intercourse not carried out by the degree of violence or intimidation or by taking advantage of a state of inability to resist required by the Criminal Act and by the Supreme Court through interpretation of the criminal norms governing rape and quasi-rape may still actually infringe the victim’s sexual self-determination in many cases. And the possibility of that is greater the more strictly the constitutive act is interpreted.\\n\\nReturning to this case, as noted above, the only issue in this case is whether impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. Therefore, if, because of the Defendant’s mistake, sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s inability to resist was objectively impossible, but, when objectively assessed in light of the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time, there was a risk of consummation, the establishment of impossible attempt is recognized. And this is also affirmed where the Defendant commenced execution with intent for quasi-rape but did not reach sexual intercourse. Yet if, instead, one says that because sexual intercourse was realized as the Defendant desired, there was no risk of infringement of the Victim’s sexual self-determination, that can only be called an inversion of the proper order of analysis. In conclusion, the majority opinion’s interpretation based on the constituent elements of the offense of quasi-rape under criminal law and the requirements for impossible attempt accords with the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state the concurring opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2018DO5475]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case and issues\\n\\na. The defendant was indicted on the charged facts of assault and attempted aggravated bodily injury: “On or about December 23, 2016, he assaulted Victim Person Not Indicted 1 and, on the same day, stabbed Victim Person Not Indicted 2 in the chest with a kitchen knife, which was a dangerous object, but Victim Person Not Indicted 2 pushed the defendant’s hand away with his hand, tearing only the victim’s clothing and resulting in an attempt.”\\nThe court of first instance applied Article 260(1) of the Criminal Act to the assault allegation among the above charged facts against the defendant and found him guilty, selecting imprisonment, and applied Article 258-2(3), (1), and Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act to the attempted aggravated bodily injury allegation and found him guilty. The statutory punishment for the assault offense selected by the court of first instance is “imprisonment for not more than 2 years,” and the statutory punishment for attempted aggravated bodily injury is “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.” Thereafter, the court of first instance, after mitigating the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense pursuant to Article 25(2) and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act (the term of punishment for attempted aggravated bodily injury became imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years), imposed aggravation for concurrent offenses on the punishment prescribed for the more severe offense of attempted aggravated bodily injury; however, because the term obtained by adding together the upper limits of attempted aggravated bodily injury and assault (7 years) was lower than the term obtained by aggravating by one-half of the upper limit of attempted aggravated bodily injury (7 years and 6 months), it determined the punishment to be imposed within the combined range (imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 7 years). And within the range of the punishment to be imposed, it sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 8 months, suspended for 2 years, and ordered probation and 120 hours of community service.\\nThe defendant appealed the judgment of the court of first instance on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence. The court below dismissed the defendant’s appeal.\\n\\nb. Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense.” A case in which the statute provides that the punishment “may be mitigated” as above is called discretionary mitigation. When a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, precedents have held to the effect that “it is not erroneous for the court below not to mitigate by law pursuant to such ground of discretionary mitigation” (see Supreme Court Decisions 91DO985 rendered on June 11, 1991, 2005DO6120 rendered on September 29, 2005, 2014DO15131 rendered on February 12, 2015, etc.), thereby taking the position that even if a ground for discretionary mitigation exists, whether to mitigate is within the court’s discretion. And if mitigation for a determinate term of imprisonment is decided, the current practice of the courts is to reduce both the upper limit and the lower limit of the term of punishment by one-half pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act.\\nHowever, there is a question whether it is proper for the court to decide in its discretion whether to mitigate when a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized. In addition, it is said that the method of mitigating both the upper limit and the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half in the case of discretionary mitigation is also improper. More specifically, in this case, it is said that the court of first instance maintained by the court below erred in reducing both the upper limit and the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half when it mitigated the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act. Therefore, the issue in this case is whether the current interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation is valid.\\n\\n2. Meaning of discretionary mitigation\\n\\nSentencing is divided into stages such as checking the statutory punishment, determining the punishment to be imposed, and determining the sentence. When sentencing, a judge must determine the sentence only within the range of the punishment to be imposed formed through aggravation and mitigation of the statutory punishment, taking into account sentencing conditions (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376 rendered on September 11, 2008, etc.).\\nArticle 25 of the Criminal Act provides that a person shall be punished as an attempted offender if the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred (paragraph 1), and that the punishment for an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense (paragraph 2). Mitigation of punishment pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act is a type of mitigation by law and is distinguished from extenuating mitigation (Criminal Act, Article 53), which is mitigation in the exercise of judicial discretion. As to mitigation by law, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act provides the method of mitigation according to the type of punishment. What constitutes grounds for mitigation by law and whether mitigation must be made when such grounds are recognized are separately and specifically provided in the Criminal Act and special statutes. Such mitigation provisions are phrased in the statutory text as “the punishment shall be mitigated” or “the punishment may be mitigated”; cases phrased as “shall be mitigated” are called mandatory mitigation, and cases phrased as “may be mitigated” are called discretionary mitigation. Mitigation of punishment pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act falls under discretionary mitigation.\\nIn the case of mandatory mitigation, if the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized, mitigation by law pursuant to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act must be made; whereas in the case of discretionary mitigation, even if the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized, the judge may or may not mitigate by law pursuant to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. Furthermore, once the existence of a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized and the judge accordingly mitigates the term of imprisonment by law, both the upper limit and the lower limit are reduced by one-half pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act. The interpretation of current precedents and practice remains valid. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. The Criminal Act specifically prescribes the method, content, and grounds of mitigation by law, and its meaning is also clear.\\nThe Criminal Act sets the statutory punishment corresponding to conduct that falls under the elements of a crime, and through aggravation and mitigation by law, as well as extenuating mitigation, it provides that the final punishment to be imposed is to be determined. In other words, the punishment to be imposed is solely the result of a judge’s application of law based on legal provisions. Whereas extenuating mitigation is to reduce punishment solely by the judge’s discretion, mitigation by law is to reduce punishment when the grounds for mitigation prescribed by the Criminal Act are recognized, and whether the method of mitigation is extenuating mitigation or mitigation by law, the method of mitigation must follow Article 55 of the Criminal Act according to the type of punishment. Mitigation by law is classified into mandatory mitigation, in which mitigation must be made when the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized, and discretionary mitigation, in which mitigation may or may not be made even if the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized. If the statute provides that punishment may be mitigated or exempted, either mitigation or exemption from punishment may be chosen.\\nSpecifically, the grounds for mandatory mitigation or reduction of punishment prescribed by the Criminal Act are termination attempt (Article 26), the provisions of special parts concerning voluntary surrender at the stage of preparation or conspiracy (Articles 90, 101, 111(3), 120, 175, 213), false testimony, false accusation, and confession and voluntary surrender (Articles 153, 154, 157), and the familial relationship between the receiver of stolen property and the principal offender (Article 365(2)). The grounds for mandatory mitigation are deafness and muteness (Article 11) and aider and abettor (Article 32(2)). The grounds for discretionary reduction or exemption are excessive self-defense (Article 21(2)), excessive emergency evacuation (Article 22(3)), excessive self-help (Article 23(2)), impossible attempt (Article 27), subsequent concurrent offenses (Article 39(1)), and voluntary surrender and confession (Article 52). The grounds for discretionary mitigation are mental and physical disorder (Article 10(2)), impeded attempt (Article 25(2)), organization of a criminal organization (Article 114), and release of a kidnapped person (Article 324-6). Meanwhile, in the en banc Decision 2017DO14609 rendered on April 18, 2019, the Supreme Court confirmed that even when mitigating punishment under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning mitigation by law applies, and thus when mitigating a determinate term of imprisonment, it cannot be mitigated to less than one-half of that term.\\n\\nb. In light of the principle of nulla poena sine lege, the current precedents and practice regarding discretionary mitigation are faithful to the text and conform to the system of the Criminal Act.\\nThe principle of nulla poena sine lege requires that crimes and punishments be prescribed by law in order to protect the freedom and rights of individuals from arbitrary exercise of the state’s punitive power. In light of that purpose, interpretation of penal statutes must be strict, and interpretation beyond the possible meaning of the language in a manner unfavorable to the defendant is not permitted under the prohibition on expansive interpretation, which is part of the principle of nulla poena sine lege (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO17847 rendered on March 10, 2016, etc.). When interpreting statutes, systematic and logical methods of interpretation may be used, taking into account legislative intent and purpose, legislative and amendment history, harmony with the overall legal order, and the relationship with other statutes, but if the text itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, in principle there is no need to use such interpretive methods, or their use is necessarily limited. This is even more so in the interpretation of penal statutes to which the principle of nulla poena sine lege applies (see en banc Supreme Court Decision 2015DO8335 rendered on December 21, 2017).\\nThe Criminal Act expresses mandatory mitigation of punishment in the text as “shall be mitigated,” while in the case of discretionary mitigation, like extenuating mitigation, it expresses the punishment in the text as “may be mitigated.” The words “may” denote the possibility or general ability of some proposition and include the meaning that it “may not” be done. In light of the meaning of the phrase “may,” the legislator, in cases of discretionary mitigation, has allowed punishment to be mitigated or not mitigated depending on the circumstances, and has conferred that authority or discretion on the judge. Such an interpretation is not only natural in terms of the text, but also close to everyday language usage and readily understandable to anyone. So long as it accords with the text and the legislator’s intent, it does not constitute analogical interpretation prohibited under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\nMeanwhile, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act prescribes the method of mitigation by law according to the type of punishment, and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act provides that “When reducing determinate imprisonment or determinate penal detention, the term shall be reduced by one-half.” It is clear from the text that, when reducing a determinate term of imprisonment, not only one of the “minimum term” or “maximum term” is reduced by one-half, but the “term of punishment,” that is, both the maximum and minimum statutory terms, are reduced by one-half. Since the punishment to be imposed becomes the final standard for the sentence, its scope must be strictly determined according to law, and unless there is a separate express provision, it is not possible to recognize other grounds for mitigation of a different nature that do not fall within the grounds for aggravation or mitigation enumerated in Article 56 of the Criminal Act (see en banc Supreme Court Decision 2017DO14609 rendered on April 18, 2019). Accordingly, in the case of mitigation by law for a determinate term of imprisonment, methods such as reducing only either the maximum term or the minimum term by one-half, or mitigating beyond one-half, instead of reducing both the maximum and minimum terms as provided in Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, cannot be permitted under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nc. The Criminal Act distinguishes discretionary mitigation from mandatory mitigation, and precedents and practice clearly distinguish the two.\\nAs noted above, most grounds for mitigation by law are grounds related to the requirements for the establishment of a crime, such as satisfaction of the elements of an offense, unlawfulness, or culpability, or are grounds related to the degree of illegality or the degree of infringement of the protected legal interest. The legislator, after designating important matters related to the establishment and punishment of crimes as requirements for mitigation by law, has classified and prescribed them as mandatory mitigation or discretionary mitigation, comprehensively considering the general effect or importance that such requirements have on the establishment of crimes or determination of the scope of punishment.\\nConsidering the purpose of distinguishing and prescribing grounds for mandatory mitigation and grounds for discretionary mitigation as above, their legal effects must also be clearly distinguished. For example, impeded attempt, in which execution of the crime has been commenced but completion of the criminal act has not been achieved due to external circumstances, is prescribed as discretionary mitigation, whereas termination attempt, in which execution of the crime has been commenced but the act is voluntarily discontinued or the result is prevented before completion, is prescribed as mandatory mitigation; accordingly, their legal effects must be clearly distinguished. The legal evaluation of cases in which the offender commenced execution to realize the unlawful act and thereby created a risk of infringement of a legal interest but then made efforts to return to legality on his or her own (termination attempt), and cases in which the offender’s intent to realize the unlawful act remains unchanged but the result of infringement of the legal interest did not occur due to external factors (impeded attempt), must inevitably differ significantly. Under current practice and precedents, in the case of termination attempt, both the upper and lower limits of the statutory punishment are reduced by one-half, whereas in the case of impeded attempt, depending on the degree of risk created to the legal interest, mitigation of the statutory punishment may not be made or both the upper and lower limits may be reduced by one-half, and the choice is left to the judge’s discretion. However, if, unlike this, one interprets the minimum term of the statutory punishment as being reduced by one-half in both termination attempt and impeded attempt, and the maximum term of the statutory punishment as being reduced by one-half only in the case of termination attempt and not reduced in the case of impeded attempt, one ignores the need for legal evaluation of termination attempt and impeded attempt as well as the judge’s case-specific evaluation according to individual circumstances, thereby rendering meaningless the legislative purpose of distinguishing mandatory mitigation from discretionary mitigation.\\nd. There is no error in the current practice that if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, there is no need to bother with discretionary mitigation.\\nThe Criminal Act provides, with respect to the order of application when grounds for aggravation and mitigation of punishment coexist, that aggravation by the principal provision of the special part, aggravation under Article 34(2), aggravation for recidivism, mitigation by law, aggravation for concurrent offenses, and extenuating mitigation are applied in that order (Article 56), and the punishment to be imposed is calculated through the process of aggravation and mitigation according to this order. Discretionary mitigation is a type of mitigation by law, and when the existence of the relevant ground for mitigation is recognized, whether to actually perform the corresponding mitigation should be independently determined by considering the weight the ground for mitigation such as diminished capacity, attempt, or voluntary surrender has in the act’s unlawfulness or the illegality of the result, and the degree to which it affected the offense. However, to assess the extent to which the relevant ground for discretionary mitigation occupies in the unlawfulness of the act or illegality of the result of the offense, consideration of other sentencing conditions will inevitably be necessary.\\nIn addition, it cannot be legally or logically wrong for a judge, in the process of determining the punishment to be imposed, to decide whether to apply discretionary mitigation while mentally envisioning the final sentence, taking into account sentencing conditions for the defendant. Sentencing, that is, determination of punishment, consists of the process of selecting the type of punishment based on the statutory punishment, then aggravating or mitigating it to determine the punishment to be imposed, and then determining the specific sentence within the range of that punishment to be imposed. Mitigation by law is provided in Article 55 of the Criminal Act, together with sentencing conditions (Article 51), voluntary surrender and confession (Article 52), extenuating mitigation (Article 53), selection of punishment and extenuating mitigation (Article 54), and the order of aggravation and mitigation (Article 56), in Part 1, Chapter 3, Section 2, “Sentencing.” Discretionary mitigation is mitigation by law within the process for sentencing. In sentencing, considerations of sentencing conditions are indispensable for a judge to decide matters in which discretion is granted to the judge, such as the selection of punishment or extenuating mitigation. It is difficult to imagine a judge selecting the type of punishment or deciding whether to apply extenuating mitigation without considering sentencing conditions. Therefore, once the legislature has conferred on the judge discretion or authority regarding discretionary mitigation, it is in fact difficult for the judge, in deciding whether to mitigate, to completely exclude consideration of other sentencing conditions and to deliberate solely on the ground for discretionary mitigation.\\nIn current practice, even if there is a ground for discretionary mitigation, the method of not bothering to apply discretionary mitigation unless it is necessary to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed has been accepted. However, this practice does not mean that the sentence is first determined and then the question of discretionary mitigation is decided. As noted above, since the legislature has conferred discretionary mitigation on the judge’s discretion or authority, the judge necessarily cannot avoid considering other sentencing conditions apart from the ground for discretionary mitigation in deciding whether to apply discretionary mitigation, and in that process may to some extent mentally sketch the sentence. Accordingly, current practice can be understood to mean that, within this process of judgment, there is no practical benefit to bothering with discretionary mitigation unless it is necessary to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, and thus it is sufficient to consider it as a sentencing factor or sentencing condition under the sentencing guidelines. If there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, it should not be deemed unlawful for the current practice not to bother with discretionary mitigation.\\ne. A judge is granted broad discretion from the point a guilty verdict is affirmed to the point of determining the sentence, and the judge’s discretion regarding discretionary mitigation is one of them and cannot be regarded as improper.\\nThe Criminal Act prescribes that one offense may be punished by several types of punishment and then leaves it to the court to determine the type of punishment to be applied to the defendant (Article 54). Most penal provisions, except for treason (Criminal Act, Article 93), which prescribes only death, prescribe as principal punishments two or more of the types of punishment set forth in Article 41(1) through (8) of the Criminal Act (death, imprisonment for life, penal detention for life, determinate imprisonment, determinate penal detention, deprivation of qualifications, suspension of qualifications, fine, detention, and petty fine), thereby conferring on the judge the authority to select the type of punishment most suitable for the case and the defendant. The legislature prescribed various types of punishment and a broad range of sentencing for individual crimes and then made the judge first select the type of punishment and determine the specific sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed. This is because the legislature could not predefine in advance a proper sentence that takes into account all sentencing conditions for each individual offense, so it granted the judge considerable discretion starting with the selection of the type of punishment.\\nFurthermore, a judge may mitigate the punishment when there are grounds to consider circumstances of the offense with respect to the punishment to be imposed after all aggravation and mitigation by law have been made (Criminal Act, Article 53). This is called judicial mitigation, extenuating mitigation, or mitigation in consideration of circumstances, and is the final mitigation applied when, even after all mitigation by law has been made, a sentence lower than the punishment to be imposed must be imposed (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO985 rendered on June 11, 1991, etc.), functioning as a device to correct cases in which the statutory punishment or the punishment to be imposed after aggravation and mitigation by law is excessively severe.\\nUltimately, the judge determines the sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed, considering all sentencing conditions and referring to the sentencing guidelines of the Sentencing Commission.\\nAs such, examining the concrete sentencing process that a judge carries out to determine the sentence after the facts constituting the offense are found guilty reveals that the judge is granted broad discretion. This is a measure chosen for objective, reasonable, and specifically appropriate sentencing by fully considering all sentencing conditions in each individual case, from the selection of the type of punishment to the determination of the sentence. Considering these wide-ranging discretions granted to the judge, it cannot be said to be unreasonable to interpret that the judge has the authority or discretion to decide whether to mitigate with respect to discretionary mitigation. The need for and method of proper control of such judicial discretion are separate issues.\\n\\nf. There is no need to uniformly define the legal effect of discretionary mitigation.\\nEven if the existence of a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, there are cases in which applying mitigation by law pursuant to that ground would instead offend the notion of justice. There are cases where a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized but mitigation pursuant thereto is deemed appropriate not to be made, such as cases where, even though the offense is an attempt and the constitutive result did not occur, a result of grave severity nearly identical to a completed offense has occurred (for example, in homicide, where the victim did not die but remained in a coma for a long period or became a vegetative patient), or cases where the offense was committed while in a diminished capacity state but mitigating punishment on account of diminished capacity would be inappropriate. In other words, the Criminal Act’s provision that punishment “may be mitigated” means that even if a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, there may be cases where mitigation pursuant thereto is necessary and cases where it is not necessary, so that where the effect of reducing unlawfulness of the act or result due to discretionary mitigation is minimal or the degree of reduction of the offender’s culpability is low, punishment may be imposed with a heavier punishment to be imposed without mitigation. And the authority or discretion to make that judgment is conferred on the judge. There is no need to interpret it so as to produce a uniform legal effect without considering these various situations.\\n\\n3. Resolution of this case\\n\\na. For the reasons stated in its opinion, the court below affirmed the first-instance judgment that found both the assault offense and attempted aggravated bodily injury offense guilty and, with respect to attempted aggravated bodily injury, mitigated punishment for attempt pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act and then reduced both the upper and lower limits of the term by one-half pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, and then determined the punishment to be imposed after aggravation for concurrent offenses. In light of the legal principles noted above, the above measures of the court below are lawful.\\n\\nb. Meanwhile, the argument to the effect that the court below’s sentencing determination is unlawful because it did not reflect the settlement with Victim Person Not Indicted 1 ultimately amounts to an argument of inappropriateness of sentence. However, according to Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, a final appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence is allowed only in cases in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years has been imposed. In this case, where a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the defendant, arguments to the effect that the sentence is too severe and improper or that probation and the community service order should be reduced do not constitute lawful grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the final appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a concurring opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek to the separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Justice Lee Gi-taek’s separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The following is the face of our criminal trials.\\n\\n(1) Defendants who committed the same offense and have the same grounds for aggravation and mitigation of punishment are punished with different punishments to be imposed.\\n(2) In a guilty judgment, the sentence corresponding to the disposition is determined first, and then the punishment to be imposed, which is the range of the sentence, is determined.\\n(3) It is lawful to set the punishment to be imposed for a defendant’s same offense at 3 years to 30 years, and it is also lawful to set it at 4.5 months to 3 years and 9 months.\\n(4) When aggravation for concurrent offenses is imposed among several offenses with different punishments, which offense’s prescribed punishment is aggravated depends on the judge’s discretion.\\n(5) Even when the sentence is set at the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, an appeal may be filed on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence.\\n(6) In order to accept the appellate ground of inappropriateness of sentence and impose a lighter punishment than in the first instance, the part applying the law to determine the punishment to be imposed must be revised.\\nThe current face of criminal trials as described in (1) through (6) above appears even without applying extenuating mitigation under Article 53 of the Criminal Act, and it should be regarded not merely as undesirable but as unlawful. Nevertheless, the majority opinion seeks to continue such trials, whereas the separate opinion seeks to correct them and conduct proper trials. Below, the problems arising under the current practice regarding discretionary mitigation as in the majority opinion are identified, and solutions thereto are proposed.\\n\\nb. In the Criminal Act, the provision that punishment “may be mitigated” as a ground for mitigation of punishment is called discretionary mitigation in practice. The current practice of the courts understands the above text as conferring on the judge authority or discretion to mitigate or not mitigate. Because of such authority or discretion, in the case of discretionary mitigation, the punishment to be imposed exists in two forms. Taking the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense under Article 258-2(3), (1), and Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act (imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years) as an example, if the punishment is mitigated pursuant to Article 25(2) and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, the punishment to be imposed appears in the form of “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years”; if the punishment is not mitigated, the punishment to be imposed appears in the form of “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.” Current practice allows the judge to determine the punishment to be imposed by choosing one of those two forms depending on whether to apply discretionary mitigation, and then to determine the sentence within that range.
