Since whether to mitigate is within the judge’s discretion, in effect sentencing is conducted within the combined range of the two, that is, imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years.\\nThe new interpretive theory based on the correct understanding of discretionary mitigation argued below in the separate opinion (hereinafter the “new interpretive theory”) is as follows. In the case of attempted aggravated bodily injury, the statement in Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act that the punishment “may be mitigated” means that the sentence may be determined across both the range “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years,” in which mitigation is made pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, and the range “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” in which no mitigation is made, which ultimately means that the punishment to be imposed is determined as “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years,” combining the two ranges. As a result, the same conclusion is reached as if only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half while the upper limit is left unchanged, but this is the result of combining the above two ranges and does not mean that the upper limit is not mitigated.\\nFrom the standpoint of the legal effect of discretionary mitigation, current practice can be called an “election discretion” because one of two punishments to be imposed is selected, whereas the new interpretive theory can be called “automatic determination” because the same legal effect (the punishment to be imposed) always arises.\\nMeanwhile, before its amendment by Act No. 15982 on December 18, 2018, Article 10(2) of the former Criminal Act provided mandatory mitigation of punishment for a person with diminished capacity, but with the amendment of that statute, mitigation of punishment for a person with diminished capacity was changed to discretionary. Claims of diminished capacity and the determination thereof are frequently at issue in practice, so the importance of the interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation has increased as a result of the amendment of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nc. The current practice regarding discretionary mitigation has understood that when there is a ground for mandatory mitigation, mitigation by law is always made, but when there is a ground for discretionary mitigation, it is “not necessary to mitigate unless needed to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed.” Taking attempted aggravated bodily injury as an example, as noted above, depending on whether the judge mitigates for attempt, two forms of punishment to be imposed are possible, such as “imprisonment from 6 months to 5 years” and “imprisonment from 1 year to 10 years.” However, because mitigation is limited to cases where the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed and is “needed to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed,” in the end the judge is made to determine the sentence first, then if the sentence is less than 1 year apply mitigation, and if the sentence is 1 year or more not apply mitigation. As seen in the above example, “where needed to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed” means where the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed before mitigation, and this means that discretion as to whether to mitigate is ultimately a sentencing consideration. The process of determining the punishment to be imposed and sentencing should be distinguished. According to the majority opinion seeking to maintain the current practice, the following problems arise.\\n\\n1) Current practice does not faithfully reflect the actual decision-making process of judges in criminal trials.\\nIn the case of attempted aggravated bodily injury, according to current practice, depending on whether attempt mitigation is applied, two punishments to be imposed are possible: imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, and imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years. Current practice in effect determines the sentence within the range of imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years, and then notes in the judgment whether mitigation has been applied depending on which of the two punishments to be imposed the sentence falls into. According to the wording of the judgment, the process consists of two stages: discretionary selection of the punishment to be imposed and determination of the sentence. However, this differs greatly not only from the actual decision-making process of judges handling criminal trials, but also from decision-making in our everyday life.\\nFor example, in an everyday situation, if one is to purchase an item by first choosing either the range of “300,000 won to 700,000 won” or the range of “500,000 won to 1,000,000 won,” and then purchasing within the chosen range, a reasonable person would think this is equivalent to being able to purchase within the entire range of “300,000 won to 1,000,000 won.” One would not first determine one of the two ranges and then think of purchasing within that range. Nevertheless, in the above example, the current practice is to choose the range “300,000 won to 700,000 won” from the ranges “300,000 won to 700,000 won” and “500,000 won to 1,000,000 won,” and then purchase an item worth 600,000 won within that range, whereas the new interpretive theory is to directly purchase an item worth 600,000 won within the combined range of “300,000 won to 1,000,000 won.” Judges handling actual criminal trials also do not in fact think in the unnecessary two-stage structure of deciding whether to apply discretionary mitigation and then selecting the sentence accordingly as in current practice; rather, taking into account the fact that grounds for discretionary mitigation exist, they determine the sentence within the combined range of the above two punishments to be imposed (in the case of attempted aggravated bodily injury, imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years). Thus, current practice, while failing to reflect the actual decision-making process of judges, adopts an unnecessary two-stage judgment structure that does not conform to reality.\\nBy contrast, the new interpretive theory directly determines the sentence within the combined range of the above two ranges by setting as the punishment to be imposed a range in which only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half. This is consistent with the actual decision-making process of judges.\\n\\n2) Current practice is contrary to the structure of judicial reasoning and violates Article 56 of the Criminal Act.\\nThe structure of judicial reasoning is no different from a judge’s structure of reasoning. A judge reaches a conclusion by determining the arguments and facts of the parties that may affect the result of the trial in a legal, logical, and systematic order of reasoning. In other words, once the judicial reasoning structure is followed, the conclusion (the disposition) is automatically derived. Here, arguments and facts that may affect the conclusion are called “legal requirements,” the result of applying law thereto is called the “legal effect,” and the legal, logical, and systematic order of reasoning can be called the “reasoning structure.” A trial is the process of deriving the legal effect corresponding to the legal requirements according to the reasoning structure. Changing or modifying the order in which legal requirements are determined as established in the reasoning structure cannot be permitted. In civil cases, after determining the cause of action and defenses, the court determines a rejoinder, but depending on how the rejoinder is decided, the court cannot retroactively revise its determination of the cause of action or defenses. Furthermore, after the disposition is determined, revising the determination of the cause of action or defenses again is even less permissible.\\nIn criminal trials, if the judge finds the facts constituting the offense through evidence examination, the judge determines the punishment to be imposed through the process of applying the relevant statutes, and then determines the sentence within that range. Application of the law means first identifying the statutory provision applicable to the relevant facts and checking the statutory punishment, and then, pursuant to Article 56 of the Criminal Act, aggravation and mitigation are applied in the following order: “1. aggravation by the principal provision of the specific part; 2. aggravation under Article 34(2); 3. aggravation for recidivism; 4. mitigation by law; 5. aggravation for concurrent offenses; 6. extenuating mitigation,” thereby determining the punishment to be imposed. Within the range of the punishment to be imposed thus determined, the judge determines the sentence by considering all sentencing conditions for the defendant. Since this process is the reasoning structure for determining the sentence, which may be called the final conclusion of a criminal trial, failure to follow or going against this process cannot be permitted. However, as noted above, current practice limits discretionary mitigation to situations where “the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed,” which is no different from first determining the final sentence and then deciding or modifying whether mitigation by law regarding discretionary mitigation should apply, thereby adjusting the punishment to be imposed to fit the sentence. The process of reasoning regarding the punishment to be imposed and the sentence under current practice is no different from the proposition that when a set of legal effects (no mitigation) resulting from applying the legal requirements (attempt, etc., grounds for discretionary mitigation) do not conform to the conclusion (sentence), those legal effects can be differently applied in the exercise of discretion (mitigation applied). This is logically improper, and making the determination of mitigation by law after first determining the sentence violates Article 56 of the Criminal Act, which prescribes the order of aggravation and mitigation of punishment, and is unlawful.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, if a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the same legal effect, namely a changed punishment to be imposed, always arises, so the problem of deciding or revising the determination of mitigation by law according to the sentence in contravention of the structure of criminal adjudication does not occur.\\n\\n3) Current practice is contrary to the principle of nulla poena sine lege in that the punishment to be imposed becomes unclear when grounds for discretionary mitigation are recognized.\\nThe principle of nulla poena sine lege provided in Article 12(1) of the Constitution has as its core content the requirement that crimes and punishments be prescribed by formal statutory law enacted by the legislature; furthermore, even if prescribed by formal statutory law, it requires that the elements of the offense be clearly defined so that anyone can foresee what conduct the relevant provision seeks to punish and what punishment attaches thereto, and thus decide his or her own conduct accordingly (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO3600 rendered on November 14, 2003). Under the principle of nulla poena sine lege, not only crimes but also punishments must be clearly prescribed by law. Since a judge determines the sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed derived through aggravation and mitigation prescribed by law on the statutory punishment set by the penal provision, matters concerning aggravation and mitigation of punishment for deriving the punishment to be imposed, as well as the provisions concerning the statutory punishment, must be clearly prescribed by law, and interpretation thereof must likewise be clear so as to ensure the foreseeability of punishment.\\nHowever, even though it has been clearly established through adjudication that a ground for discretionary mitigation of punishment exists, if the application of that ground is determined solely at the judge’s discretion, this in effect leads to a result contrary to the principle of clarity, a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege. If a ground for mitigation of punishment is prescribed by law and exists, yet whether to mitigate is interpreted as a judge’s discretion (the so-called “OX discretion”), and no standard is provided regarding the reasonable scope and exercise of such discretion, the defendant is effectively unable to know the range of punishment to be imposed for his or her act, and it opens the door to arbitrariness in the judge’s determination of the punishment to be imposed, thereby violating the principle of clarity under nulla poena sine lege. In the example of attempted aggravated bodily injury, the defendant is placed in an unstable situation, not knowing whether he or she will be punished by the punishment to be imposed of “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years” or “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years.” Furthermore, if one assumes a case in which a person commits attempted robbery under Article 342 and Article 333 of the Criminal Act while in a diminished capacity and then voluntarily surrenders (the choice of exemption is excluded from consideration; the same applies hereinafter), the statutory punishment for robbery is “imprisonment for not less than 3 years and not more than 30 years,” and depending on how many times the judge applies mitigation by law due to the three grounds for discretionary mitigation—diminished capacity, attempt, and voluntary surrender—four different forms of punishment to be imposed may arise. Specifically, if no discretionary mitigation is applied at all, the punishment to be imposed becomes “imprisonment for not less than 3 years and not more than 30 years,” whereas if all three grounds for discretionary mitigation above are applied, it becomes “imprisonment for not less than 4.5 months and not more than 3 years and 9 months,” showing that the deviation in the punishment to be imposed based solely on the judge’s discretion is excessively large.\\nMeanwhile, in the example of attempted aggravated bodily injury, if attempt mitigation is not applied, the range of the punishment to be imposed is “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” whereas if attempt mitigation is applied, the range becomes “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years,” making it possible to impose a sentence between 6 months and 1 year. Considering that the punishment to be imposed means the final range from which the sentence can be determined after aggravation and mitigation of punishment, the punishment to be imposed, which serves as the final standard for the sentence, should be interpreted so as to include the area in which a sentence can be imposed, namely “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and less than 1 year.” Nevertheless, according to current practice, in the above example the judge may, solely at his or her discretion, choose not to apply attempt mitigation, in which case the “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and less than 1 year” portion is excluded from the range of the punishment to be imposed; such current practice regarding discretionary mitigation is an interpretation that renders the punishment to be imposed unclear and is therefore improper in violation of nulla poena sine lege.\\nAs noted above, while the determination of the punishment to be imposed is a matter of application of law, the part of determining the sentence through extenuating mitigation is a matter of sentencing. Discretionary mitigation is one of the mitigation by law rules that affects the determination of the punishment to be imposed and is not a matter of sentencing. However, current practice wrongly treats discretionary mitigation as a matter of de facto sentencing rather than a matter of application of law, and the result appears in the form of a violation of nulla poena sine lege as noted above.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, one punishment to be imposed corresponding to the ground for discretionary mitigation is clearly determined, thereby guaranteeing the defendant foreseeability of punishment and conforming to nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n4) Current practice, in that it causes differences in the punishment to be imposed by the judge’s discretion for defendants who committed the same offense, may amount to discrimination without a reasonable basis.\\nThis interpretation, under which the very range of the punishment to be imposed differs according to the judge’s discretion even though the same offense has been committed, is a result that is difficult for the general public to accept, and recognizing different legal effects through the judge’s discretion even though the same legal requirements have been satisfied also runs counter to the general principles of law and the principle of nulla poena sine lege. For example, if two defendants are sentenced in the same courtroom on the same day for attempted aggravated bodily injury, the judge may say to one defendant, “Because attempt is recognized in your case, I will apply discretionary mitigation, so the punishment to be imposed is between 6 months and 5 years of imprisonment,” and to the other defendant, “Although attempt is recognized in your case, I will not apply discretionary mitigation, so the punishment to be imposed is between 1 year and 10 years of imprisonment.” Furthermore, if both of the above defendants are found to be in a diminished capacity state and to have voluntarily surrendered, the gap in the punishment to be imposed may widen to between “imprisonment for 1 year to 10 years” and “imprisonment for 1.5 months to 1 year and 3 months.” Current practice, under which such differences in the punishment to be imposed may arise between defendants who are charged with the same offense and for whom the same grounds for mitigation are recognized, depending on the judge’s discretion regarding whether to apply discretionary mitigation, is an interpretation of law that cannot be accepted under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\nSetting aside the fact that the actual sentence varies depending on specific sentencing conditions, it is proper that the punishment to be imposed as the legal effect should be applied identically to defendants who fall under the same legal requirements of attempted aggravated bodily injury. It is likewise improper that, under current practice as described above, the possibility remains that different punishments to be imposed may be applied depending on the judge’s discretion among defendants who share the same legal requirements, because this is no different from enabling discrimination without a reasonable basis.\\nFurthermore, according to Article 56 of the Criminal Act, aggravation for concurrent offenses is to be applied after mitigation by law, but even where the offense subject to aggravation is determined by comparison of punishments rather than by the nature or character of the offense, the offense subject to aggravation for concurrent offenses may differ. For example, if one assumes the commission of theft under Article 329 of the Criminal Act (imprisonment for not more than 6 years or a fine not exceeding 10 million won, with imprisonment selected) and attempted fraud under Article 352 and Article 347(1) of the Criminal Act (imprisonment for not more than 10 years or a fine not exceeding 20 million won, with imprisonment selected), under current practice the offense subject to aggravation for concurrent offenses may be theft or attempted fraud depending on whether attempt mitigation is applied to the attempted fraud. However, no reasonable explanation is possible for the basis on which such a difference arises.\\n\\n5) The phrase “may” cannot be interpreted as conferring on the judge discretion or authority to decide whether to mitigate.\\nThe majority opinion argues that, in light of the text “may,” it is proper to interpret it as meaning “discretion or authority to mitigate or not.” However, the phrase “may” expresses various meanings depending on context, such as conjecture, ability, possibility, or permission, but at its core converges on the meaning of “potential or actual possibility.” And unlike cases where the object of “may” is, by its nature, one in which a yes-or-no choice must be made, such as permission or confiscation, in the case of discretionary mitigation the object is a numerical range, so it is also textually proper that the result of its application appears as a changed numerical range. Therefore, it cannot be said that, as the majority opinion contends, interpreting it as meaning the judge’s discretion or authority is proper in textual interpretation. It is proper to interpret it from the standpoint of possibility, and further proper to interpret it from the standpoint of a range encompassing all such possibilities.\\nArticle 38(1)2 of the Criminal Act concerning aggravation for concurrent offenses provides that “where the punishments prescribed for each offense are of the same kind, other than death, imprisonment for life, or penal detention for life, the term or amount shall be increased by up to one-half of the longest term or highest amount prescribed for the most serious offense, but the aggregate term or amount of punishment prescribed for each offense shall not be exceeded. However, petty fines and petty fines, confiscation and confiscation may be cumulatively imposed.” The prevailing view and practice interpret the phrase “may be cumulatively imposed” in the proviso not as meaning “they may or may not be cumulatively imposed,” but as meaning that “petty fines and petty fines, confiscation and confiscation are not aggravated but are cumulatively imposed.” No view can be found that the judge has discretion not to cumulatively impose them. In addition, Article 55(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “If there are multiple grounds for mitigation by law, mitigation may be repeated,” but the meaning of “may” here is also understood as opening the possibility of repeated mitigation, not as meaning that the judge may, in his or her discretion, either repeatedly mitigate or not. For example, if a deaf-mute person commits termination attempt of homicide, since both deafness and muteness and termination attempt are mandatory grounds for mitigation, the practice is to repeatedly apply mitigation for each ground, and this is not interpreted to mean that whether to repeat mitigation is within the judge’s discretion. And Article 398(2) of the Civil Act provides that “if the predetermined amount of damages is unjustly excessive, the court may reasonably reduce it,” but the Supreme Court has held to the effect that “it was erroneous for the court to recognize the full amount of the predetermined amount of damages without any reduction even though the predetermined amount of damages was unjustly excessive, without properly examining whether the predetermined amount of damages was excessive” (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA19051 rendered on February 26, 2009).\\nThus, the mere fact that the phrase “may” is used in the statutory text does not always mean that discretion or authority is conferred on the judge. In this respect, the majority opinion’s argument that, by interpreting the phrase “may be mitigated,” the judge is granted discretion to mitigate or not mitigate has lost its principal basis. These provisions set out together with the provisions on discretionary mitigation in the General Part of the Criminal Act, as well as the textual interpretation of the “may” in the above Civil Act provision, clearly show that the core grounds of current practice regarding discretionary mitigation are not valid.\\n\\n6) Current practice treats discretionary mitigation as the judge’s discretion, yet it has not engaged in any discussion of control over that discretion to ensure it is properly exercised.\\nThere can be no dispute that even discretionary matters are unlawful if they are deviated from or abused. When an administrative disposition is a matter of administrative discretion, discussions to properly control the discretion are active, discretionary rules setting out the reasonable scope and standards of discretion have been enacted and implemented, and considerable precedents concerning deviation from and abuse of discretionary power have accumulated. Even with sentencing discretion, there have long been numerous discussions for the proper exercise of discretion. Moreover, after the Sentencing Commission was launched and sentencing guidelines were implemented, in-depth discussions on sentencing discretion have continued through the establishment and revision of sentencing guidelines.\\nHowever, there is no discussion whatsoever regarding the judge’s discretion or authority over discretionary mitigation. Since the range of the punishment to be imposed varies depending on whether discretionary mitigation is applied, if this is regarded as the judge’s discretion, it would correspond to one of the most important discretions in criminal procedure; therefore, in light of the seriousness of its effect, there should rightly be discussion on reasonable exercise and control thereof. For example, in a case where a person commits attempted homicide under Article 254 and Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act and then voluntarily surrenders, there should be standards and scope for proper control of discretion regarding discretionary mitigation, such as whether attempt mitigation should or should not be applied depending on whether injury occurred or the degree of injury, or whether voluntary surrender mitigation should not be applied if the offender surrendered only after the offender had been identified and an arrest warrant issued, but should be applied if the offender surrendered before being identified. However, there is no discussion whatsoever concerning control of the judge’s discretionary power regarding discretionary mitigation. It is difficult to understand that the judge is granted discretion or authority concerning the determination of the punishment to be imposed, which is an important process leading to the conclusion of a criminal trial, yet nothing is discussed about it.\\nDiscretionary mitigation, being a type of mitigation by law, must be carried out before aggravation for concurrent offenses and extenuating mitigation, and thus is not a matter to be decided in relation to specific sentencing by the judge’s discretion. Nevertheless, it is wrong for current practice to leave the decision whether to mitigate pursuant to discretionary mitigation, which is a ground for mitigation by law, to the judge’s discretion and yet exercise no control over that discretion.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the corresponding legal effect is automatically determined immediately, so discussion of control over discretion regarding discretionary mitigation is unnecessary. Perhaps the reason there has been no discussion to date concerning control over discretion in discretionary mitigation is that judges in practice are actually deciding in the same way as the new interpretive theory, namely by determining the punishment to be imposed within the combined range of the range in which mitigation has been applied and the range in which it has not; thus, discussion of control over discretion was not originally necessary.\\n\\n7) Current practice provides a theoretical basis that justifies the court’s omission of a determination on the defendant’s argument.\\nThe Supreme Court has held that “According to Article 52 of the Criminal Act, it is clear that voluntary surrender is not a ground for mandatory mitigation or exemption from punishment; therefore, the assertion regarding voluntary surrender is merely a matter affecting sentencing and cannot be said to constitute a reason that must be stated in a guilty judgment under Article 323 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus even if the court below made no determination on the defendant’s above argument, it cannot be said that there is illegality of omission of determination” (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DO945 rendered on July 7, 1987, 98DO492 rendered on April 28, 1998, etc.). In other words, precedents have interpreted the decision whether to apply discretionary mitigation as being solely within the judge’s discretion, and as a result they hold that even if the court omits a determination on the defendant’s assertion concerning a ground for discretionary mitigation, it is not unlawful. In practical terms, this can be understood to mean that there is not even a need to examine whether the ground for discretionary mitigation exists.\\nThis stands in contrast to the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DA19051 concerning the predetermined amount of damages under Article 398(2) of the Civil Act. Although the wording in both provisions is similar, namely “may be reduced” and “may be mitigated,” there is a Supreme Court decision holding that failure to reduce the predetermined amount of damages is unlawful, whereas with respect to discretionary mitigation there is a Supreme Court decision holding that because the judge has discretion as to whether to mitigate, it is not unlawful to fail to determine the assertion. It is not easy to accept that the Supreme Court’s ruling in a civil matter regarding similar wording is stricter than its ruling in a criminal matter.\\nGrounds for discretionary mitigation such as voluntary surrender, diminished capacity, and attempt are factors that bring about changes in the punishment to be imposed and are important grounds that greatly affect the determination of the sentence. In practice, a defendant or defense counsel who raises such grounds in court believes that they will significantly affect the final sentence depending on whether such grounds exist and makes great efforts to prove them. However, to say that whether mitigation is applied for such grounds for discretionary mitigation depends solely on the judge’s discretion, so that even if proof succeeds the corresponding legal effect may not arise and even omission of a determination or no examination at all is not unlawful, is a conclusion that is difficult for a defendant and defense counsel to accept. Moreover, if the defendant argues discretionary mitigation but the first-instance judgment makes no determination regarding it, the defendant cannot know whether the asserted ground for discretionary mitigation was found not to exist, or whether the ground existed but mitigation was not applied due to sentencing considerations, and furthermore cannot know what procedural efforts should be made in the second instance. Meanwhile, there is also practice in which the first instance accepts the defendant’s argument and applies discretionary mitigation, but the second instance renders a judgment not applying discretionary mitigation without explanation, and according to the precedents noted above, such a judgment is not unlawful. Thus, this practice, which is difficult for a defendant and defense counsel to accept, is being carried out with the support of precedent. Current practice in this form cannot but be said to constitute a serious obstacle to the defendant’s right of defense.\\nThis wrongful appearance of practice stems from the perception that whether to apply discretionary mitigation is a matter of the judge’s discretion. However, under the new interpretive theory, once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the court must make a determination reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half, and failure to do so becomes unlawful. Therefore, an argument concerning a ground for discretionary mitigation naturally falls under the statement of facts constituting the reason for aggravation or mitigation of punishment under Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and a determination thereon must be expressly stated in the guilty judgment. This can be naturally corrected through the new interpretive theory.\\nA considerable number of scholars, while regarding discretionary mitigation as within the court’s discretion as in current practice, also consider it proper to state a determination in the reasons for a guilty judgment pursuant to Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act with the intent of carefully considering the party’s argument and ensuring the objectivity of the judgment. There are also many practitioners who concur with this view.\\nMeanwhile, as will be discussed below, although diminished capacity was changed from mandatory mitigation to discretionary mitigation by the 2018 amendment to the Criminal Act, most current practice appears to expressly state the determination even when the defendant’s claim of diminished capacity is not accepted. This attitude of practice is not only entirely proper, but also reveals a latent awareness of the problems in current practice regarding discretionary mitigation.\\n\\n8) According to current practice, a logically difficult problem arises in relation to the defendant’s appeal against a judgment that imposed the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without discretionary mitigation.\\nAs an example in the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense, assume that the defendant confessed to the offense and wished to have the statutory minimum sentence of 6 months’ imprisonment imposed within the range of punishment to be imposed after attempt mitigation, but the court of first instance, without applying attempt mitigation, imposed the minimum sentence of 1 year’s imprisonment within the range of “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.” In such a case, the issue is on what grounds the defendant, who wanted a sentence of 6 months’ imprisonment, could appeal. First, one might argue that the defendant could raise violation of law as a ground for appeal by pointing out that attempt mitigation was not applied; however, as noted above, precedents take the position that whether to apply discretionary mitigation is a matter of judicial discretion and that failure to mitigate is not unlawful, so even if violation of law is asserted as a ground for appeal, it is difficult to have it accepted. If accepted, this would also negate the current practice regarding discretionary mitigation. Next, one might argue that the appeal may be filed on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence. However, because the first instance imposed the lowest sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed, it rendered the most favorable judgment to the defendant within the scope of sentencing discretion, so an appeal against such a first-instance judgment on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence is logically not proper. The substance of the defendant’s appeal against the above first-instance judgment would be an objection to the part that did not apply attempt mitigation, which is a discretionary mitigation. However, as current practice wrongly understands discretionary mitigation as the judge’s discretion lacking control over discretion, there is no ground of appeal that can effectively express the defendant’s intention to object to a judgment that imposed the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without discretionary mitigation.\\nFurthermore, a serious contradiction also arises in appellate proceedings. In the above example, suppose the appellate court determines that the sentence of 1 year’s imprisonment is excessive and quashes it and imposes 6 months’ imprisonment. In such a case, the question is for what reason the appellate court will quash the first-instance judgment. According to the precedential view that whether to apply discretionary mitigation is a matter of judicial discretion, the first-instance judgment cannot be quashed on the ground of violation of law, and since the quashing is based on the determination that the sentence in the first-instance judgment is excessive, it may be considered proper to quash it on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence. To regard this as a matter of legal misinterpretation or violation of law would also be tantamount to acknowledging the error of current practice. Therefore, current practice appears to quash the first-instance judgment on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence in such cases. However, in order for the appellate court to quash the first-instance judgment that imposed 1 year’s imprisonment, which is the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without attempt mitigation, and then impose 6 months’ imprisonment, the appellate court must newly apply attempt mitigation by modifying the part applying the law in the first-instance judgment when drafting the new appellate judgment. In the end, there is a difference in the application of law between the first-instance and appellate judgments, which creates a contradiction with the fact that the ground for quashing is inappropriateness of sentence. The appellate court’s determination in such cases is in substance no different from viewing the first-instance judgment as having an error of violation of law. This problem is also the result of wrongly understanding discretionary mitigation as judicial discretion.\\nThe phrase commonly encountered in practice, “legal suspension of sentence is impossible,” is an expression based on the range of the punishment to be imposed stated in the judgment, but premised on current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, this phrase becomes highly inaccurate as well. Taking the case of homicide under Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act (death penalty, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for not less than 5 years) and voluntary surrender as an example, according to current practice, even if the fact of voluntary surrender, which is a ground for discretionary mitigation, is recognized, the court may not mitigate and may omit any mention thereof in the judgment. According to such a judgment, because the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed is 5 years’ imprisonment, suspension of sentence becomes impossible. However, in fact, if mitigation based on voluntary surrender is applied and the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed becomes 2 years and 6 months’ imprisonment, suspension of sentence becomes possible. In other words, it means that legal suspension of sentence is not impossible. Under current practice, which does not state in the judgment the determination when mitigation is not applied even though a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, whether grounds such as suspension of sentence can be asserted as inappropriateness of sentence may be a separate issue, but from the judgment alone it is difficult even to know whether such an argument is legally available, and one must necessarily review the litigation record to know. It would mean that one should not simply trust the punishment to be imposed stated in the judgment, and one wonders whether this is truly consistent with our trial practice.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, there is no room for such confusion. Once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the effect of changing the punishment to be imposed always arises; if such action is not taken, it is a violation of law, and if such action is taken, only inappropriateness of sentence is at issue. Whether a ground of appeal based on inappropriateness of sentence, including suspension of sentence, is legally available can be clearly known from the wording of the judgment alone, and only at the stage of determining whether the claim will be accepted is it necessary to examine the litigation record.\\n\\n9) According to current practice, there may arise a problem in which the range of the punishment to be imposed is segmented, creating a gap where a sentence cannot be selected between the highest and lowest points of the punishment to be imposed.\\nUnder the current Criminal Act, the range of determinate imprisonment is not less than 1 month and not more than 30 years, and when aggravated, a sentence up to 50 years may be imposed; however, under the former Criminal Act before amendment by Act No. 10259 on April 15, 2010 (hereinafter the “former Criminal Act”), the range of imprisonment was not less than 1 month and not more than 15 years, and when aggravated, a sentence up to 25 years could be imposed. Taking, as an example, the offense of robbery causing death under the former Article 338 of the former Criminal Act, as amended by Act No. 5057 on December 29, 1995 and before its amendment by Act No. 10259, the statutory punishment is life imprisonment or determinate imprisonment for not less than 10 years; if determinate imprisonment is selected, under the former practice the range of the punishment to be imposed varies depending on whether discretionary mitigation is applied for voluntary surrender. If voluntary surrender mitigation is not applied, it becomes “imprisonment for not less than 10 years and not more than 15 years”; if voluntary surrender mitigation is applied, it becomes “imprisonment for not less than 5 years and not more than 7 years and 6 months.” In the end, for the above defendant, depending on whether voluntary surrender mitigation is applied, a sentence ranging from a minimum of 5 years’ imprisonment to a maximum of 15 years’ imprisonment could be imposed, but the problem is that the area of “more than 7 years and 6 months and less than 10 years” cannot be imposed. While it is understandable that a sentence of 5 years or 15 years may be imposed in determining the sentence, it is hard to accept that 8 years or 9 years cannot be imposed. In the above example, if recidivism aggravation is imposed up to twice the maximum and minimum terms of the punishment for robbery causing death pursuant to Article 3 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Specific Violent Crimes (hereinafter the “Specific Violent Crime Act”), or if additional discretionary mitigation grounds such as juvenile delinquency are added, or if extenuating mitigation is also applied, the gap between the minimum and maximum of the punishment to be imposed becomes even larger. The same applies to the current Criminal Act. Under the current Criminal Act as well, this applies where the lower limit of determinate imprisonment exceeds 15 years. If recidivism aggravation is imposed pursuant to Article 3 of the Specific Violent Crime Act, the same problem arises if there is an offense with a lower limit of the statutory punishment exceeding 12 years and 6 months. Put differently, it is no different from having a penal provision with a statutory punishment of, for example, “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 5 years, or imprisonment for not less than 8 years and not more than 15 years.”\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, in the case of discretionary mitigation the punishment to be imposed is the range obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half, so the problem of segmentation of the range of the punishment to be imposed and the resulting sentencing gap does not arise as described above.\\n\\n10) Current practice obscures the legislative intent behind the legislature’s establishment of a stepwise system of mitigation by law.\\nThe Criminal Act, while establishing a system of mitigation of punishment according to the degree of illegality and the degree of culpability, etc., distinguishes and treats differently, in order of lighter criminal responsibility: (1) mandatory mitigation, (2) discretionary mitigation, and (3) cases with no ground for mitigation.\\nCurrent practice either applies mitigation for discretionary mitigation at the judge’s discretion and treats it the same as mandatory mitigation, or does not apply it and treats it the same as cases with no ground for mitigation. Taking attempted aggravated bodily injury as an example, in the former case the punishment to be imposed becomes imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years, thus becoming the same as mandatory mitigation; in the latter case it becomes imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, thus becoming the same as when there is no ground for mitigation. Such interpretation renders meaningless the purpose and legislative choice of the Criminal Act’s mitigation system. Something that was divided into three categories in law has been reduced to two through interpretation. The majority opinion, while claiming that mandatory mitigation and discretionary mitigation are clearly distinguishable, can be said to be undermining that distinction itself.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, differences in the punishment to be imposed according to each ground for mitigation are clearly revealed. In the example of attempted aggravated bodily injury, in case (1) the punishment is imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years, in case (2) imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years, and in case (3) imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.\\n\\n11) Before amendment by Act No. 15982 on December 18, 2018, Article 10(2) of the former Criminal Act provided that “The act of a person whose ability under the preceding paragraph is deficient due to mental and physical disorder shall be mitigated,” thereby prescribing diminished capacity as a ground for mandatory mitigation. Accordingly, if the defendant asserted diminished capacity, a determination thereon had to be stated in the judgment, and if diminished capacity was recognized, mitigation by law pursuant to Article 55 of the Criminal Act had to be made. However, the current Article 10(2) of the Criminal Act, as amended above, provides that “The act of a person whose ability under the preceding paragraph is deficient due to mental and physical disorder may be mitigated,” thereby prescribing diminished capacity as a ground for discretionary mitigation. According to current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, the above amendment to the Criminal Act should naturally have brought a significant change to the practice concerning diminished capacity. That is, even if the defendant asserts diminished capacity, the court need not make a determination thereon, and even if diminished capacity is recognized, if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed according to the sentence, the punishment need not be mitigated.\\nHowever, current practice regarding diminished capacity appears to operate in a manner not very different from when it was a ground for mandatory mitigation. Even if the defendant’s claim of diminished capacity is not accepted, the determination is stated in the judgment, and even where diminished capacity is recognized, the general practice appears to be to mitigate by law even when it is not a case requiring lowering the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed. Such practice is consonant in part with the new interpretive theory. This aspect of practice concerning diminished capacity may be said to be an example showing that current practice regarding discretionary mitigation is not based on legal or logical grounds but is the result of simply inheriting a mistaken custom.\\n\\nd. Discretionary mitigation should be newly interpreted as follows.\\n\\n1) As noted above, since the meaning of “may” can be interpreted in multiple ways, it should be interpreted as closely as possible in conformity with the legislator’s intent. “May” should be understood to mean that the sentence can be determined across both the “range in case of mitigation” and the “range in case of no mitigation.” In other words, taking into account that both mitigation and no mitigation are possible, the punishment to be imposed should be determined by combining the ranges of the two cases. Then the range between the upper limit of the range where no mitigation is applied and the lower limit of the range where mitigation is applied becomes the range of punishment to be imposed for discretionary mitigation. Put simply, it may also be understood that only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is mitigated. Taking attempted aggravated bodily injury as an example, the statement that attempt mitigation may “mitigate the punishment” means that the sentence may be determined across both the range “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years,” in which attempt mitigation has been applied, and the range “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” in which it has not been applied, which means that the punishment to be imposed is determined as “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years.” In the end, it can be said that only the lower limit, namely 1 year, is reduced by one-half while the upper limit, namely 10 years, is left unchanged.\\nUnder the discretionary mitigation method according to the new interpretive theory, the area obtained by combining the mitigated range and the non-mitigated range is automatically determined as the punishment to be imposed without room for judicial discretion, and accordingly the range of the punishment to be imposed is viewed as the upper limit of the non-mitigated range and the lower limit of the mitigated range. The result is the same as reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half. Although extremely exceptional, if discretionary mitigation is viewed as “election discretion,” the problem of segmentation of the punishment to be imposed and the resulting gap, as noted above, cannot be resolved. On the other hand, the new interpretive theory, by taking the form of reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half in the end, leaves no room for such a problem and is simpler and clearer.\\nMeanwhile, according to the new interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation, in cases of offenses for which the lower limit of the statutory punishment is not prescribed, even if mitigation is applied, the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed can no longer be lowered, so the punishment to be imposed does not change, but the grounds for mitigation must be stated in the part applying the law in the judgment as a process leading to the sentence.\\nThe foregoing discussion has centered for convenience on determinate imprisonment, but the same discussion applies to other types of punishment such as fines.\\n\\n2) When the legal requirements corresponding to grounds for discretionary mitigation such as diminished capacity, attempt, or voluntary surrender are satisfied, according to the interpretation of the wording that the punishment “may be mitigated,” the legal effect noted above arises, namely that only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half. If the existence of a ground for discretionary mitigation, that is, the legal requirements, is recognized, the above legal effect naturally arises, so there is no room for judicial discretion to intervene in whether to mitigate. Therefore, if the existence of the legal requirements corresponding to grounds for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the corresponding legal effect always arises, and since that legal effect makes a difference in the range of the punishment to be imposed, whenever a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized the court must always include a notation to that effect in the part applying the law. The same applies even if the defendant does not assert a ground for discretionary mitigation. Furthermore, since grounds for discretionary mitigation always have the effect of lowering the punishment to be imposed, if the defendant asserts a ground for discretionary mitigation, the guilty judgment must state a determination thereon pursuant to Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n3) As above, with the new understanding of discretionary mitigation, it is necessary to newly understand the grounds for mitigation that have traditionally been contrasted as mandatory mitigation and discretionary mitigation. As noted above, discretionary mitigation has the effect of lowering only the lower limit, whereas mandatory mitigation has the effect of lowering both the upper and lower limits. In the case of mandatory mitigation, when the relevant ground is recognized, the effect arises that not only is a sentence lower than the lower limit within the statutory punishment permitted, but also the upper limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half so that no sentence above that may be imposed. By contrast, in the case of discretionary mitigation, since the degree of reduction of culpability is considered smaller than in the case of mandatory mitigation, a sentence lower than the lower limit of the statutory punishment may be imposed, but all sentences within the original range of the statutory punishment may also be imposed. When understood in this way, the traditional distinction between mandatory mitigation and discretionary mitigation becomes terminologically inappropriate in that once the requirements for a ground for mitigation are satisfied, the corresponding legal effect naturally arises. Accordingly, what was traditionally called mandatory mitigation appears proper to call “upper-and-lower-limit mitigation,” while discretionary mitigation appears proper to call “lower-limit mitigation.” It is my view that the current practice with several problems, as noted above, has become entrenched in part because of the erroneous use of the term “discretionary” mitigation.\\n\\n4) I have thus examined the content of the new interpretive theory on discretionary mitigation. But on reflection, the new interpretive theory is not materially different from current practice. It is, in fact, not new at all.\\nFirst, there is no difference between current practice and the new interpretive theory in that the punishment to be imposed means the final range from which the judge can select the sentence. Current practice allows the judge to determine whether to apply discretionary mitigation, and accordingly the mitigated range and the non-mitigated range each become punishments to be imposed; but because the judge can determine the sentence within both the mitigated and non-mitigated ranges, this is no different from the new interpretive theory, which regards the combined range of the two as the punishment to be imposed.\\nNext, the rule is that if a legal requirement is recognized, the corresponding legal effect follows, and the new interpretive theory seeks to create for discretionary mitigation the same logical structure as this general rule. Current practice understands the legal effects of other grounds for aggravation and mitigation as “automatic determination,” but only discretionary mitigation as “election discretion”; the new interpretive theory interprets the legal effects of all grounds for aggravation and mitigation as “automatic determination.” From the perspective of trial practice, there is nothing at all new.\\n\\ne. 1) The majority opinion says that the current practice of “there is no need to bother with discretionary mitigation if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed” does not mean that the sentence is determined and then the decision whether to apply discretionary mitigation is made, and therefore the practice is not erroneous.\\nHowever, according to current practice, the sentence must inevitably be determined before the punishment to be imposed is fixed. The practice that “there is no need to bother with discretionary mitigation if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed” has been used for a long time and can be confirmed in court training materials from the past and present, and under this practice, whether to apply discretionary mitigation is decided depending on whether it is necessary to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed in light of the sentence. But the need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed means that the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed, so without determining the sentence one cannot know whether the lower limit needs to be lowered. In the end, under current practice, one has no choice but to determine the sentence before fixing the punishment to be imposed in order to decide whether discretionary mitigation applies. Moreover, precedents support the current practice in which whether to apply discretionary mitigation is determined in the process of deciding the sentence by holding that the assertion of voluntary surrender, which is a ground for discretionary mitigation, is merely a sentencing factor (see the above Supreme Court Decision 98DO492, etc.). Furthermore, the sentencing guidelines established by the Sentencing Commission recommend that “where a sentencing factor constituting a ground for discretionary mitigation by law exists and the recommended sentencing range reflecting it is lower than the statutory punishment, it should be considered as either a ground for mitigation by law or a ground for extenuating mitigation,” which means adjusting the punishment to be imposed to fit the recommended sentencing range and is in substance the same as current practice. Therefore, the majority opinion that current practice does not first determine the sentence and then decide whether to apply discretionary mitigation is not valid.\\nMeanwhile, the fact that there is no discussion at all in current practice regarding discretion over discretionary mitigation shows that judges handling practice actually determine the punishment to be imposed for discretionary mitigation, like the new interpretive theory, within the combined range of the mitigated and non-mitigated ranges. The reason current practice has been able to remain unchanged without much sense of problem despite being wrong is not because current practice can be construed as in the manner of the majority opinion, but because judges, in their actual work, avoid judgments according to current practice and instead decide in the same way as the new interpretive theory, thereby avoiding the problems that would arise if current practice were followed as is.\\n2) The majority opinion says that, when mitigation by law is applied for a determinate term of imprisonment, a method that reduces only either the upper limit or the lower limit by one-half, rather than reducing both the upper and lower limits by one-half as provided in Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, cannot be permitted under the principle of nulla poena sine lege. If the majority opinion above understood the separate opinion to mean that the upper-limit portion of Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act is not applied, I clarify that this is a misunderstanding.\\nAs explained in detail above, the separate opinion means that in the case of discretionary mitigation, because mitigation by law is applied pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, the sentence may be determined across both the range in which both the upper and lower limits are reduced by one-half and the range in which no mitigation is applied, and this ultimately appears as the same result as reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half while leaving the upper limit unchanged. In other words, this is merely a shorthand expression of the result obtained by combining both the case in which mitigation by law under Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act is applied and the case in which it is not applied; it does not recognize a mitigation by law that reduces only the minimum term by one-half contrary to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act.\\n3) The majority opinion says that, from the point a guilty finding is made to the point of determining the sentence, the judge is granted broad discretion, such as in selecting the type of punishment, and that the judge’s discretion regarding discretionary mitigation is only one of them.\\nFor example, in the case of theft under Article 329 of the Criminal Act, because imprisonment and fines are provided as alternatives, selection of the type of punishment is inevitable in determining the sentence, and before that selection, the same punishment to be imposed is always indicated. However, in current practice regarding attempted aggravated bodily injury, if attempt mitigation is not applied, the range of imprisonment for not less than 6 months and less than 1 year is excluded from the punishment to be imposed for that defendant from the outset. In the former case, the same punishment to be imposed is applied to all defendants, whereas in the latter case the punishment to be imposed differs depending on the defendant. In this respect, the problem of selecting the type of punishment and the problem of discretionary mitigation are entirely different matters.\\n4) As noted above in item 7) of section c., there is a view that, while maintaining current practice, the claim of a ground for discretionary mitigation should be regarded as falling under the “statement of facts constituting the reason for aggravation or mitigation of punishment” in Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and that a determination thereon should be expressly stated. However, precedents have steadfastly maintained the position that even if the court omits a determination on the defendant’s argument concerning a ground for discretionary mitigation, it is not unlawful, and as noted above in item 7) of section c., current practice regarding discretionary mitigation provides a theoretical basis for justifying the court’s omission of a determination on the defendant’s argument. While a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, under current practice the occurrence of the legal effect of changing the punishment to be imposed is uncertain; maintaining that practice and at the same time requiring that determinations on arguments regarding grounds for discretionary mitigation be expressly stated seems logically difficult.\\nEven if current practice regarding discretionary mitigation were maintained but changed so that determinations on arguments regarding grounds for discretionary mitigation had to be stated, various difficulties are foreseeable. If, as a result of examination of the defendant’s argument, a ground for discretionary mitigation such as voluntary surrender is not recognized, there would be no particular problem. However, the problem arises when the ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized but the judge decides not to mitigate. In particular, it would be difficult to distinguish and state the reasons why one defendant is mitigated and another is not. And because the process of fixing the punishment to be imposed and the sentencing for determining the concrete sentence must be distinguished, it would be desirable to explain the determination on whether to mitigate by referring to circumstances other than sentencing conditions, but that is very difficult. In the end, in order to avoid such difficulties, practice will be operated in the direction of always mitigating pursuant to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, which would completely undermine the distinction between discretionary mitigation and mandatory mitigation and damage the purpose of the Criminal Act’s separate provisions for discretionary and mandatory mitigation.\\nThis problem can be confirmed by looking at recent practice involving claims of diminished capacity mentioned above in item 11) of section d. Looking more concretely at practice after diminished capacity was changed from mandatory mitigation to discretionary mitigation, one can readily find cases in which the defendant’s argument is rejected because diminished capacity is not recognized, cases in which diminished capacity is recognized and mitigation for diminished capacity is applied, and cases in which mitigation for diminished capacity is applied even though the case is not one requiring lowering the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed. However, it is difficult to find a case in which diminished capacity is recognized but mitigation for diminished capacity is not applied and the reason is stated in the judgment. Such operation of practice is no different from deciding whether to mitigate depending on whether diminished capacity is recognized, and thus is in substance the same as mandatory mitigation. If, while maintaining current practice in this way, determinations on arguments for discretionary mitigation are required to be stated in the judgment, there is a high possibility that it will in practice operate in the same way as mandatory mitigation, making it difficult to distinguish between the two.\\n5) Most issues of statutory interpretation encountered in trials concern legal requirements, and in such cases which legal effect is granted depends on which view is chosen. Put differently, the gains and losses of legal effect hinge on how the boundaries of the legal requirements are drawn. There are things to “gain” and “lose.”\\nHowever, broadly speaking, the issue of discretionary mitigation addressed in this judgment is not wrong to describe as a discussion about, while in substance agreeing on the range of punishment that may be imposed on the defendant, which interpretation is legally and logically better for expressing that in the judgment. It might be more appropriate to call this a discussion about improving the practice of drafting criminal judgments. Through the new interpretive theory, many of the problems of current practice can be resolved, and it is difficult to find new legal or practical problems arising from it. I do not understand what the insistence on maintaining the current practice of drafting criminal judgments, which cannot even clearly communicate the range of the punishment to be imposed, is intended to preserve. It is difficult to know precisely what the majority opinion opposes and for what reason.\\n\\nf. As above, examining the problems raised in the beginning based on the new interpretive theory of discretionary mitigation, one can see that all problems are naturally resolved as follows.\\n\\n1) According to the new interpretive theory, whenever a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the effect is that the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half, so defendants who committed the same offense and have the same grounds for aggravation and mitigation of punishment are always punished by the same punishment to be imposed. If a ground for mitigation by law is recognized, the legal effect is always the same, so the punishment to be imposed is likewise determined identically.\\n\\n2) According to the new interpretive theory, unlike current practice, whether to apply mitigation by law to a ground for discretionary mitigation is not decided at the judge’s discretion; rather, because the effect of changing the punishment to be imposed always arises, discretionary mitigation is not limited as in current practice to cases where the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed, and furthermore there is no room for the judge, after determining the sentence, to go back and add discretionary mitigation in the part applying the law when the sentence does not correspond to the punishment to be imposed.\\n\\n3) Under current practice, if there are several grounds for discretionary mitigation—for example, if voluntary surrender and diminished capacity are added to attempted robbery—multiple punishments to be imposed may appear, such as “imprisonment for not less than 3 years and not more than 30 years,” “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and 6 months and not more than 15 years,” “imprisonment for not less than 9 months and not more than 7 years and 6 months,” and “imprisonment for not less than 4.5 months and not more than 3 years and 9 months.” Under the new interpretive theory, however, when there are multiple grounds for discretionary mitigation as above, the lower limit is repeatedly reduced by one-half, so the punishment to be imposed is always “imprisonment for not less than 4.5 months and not more than 30 years.”\\n\\n4) According to Article 56 of the Criminal Act, mitigation by law must be applied before aggravation for concurrent offenses. Under current practice, however, even where the most serious offense subject to aggravation among several offenses in a concurrent-offense relationship is determined by comparison of punishments rather than by the nature or character of the offense under Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act, the offense with the highest punishment may vary depending on the judge’s discretion regarding discretionary mitigation; but under the new interpretive theory, if a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the lower limit of the statutory punishment is always reduced by one-half and the same punishment to be imposed results, so based on this, the offense with the highest punishment subject to aggravation for concurrent offenses is always consistently determined.\\n\\n5) As noted above, according to current practice there arise cases in which, even when a sentence equal to the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed is imposed, an appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence must be allowed. Under the new interpretive theory, however, if a ground for discretionary mitigation exists, the punishment to be imposed always includes the full maximum range within which the judge can determine a specific sentence, and because the sentence is determined within the range of the punishment to be imposed expanded in this way to all possible areas, if the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed has been imposed, it necessarily means that the most favorable punishment possible has been imposed on the defendant. Accordingly, in such cases there is no room for an appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence, and it is evident that such an interpretation conforms to the structure of our criminal procedure. As noted above, the phrase “legal suspension of sentence is impossible” can also be highly inaccurate under current practice regarding discretionary mitigation.\\n\\n6) According to current practice, if the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without discretionary mitigation is imposed at first instance, the appellate court may impose a lower sentence than the first instance, and to do so it must modify the part applying the law in the first-instance judgment in order to apply discretionary mitigation and lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed. However, under the new interpretive theory, as noted above, discretionary mitigation always has the same legal effect, so the situation in which the part applying the law in the first-instance judgment is modified simply to accept an appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence and newly apply discretionary mitigation does not occur.\\n\\ng. I will examine the court below’s determination in light of the new interpretive theory concerning discretionary mitigation.\\nThe court of first instance, according to current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, applied attempt mitigation, which is discretionary mitigation, to the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, and then mitigated it pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act. As a result, the punishment to be imposed for attempted aggravated bodily injury became imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years, and based on that term, the punishment to be imposed was determined after aggravation for concurrent offenses.\\nHowever, according to the new interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation, attempt mitigation for attempted aggravated bodily injury should be applied by “Article 25(2) and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act” (lower-limit mitigation only), thereby using as the basis for aggravation for concurrent offenses the term in which only the lower limit of the punishment for attempted aggravated bodily injury is reduced by one-half (imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years); but because the term obtained by adding together the upper limits of attempted aggravated bodily injury and assault (12 years) is lower than the term obtained by aggravating by one-half the upper limit of attempted aggravated bodily injury (15 years), the punishment to be imposed should be determined within the combined range (imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 12 years), and the sentence should be determined within that punishment-to-be-imposed range.\\nThe court below’s judgment, which failed to correct the above error of the court of first instance, contains an error of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning discretionary mitigation; however, because the punishment to be imposed that the court of first instance, maintained by the court below, used as the standard for sentencing falls within the range of the punishment to be imposed under the new interpretive theory and is not unfavorable to the defendant, the above error does not appear to have affected the judgment in the end. The determination regarding the defendant’s grounds for final appeal is the same as in the majority opinion.\\nIn this way, I concur with the majority opinion in concluding that there is no ground for quashing the judgment below, but because my reasoning differs, I state this in a separate opinion.\\n\\n6. Justice Lee Gi-taek’s supplementary opinion on the separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The issue in this case is whether the current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, including attempt mitigation under Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, is valid. Because current practice treats attempt mitigation the same as other discretionary mitigation, the separate opinion discussed the new interpretive theory on discretionary mitigation generally without distinguishing attempt mitigation from other discretionary mitigation. However, as will be discussed below, attempt mitigation has certain differences from other discretionary mitigation in relation to “mitigation of punishment.” In other words, other discretionary mitigation concerns, as discussed in the separate opinion, the meaning of the “mitigation of punishment” provision in determining the “range of the punishment to be imposed” on the premise of the statutory punishment prescribed in the penal provision, whereas attempt mitigation concerns the meaning of the “mitigation of punishment” provision in determining the “statutory punishment for an attempted offense,” which is not prescribed in the individual penal provision. Below, I will examine the legal structure of punishing attempted offenses.\\nCurrent practice and the prevailing academic view understand the attempt under Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act (hereinafter simply the “attempt”) as, in principle, punishing it with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense, but merely a ground for discretionary mitigation under paragraph 2 of the same Article. However, the above understanding of attempt under current practice is wrong. An attempt is a separate offense distinguished from a completed offense, has its own statutory punishment, and that statutory punishment is properly understood to be the range obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment for the completed offense by one-half.\\nFirst, the subject of punishment as an attempt is determined by the provision “The offenses punishable as attempts shall be prescribed in each principal provision” in Article 29 of the Criminal Act and the provision “Attempts under Article ___ above shall be punished” in the specific parts of the Criminal Act. Next, the elements of an attempted offense are determined by combining the provision in Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act—“When the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender”—with the elements-of-offense provisions for completed offenses in the specific parts of the Criminal Act. And the statutory punishment for an attempted offense is determined by combining the provision in Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act—“The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense”—with Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act regarding the meaning of mitigation and the statutory punishment provisions for completed offenses in the specific parts of the Criminal Act. For example, the offense of attempted homicide under Article 254 and Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act is determined, in combination with Article 25(1) and (2) of the Criminal Act, to have the attempt-specific elements and statutory punishment stating that “a person who has commenced the execution of an act of killing another and whose result has not occurred shall be punished by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for not less than 2 years and 6 months.”\\nThe specific reasons why a new understanding of the punishment of attempted offenses is needed are as follows. For convenience, I will discuss it centered on result crimes.\\n1) Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “When the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender.” In the case of an attempt, punishment cannot be imposed based solely on Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act, nor can an attempted offender be punished based only on the punishment provision for the completed offense. The elements of an attempted offense are completed only when the punishment provision for the completed offense and Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act are combined, and only then do they have legitimacy as the basis for punishing an attempted offense. Taking the offense of attempted homicide under Article 254 and Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act as an example, the provision in Article 254 that “attempts under the preceding four Articles shall be punished” becomes the basis for punishing attempted homicide, and the provision in Article 250(1) that “a person who kills another...” and the provision in Article 25(1) combine to complete the elements of attempted homicide, namely, “when a person has commenced the execution of an act of killing another and the result of death has not occurred.” The concept of attempt as an element of offense becomes clear only through Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n2) Like the elements of offense, the statutory punishment for an attempted offense should also be understood as being determined by combining the punishment provision for the completed offense and Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act. Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense,” and according to the new interpretive theory on discretionary mitigation, the statutory punishment for an attempted offense is determined as the range obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment for the completed offense by one-half.\\nCurrent practice understands Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act concerning punishment for attempts as a provision of discretionary mitigation.
