That is, it interprets that an attempted offender is, in principle, punished with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense, but punishment may or may not be mitigated pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act. However, there is no textual basis for punishing an attempt with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense. Moreover, although there is an obvious difference in the illegality of the result between a completed offense and an attempted offense, the fact that their statutory punishments are the same has an aspect that is hard to accept in criminal law doctrine. Furthermore, considering that there are countless offenses for which attempts are not punishable, it is improper to regard the statutory punishment for an attempt as, in principle, identical to that of the completed offense.\\n3) The legislature used a legislative technique of concisely and efficiently prescribing the elements and statutory punishment of attempted offenses in the General Part, but current practice mistakenly takes this mode of expression as discretionary mitigation. Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “When the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender”; Article 25(2) provides that “The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense”; Article 29 provides that “The offenses punishable as attempts shall be prescribed in each principal provision”; and the specific parts of the Criminal Act prescribe the punishment for attempted offenses in the form that “attempts under Article ___ above shall be punished.” Such a form of provision reflects the legislature’s use of a legislative technique in which, instead of separately and complexly prescribing the elements and statutory punishment for attempts for each offense, the general rule for punishing attempts is prescribed in the General Part, and then the offenses punishable as attempts are designated in the specific parts so that the relevant elements and statutory punishment are automatically completed. If the current Criminal Act merely provided in Article 254 that “attempts under the preceding four Articles shall be punished” concerning attempted homicide, the elements and statutory punishment of the attempt would be automatically completed; without such a legislative technique, it would have been necessary to separately prescribe the elements and statutory punishment for every attempted offense.\\nIn other words, instead of separately and complexly prescribing the elements and statutory punishment of attempts for each offense, the Criminal Act places in Article 25 of the General Part common provisions for attempts as to elements of offense (paragraph 1) and statutory punishment (paragraph 2), and then combines them with the individual provisions on completed offenses so that the elements and statutory punishment of attempts are derived. In addition, it is proper to view the legislature as having expressly indicated through such a form of provision that the statutory punishment for attempts is reduced only in the lower limit by one-half from that of the completed offense. If the statutory punishment for an attempted offense had been prescribed individually, it would have been very difficult to express such legislative intent. Therefore, the current practice of viewing the statutory punishment for an attempt as, in principle, identical to that of the completed offense, but merely capable of discretionary mitigation under Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, is not valid.\\nBased on this new understanding of attempts, it can be seen that the legislature classifies offenses with respect to attempts as follows: (i) offenses for which attempts need not be punished because they are minor offenses do not have attempt punishment provisions; (ii) where punishment is necessary for the danger of result occurrence caused by commencement of execution even though the constitutive result has not occurred, attempt punishment provisions are provided and the offense is punished by a statutory punishment obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment for the completed offense by one-half pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act; and (iii) where the offense is an attempt but strong punishment is required, as in the precedent cases discussed below, the statutory punishment for the attempt is separately specified so that the application of Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act is excluded.\\n4) The statutory punishment refers to the range of punishment generally evaluating the typical unlawfulness of each element of offense as prescribed by the legislature in each element of offense. In other words, once the elements are satisfied, the scope of punishment predetermined by the legislature is determined, and that is the statutory punishment. Then any setting or alteration of the range of punishment resulting from the element of attempt should all be regarded as part of the determination of the statutory punishment. It is not appropriate to view this, as current practice does, as a ground for mitigation of punishment after determination of the statutory punishment. Furthermore, under the principle of prohibition against double evaluation, matters constituting signs of the elements of the offense must not be considered again in the sentencing process. The circumstance that the execution of a crime was commenced but the result did not occur and the offense remained an attempt is a sign of the elements of an attempted offense, so understanding this as a ground for mitigation by law may amount to double evaluation, and such legal interpretation should be avoided unless unavoidable.\\n5) The Supreme Court has traditionally held to the effect that “where a special statute such as the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter the ‘Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act’) expressly prescribes the statutory punishment for an attempt to a specific offense in the same manner as the completed offense (e.g., Article 5-4(6), Article 11(1), etc.), mitigation of punishment for attempt under Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act is not permitted” (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DO1635 rendered on September 22, 1987, 2000DO3947 rendered on November 14, 2000, 2010DO11620 rendered on November 25, 2010, etc.). However, according to current practice, since the statutory punishment for an attempted offense and a completed offense is basically the same and Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act merely means that an attempted offense may be mitigated at the judge’s discretion, even if a special statute expressly provides that an attempt is punished with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense, this merely confirms the principle that “the statutory punishment for a completed offense and an attempt is the same,” and it is difficult to find a basis for interpreting this as excluding the mitigation provision for attempts in the General Part of the Criminal Act. Therefore, according to current practice, the discretionary mitigation provision in Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act should naturally apply to attempt punishment provisions in the above special statutes as well. In the end, the attitude of the above Supreme Court precedents and current practice contradict each other and are difficult to harmonize.\\nHowever, according to the new understanding that the statutory punishment for an attempted offense is recognized as above, the statutory punishment for the attempt is determined by combining the statutory punishment for the completed offense and Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act; but if the special statute separately specifies the statutory punishment for the attempt, there is no longer any need for the interpretive process of law to fix the statutory punishment, so Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, which serves to fix the statutory punishment, has no room to operate. In this way, the above Supreme Court precedents can be explained consistently and harmoniously through the new understanding of attempts.\\n6) In short, Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act prescribes the elements of an attempted offense, and paragraph 2 prescribes its statutory punishment. To say, without express statutory basis, that the statutory punishment for an attempt is the same as that for the completed offense is an interpretation contrary to nulla poena sine lege. Before Article 25 of the Criminal Act operates, there is neither the elements of an attempted offense nor its statutory punishment.\\n\\nb. As a related matter, I would like to make one point regarding subject-matter jurisdiction.\\nIt is proper to interpret that the phrase “cases corresponding to death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more” subject to the collegiate panel under Article 32(1)3 of the Court Organization Act means cases in which the lowest among the alternative punishments enumerated as statutory punishment is imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more, and that it does not include cases in which a lighter punishment such as a fine is provided as an alternative punishment rather than imprisonment or penal detention. The reasons are as follows.\\n1) The Court Organization Act, while in principle vesting the trial power of district courts and their branches in a single judge, exceptionally requires a collegiate panel to try the cases listed in each subparagraph of Article 32(1), and, in the interest of taking caution in handling serious cases in which the statutory punishment is severe, it designates as within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction “cases corresponding to death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more” (subparagraph 3 of the same paragraph). Current practice takes the position that if the statutory punishment provides imprisonment with a minimum term of 1 year or more, even if a fine is provided as an alternative punishment, the case is within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction. According to this, Article 16(1) of the Act on Special Measures for Registration, etc. of Real Estate Ownership Transfer (hereinafter the “Act on Registration of Real Estate Ownership Transfer”) provides that a person who prepares a false certificate or obtains a certificate by false means, etc., shall be punished by “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, or a fine of not less than 10 million won and not more than 100 million won,” so a violation of Article 16(1) of the Act on Registration of Real Estate Ownership Transfer falls under the jurisdiction of the collegiate panel. The offense of riot under Article 115 of the Criminal Act also has a statutory punishment of “imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, or a fine not exceeding 15 million won,” and thus is within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction.\\n2) However, the phrase “cases corresponding to death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more” subject to the collegiate panel under Article 32(1)3 of the Court Organization Act should be determined solely on the basis of the statutory punishment itself, which can be said to be the stage before selection of the type of punishment. The above current practice appears to focus on the fact that even if a fine is provided as the statutory punishment, if imprisonment is selected, the term becomes 1 year or more, but subject-matter jurisdiction should be determined based on the statutory punishment. Since a fine is lighter than “imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more,” it cannot be viewed as satisfying the above requirement. Therefore, it is proper to interpret the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction only where the lightest available punishment among the statutory punishments, that is, the lowest among the alternative punishments enumerated as statutory punishment, is imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more; accordingly, where a lighter fine is prescribed as an alternative punishment, it is proper to regard the case as within the jurisdiction of a single judge. In the case of the above violation of Article 16(1) of the Act on Registration of Real Estate Ownership Transfer or riot, since a fine may be selected, it is proper to regard the case as within the jurisdiction of a single judge.\\n3) And according to the new understanding of attempted offenses, the statutory punishment for an attempt is the same as the reduction by one-half of only the lower limit of the completed offense’s statutory punishment, and jurisdiction over an attempted offense should be based on the statutory punishment for the attempt. Taking the offense of attempted destruction of public goods under Article 143 and Article 141(2) of the Criminal Act as an example, the statutory punishment for destruction of public goods is “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” and the statutory punishment for attempted destruction of public goods is “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years,” so while destruction of public goods falls within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction, attempted destruction of public goods is properly regarded as within the jurisdiction of a single judge.\\n\\nI hereby state the supplementary opinion to the separate opinion as above."}

{"[75DO1549]": "Judgment on the Grounds for the Prosecutor’s Appeal\\n\\nSince it should be understood that the “offense of another” in the provision of Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act, which states that a person who aids another’s offense shall be punished as an accessory, refers to a case in which the principal offender has commenced the commission of the offense in order to realize it, accessory liability can arise only where there has been a commencement of execution by the principal offender; and where the principal offender has remained merely at the preparatory stage without reaching commencement of execution, the act of assistance thereto cannot be punished as accessory liability, except where such act becomes co-principal liability for preparation.\\n\\nThis is because, in terms of the concept of the constituent elements of a crime, the act of execution of a preparatory offense is an unstructured and indefinite act, and the act of an accessory is likewise unstructured and indefinite; and because Article 28 of the Criminal Act provides that where a conspiracy or preparatory act for a crime has not reached commencement of execution, it shall not be punished unless there is a special statutory provision, thereby prohibiting unjust analogical or expansive interpretation of the constituent elements of a crime that would arise from punishment of a preparatory offense, it is not possible to directly include within the concept of an independent constituent offense the provisions in the Specific Part of the Criminal Act punishing preparatory offenses, and this interpretation is also consistent with the principle of nulla poena sine lege. Therefore, in light of the spirit of the Criminal Act as a whole, it is a reasonable interpretation to regard accessory liability as not being established at the preparatory stage.\\n\\nThe ground of appeal that the preparatory offense of robbery in this case is a crime corresponding to an independent constituent offense under the Criminal Act is, as stated above, an untenable independent view; and even if the purport of the judgment of the court below differs somewhat from this, it is proper in that it denied the establishment of accessory liability for a preparatory offense, and the ground of appeal disputing this is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}
{"[99DO3801]": "Each appeal is dismissed. As to Defendant 2, 115 days out of the days of detention after appeal shall be credited to the principal sentence."}

{"[99DO424]": "1. Regarding the first ground of appeal by the court-appointed defense counsel\\nArticle 28 of the Criminal Act provides that when a conspiracy or preparatory act for an offense has not reached the commencement of execution, it shall not be punished unless there is a special provision of law; Article 182(2) of the Customs Act provides that a person who has made preparations with the intent to commit a customs evasion offense, etc. prescribed in Article 180 shall be punished, together with an attempted offender, in the same manner as the principal offense; and Article 6(7) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes provides for aggravated punishment, under certain requirements, of a person who has committed an offense prescribed in Article 182 of the Customs Act. This is because customs offenses, including customs evasion offenses, have a significant effect on the national economy, have the characteristics of profit-making offenses equipped with organization, expertise, intelligence, and internationality, and because, in terms of the possibility or risk of infringement of legal interests, there is not a substantial difference between completion and attempt, or between attempt and preparation; accordingly, the provisions punishing preparatory acts are established solely for the purpose of achieving the legislative objective of the Customs Act and for maintaining order and public welfare, and are not intended, without rational basis, to discriminate a particular person from the general public or to specially crack down on customs evasion offenses, etc. different from other specific offenses such as tax evasion offenses under the Punishment of Tax Offenders Act; therefore, the above provisions concerning the preparatory offense of customs evasion cannot be deemed to violate the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution or the principle of guaranteeing basic human rights under Article 10 of the Constitution.\\n\\n2. Regarding the second ground of appeal by the court-appointed defense counsel and the first and second grounds of appeal by the Defendant\\nA comparison of the judgment of the court below and the evidence expressly stated in the first-instance judgment as cited by the court below with the record shows that the court below rightly found that the Defendant, etc. on 1998. 2. 17. executed a contract with a Chinese non-party limited liability company for the import of 1,000 tons of mung beans, and also submitted that contract as it was when applying on the 25th of the same month for advance review of the taxable price, but in fact decided to evade the customs duties corresponding thereto by paying the Chinese company an amount additionally equivalent to 10% of the imported quantity, importing that much additional quantity, and not filing an import declaration with respect to that portion, and thereafter, by July 7 of the same year, imported and cleared through customs 330 tons of mung beans in three installments and attempted to import the remaining 770 tons; and there is no illegality in fact-finding due to violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\nMeanwhile, according to Article 9-2(1) of the Customs Act, a person obligated to pay customs duties shall, at the time of filing an import declaration, declare to the head of the customs office the price of the relevant goods in accordance with the Presidential Decree; however, Article 9-15 of the same Act provides that when a person who is required to file a tax declaration has doubts concerning matters forming the basis for the determination of the taxable value, he/she may, before filing a price declaration, apply to the Commissioner of the Korea Customs Service or the head of the customs office for prior examination by preparing the documents prescribed by the Presidential Decree, and that when the head of the customs office recognizes that, in the case where the person obligated to pay customs duties files a tax declaration by such advance examination report, the relevant person obligated to pay and the applicant for advance examination are identical and the imported goods and the declaration of taxable value are identical to the contents of the advance examination report, the taxable value shall be determined according to the contents of the advance examination report unless there is a special reason prescribed by the Presidential Decree. Therefore, it is appropriate to regard the act of falsely declaring the taxable value and obtaining in advance an advance examination report on the taxable value by attaching a contract stating a lower quantity and price of goods to be imported, and applying for prior examination of the taxable value for all scheduled imported quantities, as an external preparatory act for the realization of the customs evasion offense. In this purport, the court below correctly held that the preparatory offense of customs evasion prescribed in Article 182(2) of the Customs Act applies to the remaining 770 tons, excluding the 330 tons of mung beans actually imported and cleared through customs by the Defendant, etc., and applied Article 6(7) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the preparatory offense of customs evasion.\\nAlso, upon examining the record, the fact that the validity period of the above advance examination report on taxable value was entered as until 1998. 8. 25. does not mean that it was impossible for the Defendant, etc. to actually import the remaining 770 tons of mung beans; moreover, no circumstance is recognized that the Defendant, etc. voluntarily abandoned such import, and furthermore, desistance offense means a case in which, after commencement of the execution of a crime, the person voluntarily ceases the act, and in the case of punishing an act of conspiracy/preparation before commencement of execution, the concept of desistance offense cannot be recognized (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO436, rendered on 1991. 6. 25.), so the argument in the grounds of appeal on this point also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Regarding the Defendant's third ground of appeal\\nIn a case such as this, where a sentence of imprisonment of less than 10 years was imposed, the argument that the sentencing is too severe and therefore unjust cannot constitute a lawful ground of appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and 55 days out of the detention after the appeal are included in the principal sentence, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the order by unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning accomplices is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: The intent required of an aider and abettor regarding the principal offender, etc. need not involve awareness of the specific content of the crime realized by the principal offender; conditional intent or foresight is sufficient, but this is not inconsistent with the point that awareness of the unlawfulness of the principal offender’s act, etc. is required.
B: The legal principle that the general provisions of the Criminal Act concerning accomplices cannot be applied to reciprocal offenses applies not only to reciprocal offenses that are necessary accomplice offenses, but also to cases in which, in terms of the statutory elements, the offense is structured so that it can be committed by a single person but is merely carried out in the form of a reciprocal offense.
C: If a person who does not have the status relationship of being engaged in business conspired with a person who has such a status relationship and committed the crime of occupational breach of trust, the accomplice without such status relationship must, pursuant to the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act, be punished by the sentence prescribed for the crime of simple breach of trust.
D: For the formation of co-principal liability, the common intent to jointly engage in the act is insufficient if it merely consists of recognizing another person’s criminal act and tolerating it without preventing it; it must instead consist of becoming united to carry out a specific criminal act by common intent and, by using the acts of another person, carrying one’s own intent into execution.
E: In order for aider and abettor liability to be established, the act of assistance must be closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime; therefore, if a person merely assisted an act that is not closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, aider and abettor liability does not arise.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DO576]": "Judgment on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The gist of the reasoning of the judgment below is as follows.\\n\\nA. The gist of the criminal facts against the Defendants found by the court below is that: \"The Defendants, (1) together with Nonparty 1, the crew members of the regular cargo vessel Pegasus Pride, and trailer driver Nonparty 2, etc., after resolving that the said crew members would each invest KRW 20,000,000 to purchase goods in Japan and then import them without declaration by using the said vessel, whereupon Nonparty 1 proposed to the Defendants that he was going to smuggle goods from Japan and asked them to purchase the smuggled goods, and proposed to Nonparty 2 to transport them, thereby obtaining each of their consent and then sequentially conspiring, and thereafter, when Nonparty 1, etc. purchased camcorders, etc. in Japan, loaded them on the said vessel, and entered Busan Port, Nonparty 2 used his own trailer to clandestinely remove them from the pier, then met Defendant 1 on the road and transferred them to the vehicle driven by Defendant 1, thereby importing camcorders, etc. without an import declaration as stated in Attached Table 1 of the List of Crimes appended to the judgment below; and (2) together with Nonparty 3, the crew members of Meristar, a vessel belonging to Namseong Shipping Co., Ltd., and the said Nonparty 2, etc., after resolving that the said crew members would purchase liquor in Japan and then import it without declaration by using the said vessel and, if it were smuggled into the country, Nonparty 2 would clandestinely remove it from the pier and sell it to the Defendants, thereby sequentially conspiring, and thereafter, when Nonparty 3, etc. purchased liquor in Japan, loaded it on the said vessel, and entered Busan Port, Nonparty 2 used his own trailer to clandestinely remove it from the pier, then met Defendant 1 on the road and transferred it to the vehicle driven by Defendant 1, thereby smuggling liquor without an import declaration as stated in Attached Table 4 of the List of Crimes appended to the judgment below.\"\\n\\nB. The Defendants have consistently denied the offenses from the investigative authorities to the proceedings in the court below, asserting that although they purchased liquor or camcorders, etc. from Nonparty 2 or Nonparty 1, etc., they had never conspired in advance with them in the smuggling offenses or participated therein at all. As to this, the court below, comparing the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the trial court with the record, determined that it was sufficiently established that the Defendants, together with Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc., committed the smuggling offenses by acting as one entity with a common intent and by using the acts of different persons, and thus recognized and punished the Defendants as co-principals of the smuggling offenses stated in its holding.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal concerning the misapprehension of the legal principles on co-principal liability\\n\\nIn order for co-principal liability to be established, there must, as a subjective requirement, be a common intent to jointly engage in the offense, and, as an objective requirement, execution of the offense through functional control over the act based on a common intent; the common intent as a subjective requirement is not satisfied merely by recognizing another person's offense and yet failing to stop it and tolerating it, but must consist of becoming one entity for the purpose of committing a particular criminal act with a common intent and thereby carrying out one's own intent by using the acts of another person (see Supreme Court Decisions 95DO2461, rendered January 26, 1996, 97DO3297, rendered June 26, 1998, and others).\\n\\nAccordingly, in order to punish the Defendants in this case as co-principals of the smuggling offenses stated in the judgment below, it is not enough to show only that the Defendants knew in advance of and tolerated the smuggling offenses of Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc.; at least the Defendants' intent must have reached the point where it could be evaluated as intending to become one entity with them for the smuggling offenses and to execute their own intent to smuggle by using their acts.\\n\\nHowever, no matter how closely the record is examined, it is difficult to find sufficient materials to conclude that the Defendants expressed an intent, for the smuggling offenses, to become one entity with Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc. and to carry out their own intent to smuggle by using their acts. Rather, according to the record, the Defendants, a married couple engaged in the business of selling imported goods, received a proposal from Nonparty 1, a crew member of Pegasus Pride, that he would bring goods such as camcorders from Japan and asked them to sell them, and responded, \"Since orders for camcorders are already coming in from Seoul, and I cannot sell any because I do not have any, bring them and I will sell them.\" Thereafter, when the crew members including Nonparty 1 smuggled in camcorders, etc. from Japan, took them out of the pier through Nonparty 2, met them at a rendezvous place, received the goods, paid the price at a price predetermined according to the then market price, and thereafter disposed of them elsewhere at a profit, and in the meantime trailer driver Nonparty 2 recommended that they also purchase liquor, so they began purchasing liquor smuggled in by the crew members of Meristar, including Nonparty 3; and unlike the camcorders, etc., they did not directly contact the crew members regarding the liquor, but negotiated the price with Nonparty 2, paid the price to Nonparty 2, received the liquor, and disposed of it.\\n\\nIf, as above, what the Defendants did in relation to the smuggling offenses in this case was merely to agree, after being asked by Nonparty 1 whether they would sell camcorders, etc. smuggled in from Japan, to sell them, or after being urged by Nonparty 2 to also purchase liquor, to agree to that, and thereafter, when the crew members smuggled goods in, to pay the price, receive the goods, and dispose of them to others, then it cannot be said that this constituted sharing the acts of execution of the smuggling offenses in this case or that the Defendants had the common intent required for the establishment of co-principal liability. The Defendants' statement that they would sell the goods if they were smuggled in can only be viewed as an expression of intent to acquire the goods or to mediate their sale if the goods were smuggled in, and cannot be viewed as an expression of an agreement to jointly commit the smuggling offenses.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below determined that the Defendants conspired with Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc. and committed the smuggling offenses in this case, and recognized and punished the Defendants as co-principals of the smuggling crimes stated in its holding. This is an error of law as to the requirements for the establishment of co-principal liability, or an illegality of finding facts without evidence in violation of the rules of evidence. The portion of the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment below and, in order to have the case retried and redetermined, remand it to the court below. The decision is rendered with the concurrence of the Justices participating in the case, and is so ordered."}

{"[2018DO10047]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Fraud against Victim Nonparty 1\\n\\nThe lower court found the fraud against Victim Nonparty 1 among the facts charged in this case to be guilty. Looking at the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the evidence duly admitted, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it did not conduct the necessary examination and thereby went beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal doctrine on the crime of fraud.\\n\\n2. Breach of Trust in the Course of Business\\n\\na. Claim of misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning accomplice and status\\n\\n(1) The crime of breach of trust in the course of business is established when a person who is in a position to handle another’s affairs in the course of business acquires a property gain, or causes a third person to acquire such gain, by an act in violation of that person’s duty, thereby causing damage to the principal. In terms of being in a position to handle another’s affairs, this is an aggravated provision for the crime of ordinary breach of trust, and thus it is a case where there is a difference in the severity of punishment by reason of a status relationship. Accordingly, if a person who does not have such a status relationship of a duty in the course of business conspired with a person having such a status relationship and committed the crime of breach of trust in the course of business, then, with respect to the accomplice without such status relationship, punishment must be imposed under the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act with the punishment prescribed for ordinary breach of trust. In such a case, the status offense of breach of trust in the course of business is established at least against the accomplice without such status relationship under the main text of the same Article, but only in sentencing is the statutory punishment for ordinary breach of trust, rather than the heavier punishment, applied (see Supreme Court Decision 86DO1517, decided October 28, 1986; Supreme Court Decision 2010DO6507, decided September 9, 2010, etc.).\\n\\n(2) The facts charged in this part are that the Defendant conspired in the act of breach of trust in the course of business by Nonparty 1, who was in the position of handling another’s affairs in the course of business, with respect to Victim Nonparty 2; therefore, as to the Defendant, who does not have the status relationship of a duty in the course of business, the crime of breach of trust in the course of business, which is a status offense, is established at least under the main text of Article 33 of the Criminal Act, but in sentencing the statutory punishment for ordinary breach of trust must be applied under the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act. Nevertheless, the lower court applied only Articles 356, 355(2), and 30 of the Criminal Act to the breach of trust in the course of business in this case, and selected imprisonment from among the statutory punishments under Article 356 of the Criminal Act applicable to the crime of breach of trust in the course of business; therefore, the lower court judgment misapplied the law by failing to apply the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\n(3) However, because the lower court determined the punishment to be imposed by aggravating the punishment prescribed for the crime of fraud against Victim Nonparty 1, which is in a relation of concurrent crimes with the above crime of breach of trust in the course of business and is more serious in terms of gravity than the crime of breach of trust in the course of business, the error in the lower court judgment seen in (2) above does not affect the result of the judgment. The ground of appeal on this point is ultimately without merit.\\n\\nb. Remaining arguments\\n\\nThe lower court recognized the breach of trust in the course of business among the facts charged in this case as guilty. Looking at the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the legal doctrine seen above and the evidence duly admitted, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it did not conduct the necessary examination and thereby went beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal doctrine on the crime of breach of trust in the course of business.\\n\\n3. Claim of improper sentencing\\n\\nAccording to Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal may be taken on the ground of improper sentencing only in cases where death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for 10 years or more has been imposed. Therefore, in this case, in which a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the Defendant, the argument that the sentence is too severe and therefore improper is not a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is without merit, and it is ordered to dismiss it; accordingly, the Court renders judgment as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2020DO7866]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the aiding-and-abetting portion of the facts charged in this case, concerning a violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Prevention of Illegal Trafficking in Narcotics, etc. (hereinafter, the “Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act”)\\nThe Defendant, knowing that the non-indicted person used so-called a “borrowed-name bank account” in order to evade tracking by investigative authorities, nevertheless, at the request of the non-indicted person, while purchasing cannabis on 4 occasions by depositing the purchase price for cannabis into a borrowed-name account under the name of a third party by means of deposit without a passbook, aided and abetted the non-indicted person’s act of concealing the source and attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc. for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the discovery of narcotics offenses.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the court below\\nThe court below reversed the first-instance judgment, which had found the above facts charged guilty, and found the Defendant not guilty for the following reasons.\\nIn the type of offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act, where the offense requires the existence of another person’s mutually opposing act in order to be committed, leaving aside the question whether a person in such mutually opposing relationship may become an instigator or co-principal where he or she actively participates in the entire process of the “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” offense or instigates the offense, if the person merely performed the mutually opposing act in accordance with the request, etc. of the offender (the principal offender), the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act cannot be applied to punish that person together with the offender (the principal offender) who committed the “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” offense.\\nThe Defendant’s mutually opposing act as the purchaser of cannabis (depositing the purchase price into a borrowed-name bank account while purchasing cannabis) is an indispensable element of the non-indicted person’s offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.”; therefore, it is not appropriate to apply the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act to the Defendant’s act and punish the Defendant together with the non-indicted person, who is the principal offender and also the cannabis seller, and there are no circumstances indicating that the Defendant actively participated in the non-indicted person’s violation of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act.\\n\\n3. Supreme Court determination\\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be accepted.\\n\\na. The general provisions of the Criminal Act concerning accomplices cannot be applied to reciprocal offenses that require the existence of mutually opposing acts by 2 or more persons (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2004. 10. 28. 2004DO3994). This legal principle presupposes reciprocal offenses, which are necessary accomplices, in which the constituent elements of the punishment provision itself require the existence of mutually opposing acts by 2 or more persons. It cannot be said that this legal principle applies where the constituent elements are structured in a form that can be committed by a single person, but are merely carried out in the form of a reciprocal offense.\\n\\nb. Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act criminally punishes, as the offense of concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc., “a person who, for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the discovery of narcotics offenses or the source of illicit proceeds, etc. or evading confiscation of illicit proceeds, etc., conceals or disguises the nature, location, source, or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” Among such acts, the act of “concealing or disguising the source or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” means an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning the cause of acquisition as if the illicit proceeds, etc. were lawfully acquired, or an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning attribution as if the illicit proceeds, etc. were not attributed (see Supreme Court Decision of 2014. 9. 4. 2014DO4408).\\nAccordingly, because the act of “concealing or disguising the source or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act does not require, in the constituent elements of the punishment provision itself, the existence of mutually opposing acts by 2 or more persons, the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act apply to the act of participating in such act by the principal offender.\\n\\nc. Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act provides: “A person who aids and abets another’s crime shall be punished as an accessory.” Aiding and abetting refers to a supportive act that, with knowledge of the principal offender’s specific preparation for or facts of the offense, makes the act of execution possible, promotes, or facilitates it, or to an act that, before the principal offender’s criminal act is completed, strengthens or increases the infringement of the legal interest by the principal offender, namely an act closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2012. 8. 30. 2012DO6027).\\nIn addition, an accessory must have the so-called “intent to aid and abet” to aid the principal offender’s execution and the “principal offender’s intent” as to the fact that the principal offender’s act is an act corresponding to the constituent elements (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2021. 9. 9. 2017DO19025). With regard to the intent to aid and abet and the principal offender’s intent required for the establishment of an accessory to the principal offender’s offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” under the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act, this means, for example, that a cannabis purchaser, while purchasing cannabis from the principal offender who is a cannabis seller, deposits the cannabis sale price under the name of a third party into a borrowed-name account at the request of the cannabis seller, and must recognize that such act is unlawful as aiding the principal offender’s execution. Of course, the principal offender’s intent required in an accessory need not include awareness of the specific details of the crime realized by the principal offender, and conditional awareness or foresight is sufficient (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2005. 4. 29. 2003DO6056), but this does not conflict with the requirement that awareness of the unlawfulness of the principal offender’s crime, etc. is necessary (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2021. 9. 9. 2017DO19025).\\n\\nd. The court below should have examined whether the Defendant’s act constituted aiding and abetting the violation of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act arising from the principal offender, the non-indicted person’s act of “concealing or disguising the source or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” as prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act, and whether the Defendant had the intent to aid and abet.\\nNevertheless, the court below found the Defendant not guilty on the ground that the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act do not apply to the Defendant who purchased cannabis and deposited the purchase price without a passbook into a borrowed-name bank account. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the establishment, etc. of an accessory to the offense of violating the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act through concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc., and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and the grounds of appeal pointing this out are justified.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons stated above, the not guilty portion of the judgment of the court below must be reversed. Where, among several criminal facts charged as concurrent offenses, the court below rendered a guilty verdict for some and a not guilty verdict for others, and the prosecutor appealed only the not guilty portion, while neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed the guilty portion, the guilty portion becomes final upon lapse of the appeal period, so even if the appeal as to the not guilty portion is meritorious, only the not guilty portion must be reversed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2007. 6. 28. 2005DO7473). Since the portions concerning the offense of violating the Act on the Management of Narcotics, etc. (cannabis), arising from cannabis sale, cannabis smoking, and attempted cannabis sale, which are in a concurrent-offense relationship with the not guilty portion of the judgment of the court below, were found guilty by the court below and neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed them, they became final; therefore, the scope of reversal of the judgment of the court below is limited to the not guilty portion.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nThe not guilty portion of the judgment of the court below is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for rehearing and determination on that portion. It is so adjudged unanimously by the Justices as stated in the dispositive part."}

{"[2020DO7866]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the portion of the facts charged in this case constituting aiding and abetting a violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Prevention of Illicit Trade in Narcotics, Etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Narcotics Trade Prevention Act”)\\nThe Defendant, while knowing that the non-indicted person used a so-called “borrowed-name bank account” in order to evade tracing by investigative authorities, purchased cannabis on four occasions by depositing, at the request of the non-indicted person, the purchase price for cannabis into a nominee account in the name of a third party by cash deposit, and thereby aided the non-indicted person in concealing the source and relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc. for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the detection of narcotics-related crimes.\\n\\n2. The lower court’s determination\\nThe lower court, for the following reasons, reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the above facts charged guilty and held the Defendant not guilty.\\nIn the type of offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act, where the commission of the offense necessarily requires another person’s reciprocal act, apart from the issue of whether a person in a reciprocal relationship may be an instigator or co-principal by actively participating in the principal offender’s offense, such as by being involved in the entire process of the offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.” or by instigating the offense, if a person merely performed a reciprocal act in accordance with the request, etc. of the offender (principal offender), the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act cannot be applied to punish such person as an accomplice of the offender (principal offender) who committed the act of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.”\\nThe reciprocal act of the Defendant, a purchaser of cannabis (depositing the purchase price into a borrowed-name bank account while purchasing cannabis), is an indispensable element of the non-indicted person’s offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.”; therefore, it is not appropriate to apply the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act to the Defendant’s act and punish the Defendant together with the non-indicted person, who was both the principal offender and the cannabis seller, and there are no circumstances suggesting that the Defendant actively participated in the non-indicted person’s violation of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\nHowever, the above determination of the lower court cannot be accepted.\\n\\na. The provisions of the General Part of the Criminal Act concerning complicity cannot be applied to reciprocal offenses that require the existence of reciprocal acts by two or more persons (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3994, decided October 28, 2004). This principle presupposes reciprocal offenses, which are necessary accomplice offenses requiring, in the elements of the offense itself, the existence of reciprocal acts by two or more persons. It cannot be said that the principle concerning reciprocal offenses applies merely because, although the offense is structured in a form that can be committed alone in terms of the elements of the offense, it happens to be committed in the form of a reciprocal offense.\\n\\nb. Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act criminally punishes, as the offense of concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc., “a person who conceals or disguises the nature, location, source, or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc., for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the detection of narcotics-related crimes or the source of illicit profits, etc. or evading confiscation of illicit profits, etc.” Among such conduct, the act of “concealing or disguising the source or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc.” means an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning the cause of acquisition so as to make illicit profits, etc. appear to have been lawfully acquired, or an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning attribution so as to make illicit profits, etc. appear not to be attributed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2014DO4408, decided September 4, 2014).\\nAccordingly, since the act of “concealing or disguising the source or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act does not, in the elements of the offense itself, require the existence of reciprocal acts by two or more persons, the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act apply to acts of participating in such conduct by the principal offender.\\n\\nc. Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act provides, “A person who aids another person’s crime shall be punished as an accessory.” Aiding and abetting means, with knowledge of the principal offender’s concrete preparation for or facts of the offense, an act of support that makes the execution possible, promotes, or facilitates it, or an act that, before the principal offender’s criminal act has ended, strengthens or increases the infringement of legal interests by the principal offender; it refers to an act closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO6027, decided August 30, 2012).\\nIn addition, an accessory must have the so-called “intent to aid,” namely the intent to aid the principal offender’s execution, and the “intent of the principal offender” as to the fact that the principal offender’s act constitutes an act falling under the elements of the offense (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO19025, decided September 9, 2021). As to the intent to aid and the principal offender’s intent required for the establishment of an accessory to the offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.” under the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act, this means, for example, that when a purchaser of cannabis buys cannabis from the principal offender who is the cannabis seller and, at the request of the cannabis seller, deposits the cannabis purchase price into a nominee account in the name of a third party, the purchaser must recognize that such act is unlawful as it aids the principal offender’s execution of the offense. Of course, the principal offender’s intent required for an accessory need not involve recognition of the concrete content of the crime realized by the principal offender, and conditional awareness or foresight is sufficient (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DO6056, decided April 29, 2005), but this does not contradict the requirement that there be recognition of the unlawfulness of the principal offender’s offense, etc. (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO19025, decided September 9, 2021).\\n\\nd. The lower court should have examined whether the Defendant’s act constituted aiding and abetting a violation of Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act by the principal offender, the non-indicted person, through the act of “concealing or disguising the source or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc.,” and whether the Defendant had the intent to aid.\\nNevertheless, the lower court held that the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act did not apply to the Defendant, who purchased cannabis and deposited the purchase price by cash deposit into a borrowed-name bank account, and thus found the Defendant not guilty. The lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment, etc. of an aider and abettor to a violation of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act resulting from an act of concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc., and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and the argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons stated above, the not-guilty portion of the lower court judgment must be reversed. Where, among several criminal facts charged as concurrent offenses, the lower court separately rendered a guilty judgment on some and a not-guilty judgment on others, and the prosecutor appealed only the not-guilty portion while neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed the guilty portion, the guilty portion becomes final upon expiration of the appeal period; therefore, even if the appeal as to the not-guilty portion is well-founded, only the not-guilty portion must be reversed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO7473, decided June 28, 2007). The portions of the lower court judgment concerning the offense of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (cannabis) resulting from the sale and purchase of cannabis, cannabis smoking, and attempted sale of cannabis, which are in concurrent-offense relation with the not-guilty portion of the lower court judgment, were found guilty by the lower court, and since neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed them, they became final; therefore, the scope of reversal of the lower court judgment is limited to the not-guilty portion.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the not-guilty portion of the lower court judgment is reversed and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination on that portion, and the judgment is rendered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2022DO15537]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles  \\n“Aiding and abetting” refers to an act of assistance that, by knowing the principal offender’s specific preparation for or facts of the offense, makes the execution act possible, promotes it, or facilitates it, or to an act that, before the principal offender’s criminal conduct is completed, strengthens or increases the infringement of the legal interest by the principal offender, that is, an act closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime. An aider and abettor must have both the so-called intent to aid, namely the intent to aid the principal offender’s execution, and the principal offender’s intent as to the fact that the principal offender’s act is an act falling under the constituent elements of the offense; and because it is a crime established subordinately to the principal offender, a causal relationship is required between the aiding act and the realization of the principal offender’s crime. In order for aiding and abetting to be established, the aiding act must be closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime and must be capable of being evaluated as having actually contributed to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, such as by causing the principal offender to realize a concrete risk or by increasing the opportunity to bring about the criminal result. Where the act merely assisted conduct not closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, aiding and abetting is not established (see Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on September 9, 2021, 2017DO19025, Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 16, 2021, 2015DO12632, etc.).\\n\\n2. Lower court determination  \\nThe lower court determined that the operators of Baksa-bang created the Telegram group described in the opinion (hereinafter referred to as the “Mission Room”) and, by ordering the so-called “real-time search ranking challenge” by which participants in the Mission Room would cause a specific search term to appear as a real-time trending search term by simultaneously entering a specific search term on the Internet portal Naver at specific times (2019. 12. 1. 20:00, 21:00, 22:00, 23:00 and 2019. 12. 2. 00:00, 01:00, 02:00, 03:00, 08:00, 21:00), caused an unspecified number of Telegram users to participate in the Mission Room at the designated times, and then, around 2019. 12. 2. 21:20, posted obscene materials concerning the victim, the non-indicted person, in the Mission Room; and, in relation thereto, the court found that the Defendant, while recognizing the operators of Baksa-bang’s intent to distribute obscene materials concerning the victim, the non-indicted person, entered search terms on four occasions from 2019. 12. 1. 21:00 to 2019. 12. 2. 00:00 in accordance with their instructions with the intent to facilitate the same, and by posting and certifying the fact of the searches in the above Mission Room and the channel related to Baksa-bang, facilitated the act of distributing obscene materials for children and juveniles by the operators of Baksa-bang and thereby aided and abetted it.\\n\\n3. Supreme Court determination  \\na. According to the legal principles examined above, in order for aiding and abetting to be established, not only must there be the intent to aid, namely the intent to aid the principal offender’s execution, and the principal offender’s intent as to the fact that the principal offender’s act is an act falling under the constituent elements of the offense, but also the relevant act must be closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime and must be capable of being evaluated as having actually contributed to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, such as by causing the principal offender to realize a concrete risk or by increasing the opportunity to bring about the criminal result; accordingly, it is difficult to recognize the establishment of aiding and abetting merely because a person performed or was involved in an act not closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime. In light of the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court, the lower court’s determination cannot be upheld for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) As to the total of four searches listed in the attached schedule of offenses of the lower court judgment, it is acknowledged that, for some of those searches, the time gap between the time the search terms were announced in the “Mission Room” and the time the Defendant searched was quite short (items 2 and 3), or the time gap between the announced designated search time and the time the Defendant searched was quite short (items 1 and 4). However, such circumstances cannot immediately be said to constitute indirect facts supporting the proposition that the Defendant recognized that the “real-time search ranking challenge” was being carried out as a means of realizing the crime of distributing obscene materials concerning the victim, the non-indicted person, by the operators of Baksa-bang, or that the Defendant actually participated in the “Mission Room.” In other words, from the investigative stage to the trial, the Defendant consistently stated that he conducted the searches in this case out of curiosity after reading a post concerning the non-indicted person in “△△,” and submitted evidence related to “△△” consistent therewith; ① the evidence related to “△△” submitted by the Defendant clearly shows a situation in which the same keyword was repeatedly searched, without any particular reason or explanation, starting approximately 30 minutes before the time when the Mission Room announced the search keyword for item 2 of the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment; and ② even according to the evidence submitted by the prosecutor, it can be seen that the first certification by a participant had already been completed approximately 10 minutes before the time when the Mission Room announced the search keyword for items 1 and 3 of the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment. This shows circumstances indicating that the search terms listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment were being widely searched across various websites and multiple chat rooms, including “△△,” which was unrelated to Baksa-bang, even before the instructions of the operators of Baksa-bang; if so, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that the Defendant searched them after seeing them on other sites such as “△△” rather than in the “Mission Room,” as he contended, and the possibility that the operators of Baksa-bang also issued the instructions listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment in the sense of riding on the above widespread existing search state. This is even more so in light of the fact, as recognized in the first-instance judgment, that the victim, the non-indicted person, was a person who became famous by appearing in the ○○ program, that at that time numerous posts actually related to the non-indicted person were being uploaded on △△ and the like, and that the Defendant also ordinarily liked □□ music and had applied for the above ○○ program. Therefore, the time gap between the Defendant’s search time and the time the search terms were announced in the Mission Room or the announced designated search time is difficult to regard as having significant meaning in relation to the facts charged in this case.\\n\\n2) Even in light of the fact that there were approximately 2,700 participants in the “Mission Room,” whereas approximately 12,000 people searched for the “non-indicted person” on Naver from 2019. 12. 1. to 2019. 12. 2., it is difficult to exclude the possibility that they searched for it through various routes and motives unrelated to the posting and search instructions of the operators of Baksa-bang, rather than pursuant thereto. In particular, in the absence of any evidence to acknowledge that the chat room the Defendant entered through △△ and the “Mission Room” described in the facts charged in this case are the same, the mere fact that the Defendant searched for the same phrase as the search term announced in the “Mission Room” at a time close to a particular point in time, or certified some search screen in the chat room he entered, cannot justify the inference that he knew of the content of the instructions, such as the real-time search ranking challenge posted in the “Mission Room” by the operators of Baksa-bang, and acted pursuant thereto. The Defendant himself also consistently asserted, in substance, that “as a fan of the non-indicted person, he searched after seeing rumors about the non-indicted person posted on △△ and the controversy surrounding their truthfulness.” If the Defendant had known the contents of the instructions in the “Mission Room” and searched in accordance with those instructions, it would be possible to infer that he would have participated in all real-time search ranking challenges, if only to avoid being forcibly expelled as posted; yet the Defendant, apart from the searches listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment, additionally searched for the “non-indicted person” seven times until around 03:30 on 2019. 12. 2. at times unrelated to the designated search times announced in the “Mission Room,” and except for that, he does not appear to have entered the relevant search terms at the designated search times announced in the “Mission Room.” Even considering that most of the Defendant’s search times make it difficult to conclude that they were related to the designated search times announced in the “Mission Room,” it cannot be said that the Defendant participated in the real-time search ranking challenge according to the instructions of the “Mission Room”; rather, in light of the fact that, even under such circumstances, he was not forcibly expelled from the chat room, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that the chat room in which the Defendant participated was not the “Mission Room” opened by the operators of Baksa-bang, and this constitutes circumstances inconsistent with the facts charged in this case and indirect facts supporting the Defendant’s assertion.\\n\\n3) As such, inasmuch as it is difficult to find that the Defendant participated in the “Mission Room” and thereby recognized the instructions and announcements of the operators of Baksa-bang, or that he knew, from the search terms alone, that they were for the criminal act of “distributing obscene materials for children and juveniles,” it is difficult to conclude that there was, with respect to the facts charged in this case, the intent to aid and abet, much less the principal offender’s intent concerning the distribution of obscene materials for children and juveniles. Furthermore, adding to the above search circumstances the fact that the operators of Baksa-bang distributed obscene materials for children and juveniles only at a point approximately 21 hours to 24 hours after the Defendant’s search times listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment, the act of merely entering search terms encountered through various routes at the time in question, as in this case, rather than actively participating in the operators’ “Mission Room” and entering search terms and certifying in accordance with its instructions, may be viewed as having been merely utilized in the real-time search ranking challenge, etc. that the operators of Baksa-bang initiated with the intent to entice persons interested in the fact that a specific search term was then a hot issue into the “Mission Room” and thereby promote the sale of obscene materials, and it is difficult otherwise to acknowledge a close relationship or causal relationship between each of the Defendant’s acts and the realization of the principal offender’s crime, or to conclude that each of the Defendant’s acts actually contributed to the realization of the principal offender’s crime.\\n\\nb. Nevertheless, the lower court found the facts charged in this case guilty solely on the grounds stated in the opinion. In so doing, the lower court erred by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning aiding and abetting, and such error affected the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Of A, who has one of the following <CRIMINAL_RECORDS>, if A is indicted on November 10, 2023, for one or more of the following <CRIMINAL_FACTS>, and those <CRIMINAL_FACTS> are found to be true, which of the following statements is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents) <CRIMINAL_RECORD> Ⓐ On April 10, 2023, at the Seoul Central District Court, he was sentenced to a fine of 5,000,000 won for habitual theft, and that judgment became final on April 18, 2023. Ⓑ On May 10, 2023, at the Seoul Central District Court, he was sentenced to imprisonment for 6 months for theft, and that judgment became final on May 18, 2023. <CRIMINAL_FACTS> ㉠ Habitually, around February 10, 2023, at X convenience store, he took one mobile phone owned by victim M and stole it [habitual theft]. ㉡ Around March 8, 2023, at Y coffee shop, he lied to victim N, saying, “There is a virtual asset that will be listed on a famous virtual asset exchange within a few days, and if you invest money in me, you can obtain a profit of several hundred times or more,” and around March 10, 2023, received 10,000,000 won from victim N and thereby defrauded him [fraud]. ㉢ Around June 10, 2023, at Z entertainment bar, he struck victim O on the cheek several times and kicked the victim’s leg with his foot, assaulting the victim [assault].
A: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉠ offense, and it is recognized that the ㉠ criminal fact and the Ⓐ criminal fact were committed by the same habitual pattern, a judgment of dismissal of prosecution under Article 326, item 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act must be rendered.
B: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉠ offense, even if it is recognized that the ㉠ criminal fact and the Ⓑ criminal fact were committed by the same habitual pattern, a judgment of dismissal of prosecution under Article 326, item 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act cannot be rendered.
C: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉡ offense, it is in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the Ⓐ offense, for which the judgment has become final.
D: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉡ and ㉢ offenses, since the ㉡ offense is in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the Ⓑ offense, for which the judgment has become final, the court must, when rendering a judgment simultaneously on the ㉡ and ㉢ offenses, sentence one punishment for the ㉡ offense and one punishment for the ㉢ offense, respectively.
E: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉡ and ㉢ offenses, even when the punishment is reduced for the ㉡ offense under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation applies, and when reducing a fixed-term imprisonment, it cannot be reduced to less than one-half of the term.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO7864]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nEven if the criminal facts for which a final judgment has been rendered and the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the judgment of fact in that final judgment can be evaluated as falling under a single comprehensive offense as a habitual offender, in order for the res judicata effect of that final judgment to extend even to the criminal facts committed before that time, the defendant concerned must have been indicted and punished as a habitual offender in that final judgment; if the defendant was punished only for the basic constituent offense and not as a habitual offender, then even if the criminal facts for which the final judgment was rendered and the criminal facts committed before that time are comprehensively considered and are thus determined to constitute a single comprehensive offense as a habitual offender only at that point, it cannot be deemed that the res judicata effect of that final judgment extends to the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the judgment of fact (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2001DO3206 rendered on September 16, 2004).\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that it did not render a judgment of dismissal for the crime of fraud in this case is correct, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and part of the number of days of detention after the appeal is to be included in the principal sentence for each of the offenses set forth in Paragraph 1 of the holding, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2006DO7864]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nEven if the criminal facts for which a final judgment has been rendered and the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the fact-finding judgment in that final judgment may be evaluated as constituting a habitual offense and thus a comprehensive single offense, in order for the res judicata effect of that final judgment to extend to the criminal facts committed before that time, in that final judgment the defendant in question must have been indicted and punished as a habitual offender; where the defendant was only punished for an offense comprising the basic constituent elements, not for a habitual offense, even if the criminal facts for which the final judgment was rendered and the criminal facts committed before that time are combined and only then determined to all correspond to a comprehensive single offense as a habitual offender, the res judicata effect of that final judgment cannot be deemed to extend to the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the fact-finding judgment (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2001DO3206, decided September 16, 2004).\\n\\nOn the same reasoning, the appellate court's determination not to render a judgment of dismissal of prosecution with respect to the criminal facts of the fraud offense in this case is correct, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of law, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and part of the number of days of detention after the appeal is credited toward the principal punishment for each offense in Paragraph 1, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, with the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

{"[2014DO469]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal (the statements in a supplemental statement of grounds for final appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal has elapsed shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\nIn light of the wording and legislative purpose, etc. of the latter part of Article 37 and Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, where an offense that has not yet been adjudicated could not be adjudicated together with an offense for which judgment has already become final and conclusive, it is reasonable to interpret that the relation of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act cannot arise, and that a sentence may not be imposed, reduced, or exempted by considering equity with a case in which the offenses are adjudicated together under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO9948 rendered on October 27, 2011; Supreme Court Decision 2012DO9295 rendered on September 27, 2012). Meanwhile, where several offenses that have not yet been adjudicated were committed before and after the judgment became final and conclusive, if the offenses committed before the judgment became final and conclusive could not be adjudicated together with the offenses for which judgment had already become final and conclusive, it cannot be said that the relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized between those several offenses as if no final and conclusive judgment existed, and that Article 38 of the Criminal Act applies; therefore, a sentence can only be separately determined and imposed for each offense committed before and after the judgment became final and conclusive (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO2351 rendered on June 10, 2011).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the offenses of violating the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc.
