(psychotropic drugs) committed on January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case were committed before the judgment sentencing the Defendant to imprisonment for 8 months, suspended for 2 years, for the same offense at the Seoul Central District Court became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012; however, separate from the above prior conviction, the Defendant has another prior conviction in which the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to imprisonment for 1 year, suspended for 2 years, for the same offense, etc., and which became final and conclusive on November 26, 2011, and the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 were committed before the judgment became final and conclusive on November 26, 2011, so it can be seen that the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 and the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case could not, from the outset, be adjudicated together.\\n\\nTherefore, no relation of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act can arise between the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 and the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case, and Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, which requires consideration of equity with a case in which the offense and the offense for which judgment has become final and conclusive are adjudicated together when imposing a sentence for an offense that has not yet been adjudicated among concurrent offenses, has no room for application here. Nor does it follow that, as if the judgment that became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 did not exist, the relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized between the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012, which were committed before the above judgment became final and conclusive, and the remaining offenses committed after the above judgment became final and conclusive, and that Article 38 of the Criminal Act applies. Therefore, a sentence can only be separately determined and imposed for the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 and the remaining offenses in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court correctly determined that no relation of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act can arise between the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 and the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case. However, the lower court, on the premise that the relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized between the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case, which were committed before the above judgment became final and conclusive, and the remaining offenses committed after the above judgment became final and conclusive, determined and imposed a single sentence for all of the offenses in this case, which contains illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nTherefore, without reaching the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court, and it is so adjudged as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2017DO14609]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Procedural History and Issues\\n\\na. On December 9, 2016, the Defendant was convicted by the Daejeon High Court of the offense of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) and sentenced to imprisonment for 4 years on the factual finding that “from March 11, 2015, to August 7, 2015, he sold psychotropic drugs on 33 occasions.” That judgment became final by the Supreme Court’s decision dismissing the appeal on February 10, 2017 (hereinafter referred to as “the prior conviction in this case”).\\n\\nb. While the above trial was still pending before the Daejeon High Court, on November 22, 2016, this indictment was filed against the Defendant at the Gongju Branch of the Daejeon District Court on the counts of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics), alleging the following facts (hereinafter referred to as “the offense in this case”): “in early October 2015, he sold psychotropic drugs once, and on November 8, 2015, he attempted to sell psychotropic drugs once but failed.” The offense in this case constitutes the sale and attempted sale of psychotropic drugs; accordingly, Article 58(1) 3 and Article 58(3), Article 58(1) 3 of the Narcotics Control Act apply, and the statutory punishment is life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years.\\n\\nc. The latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act provides that “an offense committed before the final judgment of an offense for which a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier has been imposed and an offense committed before the finality of that judgment shall be concurrent offenses.” Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense for which judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time. In such case, the sentence may be mitigated or remitted.” Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act provides that “when mitigating a determinate term of imprisonment or confinement, the term shall be reduced to one-half thereof.”\\n\\nd. The trial court selected determinate terms of imprisonment for the offense in this case, found that the offense in the prior conviction in this case and the offense in this case were in the relation of concurrent offenses under the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “latter-part concurrent offenses”), and, pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, applied Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act to grant statutory mitigation. It then applied, in sequence, the aggravation for concurrent offenses under the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1), and discretionary mitigation, and within the range of the sentence to be imposed thus calculated (imprisonment from 1 year and 3 months to 11 years and 3 months), sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 1 year and 6 months.\\n\\ne. The appellate court reversed the trial court judgment and sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months for the following reasons. That is, where, as in this case, the offense falling within latter-part concurrent offenses committed before the judgment imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier becomes final is subject to a statutory minimum sentence, and where the sentence prescribed for that offense and the sentence prescribed for the offense whose judgment has become final are the “same type of sentence other than death, life imprisonment, or life confinement” as provided in Article 38(1) 2 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “the issue at hand”), then in mitigating punishment pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, no limit may be imposed on the extent of mitigation. Therefore, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation does not apply, and the sentence should be determined fairly and appropriately in consideration of equity with the case where punishment is imposed as former-part concurrent offenses under the former sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “former-part concurrent offenses”).\\n\\nUltimately, the appellate court selected determinate terms of imprisonment for the offense in this case, found it to be in the relation of latter-part concurrent offenses with the offense in the prior conviction in this case, applied the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act to aggravate punishment for concurrent offenses, then applied Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act to mitigate punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses, and thereafter applied discretionary mitigation.\\n\\nf. The gist of the prosecutor’s grounds for appeal is that, when mitigating punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses pursuant to the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, the statutory mitigation method under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act must be followed.\\n\\ng. The issue in this case is whether, when mitigating punishment pursuant to the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses for which a statutory minimum sentence has been set, as in the present issue, in the case of imprisonment it should be deemed possible to mitigate only within one-half of the term of imprisonment by applying Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act, or whether the application of Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act should be excluded so that mitigation below one-half of the term of imprisonment is possible.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s Determination\\n\\na. According to existing Supreme Court precedents, even when mitigating punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation applies, and when mitigating a determinate term of imprisonment, mitigation below one-half of the term is not allowed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DO6627, decided December 21, 2006). These Supreme Court precedents are sound and should be maintained going forward. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nb. 1) Sentencing is divided into stages such as confirmation of the statutory punishment, determination of the sentence to be imposed, and determination of the sentence to be pronounced. When imposing a sentence, a judge must determine the sentence to be pronounced only within the range of the sentence to be imposed, formed through aggravation and mitigation of the statutory punishment, while considering sentencing factors; this also applies to latter-part concurrent offenses (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376, decided September 11, 2008).\\n\\nArticle 56 of the Criminal Act prescribes the order of aggravation and mitigation when causes for aggravation and mitigation of punishment coincide in the following order: “1. aggravation under the main text of each respective provision, 2. aggravation under Article 34(2), 3. repeat-offender aggravation, 4. statutory mitigation, 5. aggravation for concurrent offenses, 6. discretionary mitigation.” Since statutory mitigation is to be applied first and discretionary mitigation last, where there is a cause for statutory mitigation, it must be applied before discretionary mitigation; discretionary mitigation is applied when, even after such statutory mitigation has been fully applied, the range of the sentence to be imposed is to be eased so as to pronounce a lower sentence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 91DO985, decided June 11, 1991, and 2005DO6120, decided September 29, 2005). Where Article 55 and Article 56 of the Criminal Act apply to an offense with a statutory minimum sentence, the mitigated minimum is maintained even after statutory mitigation and discretionary mitigation.\\n\\n2) In light of the above provisions of the Criminal Act, since the sentence to be imposed becomes the final standard for the sentence to be pronounced, its scope must be strictly determined according to law, and unless there is a separate express provision, no mitigation ground of a different nature from the causes for aggravation and mitigation listed in Article 56 of the Criminal Act may be recognized.\\n\\nThere are statutory mitigation and judicial mitigation, namely discretionary mitigation. Aside from discretionary mitigation, all mitigation prescribed in various provisions of the law falls within the single framework of statutory mitigation. Accordingly, mitigation prescribed in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act naturally constitutes statutory mitigation. The wording “the sentence may be mitigated or remitted” in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act is no different from other statutory grounds for mitigation. If Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act were to be understood as establishing a new type of mitigation, then, with respect to it, a different extent or method of mitigation from ordinary statutory mitigation would have to be provided, and the order of mitigation should also have been separately prescribed; yet no such provision exists. Unless the extent, method, or order of mitigation is otherwise provided, it is entirely natural to view Articles 55 and 56 of the Criminal Act, which are general provisions on the method of statutory mitigation, as applicable even to latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nc. The problem of latter-part concurrent offenses arises because, although the offense and the offense whose judgment has become final could have been adjudicated together as former-part concurrent offenses, they were not, and thus the defendant may be disadvantaged compared with the case of simultaneous adjudication. However, how latter-part concurrent offenses should be handled is fundamentally a matter of legislative policy. Whether to consider this at the sentencing stage, whether to consider it at the execution stage, and, if considered at either stage, how it is to be considered, all must follow the legislature’s intent.\\n\\nSince the enactment of the Criminal Act until it was amended by Act No. 7623 on July 29, 2005, into its present form, Article 39 had provided in paragraph 1 that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense,” and in paragraph 2 that “where there are several judgments under the preceding paragraph, they shall be executed according to the example of the preceding Article.”\\n\\nAlthough the current Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act aims to eliminate disparities in punishment between latter-part concurrent offenses and former-part concurrent offenses, it does not state that, where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, one should “determine the total sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed calculated by applying Article 38 of the Criminal Act to that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final, and then pronounce, as the sentence for the offense not yet adjudicated, the remainder after deducting the sentence for the offense whose judgment has become final from that total sentence,” or that one should “pronounce, as the sentence for the offense not yet adjudicated, a sentence such that the total of the sentences pronounced for that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final falls within the range of the sentence to be imposed calculated by applying Article 38 of the Criminal Act to both offenses.” Rather, by providing that a sentence is to be imposed for the offense not yet adjudicated “taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time,” the legislature adopted a flexible legislative form enabling the court to determine a reasonable and appropriate sentence, taking into account that determining the total sentence or limiting the range of the sentence to be imposed in the manner described above could amount to a second adjudication of the offense whose judgment has already become final, thereby potentially violating the principle against double jeopardy, and could unduly restrict the range of the sentence that may be imposed for latter-part concurrent offenses sentenced later, making it impossible or extremely difficult to determine a reasonable and appropriate sentence corresponding to responsibility (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376, etc.).\\n\\nDuring the above legislative amendment process, there was a proposed amendment to include in the current Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act a provision that “mitigation may be made even below the mitigation limit under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act,” thereby enabling mitigation without a lower limit, but it was not ultimately adopted. In other words, although the legislative process presented the view that the application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should be excluded when mitigating latter-part concurrent offenses, that view was not accepted. In light of this, it is not only consistent with textual and systematic interpretation to regard mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses as one form of ordinary statutory mitigation and to require compliance with Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act in mitigating latter-part concurrent offenses, but it also accords with teleological interpretation considering the legislature’s intent and legislative history.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, the introductory sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time.” This merely expresses the intent to determine punishment by taking equity into account at the sentencing stage, rather than at the execution stage as had previously been done for latter-part concurrent offenses, and cannot be understood as declaring that, for latter-part concurrent offenses, mitigation may be made without any restriction on the extent of mitigation so as to achieve perfect equity with simultaneous adjudication.\\n\\nThat is, the provision that a sentence shall be imposed “taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time” declares the principle that the court shall impose a sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses within the range of the sentence to be imposed, taking into account equity with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are adjudicated together, thereby presenting an additional consideration relevant to sentencing under Article 51 of the Criminal Act. This means that, in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses, if in the sentencing process the resulting punishment is deemed inequitable compared with punishing the offense whose judgment has become final together with the latter-part concurrent offense, the punishment must, as far as possible, be made equitable through mitigation or exemption from punishment as provided in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act. If, in light of sentencing discretion, it is considered impossible to reach an equitable result by mitigation alone, exemption from punishment suffices. Whether to mitigate or exempt punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses is, in principle, a matter that the court adjudicating the offense may determine at its discretion (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376, etc.). Therefore, there is not much need to view the law as permitting a sentence outside the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed, contrary to the significant principle that even when mitigating offenses with a statutory minimum, a certain minimum must be maintained. It is also difficult to say that a judge’s sentencing discretion is seriously infringed or that appropriate sentencing becomes impossible.\\n\\ne. It cannot be categorically said that, in mitigating punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses, maintaining a lower limit for the term of punishment is disadvantageous to the defendant, or that not maintaining such a lower limit is advantageous to the defendant. If, after eliminating the lower limit of punishment so that the sentence to be imposed becomes continuous up to exemption from punishment, the sentence is determined, then this would run counter to the purpose of the law, which, while requiring that a sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses be imposed taking into account equity with the case where the offense is punished together with the offense whose judgment has become final, allows not only mitigation but also exemption from punishment, and may in fact produce a disadvantageous result for the defendant. If Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is applied to mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses, then after mitigation the sentence is determined within the range of the sentence to be imposed, that is, with a lower limit of punishment maintained; at that time, if it is considered inequitable compared with punishing the offense together with the offense whose judgment has become final, the court will choose exemption from punishment rather than pronouncement of sentence, because such exemption is more favorable to the defendant than pronouncing a sentence with the lower limit removed.\\n\\nf. Exemption from punishment is not the case where the sentence to be imposed is “0.” The fixation of the sentence to be imposed is carried out at a stage prior to pronouncement of sentence, whereas exemption from punishment means that although the offense is established and the power to punish has arisen, punishment is not imposed for certain reasons; in other words, it is a guilty judgment but no sentence is pronounced, so it does not presuppose a sentence to be imposed. Also, the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act regarding latter-part concurrent offenses provides that “in such case, the sentence may be mitigated or remitted,” and does not provide that “in such case, the sentence may be mitigated and remitted,” so it is clear from the wording that mitigation and exemption from punishment are not compatible. Therefore, if one chooses mitigation, one cannot reflect the result of exemption from punishment. But if one accepts that there is no lower limit for mitigation, then no meaning remains for separately providing exemption from punishment apart from mitigation.\\n\\n3. Resolution of this Case\\n\\nIn light of these legal principles, the appellate court, having selected determinate imprisonment from among the statutory punishment of life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years and having decided to mitigate punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses and to apply discretionary mitigation, should have aggravated and mitigated punishment in the order prescribed by Article 56 of the Criminal Act—namely, mitigation pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act (Article 56 4), aggravation for concurrent offenses (Article 56 5), and discretionary mitigation (Article 56 6)—and, in doing so, should have mitigated in accordance with Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act to “one-half of the term of that punishment,” and thus should have determined the Defendant’s sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed, namely imprisonment from 1 year and 3 months to 11 years and 3 months.\\n\\nNevertheless, contrary to this, the appellate court, on the erroneous premise that Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act does not apply when mitigating punishment prescribed by Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses, sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months, which fell below the statutory lower limit of the sentence to be imposed as described above. There is error in the appellate court’s judgment in misapprehending the legal principles concerning mitigation of punishment prescribed in Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, thereby affecting the judgment. The prosecutor’s grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appellate judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the appellate court for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged as set forth in the disposition. In this judgment, apart from the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Ahn Cheol-sang, Kim Seon-soo, and Justice Lee Ki-taek, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a supplemental opinion to the majority opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, and Lee Dong-won.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Ahn Cheol-sang, and Kim Seon-soo\\n\\na. When mitigating punishment under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses under the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (“an offense committed before the final judgment of an offense for which a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier has been imposed and an offense committed before the finality of that judgment”), does Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, which prescribes the limit of statutory mitigation, apply?\\n\\nIn interpreting statutes, if neither wording nor system gives clear priority to one of two possible interpretations, the purpose and orientation of the statute become more important. Considering not only the wording and system of the statute at issue in this case but also its purpose, when mitigating latter-part concurrent offenses, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should not apply, and it should be understood that mitigation may be made to a sentence lower than “one-half of the term of that punishment,” which is the lower limit of statutory mitigation. In contrast, it is difficult to agree with the majority opinion that Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act applies even to mitigation under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\nb. First, as to the wording of the statute, there is no reason to apply Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation to the case of latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nArticle 39(1) of the Criminal Act is a provision concerning how to determine the sentence to be pronounced for latter-part concurrent offenses. The introductory sentence of this provision declares that, for offenses among concurrent offenses not yet adjudicated, “a sentence shall be imposed taking into account equity with the case where they are adjudicated at the same time,” and the latter sentence additionally provides that “in such case, the sentence may be mitigated or remitted.” It imposes on the judge the duty to impose a sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses while necessarily considering equity, and declares the principle that the defendant should not be disadvantaged, but may be granted mitigation or exemption from punishment if necessary. Here, “mitigation” is provided together with “exemption from punishment” as a means of considering equity with the case where latter-part concurrent offenses are adjudicated together. The latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act supplements the preceding phrase “a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity,” and the meaning of the introductory sentence cannot be narrowed or limited on the basis of the wording of the latter sentence.\\n\\nOther mitigation provisions in statutes outside this provision (for example, Article 153 of the Criminal Act provides that “where a person who has committed the offense in the preceding Article confesses or surrenders before the trial or disciplinary action regarding the stated case becomes final, the sentence shall be mitigated or remitted”) allow, where a ground for mitigation exists, mitigation or exemption from punishment as its effect. In such cases, the “sentence” subject to mitigation refers either to the statutory punishment or, where there are other statutory grounds for mitigation, the “sentence to be imposed” after mitigation pursuant thereto.\\n\\nBy contrast, Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act sets forth in its introductory sentence the requirement that there be “an offense among concurrent offenses not yet adjudicated” and the effect that follows from that requirement, namely that “a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity with the case where it and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time,” and then in the latter sentence provides that by that method the sentence may be “mitigated or remitted.” Apart from Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, no mitigation provision with such wording and structure can be found even upon examining both the Criminal Act and special criminal statutes.\\n\\nThe most important principle in interpreting the provision on latter-part concurrent offenses under the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is that the defendant should not suffer disadvantage merely because the offense is adjudicated in separate proceedings, as compared with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are adjudicated together. The principle of proportionality between crime and punishment, which requires an appropriate balance between crime and punishment, and the principle of culpability, which requires punishment to be based on culpability and proportional thereto, are basic principles of criminal responsibility. The exceptional and independent form of the provision concerning latter-part concurrent offenses is based on the demand that the court adjudicating latter-part concurrent offenses, when punishing such offenses, discover a sentence consistent with the principle of proportionality and the principle of culpability so that the defendant is not disadvantaged merely because the offense is tried in separate proceedings, compared with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are adjudicated together.\\n\\nIn light of this independent form and content of the provision and its legislative purpose, “a sentence shall be imposed taking into account equity” means that the sentence may be mitigated within an appropriate range, or exemption from punishment may be granted, and at this time Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should be understood not to apply. If, when mitigating pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, one were to deem it subject to the limitations of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, the result could be inequitable.\\n\\nMoreover, since the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act does not expressly provide that Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is to be applied as the method of mitigation, whether that provision applies in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses is left to interpretation. Even though Article 56 of the Criminal Act provides that discretionary mitigation follows statutory mitigation in the order of mitigation, it is difficult to say that it declares a principle that all statutory mitigation must preserve a lower limit. There is no rational reason to leave a gap in the range of the sentence to be imposed between the lower limit and exemption from punishment by imposing a lower limit on mitigation, when exemption from punishment is available in order to provide the court with the broadest possible means to determine a sentence taking into account equity. Even if one interprets that there is no lower limit for mitigation of latter-part concurrent offenses, there is no problem in terms of consistency within the criminal law system.\\n\\nIn short, while mitigation directed at the statutory punishment or the sentence to be imposed is properly construed as mitigation subject to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act should be construed as confirming the content of the introductory sentence and, at the same time, as providing a separate means of equity for which the sentence may be mitigated within an appropriate range or punishment may be remitted, and thus as mitigation not subject to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nc. Applying Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act to latter-part concurrent offenses produces highly unreasonable results, such as unexpected disadvantage to the defendant.\\n\\nIf, in mitigation pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, the mitigation method of “one-half of the term of punishment prescribed for each offense or the amount” prescribed in Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act applies, and the lower limit of mitigation is maintained even after statutory mitigation and discretionary mitigation, then this would not accord with the purpose of ensuring that, in latter-part concurrent offenses, the defendant is not disadvantaged merely because the offense is punished in separate proceedings compared with the case where the offense is punished together with the offense whose judgment has become final. Such an interpretation runs counter to the constitutional principles of equality and culpability. Where, among multiple offenses in a concurrent-offense relationship, the sentence discovered by considering equity with simultaneous punishment is not so low as to justify exemption from punishment, but is even lower than the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed after statutory mitigation, sentencing in accordance with the purpose of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act becomes impossible, thereby infringing the judge’s sentencing authority and violating culpability, as well as the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nIf several offenses with statutory minimum sentences were punished simultaneously, Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act would apply, and only the maximum term or maximum amount prescribed for the most serious offense would be aggravated by up to one-half. However, if the same offenses are punished in separate proceedings and, as the majority opinion asserts, a sentence lower than the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed cannot be pronounced, the defendant may be excessively punished. In such a case, because the sum of the lower limits of the sentence to be imposed for the offense whose judgment has become final and the sentence to be imposed for the latter-part concurrent offense becomes the new lower limit, punishment different from that in simultaneous punishment is unavoidable merely because the offenses are punished in separate proceedings.\\n\\nIn a case such as this, where the defendant has a prior conviction for an offense punishable by life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years and is again indicted for the same offense, for the latter-part concurrent offense the court must either sentence him to imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months or more (or 1 year and 3 months or more if discretionary mitigation is also applied) or exempt him from punishment. If the court chooses the mitigated lower limit of punishment, the defendant will receive harsher punishment than in the case of simultaneous punishment, because the sum of the lower limits of the sentence to be imposed for the offense whose judgment has become final and the sentence to be imposed for the latter-part concurrent offense becomes the new lower limit. By contrast, if the court exempts punishment to avoid this result, the defendant receives more favorable treatment than in the case of simultaneous punishment, which leads to the irrational result that the defendant is treated more favorably without any justification compared with simultaneous punishment. Such a result, merely by maintaining a lower limit on statutory mitigation, causes the punishment range for the defendant to differ according to the prosecutor’s charging method without any rational reason, and thus irrationally discriminates between defendants punished simultaneously and defendants punished in separate proceedings, violating the principle of equality and the principle of culpability.\\n\\nThe appellate court, in addition to considering equity with the offense in the prior conviction in this case, for which the defendant received and finalized a sentence of imprisonment for 4 years, also took into account that the offense in this case, while identical to the offense in the prior conviction in terms of criminal method and type of drug involved, involved fewer than one-tenth of the number of offenses or profits obtained, and only about one-eighth of the amount of drugs handled, and that the investigative authorities, after investigating all 35 narcotics offenses committed by the defendant, prosecuted only the offenses involving 33 occasions first without special circumstances and separately indicted the offense in this case; as a result of considering these various circumstances, the appellate court determined that the punishment appropriate to the defendant’s responsibility for the offense in this case was imprisonment for 6 months.\\n\\nSuch sentencing judgment by the appellate court should be respected. If Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is construed, as the majority opinion does, to apply to latter-part concurrent offenses, the appellate court’s sentencing authority is infringed as the court becomes unable to pronounce the punishment most appropriate to the defendant’s responsibility for the offense in this case. Even if the appellate court could choose exemption from punishment or suspend the execution of the sentence, the result remains the same: it cannot impose a sentence of imprisonment for 6 months that fits the responsibility, which leads to an unfair outcome. A principle that the lower limit of statutory mitigation must be maintained should not force the judge to determine punishment contrary to culpability.\\n\\nd. In light of the legislative history and legislative purpose, it is desirable to interpret Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act flexibly.\\n\\nThe legislature’s purpose in amending Article 39 of the Criminal Act by Act No. 7623 on July 29, 2005 was to ensure that, in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses, the defendant would not suffer disadvantage merely because the offense was punished in separate proceedings, and that a sentence consistent with the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment and the principle of culpability would be found. Before the amendment, Article 39 of the Criminal Act provided in paragraph 1 that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses not yet adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense,” and in paragraph 2 that “where there are several judgments under the preceding paragraph, they shall be executed according to the example of the preceding Article.” The Supreme Court interpreted this to mean that “execution according to the example of Article 38(1) 2 does not mean that each sentence pronounced by those judgments is reduced and executed pursuant to that provision, but rather that the terms of imprisonment pronounced by the respective judgments are aggregated and executed within the term-of-imprisonment range obtained by adding one-half to the maximum term prescribed for the most serious offense among the concurrent offenses according to that provision” (see Supreme Court Decision 67CHO6, dated March 6, 1967). As a result, by effectively executing each sentence in full, there arose the irrationality that, in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses, the defendant was punished more severely than in former-part concurrent offenses for reasons not attributable to the defendant’s responsibility, such as separate indictment, and to resolve this at the sentencing stage the provision was amended into the current Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nIn Austria and Switzerland, the system adopted is to determine an aggregate sentence matching the sentence that would have been imposed if the finalized offense and the latter-part concurrent offense had been punished simultaneously, and then, for the latter-part concurrent offense, to impose an additional sentence by deducting the sentence already imposed for the prior conviction from the aggregate sentence (Article 31(1) of the Austrian Criminal Code, Article 49(2) of the Swiss Criminal Code). Germany, too, imposes a new subsequent aggregate sentence for the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense, as if they were punished simultaneously (Articles 55(1), 53, and 54 of the German Criminal Code). These legislative examples show an intention not to disadvantage the defendant merely because the latter-part concurrent offense was punished in separate proceedings, and the purpose of our Criminal Act amendment is the same.\\n\\nAt the time of amendment to our Criminal Act, the original proposal was to determine one aggregate sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed calculated by applying Article 38 of the Criminal Act to the latter-part concurrent offense and the offense whose judgment had become final, and then to impose an additional sentence for the latter-part concurrent offense. However, in our Criminal Act, Article 38(1) 2 with respect to determinate imprisonment merely states that one may increase “the maximum term or maximum amount prescribed for the most serious offense by up to one-half, but not exceed the aggregate of the maximum terms or amounts prescribed for each offense,” and does not separately determine punishment for individual offenses. Practical problems were also raised, namely that it is difficult to determine an aggregate sentence because it is difficult to obtain sentencing materials again concerning the offense whose judgment has become final. Reflecting such circumstances, the legislature adopted a rule declaring the principle that even in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses equity with the case of simultaneous trial must be maintained, but instead of introducing a method of re-determining the aggregate sentence, it adopted the method of “mitigation or exemption from punishment.” However, the fact that the method of determining the aggregate sentence and then determining the sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses was not adopted does not mean that the necessity of preventing disadvantage to the defendant merely because the offense is tried in separate proceedings was overlooked; rather, that legislative purpose should be respected.\\n\\nDuring the deliberations on the amendment to the Criminal Act, a proposal to add the phrase “(when mitigating or exempting punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses) mitigation may be made even below the mitigation limit under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act” was not ultimately adopted. However, in light of the above legislative purpose and legislative history, it is difficult to say that, merely because the legislature did not expressly specify the method of mitigation, the intention was to require application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act in the case of this kind so that the sentence could not be mitigated below the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed, thereby punishing the defendant more disadvantageously than in the case of simultaneous punishment of latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\ne. Even from the perspective of constitutional interpretation, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should not be applied to latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nThe authority to determine, in adjudicating concrete disputes, the meaning, content, and scope of application of statutes or statutory provisions—that is, the authority to interpret and apply statutes—is an essential component of judicial power, and interpreting statutes so that they are harmonized with constitutional norms is a fundamental principle in statutory interpretation and application. Where multiple interpretations of a statutory provision are possible, a judge should, in principle, choose the interpretation consistent with the Constitution, that is, a constitution-conforming interpretation (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DU10289, decided February 12, 2009; Constitutional Court En Banc Decision 89HEONMA38, decided July 21, 1989, etc.).\\n\\nThe legislature cannot exercise unlimited legislative discretion in defining conduct as a crime and imposing punishment. When comparing punishments for crimes similar in criminal nature and protected legal interests, if it is manifest that the justice and balance of the punishment system are substantially lost, the provision is unconstitutional not only for violating the basic constitutional principle guaranteeing human dignity and worth but also for violating the principle of equality (see Constitutional Court En Banc Decision 2008HEONBA9, 43, etc.). The balance of the punishment system and the principle of equality mean that crimes similar in criminal nature and protected legal interests must, within a reasonable range, be punished with similar statutory punishments (see Constitutional Court En Banc Decisions 2006HEONGA7, decided June 29, 2006; 2012HEONBA275, decided September 26, 2013; 2015HEONBA225, decided December 29, 2016, etc.).\\n\\nIf, in the process of interpreting the wording of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, both an interpretation affirming and an interpretation denying the application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act are possible, then an interpretation that results in harsher or more favorable punishment merely because the offense is punished in separate proceedings compared with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are punished together would infringe the justice of the punishment system and violate the constitutional basic principles guaranteeing human dignity and worth as well as the principle of equality; therefore, such interpretation should be avoided and a constitution-conforming interpretation should be adopted.\\n\\nThere are also limits, grounded in the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment and the principle of culpability, on legislation concerning punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses. If latter-part concurrent offenses are interpreted as the majority opinion does, then in order to realize these principles of criminal law, a new legislative measure must be enacted so that no disadvantage is suffered merely because the case is tried in a separate proceeding, compared with the case where latter-part concurrent offenses are adjudicated together. There is no reason to take the difficult path when there is a method of statutory interpretation that can easily escape an unconstitutional situation without departing from the possible meaning of the wording.\\n\\nMeanwhile, even if one were to interpret that, for latter-part concurrent offenses with a statutory minimum sentence, mitigation pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act may be made below the mitigation limit prescribed by Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act and pronounced, that would be an interpretation favorable to the defendant and thus would not violate the principle of nulla poena sine lege, nor is there any reason to construe it strictly. The request that criminal statutes be strictly construed is intended to prevent arbitrary interpretation and application of the law to the disadvantage of the public; it is not intended to prohibit interpretation in a way that is not unfavorable to the public and is reasonable, so long as the legislative spirit is not undermined (see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 78DO246, decided April 25, 1978, etc.).\\n\\nf. In light of these legal principles, the appellate judgment should be examined.\\n\\nThe appellate court selected determinate terms of imprisonment for the offense in this case, for which the statutory punishment is life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years, and found that it was in the relation of latter-part concurrent offenses with the offense in the prior conviction in this case. It then applied the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act to aggravate punishment for concurrent offenses. Thereafter, applying Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, it mitigated punishment; in doing so, it did not apply Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, and, taking into account equity with the case where the offense would be punished as former-part concurrent offenses, it determined the sentence and, after discretionary mitigation, ultimately sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months. Although there is an inappropriate aspect in the order in which the law was applied, the appellate court did not err in a way that affected the conclusion of the judgment, such as by misapprehending the legal principles concerning mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses. Therefore, the appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nThese are the reasons for dissenting from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek\\n\\na. The majority opinion construes the provision “the sentence may be mitigated or remitted” in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, in imposing punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses for which a statutory minimum sentence is set, as having a segmented meaning in which one must choose between “mitigation” and “remission,” so that in the case of mitigation the sentence may be mitigated only within the range prescribed by Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, and if one wishes to mitigate to a lower sentence, punishment must be remitted. However, I cannot agree with the majority opinion’s segmented interpretation of the meaning of “mitigated or remitted.”\\n\\nThe Criminal Act uses the provisions “the sentence may be mitigated or remitted” in Articles 21 (self-defense), 22 (necessity), 23 (self-help), 27 (impossible offense), 39 (latter-part concurrent offenses), 52 (voluntary surrender), etc., and uses the provisions “the sentence shall be mitigated or remitted” in Articles 26 (abandoned offense), 153 (confession of perjury, voluntary surrender), 157 (confession of false accusation, voluntary surrender), etc. The legal effect of “mitigated or remitted” is a matter not limited to latter-part concurrent offenses like the present case; rather, it is a general issue that applies whenever the Criminal Act or special criminal statutes contain provisions on “mitigation or remission” of punishment. Of course, it concerns only one type of punishment after the choice of the type of punishment has been made under Article 54 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nBelow, I will examine the legal effect of “mitigation or remission.” For convenience of discussion, however, I will not consider discretionary mitigation when mentioning the lower limit of punishment by mitigation.\\n\\nb. Provisions on “mitigation or remission” of punishment function to determine the modified sentence to be imposed. First, it is clear that mitigation determines the range of the sentence to be imposed, and further, because there are no separate provisions concerning different requirements or effects for “remission” that differ from those for other ranges of the sentence to be imposed, remission likewise falls within the ordinary range of the sentence to be imposed.\\n\\nProvisions on “mitigation or remission” of punishment present to the judge the range of the sentence to be imposed as modified by those provisions as the limit of sentencing, and it is proper to view the legal effect as meaning a single integrated domain. Once the choice of the type of punishment has already been made, there is no reason or necessity for a provision that changes the range of punishment to require the judge to choose anew between two separate domains.\\n\\nExemption from punishment is a type of guilty judgment in which the offense is established but no punishment is imposed, and it is a case where the defendant’s sentencing responsibility is at the level of “0.” In other words, exemption from punishment may be understood as setting the sentence to be imposed at “0.” If exemption is understood in this way, then when “mitigation or remission” is applied to a statutory punishment with a minimum limit, the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed is set at “0.” Since there can be only one lower limit of the sentence to be imposed, once the lower limit is set at “0” by remission, there is no need to refer to the general provision of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act in order to confirm the lower limit of punishment resulting from “mitigation or remission.” In this case, because the upper limit of the sentence to be imposed is not separately provided in the individual statutory provision that prescribes “mitigation or remission,” reference must be made to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nIf the meaning of “mitigation or remission” is understood as above, then where “mitigation or remission” is provided together with “mitigation,” it should be understood as a single integrated concept, not as a segmented meaning. Accordingly, the range of the sentence to be imposed by “mitigation or remission” has a lower limit of “0” and an upper limit of one-half of the maximum term or amount, with no room for a gap in between.\\n\\nAlthough not directly relevant to this part of the discussion, I add the following to avoid misunderstanding. Unlike the case of “shall mitigate or remit,” where the wording is “may mitigate or remit,” the range of the sentence to be imposed in the event of no such action also includes the range before mitigation or remission (that is, the statutory punishment or sentence to be imposed before mitigation or remission), so naturally the maximum term does not change. Current practice is the same.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 56 of the Criminal Act prescribes the order of aggravation and mitigation, but does not expressly provide for “mitigation or remission.” If the legal effect of “mitigation or remission” is understood as above, then “mitigation or remission” may be regarded as falling under “statutory mitigation” under Article 56 4 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nc. Where a statutory minimum is set, if the legal effect of “mitigation or remission” is not understood, as above, as a single integrated concept in which the sentence to be imposed continuously ranges from “0” to the upper limit, but instead, as the majority opinion does, “mitigation or remission” is understood in a segmented sense, it results in an unjustified gap in the range of the sentence to be imposed between “0” and the lower limit mitigated under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) The legislature presents judges with a certain kind and range of punishment proportionate to responsibility for all crimes, and judges determine a specific sentence corresponding to the principle of individual act responsibility and the preventive purpose of punishment within the range of the sentence to be imposed for each offense. Punishment appropriate to responsibility exists as a certain range of responsibility or judgment within the range of the sentence to be imposed; if there is a gap between the upper and lower limits of the sentence to be imposed, the range of punishment appropriate to responsibility cannot be properly determined, which is contrary to culpability.\\n\\nThere is no case in which a gap exists between the lower and upper limits of the statutory punishment for any offense prescribed in the Criminal Act or in special criminal statutes. For example, one cannot find legislative examples where the statutory punishment is “imprisonment for up to 3 years, or imprisonment for between 7 and 15 years,” and it is probably self-evident that such legislation would be impossible. The legislature, too, knows all too well that a gap in a certain range between the lower and upper limits of punishment is inconsistent with responsibility and may permit sentencing that does not accord with responsibility, and therefore legislates so as not to create any gap between the lower and upper limits of punishment. Also, under the current criminal justice system, there is no case where the lower and upper limits of the sentence to be imposed are separated by a gap even when punishment is aggravated or mitigated. Yet the only area in which continuity between the lower and upper limits is severed and a gap arises is the case of “mitigation or remission” of punishment. The legislature permitted judges to “mitigate or remit” punishment so as to impose punishment appropriate to responsibility; it could never have intended that “mitigation or remission” would create a gap between the lower and upper limits of punishment. The majority opinion is essentially no different from enacting a statute that leaves a gap in the statutory punishment.\\n\\n2) “Mitigation or remission” of punishment is a matter of determining the degree and amount of punishment. However, in ordinary social understanding, it is difficult to imagine leaving a gap of a certain range in the middle of the question of degree and amount. Even if such a gap were created, there would be almost no case in which it could be accepted in ordinary social understanding.\\n\\nFor example, can one imagine a situation in which, when an employer negotiates wages with workers, the wage must be set either at 55 million won or more, or at 50 million won or less, and the amount between 50 million won and 55 million won can absolutely not be set? If a school teacher, when assigning exam scores to students on a scale from 0 to 100, says that scores between 70 and 80 can never be assigned, could that truly be considered normal? Can one even imagine a legal order in which the state, when imposing taxes on taxpayers, sets taxes of at least 500,000 won but less than 750,000 won at 500,000 won, and taxes of at least 750,000 won but less than 1,000,000 won at 1,000,000 won, so that taxes between 500,000 won and 1,000,000 won cannot be recognized? In light of ordinary social common sense, such a situation is impossible.\\n\\nThe same is true for “mitigation or remission” of punishment. If “mitigation or remission” is understood in the segmented sense, as the majority opinion does, then where a statutory minimum is set, a judge can only determine the sentence to be pronounced within the sentence-to-be-imposed range with “0” or with a lower limit mitigated within one-half of the punishment as the lower limit, and cannot pronounce a sentence between “0” and that lower limit mitigated by statute. A gap arises in the sentence-to-be-imposed range within a certain band, and even if the judge, after reviewing the various sentencing factors prescribed in Article 51 of the Criminal Act, concludes that a sentence between “0” and that statutory mitigated lower limit is most appropriate to responsibility, the judge cannot pronounce that sentence. The judge is forced either to pronounce a sentence not less than the lower limit mitigated within one-half or to exempt punishment. It is self-evident that such a result is unreasonable in ordinary social understanding.\\n\\nd. Let us apply the foregoing discussion to this case. In this case, the statutory punishment is “life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years.” According to the majority opinion, if the judge selects determinate imprisonment and then aggravates punishment for concurrent offenses and, pursuant to statutory mitigation, “mitigates or remits,” the judge will have to exempt punishment or determine the sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed of imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months or more (the upper limit is not separately mentioned because it is not an issue in this case). The judge can choose only one of “0” or “imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months or more.” From the standpoint that “mitigation or remission” is a single integrated concept, the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed for each offense in this case becomes “0” by virtue of exemption from punishment, and there is no gap up to the upper limit.\\n\\nViewing the above result, from the standpoint of criminal policy it cannot possibly be said that understanding “mitigation or remission” as a single integrated concept so as not to create a gap in the sentence to be imposed is an interpretation or application of the law unfavorable to the public, nor can it be said to unnecessarily strengthen the state’s punitive power by granting judges excessive sentencing discretion. It simply makes the criminal justice order a rational legal order in accordance with natural principle.\\n\\ne. When a judge is deliberating between imprisonment for 3 years and exemption from punishment, which citizen would say, “Why not make it 1 year or 2 years?” Is there any lawyer who can explain that the judge’s deliberation is unavoidable?\\n\\nThe parts of the world and of life that need to be regulated by legal order are made law; one cannot make into law what does not exist in the world. In matters of degree and amount, there is no world in which a gap exists in the middle.\\n\\nf. Examining the reasons of the appellate judgment in light of the above legal principles and the evidence adopted by the appellate court, the appellate court, after finding that the offense in this case was in the relation of latter-part concurrent offenses with the offense in the prior conviction in this case, applied the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act to aggravate punishment for concurrent offenses, then applied Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act to mitigate punishment, and, without applying Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, determined the sentence while considering equity with the case where punishment is imposed as former-part concurrent offenses, and after discretionary mitigation finally sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months. Although there is an inappropriate aspect in the order in which the law was applied, the appellate court’s judgment does not contain an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment, such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning mitigation of punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses. Therefore, the appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nThis is the reason for setting forth the dissenting opinion against the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplemental Opinion of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, and Lee Dong-won on the Majority Opinion\\n\\na. Statutory mitigation, as used in the Criminal Act, does not itself denote a special type of mitigation. Rather, it refers to all cases, except for discretionary mitigation, where the Criminal Act or other statutes provide for mitigation of punishment. The dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Ahn Cheol-sang, and Kim Seon-soo (hereinafter referred to as “the dissenting opinion”) seeks to bolster its basis by pointing out that there is no express provision requiring Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act to be applied as the method of mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses. The dissenting opinion appears to affirm that mitigation other than mitigation of latter-part concurrent offenses generally constitutes statutory mitigation, but one can hardly find any case in which a dissenting opinion that recognizes statutory mitigation includes an express provision in the relevant individual article requiring application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is not applied because the individual provision expressly provides for its application; rather, on the premise that cases where the Criminal Act or other statutes provide for mitigation of punishment, other than discretionary mitigation, all fall under statutory mitigation, it is prescribed that such mitigation shall be made under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. In the case of discretionary mitigation, although the Criminal Act does not expressly say so, it is understood by interpretation to be a mitigation method similar to statutory mitigation. Therefore, it is not appropriate to build an argument on the basis that there is no provision requiring mitigation under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nb. If mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses were not statutory mitigation but an independent form of mitigation, there must follow an explanation that coherently, within the Criminal Act system, shows how that mitigation differs from statutory mitigation.\\n\\nThe mitigation of latter-part concurrent offenses discussed by the dissenting opinion includes not only mitigation of the lower limit but also mitigation of the upper limit, yet there is no explanation whatsoever as to the upper limit. It is necessary to explain by what method the upper limit is mitigated, and whether mitigation of the upper limit is the same as statutory mitigation. If mitigation of the upper limit is the same as statutory mitigation, then the dissenting opinion must also explain on what basis the upper limit is mitigated in the same manner as statutory mitigation despite claiming that it is not statutory mitigation, and why, unlike the lower limit, it follows the method of statutory mitigation.\\n\\nIn addition, with respect to aggravation and mitigation of punishment, explanation is needed regarding the order of aggravation and mitigation under Article 56 of the Criminal Act. It is necessary to explain at which stage mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses is carried out, particularly its order relative to discretionary mitigation. Under the dissenting opinion’s logic, discretionary mitigation itself might not be necessary in cases of latter-part concurrent offenses, so an explanation is also needed as to whether discretionary mitigation is separately recognized. If discretionary mitigation is unnecessary, an explanation is also needed as to why the most fundamental and ultimate method of mitigation under the Criminal Act, namely discretionary mitigation, is excluded without basis.\\n\\nWhile there may be no difference between the majority opinion and the dissenting opinion on the fundamental distinction between exemption from punishment and pronouncement of punishment, under the dissenting opinion it is difficult to explain the independent meaning of providing for exemption from punishment, in addition to providing for mitigation of punishment as a method to impose a sentence taking into account equity with the case where the offense is adjudicated together with the offense whose judgment has become final in cases of latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nc. Judicial sentencing discretion is granted within the range of the sentence to be imposed, and the dissenting opinion does not appear to take a different view, but when the dissenting opinion says that the majority opinion excessively infringes the judge’s sentencing discretion with respect to latter-part concurrent offenses, it is speaking about the question of how to determine the range of the sentence to be imposed and then invoking the judge’s sentencing discretion, which is an issue at the next stage; this is deeply improper. Under the dissenting opinion, one may misunderstand as if judges have sentencing discretion notwithstanding the sentence to be imposed, and that the majority opinion’s limitation of the range of the sentence to be imposed infringes the judge’s sentencing discretion.\\n\\nd. In determining punishment, the notion of imposing punishment taking equity into account necessarily presupposes that punishment is imposed taking equity into account within the range of the sentence to be imposed. The dissenting opinion also does not seem to take the position that taking equity into account means that the same punishment as in simultaneous adjudication must be imposed. If the offense whose judgment had become final and the offense of latter-part concurrent offenses had both been before the court, what sentence would have been imposed is something that the court trying the latter-part concurrent offense could not know and cannot impose a corresponding sentence with certainty. Where it appears that determining the sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses within the fixed range of the sentence to be imposed would be inequitable compared with simultaneous adjudication, the law has provided a basis for mitigation so that the sentence can be determined by changing the sentence to be imposed. Furthermore, where mitigation alone is clearly insufficient to avoid inequity, exemption from punishment is allowed. For that reason, the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376 said that the Criminal Act provisions concerning latter-part concurrent offenses adopted a flexible legislative form enabling the court to determine a reasonable and appropriate sentence. A judge trying latter-part concurrent offenses must exempt punishment, rather than merely mitigate it, if setting the sentence with a lower limit of mitigation for a defendant punished as latter-part concurrent offenses would be so disadvantageous, compared with simultaneous punishment, as to violate the principle of equality or culpability.\\n\\nIt is difficult to accept how such an interpretation of mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses could violate the principle of equality or culpability.\\n\\nFurthermore, according to the dissenting opinion, the sentencing and execution under the former Article 39(1) and (2) of the Criminal Act, under which, unlike the current law, neither mitigation nor exemption from punishment was possible for latter-part concurrent offenses, would be even more contrary to culpability and equality. If so, it would mean that until the above statutory provisions were amended, the Supreme Court had never once raised an objection and had continued to render judgments contrary to culpability and equality, which is also unacceptable. As noted above, one must remember that how latter-part concurrent offenses should be handled fundamentally depends on legislative policy.\\n\\nThis concludes the supplemental opinion on the majority opinion."}

{"[2017DO7287]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\nSince the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act provides that “an offense for which a judgment imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or a heavier punishment has become final and binding, and an offense committed before the final and binding judgment” shall constitute concurrent offenses, an offense for which a fine judgment or a summary order has become final and binding cannot constitute concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the court below found that the theft offenses and fraud offenses for which each of the summary orders stated in the judgment had become final and binding, and each of the offenses stated in the judgment committed before the date on which each of the above summary orders became final and binding, were in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, and accordingly determined separate punishments for each of the offenses stated in the judgment committed before the date on which each of the above summary orders became final and binding and each of the offenses stated in the judgment committed after the date on which each of the above summary orders became final and binding, thereby sentencing the Defendant to three punishments.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the legal principles set forth above, the offenses stated in the judgment committed by the Defendant before and after the final and binding of each of the above summary orders cannot constitute concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, and all are in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, so one punishment should have been imposed thereon. Nevertheless, the court below determined otherwise; therefore, there is illegality that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal doctrine of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning offenses of negligence and aggravated offenses by result are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) Under the Criminal Act, the offense of special obstruction of the performance of public duties causing bodily injury is an improper aggravated offense by result that includes not only cases where the serious result was not foreseen despite foreseeability, but also cases involving intent. (b) In a negligent offense, unconscious negligence is a case in which there is no awareness whatsoever of the possibility of the occurrence of the result, and it shall be regarded as negligence liability as a normative reality, namely, carelessness in failing to recognize the occurrence of the result. (c) With respect to an accident that occurred while a construction company, during construction work, had the installation work of a tower crane subcontracted to a specialist and the tower crane was being installed, if A, the site agent of the construction company, did not have actual authority to direct and supervise the installation work of the tower crane so as to manage and control it, he cannot be deemed to have been negligent in violation of the duty of care in the course of business. (d) If A, with intent to kill A, set fire to the house where A was sleeping, and the fire reached the ceiling of the master bedroom in A's house, but A woke up and got out of the house, thereby failing to achieve the purpose of killing, then A is punished as an attempted offender of arson of an inhabited building resulting in death. (e) Where a person instigated assault, but the person instigated went beyond this and committed homicide, the instigator becomes an accessory by instigation to the offense of assault; however, in such a case, if the instigator had negligence or foreseeability with respect to the result of the victim's death, it becomes an ideal concurrence of an accessory by instigation to the offense of assault and negligent homicide.

{"[2007Do10058]": "We determine the grounds of appeal (the statements in the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal has elapsed are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. As to the first ground of appeal\\nUnder Article 9(1) of the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Violence Crimes and Protection of Victims Thereof, not only a person who commits the crime of special rape as prescribed in Article 6(1) of the same Act, but also where special rape remains at the attempted stage, if the victim thereby suffers injury, the crime of special rape resulting in bodily injury is established; and the punishment provision for an attempt under the above Article 9(1) prescribed in Article 12 of the same Act applies to cases where the offense of special rape inflicting injury, which is prescribed together with the offense of special rape resulting in bodily injury in Article 9(1), remains at the attempted stage, that is, where a person who commits or attempts special rape, with intent to cause injury to the victim, attempts to injure the victim but the attempt fails.\\nConsidering the evidence cited in the judgment below as a whole, the court below found that the Defendant, by placing an electroshock device, which is a dangerous object, against the victim’s waist and assaulting the victim in an attempt to rape her, only to the extent of an attempt, and thereby causing the victim injuries such as a contusion to the face requiring approximately 2 weeks of treatment, and the court below further found that this constituted the consummated offense of special rape resulting in bodily injury under the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Violence Crimes and Protection of Victims Thereof. In light of the record and the legal principles stated above, that determination is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law regarding the doctrine of an attempted offense of a consequential aggravated offense, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the second ground of appeal\\na. As to whether the medical certificate has evidentiary admissibility\\nExcept where the entries in the trial transcript are due to an obvious clerical error or mistake, matters entered in the trial transcript as procedural acts on the trial date must be proved by the transcript alone, and its probative force is absolute in that contrary proof by materials other than the trial transcript is not permitted (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO6557 rendered on December 22, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2002DO2134 rendered on July 12, 2002, etc.).\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that at the first hearing date of the first instance, the Defendant consented to the admission of the medical certificate submitted by the prosecutor, and that fact is stated in the list of evidence; and since there is no material showing that such entry was the result of an obvious clerical error or mistake, the ground of appeal challenging the evidentiary admissibility of the above medical certificate contrary to the entry in the list of evidence is not accepted.\\nb. As to the injury count and the credibility of the medical certificate\\nThe arguments disputing the lower court’s determination regarding the injury count and the credibility of the medical certificate ultimately complain of the selection and weighing of evidence and the finding of facts, which are within the exclusive province of the lower court as the trier of fact, and therefore all cannot be accepted; nor is any illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence, insufficiency of deliberation, or error of law otherwise apparent in the lower court judgment. The Supreme Court decisions pointed out in the grounds of appeal concern different matters from this case and are not appropriate for invocation here.\\n\\n3. As to the third ground of appeal\\nExamining the evidence admitted by the court below in light of the record, it is recognized that the Defendant possessed an electroshock device without obtaining permission from the competent chief of police, and therefore the lower court’s determination that the Defendant violated the Control of Firearms, Swords, Explosives, Etc. Act is proper; the Defendant’s argument criticizing this point cannot be accepted, and no illegality such as insufficiency of deliberation or error of law is otherwise apparent in the lower court judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and with the concurrence of all participating Justices of the Supreme Court, it is decided as set forth in the disposition that a part of the period of detention after appeal shall be included in the principal sentence."}

{"[83Do3007]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal against Defendant 1, the terms “a person who, by reason of the mental and physical disorder under Article 10 of the Criminal Act, lacks the ability to distinguish things or to decide his or her will” and “a person whose such ability is weak” both refer to a person in a state of mental and physical disorder; the difference between the two lies only in the difference in degree of the severity of the disorder, and they mean, in one case, a person who, due to mental disorder, lacks the ability to distinguish right from wrong or good from evil in matters, or to act according to what has been so distinguished, and, in the other case, a person whose mental disorder has not reached the degree of depriving him or her of such ability, but whose ability has been markedly diminished.
