The Minister of National Defense is here too, so bring the Prime Minister to the Army Headquarters banka,” and the Prime Minister and ministers of Home Affairs and Justice went there. A’s act of emphasizing security to the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers and inducing martial law declaration was merely a process to calmly proceed with restoring order after the killing of the President and others and to achieve the purpose of the planned act. There is no evidentiary material showing that the act itself was a riot or that the riot continued until he was arrested. And the fact that Defendant thought A had taken control of the military after enticing the Army Chief of Staff and went to the Army Headquarters banka can only mean that he thought A had taken control of the military without any riot. Defendant said there that declaring emergency martial law on the ground of the President’s absence would be better, and while watching how things developed he took the opportunity to have A arrested. Thus, after the killing of the President and others, the riot ended, and there were no subsequent riotous acts; one cannot say there was a continuing riot. Even if one assumed that the riot was continuing, there is no evidence that Defendant participated in it or engaged in conspiratorial acts.\\n\\nAccordingly, there is no room to recognize Defendant’s attempted major participation in insurrection, which presupposes involvement in riot. Nevertheless, the lower court found and applied that offense. This is either a factual mistake in violation of the rules of evidence or a misunderstanding of law or defect for lack of reasons that affected the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.\\n\\nI consider together point 1 of the grounds of appeal by Defendant D’s counsel N, point 3 of the grounds of appeal by counsel O for Defendants E and F, and point 3 of the grounds of appeal by counsel P for Defendant G.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons in the lower judgment, at around 19:00 on the day of the incident, when Defendant A left the banquet table with the President and T in the restaurant and put one pistol prepared in advance in the second-floor bedroom of the main office into his pants watch pocket and was entering the banquet table, at around 19:10 in the old building garden adjacent to the restaurant he instructed Defendant D and first-instance defendant Park Heung-ju, saying, “I will take care of it today, so be prepared. I will handle the President and others directly, so as soon as you hear gunshots, pick three smart men and deal with the security guards,” and informed them that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director were in the office, thereby urging them to solidify their will to participate in the offense, and received a promise from Defendant D that he would finish preparations within 30 minutes. Then, at around 19:15 in the west garden of the restaurant, Bureau Chief Kim Sun-ho instructed Defendants F and E, saying, “This is an order from the chief. If things go well today, you will get a share. When the chief fires from inside, shoot the security guards in the kitchen,” and received their assent. Defendant C, in the guard waiting room opposite the restaurant, received from Defendant D instructions to shoot the security guards if they came from the Blue House, and also, at around 20:05, received from Defendant E instructions to fire a confirmation shot at persons in the restaurant who were not yet fully dead. Defendant C then entered the security guards’ waiting room inside the restaurant, saw the guards being shot, recognized that this was a state of national upheaval, and agreed to participate according to the instruction. Thus each Defendant sequentially conspired to participate in killings for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. According to the same conspiracy, when at around 19:40 the sound of Defendant A’s pistol shot was heard as a signal, Defendant D fired his pistol toward the security guards in the waiting room in front of the restaurant entrance; Defendants E and F, together with Park Heung-ju, fired their pistols toward the President’s driver and security guards in the kitchen of the restaurant; and Defendant G, at around 20:05, carrying an M16 rifle, fired at the security guards lying in the restaurant waiting room and kitchen, as well as T groaning in the banquet table, thereby Defendant D, E, F, and G also jointly with Defendant A killed the President and others for the purpose of subverting the Constitution.\\n\\nHowever, even if one carefully examines the evidence adopted by the lower court against the record, the offense plan in this case, as mentioned in the lower judgment, was independently devised by Defendant A for security reasons, and the words “I will take care of it today” said to Defendant D and first-instance defendant Park Heung-ju were first spoken to those two persons at around 19:10 that day. If at that time A gave the instruction that “I will take care of the President and others directly, so as soon as gunshots are heard, you take care of the security guards,” the natural meaning would be that they should cooperate in killing the President and others. Even if Defendant D knew that killing the President would bring about state upheaval, in this case there is no record showing any other particular instruction regarding the purpose of the act or other matters. Therefore, it would be a leap of logic inconsistent with our experience and logic to conclude that the Defendants participated in and carried out a killing of natural person B, the President, rather than a killing for the purpose of subverting the constitutional organ itself, the President, by force or making the exercise of its powers impossible. Even if Defendant D knew that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency were in the main office at the time, that alone cannot change the conclusion.\\n\\nDefendants E and F were those who received from Defendant D the instruction to “shoot the security guards in the kitchen when gunshots are heard” (according to the record, they are recognized as having received instruction to drive the security guards into the kitchen and return fire if the guards shot), and Defendant D said, “If today goes well, you will get a share.” However, those words were not spoken by A but were an independent remark by Defendant D. Even if the restaurant guards or drivers, no more than that, thought that getting a share would mean advancement or something major, and even if they knew that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency were present, or even thought that this was a coup d’état bringing about upheaval against the State, that would merely reflect the Defendants’ awareness or thoughts in a system in which they blindly obeyed a superior’s directive. There is no basis for recognizing that “coup d’état” means the purpose of subverting the Constitution here, and such thoughts alone cannot constitute evidence of mutual conspiracy.\\n\\nDefendant G, further down the chain, was the one who received from E the instruction to perform a confirmation killing on persons in the restaurant who had not yet died. It is shown that he did not think a state upheaval had occurred at the time, and he denies having ever muttered to himself that “the die is cast,” and there is no evidentiary material to the contrary.\\n\\nAccordingly, not only Defendant G, but also Defendants E and F and Defendant D are properly viewed as unrelated to murderous acts for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Yet the lower court recognized all of those Defendants as co-principals in murder with the purpose of subverting the Constitution. This cannot be denied to be a factual error without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence, and this affected the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.\\n\\n3. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Im Hang-jun\\n\\nAccording to the appellate judgment, the lower court held that the acts of the Defendants other than Defendant C H corresponded to both the crime of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 of the Criminal Act and the crime of attempted insurrection under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, and that the two offenses are in imaginary concurrence; and it held that Defendant C’s acts corresponded to both murder and attempted insurrection. However, the lower court’s above holdings contain the following unlawful grounds:\\n\\n(1) In this case, the Defendants cannot be regarded as a combination of a number of persons sufficient to constitute a riot under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, and therefore cannot be subjects of the crime of insurrection under Article 87. Even if, as the lower court held, the acts of the Defendants are viewed as a combination of a number of persons sufficient for a riot, they correspond only to one offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 of the Criminal Act, and cannot also be said to correspond to Article 87 so as to be punished as imaginary concurrence.\\n\\n(2) There is insufficient evidence to hold that the criminal acts of Defendants E, F, and C were murder with insurrectionary purpose; they should be viewed as simple murder.\\n\\n(3) There is no evidence to hold that Defendant C was a conspiracy co-principal in the killing of T with Defendant A, so the lower judgment appears to contain a misinterpretation of the law concerning conspiracy co-principal liability or a mistake in recognizing the conspiracy without evidence.\\n\\nI will set forth the reasons as follows.\\n\\n(4) Finally, I will add opinions concerning Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act and the right of resistance.\\n\\n1. Article 87 of the Criminal Act provides that “A person who riots for the purpose of usurping the territory or subverting the Constitution ...” and thus makes riot a constituent element. Here, riot means a combination of many persons that through violence or intimidation disturbs the peace of a locality. Therefore, for the crime of insurrection to be established, a combination of many persons is absolutely required.\\n\\nThus, the crime of insurrection, together with the crime of riot, is called a collective crime, mob crime, or group crime.\\n\\nThen why is the subject of the crime in insurrection or riot necessarily a combination of many persons? It is because when a large number of persons gather, merely from the fact that they are assembled, the so-called mob psychology arises, and the rational functioning of each individual in the group declines or recedes. The assembled mass tends, through suggestion, imitation, emotional contagion, etc., to exhibit irrational emotions or destructive behavior that is completely different from what each would do alone and that would not normally be expected. Therefore, the Criminal Act specially provides punishment provisions for collective crimes and mob crimes in order to guard against the concentration and explosion of the power of the mob, which would produce unpredictable results.\\n\\nAccordingly, first of all, for the crime of insurrection to be established, a combination of many persons is indispensable. Here, “many persons” means the type of many persons among whom the collective consciousness or mob psychology has formed, producing not a simple arithmetic aggregation of each individual’s thoughts and acts, but a completely different blind emotion or irrational and destructive conduct, sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality and to commit violence or intimidation. Therefore, a gathering of around 10 persons cannot be regarded as a “many persons” combination from which such collective consciousness or mob psychology arises. In this case, only A, Park Heung-ju, and D, three persons, conspired to shoot at the President and others, and even if one adds all those who did not know the reasons and motivations of those who committed the offense, there are only six or seven persons. Such number cannot be regarded as a “many persons” sufficient to commit a riot under Article 87 of the Criminal Act. Therefore, the acts of the Defendants cannot correspond to Article 87. The lower court’s decision to the contrary misinterpreted the law concerning riot.\\n\\nEven if, as the majority opinion says, the acts of the Defendants were a “many persons” combination sufficient to commit a riot under Article 87, once the Defendants committed murder, they would constitute only one offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88, and would not correspond to attempted insurrection under Article 87. Yet the lower court held that they also correspond to attempted insurrection under Article 87 and that the two offenses were in imaginary concurrence. This cannot be said to be proper. If the lower court’s theory were followed, then a person who caused death by injury would have to be in imaginary concurrence between assault and bodily injury causing death, and a person who committed robbery murder would have to be punished as an imaginary concurrence of robbery and robbery murder. That is the consequence of the lower court’s theory.\\n\\n2. There is no evidence that the acts of Defendants E, F, and G correspond to murder with insurrectionary purpose.\\n\\nThe crime of insurrection is a crime whose protected legal interest is the existence of the State. To have insurrectionary purpose, there must be a purpose to unlawfully destroy or transform the democratic basic order of Korea. We examine whether these three Defendants, as a subjective requirement, knew that A and others had such purpose and participated in the criminal acts.\\n\\nAs to Defendants E and F, they were told only by Defendant D, as instructed by the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, that if gunshots were heard inside, they should drive the Blue House security guards to one side, and if those guards tried to shoot, they should shoot back. They merely carried that out. They never heard that the President was to be shot, and Defendants E and F did not know what the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency was doing inside. It cannot be said that they participated while knowing that A and others had the purpose of subverting the Constitution. To recognize a criminal fact there must be strict proof, and one cannot infer that these Defendants also had insurrectionary purpose merely by conjecture.\\n\\nMoreover, Defendant G was on guard in a building separated from the building where the incident occurred and did not know what had happened there. Later, at the instruction of Defendants D and E, he performed the confirmation killing on three or four of the victims who had been shot and fallen down, without knowing who those victims were or why they had been shot. Defendant G was told by Defendant E that the President, Chief Secretary C, and the Central Intelligence Agency director had already escaped from the scene, and then he performed the confirmation killing. What evidence supports that Defendant G had insurrectionary purpose? No such evidence appears in the record.\\n\\nAlso, the so-called confirmation killing by Defendant G took place after a considerable time had passed since the occurrence, and even according to the evidence appearing in the record, it is not clear whether Defendant G fired at already dead bodies or at victims before death. The hearing on this point cannot be said to have been fully conducted.\\n\\n3. There is no evidence that Defendant C conspired with Defendant A, who killed T, as a conspiracy co-principal.\\n\\nIn general, it is beyond dispute that a person who participates in a conspiracy or plot to commit a crime cannot escape co-principal liability for the criminal acts executed by other conspirators even if he does not directly participate in the execution. But the lower court and the majority opinion have misunderstood the law of conspiracy co-principal liability, confusing or equating the elements of execution co-principal liability and conspiracy co-principal liability, or making evidentiary judgments contrary to logic and experience.\\n\\nThat is, in execution co-principal liability, a conspiracy may exist if there is an agreement in the broad sense such as “common awareness of joint crime” or “communication of intent.” But for conspiracy co-principal liability to be recognized, such broad agreement is insufficient; there must be a higher-level agreement approaching indirect perpetration.\\n\\nTherefore, conspiracy or plot in conspiracy co-principal liability must be strictly construed as existing only where there is a “high-level plot” among two or more persons to become one with a shared intent for a specific crime, using each other’s acts to carry out their own intent. For conspiracy co-principal liability to be recognized, the following additional requirements must be met:\\n(1) such high-level conspiracy or plot among several persons,\\n(2) one of them must have carried out the planned offense,\\n(3) the execution of the crime must have been caused by the conspiracy or plot under item (1).\\n\\nThus, we must determine from the evidence in the record:\\n① whether Defendant C and A made a sufficiently high-level agreement to kill T as described above;\\n② whether A killed T because of the conspiracy with C, that is, whether A killed T because of the agreement with C to kill him.\\n\\nThe lower court and the majority opinion cite as evidence A’s statement to the military prosecutor that, while sitting on the curb in the garden in front of the restaurant, when A said to C around 17:50 that “Shall I get rid of that guy” referring to T, he looked at C’s expression and C nodded his head, and that when he said “Please take care of what happens after this,” C nodded again. They also rely on similar statements by Defendant C. But A said in the first-instance court that he never told the prosecutor that C nodded when he said that, and that he only said C appeared to nod. A further stated that when he sat with C on the curb and casually said, “Shall I get rid of T?”, he thought C would understand it as simply making T look bad, and he did not think C would imagine that T would be shot in front of the President. C also stated that he was not the kind of person who would agree with A’s actions and participate in them. At the first-instance court, C stated that while waiting for the President’s arrival in the restaurant garden, he never heard words about getting rid of T or about taking care of the aftermath, and that A had often previously used the expression “get rid of him” about T. Thus, the prosecutor’s interrogation statement that C nodded when A said “Shall I get rid of T?” is insufficient to establish that fact as it stands. Even if the facts in the prosecutor’s record are accepted as they are, it still cannot be said that the two agreed in the restaurant garden to kill T. That is, A had already firmly resolved to shoot T and the President long before meeting C, and after completing preparations such as checking the pistol upon arriving at the Gungjeong-dong restaurant, he only told C at around 17:40. Then, can we conclude from the short interval while waiting for the President’s arrival that, in the garden in front of the restaurant, an agreement to kill the President’s security chief was formed through a casual “shall we get rid of him” and a nod? The prosecutor’s statement alone does not support that A and C became one in order to kill T, with C using A’s act to carry out C’s own resolution to kill T.\\n\\nFurthermore, for conspiracy co-principal liability to be recognized, the third requirement above must be met, namely that A’s act of killing T was carried out because of the conspiracy with C. Can A’s act really be seen as having been carried out pursuant to a conspiracy with C and as executing the content of the conspiracy? A did not execute a conspiratorial plan with C; rather, he had already fully fixed his intent before meeting C and then killed T pursuant to that intent, which is a clear fact on the record. Thus, C cannot be a conspiracy co-principal in the killing of T from that point of view either.\\n\\nNot only that, but all evidence in the record lacks even the material to show the high-level agreement needed for conspiracy co-principal liability between C and A; it is not even enough to say that C knew in advance that A would kill T in front of the President.\\n\\nIn the end, although the lower court and majority opinion seem to accept that because A shot the President and T, the bias from that offense caused them to take A’s “shall I get rid of T?” as meaning he would kill T, and that C understood it that way, the phrase “shall I get rid of T” does not necessarily mean killing T, and given the circumstances that day at the President’s presence, it is far removed from our rules of experience to infer that A’s ambiguous and fragmentary remark meant he would kill T in front of the President. Therefore, Defendant C cannot be regarded as a conspiracy co-principal in T’s killing. Nor can there be said to be communication of intent even in the broader sense, so C cannot be said to have known A would kill T. Even if C had known A would kill T, mere passivity despite knowing another’s crime is not punishable by any provision. In any event, C cannot be regarded as a joint principal who aided in killing T.\\n\\nAs to Defendant C’s attempted insurrection offense, as stated in item 1 above, there was no riot by a combination of many persons using violence or intimidation, so there is no room to apply attempted insurrection to C.\\n\\nEven if, as the majority opinion says, the acts of the Defendants in this case correspond to a riot under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, the lower court’s conclusion that when A came out after the offense and said to C, “Please keep security,” C responded and that this proves he was a major participant under Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act is a misunderstanding of Article 87(2). If everyone who receives a unilateral request from A to keep security and does not resist is recognized as a major participant in insurrection, then if some persons were also present at the offense scene and A asked them not to tell anyone, and they complied without objection, they too would become major participants in insurrection. That result is untenable.\\n\\n4. Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act and Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act provide that where the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for 10 years or more is imposed, and there is a manifest reason to recognize that the sentence is grossly improper, such can be a ground for appeal. However, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision allowing appeal on the ground of excessive sentence. We therefore examine whether civilians, not military personnel or military employees, who were tried by a military court may appeal on the ground of excessive sentence, and whether the right of resistance can be recognized in our country and applied as a judicial norm.\\n\\n(1) The issue of Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act\\n\\nAs a general question, regardless of whether the sentence in this case against the Defendants was excessive, there is a doubt as to the argument that a person tried by a military court cannot appeal on the ground of excessive sentence, so I note this.\\n\\nWhereas Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the above-mentioned heavy sentence may be a ground of appeal, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain such a provision among the grounds of appeal, so a person tried by a military court cannot appeal on the ground of excessive sentence. This may be justifiable if the person tried by the military court was a military member or military employee in view of the particularity of that status and service. But if a civilian who is neither military personnel nor military employee is sentenced to such punishment by a military court, there is no distinction from a person tried by an ordinary court, and there is no rational basis to treat them differently. Therefore, depriving them of the right to appeal on the ground of excessive sentence merely because they were tried by a military court cannot be regarded as a rational measure in light of Article 9 of the Constitution, which provides equality before the law. Thus, for civilians who are not military personnel or military employees, even if tried by a military court, there is no reason to distinguish them from those tried by an ordinary court, and it may be interpreted that they can appeal under Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act on the ground of excessive sentence. If, however, even civilians must be interpreted as unable to appeal on the ground of excessive sentence under the express language of Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act, then at least as to civilians, there may arise the issue that Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act violates Article 9 of the Constitution.\\n\\nAccording to Article 525 of the Military Court-Martial Act, members of the military and military employees tried by a military court in an area under emergency martial law are prohibited from appealing, while civilians who are not military personnel or military employees are not restricted in their right to appeal even if tried by a military court. This shows that, for civilians, even if they were tried by a military court, the right to appeal is not restricted in order to maintain parity with the case of trial in an ordinary court. If Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act is interpreted as treating civilians the same as military personnel and military employees, then it is a provision that discriminates against the exercise of civil rights equally guaranteed to anyone.\\n\\n(2) The issue of the right of resistance\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that it will maintain this Court’s decision dated April 8, 1975, 74DA3323, holding that an argument invoking the right of resistance, an extra-legal concept of right, to justify acts contrary to positive law cannot be accepted. It is not clear whether that precedent denies the existence of the right of resistance itself in Korea or whether it merely means that the right of resistance cannot be applied as a judicial norm. In this case, the acts of Defendant A and others cannot be regarded as an exercise of the right of resistance given the content of the offense, so there is no need to discuss the right of resistance in connection with this case. However, as a general matter, I wish to point out the following doubts as to whether one can deny the existence of the right of resistance in our country or deny its application as a judicial norm.\\n\\nWhere a serious infringement by a state organ is committed against the democratic order centered on human dignity, which is the basic political order of our country, and the majority of the people judge that the existence itself of the democratic constitution is objectively being denied, if there is no way to remedy it by means available under positive law at that time, the people cannot simply watch passively or promote it. In such a case, for the protection of human rights and the basic order of the democratic constitution, the right of resistance consisting of refusal to comply with duties under positive law or to obey positive-law commands that formally appear lawful but substantively violate human rights and the democratic basic order should be recognized as a kind of natural-law right even if not explicitly written into the Constitution. If such a right of resistance is recognized, there is no basis to exclude its function as a judicial norm.\\n\\nAs grounds for denying the existence of such a right of resistance, the Preamble to our Constitution declares that it inherits the spirit of the April 19 democratic movement and ... establishes a new democratic republic; although the events of April 19, viewed under the positive law then in force, were complete criminal acts and unlawful, the Constitution’s Preamble designates them as a revolutionary act and declares inheritance of its spirit. If one evaluates the Preamble legally, one can only interpret it as meaning that our Constitution viewed the April 19 uprising as an exercise of the people’s right of resistance to preserve or defend a democratic order that was being destroyed. One wonders whether a right of resistance recognized by our Constitution can be denied in judicial judgment, and whether, once recognized, there is any rational reason to deprive it of effect by saying it cannot be applied as a judicial norm. The majority opinion states that the right of resistance has no basis in positive law and therefore cannot be applied as a judicial norm. However, there can be no legal principle that natural-law rights can never function as judicial norms, and the above-mentioned Preamble of our Constitution may also be seen as a positive-law basis for the right of resistance.\\n\\n4. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Kim Yun-haeng\\n\\nArticle 87 of the Criminal Act is the so-called collective offense of insurrection, and “riot” here means violence or intimidation by a combination of a mob sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality. In this case, taking the view that the acts of the Defendants do not constitute such a mob combination, I share the theory already expressed by Justice Im Hang-jun concerning that the six Defendants A, C, D, E, F, and G, excluding Defendant H, cannot be subject to the crime of insurrection, and also concerning that as to Defendant C, the lower judgment’s finding of conspiracy co-principal liability with A for the killing of T cannot be established.\\n\\nFurther, even if the insurrection (attempt) offenses recognized by the lower court could apply to the Defendants, the lower court recognized as to the remaining Defendants other than Defendant C the relation of imaginary concurrence on the ground that their acts also corresponded to murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88. I point out that this legal application was mistaken for the following reasons.\\n\\nThe reason is that the crime of insurrection takes as its constituent element a riot for the purpose of insurrection, and the riot referred to here is, by virtue of Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act concerning insurrection, broad enough to include “a person who executes an act of killing” as well as one who participates in plotting, directs, or engages in other important duties. Therefore, it is a concept that broadly includes acts from simple violence and intimidation to acts such as murder, injury, and arson. Accordingly, in a riot for insurrectionary purpose, even if someone is killed during the riot process, this constitutes a single insurrection offense, and depending on the position and role forming the group, they are separately punished under Article 87(1) through (3) as leader, participant in plotting, director, major-duty participant, or mere participant. By contrast, Article 88 of the Criminal Act, which defines murder with insurrectionary purpose, only says “a person who kills another for the purpose of insurrection,” which clearly means a case in which a person is killed not by riot but otherwise. Therefore, even if a person kills another for the same insurrectionary purpose, if it is carried out in the course of a riot, it is absorbed into the insurrection offense and becomes only an insurrection offense under Article 87; if it is not carried out by riot, then it is only a single offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88.\\n\\nIf, as the lower court thought, such cases always become imaginary concurrence, then in the case of a leader of insurrection, the statutory penalty is death, life imprisonment, or life imprisonment without labor, and murder with insurrectionary purpose also has the same statutory penalty, so one might say that in the case of the leader there is no practical effect. However, in the case of “a person who executes an act of killing” in the course of riot under insurrection, that person is punished, as noted above, with the same punishment as a conspirator, director, or other important-duty participant, and the penalty is death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for at least 5 years. In some cases, the person could be punished by imprisonment or imprisonment without labor for a fixed term of at least 5 years. By contrast, in imaginary concurrence, Article 40 of the Criminal Act requires punishment according to the heaviest penalty prescribed for the most serious offense, so the person would always be punished by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment without labor under Article 88, which makes no balance with Article 87(2), which prescribes imprisonment or imprisonment without labor for at least 5 years. (That the penalty for murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 is prescribed as heavier than that under Article 87(2) for “a person who executes an act of killing” in the course of insurrectionary riot is somewhat difficult to understand and not fully balanced, but in insurrection offenses, because mob psychology operates in collective crime and people often act rashly without deep thought, the expectation of compliance is low; thus, I understand the difference in statutory penalties between this and non-riot murder with insurrectionary purpose.) In light of this, in this case the lower court, while describing the acts of Defendants D, E, F, and G as those of persons engaged in important duties in the riot constituting insurrection, nevertheless applied to them the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and punished them by the heavier penalty of murder with insurrectionary purpose. This amounts to a case where the application of law was wrong and it affected the judgment. Therefore, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that maintains such lower judgment, and the lower judgment should also be reversed on this point.\\n\\n5. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Jeong Tae-won\\n\\nThis is the same as part (2) of the opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong below concerning Defendants E and F, and part (3) concerning Defendant G.\\n\\n6. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong\\n\\nIn view of the facts and evidence in this case, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the lower judgment finding all charges against Defendants C, E, F, and G guilty for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) As to Defendant C\\n\\nFirst, regarding the offense of murder by conspiracy co-principal liability against this Defendant, the point of the lower court (Army High Military Court) in finding this guilty is ultimately that the Defendant conspired with co-defendant A to kill the deceased T, the President’s security chief, and although he did not directly act, he caused A to carry out the killing and thus achieved the purpose. The supporting facts and evidence are summarized as follows: two hours before the shooting as execution of the murder by A (the shooting occurred at 19:40 on October 26, 1979, and the meeting between Defendant and A was at 17:50 on the same day, so less than two hours had passed), when the Defendant met A at the curb in the garden at the entrance to the Gungjeong-dong office, the Blue House branch of the Central Intelligence Agency, A said “I will get rid of the chief T,” and the Defendant nodded; he did not restrain A’s conduct at the shooting scene; and later that day, when the situation developed and Defendant met A in the restroom of the Army Headquarters banka and rebuked him, saying “Why did you even kill the President?”, from these things it was inferred that he intended the gunshot killing of T.\\n\\nHowever, the so-called conspiracy co-principal liability is a concept concerning an execution principal. In light of social reality, in crimes by multiple persons there are cases where the substantive principal plans the crime behind the scenes and causes the execution act to be carried out by subordinates or persons under the principal’s control, and in such cases simple instigation or aiding and abetting is not enough. This theory emerged from judicial necessity. Even in such cases, the substantive principal must have the subjective intent to commit the crime as his own. Merely inducing another’s intent or tolerating or using another’s crime does not fall within this category. (The Supreme Court seems already in Decision 57DO380 dated June 12, 1959 to have expressed this through the terms “subject of intent” or “single body of intent,” and the Japanese Supreme Court in Decision of May 28, 1958, Case No. 29(ka)1056, expressly held that subjective intent is required.) In this case, the lower court’s reasoning concerning Defendant C and the supporting facts are plainly not of that nature. No one can deny that the true subject of this shocking offense of assassinating the President was A, not Defendant C, but it is hard to understand that only with respect to the part of killing T the Defendant is treated as the principal and A as the executor under Defendant’s direction. Even if it is true that the Defendant nodded when A said “get rid of him,” that would, at most, mean he tolerated murder, and it is unclear why that can become a joint plot to kill. Likewise, even if he did not restrain A at the scene of the killing, that was merely passivity toward murder. More inexplicable still, the fact that the chief secretary Defendant did not restrain the shooting death of the President at the scene is not reproached in this case, yet failing to restrain the killing of the security chief is treated as conspiracy co-principal liability for murder. Also, the conversation in the Army banka restroom with A as a post hoc support for the plot is hard to accept when the plot itself is a major fact requiring strict proof.\\n\\nSecond, as to the attempted insurrection offense against the same Defendant, insurrection is a crime under Article 87 of the Criminal Act with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, and the concrete content of the Constitution at issue in this case is that the constitutional order was to be changed by assassinating the President. Therefore, whether Defendant had the intent to assassinate the President is indispensable for recognizing the purpose of insurrection against him.\\n\\nHowever, at the time of filing the original indictment, it was stated as a factual allegation that Defendant also conspired with A to assassinate the President, but this part of the indictment was later amended in the lower court, and the lower court’s factual findings also finalized that Defendant had no relation to the assassination of the President. Therefore, attempted major participation in insurrection cannot be established against Defendant. Although the record suggests some doubt that on the day of the incident Defendant may have, in the sequence of acts he performed until A was arrested, either cooperated with A’s conspiracy or aided it, that doubt arises only from inference and circumstances. Since insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the evidence or facts to establish that purpose are major facts requiring strict proof. Thus, the fact that Defendant did not immediately report A after the crucial shooting cannot be deemed a suspicious circumstance from which it reflexively follows that he participated in the major duties of insurrection. Especially given the situation at the time, there was no guarantee that Defendant himself would not be shot by A. To say that merely because he did not disclose A’s offense until four hours after the assassination, when reporting to the Minister of National Defense and the Army Chief of Staff, he did so for the purpose of insurrection is a leap in logic. Moreover, in this case, where no one can deny that A’s attempt at insurrection failed because of Defendant’s report, it is not proper under the principle of fairness to infer from the reporting fact a basis unfavorable to the Defendant and thereby convict him.\\n\\nTherefore, as to Defendant C, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the lower judgment, which does not establish the several decisive circumstances set forth above. The grounds of appeal on these points are meritorious.\\n\\n(2) As to Defendants E and F\\n\\nThe lower judgment finding these Defendants guilty of attempted insurrection and murder with insurrectionary purpose also cannot be left standing. It is undeniable that, as co-defendants and subordinates of D, they shot and killed U and X, security guards of the Presidential Security Service, while staying at the Gungjeong-dong intelligence restaurant on the day of the offense. However, for that act to be murder with insurrectionary purpose, there must be awareness of the insurrectionary purpose, namely subversion of the Constitution. On this point, the only materials the lower court or the majority opinion regarded as evidence are the statements the Defendants made during the military investigation. Their statements merely amount to saying they thought that if things went well, they would be promoted or get a share. To say that those statement entries are sufficient evidence that they knew of subversion of the Constitution, i.e. the assassination of the President, and participated in the offense exceeds the bounds of free conviction.\\n\\nAs to how those statements were made, the record shows they were the result of leading questions and inferences made by the military investigative authorities, so one cannot distinguish whether they are opinions or statements of fact. It is hard to understand how they can be linked to awareness of the assassination of the President or subversion of the Constitution. Regarding the circumstances by which the Defendants came to shoot, co-defendant D merely instructed them to “drive the security guards in the restaurant into a corner and, if they resist, return fire.” Defendant F was D’s driver, and E was also a guard at Gungjeong-dong with little education. Even if one has difficulty asking them about the meaning of subverting the Constitution, the minimum would be awareness of the assassination of the President. Yet there is no clear material in this case showing even that awareness on their part. To uphold a death sentence by recognizing that all of this existed is unacceptable.\\n\\n(3) As to Defendant G\\n\\nThis Defendant is recognized by the lower court as having committed attempted insurrection and murder with insurrectionary purpose by carrying out so-called confirmation killing 30 minutes after the gunfire in this case, thereby completely extinguishing the lives of T and U, who were still alive at the time. This part also cannot be left standing.\\n\\nThe time of the above confirmation killing by the Defendant is fixed by the lower court as 20:05 on that day, whereas the shooting of Chief T by A was at 19:40. Then it is difficult, in view of the various materials, to conclude that even 25 to 30 minutes after the first shot T was still groaning and had not died. On that day A shot T, then fired at the President, and shortly thereafter hid in the restroom, then fired the final shot into T’s abdomen and again shot the President; the record and the lower court both accept this. Then T’s time of death would have been at least before, or at the same time as, the President’s death. The hospital authorities stated that the President’s time of death was five minutes before the time the body was transported to the military hospital, that is, before 19:57 that day. In the end, if the President’s time of death can be estimated as 10 to 12 minutes after A’s first shooting, then T’s time of death would also be 19:50 or 19:52. Then it would be reasonable to conclude that at the time of Defendant G’s confirmation killing at 20:05, the victim T had already died. Otherwise, because the autopsy report and photographs of the body are in the record and the exact location of the gunshot wounds is clearly shown, the court should have had an expert assess the time of death and conducted a hearing accordingly.\\n\\nNevertheless, without taking such measures, to recognize murder with insurrectionary purpose and even impose the death penalty merely on the Defendant’s statement that T seemed to be making some sound at the time of the confirmation killing is utterly incomprehensible. Therefore, failing to examine this point and determine whether it was murder or merely a gunshot at a corpse amounts to a failure of hearing or defect for lack of reasons. Moreover, the record does not show where or what the Defendant was doing before the confirmation killing. To recognize guilt for insurrection on the ground that the killing was for an insurrectionary purpose is also not free from the criticism of finding facts without evidence.\\n\\nFor these reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the Army High Military Court judgment on Defendants C, E, F, and G, and I state that the grounds of appeal on these points are meritorious.\\n\\n1980. 5. 20."}

{"[84DO114]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the statement of reasons of the judgment of the first instance upheld by the lower court, the first instance court, by synthesizing the evidence cited therein, found that the Defendant, on or about 1982.10.29. 14:00, at Courtroom No. 217 of the Seoul Civil District Court, after taking the oath as a witness for the Plaintiff in case 82NA1174, an action for damages between Plaintiff Jo Bo-gyeong and Defendant Yi Wol-bun, made a false statement contrary to her memory to Judge Jeon Chung-hwan of that court, saying, “The Plaintiff received the balance of 134,800 won after deducting 165,200 won from 300,000 won,” thereby committing perjury, even though she did not know the contents thereof but stated as if she knew them.\\n\\nIn perjury, the false statement referred to does not mean that the objective fact is false, but means a statement made contrary to one’s memory of facts personally experienced, that is, a fact contrary to memory; and according to the record of this case, not only has the Defendant consistently denied criminal intent, but even according to the respective entries in the statement prepared by the judicial police officer concerning the complainant Yi Wol-bun and the written statement prepared by Yi Wol-bun, the said Yi Wol-bun herself stated that, between her and the above Jo Bo-gyeong, there were transaction relations concerning a mutual-aid fund and the management of a teahouse, as well as transaction relations concerning deposits, and that there was an occasion when she applied 165,200 won out of the deposits to the mutual-aid fund and deducted it, and gave the remaining 34,800 won to Jo Bo-gyeong (however, she claimed that the deposit was 200,000 won, and thus, after deducting the above 165,200 won, the remainder was 34,800 won, so that there is a difference of 100,000 won each between the deposit and the payment). Although Yi Wol-bun denies the fact of running a teahouse as a partnership with Jo Bo-gyeong, stating that she employed Jo Bo-gyeong as the teahouse madam, and denies having received 700,000 won as partnership funds, what this means is that, separate from such transactions, there was a deposit to be returned to Jo Bo-gyeong, and that she returned the remaining money after deducting 165,200 won therefrom; accordingly, it cannot be concluded that the Defendant’s testimony, in light of the above facts, was a false statement contrary to memory, and no other evidence can be found sufficient to establish that the Defendant’s testimony was a false statement contrary to memory. Therefore, if the trier of fact was to recognize the Defendant’s criminal intent, it should first have further examined the various transaction relations between the above Jo Bo-gyeong and Yi Wol-bun and determined whether the Defendant’s testimony was wholly implausible; nevertheless, without fully conducting such examination, it held that testimony which substantially accorded even with the objective facts asserted by Yi Wol-bun was a false statement, and thus it is deemed to have erred by misunderstanding the legal principle of the offense of perjury, by failing to conduct sufficient examination, and by violating the rules of evidence and misapprehending the facts.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal are well taken.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court judgment is reversed, and, in order to have the lower court conduct a new trial and determination, the case is remanded to the collegial division of the Seoul Criminal District Court; the opinions of the participating judges being in agreement, judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[88DO650]": "The grounds of appeal filed by the Defendants and by the court-appointed defense counsel are considered together.\\n\\nBased on the evidence adopted by the judgment of the court of first instance, which the court below affirmed, the court below found that Defendant <REDACTED> had long harbored intense resentment over the victim <REDACTED> teasing the wife of the co-defendant, who was somewhat mentally retarded, by asking her for breast milk, and that, on 1987. 8. 8. around 23:30, while drinking with the victim at the village store in <REDACTED>, Goesan County, Chungcheongbuk-do, he heard from the owner of said store, non-party <REDACTED>, that even during the daytime of that day the victim had teased the wife of the co-defendant by asking her for breast milk, whereupon he struck the victim’s cheeks several times and otherwise assaulted him. Thereafter, as the three of them, namely Defendant <REDACTED>, who had come there, the victim, and Defendant <REDACTED>, were heading together to a nearby <REDACTED> in order to drink more liquor, when they reached the farm road in front of the village, the victim, who was in a state of heavy intoxication, made a gesture with his fingers as if to gouge out their eyes and used abusive language, such as saying, “If this bastard keeps fooling around, I will kill him,” whereupon Defendant <REDACTED> struck the victim’s cheeks several times with the palm of his hand, and Defendant <REDACTED> also struck the victim’s abdomen twice, causing the victim to fall down. Then, in a moment of erupting anger, they resolved to kill the victim, and Defendant <REDACTED> climbed onto the victim’s body and struck the victim’s chest twice with a stone measuring 20 centimeters in width and 10 centimeters in length (Prosecution Exhibit No. 1), and Defendant <REDACTED> likewise joined in and struck the victim’s head twice with a stone measuring 13 centimeters in width and 7 centimeters in length (Prosecution Exhibit No. 2). Thereafter, they again raised the victim to his feet, and Defendant <REDACTED> struck the victim’s abdomen once, causing him to fall backward; and when the victim lost consciousness and went limp due to concussion and the like, they mistook him for dead and, for the purpose of secretly burying the corpse and destroying evidence, dragged the victim to a stream about 150 meters away from there, dug a pit with a shovel, and buried the victim, thereby causing the victim to die of suffocation. Upon comparing this with the record, the above finding is proper, and there is no illegality in having erred in fact-finding by violating the rules of logic and experience in evaluating evidence, as alleged in the grounds. Further, even if, as stated above, the victim did not directly die from the assault committed by the Defendants with intent to kill, but instead died from the burial conducted for the purpose of destroying the traces of the crime, if the entire course is viewed comprehensively, the initially foreseen fact of the victim’s killing was ultimately realized, and the Defendants cannot escape criminal liability for homicide; accordingly, the court below’s decision, in the same sense, to uphold the first-instance judgment convicting the Defendants of homicide is proper, and there is no error whatsoever therein.\\n\\nFurther, according to the record, it is recognized that Defendant <REDACTED> was somewhat intoxicated at the time of the above offense, but it does not appear that, as a result, said Defendant had reached the level of diminished mental and physical capacity; therefore, the argument on this point is also without merit.\\n\\nIn addition, in this case, in which a sentence of less than 10 years’ imprisonment was imposed, the argument that the court below’s sentencing is too severe cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal in light of Article 383, item 4, of the Criminal Procedure Act. All of the grounds are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeals of the Defendants are all dismissed, and each Defendant shall have a portion of the days of detention after appeal credited toward the principal sentence, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating.\\n\\n1988. 6. 28."}
{"[93DO1002]": "The appeal is dismissed."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning property crimes are incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents) (a) Even if A, a vehicle owner-operator entrusted by the entrusting company with the vehicle’s operation and management rights, effectively disposes of a vehicle in custody without the entrusting company’s consent, embezzlement is not established because he has no legal authority to dispose of it. (b) The act of A, after pretending as if he were going to purchase precious metals at a jewelry store operated by the victim, receiving a gold necklace from the victim, and then fleeing under the pretext of going to the restroom, constitutes theft. (c) Even if A deceives A, the owner and seller of land, into signing and sealing a contract for the creation of a mortgage, etc., and into handing over a certificate of seal impression, by falsely stating that they are documents necessary for land transaction permission, etc., and then uses them to create in favor of B a mortgage on land owned by A, with A as the debtor, and borrows money, A’s intent to dispose is recognized, and thus it constitutes fraud. (d) Where A, after agreeing with A to provide his automobile as security by transfer, arbitrarily sells it to B and has the transfer registration completed in B’s name, a debtor who has entered into a transfer-security agreement with respect to automobiles, etc., which are assets requiring registration, is recognized as being in a position to handle the creditor’s affairs, and if, in breach of that duty, he disposes of it to another, breach of trust is established. (e) If A, due to a mistake by the rightful holder or an error in the virtual asset operating system, etc., transfers virtual assets that were transferred to his electronic wallet without legal cause to another of his electronic wallets without returning them, the doctrine of mistaken remittance applies and breach of trust is established.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2015DO1944]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal (the contents of a petition submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. a. Embezzlement is established when a person who keeps in custody another’s property embezzles that property or refuses to return it (Article 355(1) of the Criminal Act). In embezzlement, custody of property means a state in which one has factual or legal control over the property (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 87DO1778, rendered October 13, 1987), and an act of embezzlement means any act that realizes an intent of unlawful appropriation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DO5904, rendered December 9, 2004). Accordingly, where a person who has taken delivery of and is keeping in custody a vehicle owned by another person, the acquisition of ownership of which requires registration, disposes of it in fact, embezzlement is established, and neither the person who entrusted the custody nor the custodian need be the registered title holder of the vehicle. And this legal principle likewise applies where, with respect to a vehicle owned by a title-leasing company, a title-lessee who has been entrusted by the title-leasing company with the right to manage operation disposes of the vehicle in custody in fact without the title-leasing company’s consent, or where a person entrusted by a title-lessee with custody of the vehicle disposes of the vehicle in custody in fact without the title-lessee’s consent.\\n\\nIn contrast, Supreme Court Decision 78DO1714, rendered October 10, 1978, Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3276, rendered December 22, 2006, etc., to the extent they state that, in the offense of embezzlement involving a vehicle whose acquisition of ownership requires registration, the status of a person who keeps in custody another’s property should, unlike in the case of ordinary movables, be determined not by whether he or she possesses the vehicle but by whether he or she has the authority to validly dispose of the vehicle in law to a third party by registration, are hereby modified to the extent inconsistent with this Decision.\\n\\nb. According to the record, as to the portion of the indictment alleging that the Defendant purchased and acquired stolen goods by acquiring the vehicles embezzled through the act that Nonparty 2, the representative director of Nonparty 1 Co., Ltd., kept in custody and then disposed of in fact the four vehicles title-leased by Nonparty 1 Co., Ltd., which were owned by the respective title-leasing companies, and the remaining two vehicles owned by Nonparty 1 Co., Ltd., the court below upheld the conclusion of the first instance court that found this guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the first instance judgment and the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principle and the duly admitted evidence, the above determination by the court below is acceptable, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle regarding the ownership relationship of title-leased vehicles or the status of a custodian in embezzlement.\\n\\n2. The finding of criminal facts must reach proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 307(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), but the selection and weighing of evidence conducted as the premise of fact-finding fall within the discretion of the court of fact, so long as they do not exceed the bounds of free evaluation of evidence (Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below determined that the Defendant had participated in the acquisition of stolen goods, forgery of private documents, and uttering of forged private documents in this case by tacit and sequential conspiracy with co-defendant 1 at the court below and others, and it rejected the appellate arguments alleging factual error and misapprehension of law challenging this determination.\\n\\nThe grounds for final appeal challenging such fact-finding by the court below are, in substance, nothing more than criticizing the court below’s determination regarding the selection and probative value of evidence, which falls within the free judgment of the court of fact. And even upon examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles stated by the court below and the duly admitted evidence, there is no illegality in the above determination by the court below, such as misapprehending the legal principle on co-principal liability, failing to conduct the necessary deliberation, or exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n3. Under Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, a final appeal on the ground of unfairness in sentencing is permitted only in cases in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or detention for 10 years or more has been imposed; accordingly, in this case, in which a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the Defendant, an argument to the effect that the sentencing is unfair does not constitute a lawful ground for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2016DO13362]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the primary charges among the acquittal portion\\n\\n(a) Fraud is an offense constituted by deceiving another person, causing that person to fall into error, inducing the person deceived thereby to engage in a disposition act, and thereby obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit. Therefore, for fraud to be established, there must be the actor’s deceitful act, the person deceived’s error and the ensuing disposition act, and the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit, and there must be a sequential causal relationship among them (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 11, 1989, 89DO346, Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 27, 2000, 2000DO1155).\\n\\nIn fraud, the disposition act mediates and connects in the middle the final result of the person deceived’s error caused by the actor’s deceitful act and the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit, while at the same time playing the role of distinguishing fraud, which is essentially characterized by obtaining property by taking advantage of the victim’s act falling into error, from theft, in which the actor obtains property by means of taking it away without relying on the victim’s act. Considering this role and function of the disposition act, if it can be assessed that the actor obtained property or a pecuniary benefit through some act based on the will of the person deceived, the disposition act contemplated in fraud is recognized.\\n\\n(b) As to such disposition act, however, the Supreme Court has traditionally held that, subjectively, the person deceived must have a disposition intent, that is, awareness of the disposition result, and, objectively, there must be an act governed by such intent (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on October 26, 1987, 87DO1042, Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 9, 1999, 99DO1326, Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 14, 2011, 2011DO769). According to this view, even if the victim, deceived, engaged in an act causing property damage to himself or herself, fraud is not established because the disposition act cannot be recognized unless there is awareness of the resulting consequence.\\n\\nHowever, fraud is originally an offense in which the actor, by means of deceitful conduct, causes the person deceived to fall into error and thereby makes the person deceived engage in a disposition act in a state where the person does not properly know what consequence his or her act will bring about. If the person deceived accurately recognizes the consequence his or her act will bring about, that means, in the end, that the person was not deceived or was not caused by deceitful conduct to fall into error, and thus fraud cannot be established. Accordingly, the previous view that disposition intent can be recognized only when the person deceived is aware of the disposition result needs to be reconsidered. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Fraud is established where property is transferred by a disposition act based on the person deceived’s defective intent. Therefore, a disposition act must not only be attributable to the person deceived’s act, but also, even if defective, must be attributable to the person deceived’s intent; thus, acts by a person lacking capacity to intend or acts done in a state of unconsciousness cannot constitute a disposition act. In this respect, disposition intent may be said to be the subjective element of the disposition act.\\n\\nIn fraud, the person deceived’s disposition intent is a defective intent formed in a state of error caused by the deceitful act, and thus is necessarily incomplete or defective. It is rather natural that the person deceived’s subjective recognition of the legal meaning or economic effect of the disposition act and the actual consequence brought about do not coincide, and this is the essential characteristic of fraud. Therefore, disposition intent is sufficiently established if the person deceived, having fallen into error, recognizes that he or she is performing some act; it cannot be said that awareness of the consequence brought about by that act is also required.\\n\\n(2) As an element constituting fraud, deceitful conduct means broadly conduct contrary to the principle of good faith that should be observed in transactional relations, causing a person to fall into error, and error means an awareness not in conformity with the facts, regardless of whether it concerns facts, legal relations, or legal effects (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 14, 1984, 83DO2995, Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 26, 2006, 2005DO1160). In addition, the defective awareness of the person deceived that does not accord with the facts may concern the motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act, or the disposition act itself, without limitation. Therefore, even if, as a result of deception, the person deceived does not properly recognize the meaning of his or her act or omission and thus does not recognize the consequence brought about by such act, if that person came to engage in an act causing property damage in such a state of error, the person deceived’s disposition act and the corresponding disposition intent must be recognized.\\n\\nIf, on the contrary, disposition intent can be recognized only when the person deceived is aware of the consequence resulting from his or her own act, then the more the actor, by using a cunning and intelligent method, causes the person deceived to fall deeply into error to the extent that the person does not recognize the consequence of his or her act, the more likely it becomes that disposition intent will instead be denied. This is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(3) When determining whether the victim had disposition intent, it is not proper to transplant as is the interpretive theory concerning the actor’s criminal intent and interpret it so that disposition intent is recognized only when the victim recognized the consequence of the disposition act.\\n\\nArticle 13 of the Criminal Act provides: “An act committed without awareness of the facts constituting the elements of a crime shall not be punished.” This is an expression of the principle of culpability, namely, that only conduct attributable to the actor’s responsibility by reason of the actor’s awareness of the facts constituting the elements of a crime shall be punished. Therefore, for the actor’s criminal intent to be recognized in fraud, awareness of all the elements constituting fraud is required: the actor’s deceitful act, the person deceived’s error and the ensuing disposition act, and the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit. In the end, the actor’s criminal intent can be recognized only when there is awareness of the result of the act, that is, awareness of the element of the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit.\\n\\nHowever, fraud is not established only if the victim, namely the person deceived, is aware of the actor’s deceitful conduct or of his or her own error caused thereby. Rather, if the victim were aware of the actor’s deceitful conduct or his or her own error caused thereby, fraud could not be established. Likewise, there is no reason to think that the victim must be aware of the element of the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit, which is the consequence of the disposition act. The object of awareness for the actor’s criminal intent comprises all elements constituting fraud, whereas the object of awareness for the victim’s disposition intent is confined to the disposition act itself among the elements constituting fraud. This is because the victim’s disposition intent, unlike the actor’s criminal intent, has no relation whatsoever to the principle of culpability and is nothing more than the subjective element of the disposition act.\\n\\nThe ground for requiring disposition intent in the victim’s disposition act is that, when it is recognized that the disposition act was performed by the victim with awareness of it, that disposition act can be regarded as an act performed by the victim. In other words, the function of the victim’s disposition intent in fraud is only to serve, on the subjective side, to confirm the objective fact that the victim’s disposition act exists. Therefore, if the victim recognized and performed some act that is evaluated as a disposition act, the victim’s disposition intent can be said to exist. In the end, it is not necessary for the victim to be aware even of the consequence of the disposition act.\\n\\n(c) In conclusion, in light of the nature and structure of fraud, the function and role of the disposition act and its volitional element, namely disposition intent, and the meaning of deceitful conduct and error, even if the person deceived did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the person deceived’s act or omission is evaluated as a patrimonial disposition act directly causing property damage and such act or omission was recognized and performed by the person deceived, the disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act is recognized. Put differently, it is not necessary that the person deceived recognize even the consequence of his or her own act or omission in order for disposition intent to be recognized.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decision rendered on October 26, 1987, 87DO1042, Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 9, 1999, 99DO1326, Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 14, 2011, 2011DO769, and the like, which held that for a disposition act contemplated in fraud to be recognized, the person deceived must be aware of the disposition result, are to be changed to the extent they conflict with this judgment.\\n\\n(d) Further, we examine how to identify the disposition act and disposition intent when the person deceived’s disposition act is carried out in the form of a legal act or declaration of intent and the person deceived’s inner intent does not coincide with the intent manifested externally and objectively recognized.\\n\\n(1) The so-called “signature fraud” issue in this case concerns a case where, due to error induced by deceitful conduct, the person deceived signed or affixed a seal to a disposition document different from his or her inner intent, thereby causing property damage. Here, the actor’s own deceitful conduct essentially exploits a situation in which the person deceived cannot properly recognize the meaning or content of his or her own disposition act, or prevents the person deceived from recognizing the consequence of his or her own act. As a result, the person deceived falls into error and fails to recognize the consequence of signing or affixing a seal to the disposition document. The essence of fraud is the use of the person deceived’s defective disposition act; in a signature-fraud case, the defect exists in the very process of formation of the declaration of intent itself.\\n\\n(2) In such a signature-fraud case, even if the person deceived did not properly recognize the content of the disposition document and signed or affixed a seal to it, resulting in a discrepancy between the inner intent and the intent objectively and externally recognized through the disposition document, the reason one can say that the actor obtained property or a pecuniary benefit by the person deceived’s act is that the disposition document containing the transfer of property can be viewed as having been prepared by the person deceived. Thus, if, as a result of the person deceived falling into error due to the actor’s deceitful conduct, the person deceived signed or affixed a seal to a disposition document whose content caused a result different from the inner intent, and property damage according to the content of the disposition document was thereby caused, the act of the person deceived who signed or affixed a seal to such disposition document constitutes the disposition act contemplated in fraud. In addition, even if the person deceived did not yet recognize the disposition result, namely the specific content of the document and its legal effect, if the person deceived himself or herself signed or affixed a seal to some document and thus had awareness of the act of signing or affixing a seal to that disposition document, the person deceived’s disposition intent is also recognized.\\n\\n(e) According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the evidence duly admitted and examined by the first instance court and the court below, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(1) The Defendant and Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., around November 29, 2010 and December 3, 2010, deceived Victim Non-Indicted Person 2, the seller of each land identified in the judgment below, by telling him that the documents were necessary for land transaction permission, etc., thereby causing the victim to sign and affix a seal to the mortgage creation agreement, etc.; after receiving the victim’s seal certificate, they used it to establish in favor of Non-Indicted Person 3, etc. a mortgage with a maximum secured claim amount totaling KRW 1,050,000,000 on each of the lands owned by the above victim, with the Defendant as debtor, and borrowed KRW 700,000,000.\\n\\n(2) In addition, on December 29, 2010, the Defendant and Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., deceived Victim Non-Indicted Person 2 and Non-Indicted Person 4, the sellers of each land identified in the judgment below, by telling them that the documents were necessary for land transaction permission, etc., thereby causing the victims to sign or affix a seal to a loan payment agreement, etc. stating that the above lands were provided as security; after receiving the victims’ seal certificates, they used them to establish in favor of Non-Indicted Person 5 a mortgage with a maximum secured claim amount of KRW 180,000,000 on each of the lands owned by the victims, with the Defendant as debtor, and borrowed KRW 120,000,000.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, ① the Defendant and Non-Indicted Person 6 conspired to borrow KRW 100,000,000 by providing as security the land identified in the judgment below owned by Victim Non-Indicted Person 7 and then use the remaining money, except for the down payment of KRW 30,000,000, themselves; thereafter, around April 5, 2011, they proposed to the victim to sell the above land for KRW 300,000,000 and demanded that a mortgage be established regarding the borrowing of the down payment of KRW 30,000,000, thereby obtaining the victim’s consent; ② on April 7, 2011, at the place where the sales contract for the above land was concluded, they obtained from the victim, who mistakenly believed them to be documents necessary for establishing a mortgage for the borrowing of KRW 30,000,000, signatures and seals on a mortgage creation agreement with a maximum secured claim amount of KRW 30,000,000, debtor the Defendant, mortgagee Non-Indicted Person 8, and a mortgage creation agreement with a maximum secured claim amount of KRW 120,000,000, debtor the Defendant, mortgagee Non-Indicted Person 9, and also obtained seals on each mortgage creation registration application and power of attorney, while receiving the victim’s seal certificate; ③ using these, they established mortgages in favor of the above mortgagees and borrowed a total of KRW 100,000,000.\\n\\n(f) Examining these facts in light of the legal principles stated above, (1) Victim Non-Indicted Person 2 and Non-Indicted Person 4, as a result of falling into error due to the Defendant’s and others’ deceitful conduct, mistakenly believing the documents to be those necessary for land transaction permission, etc., signed or affixed a seal to the mortgage creation agreement, etc., which are disposition documents, thereby engaging in acts causing property damage. Accordingly, the victims’ acts as above constitute the disposition act contemplated in fraud, and (2) Victim Non-Indicted Person 7 also, as a result of falling into error due to the Defendant’s and others’ deceitful conduct, mistakenly believed the documents to be security-provision documents necessary for the Defendant and others to borrow KRW 30,000,000, and signed or affixed a seal to the mortgage creation agreement, etc. for borrowing KRW 100,000,000, thereby engaging in acts causing property damage. Accordingly, the victim’s acts as above also constitute the disposition act contemplated in fraud. Moreover, even if the victims did not yet recognize the exact content of the documents they signed or affixed a seal to, and the consequence of drafting those documents, so long as they believed the documents to be for land transaction permission or the agreed mortgage creation and themselves signed or affixed a seal to documents containing contents concerning a different mortgage creation agreement, they had awareness of the act of signing or affixing a seal to such documents, and thus disposition intent is also recognized.\\n\\n(g) Nevertheless, the court below, on the contrary, erroneously determined that because the victims had no intent to establish a mortgage on their lands, the victims could not be said to have engaged in a disposition act, and therefore found all of these primary charges not guilty. Accordingly, the court below’s judgment contains error that affected the conclusion by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the disposition act contemplated in fraud. The grounds of appeal pointing out this error are meritorious.\\n\\n2. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the portions of the judgment below concerning the primary charges of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud), the charge of fraud on December 29, 2010, and the charge of fraud on April 7, 2011 must be reversed, and since those primary charge portions are reversed, the alternative charge portions concerning violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud) and each charge of fraud must also be reversed as a matter of course. Furthermore, because the court below, including the alternative charge portion concerning the charge of fraud on April 7, 2011 that is reversed as above, imposed a single sentence on the remaining guilty portion on the view that they were in a concurrent offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, the judgment below must ultimately be reversed in its entirety.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and so decide as stated in the operative part. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Sang-hoon, Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, Cho Hee-dae, Park Sang-ok, and Lee Ki-taek, the opinions of the participating justices are unanimous. There are supplemental opinions by Justice Park Byeong-dae to the majority opinion, supplemental opinions by Justices Kim Chang-seok and Kwon Soon-il, and a supplemental opinion by Justice Kim Shin.
