There are supplemental opinions to the dissenting opinions by Justices Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, and Park Sang-ok, and a supplemental opinion by Justice Cho Hee-dae.\\n\\n4. The dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Sang-hoon, Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, Cho Hee-dae, Park Sang-ok, and Lee Ki-taek to the majority opinion as to each primary charge among the acquittal portion of the judgment below are as follows.\\n\\n(a) The majority opinion states that, even if the person deceived did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the person deceived’s act or omission is evaluated as a patrimonial disposition act directly causing property damage and such act or omission was recognized and performed by the person deceived, the disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act is recognized, and that it is not necessary to recognize even the consequence resulting from one’s own act or omission in order to recognize disposition intent. However, we find it difficult to agree with the logic of the majority opinion, which abruptly changes the previous precedents that have understood awareness of the disposition result as disposition intent for the purpose of punishing signature-fraud cases, for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) Theft is obtaining property by the offender’s act of taking it away, while fraud is obtaining property through the victim’s disposition act; the two are distinguished by the disposition act. In this sense, fraud is explained as an offense of self-harm, while theft is an offense of harm to another. In fraud, in order for the essence of the disposition act as such self-harm to be satisfied, the victim must necessarily have a will to decide upon the disposition of his or her own property. Put differently, only an act or omission governed by a will formed on the basis of the recognition that the victim’s act is related to his or her own property rights can normatively be evaluated as the disposition act contemplated in fraud. A disposition act with no awareness or intent at all concerning the disposition result is, in itself, a contradiction. In short, a fraud case in which the victim does not even recognize what he or she did with respect to his or her own property runs counter to the essence of fraud as an offense of self-harm.\\n\\nThe reason the Supreme Court has consistently interpreted the disposition act contemplated in fraud to mean a patrimonial disposition act, requiring subjectively that the person deceived have a disposition intent, namely awareness of the disposition result, and objectively that there be an act governed by such intent, is likewise a proper theory of interpretation derived from a deep insight into the essence of fraud and the meaning of the disposition act and its volitional element, disposition intent, and is by no means a view to be changed.\\n\\nIn the end, the majority opinion, which says that even where the person deceived has no awareness of the disposition result, disposition intent and the disposition act contemplated in fraud can be recognized, is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion also takes the view that for the disposition act contemplated in fraud to be recognized, disposition intent, which is the subjective intent of the person deceived, is necessary. However, even apart from further discussion of the essence of fraud, the very concept of “disposition” intent already presupposes the person deceived’s awareness and intent corresponding to the content of the disposition act. A disposition intent with no awareness whatsoever of the result of the disposition act cannot be the subjective intent of the disposition act.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that disposition intent in a disposition act is sufficiently established if the person deceived, having fallen into error, has awareness that he or she is performing an act that is evaluated as a patrimonial disposition act; looking at its substantive meaning, however, this merely means that the person deceived who performed the act has only a factual intent to perform an act, distinguishable from the act of a person lacking capacity to intend or an unconscious act. But such an intent to act cannot be evaluated as a “disposition” intent corresponding to the disposition act.\\n\\nThus, the majority opinion confuses the disposition intent contemplated in fraud with the victim’s general intent to act, and while stating that disposition intent is necessary for the disposition act, it is itself falling into contradiction by independently interpreting the meaning of disposition intent in a way that in no way accords with the concept of disposition intent. Even in light of this, the majority opinion’s logic is improper.\\n\\n(3) The elements of fraud must be interpreted in accordance with the essence of fraud, and an interpretation of the elements that contradicts that essence can hardly be recognized as justified. As noted above, in interpreting the disposition act that characterizes fraud as an offense of self-harm and distinguishes it from theft, awareness of the disposition result is naturally required for the person deceived; in interpreting the other elements of fraud, namely error and deceitful conduct, an interpretive theory contrary thereto cannot be developed. In other words, according to the essence of fraud and the meaning of disposition intent derived therefrom, fraud can be established only where the person deceived, having fallen into error, performs the disposition act while aware of the meaning and consequence of his or her act; accordingly, the person deceived’s error as an element of the offense is also confined to matters concerning the motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act, and error concerning the disposition act itself, lacking even awareness of the disposition result, cannot be subsumed under the error contemplated in fraud. The proper interpretive theory concerning deceitful conduct as an element of the offense is no different. In the end, the majority opinion’s argument that awareness of the disposition result by the person deceived is not indispensable, relying on an improper interpretation of error and deceitful conduct detached from the essence and specificity of fraud, is nothing more than a reversed-order interpretive theory and cannot be accepted as is.\\n\\n(4) Under the majority opinion, which interprets disposition intent in fraud as not requiring awareness of the disposition result by the person deceived, the question whether fraud is established becomes uncertain, and as a result the scope of punishment is also likely to expand. In numerous cases involving the actor’s deceitful conduct, it is doubtful whether one can clearly distinguish fraud from non-fraud without considering the person deceived’s awareness at all. For example, in the so-called “trick theft” case where the offender falsely says he wishes only to look at a book or a piece of jewelry, receives it from the person deceived, and then simply takes it away, the Supreme Court has punished the conduct as theft, viewing the book or jewelry as still being in the person deceived’s possession notwithstanding the delivery act, and treating the defendant’s taking act as an act of trespass upon possession (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 22, 1983, 82DO3115, Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 12, 1994, 94DO1487). However, even in such a trick-theft case, it is by no means easy, considering only the objective and external delivery act without any regard to the victim’s awareness or intent, to determine clearly whether the person deceived still retained possession of the book or jewelry or had completely transferred possession. In the end, it is clear that disposition intent, with awareness of the disposition result as its content, is an important element for distinguishing fraud from theft and should not be abandoned in interpreting fraud.\\n\\n(5) Article 2, item 2 of the Special Act on the Prevention of Damage from Telecommunications-Based Financial Fraud and Refund of Damages (hereinafter the “Telecommunications-Fraud Damage Refund Act”) defines “telecommunications-based financial fraud” as the following acts committed by deceiving or extorting another person by using telecommunications under Article 2, item 1 of the Framework Act on Telecommunications to obtain a pecuniary benefit or to cause a third party to obtain a pecuniary benefit, and lists as one such act “causing funds to be remitted or transferred.” Article 15-2, paragraph 1, item 1 (hereinafter the “punishment provision of this case”) provides that a person who, for the purpose of telecommunications-based financial fraud, causes another person to enter information or commands into a computer or other information-processing device shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 10 years or a fine not exceeding KRW 100,000,000. This punishment provision was newly enacted to punish even such offenses in light of the need to punish variant voice-phishing crimes in which the offender deceives the victim by promising a tax refund, lures the victim to an ATM, and causes the victim to remit or transfer money from his or her own account to a voice-phishing account, since whether fraud applies was unclear because the deceived victim did not remit or transfer money with awareness of disposing of his or her property. As a result, conduct in which a victim is deceived by using telecommunications and is caused to remit or transfer money without even awareness of the consequence of his or her own act is punished through this punishment provision.\\n\\nAs can be seen from the enactment history of this punishment provision under the Telecommunications-Fraud Damage Refund Act, if one seeks to criminally punish the actor who obtained a pecuniary benefit through unlawful deceit causing the person deceived not to recognize the consequence of his or her own act in time, the proper solution is to enact separate legislation, rather than arbitrarily changing the basis of the established jurisprudence on fraud as the majority opinion does.\\n\\n(b) The majority opinion further states that in a signature-fraud case such as the one at issue here, even if the person deceived signed or affixed a seal to the disposition document without properly recognizing its content, fraud is established because property damage was caused according to the content of the disposition document, and because the person deceived had awareness of the act of signing or affixing a seal to that disposition document by signing or affixing a seal to it himself or herself, the disposition act by disposition intent can be recognized. However, we cannot agree with this for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) As repeatedly emphasized, in light of the nature and structure of fraud, the disposition act contemplated in fraud must be an act governed by disposition intent, and such disposition intent naturally presupposes awareness of the consequence resulting from one’s own act. Consequently, in the so-called signature-fraud case, where the person deceived, due to the deceitful conduct, misapprehends the content of the document and signs or affixes a seal to a document whose content differs from the inner intent, thereby causing the actor, etc. to obtain property or a pecuniary benefit, even if the person deceived was aware that he or she was signing or affixing a seal to the document, disposition intent and the disposition act cannot be recognized because there was no awareness whatsoever of the disposition result.\\n\\n(2) (a) Whether a patrimonial disposition act or disposition intent as its element exists can only be determined from the standpoint of the person deceived who performed the disposition act. If the person deceived, having been deceived as to the content of a document and without any awareness thereof, signed or affixed a seal to a written document presented by the actor, then rather it is a case where a document contrary to the will of the person deceived, who is the nominal author, has been prepared; for the person deceived who did not know the meaning of the document, he or she was merely used in the commission of forgery of a document in his or her name (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 13, 2000, 2000DO778), and it cannot be evaluated that there was a disposition act based on his or her will.\\n\\nIn fact, in a case like this one, where the actor, by deceiving the landowner as to the content of the document, caused the landowner to sign or affix a seal to the mortgage creation agreement, etc., thereby fraudulently obtaining the signature and then completing the mortgage creation registration in favor of the lender by using it, the act of the person deceived is merely the signing or affixing of a seal to a document labeled as a mortgage creation agreement; he or she had no intent to prepare a document with such content, nor any awareness itself of such preparation. The document is nothing but a forged document prepared without the person deceived’s will, and even if mortgage creation or similar acts were done using the forged document, such act or the consequence thereof was entirely unrecognized or unintended by the person deceived and rather contrary to the person deceived’s will, so one cannot say that the person deceived’s disposition intent toward a third party was contained therein. In the end, in relation to the person deceived, such consequence remains merely something to be eliminated, and it cannot be said that the person deceived performed a disposition act toward a third party with respect to that consequence.\\n\\n(b) The Supreme Court has held, in so-called “seal fraud” cases where a person who purchased only part of a parcel of land, by falsely saying that only that part would be subdivided and transferred, received the owner’s seal stamp and then completed ownership transfer registration for the entire parcel, that fraud is not established as to the registration concerning the non-purchased portion because there was no disposition act by the owner-victim (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 9, 1982, 81DO1732).\\n\\nIn both the above seal-fraud case, where the actor-defendant himself prepared the documents necessary for transfer of ownership without the landowner’s involvement, and the signature-fraud case at issue here, where the landowner is deceived into signing or affixing a seal to a mortgage creation agreement without any awareness of the content of the document, the defendant’s conduct is merely one among various forms of document forgery, and its substance is the act of forging a document in the name of the landowner rather than fraud; there is no substantial criminal-law difference between the two.\\n\\n(c) According to the majority opinion recognizing fraud in signature-fraud cases, the question whether fraud is established varies depending on the extent of the document’s description or completeness, or the manner in which the person deceived signed, thereby causing confusion and unreasonable results.\\n\\nEven under the majority opinion, it is unclear to what extent the content of the document must be specified at the time the person deceived signs or affixes a seal in order to recognize the person deceived’s disposition intent. For example, in the case of fraudulent signature on a mortgage creation agreement, it is difficult to know what entries must be included in the document at the time of the person deceived’s signing or sealing for fraud to be established, namely, whether fraud is established even if some matters among the indications of the mortgagee or debtor, the maximum secured claim amount, the content and scope of the secured obligation, or the mortgaged property are omitted, and if fraud is established, which omissions are permissible.\\n\\nFurthermore, it is not easy to distinguish between signature-fraud cases, in which the majority opinion recognizes the existence of disposition intent, and cases in which the actor received authority from the person deceived to sign on his or her behalf; there is also concern that the scope of punishment for fraud may become vague or overly expanded. Even under the majority opinion, if the deceived person, after being deceived by the actor, immediately authorizes the actor to sign on his or her behalf, this could be evaluated as the deceived person’s act of preparing a document and thus, like signature fraud, fraud could be seen as established. However, if the proxy signing is done without the person deceived’s participation—for example, if the actor first obtains from the person deceived prior authorization to sign land transaction permission documents and then, at a contract-conclusion scene where the person deceived is absent, signs on behalf of the person deceived a mortgage creation agreement that is a disposition document with entirely different content—it is not easy to know whether the person deceived’s disposition intent or disposition act is recognized and thus fraud is established, or whether only the crime of forgery of a document is established, or, if the outcome varies depending on the concrete circumstances or situation, what the distinguishing standard is.\\n\\n(3) If, in a signature-fraud case, the actor used the forged writing to borrow money from a lender who did not know the truth, there is certainly room for the fraud offense of obtaining money by deception to be established against the lender as well. In light of this, it is difficult to say that if fraud is not established against the landowner, this necessarily creates an obstacle to the proper exercise of punitive authority or results in punishment imbalance. Rather, in a signature-fraud case, because document forgery is carried out under the involvement of the person deceived landowner’s act or intent, it cannot be said that the punishability is necessarily smaller than in a seal-fraud case where the offender himself commits the forgery of the document without any involvement by the person deceived.\\n\\nMoreover, it is also doubtful whether it is proper to punish separately by recognizing, apart from fraud against the lender, fraud against the landowner as the victim in such cases. If the offender forged a document in the name of the landowner from the outset with the intent to obtain money by deception, the document forgery following the signature-fraud offense should be regarded as either a means for the series of fraudulent offenses of obtaining money through deception of the lender or as an act included in the execution act thereof. Therefore, the mortgage that the offender allegedly obtained overlaps with the economic value of the borrowed money, and it is difficult to assess each patrimonial benefit obtained by the offender during the course of the series of offenses as separate items distinct according to each counterpart of the deceitful conduct. The signature-fraud act would already be included in the punishable evaluation of fraud against the lender. This is even more so considering, in civil-law terms, that it is difficult to view the defendant-actor as being in a position to compensate simultaneously both the loss resulting from the creation of security against the landowner and the loss equivalent to the borrowed money against the lender.\\n\\nNot every act of obtaining property by means of deception can be subject to criminal punishment, and even if such an act does not satisfy the elements of fraud, it must not be punished recklessly merely because its punishability is high. If a person deceived has no awareness of the disposition result yet is punished for fraud solely because the deceitful conduct is highly punishable, that directly undermines the freedom-guaranteeing function of criminal law.\\n\\n(c) In sum, considering these circumstances collectively, in order for the disposition act contemplated in fraud to be recognized, the person deceived’s subjective awareness of the disposition result is required, and in a signature-fraud case, because the person deceived has no awareness whatsoever of the content or legal effect of the disposition document he or she signs or affixes a seal to, it is proper to deny disposition intent and the disposition act based thereon.\\n\\n(d) On the same reasoning, the court below’s determination that fraud cannot be established as to these primary charges, on the ground that the victims, who are the owners of each parcel of land identified in the judgment below, had no intent to establish mortgages, etc. on their respective lands and thus cannot be said to have engaged in a patrimonial disposition act, contains no error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the disposition act or disposition intent contemplated in fraud, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we state that we cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Justice Park Byeong-dae’s supplemental opinion to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\nThe core of a legal act or declaration of intent under the Civil Act is the intention as to effect. This is because a legally meaningful act must presuppose the actor’s awareness of the legal effect he or she seeks to accomplish. The logic that, in fraud, for a disposition act by deception to be recognized, the actor (victim) must be aware of the result of the act is similar in structure to the requirement that there be an intention as to effect in a legal act under the Civil Act. However, the victim’s disposition intent in fraud necessarily involves error by its nature. Whether the error concerns the legal consequence of the disposition act or its economic effect, there exists error as to the fact that a result different from the inner expectation is brought about by another’s deceitful conduct. Such error usually corresponds to error as to motive. Typical cases are property fraud such as deception as to the efficacy of an item, loan fraud, or investment fraud. The signature fraud at issue here falls under error in the manifestation. The inner intent was to apply for land transaction permission, but as a result of deception, in fact the person signed the documents for registration of a mortgage creation. The inner intent as to effect and the manifested intent as to effect did not coincide. Viewed from the perspective of the declaration of intent under the Civil Act, there is room to regard this as absence or non-formation of a declaration of intent in that there is no inner intention to effect corresponding to the manifested disposition act. However, even in civil-law theory, there appears to be little support for the view that judges the existence of a legal act solely by whether there was an inner intention to effect matching the act of manifestation. Since the core of intention as to effect is the intent inferred and judged externally through the act of manifestation, the dominant majority view understands that, even if the inner intent and the manifested intent do not coincide, the declaration of intent or legal act in accordance with the manifested intention as to effect is formed and exists. And, unlike this, even in the view that regards the inner intent as the core of the intention as to effect, or in the view that also considers the awareness of engaging in an act of manifestation according to the intention as to effect, namely manifestation intent, as an element of the declaration of intent, when the declarant has performed an act of manifestation that can only be understood as different from the inner intention as to effect, the disadvantage arising therefrom should be borne by the declarant himself or herself who caused the inconsistency between intent and manifestation, which accords with the principle of self-responsibility, and thus a normative interpretation is inevitable to deem the declaration of intent to be formed according to the content of the act of manifestation. Therefore, when an act of manifestation differing from the inner intent is brought about by another’s deceitful conduct, the question of what responsibility the declarant bears is organized by the principle of self-responsibility and the doctrines concerning declarations of intent by fraud or mistake, on the premise that the “existence” of the declaration of intent inferred from the act of manifestation is recognized.\\n\\nIf this is so in discussions of declarations of intent under civil law, then in the sphere of determining whether the deceiver’s fraud offense is established under criminal law, to say that in signature fraud the disposition act does not exist or is not formed because intent and manifestation do not coincide is to turn back the clock to the theory of primitive intentionism. Inducing the declarant by deception to perform a manifested act inconsistent with the inner intent is the deceiver’s original purpose, and even though the act of manifestation was performed as intended, to say that the disposition act of fraud does not exist because the inner intent does not coincide with the manifestation is contrary to the fundamental purpose of fraud and also to the criminal law principle of responsibility. Whether one follows the natural interpretation theory, which emphasizes the inner intent, or the normative interpretation theory, which stresses the act of manifestation, as the method of interpreting declarations of intent, it is naturally correct, when determining the existence of a disposition act in fraud, to follow the normative interpretation based on the act of manifestation. If the inconsistency between intent and manifestation was caused by deceitful conduct, it cannot be interpreted in a way that makes that circumstance operate rather in favor of the deceiver. If the cause of the mistaken manifestation is deceitful conduct, it is appropriate to hold the deceiver responsible according to the manifestation.\\n\\nIn short, even in the theory of legal acts under the Civil Act, where intention as to effect must inevitably be the core index of the act, there is almost no theoretical dispute that intention as to effect must be regarded not as a concept of the actor’s inner subjective intent as a natural fact, but as the object of normative evaluation. In other words, even in civil-law theory, it is not said that a declaration of intent is fundamentally “nonexistent” merely because, due to a mistake in the manifestation arising from inconsistency between intent and manifestation, there is no intention as to effect according to the manifestation. Nor is it regarded that the inner intent becomes the content of the legal act merely because it is confirmed that the party’s inner intent differs from the act of manifestation. Much less, in the context of fraud under criminal law, where the victim’s disposition act is at issue, is it balanced to say that disposition intent can be recognized only if there is a stricter factual coincidence between the inner intent and the manifested intent than the concept of intention as to effect under civil law. There is no reason to require conformity between intent and manifestation more strongly in fraud. If one insists on comparing the civil-law intention as to effect and the disposition intent in fraud and then sorts out the scope of their coverage, narrowing the concept of the criminal-law disposition act to something smaller than the concept of a civil-law legal act is neither normatively appropriate nor natural. Nor is there room for the unique criminal-law logic such as the principle of strict interpretation for protecting the defendant’s interests to come into play there.\\n\\nMeanwhile, when a declaration of intent by mistake is induced by deception, whether to construct it as a declaration of intent by fraud or a declaration of intent by mistake has practical significance in civil-law discussion. This is because whether cancellation is possible when the declarant is grossly negligent may differ. However, in a situation where the issue is whether fraud is established under criminal law, there is no clear practical benefit in distinguishing whether the declaration of intent was by fraud or by mistake, or whether it constitutes error as to motive or error in the manifestation. The statement that the victim’s disposition act in fraud must be a defective declaration of intent induced by deception is primarily an issue in relation to causation between the defendant’s deceitful act and the victim’s disposition act; it should not be understood as meaning that whether fraud is established depends on what inner intent the victim had when performing such disposition act. Moreover, there is no rational reason in civil law to exclude from the category of disposition act in fraud only the case of error in the manifestation, among declarations of intent “by fraud” and “by mistake.”\\n\\nHowever, signature fraud such as in this case is not merely obtaining a signature on a blank paper. The document itself expressly states the purpose of a patrimonial disposition act, and the actor deceived the victim into signing by saying it was a document of a different purpose. In other words, the signature here is, of course, not an unconscious act, nor is it a mere factual act. It is an act externally manifesting an intent that, together with the content of the document, constitutes a patrimonial disposition act. It is only that, having been deceived, the actor did not recognize that the manifested act had a meaning different from the inner intent. Where a disposition act of property is embodied in a written disposition document, if the objective meaning of the wording is clear, the established precedents require that, absent special circumstances, existence and content of the declaration of intent be recognized according to the wording. There is no reason for a different rule to apply merely because the document was prepared through signature fraud. When a mortgage is established in favor of a third party by using a document obtained through signature fraud and the validity of the underlying act becomes an issue, there is no example of recognizing absence of a declaration of intent. The issue is only whether the legal act exists according to the wording of the forged mortgage creation agreement and whether it is valid or invalid by the logic of fraud, mistake, or unauthorized agency. Nevertheless, in relation to criminal fraud, to say that there is no awareness of the disposition result in signature fraud and therefore the disposition act does not exist is neither logically consistent nor in accord with the normative purpose unique to criminal law. Recognizing in civil-law relations that a legal act exists while saying in criminal-law relations that it is not a disposition act merely because of one and the same act only causes confusion in the coherence of the normative order.\\n\\nThe reason precedent held that taking an motorcycle after receiving it under the pretext of a test drive and fleeing constitutes theft rather than fraud is that the act of handing over the motorcycle, viewed in light of the circumstances at the time, was not a disposition act having the appearance of transferring the power of disposition. In a case of signature fraud involving a disposition document, the appearance of the act is the content of the disposition document itself; thus the legal interpretation cannot be the same as in the motorcycle-taking case.\\n\\nTherefore, the previous line of some precedents that required, for the disposition act of a fraud victim, disposition intent in the strict sense of awareness of the disposition result is not only inconsistent with the framework of criminal-law regulation but also unharmonious even within the framework of civil-law legal-act theory. In fraud as well, as in the general theory of declarations of intent under civil law, it is proper to recognize intention as to effect as a normative-evaluation concept inferred from the manifested act, and if such manifested act was based on the victim’s defective intent, the victim’s disposition intent should be deemed to exist. This accords with the essence of the theory of conduct that runs through civil and criminal law.\\n\\nThis is the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. The supplemental opinion of Justices Kim Chang-seok and Kwon Soon-il to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\n(a) The Supreme Court has traditionally held that, for there to be a disposition act by the person deceived in fraud, there must be a corresponding disposition intent by the person deceived, and for disposition intent by the person deceived to be recognized, the person deceived must go beyond recognizing the act itself evaluated as a disposition act and must also recognize the consequence resulting therefrom. However, according to this, acts that should properly be punished as fraud are excluded from the scope of fraud’s establishment, and because such a result is also not correct theoretically, we seek to change the previous view.\\n\\n(1) The dissenting opinion argues, as grounds for maintaining the previous view, that in order for the essence of a disposition act as a self-harm act in fraud to be satisfied, the victim must necessarily have a will to decide upon the disposition of his or her own property; and only an act or omission governed by a will formed on the basis of the recognition that the victim’s act is related to his or her own property rights can normatively be evaluated as the disposition act contemplated in fraud.\\n\\nIf one seeks to attribute responsibility for the result of a disposition act to the person who performed the disposition act, then it can be said that the person who performed the disposition act must recognize the consequence of the disposition act. This is a natural result under the principle of culpability that if the actor does not recognize the facts constituting the elements of the offense, they cannot be attributed to his or her responsibility. However, the reason for requiring disposition intent by the victim in fraud is not to attribute responsibility for the consequence of the disposition act to the person who performed it.\\n\\nThe most prominent feature of fraud is that property is transferred directly by the victim’s disposition act. However, in order to say that the victim engaged in a disposition act, it is insufficient that an act evaluable as a disposition act was performed by the victim in the objective sense; a corresponding disposition intent must also be recognized. Therefore, the function of disposition intent does not go beyond confirming that the victim recognized and performed an act evaluated as one causing property damage to the victim and resulting in acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit by the actor, etc. From this perspective, the majority opinion is that the object of the victim’s awareness necessary for recognizing disposition intent is sufficiently the act itself that can be evaluated as a disposition act, and it need not be extended to the consequence resulting therefrom. In the elements of fraud, the disposition act is clearly distinguished from the result of that disposition act, namely the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit, and the subjective element corresponds to the objective element; limiting the object of the victim’s awareness necessary to recognize disposition intent to the act itself evaluated as a disposition act also fits that criterion.\\n\\n(2) Under the previous view, if the victim did not recognize that the actor’s deceitful conduct or the resulting error existed and performed a disposition act, but did recognize the occurrence of the result, fraud is affirmed; further, if the victim performed the disposition act without even recognizing the occurrence of the result, fraud is denied. The dissenting opinion argues that such a result accords with the essence of fraud as an offense of self-harm.\\n\\nHowever, in either case, the actor’s deceitful conduct and the resulting victim’s error exist, the victim’s act based on such error exists, and the victim’s property damage resulting from such act exists. In either case, one must conclude that there is a self-harm act. Nevertheless, the dissenting opinion says that without awareness of the disposition result, fraud as an offense of self-harm cannot be established. This is understood as the logic that, because the victim’s freedom of decision cannot be regarded as having been properly exercised, the act cannot be regarded as the victim’s act. Fraud is an offense established when property is transferred by the victim’s act but the victim, due to the actor’s deceitful conduct, cannot properly exercise freedom of decision. In this respect, it is not proper to exclude from self-harm offenses the cases in which the victim’s freedom of decision is more severely infringed by the actor’s deceitful conduct.\\n\\n(b) The dissenting opinion argues that, by the nature of disposition intent derived from the essence of fraud, the person deceived’s error is confined to matters concerning motive, intention, or purpose, and that error concerning the “disposition act itself,” which lacks even awareness of the disposition result, cannot be subsumed under the error contemplated in fraud. This argument is tantamount to limiting the scope of error so that, among the elements of fraud, error must exist at the stage preceding the disposition act and must not exist in the disposition act itself.\\n\\nIf the dissenting opinion’s interpretation—that the person deceived’s inner intent and externally manifested intent must coincide, so that the declaration of intent itself must have no defect—is applied to a signature-fraud case, then unless the person deceived knew the specific content of the document and the consequence its preparation would bring about, and signed or affixed a seal with the inner intent to produce effect according to the manifested intent in that document, disposition intent cannot be recognized. In a signature-fraud case, since deceitful conduct exists in the course of the actor drawing out the person deceived’s declaration of intent, it is a situation in which it is impossible for the person deceived to notice the meaning and effect of the declaration of intent objectively recognized on the basis of the externally manifested intent. Yet the dissenting opinion insists, in fraud types requiring the person deceived’s declaration of intent, that even as to that declaration of intent, the person deceived’s inner intent and manifested intent must coincide so that it is defect-free; this is difficult to accept.\\n\\nMeanwhile, under criminal law, when the disposition act is a legal act, whether it is valid, void, or voidable does not affect the establishment of fraud. In a signature-fraud case, although obtained by deception, an externally manifested declaration of intent objectively exists through the victim’s preparation of the disposition document. Such a declaration of intent is evaluated as a disposition act that directly produces the effect of allowing the actor, etc. to acquire property. Even from the civil-law perspective, although the inner intent as to effect and the manifested intent as to effect do not coincide as a result of error, because there is clearly an external act—namely a manifested act—through the preparation and delivery of the disposition document by signing or affixing a seal thereto, in which such intent can be recognized, in a signature-fraud case the declaration of intent according to the content of the disposition document is evaluated as having been formed and existing. Moreover, even if the person deceived did not know the content of the disposition document due to the actor’s deceitful conduct, so long as the person deceived himself or herself signed or affixed a seal to the disposition document and prepared it, the authenticity of the document’s formation is recognized. Even if the actor was punished for forgery of a private document with respect to the signature-fraud act, one cannot say that the declaration of intent externally manifested through document preparation is nonexistent or that there was no manifested intention as to effect. It is difficult to accept denying fraud on the ground that, although the actor’s deceitful conduct caused the person deceived to fall into error and the person deceived then performed some act such as preparing a disposition document objectively recognized as a declaration of intent, and on that basis property or a pecuniary benefit was transferred and property damage occurred as a result, disposition intent cannot be recognized merely because the person deceived’s inner intent and externally manifested intent do not coincide.\\n\\n(c) (1) It is also difficult to say that, because disposition intent in fraud does not require awareness of the disposition result by the person deceived, as the dissenting opinion mentions, the question whether fraud is established becomes unclear or the scope of punishment is unreasonably expanded.\\n\\nThe majority opinion does not abandon the concept of disposition act as an element of fraud; it merely says that disposition intent does not require awareness of the disposition result. In each individual case, the question whether fraud is established is determined based on whether there exists a disposition act by the person deceived, that is, a patrimonial disposition act directly causing property damage as an act or omission governed by the person deceived’s defective intent. In the prior precedents holding that fraud was not established as to a pecuniary benefit, namely the case where a person fled from a hospital to avoid performing the obligation to pay medical expenses (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 22, 1970, 70DO1615), or the case where a forged promissory note was delivered in relation to an existing debt (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 28, 1982, 82DO1759), even without considering whether the person deceived had awareness of the disposition result, the conclusion that fraud was not established can be reached without difficulty because there simply was no patrimonial disposition act by the person deceived that caused property damage.\\n\\nAlso, in the so-called “trick theft” example mentioned by the dissenting opinion, where the victim hands over an item believing it will be purchased and the offender then runs away with it, from the victim’s standpoint the victim has only temporarily transferred possession to someone who is going to look at the item as a prospective buyer. The taking of the property did not occur because there was a disposition act governed by the victim’s defective intent; rather, the property was acquired by the actor’s additional act of running away with it. Accordingly, it is a case in which fraud cannot be established because the existence of the disposition act cannot be recognized. Even when judged by the objective and externally recognized delivery act, it is easy to see that the victim did not completely transfer possession of the item to the actor. In short, since the existence of the disposition act itself determines whether fraud is established in such a case, it is not necessary to include awareness of the disposition result in order to distinguish fraud from trick theft.\\n\\n(2) As the dissenting opinion points out, with the enactment of the Telecommunications-Fraud Damage Refund Act, numerous punishment provisions related to telecommunications-based financial fraud were newly established, and clear grounds for punishment were provided for various types of fraud committed using telecommunications, including cases where the victim has no awareness of remitting or transferring money. However, even though such punishment provisions were newly enacted to clarify parts that had been controversial regarding the establishment of fraud under the Criminal Act and to deal effectively with new types and variants of voice-phishing crimes, that does not lead to the interpretive theory that awareness of the disposition result is required to recognize disposition intent. Nor is it desirable to interpret the current law in a way that narrows the scope of fraud’s establishment, and then argue that legislative resolution is needed again to fill the gap.\\n\\n(d) (1) The so-called “seal-fraud case” and “signature-fraud case” are essentially different. If one imagines a seal-fraud case in which the offender deceives the landowner as to the use, receives the owner’s seal stamp, and then completes, in favor of a third party, a mortgage creation registration on the owner’s land, in such a case there is no external declaration of intent that can be called the victim’s disposition act. Only the act of forging the documents necessary for the mortgage creation registration in the victim’s name using the seal fraudulently obtained by the offender exists, so it is clear that fraud cannot be punished. By contrast, in a signature-fraud case, there undeniably exists the victim’s external manifestation of intent through the mortgage creation agreement, etc., which constitutes a disposition act causing property damage. Considering that in a seal-fraud case, because there is no declaration of intent by the victim concerning the mortgage creation agreement, the registration completed by means of the fraudulently obtained seal is inevitably a registration void for lack of cause and thus subject to cancellation, it cannot be said to be unreasonable to treat it differently in legal evaluation from the signature-fraud case.\\n\\n(2) In a signature-fraud case involving a mortgage creation agreement like this one, in civil law the victim who is the landowner may seek cancellation of the mortgage creation agreement on the ground of mistake in signing or affixing a seal and request cancellation of the mortgage creation registration made in favor of the lender (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on May 27, 2005, 2004DA43824, Supreme Court Decision rendered on October 27, 2006, 2006DA41778). However, cancellation is barred where the declarant-victim was grossly negligent (proviso to Article 109(1) of the Civil Act). In the case of a claim for cancellation on the ground of a declaration of intent by fraud, cancellation is permitted only where the third-party mortgagee knew or could have known that the declaration of intent was induced by fraud (Article 110(2) of the Civil Act). Furthermore, such cancellation cannot be asserted against a good-faith third party who established new legal relations, such as by acquiring the status of a mortgagee based on the mortgage creation agreement (Articles 109(2) and 110(3) of the Civil Act).\\n\\nIn the end, it is not always possible for the victim landowner to recover his or her rights by canceling the mortgage creation registration established on the land by invoking fraudulent signature or seal. Accordingly, the need for criminal-policy protection of the landowner as a fraud victim is clearly recognized.\\n\\n(e) (1) The fact that fraud involving a loan against the lender may be established in a signature-fraud case cannot serve as a basis for denying the establishment of fraud against the landowner. The two fraud offenses have different victims, and the content of the deceitful conduct also differs. The property obtained by the offense is also clearly distinguishable: in the former case, money, which is tangible property, whereas in the latter, a pecuniary benefit consisting of the ability to use another’s real estate as security. The two offenses are not in an impossible or mutually exclusive relationship. Nor is the signature-fraud offense against the landowner generally or typically joined with and incidental to the fraud offense against the lender. Yet the dissenting opinion, overly focusing on the fact that the actor obtained money as a result of the offense, overlooks the fact that different harms to different legal interests resulted to multiple victims depending on the offense.\\n\\nAlso, if property is obtained by causing the person deceived to sign or affix a seal to a disposition document containing a declaration of intent of donation to the actor or a third party, or of exemption from debt, there is no room for establishing any separate fraud offense apart from the fraud offense with the person deceived as victim. Moreover, in cases like this one, because proof in criminal procedure may be insufficient and fraud against the lender may not be established, and because the security-right creation agreement may be recognized as valid in civil law, the lender may not necessarily question the actor’s criminal responsibility. Contrary to the dissenting opinion, the concern that a gap may arise in punishment can be confirmed directly in this case.\\n\\n(2) It cannot be said that punitive authority is properly realized merely because the actor may be punished for forgery of a private document in a signature-fraud case. The substance of a signature-fraud case is an offense of obtaining property through deception. Nevertheless, not punishing the core and essential part of such punishable conduct and punishing only the instrumental act of document forgery cannot be said to be a proper exercise of punitive authority commensurate with the unlawfulness of the act and result. Moreover, because the statutory penalty for fraud and forgery of a private document differs greatly, and while fraud is subject to aggravated punishment by special statutes depending on the amount obtained, forgery of a private document has no such provision, a sentencing imbalance arises whereby even if the actor, etc. obtained a substantial pecuniary benefit through signature-fraud, the punishment is limited to the lighter offense of forgery of a private document.\\n\\n(f) (1) The question of how specifically the content of a disposition document must be identified at the time the person deceived signs or affixes a seal is of a nature that must be determined by comprehensively considering all circumstances in each case. Because the forms of criminal conduct vary widely, a uniform standard that can encompass all the special circumstances of individual cases cannot be set forth. In light of the role and function that the disposition act occupies in fraud, the key criterion is whether the document on which the person deceived signed or affixed a seal has the appearance of a disposition document such that it can directly cause the actor, etc. to obtain property or a pecuniary benefit, and whether, by signing or affixing a seal to that disposition document, it can be evaluated that the victim’s declaration of intent to dispose of property was externally and objectively made. Put differently, the question is whether the person deceived’s act of signing or affixing a seal made an essential contribution to the occurrence of such consequence. In the end, it can be seen that this is merely the frequently encountered issue of subsumption under the elements of the offense in relation to whether the offense is established.\\n\\n(2) Fraud is such that, unless there is a disposition act by the person deceived himself or herself rather than by the actor, and unless such act can be assessed as causing the actor’s acquisition of property, the person deceived’s disposition act cannot be recognized. Accordingly, unless the actor or a third party, in a manner that is treated by social common sense as equivalent to the person deceived’s own signing or sealing, mechanically signs or affixes a seal on behalf of the person deceived like his or her hands and feet, then even if the actor deceives the person deceived as to the content to be stated in a disposition document and receives authorization to sign or affix a seal on behalf of the person deceived, and then signs or affixes a seal on behalf of the person deceived to a disposition document causing property damage to the person deceived, this is no different from a seal-fraud case and cannot be said to mean that the person deceived performed the disposition act.\\n\\nThis is the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Justice Kim Shin’s supplemental opinion to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\n(a) Even if the person deceived did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the person deceived’s act or omission directly causes property damage and is governed by the defective intent of the person deceived who fell into error, and as a result the Defendant obtained property or a pecuniary benefit, fraud is established, and awareness of the consequence resulting from the person deceived’s act or omission is not required. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Whether fraud is established must be determined by whether the elements prescribed by the Criminal Act are satisfied, and whether a disposition act involving awareness of the disposition result by the person deceived is required for fraud’s establishment must also be determined on the basis of interpretation of the statutory text.\\n\\nThe Criminal Act provides that a person who, by deceiving another, obtains delivery of property or acquires a pecuniary benefit, or causes a third party by the same method to obtain delivery of property or a pecuniary benefit, shall be punished for fraud (Article 347 of the Criminal Act). By the wording, it is clear that the statute defines as the elements of the offense only the Defendant’s act of obtaining delivery of property or acquiring a pecuniary benefit, and does not make it an element that the person deceived recognizes the disposition result and performs a disposition act.\\n\\nHowever, for fraud to be established, as a premise for the Defendant’s obtaining delivery of property or a pecuniary benefit, there must be a person deceived’s delivery of property or an act causing property damage. For some act to be evaluated as an act by the person deceived, awareness by the person deceived of the natural act itself is necessary, and it is natural that an unconscious behavior lacking even such awareness cannot be evaluated as the person deceived’s act. However, if the person deceived’s act or omission is recognized as an act directly causing property damage and governed by the person deceived’s will, there is no reason to evaluate it as not the person deceived’s act.\\n\\nThe essence of fraud lies in obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit by deception, and when the Defendant obtains delivery of property or acquires a pecuniary benefit, the victim, namely the person deceived’s disposition act intervenes. There is no legal basis or logical necessity for requiring, in such a disposition act, awareness by the person deceived of the disposition result as a necessary condition, even though the disposition act by the person deceived is merely a premise for the Defendant’s obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit. This is not the result of emphasizing the necessity of punishment or the protective function of criminal law from a criminal-policy perspective, but rather the result of the natural interpretation of the Criminal Act’s provisions.\\n\\n(2) For the unified interpretation of the various forms in which the Defendant obtains property or a pecuniary benefit in fraud, it cannot be said that fraud is established only when the person deceived, aware of the disposition result, performs the disposition act.\\n\\nWhat the Criminal Act seeks to protect by fraud is not the victim’s freedom of decision but the victim’s property as a whole. Therefore, the person deceived’s disposition act, which is the premise for the Defendant’s obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit in fraud, need not be a legal act under the Civil Act if it objectively directly causes property damage; it also includes factual acts in the pure sense, regardless of whether they are valid, void, or voidable.\\n\\nHowever, if the disposition act takes the form of a declaration of intent or legal act, there may be a situation in which the person deceived has an intent to recognize the disposition result. Yet even in the case where the disposition act is a factual act in the pure sense, recognizing such intent means nothing more than viewing awareness of the person deceived’s act itself as awareness of the disposition result. The attempt to require, for the person deceived’s disposition act which is the premise for the Defendant’s obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit, an intent requiring awareness of the occurrence of the result, a notion conceivable only in civil-law legal acts, and further to interpret such disposition intent as an element of fraud, results in abandoning a unified interpretation of cases where the Defendant obtains property or a pecuniary benefit by the person deceived’s factual act and cases where the Defendant obtains property or a pecuniary benefit by the person deceived’s legal act.\\n\\n(3) The object punished by fraud is the Defendant’s act, and the object to be evaluated in determining whether fraud is constituted is also the Defendant’s act, not the person deceived’s act. Therefore, whether fraud is established is a matter to be determined by evaluating the Defendant’s act, not by evaluating the person deceived’s act.\\n\\nThe attitude of understanding the victim’s disposition intent as meaning awareness of the disposition result and as an element of the offense appears to be in the same context as the interpretive theory of declarations of intent under civil law, in that it seeks to assess the validity of the declaration of intent when there is a discrepancy between the person deceived’s subjective intent and the objective manifested act. However, while the interpretive theory of declarations of intent under civil law is a matter of determining whether the person deceived’s declaration of intent is nonexistent, or whether it contains a defect constituting grounds for invalidity or cancellation, and thereby deciding the legal effect to be given to the declaration of intent, the question whether fraud is established is a matter of determining whether the Defendant’s act, which caused such a state and thereby obtained property or a pecuniary benefit, is conduct subject to punishment under the Criminal Act. Since fraud in this way punishes the Defendant’s act, the person deceived’s disposition act, which is the premise for the Defendant’s obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit, is merely a means to evaluate whether the Defendant’s act satisfies the elements of fraud. Thus, unlike a legal act under civil law, there is no reason or need for it to be a declaration of intent in the complete sense, and if there is no disposition act, it merely has the negative meaning that, as a logical consequence, the Defendant cannot be recognized as having obtained property or a pecuniary benefit.\\n\\nObjectively viewed, if it is recognized that the Defendant directly obtained property or a pecuniary benefit through the person deceived’s disposition act and that this has a causal relationship with the Defendant’s deceitful conduct, fraud is established. Whether a legal effect arises according to the person deceived’s inner intent is a matter to be separately discussed in a civil case, and even if, when the Defendant acquires a pecuniary benefit according to the content of the disposition document prepared by the person deceived’s act, a legal effect different from the person deceived’s inner intent arises, it is difficult to find any reason to exclude this from fraud.\\n\\n(b) The core of the dissenting opinion is that, by the nature of fraud as an offense of self-harm, the person deceived’s disposition act must be governed by a will formed on the basis of the recognition that it is related to property rights, and because a will lacking awareness of the disposition result cannot be regarded as disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act, the person deceived’s error as an element of the offense is confined to matters concerning motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act, and error concerning the disposition act itself, lacking even awareness of the disposition result, cannot be included in the error contemplated in fraud. However, for the following reasons, this dissenting opinion is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(1) It is understandable that fraud is an offense of self-harm and that the person deceived’s act must intervene in its nature, but from such circumstance alone one cannot reach the conclusion that for fraud to be established, awareness by the person deceived of the disposition result is necessarily required.\\n\\nThat fraud is an offense of self-harm means that the person deceived’s act intervenes so that the Defendant obtains property or a pecuniary benefit, and unlike theft or similar offenses of taking away property, the behavior induced by the person deceived’s error directly causes a reduction in the person deceived’s property and an increase in the property of the Defendant or a third party without the Defendant’s criminal intermediate act. However, the mere fact that the person deceived’s act intervenes does not mean that awareness by the person deceived of the disposition result constitutes an element of the offense as the indicator distinguishing theft and fraud. The victim’s subjective awareness is merely an important factor to be considered when determining whether the transfer of property or pecuniary benefit is a direct result originating from an act governed by the victim’s will or a direct result originating from the Defendant’s act.\\n\\nEven according to the view that fraud requires the person deceived’s awareness of the disposition result, it is not the case that disposition intent is recognized only where the person deceived precisely recognizes that the property which became the object of the disposition act is completely separated from his or her property and belongs to the Defendant or a third party. If fraud were interpreted as requiring a perfect and strict disposition intent by the person deceived, then in cases where property is delivered to a person who asks to borrow it without intent to return it, one would reach the absurd conclusion that fraud is never established because there was no awareness of the disposition result. In the end, depending on the case, it may be difficult even to specify what “awareness of the disposition result” as disposition intent of the person deceived means. The Supreme Court has in precedents described the person deceived’s subjective awareness of the meaning of a disposition act and the consequence it brings about as awareness of the disposition result, but this should be understood as an expression used for the subjective awareness necessary for fraud to be established in that case. The concept of awareness of the disposition result by the person deceived does not naturally follow from the essence of fraud as an offense of self-harm, nor does it appear to be an effective and proper standard distinguishing fraud from other offenses.\\n\\n(2) In this respect, the dissenting opinion’s assertion that if disposition intent is required for a disposition act, awareness of the disposition result must become an element of fraud is difficult to accept.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion mainly assumes fraud in which the Defendant obtains a pecuniary benefit, and assumes cases where the person deceived’s disposition act takes the form of a declaration of intent or legal act, and states that awareness by the person deceived of the disposition result is necessary. However, it is not clear whether this interpretive approach can apply as is even in fraud involving receipt of property.\\n\\nGenerally, when the person deceived’s disposition act is the delivery of property, the person deceived’s subjective intent is understood as being sufficiently satisfied by awareness of the transfer of possession alone, and it is difficult to find a view interpreting that the person deceived must accurately recognize the consequence of delivering the property. Yet the Criminal Act expressly provides that the Defendant obtaining delivery of property by deceiving the victim is a primary type of fraud, and there is no doubt that obtaining a pecuniary benefit by deceiving the victim is a corresponding type of fraud. Fraud involving property and fraud involving a pecuniary benefit are not essentially different, and the act of obtaining delivery of property and the act of obtaining a pecuniary benefit are corresponding elements of the offense. Even though, in fraud involving property, the subjective element required for recognizing the person deceived’s disposition act is sufficiently satisfied by awareness of the act of transferring possession itself, there is no reason whatsoever to think that in fraud involving a pecuniary benefit, as a corresponding subjective element, one must require awareness of the disposition result rather than awareness of the act itself causing property damage.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion says that, if disposition intent is required in fraud, the conclusion that awareness of the disposition result is required inevitably follows, yet the majority opinion, by independently interpreting disposition intent, fell into contradiction. However, beyond opposing the very expression of a will lacking awareness of the disposition result as disposition intent, it is doubtful whether this serves as a ground justifying the conclusion that awareness by the person deceived of the disposition result is an element of the offense. If the point is merely that one can characterize as disposition intent only the awareness of the disposition result by the person deceived, and that awareness of the act itself is necessary as a criterion for distinguishing the person deceived’s disposition act from an unconscious act, so that there is no need to separately call such awareness disposition intent, then the majority opinion can be understood as expressing the view that such disposition intent, in the sense limited by the dissenting opinion, is not necessary.\\n\\n(3) Consequently, the person deceived’s error as an element of the offense cannot be confined to matters concerning the motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act.\\n\\nEven if one repeatedly examines the elements of fraud under the Criminal Act, one cannot find any provision suggesting that the actor’s deceiving conduct toward the person deceived should be confined to matters concerning the motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act. The Criminal Act takes the Defendant’s act as the object of evaluation and defines as fraud the act of deceiving a person and obtaining delivery of property or acquiring a pecuniary benefit, with the victim’s disposition act only intervening as a premise for the Defendant’s obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit. Whether the Defendant’s deceitful conduct corresponding to the elements of fraud concerns the motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act or the disposition act itself, it can still be evaluated as conduct deceiving the victim; and if, by reason thereof, the victim, based on a defective intent, delivered property or engaged in an act causing property damage, and the Defendant obtained delivery of property or acquired a pecuniary benefit, there is no reason to exclude this from fraud.\\n\\nFraud is established only when the Defendant obtains property or a pecuniary benefit by the other party’s defective declaration of intent; if the Defendant, through deceit, causes the other party to have a defective intent, the matters concerning the motive, intention, or purpose of the disposition act are naturally deceived as well. That is, in typical fraud cases where fraud is established, there are bound to be many instances of the Defendant deceiving circumstances concerning the motive, intention, or purpose of the victim’s disposition act. But to infer from such circumstances that fraud is established only in such cases is an overgeneralization and cannot be adopted.\\n\\n(c) The Criminal Act does not define as an element of fraud a disposition act performed by the person deceived while aware of the disposition result, and the person deceived’s disposition act may be either a factual act or a legal act. Therefore, so long as the person deceived’s act or omission directly causing property damage is governed by the will of the person deceived who has fallen into error, the subjective element necessary to recognize the person deceived’s disposition act is sufficiently awareness of the act itself, and if such awareness is not recognized, it merely has the negative meaning that it cannot be regarded as the person deceived’s disposition act. One may separately evaluate a will that does not go beyond awareness of the act accompanying the disposition act and call it disposition intent, or one may say that disposition intent is unnecessary because it is naturally subsumed within the disposition act itself. This is merely a difference of classification or naming, and the substantive meaning is not different. However, in fraud, it cannot be said that the disposition act requires even awareness of the disposition result; this is a natural consequence of interpreting our Criminal Act by evaluating whether fraud is established from the standpoint of the Defendant’s act.\\n\\nThis is the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n8. The supplemental opinion of Justices Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, and Park Sang-ok to the dissenting opinion is as follows.\\n\\n(a) (1) The principle of culpability is the grand principle of criminal law, and the principle of private autonomy or the principle of self-responsibility is the grand principle of civil law. The idea penetrating these grand principles is liberalism, according to which a person is bound by and responsible for the acts and consequences he or she has chosen and performed according to free will. However, in the real world, because differences exist among people due to disparities in capacity of will or capacity to act, etc., one party is sometimes unable to realize his or her original intention. Accordingly, proper consideration is afforded through a legal system supported by democracy, and this is the principle of culpability and the principle of private autonomy or self-responsibility in their modern sense. In the end, with respect to legal relations formed by people’s intent, appropriate allocation and interpretation must be given on the basis of that intent and legal system.\\n\\n(2) According to this principle of culpability, the Criminal Act provides that an act committed without awareness of the facts constituting the elements of a crime shall not be punished, except where a special provision exists in the law (Article 13), and that an act committed without awareness of facts constituting a particularly serious crime shall not be punished as the more serious crime (Article 15(1)), and that in an offense punishable more severely due to the result, if the occurrence of that result could not have been foreseen, it shall not be punished as the more serious crime (Article 15(2)).\\n\\n(3) In property crimes, infringement of legal interests may be divided into a type where the perpetrator’s act unilaterally infringes the victim’s legal interests, as in theft, and a type where the result of infringement arises through the victim’s act, as in fraud. More specifically, the latter can be said to be an offense of self-harm in which the legal-interest infringement arises as a result of the victim’s own decision to choose and accept it. The essence of fraud is that the accepted result of the victim’s patrimonial act, chosen by a will determined on the basis of a mistaken perception induced by the perpetrator’s deceitful conduct, directly leads to the victim’s property damage; and because the law values the infringement of freedom of decision through deceit that occurs beyond the occurrence of property damage, the Criminal Act punishes fraud more severely than theft. In the end, the actor’s deceitful conduct and acquisition of a pecuniary benefit, and awareness thereof on either side, and, on the other side, the victim’s patrimonial act performed in a state where freedom of decision has been infringed by deceit and the occurrence of property damage as its result become the realm in which the principle of culpability, the ideological foundation of state punitive power, operates.\\n\\n(b) (1) Until now, the Supreme Court has interpreted fraud as established when one deceives another and causes that person to fall into error, thereby inducing the disposition act and obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit, and has interpreted that the disposition act, as a patrimonial disposition act, subjectively requires that the person deceived have disposition intent, namely awareness of the disposition result and intent to realize that result, and objectively requires an act governed by such intent. It has also held that an omission, in which the person deceived, by free will, either proceeds to an act directly causing property damage or comes to omit the exercise of a claim, is a disposition act, thereby holding that an omission not to exercise a claim also constitutes a disposition act on the premise that it is an act by free will.\\n\\n(2) The omission that constitutes a disposition act here is not a mere omission of doing anything, but the so-called improper omission, in which a person does not exercise a certain right that he or she can or should exercise, such as postponement or waiver of a right, and which can be evaluated as a patrimonial disposition act. Accordingly, like an act, such omission requires awareness of the consequence resulting from the omission and intent to realize that consequence by omission, namely disposition intent; indeed, awareness and intent concerning such an omission can be said to be an essential element distinguishing omission as a disposition act from other simple omissions.\\n\\n(3) In the end, the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the disposition act and of disposition intent as its volitional element, as above, is based on the theory of conduct and the essence of fraud discussed above, and is proper and should not be changed.\\n\\n(c) The majority opinion states, as to the signature-fraud case at issue here, that although fraud requires the person deceived’s disposition act and disposition intent, so long as the person deceived has awareness of merely performing some act by his or her will, disposition intent is recognized even without awareness of the consequence brought about by that act; further, even as to an act where the person deceived did not recognize the specific content and legal effect of the document and merely signed or affixed a seal, it recognizes the disposition act by deeming that a declaration of intent according to the content of the document was made, and explains that disposition intent is recognized so long as the person deceived signed or affixed a seal. Although it does not clearly state in what respect the intent to sign or affix a seal differs from the disposition intent concerning another act, it appears to mean that, because a defective declaration of intent is established by the preparation of the document through the person deceived’s signing or affixing a seal, awareness of signing or affixing a seal corresponds to awareness of the declaration of intent that is the disposition act and thus amounts to disposition intent.\\n\\nHowever, if the meaning of disposition intent in signature fraud is understood as the majority opinion does, then even where there is no inner intent corresponding to document-preparation or manifestation, and even where there is no awareness of producing any legal effect or even any manifested act cannot be recognized at all, one would still recognize the person deceived’s declaration of intent and disposition intent therefor, ultimately treating the mere act of signing or affixing a seal to a document as a disposition act. This is difficult to accept because it is contrary to the theory of conduct discussed above and to the essence of fraud requiring a disposition act.\\n\\nBelow, we specifically examine the various legal problems inherent in this new theory of disposition act presented by the majority opinion.\\n\\n(1) When discussing what act a party performed, one cannot separate that from what the party’s true intent was. True intent and external act usually coincide, but when they do not, the issue is how to interpret them and what legal effect to give them. In interpreting declarations of intent under civil law, it is explained that interpretation based on intent inferred from externally manifested conduct rather than the party’s inner intent is proper; however, this is a theory of interpretation where the party’s true intent is not known, and if the party’s true intent is known, it is that true intent, not the externally manifested conduct, that becomes the content of the declaration of intent or legal act. In other words, intent determines the act and forms the content of the act; one cannot say that intent is deemed by the outward form of an act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the majority opinion explains that even if the person deceived did not accurately recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the person deceived merely had the intent to perform an act, then there is disposition intent accompanying the disposition act, and on that basis, in a signature-fraud case, so long as the person deceived signed or affixed a seal, disposition intent is recognized and there is a disposition act according to the document. However, this disregards the relationship between act and intent, and between disposition act and disposition intent, and also evades the argument concerning the subjective element, namely disposition intent, required as a premise for recognizing the disposition act. It means that, although the person deceived merely recognized that he or she was preparing a document, one recognizes a disposition act by disposition intent with respect to the prepared document; this not only contradicts the essence of the theory of conduct, but also contains a circular error that because there is a disposition act there is disposition intent.\\n\\n(2) Moreover, among signature-fraud cases, there are cases where the person deceived had no consciousness of performing an act disposing of rights, namely, in civil-law terms, no awareness or intent to perform a legal act at all.\\n\\nIf, as a result of falling into error due to deceitful conduct, the person deceived signs a document with no intent whatsoever to prepare a document having any legal meaning, or signs according to the awareness that he or she is preparing a document wholly unrelated to legal acts, such as a confirmation or petition, and the prepared document contains matters concerning the disposition of rights, then from the standpoint of the person deceived, there is of course no intent to produce a concrete legal effect such as the content stated in that document through the signature on that writing, and there is no awareness itself that any legal effect will arise by the person’s own act.
