Where there is no intent concerning the legal act itself, the act is no different from an act performed without any consciousness, and such an act cannot be said to be a disposition act.\\n\\nAs seen below, although error is discussed in civil law where the inner intention as to effect and the act of manifestation do not coincide, in a case where neither the person deceived nor the deceiver has any intent at all to perform some legal act, one cannot import the discussion of error in declarations of intent and, merely because there is a discrepancy from the standpoint of the person deceived between the inner intent and the content of the prepared document, conclude that the person deceived’s disposition act according to the content of the document was made between the person deceived and the deceiver, let alone that the person deceived had disposition intent with respect thereto. Moreover, under the Civil Act, if the other party to the declaration of intent could know that the declarant was not acting in accordance with true intent, that declaration of intent is void (Article 107(1) of the Civil Act), and a false declaration of intent made in collusion with the other party is also void (Article 108(1) of the Civil Act). Yet, paradoxically, even where the discrepancy is greater, as in this case where neither the person deceived nor the deceiver had even an awareness or intent to perform the legal act of establishing a mortgage during the document preparation process, to treat it merely as a declaration of intent by mistake or deception and say that only grounds for cancellation exist (Articles 109(1) and 110(1) of the Civil Act) is contrary to the system of provisions on declarations of intent under civil law and also unfair.\\n\\nAnd until now, the Supreme Court has regarded cases where a thing was handed over under the pretext of purchase and then the offender fled while carrying it as theft, and it has similarly treated cases where one drove a motorcycle out of a shop under the pretext of a test drive and fled (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 12, 1994, 94DO1487, Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 11, 2009, 2009DO3139). This appears to mean that, notwithstanding the external appearance of delivery/use of the item, there is no substance of a disposition act transferring possession and control by the victim, and it is not an act intended to produce such legal effect. There is no meaningful difference from the case here, where one simply prepared a document without any substance of performing a legal act between the deceiver and the victim and without intending any legal effect. If one were to recognize disposition act and disposition intent based on the external form of preparing a document by signing or affixing a seal, or on the result of using that document, then even in the motorcycle test-drive case one would likewise have to recognize corresponding disposition act and disposition intent, resulting in fraud and conflicting with the established precedents.\\n\\nIn the end, to say that there is disposition act and disposition intent as a declaration of intent merely from the result of document-signing, even though there is no awareness or intent whatsoever regarding the disposition that produces legal effect, is to deem nonexistent awareness, intent, and disposition act as existing, which exceeds the limits of interpretation concerning disposition act.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the majority opinion develops its discussion on whether the act of signing in a signature-fraud case constitutes a disposition act by relying on civil-law interpretive theory of declarations of intent by considering that a declaration of intent whose content produces effects different from the inner intent is manifested in the disposition document. But it is doubtful whether it is proper to explain the criminal-law disposition act, which is the standard for determining whether fraud is established, by using civil-law interpretive theory of declarations of intent or legal acts. Moreover, the majority opinion’s logic, which evaluates the act of signing or affixing a seal itself as a patrimonial disposition act in the form of a declaration of intent according to the content of the document and then finds disposition intent to exist, is difficult to regard as proper because it confuses the preparation of the document with the declaration of intent.\\n\\n(a) Under civil law, a declaration of intent is the external manifestation by the declarant of the intention as to effect, and there is no limitation on the manner of manifestation. Documents such as contracts are a means of clearly setting forth such declarations of intent or legal acts, and the preparation of the document itself is a factual act, while the content of the declaration of intent formed between the parties through the preparation of the document constitutes the legal act. When there are differences between the parties regarding the interpretation of a contract and the question arises of interpreting the parties’ intent appearing in a disposition document, it is also explained that the content of the wording, the motives and circumstances by which such agreement was reached, the purpose sought to be accomplished by the agreement, and the parties’ true intent should be considered comprehensively and reasonably interpreted according to logic and rules of experience. The mere fact that something is written in a document cannot be immediately concluded to be an externally manifested declaration of intent.\\n\\nAccordingly, preparation of a document may be strong evidence that a declaration of intent or legal act was made, but one cannot say that a declaration of intent is deemed to exist merely because the document was prepared, even if no corresponding declaration of intent exists. For example, if a father who prepared a document has not yet decided whether to make a gift to his son and simply prepares a gift contract, this cannot be called a legal act; even if possession of the document is transferred to the son during a move, one cannot say there was a legal act of gift between father and son; and even if deceptive means by the son were used in the process of transferring possession of the document, the absence of the legal act does not change. In other words, it is not the mere fact of document preparation, but the preparer’s substantive intent to produce the same legal effect as the content of the prepared document that constitutes the declaration of intent; preparation of a document without such intent is nothing more than a factual act of making a paper document.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court regards the fraudulent obtaining of a signature on a document as forgery. Forgery means preparation contrary to the intention of the person in whose name the document is prepared; therefore, treating a document prepared by fraudulent obtaining of a signature as forgery means that, although the nominal author signed, the document or the content contained therein was prepared contrary to the nominal author’s will. In the end, despite the signature, the content contained in the document is not the nominal author’s intent, nor is there a declaration of intent or legal act according to the content of the document, and one cannot say merely from the fact that the document was prepared that there was a declaration of intent or disposition act according to its content.\\n\\n(b) The act of manifestation for the formation of a declaration of intent is recognized to exist where there is an external act from which the declarant’s intention as to effect can be inferred.\\n\\nIn a case such as this one, where the Defendant fraudulently obtained the person deceived’s signature and then used a mortgage creation agreement in the name of the person deceived to establish a mortgage in favor of a third party and borrow money, in order for the Defendant’s conduct to constitute fraud obtaining property or a corresponding pecuniary benefit from the person deceived through the mortgage, it is natural that the person deceived’s patrimonial disposition act or declaration of intent establishing a mortgage in favor of a third party is required.\\n\\nHowever, where the counterpart to the declaration of intent or patrimonial disposition act is a third party, not the deceiver, one cannot, based only on the document-preparing act between the deceiver and the person deceived, say that the person deceived manifested an intent to dispose of property to the third party or performed a disposition act toward the third party; rather, the disposition act toward the third party appears to be performed not by the person deceived but by the deceiver. Furthermore, to regard the deceiver’s use of the prepared document to establish a mortgage in favor of the third party as the person deceived’s declaration of intent to establish the mortgage, there must be authorization by the person deceived concerning the deceiver’s declaration of intent or contract to establish the mortgage. If there is no such authorization, it is nothing more than an unauthorized agency act or unauthorized proxy act by the deceiver. Therefore, a mortgage-creation act performed without such authorization can by no means be viewed as the person deceived’s disposition act performed by the person deceived’s disposition intent. Nevertheless, the majority opinion appears to recognize fraud by obtaining a mortgage in such cases, which is difficult to accept.\\n\\nAnd if, according to the majority opinion, recognizing the person deceived’s disposition act means that the disposition act must be the person deceived’s own document preparation, then it is unclear whether, if the deceiver fraudulently obtained the signature and then did not deliver the document to a third party, the person deceived’s disposition act is recognized and fraud is immediately established; or whether fraud is established only once the document is delivered to a third party; or whether, if at the time of document preparation fraud has merely been initiated and fraud is consummated only when a mortgage creation agreement is concluded with a third party and money borrowed or a mortgage creation registration completed. This is because, apart from document preparation, the person deceived performed no other act, and the act the deceiver arbitrarily performed after the document was prepared cannot be regarded as the person deceived’s act.\\n\\nIn the end, the majority opinion seems to have erred in its line of reasoning by regarding, as a disposition act, the mere preparation of a document on the theory that a declaration of intent matching the content of the document was externally made, while overlooking the process of formation of the declaration of intent and failing to properly examine the conduct after document preparation, all in light of the need to punish signature-fraud cases.\\n\\n(c) Furthermore, the Supreme Court has held, in civil cases, that a declaration of intent by fraud means a situation where, as a result of being caused to fall into error by another’s deceitful conduct, a declaration of intent is made; therefore, there can be no inconsistency between intent and manifestation there, and it is merely an error in the process of formation of the intent, namely a mistake in the motive for the declaration of intent, and on this point it is distinguished from a declaration of intent by mistake in the proper sense. Accordingly, in a case like this one, where the person deceived had the intent to sign or affix a seal to the disposition document but, while in a state of error, signed or affixed a seal to a writing containing content different from his or her own intent and thereby caused the inner intention as to effect and the manifested intention as to effect not to coincide, even if that error arose by a third party’s deceitful conduct, the doctrine concerning a declaration of intent by fraud should not be applied; rather, the doctrine concerning a declaration of intent by mistake should apply (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on May 27, 2005, 2004DA43824).\\n\\nThis Supreme Court decision distinguished document preparation by deception from declaration of intent by deception, and clarified that one cannot say merely from the fact of document preparation that there was intent to make the legal act corresponding to the content of the document; in this respect it corresponds to the criminal precedents denying disposition intent regarding signature fraud. That Supreme Court decision recognized the above signature fraud as civil-law mistake, and because civil-law mistake means that there is no inner intention or intention as to effect and thus there is inconsistency with the act of manifestation, it follows that even if civil-law mistake is recognized, the premise that there is no disposition intent corresponding to the externally manifested result remains unchanged.\\n\\nThus, if one recognizes, as the majority opinion does, that the externally manifested content was made by the person deceived’s will even though there was no inner intent corresponding to the person deceived’s external act of manifestation, and thereby acknowledges the establishment of fraud, this produces an untenable result in which conduct that in civil legal relations is merely a mistake and not fraud is evaluated criminally as fraud, and it reaches an unreasonable conclusion inconsistent with the Supreme Court’s existing interpretation concerning declarations of intent.\\n\\n(d) Meanwhile, the majority opinion states that the victim’s disposition intent, unlike the actor’s criminal intent, has no relation to the principle of culpability and is merely the subjective element of the disposition act, so the object of awareness for the actor’s criminal intent covers all elements constituting fraud, whereas the object of awareness for the victim’s disposition intent is limited to the disposition act itself among the elements of fraud. We therefore examine whether, as the majority opinion says, the actor’s criminal intent and the victim’s disposition act are really separate matters.\\n\\n(1) According to the principle of culpability, the main text of Article 13 of the Criminal Act provides that an act committed without awareness of the facts constituting the elements of a crime shall not be punished. Under this principle of culpability, Article 347(1) of the Criminal Act provides that fraud is established when a person deceives another and obtains delivery of property or acquires a pecuniary benefit. Therefore, the actor in fraud must have, in addition to the deceitful act, awareness that he or she obtains delivery of property or acquires a pecuniary benefit, that is, awareness that he or she obtains property.\\n\\n(2) In the signature-fraud case, we examine the actor’s criminal intent. The Defendant and Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., deceived the owner of real estate into signing or affixing a seal to the mortgage creation agreement, etc. by saying that the documents were necessary for land transaction permission, etc.; after receiving the owner’s seal certificate, they used it to establish mortgages on each parcel of land in favor of a lender, with the Defendant as debtor, and carried out a series of acts of borrowing money. The point at which the Defendant, etc. recognizes that they obtain property through these series of acts can be said to be when they obtain the money of the loan, namely the borrowed money.\\n\\nAt the earlier stage, the mortgage creation agreement, etc. signed or sealed by the owner of the real estate are merely a means by which the Defendant, etc. obtains the borrowed money; they are not property in themselves. Then, in relation to the act of obtaining the signature or seal on the mortgage creation agreement, etc., the Defendant, etc. had no awareness concerning the acquisition of property, which is an element of the offense. This is not substantially different from the awareness of receiving a seal on a deed of transfer or the awareness of receiving a seal for preparation of a transfer document, as in the seal-fraud case discussed below.\\n\\n(3) However, the Defendant, etc. used not one, but two, deceitful acts in this series of processes. The first deceitful act is the deceit toward the signer of the mortgage creation agreement, and the second deceitful act is the deceit toward the lender of the borrowed money. As to the latter act of obtaining the borrowed money through deceit, the majority opinion also appears, apart from issues of proof, to take the position that it is fraud, so we will focus the discussion on the former.\\n\\n(a) Let us compare the former deceitful act with trick theft. In a jewelry store, if the actor drops a gold necklace on the floor from the display case, picks it up, says it was his own, and the owner, believing that, lets him take it away, it would be difficult to call this fraud. It may also be viewed from the standpoint of the victim’s disposition act, but from the standpoint of the actor’s criminal intent as well, the actor has only an intent to steal, not an intent to defraud.\\n\\n(b) However, if in a jewelry store the actor poses as a gold trader and tells the owner that the purity of the gold to be sold is only 30%, then manipulates a machine measuring purity to make the owner believe it, and purchases the gold by paying only 30% of its market price, this would be fraud. This too may be viewed from the standpoint of the victim’s disposition act, but also from the standpoint of the actor’s criminal intent, because there is intent to defraud.\\n\\n(c) The former deceitful act is very similar to trick theft, as the dissenting opinion has repeatedly discussed. Just as in the seal-fraud case the Supreme Court did not regard it as fraud and held that if a document was completed by means of the fraudulently obtained seal it was forgery, if one fraudulently obtains a signature on a document whose form as a mortgage creation agreement is unclear and completes the mortgage creation agreement, this is merely forgery. Viewed from the standpoint of the actor’s criminal intent, the actor has only the intent for forgery, in the sense that he or she obtained the nominal author’s signature or seal by exploiting the nominal author’s misapprehension, rather than obtaining property; and further, only the intent to use this as a means for subsequent fraud.\\n\\n(d) The Supreme Court has in the past taken this position, holding that where one, having bought only part of the total land area, nevertheless thinking of obtaining transfer registration for the entire parcel, told the registered owner that a seal was necessary for the transfer registration of the part area and thus received a signature or seal on the transfer document for the entire parcel, this constituted forgery of a private document because the document was prepared in content different from the preparer-nominal owner’s will, since the nominal owner who prepared the document was deceived as to its content by receiving the seal (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 29, 1970, 70DO1759). On the same view, it was also held that where one deceived the victim as to the true purpose and received the victim’s seal stamp, prepared the documents necessary for ownership transfer registration of real estate and completed ownership transfer registration in that name, there was no disposition act by the victim, and if the offender had no intent to appropriate the seal stamp as property, it was correct to render a not-guilty verdict on the fraud charge (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 27, 1990, 89DO335).\\n\\n(4) We examine the case where the loan amount was not obtained in a signature-fraud case. If the offender tried to obtain the signature or seal of the nominal author of the mortgage creation agreement by deception, but the nominal author noticed this and did not sign, then under the majority view it would be an attempted fraud. However, as stated above, what the actor sought to obtain through the nominal author of the mortgage creation agreement was not property or a pecuniary benefit but merely the nominal author’s signature or seal, and he or she failed in trying to obtain it. The actor intended to use this as a means of fraud to obtain money from the person holding the borrowed money, and awareness of this point is the criminal intent with awareness of the facts constituting the offense of obtaining property. Therefore, the actor merely commenced execution of forgery and remained at attempt, which accords with the Supreme Court’s attitude toward forgery discussed above.\\n\\nIf, after fraudulent obtaining of a signature or seal, the mortgage creation registration was completed but the lender, after confirming with the nominal author, ceased lending and no loan money was delivered, it is doubtful, under the majority opinion, whether the security-creation act is complete and thus the offense of fraud is consummated because a pecuniary benefit was obtained. Under the dissenting opinion, there is no particular doubt because forgery is consummated and fraud remains at the attempted stage. Going one step further, if the actor and the lender are co-perpetrators and they merely created the appearance, after fraudulent obtaining of a signature or seal and completion of the mortgage creation registration, of borrowing money, but there was in fact no lending, and the false lender, using the mortgage as leverage, deceived the signer into paying money under the guise of repaying the loan and obtaining cancellation of the mortgage creation registration, then it is doubtful whether, as the majority opinion suggests, the act of signing or affixing a seal can be treated as a disposition act. Under the dissenting opinion as well, there is no particular doubt in recognizing the establishment of forgery and fraud.\\n\\n(5) We examine accomplice relations in the signature-fraud case. Suppose there is an accomplice who recognized only the result of obtaining the signature or seal and participated only in that act, and another accomplice who recognized the entire offense; if, immediately after obtaining the signature or seal on the mortgage creation agreement, they are arrested or otherwise prevented from obtaining the borrowed money, then under the dissenting opinion there may be accomplice liability for forgery of a document, but under the majority opinion it is unclear whether they are accomplices to forgery, accomplices to attempted fraud, or whether one should be treated as guilty of forgery and the other of attempted fraud.\\n\\n(6) We have examined the actor’s criminal intent from various angles, and it cannot but be questioned whether the criminal intent as described by the majority opinion accords with the principle of culpability. If one examines the actor’s criminal intent according to the principle of culpability, the intent is divided into the intent to fraudulently obtain the signature or seal and the intent to fraudulently obtain the loan money; the former is the intent for forgery and the latter is the intent for fraud. Nevertheless, the majority opinion regards both the former and the latter as intent for fraud, and especially in the former case, by treating the actor’s series of criminal plans leading to obtaining money in the form of a loan as the object of awareness for the actor’s criminal intent, which comprises all elements of the offense, it moves away from the principle of culpability. In the end, insofar as one looks at the actor’s criminal intent according to the principle of culpability, awareness of the result of transfer of property is required also in the disposition act, and the actor’s criminal intent and the person deceived’s disposition act are two sides of the same coin.\\n\\n(e) In conclusion, just as an act detached from intent is meaningless, there can be no disposition act independently existing apart from disposition intent, and one cannot recognize as having the intent to dispose of the property, or as having performed a disposition act, a person deceived who does not even know whether he or she has disposed of the property. If the actor and the person performing the disposition act have no awareness that property is being handed over and received, the actor lacks awareness of the delivery of property or acquisition of a pecuniary benefit, which are elements of fraud, and the person performing the disposition act lacks awareness of the disposition act, so fraud cannot be established. Yet the majority opinion, while presupposing that the person deceived’s disposition act and disposition intent are necessary in relation to fraudulent obtaining of a signature on a document, nonetheless recognizes the disposition act by deeming the result of document preparation, which is unrelated to and rather contrary to the person deceived’s internal consciousness regarding the concrete result, as a result of the person deceived’s own will, namely disposition intent. This is contrary to the legal principles based on the theory of conduct that the Supreme Court has consistently stated and to the essence of fraud, and thus cannot be supported. In addition, because this majority opinion is contrary to the principle of culpability that an act committed without awareness of the facts constituting the elements of a crime, that is, an act without criminal intent, shall not be punished, it also cannot be supported.\\n\\nThis is the supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n9. Justice Cho Hee-dae’s supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion is as follows.\\n\\n(a) The so-called “signature fraud” issue in this case concerns a case where, due to deceitful conduct, the person deceived signed or affixed a seal to a document different from his or her inner intent, thereby causing the actor to obtain a pecuniary benefit according to the mortgage creation registration.\\n\\n(b) For fraud to be established, there must be the actor’s deceitful conduct, the person deceived’s error and the disposition act resulting therefrom, and the actor’s acquisition of property or a pecuniary benefit, and there must be a sequential causal relationship among them. In particular, in fraud, the disposition act serves the role of distinguishing fraud, which is essentially characterized by obtaining property by using the victim’s act, from theft, in which the actor obtains property by taking it away without relying on the victim’s act. As to such disposition act, the Supreme Court has traditionally held that the person deceived must subjectively have disposition intent, namely awareness of the disposition result, and objectively there must be an act governed by such intent.\\n\\n(c) However, the majority opinion says that even if the person deceived did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the person deceived’s act or omission is evaluated as a patrimonial disposition act directly causing property damage and such act or omission was recognized and performed by the person deceived, the disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act is recognized, and it is not necessary for the person deceived to recognize even the consequence resulting from his or her own act or omission in order to recognize disposition intent. Therefore, in a signature-fraud case like this one, ① if property damage according to the content of the disposition document is caused by the person deceived, as a result of falling into error due to the actor’s deceitful conduct, signing or affixing a seal to a disposition document whose content produces effects different from the inner intent, then the act of the person deceived who signed or affixed a seal to that disposition document constitutes the disposition act contemplated in fraud; and ② in addition, even if the person deceived did not yet recognize the disposition result, namely the specific content of the document and its legal effect, the person deceived’s disposition intent is also recognized so long as the person deceived himself or herself signed or affixed a seal to some document and thereby had awareness of the act of signing or affixing a seal to that disposition document.\\n\\nThis majority opinion has several problems besides those already stated in the dissenting opinion, and we examine them below.\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion appears to mean that if the person deceived signs or affixes a seal to a document while recognizing that he or she is signing or affixing a seal to some document, and that document includes the content of a disposition causing property damage, then even if the person deceived did not recognize the concrete content and legal effect of the document, the person deceived’s disposition act and disposition intent are recognized.\\n\\nHowever, this commits the error of understanding the act and intent under criminal law solely by external result, completely disregarding the content of awareness, and is therefore impossible to accept.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion appears to regard the person deceived’s act of signing or affixing a seal to some document as the disposition act.\\n\\nHowever, in fraud, the disposition act means an act that causes property to be delivered to the actor, etc. or directly causes acquisition of a pecuniary benefit.\\n\\nFor example, in a signature-fraud case, if one fraudulently obtains a signature on a disposition document containing a declaration of intent to exempt a debt, then because the declaration of intent confirmed through the disposition document itself can directly result in acquisition of a pecuniary benefit, it may be regarded as the disposition act contemplated by the majority opinion.\\n\\nBy contrast, if one fraudulently obtains a signature on a mortgage creation agreement, the Civil Act adopts the principle of constitutive effect for real rights arising from legal acts concerning real estate, under which a transfer or creation of a real right has no effect solely by the parties’ declaration of intent and becomes effective only upon registration (Article 186 of the Civil Act). Thus, even if one takes the view that both the obligation act and the real right declaration of intent are involved, the mere preparation of a mortgage creation agreement does not bring about the effect of a change in real right; only when the documents necessary for registration are prepared and registration is completed can a pecuniary benefit be acquired. Therefore, the mere circumstance that a disposition document containing a transfer of property is prepared by the person deceived’s signing or affixing a seal, and that an externally recognized obligatory or real-right declaration of intent is thereby present, does not, apart from the question whether the actor may be guilty of forgery of a private document or whether the offense of obtaining a document by fraud may be established, suffice to evaluate that a criminal-law disposition act directly causing acquisition of a pecuniary benefit has occurred. Put differently, the act of signing or affixing a seal to a document whose content is unknown to the person deceived is, even if that document is a disposition document such as a mortgage creation agreement, merely an act of preparing a document containing a disposition-oriented declaration of intent; it cannot be regarded as a criminal-law disposition act directly causing the actor, etc. to acquire a pecuniary benefit equal to the security value resulting from completion of mortgage creation registration.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion appears to premise that disposition intent is necessary and that disposition intent must be intent corresponding to the disposition act.\\n\\nHowever, even if one were to regard the act of preparing a disposition document rather than the mortgage creation itself as the disposition act, as the majority opinion states, at a minimum there must be awareness corresponding to the content of the disposition document in order to say that disposition intent exists. Yet the majority opinion says that disposition intent exists if there is no intent corresponding to the content of the disposition document and merely awareness that one is signing or affixing a seal to some document, which is logically difficult to understand.\\n\\nAnd as mentioned in the dissenting opinion, only awareness of the disposition of property and decision-making based thereon can be disposition intent consonant with the essence and characteristics of fraud, and only acts based on such intent can be evaluated as disposition acts. As a result, in a signature-fraud case where there is no awareness whatsoever of the content or consequence of the disposition document, the person deceived’s disposition intent cannot be recognized.\\n\\n(4) While the Criminal Act separately provides for theft and fraud, it punishes in fraud cases both obtaining delivery of property and obtaining a pecuniary benefit, whereas in theft the object is limited to property, and it sets the statutory penalty for fraud far higher than that for theft. Meanwhile, separate from fraud, the Criminal Act also separately provides for punishment of a person who, by exploiting a minor’s lack of judgment or a person’s mental or physical disability, obtains delivery of property or acquires a pecuniary benefit (Article 348 of the Criminal Act). Accordingly, as an element of fraud that characterizes the offense, distinguishes fraud from theft when the object of the property-infringement conduct is property, and performs the function of distinguishing punishable fraud from nonpunishable theft of a pecuniary benefit when the object is a pecuniary benefit, the disposition act and disposition intent must be strictly construed according to the general principles of interpretation of criminal law. In the signature-fraud case at issue here, the majority opinion’s reasoning affirming fraud expands, by interpretation adverse to the defendant or by analogy, the meaning of the disposition act, an element of fraud, and the disposition intent, its element, thereby excessively expanding the scope of punishment for fraud. This is not only inconsistent with the system and regulatory content of our Criminal Act concerning fraud and theft, but is also contrary to the principle of legality, which underlies the rule of law.\\n\\n(d) The majority opinion also does not accord with the recent trend in Supreme Court decisions strictly interpreting criminal-law provisions relating to property offenses.\\n\\nWith respect to breach of trust, the Supreme Court has held that a debtor’s obligation to perform the registration procedure for ownership transfer of real estate pursuant to a contract for substitutional performance is merely incidental to what is required of the debtor to secure performance of the loan-repayment obligation, and therefore cannot be regarded as “the affairs of another” to protect or manage the creditor’s property based on the fiduciary relationship contemplated in breach of trust (see Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on August 21, 2014, 2014DO3363). Also, in aggravated breach of trust in the course of business, it has held that the risk of financial loss that can be assessed as property damage must reach the level of a concrete and realistic risk, and a mere vague possibility is insufficient (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 10, 2015, 2015DO6745). With respect to embezzlement, too, considering that the essence of embezzlement lies in unlawfully appropriating property entrusted on the basis of a fiduciary relationship, it is proper to limit the entrustment-fiduciary relationship to one based on trust worthy of protection by embezzlement; accordingly, in a case where a middle-omission registration type title trust was made in violation of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, the Supreme Court held in an en banc decision that the trustee’s arbitrary disposal of the entrusted real estate does not constitute embezzlement (see Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on May 19, 2016, 2014DO6992).\\n\\nThrough these recent decisions, the Supreme Court appears to have been forming a line of precedents that, even in cases where criminal punishment seems necessary on the face of it and even in cases that have long been criminally punished, faithfully applies the basic principles of interpreting criminal law provisions and strictly interprets the elements of offenses so as to exclude them from criminal punishment, thereby guarding against arbitrary exercise of state punitive power in property offenses. Nevertheless, the majority opinion, by invoking only the concrete need for punishment in the individual case, abruptly discards numerous precedents that had been maintained for a long time with reasonable grounds concerning the interpretation of fraud, without a clear theoretical reconstruction, and newly seeks to punish the conduct. This is not in accord with this trend of the Supreme Court and, as a result, creates renewed confusion regarding not only fraud but also the direction of interpretive theory for property offenses, which is not desirable.\\n\\nThis is the supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2020DO9789]": "The grounds for appeal are reviewed.\\n\\n1. Summary of the alternative charge\\n\\nThe gist of the alternative charge, namely violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter the “Specific Economic Crimes Act”) (breach of trust), is as follows.\\n\\nThe Defendant, by an unknown process, had 199.999 Bitcoins (hereinafter the “Bitcoin at issue”) that were in the Victim’s virtual wallet at the “Hitbit” exchange transferred into his own account, and therefore had the duty to keep the Bitcoin at issue, which had been transferred by mistake, intact in order to return it; notwithstanding this, he transferred 29.998 Bitcoins thereof to his own “(account name 1 omitted)” account and 169.996 Bitcoins to his own “(account name 2 omitted)” account, thereby obtaining a total of 199.994 Bitcoins (= 29.998 Bitcoins + 169.996 Bitcoins), which constituted economic benefit worth approximately KRW 1,487,235,086 in total, and causing the Victim damage in the same amount.\\n\\n2. The judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below upheld as is the trial court judgment that found the alternative charge guilty for the following reasons.\\n\\nVirtual assets are economic benefits having economic value and are worthy of protection under the Criminal Act. Since the Defendant received and held Bitcoins owned by another person, without legal cause, transferred into his virtual asset wallet, he must return the Bitcoins to the owner by way of restitution of unjust enrichment. Embezzlement and breach of trust are property crimes of the same nature based on a relationship of trust, and the account holder who receives money transferred without a legal relationship has the obligation to return the transferred money to the remitter, so a position is recognized in which the account holder holds the money received or transferred for the remitter; there is no reason to treat cases in which virtual assets are transferred without cause differently in this respect.\\n\\nIn light of these circumstances, it is appropriate to regard the Defendant as bearing the duty to protect and manage the Victim’s property, such as by keeping the transferred Bitcoins intact in order to return them to the owner based on the principle of good faith; thus, as the subject of the crime of breach of trust, he falls under “a person who handles another’s affairs.”\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s judgment\\n\\nHowever, the judgment of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Where virtual assets are transferred into another person’s virtual asset electronic wallet without legal cause due to the mistake of the right holder of the virtual asset or an error in the virtual asset operating system, the transferee of the virtual asset may become liable to the right holder of the virtual asset, etc. for restitution of unjust enrichment. However, this is merely a civil debt between the parties, and such circumstance alone does not mean that the person who received the transfer of the virtual asset is in a position to preserve or manage the virtual asset based on a relationship of trust. In addition, there is no contractual relationship whatsoever between the Defendant and the Victim, and because it is unclear by what process the Defendant received the Bitcoin at issue, it is not clear whether the Victim or the exchange is the party entitled to claim restitution of unjust enrichment. Even if the Defendant directly bears an obligation to make restitution of unjust enrichment to the Victim, it cannot immediately be concluded that the person who received the virtual asset falls under “a person who handles another’s affairs,” the subject of the crime of breach of trust, in relation to the Victim.\\n\\nb. The Supreme Court limits the scope of the crime of breach of trust by holding that, in order to be “a person who handles another’s affairs,” the person must be engaged in preserving or managing another’s property based on a relationship of trust between them, beyond the ordinary conflict of interests in a contractual relationship, as in the case of acting on behalf of another in whole or in part with respect to the affairs of property management for another, which is the typical and essential content of the parties’ relationship (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2019DO9756, decided February 20, 2020, etc.). In a case such as this, where virtual assets are transferred and received, it is not easy to recognize a relationship of trust between the Victim and the Defendant.\\n\\nc. Virtual assets are information digitally represented by economic value granted by blockchain or other cryptographically distributed ledgers, without control by the State, and constitute economic benefits (see Supreme Court Decision 2021DO9855, decided November 11, 2021). A virtual asset reveals only the address of the electronic wallet in which it was stored, and the personal identity of the person using that address cannot be known; its transaction history is recorded in a distributed manner, and when it is sent to another account, a person other than the parties must participate, so it has characteristics distinct from ordinary assets.\\n\\nAs to such virtual assets, they are not being treated the same as legal tender, including because no regulation equivalent to legal tender has been implemented under the relevant laws to date, and transactions in them involve risk; therefore, in applying the Criminal Act, they need not be protected in the same manner as legal tender.\\n\\nd. In the present situation, where there is no express provision criminalizing the use or disposal of virtual assets, which are economic benefits, by a person who received them by transfer for unknown reasons, analogizing from the precedent that affirmed the establishment of embezzlement in the case of mistaken transfer (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO891, decided December 9, 2010, etc.) and punishing the Defendant for breach of trust on the basis of the principle of good faith would run contrary to the principle of legality.\\n\\nEven if the Bitcoin at issue was transferred from the Victim to the Defendant’s electronic wallet without a legal cause relationship, insofar as the Defendant cannot be viewed as having undertaken and handled the Victim’s affairs based on a relationship of trust, he cannot be said to fall under “a person who handles another’s affairs” in relation to the Victim.\\n\\ne. Nevertheless, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “a person who handles another’s affairs” in the crime of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (breach of trust), in finding that the Defendant falls under “a person who handles another’s affairs” as the subject of the crime of breach of trust.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the part of the judgment of the court below concerning the alternative charge contains a ground for reversal and cannot be upheld as is, and the part concerning the principal charge, namely violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (embezzlement), which is in an inseparable relation with that part, also cannot escape reversal; therefore, the entire judgment of the court below must be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is well-founded, and the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[94DO1487]": "The grounds for final appeal advanced by the Defendant and the court-appointed defense counsel are considered together.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the reasons for the judgment of the court below, its acceptance of the facts constituting the offense in this case can be affirmed; its acceptance of the habitual nature of the theft charge against the Defendant and its rejection of the assertion that the Defendant was in a state of mental and physical disorder due to taking philopon at the time of the offense can also be affirmed; and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in violation of the rules of evidence or, as argued, any misapprehension of the law concerning habitual offenders.\\n\\nIf, as the court below found, the Defendant, pretending as though he would purchase precious metals at the jewelry store operated by the victim, received a pure gold necklace and the like from the victim and then fled on the pretext of going to the restroom, then the said pure gold necklace and the like were still in the victim’s possession until the Defendant fled (see this Court’s Decision of 1983. 2. 22., 82DO3115), and therefore the court below’s disposition of classifying and adjudicating the matter as larceny is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the law as argued.\\n\\nMoreover, in this case, in which a sentence of less than 10 years’ imprisonment was imposed on the Defendant, the grounds of factual error or improper sentencing cannot be made a lawful ground for final appeal. All arguments lack merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is decided, by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating, to count part of the period of detention after the filing of the appeal toward the principal sentence, and to render judgment as stated in the order."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the crime of trespass into a dwelling (building) is correct? (In case of dispute, according to case law)
A: The mere act of pressing the doorbell of the apartment that is the object of the intrusion in order to check whether anyone is inside should be regarded as having commenced the execution of the crime of trespass into a dwelling.
B: If it constitutes adjacent appurtenant land that contributes to the use of a building, then even if the land is not demarcated or controlled by human or physical facilities, etc., and its boundary can be easily crossed by ordinary walking, it falls within the object of the crime of trespass into a building.
C: If A, for the purpose of assaulting A, his former lover with whom he had broken up several months earlier, entered by pressing the password known from the time they were dating at the entrance door of the common entrance to the officetel where A lives, then took the elevator to the front of the entrance door of A's home and attempted to intrude but failed and fled, once he entered by inputting the known common-entrance password, there is no room to recognize trespass as to the common area.
D: If A, who had raped the victim several days earlier, secretly opened the gate and entered, and, in a narrow passage between the fence and the room where the victim was residing, peered into the room through the window, then the victim's de facto peaceful condition with respect to the dwelling has been infringed, and this constitutes the crime of trespass into a dwelling.
E: If A, due to discord with his wife A, left the apartment where he had been living with A and thereafter arbitrarily entered the said apartment, even if there are special circumstances such as A having withdrawn from the shared living relationship or having lost de facto dominion and control over the dwelling, etc. of the said apartment, there is no room for the crime of trespass into a dwelling to be established.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DO1092]": "The grounds of appeal are determined as follows.\\n\\n1. Upon examining the reasons of the judgment of the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s action in upholding as is the first-instance judgment that convicted the Defendant of the offense of violating the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Crimes and Protection of Victims Thereof, etc., on the ground that there was proof of the offenses in this case, i.e., the first and second criminal facts charged against the Defendant, is deemed proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as a factual error caused by a violation of the rules of evidence or a misunderstanding of legal principles, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. The offense of residential trespass protects the factual peace of a dwelling as its protected legal interest, and if the conduct has reached a level capable of impairing the factual peace of the dwelling enjoyed by the resident, the constituent elements of the offense should be deemed satisfied (Supreme Court Decision 94DO2561, rendered September 15, 1995), and, in the offense of residential trespass, a dwelling means not merely the house itself but includes its curtilage (Supreme Court Decision 82DO1363, rendered March 8, 1983). Therefore, if the Defendant, who had already raped the Victim twice several days earlier, secretly opened the front gate and entered, and was peeping into the room through a window from a narrow passage between the wall and the room where the Victim resided, then the factual state of peace concerning the Victim’s dwelling was infringed; and the lower court, on the same purport, properly held that such conduct of the Defendant constituted residential trespass, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as a misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning residential trespass, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. According to the record, although it is acknowledged that the Defendant was in an intoxicated state at the time of each of the offenses in this case, in light of the Defendant’s usual alcohol tolerance, the circumstances leading to the offenses, the means and method of the offenses, and the Defendant’s conduct before and after the offenses, it appears that he had not reached a state of mental and physical disorder as a result thereof; accordingly, the assertion in the grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted, and, in this case where a sentence of imprisonment of less than 10 years was imposed on the Defendant, the assertion to the effect that the determination of the sentence is too severe and therefore unjust cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and 36 days out of the period of detention after the filing of the appeal shall be included in the principal sentence, and the opinion of the Justices participating is unanimous, so judgment is rendered as set forth in the Disposition."}

{"[2008DO1464]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe commencement of execution of the offense of residential trespass does not require conduct that realizes a part of the constituent elements of the offense, namely, entering a house or other structure used for residence or management against the will of the resident, manager, occupant, etc.; rather, it is sufficient to commence conduct that includes a realistic danger leading to the realization of the elements of the offense (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DO4417, decided October 24, 2003; Supreme Court Decision 2006DO2824, decided September 14, 2006). However, merely pressing the doorbell of the apartment that is the object of intrusion in order to ascertain whether anyone is inside cannot be regarded as having commenced conduct that includes a realistic danger of intrusion, or as having engaged in conduct that includes an objective danger of infringing the factual peace of the residence.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the lower court, the lower court maintained the first-instance judgment that acquitted the Defendants on the ground that they could not be deemed to have engaged in conduct constituting the commencement of execution of residential trespass with respect to the present case, in which the Defendants, who had conspired to ring the apartment doorbell and, if no one was inside, to use a master key, etc. to open the door, enter, and steal property, were moving around together, and Defendant A rang the doorbell of C’s house and said, “Didn’t you order jajangmyeon?” but, when C, who was inside the house, replied, “I did not order any,” moved to the lower floor by using the stairs. Upon comparing this with the record, no error can be found in the lower court’s process of finding the facts, and the above determination also conforms to the legal principle stated above; thus, it cannot be said that there is any illegality asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the dispositive part."}

{"[2009DO14643]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. In the crime of trespass upon residence, the “building or structure” that is the object of the act of intrusion should be deemed to include, in view of the fact that the crime of trespass upon residence in substance protects the peace and quiet of habitation as the protected legal interest, not only the building or structure itself in the strict sense, but also the curtilage appurtenant thereto; here, the term curtilage means adjacent land surrounding the building or structure, and it must be objectively and clearly apparent that a wall or the like is installed along the boundary with the outside, that the land is provided for the use of the building or structure, and that outsiders cannot freely enter therein (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DO6133, rendered on June 10, 2004). Accordingly, even if the land is adjacent appurtenant land contributing to the use of the building or structure, if there is no partition or control by human or material facilities, and if one can easily cross its boundary by ordinary walking, then it is difficult to deem it objectively and clearly apparent that entry by outsiders is generally restricted; therefore, unless there are other special circumstances, it is appropriate to regard such land as not falling within the object of the crime of trespass upon residence.\\n\\n2. The court below, comprehensively considering that: ① the facility at issue, consisting of the victim Nonindicted Person’s residential building, 4 livestock barns, and 2 vinyl greenhouses, together with the cement-paved passageway leading thereto, is shaped as if surrounded by mountains except for the entrance of the passageway, with a mountain behind the said livestock barns and no separate road from outside leading to the said livestock barns; ② at the right-hand entrance of the passageway at issue, there stands a signboard stating “No Entry Except Authorized Personnel,” and equipment and tools necessary for the operation of the livestock barns are scattered around the passageway from the residential building to the livestock barns, while the victim can perform the work necessary for operating the livestock barns, such as supplying feed to the livestock barns and discharging manure, only through the said passageway and the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns; ③ at the time of this case, the Defendants, riding in a car, entered the said passageway without the victim’s permission and stopped in the vacant lot at issue, which is not only more than 2~3 m past the residential building and the one livestock barn immediately thereafter (even according to the Defendants’ assertion, they passed the residential building and stopped in front of the one livestock barn), and when Defendant 2 got out of the vehicle and engaged in acts such as taking photographs of the livestock barn buildings, the victim strongly protested against the Defendants’ entry; ④ the Defendants were in a co-venturer relationship, and at the time of this case, Defendant 1 and the victim were engaged in ongoing disputes, including litigation, concerning the use of farmland leased by the victim to the said Defendant, and the Defendants had previously known that the victim was raising cattle in the facility at issue; ⑤ in a place such as the facility at issue where a large number of livestock are raised as a business, epidemic prevention is one of the most important issues determining the success or failure of the business, so for a livestock farmer such as the victim, it is an intolerable act for a vehicle or a person to enter near the livestock barns without permission, found that the passageway and the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns are indispensable places necessary for the operation of the livestock barns appurtenant to the residential building and the livestock barns at issue, and although the entrance of the passageway was not blocked by a gate or wall, and the facility at issue is located in a place surrounded by mountains, with the victim’s residential building and the vinyl greenhouse across the passageway located at the entrance so that the boundary with the outside is clearly apparent, and the victim installed at the entrance a sign to the effect that entry by outsiders is prohibited, the said passageway and the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns constitute the curtilage of the residential building or livestock barns at issue; and determined that the Defendants’ act of jointly entering the passageway at issue and going into the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns constitutes an act of intrusion into the building or structure at issue where the victim resides and manages; accordingly, it reversed the first-instance judgment and rendered a judgment of guilty against each of the Defendants.\\n\\n3. However, the above determination by the court below cannot be upheld.\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, the facility at issue is located directly adjacent to a road with frequent vehicle traffic leading toward Gwacheon and Indeogwon from the entrance of the village in Galhyeon-dong, Gwacheon-si, and the residential building faces the said road and can be entered directly therefrom; there are no gates, walls, or any other human or material facilities at the entrance from the said road into the facility at issue that control entry thereto, and anyone can freely come and go through the cement-paved passageway approximately 5 m wide by ordinary walking, which is no different up to the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns at issue; although the facility at issue is, except for its entrance, shaped as if surrounded by woods on a low hill, there are no walls or wire fences installed around it, and there is an unpaved path ascending from the said road, around the hill, to the rear of the livestock barn buildings, through which one can enter in front of the vinyl greenhouse opposite the livestock barn buildings; and although there is a signboard stating “No Entry Except Authorized Personnel” below a utility pole on the right side of the entrance of the passageway through which the Defendants drove in, there is a large signboard reading “○○ Livestock Farming” immediately behind it, making it difficult to say that, even from the standpoint of an ordinary person, it is readily apparent from that sign alone that entry by outsiders is restricted not only to the said vinyl greenhouse but to the entire facility at issue, passageway, and the like.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and these facts, it cannot readily be concluded that reasonable doubt is excluded as to whether the passageway or the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns through which the Defendants drove in constitutes the curtilage that is the object of the crime of trespass upon residence, and the circumstances relied on by the court below are mostly related to the victim’s primarily economic interests in the facility at issue and the passageway, or to the circumstances surrounding the entry at issue, and cannot be said to be matters that should be given substantial weight in determining whether the circumstance that entry by outsiders into the said passageway, etc. is restricted was objectively and clearly manifested.\\nNevertheless, the court below determined that the said passageway and the vacant lot in front of the livestock barns constitute the curtilage of the residential building or livestock barns at issue, and held that the Defendants’ conduct constituted trespass upon residence; in so doing, it erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the object of the crime of trespass upon residence or by finding facts in violation of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, thereby affecting the judgment. The portion of the appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2020DO6085]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Scope of review by this Court\\n\\nAmong the facts charged in this case, the first-instance court entered a judgment of not guilty on the count of violation of the 「Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc.」 (hereinafter referred to as the “Violent Acts Punishment Act”) (joint bodily injury) as to Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, and although the prosecutor appealed, the lower court dismissed it. Since the prosecutor did not appeal this, that part became final. Accordingly, as to Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, only the remaining parts excluding the portion already finally acquitted are subject to this Court’s review; therefore, we will examine only the grounds for appeal concerning that.\\n\\n2. Outline of the case and issues\\n\\nA. The gist of the facts charged subject to review is as follows.\\n\\nDefendant 1 is the husband of Non-Indicted Person 1 and the brother-in-law of Non-Indicted Person 2, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 are the parents of Defendant 1 and the parents-in-law of Non-Indicted Person 1.\\n\\n1) Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.)\\n\\nThe Defendants went to the apartment at issue, which was the residence of the victim, Non-Indicted Person 1, at around 14:30 on May 19, 2018, and demanded that the entrance door be opened. However, the victim, Non-Indicted Person 1, was out, and her younger sibling, Non-Indicted Person 2, had fastened the chain latch installed on the entrance door and did not open the door, saying, “Come when your older sister comes home.” Accordingly, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, acting jointly, with Defendant 1 inserting his hand through the open gap and repeatedly striking the chain latch downward, and Defendant 2 continuously shaking the doorknob, caused the chain latch installed on the entrance door to come off from the door.\\n\\nAs a result, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 damaged the chain latch, the value of which is unknown, owned by the victim Non-Indicted Person 1, thereby impairing its utility.\\n\\n2) Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling)\\n\\nThe Defendants jointly damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the residence where the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 was staying, at the date and place stated in paragraph 1), and then entered.\\n\\nB. The lower court determined as follows.\\n\\n1) As to the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) concerning Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, it upheld the first-instance judgment that found them guilty.\\n\\n2) As to the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 1, it held that the dwelling, which is the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act, is limited to one occupied by another person, and that where the actor is a person living together with another person, unless he or she has departed from the shared life, the relevant dwelling does not become the object of this offense; on the ground that Defendant 1 could not be deemed to have departed from the status of a co-occupant of the apartment at issue at the time of this case, it determined that the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling was not established, set aside the first-instance judgment that had found him guilty, and entered a judgment of not guilty.\\n\\n3) As to the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, it held that where there are multiple dwelling-right holders, if the entry by one person contravenes, directly or indirectly, the intention of another resident, entry into the dwelling by that person harms the peace of the dwelling of the person against whose intention it is made, namely, the peace of control and management of the dwelling, and therefore the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established; on the ground that even if Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the apartment at issue with the consent of Defendant 1, a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, they did not obtain the consent of Non-Indicted Person 1, another resident, or of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, who was entrusted by Non-Indicted Person 1 with management of entry into the dwelling, and thereby disturbed the de facto peace of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s dwelling, it upheld the first-instance judgment that found them guilty.\\n\\nC. The gist of the grounds for appeal by the prosecutor and the Defendants is as follows.\\n\\n1) Grounds for appeal by the prosecutor\\n\\nDefendant 1 had departed from the apartment at issue and lost his status as a co-occupant, and because he entered the apartment at issue together with Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 by using violent means, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established. Nevertheless, the lower court judgment, which held otherwise and found that the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established, contains error by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the law regarding the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\n2) Grounds for appeal by the Defendants\\n\\nA) As to the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) concerning Defendant 1 and Defendant 2\\n\\nDefendant 1 and Defendant 2 did not damage the chain latch as stated in the facts charged for this portion, nor did they have the intent to damage it. Even if not so, the acts of the said Defendants constitute an act of self-help or a justifiable act. Nevertheless, the lower court judgment, which found the facts charged for this portion guilty, contains error by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the law regarding the establishment of the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.), justifiable act, and self-help act.\\n\\nB) As to the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\n(1) Where a person enters a shared dwelling with the consent of one of the co-occupants, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established, unless there are special circumstances such as entering for the purpose of committing a crime against another resident. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the apartment at issue with the consent of Defendant 1, who was a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, and they did not enter for the purpose of committing a crime against Non-Indicted Person 1, another resident, or the victim Non-Indicted Person 2; therefore, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established as to those Defendants.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 did not have intent to unlawfully enter a dwelling, and the acts of the said Defendants constitute either a justifiable act not contrary to social norms as prescribed in Article 20 of the Criminal Act, or a self-help act as prescribed in Article 23 of the Criminal Act, and thus unlawfulness is excluded.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the lower court judgment, which found the facts charged for this portion against the said Defendants guilty, contains error by misapprehending the law regarding the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, justifiable act, and self-help act.\\n\\nD. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nThe crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling protects the peace of the dwelling as a de facto legal interest. The constituent act of “intrusion” in the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling must be interpreted in relation to the protected legal interest of the crime; thus, “intrusion” means entering a dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace enjoyed by a resident in the dwelling, and whether an act constitutes intrusion is, as a general rule, determined based on the objective and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry. If the entry into a dwelling is in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace, it would, absent special circumstances, be contrary to the resident’s intention; however, the mere subjective circumstance of the resident that the act of entering the dwelling itself is contrary to the resident’s intention cannot immediately be deemed to constitute intrusion (see Supreme Court en banc decision of September 9, 2021, 2020DO12630).\\n\\nE. The principal issues in this case are as follows.\\n\\n1) Premise for discussion\\n\\nThis case concerns a situation in which Defendant 1, who was a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, together with Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who are his parents and the parents-in-law of Non-Indicted Person 1, another co-occupant, were entering the apartment at issue, and the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, who was staying inside the apartment at issue by entrustment from Non-Indicted Person 1, fastened the chain latch on the apartment entrance door and did not open the door, thereby prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry, and the Defendants then exercised physical force by damaging the chain latch, etc. In light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the Defendants’ conduct at the time of entry into the apartment at issue, it can be deemed to fall within a case in which the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s state of de facto peace was harmed.\\n\\n2) Principal issues in this case\\n\\nA) The first issue is whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established even where, in a case in which one of the co-occupants enters a shared dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace of another co-occupant who prohibited that person’s entry, such entry can be evaluated as falling within the ordinary manner of use of the shared dwelling.\\n\\nB) The second issue is whether, where one of the co-occupants, in responding to another co-occupant who prohibited his or her entry into the shared dwelling, enters the shared dwelling by exercising physical force, and in such entry an outsider joins that conduct and together they enter the shared dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace of the other co-occupant who prohibited their entry, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established against that outsider if it constitutes the ordinary conduct of use of the shared dwelling by the co-occupant who consented to the outsider’s entry, or an accompanying act thereto.\\n\\n3. Determination on the prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. As to the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 1\\n\\n1) The Criminal Act provides in Article 319(1) that “a person who intrudes into another person’s residence, managed structure, vessel or aircraft, or occupied room” shall be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. The crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established when a person other than the resident of the dwelling, the manager of the structure, vessel, or aircraft, or the occupant of the room (hereinafter referred to as the “resident, etc.”) intrudes into the above dwelling, structure, vessel, aircraft, or room (hereinafter referred to as the “dwelling, etc.”). Accordingly, the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is the dwelling, etc. occupied by a person other than the actor, that is, a “third party”; therefore, even if the actor himself or herself freely enters a dwelling, etc. that he or she occupies or manages, alone or jointly with another person, it does not constitute the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. However, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling can be established only where there are special circumstances, such as where a person who had been residing in or managing a dwelling together with another person has departed from the shared life relationship or has lost de facto control and management over the dwelling, etc.\\n\\nIn this spirit, the Supreme Court upheld a lower court that held that, because the dwelling shared by the victim and the defendant did not constitute the dwelling of another person, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling was not established even if the defendant entered that dwelling (see Supreme Court decision of December 27, 2012, 2010DO16537), and held that even if one of the co-possessors freely entered a structure under joint management, the crime of unlawful entry into a structure was not established (see Supreme Court decision of April 27, 1982, 81DO2956).\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, insofar as the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling protects the peace of the dwelling as a de facto legal interest, each co-occupant living in a shared dwelling may be said to enjoy the de facto peace of the dwelling. However, each co-occupant, absent special circumstances, may enter and use the portion established as the place of common life in the shared dwelling in accordance with the purpose and nature of the shared dwelling relationship, and for the same reason, must tolerate other co-occupants entering and using it. That is also the ordinary form in which co-occupants use a shared dwelling. Thus, the de facto legal interest of peace of the dwelling enjoyed by each co-occupant in the place of common life is necessarily subject to certain limitations due to the relationship among co-occupants, and it must be deemed that the co-occupants formed the shared dwelling relationship while mutually tolerating such circumstances. Therefore, absent special circumstances, co-occupants cannot prohibit other co-occupants from freely entering and using the place of common life.\\n\\nWhere one co-occupant, without legal basis or other just cause, prohibits another co-occupant from entering the place of common life, even if the other co-occupant enters the place of common life in response, that is merely a means to use the place of common life in accordance with the pre-acknowledged purpose and nature of the shared dwelling, and cannot be regarded as an act infringing the de facto peace of the dwelling of the co-occupant who prohibited the entry; therefore, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established. Even if the co-occupant, in order to enter the place of common life, employed some physical force, such as damaging the locking device of the entrance door, thereby harming the de facto state of peace of the co-occupant who prohibited the entry, it remains the same: apart from the question of whether punishment may be imposed under a separate provision that punishes such conduct itself, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established either.\\n\\n3) The lower court held that the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) was not established as to Defendant 1 on the basis of the following factual findings and reasons.\\n\\nA) Facts found by the lower court\\n\\n(1) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 are husband and wife by law, married on September 5, 2015, and they have one child between them; they have been living as a married couple in the apartment at issue since around August 15, 2016.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 frequently argued over the sale of a newly built apartment from around January 2018, and on April 9, 2018, Defendant 1 fought with Non-Indicted Person 1 and left the apartment at issue with some of his belongings. Then, on April 13, 2018, Defendant 1 went to the apartment at issue, argued again with Non-Indicted Person 1, and left the home. Thereafter, Non-Indicted Person 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door to the apartment at issue and also installed a chain latch on the entrance door.\\n\\n(3) Through a mobile phone messenger, Defendant 1 asked Non-Indicted Person 1 on April 17, 2018 and April 19, 2018 to tell him the password for the entrance door of the apartment at issue, and on May 4, 2018, he went to the apartment at issue and asked to be let in at the entrance, but was refused.\\n\\n(4) After the incident in this case, Non-Indicted Person 1 filed a lawsuit for divorce, etc. with the court around June 28, 2018, and a divorce mediation was established between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 on September 4, 2018.\\n\\nB) Reasons for the lower court’s determination\\n\\nAt the time of this case, it is difficult to deem that there was an explicit agreement between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 to terminate the marital relationship and for Defendant 1 to leave the shared residence, the apartment at issue, and live elsewhere. In such a situation, the mere fact that Defendant 1 took some of his belongings out of the apartment, or that Non-Indicted Person 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door and prevented Defendant 1 from entering, does not justify finding that Defendant 1 had departed from, or been excluded from, the status of co-occupant. Therefore, even if Defendant 1 used a method such as damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door in the process of entering the apartment at issue, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established.\\n\\n4) We examine the reasons for the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record.\\n\\nThe evidence submitted by the prosecutor alone is insufficient to establish that Defendant 1 departed from the shared life relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it, and there is no other evidence to establish this.
