In the course of confirming the manner in which the former labor union head, Victim Non-Indicted Person 2, had handled union business during his term of office, the Defendant found somewhat unclear portions in the supporting materials and, for the purpose of informing the union members of such fact and thereby excluding the victim from the competition in future union head elections, on or about April 20, 1991, prepared and posted a large placard on the wall of the dispatch room within the said company, using imitation paper sheets, stating: “With respect to athletic uniforms, we purchased them at the outrageously high price of KRW 18,000, although they could have been purchased for KRW 10,000 per set” (hereinafter referred to as the “athletic-uniform-related placard”); “With respect to flood-disaster relief money, the branch received reports from our members on the status of flood damage and paid flood-disaster relief money, but former branch head Non-Indicted Person 2 did not even announce such fact and secretly paid KRW 50,000 each to members who had not suffered any damage at all” (hereinafter referred to as the “flood-disaster-relief-money-related placard”); and “With respect to union dues, farewell money, and congratulatory and condolence money, former officeholder Non-Indicted Person 2 irregularly paid union dues from July 1, 1988, when he executed the duties, until the present, but did not pay a single won in farewell money or congratulatory and condolence money” (hereinafter referred to as the “farewell-money etc.-related placard”), and by causing other union members to read the same, publicly stated facts and thereby damaged the victim’s reputation. The first instance applied Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act to the above recognized facts and rendered a judgment of conviction against the Defendant.\\n\\n2. Summary of the reasons of the judgment below\\n\\nIn response to the argument by counsel for the Defendant in the court below that the Defendant lacked intent to defame and that the Defendant’s act constituted truthful facts solely concerning the public interest or was not contrary to social norms, the court below held that, although some aspect of the circumstances in which the Defendant had the said placard posted may be seen as reflecting an intent to serve the union, in light of the contents described and the means used, it could not be found that the Defendant lacked intent to defame in the act at issue in this case, and that it could not be deemed to fall under a case of truthful facts solely concerning the interests of the union members or to constitute an act not in violation of the law because it was not contrary to social norms. Accordingly, the court rejected counsel’s argument and dismissed the Defendant’s appeal.\\n\\n3. The Court’s determination\\n\\na. Since Article 310 of the Criminal Act provides that “Where the act under Article 307(1) is truthful facts solely concerning the public interest, punishment shall not be imposed,” even if a person publicly states facts and thereby damages another’s reputation, where such facts concern the public interest and the facts are stated for the purpose of serving the public interest, if the truth of such facts is proven, unlawfulness is excluded and the act is not punished. The above provision of the Criminal Act should be understood as seeking harmony between the two conflicting legal interests of protection of an individual’s honor as a personality right and guarantee of the just freedom of expression under Article 21 of the Constitution. Therefore, taking into account the harmony and balance between these two legal interests, even if there is no proof that the stated facts are true, where the actor believed those facts to be true and had reasonable grounds to so believe, unlawfulness should be deemed absent (see Supreme Court Decision 4294HYEONGSANG12, rendered on May 17, 1962; Supreme Court Decision 85DAKA29, rendered on October 11, 1988, etc.). In such case, whether the stated facts concern the public interest must be determined objectively in light of the contents and nature of the facts themselves, and if the actor’s principal purpose was to serve the public interest, the application of Article 310 of the Criminal Act cannot be excluded merely because there were incidentally other private motives (see Supreme Court Decision 88DO899, rendered on February 14, 1989).\\n\\nb. We first examine whether the facts stated by the Defendant concern the public interest.\\n\\nUpon reviewing the relevant evidence in comparison with the record, it may be found that the Defendant was elected on March 21, 1991, through an election, as the branch head (hereinafter referred to as the union head) of the branch of Non-Indicted Company 1 Co., Ltd. of the Seoul Bus Branch of the National Automobile Labor Union Federation, with a term of office of 3 years, and took office on April 1. Previously, the results of the union’s operation or accounting audit had not been disclosed, and there had been misunderstandings and dissatisfaction among the union members. Accordingly, at the time of the union head election, the Defendant had pledged to disclose all union operations. It may also be found that the union officers, from April 8, 1991 through April 12, 1991, conducted an accounting audit openly pursuant to the Branch Operating Rules (trial record, pages 57 through 75), as a result of which, as the court below also found, they discovered, among the business handled by Victim Non-Indicted Person 2, the former union head, during his tenure as union head, portions, as stated in the placard at issue, where supporting materials showing disbursement of union funds were lacking or gave rise to doubt, and that the placard was posted mainly for the purpose of informing the union members thereof; and that the union officers who conducted the accounting audit strongly requested the Defendant to disclose the results of the accounting audit. It is difficult to find that the principal motive for the Defendant’s posting of the said placard was, as stated in the facts charged, to exclude the said Non-Indicted Person 2 from the union head election to be held thereafter (other than the unilateral assertion of the said Non-Indicted Person 2 contained in the statement prepared by the prosecutor, there is no evidence supporting this point).\\n\\nTherefore, the facts stated in the said placard concern whether union funds were properly disbursed during the period in which the said Non-Indicted Person 2 served as union head, and when objectively determined in light of their contents and nature, it is appropriate to deem them to fall under “matters concerning the public interest” as provided in Article 310 of the Criminal Act. Even if the manner of expression in the said placard did not take the form of a simple accounting-audit result report but instead took the form of criticizing the performance of duties by the said Non-Indicted Person 2, the former union head, since the Defendant, as union head, posted the said placard mainly for the purpose of informing the union members of the above facts, it may be deemed to have been for the public interest.\\n\\nEven if the place where the Defendant posted the said placard was the dispatch room to which the general public could enter, as recognized from the relevant evidence and the record, considering that the dispatch room was mainly used as a waiting room for driver members and that it was difficult for all members, including drivers working on a two-shift system per day, to gather in one place, posting the placard in the dispatch room may also have been the most effective method of informing all union members of the above facts. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Defendant’s act was not for the public interest merely because the Defendant posted the placard in such a place.\\n\\nc. Next, we examine whether the facts stated by the Defendant are true.\\n\\nAccording to the relevant evidence and the record, including the testimony of First-Instance Witness Non-Indicted Person 3 and Court-Below Witness Non-Indicted Person 4, which were not rejected by the court below, the photographs of the said placard filed in the investigation record (pages 13 and 14), the respective written statements prepared by Non-Indicted Person 5 and Non-Indicted Person 6 (pages 48 and 50), the simplified tax invoices (page 49), the receipts (page 51), and the respective entries in the documents concerning the disbursement of flood-disaster relief money (pages 52 through 69), the grounds on which the Defendant learned of the facts stated in the said placard as a result of the union officers’ open accounting audit may be recognized as follows: (1) with respect to the “athletic-uniform-related placard,” Non-Indicted Person 5, a union member, stated that he purchased on the market at KRW 10,000 a set of athletic uniforms having the same trademark and fabric as the athletic uniforms the union had already purchased at KRW 18,000 per set, differing only in color and design, and brought the item for comparison, whereupon it was found to be of the same quality (the Defendant displayed the athletic uniform purchased by the said Non-Indicted Person 5 together with the placard and made it public); (2) with respect to the “flood-disaster-relief-money-related placard,” Non-Indicted Person 6, a union member who had received flood-disaster relief money at that time, stated that he heard from the said Non-Indicted Person 2 that since flood-disaster relief money had come in, it would be paid if he brought a confirmation from the bank account holder, and that although he had not actually suffered flood damage, he submitted the bank account holder’s confirmation and received the flood-disaster relief money (there were six union members in total who received flood-disaster relief money at that time); and (3) with respect to the “farewell-money etc.-related placard,” it was confirmed that, while union dues, farewell money, and congratulatory and condolence money were uniformly deducted from the salaries of other union members and collected, only union dues were irregularly deducted from the salary of Kwon Jae-hwan, and farewell money and congratulatory and condolence money were not deducted from his salary. It may be recognized that the Defendant, based on such materials revealed as a result of the open accounting audit, believed the facts stated in the said placard to be true and made them public. If so, although it may not be possible to conclude that all of the contents stated in the said placard were proven to be true facts, in a situation where, during the period when the said Non-Indicted Person 2 served as union head, the union’s operations were not disclosed and thus there was room for misunderstanding, the open accounting audit revealed portions of the business handled by the said Non-Indicted Person 2 as union head where supporting materials showing disbursement of union funds were lacking or gave rise to doubt, and some important portions among them were supported by materials to the extent that truth could be proven. Accordingly, it may also be deemed that there were reasonable grounds for the Defendant to believe the contents stated in the said placard to be true.\\n\\nd. Therefore, the court below should have carefully examined and reviewed whether the Defendant believed the facts he stated to be truthful facts concerning the public interest, and whether, in light of clear materials or grounds, the Defendant had reasonable grounds to so believe, and then determined whether counsel’s argument that Article 310 of the Criminal Act should apply was well-founded. Nevertheless, the court below, solely for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that the Defendant’s act did not fall under a case of truthful facts solely concerning the public interest, and punished the Defendant for defamation. Accordingly, the judgment below contains an error of law by misapprehending the legal principles concerning unlawfulness in the crime of defamation, and since it is clear that such error affected the judgment, the argument pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered as ordered by the concurrence of the Justices participating therein."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning confiscation and collection is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)
A: If the facts charged are not established, the court’s recognizing unrelated criminal facts and imposing confiscation and collection violates the principle of no accusation and no trial.
B: Even if the bribee received a cashier’s check as a bribe, spent it, and then returned to the bribe-giver an amount equivalent to the cashier’s check, since the bribe itself was not returned, it cannot be confiscated, and the equivalent value must be collected from the bribee.
C: Even if it is recognized as having substantially contributed to the commission of the criminal act, an object that was used only in an act before commencement of the act of execution or after completion of the act of execution, and was not used in the act of execution itself, cannot be included in the “object furnished for the criminal act” subject to confiscation and collection.
D: Even if confiscation and collection are related to the facts charged, if the statute of limitations has already expired with respect to those facts charged, confiscation and collection cannot be imposed.
E: If A received KRW 100 million in connection with the intermediation of matters within the scope of a public official’s duties, but, in accordance with the purpose for which KRW 30 million thereof was received, gave it as a bribe to the relevant public official in connection with the solicitation, then only the remaining KRW 70 million, excluding that amount, may be confiscated and collected from A.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO4075]": "1. As to ground of appeal No. 1, we consider.\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below found that the Defendant, taking note of the fact that a checkout-completion sticker attached in order to prevent double billing when a person brings items purchased at a large discount store nationwide back into the same store is not retrieved by the discount store side, and of the fact that such sticker is easy to detach, decided to attach stickers to items of the same kind as those purchased by him and obtain refunds; that on July 1, 2005, at the Shinsegae E-Mart Guro Branch Co., Ltd. located in Guro-dong, Guro-gu, Seoul, he paid for one Bosch cordless drill displayed there worth approximately KRW 133,000 and went out of the above store, then reentered the store with the above drill and behaved as if he were about to purchase goods, causing a cashier there to attach a checkout-completion sticker to the above drill; that he then went out of the store again and peeled off only the above sticker, and then reentered the store, and, taking advantage of the employees’ lax supervision, attached the above sticker to one drill of the same kind as the above drill, owned by the above company and displayed there, worth approximately KRW 133,000, and then, falsely representing it to the cashier as an item lawfully purchased, carried the above drill out of the store; and that, including this, until October 23 of the same year, as stated in the attached list of offenses to the judgment of the court of first instance, he stole property owned by the victim company, Homeplus Co., Ltd., and Lotte Shopping Co., Ltd. on a total of 60 occasions in the above manner, with a total market value of approximately KRW 17,327,860, and further found that the Defendant’s theft offenses were committed habitually. In light of the record, the court below’s above finding of habit is acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality of misapprehending the law concerning habituality as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to ground of appeal No. 2, we consider.\\nThe “property provided for the commission of a criminal act” under Article 48(1)1 of the Criminal Act is not limited to property used only in the act of execution itself, such as a knife used in an act of murder, but even if it is property used in an act before the commencement of the act of execution or in an act after the termination of the act of execution, it shall be deemed included in the property provided as prescribed in the above Article, so long as it is recognized to have substantially contributed to the carrying out of the criminal act.\\nAs seen above, in the present case, whenever the Defendant visited a large discount store once and committed the offenses, he stole goods worth several hundred thousand won in 1 to 6 items and loaded them into his Sonata passenger car (Exhibit No. 1), and the size of those goods was also considerable, such as an electric rice cooker, hammer drill, sofa cover, vacuum packaging machine, massage machine, telephone, DVD player, etc., so that they were difficult to transport by public transportation; accordingly, the passenger car in this case should be deemed a car used not merely as transportation to arrive at the place of the offense, but as a car used to transport the stolen goods in this case, and therefore it may be deemed property provided for the commission of a criminal act under Article 48(1)1 of the Criminal Act.\\nIn the same purport, the court below’s measure of upholding the judgment of the court of first instance, which confiscated Exhibit No. 1 on the ground that it was clear that Exhibit No. 1 had been provided for the offenses in this case, is correct, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality of misapprehending the law concerning confiscation.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as per the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2022DO8662]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendants’ grounds for final appeal on the merits\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court found the facts charged against the Defendants to be guilty. In light of the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the relevant legal principles and duly admitted evidence, there is no error in the lower court’s failure to conduct the necessary examination, thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience or misunderstanding the relevant legal principles.\\n\\n2. Regarding Defendant 2’s grounds for final appeal concerning the confiscation of the seized Exhibits 1 and 2\\n\\na. Outline of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The victim, Non-indicted Person 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the Victim in this Case”), was deceived by a member of a voice phishing organization whose name is unknown and, on 2021. 10. 7., handed over to Non-indicted Person 2, who impersonated an employee of the Financial Supervisory Service, cash in the amount of KRW 200 million contained in a suitcase (Seized Exhibit 3), and Non-indicted Person 2, on the same day, delivered to Defendant 2, among others, the suitcase and KRW 196 million in cash.\\n\\n2) On the same day, the Victim in this Case reported the fraud damage to the Seoul Seongdong Police Station, and an investigation was initiated; and Defendant 2, when he was urgently arrested at his home on 2021. 10. 11., had confiscated, together with the suitcase, 2,686 notes of KRW 50,000 denomination (Seized Exhibit 1) and 200 notes of KRW 10,000 denomination (Seized Exhibit 2) (hereinafter the seized Exhibits 1 and 2 are collectively referred to as “the Seized Cash in this Case”), among other items.\\n\\n3) The prosecutor investigated several monetary transactions based on the WeChat conversation contents between the Defendants and “○○,” but brought charges against the Defendants only for the offense of fraud against the Victim in this Case.\\n\\n4) The first instance court, while finding the facts charged against the Defendants to be guilty, ordered the confiscation of Seized Exhibits 1 through 4 seized from Defendant 2, and Seized Exhibits 5 through 10 seized from Defendant 1, respectively.\\n\\n5) The Defendants, while appealing the first instance judgment, asserted grounds of appeal not only as to the merits but also as to the confiscation portion.\\n\\nb. The lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court upheld the confiscation portion concerning Defendant 2 in the first instance judgment for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Taking together the various provisions of the Special Act on the Confiscation and Recovery of Assets Acquired through Corruption (hereinafter referred to as the “Corrupt Property Confiscation Act”) and Article 49 of the Criminal Act, etc., a court may confiscate, with respect to the criminal proceeds property of a corruption offense committed by the defendant against whom the indictment was filed, even if such property constitutes the victim’s property from an offense not charged in the present case.\\n\\n2) The Seized Cash in this Case constitutes property acquired from the victim or property obtained by holding or disposing of such property through the Defendants’ voice phishing fraud offense, and therefore falls under “criminal proceeds property” as provided in the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act.\\n\\n3) In connection with the Defendants’ voice phishing fraud offense, there appear to be multiple victims who have not yet been identified, and recovery of damage to the Victim in this Case has not yet been fully achieved; accordingly, this falls under the case “where recovery of damage is deemed to be extremely difficult, such as because the victim cannot exercise a claim for return of property or a claim for damages against the Defendants.”\\n\\nc. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n1) The proviso to Article 49 of the Criminal Act provides that “even when a judgment of guilt is not rendered against the offender, if the requirements for confiscation are met, only confiscation may be declared.” However, because there is no system under our legal order that separately permits only confiscation to be declared without filing an indictment, in order to declare confiscation on the basis of the above provision, the requirements for confiscation must be related to the facts charged for which an indictment was filed, and it is not permissible, as it violates the principle of no indictment, no trial, for a court to recognize separate criminal facts for which no indictment was filed and to declare confiscation or collection in relation thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 92DO700, rendered on 1992. 7. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2012DO8964, rendered on 2013. 1. 16., etc.). The Corrupt Property Confiscation Act is a law enacted for the purpose of fundamentally eliminating the economic factors that encourage corruption offenses and effectively preventing and eradicating corruption offenses, thereby contributing to the establishment of a clean international order, by prescribing special measures concerning the confiscation and collection, recovery, etc. of corrupt property in order to efficiently implement the United Nations Convention against Corruption and other related international conventions (Article 1). Unlike the Criminal Act, which does not recognize confiscation or collection for victim property in property offenses, where, as to “criminal proceeds property” acquired from the victim or obtained by holding or disposing of such property through specified criminal acts prescribed in each item of Article 2(3), including electronic financial fraud under Article 2(2) of the Act on the Prevention of Damage from Telecommunications-Based Financial Fraud and Refund of Damage Amounts, it is recognized that recovery of damage is extremely difficult, such as because the criminal victim cannot exercise a claim for return of property or a claim for damages against the offender with respect to such property, such property may be confiscated or collected (Article 6(1)), and the criminal proceeds property confiscated or collected shall be returned to the victim (Article 6(2)). Meanwhile, the Enforcement Decree of the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act prescribes procedures for returning criminal proceeds property to the victim, etc., and where the prosecutor has commenced the procedure for returning criminal proceeds property, the prosecutor shall promptly notify the victim, etc. of various matters including “the court that rendered the confiscation judgment or collection judgment concerning the property subject to recovery, the date of the judgment and the date of finality, the case number, the name of the defendant who received the judgment, and the gist and offense title of the criminal facts that became the basis for the confiscation or collection” (Article 5(1)).\\n\\nTaking into comprehensive consideration the principle of confiscation and collection of victim property, the legislative purpose of the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act, and the purpose of providing a return procedure to the victim, etc. while limiting the offenses for which confiscation and collection of criminal proceeds property are permitted to specified offenses, the criminal facts that constitute the cause of confiscation and collection under Articles 6(1), 3(1), and 2(3) of the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act must be limited to the criminal facts for which an indictment was filed; “criminal proceeds property” must be limited to property acquired from the victim of the criminal facts for which an indictment was filed or property obtained by holding or disposing of such property; and confiscation and collection may be permitted only where it is recognized that recovery of damage to that victim is extremely difficult.\\n\\n2) In light of the foregoing legal principles, the facts as previously found mean that the Seized Cash in this Case, being cash acquired by Defendant 2 through the fraud offense against the Victim in this Case for which the Defendants were indicted, or cash obtained by disposing of such cash, corresponds to “criminal proceeds property,” and confiscation under the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act is permitted with respect to the Seized Cash in this Case only if it is recognized that recovery of damage to the Victim in this Case is extremely difficult.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the lower court, on the premise that even criminal facts for which no indictment was filed may constitute “criminal proceeds property” so long as they are recognized as constituting specified criminal acts prescribed in each item of Article 2(3) of the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act, held that the Seized Cash in this Case could be confiscated from Defendant 2, without clearly determining whether the Seized Cash in this Case was related to the criminal facts concerning the Victim in this Case, and on the ground that recovery of damage was deemed to be extremely difficult not only in relation to the Victim in this Case but also in relation to the victims of the Defendants’ other voice phishing fraud offenses. In this lower court judgment, there is an error that affected the judgment by failing to conduct the necessary examination due to misunderstanding the legal principles concerning “criminal proceeds property” under the Corrupt Property Confiscation Act and the requirements for confiscation, etc. The argument by Defendant 2 to that effect in this part of the grounds for final appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the lower court judgment concerning the confiscation of the Seized Cash in this Case from Defendant 2 is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; and the Defendants’ final appeal and the remaining final appeal by Defendant 2 are all dismissed. Therefore, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, the Court renders judgment as follows."}

{"[92DO700]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n(1) Determination on Ground 1 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nThe lower court found that the Defendant, while entering through Gimpo International Airport a total of 19 times during the period from 1986. 11. 25. to 1990. 11. 26., secretly smuggled in violins, cellos, etc. by deeply placing them inside travel bags and concealing them by covering them with clothes and other items; and, upon review of the record, the lower court’s above factual findings are fully supportable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality, such as a violation of the rules governing the weighing of evidence, as alleged.\\n\\nAnd, if goods subject to customs duties were concealed so as to be difficult to discover and were passed through customs, this shall constitute the evasion of customs duties by fraud or other improper means prescribed in Article 180 of the Customs Act (see this Court’s decision rendered on 1991. 2. 8., 90DO2418); therefore, it is proper that the lower court regarded the Defendant’s above act as falling under Article 180 of the Customs Act, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality, such as a misunderstanding of the legal principle regarding evasion of customs duties, as alleged.\\n\\nAll arguments are without merit.\\n\\n(2) Determination on Ground 2 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nAs to the point among the facts charged in this case that the Defendant smuggled in one Italian violin (Peter Guarnerius) on 1987. 3. 25., the lower court, finding no evidence that the Defendant smuggled in the above violin on the above date, rendered a verdict of not guilty on that point (the prosecutor did not file an appeal with respect to this part, so it has already become final), but, finding that it was established that the Defendant smuggled in the above violin on 1983. 1. 30., ordered forfeiture from the Defendant of KRW 273,181,127, which is the sum of KRW 164,356,385, the market value at the time of the offense of the other musical instruments, etc. that had been smuggled in and for which a guilty judgment was rendered, and KRW 108,824,742, the market value at the time of the offense of the above violin.\\n\\nThe proviso to Article 49 of the Criminal Act provides that even when a judgment of guilt is not rendered against the actor, only forfeiture may be declared when the requirements for forfeiture exist; therefore, it should be deemed that not only forfeiture but also collection in lieu of forfeiture may be declared on the basis of the above provision. However, under our legal system, there is no institution permitting a court to declare only forfeiture or collection separately without the filing of an indictment, so in order to declare forfeiture or collection on the basis of the above provision, the requirements for such forfeiture or collection must relate to the facts charged for which an indictment has been filed. If the facts charged are not established, it should be deemed impossible, as being contrary to the principle of no indictment, no adjudication, for the court to find criminal facts for which no separate indictment has been filed and to declare forfeiture or collection with respect thereto. Moreover, even if forfeiture or collection is related to the facts charged, if the statute of limitations has already expired with respect to those facts charged and a judgment of guilt can no longer be rendered, forfeiture or collection should likewise be deemed unavailable. If it were not so understood, it would lead to the unreasonable result that only forfeiture or collection, which are prescribed under the current law as a type of punishment, would not be subject to the statute of limitations.\\n\\nIn this case, the question of when the above violin was smuggled in should be deemed to have a significant effect on the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense; therefore, even though it is the same violin, the effect of the indictment regarding the smuggling of the violin on 1987. 3. 25. should be deemed not to extend to the smuggling of the violin on 1983. 1. 30. found by the lower court (and, as will be seen below, this is all the more so because the statute of limitations had already expired at the time this indictment was filed with respect to that point). Accordingly, the lower court’s finding of the fact of smuggling the violin on 1983. 1. 30., for which no indictment had been filed, and its ordering of collection of the market value of the above violin, cannot but be said to violate the principle of no indictment, no adjudication. On the other hand, the statute of limitations for the offense prescribed in Article 180 of the Customs Act with respect to the smuggling of the violin on 1983. 1. 30. is 7 years pursuant to Article 249(1)3 of the Criminal Procedure Act, so it must be deemed that the statute of limitations for this offense had already expired by the time the indictment in this case was filed on 1991. 7. 15., and in this respect as well the lower court’s above collection order cannot but be said to be erroneous.\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court’s finding of the fact of smuggling the violin on 1983. 1. 30., for which neither an indictment had been filed nor the statute of limitations had already expired, and its ordering of collection of the market value of that violin, constituted an illegality that misapprehended the legal principle of collection and affected the judgment; and the argument on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, pursuant to Articles 391 and 396(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, among the guilty portion of the lower court judgment, the portion ordering collection from the Defendant of KRW 273,181,127 is reversed, and KRW 164,356,385 shall be collected from the Defendant; and the Defendant’s remaining appeal is without merit, so it is dismissed pursuant to Articles 399 and 364(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[98DO3584]": "1. The grounds for appeal filed by Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and counsel for Defendant 2 concerning whether each interrogation record of the suspects, etc. as to the Defendants was voluntary are considered together.\\n\\nIf the Defendant’s confession at the Prosecutors’ Office constitutes a case in which there are substantial grounds to suspect that it was not made voluntarily because it was obtained after verbal abuse, coercion, and inducement without allowing the Defendant to sleep, then, pursuant to Article 309 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the interrogation record of the suspect lacks evidentiary admissibility (see Supreme Court Decisions 95DO1964, rendered on June 27, 1997, and 97DO3234, rendered on April 10, 1998, among others). Moreover, the purpose of denying the evidentiary admissibility of a confession lacking voluntariness is that a confession made under circumstances likely to induce or compel false statements is itself inconsistent with substantive truth and thus may lead to a mistaken judgment; and, irrespective of whether it is true or false, it is intended to prevent in advance the application of unlawful and improper pressure infringing the basic human rights of the suspect in order to obtain a confession. Therefore, where voluntariness is contested, it is not the Defendant who must prove concrete facts giving rise to reasonable doubt as to voluntariness; rather, the prosecutor must present proof resolving the doubt as to voluntariness (see the above-mentioned 97DO3234 decision).\\n\\nAccording to the record, Defendant 2 first voluntarily appeared at the Prosecutors’ Office at around 14:30 on February 11, 1998, and prepared a written statement concerning allegations of corruption, after which, following an investigation that continued until the next day, the first interrogation record of the suspect was prepared. During that investigation, the said Defendant, during a brief break taken by the prosecutor and others, slept in a chair for about one hour from around 05:00 on February 12 of the same year and then continued to undergo investigation; at around 09:00 of the same day he was urgently arrested; at around 24:00 of the same day he was placed in custody at the Seocho Police Station; at around 10:00 on February 13 of the same year he underwent judicial review of the detention warrant; the detention warrant was issued that day; the detention warrant was executed at around 17:00 of the same day; and he was confined in the Seoul Detention Center at around 20:00. At the time of the initial preparation of the written statement, the said Defendant made no mention whatsoever of the portion concerning the request for a bribe of KRW 50,000,000. However, in the first interrogation record of the suspect prepared by the prosecutor, he stated that he had asked Nonindicted 1 to lend him the money but had been refused, and with respect to the suspicion of having received a bribe from the side of Nonindicted 2, he denied it. In the third interrogation record of the suspect prepared on February 14 of the same year, the day after the Defendant was confined in the Seoul Detention Center, he stated that he had received a total of KRW 21,000,000, including KRW 5,000,000 said to have been received from Nonindicted 2 in the fall of 1995 and KRW 6,000,000 said to have been received on December 24, 1997, and he also confessed to having received KRW 30,000,000 in bribes from Nonindicted 3, the father of Nonindicted 2. However, from the trial court stage onward, he denied the receipt of each of the above amounts of KRW 5,000,000, KRW 6,000,000, and KRW 30,000,000, as well as the portion concerning the request for a bribe of KRW 50,000,000. Defendant 1 departed for Germany on February 8, 1998 to attend an academic seminar, received contact regarding the bribery corruption case at issue, left Germany by airplane at around 17:00 on February 11 of that month, arrived at Gimpo Airport the following day, was voluntarily taken to the investigators who were waiting upon the Defendant’s contact, arrived at the Prosecutors’ Office building at around 14:00 that day, submitted a surrender statement, then prepared a statement, then prepared the first interrogation record of the suspect, and was urgently arrested at around 11:00 on the 13th of the same month; the following day at around 10:00, after judicial review of the detention warrant, the detention warrant was issued; the detention warrant was executed at around 23:00 that day; and he was confined in the Seoul Detention Center. When the first interrogation record of the suspect was prepared on February 12, 1998, the Defendant stated, with respect to the folding screens, etc. received from Nonindicted 1 and others, that they were received as gifts unrelated to his official duties. As to the fact that Nonindicted 1 left KRW 50,000,000 on September 29, 1997, before returning it to Nonindicted 4, the son of Nonindicted 1, on October 16 of that year, he stated that he did not remember whether Nonindicted 4 had visited the Defendant’s house around October 10 of that year, or that he forgot to return it during the conversation, or that although he had no recollection, he wished to believe what Nonindicted 4 said regarding the matter. In the second interrogation record of the suspect prepared on February 13, 1998, he denied the fact that the USD 49,000 found during the search of the Defendant’s house that day had been received from Nonindicted 3, and initially said that it was foreign currency left over after use during overseas trips. However, in the third interrogation record of the suspect prepared on February 14 of the same month, he confessed that he had received USD 50,000 from Nonindicted 3 and USD 10,000 on each of two occasions. In the fourth interrogation record of the suspect prepared on the same day, he stated that the KRW 50,000,000 received from Nonindicted 1 had been kept with the thought of deciding later depending on the circumstances, and that when Nonindicted 4 visited the Defendant’s house around October 10, 1997, he should have returned it then; he also stated that the folding screens, etc. had been received in connection with the appointment of a professor. From the trial court stage onward, he stated that the said KRW 50,000,000 had been kept from the beginning with the intent to return it, that Nonindicted 4 had not visited the said Defendant’s house on the 10th of the same month, and that after repeated contact the Defendant finally got in touch with Nonindicted 4 around the 14th of the same month and returned the said amount to Nonindicted 4 on the 16th of the same month. Meanwhile, Defendant 2 argues that the interrogation records of the suspect of the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor were false statements made because the Defendant was not allowed to sleep for more than 30 hours at the Prosecutors’ Office, was made to kneel, was slapped on the cheek, was stabbed in the side with a ballpoint pen, and was continuously interrogated while being subjected to verbal abuse and assault and being prevented from contacting the outside world, until the Defendant, exhausted in body and mind, made the false statements in a state of despair. Defendant 1 argues, with respect to the interrogation records of the suspect of the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor, that the Defendant, having flown for more than 12 hours from Germany, was not allowed to sleep for more than 48 hours at the Prosecutors’ Office, was subjected to overnight investigation accompanied by obscenities and verbal abuse, and in the process, the Defendant’s physical strength was depleted to the utmost, with even consciousness blurred as the Defendant was forced into making statements under the coercion of certain investigators, and therefore the statements lacked voluntariness.\\n\\nIn light of these circumstances, and particularly considering that the Defendants had the right to remain silent, and considering that even though the Defendants voluntarily appeared at the Prosecutors’ Office and were investigated, they were unable to return home and instead remained continuously at the Prosecutors’ Office building until they were placed in custody at the Seocho Police Station or until the detention warrant was executed, making it strongly suspect that they could have been subjected to overnight interrogation, if the Defendants’ confessions at the Prosecutors’ Office were, as they claim, the result of continued interrogation accompanied by verbal abuse and coercion without allowing them to sleep, then there are substantial grounds to suspect that the confessions were not made voluntarily. In such a case, even if the Defendants voluntarily appeared and were investigated, proof resolving the doubt as to voluntariness, such as that they underwent investigation while staying at the Prosecutors’ Office building but obtained the necessary sleep, must be made by the prosecutor. Accordingly, unless the statements made by the Defendants at the Prosecutors’ Office are examined and determined to have been made after the overnight investigation and verbal abuse and coercion at issue in this case, they cannot ultimately be used as evidence of guilt. Nevertheless, the lower appellate court’s recognition of voluntariness solely on the basis of the reasons stated in its judgment was erroneous.\\n\\nHowever, according to the reasons stated in the trial court judgment upheld by the lower appellate court, in addition to the above, the evidence of guilt against the Defendants included the statements of witnesses Nonindicted 1, Nonindicted 2, Nonindicted 3, and Nonindicted 4; the statements recorded in each interrogation record prepared by the prosecutor concerning Nonindicted 1, Nonindicted 2, Nonindicted 3, and Nonindicted 4; the contents of each seizure record prepared by the prosecutor or the prosecutorial investigative official; and copies of each deposit passbook and copies of academic conference pamphlets attached to the investigation record. Reviewing the remaining evidence in light of the record, as will be seen below, even by the remaining evidence, the criminal facts stated in the judgment concerning the Defendants are sufficiently proven. Ultimately, the above error by the lower appellate court does not affect the result of the judgment. The argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is therefore without merit.\\n\\n2. The remaining grounds of appeal of Defendant 1 and his court-appointed counsel, as well as counsel Choi Jong-young, and the portions supplementing them among the statements in the supplemental petitions for appeal filed by counsel Choi Jong-young and Park Man-ho are considered together.\\n\\nA. Regarding the receipt of the folding screens, sofa, and golden mandarin ducks\\n\\nIf money or goods were received in connection with the official duties of a public official, the money or goods so received constitute a bribe, and even if they are given in the form of social courtesy, they constitute a bribe when they have the meaning of consideration for official conduct (see Supreme Court Decisions 96DO865, rendered on June 14, 1996, and 83DO1499, rendered on April 10, 1984, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the facts affirmed by the lower appellate court and the record, it is recognized that around February 1997, Professor Nonindicted 5, a senior professor in the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery of College △△ of ○○ University, retired upon reaching the mandatory retirement age; that around that time it was known to all persons interested in the new recruitment of professors that a professor in the field of oral and maxillofacial surgery would be newly hired in the second half of that year; and that Jin Woo-jeong was a direct disciple of Defendant 1, and Nonindicted 1 was his father, but until 1996 he had not had very frequent contact with Defendant 1 and had not given expensive gifts. Considering these points, and the fact that the said Defendant remarried on April 3, 1997, but after more than six months had passed, and moreover, it is not plausible that after gifting expensive folding screens, etc., he would again gift expensive golden mandarin ducks; considering the social status and financial condition of the said Defendant and Nonindicted 1 and Nonindicted 4; and considering that the items were expensive and were received on multiple occasions, they cannot be regarded as merely falling within the scope of simple social courtesy. Even if Defendant 1 received the above items from Nonindicted 1 and Nonindicted 4 under the pretext of ceremonial wedding congratulations and greetings, their inward intent, unlike the outwardly stated pretext, can be viewed as having received them under the pretext of requesting favors in connection with the new recruitment of professors.\\n\\nThe lower appellate court’s determination to the same effect appears correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law regarding the quid pro quo nature of the bribe or its relation to official duties, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the receipt of KRW 50,000,000\\n\\nAccording to the facts affirmed by the lower appellate court and the record, when Nonindicted 1 came with a bundle of money containing KRW 50,000,000 on September 29, 1997 and tried to give it to Defendant 1, the Defendant initially refused it but later accepted it saying he would return it, and kept it as is; in early October of that year, he received USD 50,000 from Nonindicted 2 under the pretext of overseas research activity expenses; on the 10th of the same month, when Nonindicted 4 visited the Defendant’s house and requested support in recommending the Defendant for appointment as professor, he did not return it; then on the 14th of the same month he called Nonindicted 4 and told him to come to the said Defendant’s house, and only when Nonindicted 4 visited the said Defendant’s house on the 16th of the same month did he finally return the said amount to Nonindicted 4.\\n\\nIf the facts are as above, then even if the said Defendant initially appeared to refuse to receive the said amount from Nonindicted 1, he in fact received the amount with intent to appropriate it, and although he had the opportunity to return it, he did not do so. While in that state, his mind appears to have changed as he received USD 50,000 from Nonindicted 3, the father of Nonindicted 2, who was a competitor of Nonindicted 4, and then returned it. Therefore, the fact that the Defendant returned the said amount later does not affect the establishment of the offense of bribery.\\n\\nThe lower appellate court’s determination to the same effect appears correct, and there is no illegality of factual error due to violation of the rules of evidence or misapprehension of law regarding the receipt of bribes, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Regarding the receipt of a total of USD 70,000\\n\\nThe lower appellate court, after finding that the Defendant had received from Nonindicted 3 USD 10,000 around May 20, 1997 under the pretext of a wedding congratulatory gift, USD 10,000 around mid-September of the same year under the pretext of assistance for overseas business trip expenses, and USD 50,000 in early October 1997 under the pretext of overseas research activity expenses, determined that in light of the relationship of acquaintance between the Defendant and Nonindicted 4, their social status, their financial condition, and the timing and amounts of the respective sums, which were far too large to be regarded as money given as social courtesy, the said sums, unlike the stated pretexts, should in fact be regarded as bribes received under the pretext of asking for help and promising help in connection with the new recruitment of professors. Reviewing the record, the lower appellate court’s determination is persuasive, and there is no illegality of factual error due to violation of the rules of evidence or misapprehension of law regarding the offense of bribery, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. The remaining grounds of appeal of Defendant 2 and counsel Jeong Tae-ryu, together with the portions supplementing them among the statements in the supplemental petition for appeal filed by counsel Hong Sun-hyeop, are considered together.\\n\\nA. Regarding the relation to official duties in the offense of bribery\\n\\nIn the offense of bribery, official duties mean not only the duties themselves that a public official has jurisdiction over under statutes, but also acts closely related to those duties, acts customarily or in fact under the official’s jurisdiction, and acts assisting or influencing the decision-maker (see Supreme Court Decisions 96DO3378, rendered on April 17, 1997, and 96DO5828, rendered on February 27, 1998, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower appellate court judgment, the procedure for hiring new professors at ○○ University was as follows: ① at the qualification review stage, the college in question examined whether the applicant met the qualifications through review of research and teaching experience and research achievements; ② at the substantive review stage, ㉮ after going through procedures for ability verification by research achievement review, document review, and public presentation by at least three research achievement review committee members in the college, the College Personnel Committee, chaired by the dean and composed of around 10 personnel committee members, made the final decision on whether to recommend appointment after deliberation and reported the result to the president; and when deliberating, it collected the department chair’s opinion, and ㉯ at the university headquarters, a committee chaired by the president and composed of the vice president, etc. as members examined the results of the public recruitment review submitted by the college and made the final decision on whether to submit the matter to the headquarters personnel committee; ③ at the stage of determining the prospective appointee, the Personnel Committee, chaired by the Dean of Academic Affairs and composed of 34 members, made the final deliberation on each evaluation factor, referring to the opinions of the college, and after the president’s approval, the decision on the prospective appointee was to be notified to each college and applicant. In the case of College △△, it consisted of one department, Dentistry, and had 17 divisions as a non-statutory organization. Although there was no formal procedure for collecting the opinions of the relevant division when hiring a new professor, if the relevant division presented the professors’ opinions through the chief professor, those opinions were reported to the Personnel Committee and used as reference in deliberation and decision. In practice, in the case of new faculty hiring at College △△, it was customary that the applicant recommended by the faculty meeting of the relevant division was ultimately selected as the prospective appointee, and in the hiring of new professors in the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, except for this case, all applicants recommended by the faculty meeting of that division were selected as prospective appointees. When the faculty meeting consolidated opinions, the senior professors had far stronger speaking power than the junior professors, and in most cases decisions were made according to the wishes of the senior professors. In the course of the new faculty hiring in this case, when the College △△ Personnel Committee recommended applicant Nonindicted 6 as the candidate for appointment instead of applicant Nonindicted 2 recommended by the faculty meeting of the division, the professors of that division strongly protested, saying it was contrary to custom, and there was a serious dispute between the chair of the Personnel Committee, the dean of College △△, and the professors of the division. The court found that Defendant 2 was a senior professor in the relevant division who concurrently served as head of the Oral Surgery Department of the Department of Dental Medicine at ○○ University Hospital. On that basis, it determined that Defendant 2 occupied a position that, customarily or in fact, could influence the decision-maker in the new hiring of a professor in the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery of College △△, and therefore that if money or goods were received in connection with the exercise of such authority, the offense of bribery is established. Reviewing this in light of the record, that determination appears correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law concerning the official-duty element of the offense of bribery, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding violation of the rules of evidence\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower appellate court judgment, the lower appellate court found that the said Defendant received KRW 30,000,000 from Nonindicted 1 around September 24, 1997, together with a request to help Nonindicted 4 be hired as a professor, under the pretext of research funds; that the said Defendant requested the said Nonindicted 1 in early October of the same year, saying, “I urgently need to use money, so please lend me KRW 50,000,000,” but Nonindicted 1 refused; that the Defendant requested Nonindicted 4 around late September 1997, saying, “I need money, so if you have money, please lend me around KRW 30,000,000,” and then received KRW 30,000,000 from Nonindicted 4 a few days later under the pretext of a loan; that at that time no promissory note was prepared, and there was absolutely no agreement concerning maturity or interest, and the Defendant had not repaid the money until the time he was arrested in this case. The court then first found, with respect to the money received from Nonindicted 1, etc., that in light of the acquaintance relationship between the Defendant and the said Nonindicted 1, their social status, financial condition, the fact that the time when the Defendant asked to borrow money was immediately after receiving KRW 30,000,000 as stated above, and the fact that there was fierce competition among applicants at the time over the new faculty appointment, as well as the amount the Defendant sought to borrow, the money should, unlike the stated pretext, actually be viewed as the Defendant requesting money from Nonindicted 1 in return for helping Nonindicted 4 be hired as a professor. As for the money received from Nonindicted 4, the court found that, in light of the relationship of acquaintance between the Defendant and Nonindicted 4, their social status, financial condition, the timing at which the money was given, and the fact that there was absolutely no agreement regarding interest and maturity that would ordinarily be fixed if money were truly being lent, the respective amounts were not loans in fact but bribes received under the pretext of asking for help and promising help in connection with the new faculty hiring. Reviewing the record, the lower appellate court’s factual findings and determination are persuasive, and there is no illegality such as factual error due to violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Regarding the number of offenses\\n\\nEven if the conduct consists of multiple acts by receiving bribes on several occasions, when such conduct is carried out pursuant to a single and continuous criminal intent and infringes the same legal interest, it is appropriate to punish it as a single comprehensive offense (see Supreme Court Decisions 90DO1588, rendered on September 25, 1990, 85DO1502, rendered on September 24, 1985, and 81DO1409, rendered on October 26, 1982, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the trial court judgment upheld by the lower appellate court, Defendant 2, hoping in the future to be hired as a professor in the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery of College △△ of ○○ University, can be found to have received, on six occasions from the fall of 1995 through around December 24, 1997, a total of KRW 21,000,000 in bribes offered by Nonindicted 2, who had entered the doctoral program in the relevant department of the graduate school of ○○ University around March 1995, under the pretext of requesting leniency in connection with obtaining a doctoral degree and the future professorial appointment. As such, Defendant 2’s receipt as bribes of the total sum of KRW 21,000,000 from the same bribe-giver for the same reasons, etc., must be regarded as having been committed pursuant to a single and continuous criminal intent, and therefore it should be treated as a single comprehensive offense.\\n\\nThe lower appellate court’s action of upholding the trial court judgment, which held in the same vein that the bribes received by Defendant 2 from Nonindicted 2 are in the relationship of a single comprehensive offense, is persuasive, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law concerning the number of offenses in the crime of bribery, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nD. Regarding confiscation/collection\\n\\nEven if the bribe recipient receives a cashier’s check as a bribe and consumes it, and thereafter returns an amount equivalent to the cashier’s check to the bribe-giver, because the bribe itself has not been returned, it cannot be confiscated and the equivalent value must be collected from the bribe recipient (see Supreme Court Decisions 82DO2462, rendered on April 12, 1983, and 83DO2871, rendered on February 14, 1984, among others).\\n\\nThe lower appellate court found that Defendant 2 received KRW 30,000,000 from Nonindicted 1 in the form of cashier’s checks in denominations of KRW 100,000, consumed all of it, and then returned KRW 30,000,000 plus interest to Nonindicted 1 using other funds, and then determined that KRW 30,000,000 should be collected from Defendant 2. Reviewing that decision in light of the above legal principle and the record, it appears correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law concerning collection, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAnd it cannot be said that there is any necessity to change the above-mentioned Supreme Court precedent.\\n\\n4. The grounds of appeal of Defendant 1 and counsel Choi Jong-young (including the portions supplementing them in the statement of the supplemental petition for appeal filed by counsel Park Man-ho), as well as the grounds of appeal of Defendant 2 and counsel Jeong Tae-ryu (including the portions supplementing them in the statement of the supplemental petition for appeal filed by counsel Hong Sun-hyeop), concerning misapprehension of law regarding whether there was voluntary surrender, are considered together.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower appellate court judgment, the lower appellate court, based on the record, found that although the Defendants voluntarily appeared at the Prosecutors’ Office on February 11 or 12, 1998, Defendant 2 at first at the Prosecutors’ Office admitted receiving KRW 30,000,000 from Nonindicted 1 as a bribe, but denied the charged facts regarding KRW 50,000,000 by saying that he had not requested a bribe but had merely asked to borrow money; as to the suspicion that he had received a bribe from the side of Nonindicted 2, he denied it, and only after later stating that Nonindicted 2 and Nonindicted 4 had given money and goods did he finally admit the receipt of money and goods, but he disputed the portion concerning receipt of KRW 6,000,000, saying that it was not a bribe but a loan. Defendant 1 at first at the Prosecutors’ Office admitted receiving money and goods from Nonindicted 4 and Nonindicted 1, but with respect to KRW 50,000,000, he denied the charged facts on the ground that he had received it with intent to return it and returned it immediately, so he had no intent to appropriate it, and with respect to the remaining money and goods he denied the charged facts on the ground that there was no relation to his official duties; he denied the very receipt of money and goods from the side of Nonindicted 2; after USD 49,000 was discovered in the search of the Defendant’s home on the 13th of the same month, he continued to deny the fact of receiving money and goods from the side of Nonindicted 2, but on the 14th of the same month he finally admitted that he had received USD 70,000 from Nonindicted 4 as bribes; with regard to the relation to official duties of the receipt of KRW 50,000,000, he only admitted it when giving the fourth interrogation statement as a suspect; and in court he disputed, as to all of the charges, the amount received, the intent to appropriate, and the relation to official duties. On that basis, the court determined that, except for the portion that Defendant 2 received KRW 30,000,000 from Nonindicted 1, it could not be recognized that the Defendants had voluntarily surrendered. Reviewing this in light of the record, that determination is persuasive, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law concerning voluntary surrender, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the appeals by the Defendants are all dismissed, and it is unanimously decided by the participating Justices to include 120 days of detention after appeal in each Defendant’s principal sentence, as stated in the order."}
