question: Among the explanations concerning mistake, which is correct? (In case of dispute, according to case law)
A: Article 16 of the Criminal Act, mistake of law, includes not only ignorance of the law, in which the actor does not recognize the very existence of the legal norm prohibiting his act, but also the case in which, although the act is generally punishable, he mistakenly believes that in his special case it is an act permitted by statutes and therefore not a crime.
B: If A, with intent to kill A, mistakes B, whose appearance resembles A, for A and fires a gun at B, resulting in B’s death, then according to the concrete conformity theory, an ideal concurrence of attempted murder of A and negligent homicide of B is established for A.
C: Where, in the middle of an act violating the law, there was a time when that act had temporarily been interpreted according to case law as not being subject to punishment, the actor has, in believing that his act would not be punished, “justifiable grounds for the mistake” under Article 16 of the Criminal Act.
D: If A does not recognize that A is his own father and kills A, such a mistake does not negate the intent to commit homicide of an ascendant.
E: Where a person enters a building whose access is controlled by an administrator by obtaining the administrator’s actual consent and by the ordinary method of entry, even if there is a mistake as to the motive for consent and the administrator would not have consented to the entry had he known the actor’s actual purpose of entry, the offense of trespass upon a structure is not established.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2018DO15213]": "The grounds for appeal (the prosecutor’s reference materials submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement them) are examined.\\n\\n1. Determination on the part concerning obstruction of performance of official duties by fraudulent means\\n\\na. Where a statute prohibits certain acts, prescribes penalties for acts in violation thereof, and requires public officials to monitor and enforce compliance with the prohibition, public officials have the authority and duty to monitor, verify, and enforce against the existence of acts in violation of the prohibition. Accordingly, if one used fraudulent means to prevent a public official who is specifically and actually performing monitoring and enforcement duties from carrying out those duties, the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties by fraudulent means is established. However, if the act merely consists of violating the prohibition while avoiding the public official’s monitoring and enforcement, then, apart from the question of applying penalties thereto, it cannot be said that such act constitutes the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties by fraudulent means (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2001DO7045 decided on November 13, 2003). If the public official failed to detect the Defendant’s violation of the prohibition by evading monitoring and enforcement, this is merely the result of the public official’s neglect of the duty of monitoring and enforcement and cannot be regarded as obstruction of official duties by fraudulent means.\\n\\nArticle 93(3) of the former Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Prisoners (as in effect before its amendment by Act No. 16345 of April 23, 2019; hereinafter referred to as the “former Sentences Execution Act”) provides, “If necessary for the safety and maintenance of order of the facility, a correctional officer may inspect the clothing and personal effects of persons other than inmates entering or leaving the correctional facility. In such case, if the entrant is in possession of prohibited items under Article 92, the entrant shall be required to deposit them with the correctional facility, and if the entrant does not comply, entry may be prohibited.” Article 92 subparagraph 2 of the same Act provides as prohibited items that inmates may not possess “alcoholic beverages, tobacco, firearms, cash, checks, and other items likely to harm the safety or order of the facility,” and Article 42 subparagraph 6 of the same Act provides that, where a person “commits or intends to commit an act that harms the safety or order of the facility,” a correctional officer may suspend the visitation of the inmate who is in visitation or of the other party thereto.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 42(1) of the Rules on the Duties of Correctional Officers, based on Article 10 of the former Sentences Execution Act, provides, “A correctional officer on duty at the main gate (hereinafter referred to in this Article as a ‘main gate duty officer’) shall inspect and control persons entering and leaving the main gate and items being taken out or brought in.” Article 42(2) of the same Rules provides, “When conducting the inspection and control under paragraph (1), if the main gate duty officer deems it particularly necessary, the officer may inspect the entrant’s body and personal effects.” Article 42(3) of the same Rules provides, “If the main gate duty officer discovers any unusual or suspicious point during the inspection under paragraph (1) or (2), the officer shall immediately suspend entry or exit, report the matter to a superior, receive instructions from the superior, and take appropriate measures.”\\n\\nWhen the contents and legislative intent of the foregoing statutes and regulations are considered together, the following conclusion is reached. If electronic equipment capable of recording or filming is an item that may harm the safety or order of a correctional facility and thus needs to be prohibited from being brought in, a correctional officer has the general official authority and duty to inspect and control persons entering and leaving the correctional facility and items being taken out or brought in. If a person other than an inmate brought such prohibited items into the correctional facility, this is merely an act of violating the prohibition while evading the correctional officer’s inspection and control, and it cannot be said that the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties by fraudulent means is thereby established.\\n\\nb. The court below upheld, as is, the first-instance judgment that found this part of the indictment not guilty on the ground that it could not be said that the Defendants, in collusion, obstructed by fraudulent means the lawful performance of duties by the correctional officer in charge of visitation work. Examining the reasons given in the judgment below in light of the lawfully admitted evidence, the judgment below was based on the legal principle discussed above, and there is no error, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the law concerning the establishment of the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties by fraudulent means.\\n\\n2. Determination on the part concerning violation of the Act on Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (joint trespass into a structure)\\n\\na. If one entered a structure whose access is controlled by a manager, with the manager’s consent, by the ordinary method of entry into the structure, then, even if the manifestation of intent constituting such consent is defective due to fraud, mistake, or the like, the crime of trespass upon a structure under Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act is not established, absent special circumstances. In such a case, since there was the manager’s actual consent, there is no need to consider hypothetical or presumed intent. A mere mistake in the motive for consent does not affect the validity of the consent, and therefore, even if there are circumstances under which the manager would not have consented to entry had the manager known the actor’s actual purpose of entry, it cannot be said that the crime of trespass upon a structure is established. Furthermore, where one entered a structure by the ordinary method of entry with the manager’s actual consent, such entry cannot be evaluated, in light of the objectively and externally manifested manner of conduct at the time of entry, as entry into the structure in a form that disturbed the factual state of peace.\\n\\nb. In light of the circumstances ascertainable from the reasons of the judgment below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the Defendants, as applicants for visitation, entered the civil petition office and visitation room within Seoul Detention Center by the ordinary method of entry, after obtaining the actual consent of correctional officers entrusted with control over entry to the detention center by the warden of Seoul Detention Center, who is the manager thereof. Accordingly, they cannot be regarded as having entered Seoul Detention Center in a manner that disturbed the factual state of peace against the manager’s will.\\n\\nIn this case, the Defendants secretly carried recording and filming equipment made to resemble a business card holder into Seoul Detention Center for the purpose of recording and taping the contents of a visitation session in order to interview a person detained at Seoul Detention Center, without the permission of the warden of Seoul Detention Center. Had the warden of Seoul Detention Center or a correctional officer known of this fact, they would not have consented to the Defendants entering Seoul Detention Center while carrying such equipment. However, this circumstance merely means that there was a mistake in the motive for consent, and it cannot be evaluated that the Defendants entered the detention center against the will of the warden of Seoul Detention Center or correctional officers, or that they trespassed into the civil petition office or visitation room within Seoul Detention Center in a manner that disturbed the factual state of peace. Therefore, the Defendants’ acts do not constitute trespass upon a structure.\\n\\nc. The court below upheld, as is, the first-instance judgment that found this part of the indictment not guilty. Although there is a portion in the reasons of the judgment below that is not appropriate, there is no error in the judgment below that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the crime of trespass upon a structure, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAs the prosecutor’s appeal is without merit, all of it is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2021DO10903]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the Indictment\\nThe summary of the indictment is as follows.\\nNo one shall infringe another’s copyright property rights, or other property rights protected under the Copyright Act, by means of reproduction, public performance, public transmission, exhibition, distribution, rental, or creation of derivative works.\\nDefendant 1 is a person who operates “(site name omitted 1),” “(site name omitted 2),” and “(site name omitted 3)”—link sites for replay videos—(hereinafter collectively referred to as “the instant site”), and Defendant 2 is a person who manages the advertisement revenue from the instant site and posts link articles, among other tasks.\\nAround September 2013, Defendant 1 established on the main screen of the aforementioned “(site name omitted 1)” site bulletin-board formats such as “Broadcast Dramas,” “Variety Entertainment,” “Current Affairs and Culture,” “Japanese Dramas” (Japanese dramas), “Chinese/Taiwanese Dramas,” “U.S./British Dramas” [when clicking the category, users are moved to the “(site name omitted 3)” site], and “Movies/Animation” [when clicking the category, users are moved to the “(site name omitted 2)” site]. From around April 11, 2014 to November 11, 2015, the above Defendant, at Defendant 1’s residences in Paju-si (address omitted 1), Paju-si (address omitted 2), and the like, posted on the aforementioned “(site name omitted 1)” site, under the title “(title of post omitted),” links connected to the audiovisual work “(title of work omitted)” of Complainant Nonparty 1 Co., Ltd., which an unidentified person (user with omitted ID) had unlawfully uploaded to the video-sharing platform site “(site name omitted 4),” and arranged matters so that when such link was clicked, a new pop-up window would open and the file unlawfully uploaded to the “(site name omitted 4)” site would be played immediately, thereby enabling an unspecified number of users, regardless of whether they had registered as members of the instant site or of the “(site name omitted 4)” or “(site name omitted 5)” site, to individually transmit, through PCs and mobile devices, the various works such as broadcast programs and movies uploaded by the unidentified person, at a time and place of their own choosing, without any restrictions or consideration, each time the link was clicked.\\nAt Defendant 1’s request, Defendant 2 managed the instant site and, from July 25, 2014 to January 22, 2016, received a total of KRW 27,205,900 in revenue generated from advertisements inserted in the instant site, on 25 occasions, into a Post Office account in Defendant 2’s name; and from February 20, 2014 to February 22, 2016, received advertisement revenue of KRW 51,857,242 on a total of 67 occasions into an account in the name of Defendant 2’s younger sister, Complainant Nonparty 2, with the money to be received by Defendant 1, and newly opened a Facebook account for the “(site name omitted 1)” site to provide guidance to a circumvention route site in preparation for access blocking.\\nAccordingly, the Defendants conspired to facilitate the act of infringement of the transmission right by the unidentified person as described above, and, from around April 11, 2014 to around November 11, 2015, by the same method as above, linked in pop-up-window format a total of 460 works uploaded without the copyright holders’ permission by unidentified persons to video-sharing platform sites such as “(site name omitted 4),” thereby facilitating, for profit or habitually, the infringement of the transmission right by the unidentified persons and aiding and abetting the same.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Lower Court\\nThe lower court maintained in full the first-instance judgment, which acquitted the Defendants, for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. Even if a user of the instant site clicks on a link posted by the Defendants as a direct link and is connected to a site such as “(site name omitted 4)” where content uploaded without authorization from the copyright holder is stored, the Defendants did not facilitate the principal offender’s act itself, such as by providing the space or facilities necessary therefor or by reinforcing the intent to commit the offense, with respect to the principal offender’s act of infringing the copyright holder’s public transmission right by making illegally copied videos available for use on an overseas internet video-sharing site without the copyright holder’s permission; accordingly, the linking act in this case does not constitute aiding and abetting an act of copyright property right infringement. The fact that the Defendants posted multiple content links while organizing the titles and broadcast dates and provided a content search function, or that they derived profits by attaching advertising banners to the instant site, does not alter whether the offense of aiding and abetting is established. Such circumstances are merely data for determining, after the establishment of copyright infringement or aiding and abetting copyright infringement, whether a profit-making purpose or habituality may be recognized in the Defendants.\\n\\nB. Even if the Defendants’ acts constitute aiding and abetting a violation of the Copyright Act, the Defendants mistook their acts as not constituting a violation of the Copyright Act or aiding and abetting such violation, and such mistake was with justifiable cause.\\n\\n3. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\nHowever, the lower court judgment cannot be upheld for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. Provision of links leading to infringing posts, etc., and establishment of aiding and abetting liability for infringement of the public transmission right\\n(1) Where a person who provides a link to a post that infringes the public transmission right by means of transmission, or to a webpage where such post is located, knowingly that the principal offender is infringing the public transmission right, posts such link on an internet site on a profit-making and continuing basis, or otherwise provides links to such an extent as to enable members of the public to easily access the infringing post at a time and place individually chosen by them, that person facilitates the principal offender’s crime of making the infringing post available for public use, and therefore aiding and abetting liability for infringement of the public transmission right is established. Such linking conduct has a close relation to the realization of the principal offender’s crime of making the infringing post available for public use at a stage before the principal offender’s criminal act is completed, and, by actually increasing the opportunity for the constituent result to occur, may be evaluated as facilitating the principal offender’s execution and strengthening and increasing the infringement of the legal interest known as the public transmission right. The intent to aid and abet, as well as the principal offender’s intent, may be recognized on the part of the linker (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated September 9, 2021, 2017DO19025).\\n(2) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court, the following facts may be found.\\nAn unidentified person uploaded and posted audiovisual works described in the indictment, such as motion pictures and broadcast programs, on an overseas internet video-sharing site without the permission of the copyright holder. Such conduct constitutes infringement of the public transmission right by making the audiovisual works available for use so that members of the public may access them at a time and place individually chosen by them, without the copyright holder’s permission.\\nSo long as the unidentified person does not delete the audiovisual works uploaded as above, the criminal act of infringing the public transmission right by making such audiovisual works available for access by members of the public at times and places individually chosen by them had not been completed. During the course of such infringement of the public transmission right by the unidentified person, the Defendants conspired and, while fully aware of such criminal conduct, posted links connected to a total of 460 audiovisual works on the instant site. Users of the instant site could easily access the aforesaid audiovisual works through the links posted by the Defendants, and the Defendants were fully aware of that fact.\\nThe instant site is a link site for copyright-infringing materials, established and continuously operated by the Defendants for the purpose of obtaining advertising revenue, and the Defendants separated and posted links by type, such as movies, dramas, and variety programs, so that unspecified users could easily find links to audiovisual works, and provided a search function therefor.\\n(3) Examining the above factual relationship in light of the legal principles stated above, the Defendants, by conspiracy, posted on a profit-making and continuing basis links leading to such infringing posts, etc., on the instant site while being fully aware of the criminal conduct during the course of the unidentified person’s infringement of the public transmission right, and thereby facilitated the unidentified person’s crime of making the infringing posts available for public use by enabling members of the public to easily access the infringing posts at a time and place individually chosen by them; accordingly, aiding and abetting liability for infringement of the public transmission right may be established.\\n(4) As noted in 2. above, the lower court determined the indictment against the Defendants to be not guilty on the ground that the Defendants’ linking conduct was not an act that facilitated the principal offender’s act itself and therefore could not constitute aiding and abetting an act of copyright property right infringement. The lower court judgment erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning aiding and abetting infringement of the public transmission right, and such error affected the judgment. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\nB. Mistake of Law and Justifiable Cause\\n(1) Article 16 of the Criminal Act, under the heading “Mistake of Law,” provides that an act done under the mistaken belief that one’s act does not constitute a crime pursuant to statutes shall be punishable only when there is no justifiable cause for such mistake. This generally means that, although the act constitutes a crime, if the actor mistakenly believes that, in light of his or her special circumstances, the act is permissible under statutes and therefore not a crime, and there is justifiable cause for such belief, the act shall not be punished. Whether justifiable cause exists in such a case should be determined by whether, despite having an opportunity to reflect upon or inquire into the illegality of one’s act and, if one had made every sincere effort to avoid it by fully exercising one’s intellectual capacity, there would have been a possibility of recognizing the unlawfulness of one’s own act, the actor nevertheless failed to do so and thereby failed to recognize the unlawfulness of his or her act. The degree of effort required for such recognition of unlawfulness must be evaluated differently according to the specific circumstances of the act, the individual actor’s capacity for recognition, and the social group to which the actor belongs (see Supreme Court Decision dated March 24, 2006, 2005DO3717; Supreme Court Decision dated March 15, 2017, 2014DO12773).\\n(2) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court, the following facts may be found.\\nWhen opening the instant site around April 11, 2014, the Defendants obtained information through internet searching (googling) that setting links is not illegal, but they had never made inquiries to relevant institutions and received responses therefrom, nor had they consulted legal experts.\\nThe time when the Supreme Court Decision dated March 12, 2015, 2012DO13748, which held that merely linking to a webpage, etc., infringing the copyright holder’s public transmission right does not constitute aiding and abetting infringement of the public transmission right, was rendered was after the Defendants had begun operating the instant site, a link site for copyright-infringing materials, and it is difficult to conclude that the Defendants committed the charged offense in reliance on that decision.\\n(3) Examining the above factual relationship in light of the legal principles stated above, it cannot be said that the Defendants mistook their acts as not constituting a crime pursuant to statutes, or that there was justifiable cause for such mistake.\\nAlthough Supreme Court Decision dated March 12, 2015, 2012DO13748, was rendered while the Defendants were operating the instant site, that decision was changed by Supreme Court en banc Decision dated September 9, 2021, 2017DO19025. Even if, in the middle of a violation of law, there had been a period during which precedent temporarily interpreted such conduct as not subject to punishment, that alone cannot be deemed justifiable cause for believing that one’s conduct would not be punished (see Supreme Court Decision dated October 22, 2002, 2002DO4260).\\n(4) Nevertheless, the lower court determined that, even if the Defendants’ linking conduct constituted aiding and abetting an act of copyright property right infringement, the Defendants fell within the case where there was justifiable cause for mistaking their acts as not constituting a crime. The lower court judgment erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning justifiable cause under Article 16 of the Criminal Act, and such error affected the judgment. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe Prosecutor’s final appeal is all well-founded; accordingly, the lower court judgment shall be reversed and the case remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices, as set forth in the order."}

{"[4293HYEONGSANG494]": "Reasons\\n\\nI. Although the Defendant asserted that he had no involvement in the murder and was not present at the relevant time, the trial court, by comprehensively considering the witness statements and the circumstances surrounding the scene, found that the Defendant was present at the scene and participated in the act. That finding is not contrary to the rules of logic or experience.\\n\\nII. The Defendant’s assertion that his confession was made under coercion in the course of police investigation, and that it should therefore be disregarded, cannot be accepted on the record as a basis for overturning the lower court’s finding. In light of the surrounding evidence, the confession is not rendered unreliable merely because the Defendant later gave a contrary account.\\n\\nIII. The statements of the witnesses and the objective circumstances surrounding the occurrence are consistent with the conclusion that the Defendant and the other participants went to the village, gathered the residents, and committed the murder with knives. The lower court’s determination of the facts on this point is supported by the evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s judgment is not erroneous in its fact-finding or application of law.\\n\\nCriminal Act Article 250(1), Article 37, Article 38, and Article 41."}

{"[91DO1566]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The Defendant’s act of changing the use of the building in this case, which is a neighborhood living facility, to use it as a church without permission from the mayor or county governor, was not something that first became punishable only from 1987; rather, it is clear that even at the time when the Defendant commenced the above act of changing the use on 1985.9.1., it was an act in violation of Article 54(1), the main text of Article 5(1), and Article 48 of the Building Act then in force and was punishable. In addition, Article 16 of the Criminal Act provides that a person who, in respect of his own act, mistakes that it does not constitute a crime by virtue of a statute shall not be punished only where there is a justifiable reason for such mistake; this does not refer to mere ignorance of the law, but means that where an act is generally a criminal act, yet in the particular case the person mistakenly recognizes it as an act permitted by statute and thus not constituting a crime, and there is a justifiable reason for such recognition, he shall not be punished. Therefore, the circumstance that the Defendant did not know that the act in this case was subject to permission under the Building Act is merely simple ignorance of the law, and in particular does not constitute a case in which he affirmatively and mistakenly recognized it as an act permitted by statute and thus not constituting a crime; thus, it cannot be said to be an act resulting from a mistake of law. This argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. In this case, in which a sentence of a fine was imposed on the Defendant, the reason of improper sentencing does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. This argument is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, since the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous that the appeal be dismissed, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) concerning evidence? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) To examine “a written item that is physical evidence,” the procedures of reading aloud, notifying the contents, or inspection, which are methods of examining documentary evidence, and the procedure of presentation, which is the method of examining physical evidence, must be carried out together. (b) A photograph of the injured area submitted as evidence of injury is non-statement evidence, and the hearsay rule does not apply. (c) Since “a statement prepared during the investigative process,” which is subject to Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act, means one prepared in an investigative office under the involvement of an investigative agency after the investigation has begun, a statement prepared by a suspect at a place other than the investigative office at the request of the investigative agency does not constitute a statement prepared during the investigative process. (d) If, after the prosecutor has summoned in advance, without special circumstances, and interviewed a person whom the prosecutor intends to request and examine as a witness on the trial date, that witness testifies in court to matters unfavorable to the defendant, the witness’s in-court testimony can be found credible only if it is ensured that the prosecutor did not influence the witness’s in-court testimony through coaxing or pressure, or by leading or suggesting answers, etc., during the pre-examination interview process.

supporting_precedents: {"[2007DO3906]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the assertion that the principle of indictment-only was violated\\n\\nWhen the prosecutor petitions for a summary order, he must submit to the court, at the same time as the petition for the summary order, the documentary evidence and exhibits necessary for issuing the summary order (Criminal Procedure Rules Article 170). This is because the summary procedure is a trial based on written examination, and therefore an exception to the principle of indictment-only is recognized; accordingly, it cannot be said that the principle of indictment-only was violated merely because the documentary evidence and exhibits were submitted to the court concurrently with the petition for the summary order. Nor can it be said that, even after a request for formal trial against the summary order was filed, the fact that the court retained the documentary evidence and exhibits without returning them to the prosecutor rendered the procedure of the indictment, which had already been lawfully instituted prior thereto, unlawful.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and, as argued in the grounds for appeal, there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principle concerning the principle of indictment-only, violation of the principle of due process under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, or violation of Article 254(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act and Article 61 of the Rules on the Administrative Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases.\\n\\n2. Regarding the assertion that the petition for a summary order was unlawful\\n\\nThis part of the argument was raised only at the stage of this Court and therefore does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. Moreover, even upon examination of the record, the offense subject to the petition for a summary order in this case is the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (night-time and joint injury), and the applicable provisions are Article 2(2) and Article 2(1) of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc., and Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act, so that it is capable of being the subject of a summary order; accordingly, this ground of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Regarding the assertion that the photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person are inadmissible\\n\\nA. The reason Article 55(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act grants the defendant the right to inspect or copy the trial record is to ensure the accuracy of the record by giving the defendant an opportunity, through inspection or copying of the trial record, to confirm whether the contents of the declarant’s statement correspond to the contents of the recorded minutes, and thereby to fully guarantee the defendant’s right of defense (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO3282, rendered on October 10, 2003). Therefore, even if the defendant did not inspect or copy the trial record at a time of his choosing, such as before the next trial date, if he inspected or copied it before the conclusion of oral argument, the defendant’s right under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act to request inspection or copying of the trial record cannot be deemed infringed absent special circumstances, such as where the delay in inspection or copying hindered the exercise of the defendant’s right of defense, and the trial record must be deemed admissible as evidence of guilt.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the defendant inspected and copied the trial record of the first trial date held on April 18, 2005, on which the first trial date held on October 19, 2004, had been recorded. It can be seen that the court of first instance, at the second trial date on December 16, 2004, informed the defendant, by reference to the trial record of the first trial date, of the gist of the main matters concerning the proceedings at the first trial date, and concluded oral argument on December 8, 2005. If such are the circumstances, then even if the defendant had requested inspection and copying of the first trial record on December 13, 2004, before the second trial date in the court of first instance, and was unable to inspect or copy it, there is no indication that this caused any hindrance to the exercise of the defendant’s right of defense. Accordingly, the first trial record may be used as evidence of guilt, and therefore the argument in the grounds for appeal—that because the above first trial record cannot be used as evidence of guilt, the evidentiary examination of the “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” made at that trial date is also invalid and thus those photographs cannot be used as evidence of guilt—is without merit.\\n\\nB. Even if, as argued in the grounds for appeal, there were any illegality in the procedure by which the investigative authorities arrested the defendant in flagrante delicto, the “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” were not evidence collected from the defendant, and thus cannot be deemed illegally collected evidence. This ground of appeal is also without merit.\\n\\nC. The “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” are non-testimonial evidence, to which the hearsay rule does not apply; therefore, the ground of appeal asserting that the hearsay rule should apply on the premise that the photographs are testimonial evidence cannot be accepted.\\n\\nD. The expression of consent to evidence stipulated in Article 318 of the Criminal Procedure Act may be revoked or withdrawn until the completion of the evidentiary proceeding; however, once the evidentiary proceeding has been completed, revocation or withdrawal is not recognized, and therefore evidentiary capacity already acquired prior to revocation or withdrawal is not lost (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO2611, rendered on June 25, 2004). Upon examination of the record, it can be seen that the defendant consented at the first trial date in the court of first instance to use the above photographs as evidence, and that the court of first instance thereby completed the evidentiary examination of those photographs. Accordingly, even if the defendant, at the court below, revoked or withdrew the expression of consent to evidence regarding the above photographs, as argued in the grounds for appeal, the evidentiary capacity of the above photographs is not lost. This ground of appeal is also without merit.\\n\\nE. Therefore, the court below’s measure recognizing the evidentiary capacity of the “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” is proper, and there is no illegality such as a violation of Article 55(3), Article 307, Article 310-2, Article 312(1), or Article 318(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 12(1) of the Constitution, or Article 61 of the Rules on the Administrative Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Regarding the assertion that the defendant did not inflict injury on the non-party person\\n\\nUpon examination of the evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the court of first instance, as cited by the court below, by reference to the record, the court below’s measure of finding the facts charged in this case guilty—that the defendant grabbed the victim, the non-party person, by the collar, pushed and pulled him, and thereby inflicted on the victim an injury of an unspecified number of days for treatment consisting of abrasions to the neck and chest areas—is proper, and there is no illegality, such as a violation of the rules of evidence and logic, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the order, with the concurrence of all participating Justices."}

{"[2013DO2511]": "The Court determines the grounds for appeal (the statements in the respective supplemental appellate briefs submitted by the Defendants after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Determination of the Defendants’ grounds for appeal and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\nA. As to the argument regarding the principle of indictment-only\\n\\nAs a general rule, when a prosecutor institutes a prosecution, the indictment must not attach documents or other objects that may create prejudice in the court regarding the case, nor may it cite their contents (Criminal Procedure Rules Article 118(2)). However, whether this principle against indictment by reference has been violated must be determined specifically in the particular case by considering, in light of the type and content of the offense stated in the indictment, the contents of the documents or other objects attached to or cited in the indictment, and whether, in addition to the matters required by law, the facts stated in the indictment may create prejudice in the judge and hinder the judge from grasping the substance of the criminal facts (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009. 10. 22., 2009DO7436).\\n\\nThe lower court determined that, although the indictment in this case cited written materials and photographs to be submitted as evidence, such citations were for the purpose of specifying the facts charged for each violation of the National Security Act in this case or concerned part of the objective and subjective constituent elements, and that the cited portions did not hinder the Defendants’ exercise of their defense rights nor create prejudice in the judge or hinder the judge from grasping the substance of the criminal facts, and thus could not be regarded as violating the principle against indictment by reference.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the principle against indictment by reference as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nB. As to the argument regarding the illegality of the seizure and search execution procedure and the resulting admissibility of evidence\\n\\n(1) The lower court, after comprehensively considering the circumstances as found in its reasoning, determined that it could not be deemed that the Defendants were in a de facto state of detention at the time of execution of the seizure and search warrant for the office of the National Intelligence Service investigator against Non-party 1 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Non-party 1 Company”). Examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the record, the lower court’s above factual finding and determination are proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in omitting a determination on necessary matters or in misunderstanding the legal principles regarding the guarantee of the right to participate in the execution of a seizure and search warrant or the legality of such execution.\\n\\n(2) In addition, the lower court determined that, because the columns “place and person/body to be seized, searched, and inspected” in the seizure, search, and inspection warrant of this case stated the residence of Defendant 1 and the body of Defendant 1, even though the above warrant had been presented and the seizure and search of Defendant 1’s body had been completed, the seizure and search of Defendant 1’s residence could not yet be deemed to have commenced, and on such reasons as stated in its reasoning, the act of the National Intelligence Service investigators in executing the seizure and search of Defendant 1’s residence pursuant to the above warrant was not unlawful. Examining this in light of the record, the lower court’s above determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the warrant principle, etc.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the lower court determined that, at the time of the seizure and search of Defendant 3’s residence, the investigator in charge notified Non-party 2, who was Defendant 3’s wife and was stated as a co-suspect in the seizure and search warrant, of the fact of execution of the warrant and then presented the warrant, and considering, among other things, the circumstances that, at the time of execution, the seizure and search of the office of Non-party 1 Company jointly operated by Defendant 3 took place simultaneously and Defendant 3 participated in the seizure and search of that office, Defendant 3’s right to participate in the seizure and search of the residence was not substantively infringed. Examining the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the warrant principle, etc.\\n\\n(4) Furthermore, the lower court determined that the “result of execution of restrictive measures on communications concerning e-mail,” which the trial court inspected, was directed at the contents of electronic mail that Defendant 1 sent and received in real time, obtained and recorded pursuant to the court’s warrant permitting restrictive measures on communications, and that Criminal Procedure Act Articles 219 and 123, concerning execution of warrants and the participation of the person in charge, do not apply to the execution procedure of the above permit; and it recognized the admissibility of the inspection result on the grounds, inter alia, that the trial court directly inspected in the inspection procedure whether the original electronic mail was identical to the printout. Examining this in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the legal nature of restrictive measures on communications concerning e-mail or the identity of electronic evidence.\\n\\nC. As to the argument regarding infringement of the right to a public trial and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\n(1) The latter sentence of Article 27(3) of the Constitution provides, “Any accused person shall have the right to a speedy and public trial in the absence of exceptional circumstances where a trial may be held in camera as provided by law.” Thus, it declares that the criminal defendant’s right to a public trial is guaranteed as a fundamental right. Article 109 of the Constitution and Article 57(1) of the Court Organization Act provide that trials and judgments shall be public, but that the hearing may be non-public by decision when there is a risk of harming national security, public peace and order, or good morals and manners. Article 57(2) of the Court Organization Act provides that a decision prohibiting public access concerning the hearing of a trial shall be pronounced stating the reasons. In light of the purport of these provisions, if a decision was made to prohibit public access to the hearing of a trial even though there was no ground for prohibition of public access under Article 109 of the Constitution and Article 57(1) of the Court Organization Act, such decision prohibiting public access would infringe the Defendant’s right to a public trial, and the testimony of a witness taken through that procedure would have no admissibility as evidence. This is not altered even if the defense counsel’s right of cross-examination was guaranteed (see Supreme Court Decision 2005. 10. 28., 2005DO5854), and the same applies even where the reason for the decision prohibiting public access is unknown, such as where no pronouncement of a decision prohibiting public access was made.\\n\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that at the fourth trial date of the first instance, the trial court conducted the witness examination of Non-party 3 without pronouncing a decision prohibiting public access, and that the examination was conducted in a non-public state. In light of the above legal principles, there was a procedural illegality infringing the Defendants’ right to a public trial in the witness examination procedure for Non-party 3; thus, the witness examination record for Non-party 3, a piece of evidence collected in that procedure, cannot be used as evidence of guilt against the Defendants.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s action in upholding the first-instance judgment, which otherwise used the witness examination record for Non-party 3 as evidence of guilt, contains an error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the principle of public trial and the admissibility of evidence. However, examining the relevant evidence in light of the record, even excluding the witness examination record for Non-party 3, which lacks admissibility as evidence, the remaining evidence admitted by the lower court—namely, various documents including the “organizational status report,” the respective in-court statements of witness Non-party 4, Non-party 5, and the National Intelligence Service investigators, and the images of each on-site photograph, as well as the respective entry and exit records of Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 5—sufficiently establishes the points of spy activity for the purpose of execution and special intrusion/escape among the facts charged in this case that the lower court found guilty. Therefore, the lower court’s conclusion finding this part of the facts charged guilty is proper, and ultimately the above error by the lower court cannot be deemed to have affected the judgment.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, Criminal Procedure Act Article 56 provides, “Matters entered in the trial record as procedural acts on the trial date shall be proved only by that record.” Therefore, insofar as the first-instance trial record of the 26th hearing states that the trial court, after pronouncing a decision prohibiting public access, conducted the witness examination procedure for the above investigators in a non-public state, proof or rebuttal by means other than the trial record regarding whether such decision prohibiting public access was pronounced is not permitted. In the same context, the lower court’s action determining that each of the above witnesses’ in-court statements had admissibility as evidence is proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the principle of public trial.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the lower court recognized, based on the trial record, the fact that at the fourth trial date of the first instance, in the witness examination procedure for Non-party 6, and at the fifth trial date, in the partial witness examination procedure for Non-party 7 and the witness examination procedure for Non-party 8, the trial proceeded non-publicly without pronouncing a decision prohibiting public access, and determined that the in-court statements of such witnesses lacked admissibility as evidence. The lower court’s determination on this point follows the above legal principles and is proper, and there is no illegality, such as failure to fully deliberate, as argued in the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal.\\n\\nD. As to the argument concerning the integrity and identity of documents printed from seized information storage media, and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\n(1) In order to use as evidence the character information stored by input into a seized computer disk or other similar information storage medium (hereinafter referred to only as “information storage medium”) or its printout (hereinafter referred to as “printed document”), the identity between the contents stored in the original information storage medium and the printed document must be recognized, and for this purpose, the circumstance that the original information storage medium was not altered from the time of seizure until the time of document output, that is, integrity, must be secured. In particular, in the case of a document printed from a medium that “hard-copied” or “imaged” the data stored on the storage medium in lieu of the original information storage medium, not only must the identity of the data between the original information storage medium and the “hard-copied” or “imaged” medium be recognized, but also the mechanical accuracy of the computer used in the process of verification, the reliability of the program, and the operator’s professional technical ability and accuracy at each stage of input, processing, and output must be secured (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2007. 12. 13., 2007DO7257). In this case, as a matter of principle, the fact that the printed document and the data stored in the information storage medium are identical, and that the original information storage medium was not altered until the time of document output, shall be proved by the method of receiving from the party subjected to seizure/search a written confirmation signed to the effect that the hash values of the original information storage medium and the “hard-copied” or “imaged” medium are identical and submitting it to the court; however, where proof by such method is impossible or markedly difficult, the integrity and identity may also be recognized by testimony of investigators or experts who participated in a series of procedures such as seizure, sealing, unsealing, “hard-copying,” or “imaging” of the original information storage medium, by proving circumstances such as the identical hash values between the original information storage medium and the “hard-copied” or “imaged” medium or that the original information storage medium remained sealed from the time of initial seizure until submission of evidence and was not altered at all, or by a method in which the court compares the data stored in the original and the printed document submitted as evidence. It cannot be said that proof must necessarily be made only by means such as playback of video recordings of the seizure and search process.\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court, based on the following circumstances recognized through the respective testimonies of the National Intelligence Service investigators who executed the seizure and search of the office of Non-party 1 Company or the residences of the Defendants, and the experts who participated in the “imaging” procedure at the National Intelligence Service office, namely: the National Intelligence Service investigators seized the respective information storage media indicated in the lower court’s reasoning in the presence of the Defendants or their family members and employees, then sealed them after obtaining the participants’ signatures; when the National Intelligence Service duplicated data stored in some information storage media by the “imaging” method, the seal status was checked, unsealed, and resealed after obtaining signatures from the Defendants or the above experts; and these persons signed to the effect that the hash values of the original information storage media and the hash values of the files created through the “imaging” work were identical; together with the circumstance that the trial court conducted an inspection with the participation of both the Defendants and the Prosecutor and defense counsel, and in that inspection process verified that the hash values produced in the inspection were identical to the hash values produced during “imaging” while a write-protection device was attached at the time of seizure and search, or verified that the character information of the files created through the “imaging” work and the printed documents were identical; and the circumstance that, in the case of some information storage media, the court confirmed the existence, inside the sealed envelope of the portion concerning the inspection result carried out by the lower court, of a previously unsealed envelope that appears to have been signed by the expert who participated in the “imaging” process as an expert on electronic information—all taken together, the lower court determined that the printed documents submitted as evidence, as stated in its reasoning, were not only identical to the contents stored in the original seized information storage media, but also that the original information storage media had not been altered until the time of document output, and therefore the printed documents could be used as evidence.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the method or degree of proof for the integrity, identity, and reliability of electronic evidence. Furthermore, there is also no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in the lower court’s action rejecting the Defendants’ argument to the effect that the above information storage media, etc. had been manipulated by investigative agencies or that the Defendants did not own or possess such information storage media.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, as to the MP3 file submitted as evidence concerning the point of praise and encouragement arising from possession of enemy-related expressive materials by Defendant 2, the lower court determined that the file could not be used as evidence, and acquitted on this part of the facts charged, on the grounds that, according to the trial court’s inspection result, traces of access to the hard disk on which the above MP3 file was stored appeared at a time after the seizure and search had begun, and even according to the testimony of the National Intelligence Service investigator who was in charge of the seizure and search at the time, no reasonable explanation was revealed regarding the circumstances of such access.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the record, the lower court’s determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning admissibility of evidence or in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nE. As to the application of the hearsay rule\\n\\n(1) When the character information stored by input into an information storage medium by the Defendant or a person other than the Defendant, or its printout, is used as evidence, it is in substance not greatly different from a written statement prepared by the Defendant or the non-Defendant or a document recording that person’s statement, and in light of the possibility of manipulation after seizure and during the printing process, and the fact that the opportunity for cross-examination is not fundamentally guaranteed, the hearsay rule applies to the truth of its contents. Therefore, as a general rule, such evidence may be used only when the authenticity of its formation is proved by the statement of its maker or declarant pursuant to Criminal Procedure Act Article 313(1). However, where the fact to be proved is not the truth of the contents of the character information stored in the information storage medium but the existence of such character information itself, the hearsay rule does not apply (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 99DO2317 dated 1999. 9. 3. and 2010DO3504 dated 2013. 2. 15.). Furthermore, when a certain statement is used as direct evidence of the criminal facts, even if that statement constitutes hearsay evidence, it does not necessarily become hearsay evidence when it is used as circumstantial evidence of the very fact that such statement was made or of indirect facts unrelated to the truth of the statement (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 99DO1252 dated 2000. 2. 25.).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court determined that, in the case of communication by exchanging documents with members of an anti-state organization, where the facts charged relate to having received instructions from an anti-state organization and having searched for and collected state secrets, if the received instructions and the state secrets searched for and collected exist in the form of documents, or if the object of the provision of convenience is documents, the truth of the contents of the documents is not at issue; rather, the very existence of documents containing such contents is evidence, and therefore the hearsay rule does not apply to such facts charged, and the printed documents submitted as evidence concerning that part of the facts charged have admissibility as evidence.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, most of the contents of the printed documents submitted as evidence for this part of the facts charged fall within the category where, in relation to the facts to be proved, the issue is not whether the contents of the documents are true, but the very existence of character information containing such contents is evidence. Therefore, the above determination by the lower court is proper and acceptable within that scope.\\n\\nHowever, among the contents of the above printed documents, some include contents such as “○○○ (Defendant 5) is active as a political affairs special advisor, etc. under the chairman of the election countermeasures committee of the △△ Party,” and contents reporting the Defendants’ own experiences and activities. In such cases, in relation to the “search and collection” of state secrets, which is the fact to be proved, whether the Defendants actually engaged in such experiences and activities, that is, whether the contents of the documents are true, becomes an issue, and there is room for application of the hearsay rule. Thus, it was erroneous for the lower court to conclude broadly that the hearsay rule does not apply even to the parts of the entire printed documents that describe the Defendants’ own experiences and activities. However, these document contents constitute only a very small part of the entire set of documents submitted as evidence, and according to the evidence, including the lawful in-court statement of witness Non-party 4 adopted by the first instance, together with the contents of most of the document contents that the lower court properly determined were not subject to the hearsay rule, even excluding from the evidence of guilt the parts of the printed documents concerning the Defendants’ actual experiences and activities, there is sufficient basis to recognize this part of the facts charged as guilty. Therefore, the lower court’s conclusion finding each part of these facts charged guilty is proper and acceptable. Accordingly, the above error by the lower court cannot be deemed to have affected the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, according to the reasons of the lower court judgment, with respect to Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 5’s special intrusion/escape and meeting, the court below can be seen to have relied, as one of the indirect facts supporting a guilty finding, on the fact that files containing contents such as “To Mr. Non-party 9: regarding the 2011 interview, I think it would be preferable to conduct it in Beijing with Non-party 9 and Mr. ▽▽ from January 30 to February 1” had been “saved” on Defendant 1’s computer.\\n\\nExamining this in light of the above legal principles, if one seeks to prove that Defendant 1 and Defendant 5 actually met with North Korean operatives at that time, as described in the contents, the truth of the document contents is at issue, and the hearsay rule would apply. However, the fact itself that a file containing such contents was stored on Defendant 1’s computer is unrelated to the truth of the contents and constitutes an indirect fact for proving this part of the facts charged. Therefore, the hearsay rule cannot be said to apply even in such a case. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the hearsay rule or the granting of admissibility as evidence.\\n\\nF. As to the admissibility of photographs taken overseas\\n\\n(1) Any person has the freedom not to have his or her face or appearance arbitrarily photographed; however, such freedom is not guaranteed without limitation, and to the extent necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, reasonable restrictions may be imposed within that scope. Where investigative agencies photograph in the course of investigating crime when the offense is currently being committed or has just been committed, there is a need and urgency to preserve evidence, and the photograph is taken by a generally permitted and reasonable method, the mere fact that the photography was conducted without a warrant does not necessarily make it unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO2317 dated 1999. 9. 3.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court, the video recording of Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 5 meeting with North Korean operatives in Japan or China was made because there was a need to preserve evidence of the Defendants’ meetings, and it can be seen that the Defendants were photographed while meeting with members of an anti-state organization or immediately before or after such meetings, and the locations of the photography were public places such as roads used by vehicles, the street in front of a restaurant, or the hotel front desk. Accordingly, such photography was not conducted by a method beyond what is generally permitted and reasonable, nor can it be deemed unlawful as a coercive disposition without a warrant. Therefore, under such circumstances, the lower court’s determination that the above photography was not unlawful and its recognition of the admissibility of the photographs capturing the 6mm tape video, as stated in its reasoning, are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the scope of application of the warrant principle or the legal principles concerning the right of portrait.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, according to the reasons of the lower court judgment, it can be seen that the lower court rejected the Defendants’ argument that the above video-captured photographs should be denied admissibility as illegally obtained evidence infringing the foreign territorial sovereignty that ought to be guaranteed under international law and violating the international criminal judicial cooperation procedures, and used them as evidence of guilt.\\n\\nAlthough the filming constituted an investigative act for the collection of evidence and the place of filming was within the territory of Japan or China rather than Korea, considering that the person filmed was a Korean national and that, as stated above, the filming was conducted by a generally permitted and reasonable method in a public place and thus cannot be said to be a coercive disposition, such circumstances do not constitute grounds for denying the admissibility as evidence of the evidence obtained through the filming act. In the end, the lower court’s action recognizing the admissibility of the above photographs is proper, and there is no illegality, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of application of the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nG. As to the argument concerning the “overseas residence” requirement under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314\\n\\n“Overseas residence” under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314 is not satisfied merely because the person who is to give a statement is simply located abroad; exceptionally, the requirement can be satisfied only where there are circumstances making it impossible to have that person appear in court even if all possible and reasonable means are used (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 2007DO10004 dated 2008. 2. 28. and 2011DO1013 dated 2011. 7. 14.). Although, in general, whether the requirement is satisfied is determined through procedures such as confirming the whereabouts and dispatching a summons, such procedures are not always necessary; in some cases, even if such procedures are not followed, if the court can recognize circumstances making it difficult to expect that person to be examined in court, the requirement must be deemed satisfied (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2001DO5666 dated 2002. 3. 26.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, Non-party 10 is a person who left North Korea after working as an operative of the External Liaison Department, the predecessor of North Korea’s Bureau 225, which is in charge of operations against South Korea, and after giving a statement at the National Intelligence Service on 2011. 6. 15. regarding his experiences from when he had worked as an operative, he has since his move to Japan around 2011. 7. 22. remained in a state where his residence or whereabouts are unknown except for communication by e-mail. At the time of his statement at the National Intelligence Service, he expressed his plan to move, and also stated that after moving he would find and submit materials related to his statement; the investigative agency, after confirming Non-party 10’s departure from the country, repeatedly requested his appearance as a witness via his e-mail address, which was his only contact information, together with a notice upon entry into the country, but Non-party 10 clearly indicated through a handwritten statement that he refused to testify.\\n\\nIn addition, when the circumstances that, even under the criminal judicial assistance treaty concluded between Korea and Japan, it is impossible to forcibly apprehend Non-party 10 and bring him to this court, are comprehensively considered, even if Non-party 10’s whereabouts were confirmed and a summons were sent, it would be difficult to expect that he would appear in court as a witness. Therefore, even if measures such as confirming his Japanese address and dispatching a witness summons were not fully taken, the “overseas residence” requirement under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314 must be deemed satisfied. In the same sense, the lower court’s determination recognizing the admissibility of the statement record of Non-party 10 on the basis that it satisfied not only the “overseas residence” requirement but also that his statement was proved to have been made under circumstances of special reliability is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for granting admissibility of evidence under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314 or in failing to fully deliberate.\\n\\nH. As to the argument regarding the installation of shielding facilities\\n\\nUnder Article 17 of the National Intelligence Service Employees Act, an employee of the National Intelligence Service has a duty not to divulge secrets acquired in the course of duty (paragraph 1), and where an employee intends, as a witness pursuant to law, to testify concerning matters of official secrets, prior permission from the Director of the National Intelligence Service must be obtained (paragraph 2); where the Director of the National Intelligence Service permits testimony under paragraph 2, the court may take appropriate measures, such as non-public testimony, to protect official secrets (paragraph 6).\\n\\nAccording to the record and the reasons of the lower court judgment, it can be seen that, at the 26th trial date in the first instance, during each witness examination of the National Intelligence Service investigators, the trial court pronounced a decision that the witnesses’ personal information and the witness examination procedure would be conducted non-publicly, and proceeded with the witness examination in a state where shielding facilities were installed so that the Defendants or their counsel could not see the appearance of the National Intelligence Service employees, and only the bench could see them. In light of the purport of the above provisions, the contents of the testimony concerned the circumstances of the witnesses having photographed the meeting between Defendant 1, etc. and the North Korean operative in China or Japan, and thus concerned matters of official secrets of the National Intelligence Service employees. Therefore, the trial court’s measure of installing shielding facilities to protect such secrets should be regarded as part of the “appropriate measures for the protection of official secrets.”\\n\\nFurthermore, even if, due to the installation of such shielding facilities, defense counsel could not see the witness during cross-examination, in light of the fact that detailed cross-examination was conducted regarding the above photographing circumstances, and the above witnesses answered relatively in detail regarding matters other than portions relating to some official secrets, it cannot be said that the defense counsel’s defense rights were substantively infringed or that the legitimacy of the judgment itself became impossible to recognize, and thus this cannot be deemed an illegality affecting the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO3983 dated 2007. 6. 1.). The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the guarantee of the defense counsel’s right of cross-examination, the principle of direct examination, or the scope of application of the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence.\\n\\nI. As to the argument concerning the method of examination of documentary evidence\\n\\nUnder Criminal Procedure Act Article 292 and Criminal Procedure Rules Article 134-6, when documentary evidence is examined, the applicant, in principle, shall read it aloud, but when the presiding judge deems it necessary, the applicant may be directed to state its gist in lieu thereof, and when inspection by reading is deemed more appropriate than other methods, examination may be conducted by presenting the documentary evidence and allowing it to be read. Meanwhile, under Criminal Procedure Act Article 292-2(1), when examining physical evidence, the applicant shall present it.\\n\\nIn light of the purport of these provisions, to examine the so-called “written document as physical evidence,” which is originally physical evidence but also has the nature of documentary evidence, the procedures for examination of documentary evidence—reading, disclosure of contents, or inspection—and the procedure for examination of physical evidence—presentation—must be carried out together. Therefore, as a rule, the evidentiary applicant must be made to read the document while presenting it, or in lieu thereof, disclose or inspect its contents.\\n\\nThe lower court determined that the first-instance court had adopted as evidence the books allegedly possessed by Defendant 1 and Defendant 3 as enemy-related expressive materials, and that in light of the circumstances that evidence examination was conducted by presentation and disclosure of contents for those books, the examination method was not unlawful and the admissibility of the books could not be denied. The lower court’s factual findings and determinations are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of recognition of admissibility as evidence.\\n\\nJ. As to the argument concerning the point of execution for the purpose of attaining the objective (spy activity), and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\n(1) The “state secret” prescribed in Article 4(1)2(b) of the National Security Act is limited to cases where the secret is any fact, object, or knowledge that is not already widely known to the general public domestically through lawful procedures, etc., and whose being kept secret or unconfirmed vis-à-vis an anti-state organization in matters such as politics, economy, society, or culture is in the interest of the Republic of Korea; and where disclosure of its contents is likely to cause a danger to national security, thereby having substantial value warranting secret protection. This has been the Supreme Court’s settled view since the en banc Decision 97DO985 dated 1997. 9. 16. While interpreting the general meaning of “state secret” in this limited manner, and considering that the above provision not only limits the subject of the act to “a member of an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom,” but also makes it a constituent element that the act be “an act for the purpose of carrying out the objective of an anti-state organization,” thereby imposing limitations in terms of the subject and manner of the act, it cannot be said that the provision violates the principle of definiteness required by the principle of nulla poena sine lege to the extent of being unconstitutional.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the issue of how to punish a certain crime, namely the choice of the type and range of the statutory penalty, is a matter to be determined by the legislature after comprehensively considering not only the nature of the crime and the protected legal interest, but also our history and culture, the circumstances of the times at the time of legislation, the value judgments and legal sentiments of the general public, and criminal policy aspects for crime prevention. Accordingly, broad legislative discretion or freedom of formation should be recognized in this area. Therefore, unless the statutory penalty for a crime is so excessively harsh in comparison with the nature of the crime and the responsibility of the actor that it markedly loses balance within the penal system, or departs from the degree necessary to achieve the original purpose and function of punishment for that crime, and thus clearly violates the principle of equality or proportionality, it should not be readily concluded to be unconstitutional (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 2012NO4637 dated 2012. 9. 27. and 2009DO13197 dated 2012. 10. 25.).\\n\\nExamining this in light of such legal principles, the mere circumstance that, unlike Article 11 of the Military Secrets Protection Act, which provides for a statutory penalty of imprisonment for not more than 10 years for the act of searching for and collecting military secrets, the statutory penalty for Article 4(1)2(b) of the National Security Act, which is the punitive provision in this case, provides for death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for not less than 7 years, does not mean that the above provision prescribes excessively severe punishment in violation of the principle of responsibility, nor can it be said to be a provision that violates the principle of equality because its statutory penalty has lost balance within the penal system. Nor can it be deemed to substantially infringe the judge’s authority to determine and decide sentencing.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, in order to fall under “state secret” within the above legal provision, the relevant information must, as noted above, not belong to facts, objects, or knowledge already publicly known. Whether such matters are publicly known should be determined by considering various circumstances, such as the degree of development of mass media or communication means like newspapers and broadcasting, the scope of readers and listeners, and the subject of publication, and by the standard of whether it can be judged that an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom no longer needs to search for, collect, confirm, or verify it. Whether disclosure poses a substantial risk should be determined according to sound common sense and social norms, taking into account the status of confrontation between the Republic of Korea and North Korea or other anti-state organizations and security matters at the time the secret was collected (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 97DO985 dated 1997. 9. 16.).\\n\\nApplying this legal principle, the lower court, for the reasons stated in its reasoning, determined as follows: as to the part of the facts charged that the first-instance judgment found guilty and which was maintained, on the premise that the contents of the relevant documents were facts or knowledge not publicly known and, if disclosed, there was a risk of causing danger to national security, thus constituting “state secrets,” Defendant 1, Defendant 3, and Defendant 5 were recognized as having “searched for and collected” such secrets as “a member of an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom”; whereas, as to the part of the facts charged that maintained the acquittal of the first-instance judgment or reversed the guilty portion of the first-instance judgment and was found not guilty, the contents of the relevant documents were deemed not to constitute “state secrets” on the grounds that they were facts or knowledge already publicly known through media reports, etc. at the time of search and collection, or merely subjective predictions or opinions based thereon.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the respective grounds for appeal by the above Defendants and the Prosecutor, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of “state secrets” or “search and collection” or in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nK.
