As to Defendant 4’s point of providing convenience (guilty part)\\n\\nArticle 3 of the former Act on Inter-Korean Exchange and Cooperation (before amendment by Act No. 7539 on 2005. 5. 31.) provides: “With respect to acts for the purpose of exchange and cooperation between South Korea and North Korea, such as movement, trade, cooperative projects, and provision of communication services between South Korea and North Korea, this Act shall apply in preference to other laws within the scope recognized as justifiable.” The phrase “other laws” here includes the National Security Act, but for the preferential application to apply, the act of a resident of South Korea contacting a resident of North Korea by meeting, communication, or other means must be an act “for the purpose of inter-Korean exchange and cooperation” and be “recognized as justifiable” or fall “within the scope of the purpose of the above Act,” and whether it falls thereunder must be determined objectively by comprehensively considering the circumstances leading to such act, whether reporting, etc. was made as prescribed by the same Act, and the conduct before and after the act (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO6310 dated 2012. 10. 25.).\\n\\nThe lower court, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, upheld the first-instance judgment that found Defendant 4 guilty of this part of the facts charged, on the grounds that Defendant 4’s act, in around June 2005, of taking the lead in creating and providing the Internet Chosun press information base (KPM) site to Joseon Media, an organization under Chongryon, an anti-state organization, posed a risk of endangering the existence and security of the Republic of Korea or the free democratic basic order, and that the mere circumstance that Defendant 4 had previously obtained approval from the Ministry of Unification for contact with residents could not render his act justifiable under the above Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above factual findings and determinations are proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence or in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of the offense of providing convenience.\\n\\nL. As to the points of receipt of money and valuables, special intrusion/escape, meeting/communication contact, possession/distribution of enemy-related expressive materials, and provision of convenience (each guilty part)\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the evidence admitted by the first-instance judgment cited by the lower court (excluding, however, the witness examination record for Non-party 3 discussed above) and the record, the lower court’s determination that all of the respective facts charged in this part were guilty for the reasons stated in its reasoning is proper, and there is no illegality, such as failure to fully deliberate by misunderstanding the legal principles asserted in the grounds for appeal, or in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of granting admissibility as evidence, or in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nM. As to the remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe Defendants’ remaining grounds for appeal concern violations of law that do not affect the outcome of the judgment, or they challenge the selection and weighing of evidence and factual findings, or they are matters not raised as grounds for appeal before and are asserted only for the first time in the statement of grounds for appeal, and thus do not constitute lawful grounds for appeal. Furthermore, even upon ex officio review, no illegality as argued in the grounds for appeal can be found in the lower court judgment.\\n\\n2. Determination of the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. As to the point of constituting an anti-state organization, special intrusion/escape, and meeting (not guilty part)\\n\\nThe lower court, on the premise that where the constitution of an anti-state organization or special intrusion/escape and meeting is the fact to be proved, the truth of the contents stated in the documents becomes an issue, and therefore the contents of printed documents whose authenticity of formation has not been proved by the maker cannot be used as evidence directly proving the relevant facts charged, upheld the first-instance judgment that acquitted the Defendants on the ground that the evidence related to this part, namely the existence of the documents, the in-court statement of witness Non-party 4, and records concerning the Defendants’ entry and exit, alone were insufficient to prove the crime for each of these parts of the facts charged.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in violating logic and empirical rules and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nB. As to the points of possession/distribution of enemy-related expressive materials and provision of convenience (each not guilty part)\\n\\nIn order to be recognized as enemy-related expressive materials under Article 7(5) of the National Security Act, the contents of the expressive materials must be affirmative and aggressive, threatening the existence and security of the state and the free democratic basic order, which are the protected legal interests of the National Security Act. Whether such subversive character exists in the expressive materials must be determined by comprehensively considering not only the overall contents of the expressive materials but also the motive for their creation, the manner of the expression itself, external related matters, and the circumstances at the time of the expressive act (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2010DO1189 dated 2010. 7. 23. and Supreme Court Decision 2012DO7455 dated 2012. 10. 11.).\\n\\nThe lower court, comprehensively considering circumstances such as that the expressive materials as stated in its reasoning that Defendant 1 and Defendant 4 possessed or distributed, or that Defendant 4 posted, were videos that did not use expressions sympathetic to North Korea’s assertions or doctrines, or were posted by citing domestic press materials, determined that they cannot be viewed as affirmative and aggressive materials threatening the existence and security of the state and the free democratic basic order, and that Defendant 4’s conduct in this part cannot be deemed to have had the purpose of subversive activity, and on such grounds acquitted all of the respective facts charged in this part.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning enemy-related expressive materials or the purpose of subversive activity under the National Security Act, or in violating logic and rules of experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nC. As to the point of sympathizing with enemy activity\\n\\nAs an element of the offense of praising or sympathizing with the activities of an anti-state organization, etc. under Article 7(1) of the National Security Act, “sympathizing” means to respond to or join the activities of an anti-state organization, etc. by making assertions of the same content as the propaganda, incitement, and activities of an anti-state organization, etc., or by engaging in conduct consistent therewith, and such act of “sympathizing” must reach the level of presenting a clear danger that can cause substantial harm to the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DO758 dated 2008. 4. 17. and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO3504 dated 2013. 2. 15.).\\n\\nThe lower court upheld the first-instance judgment that acquitted this part of the facts charged on the grounds that, in light of the gist of the declaration in which Defendant 3 is said to have participated, and the social discussion and circumstances at the time of the declaration, the mere circumstance that Defendant 3 engaged in search and collection of state secrets around that time does not make Defendant 3’s participation in the declaration such that it can be evaluated as praising, encouraging, or propagandizing the activities of an anti-state organization, etc., and thus cannot be said to present a clear danger that can cause substantial harm to the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning sympathy with enemy activity or in violating logic and rules of experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nD. As to the point of communication contact (not guilty part)\\n\\nThe offense of meeting/communication, etc. under Article 8(1) of the National Security Act is constituted when, while knowing that the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order are threatened, one makes contact by meeting, communication, or other means with a member of an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom, and such meeting, etc. presents a clear danger of causing substantial harm to the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DO758 dated 2008. 4. 17. and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO6310 dated 2012. 10. 25.).\\n\\nThe lower court, comprehensively considering circumstances such as that the documents as stated in its reasoning cannot be regarded as core technology of a vehicle number recognition system received from a member of an anti-state organization or as materials related to the economy, military, diplomacy, etc. of the Republic of Korea, determined that Defendant 1’s act of exchanging documents containing such contents does not present a danger to the existence and security of the Republic of Korea or the free democratic basic order, and on such grounds acquitted this part of the facts charged.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning communication contact or in violating logic and rules of experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nE. As to the remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe lower court, with respect to some of the so-called overseas photographs, recognized admissibility as evidence, and with respect to the remaining photographs denied such admissibility, and then upheld the first-instance judgment that found some of the facts charged concerning special intrusion/escape and meeting guilty on the grounds that, even excluding such evidence lacking admissibility, the other evidence as stated in its reasoning, taken together, was sufficient to recognize the related criminal facts. Therefore, the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal disputing the lower court’s determination on the admissibility of the above photographs concern matters not affecting the outcome of the judgment and cannot constitute lawful grounds for appeal.\\n\\nMeanwhile, under the interpretation of Criminal Procedure Act Article 383(4), the Prosecutor cannot assert as grounds for appeal that the lower court’s sentencing is too lenient or that the lower court violated the rules of evidence in recognizing the factual premise for sentencing against the Defendant’s interest. Therefore, this too cannot constitute lawful grounds for appeal (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2005DO1952 dated 2005. 9. 15.).\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the Court dismisses both the Defendants’ appeal and the Prosecutor’s appeal, and renders the judgment as per the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO15891]": "The grounds of appeal (the defendant’s supplemental appellate brief submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds of appeal) are determined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nThe Constitution proclaims, in the latter sentence of Article 12(1), the principle of due process, and guarantees in Article 27 the right to trial. In order to implement these principles substantively, the Criminal Procedure Act adopts as its basic principles the adversarial system and the trial-centered principle, under which the substantive examination of a criminal case must be conducted in an open courtroom through the offensive and defensive activities of both the prosecutor and the defendant, and the principles of direct examination and evidence-based adjudication, under which the finding of the facts charged must be based only on evidence directly examined in the presence of the judge. Accordingly, after a prosecution is instituted, all authority over the criminal procedure concerning that case belongs to the court seized of the case presiding over it, and the suspect who was the subject of the investigation assumes the status of a defendant, a party equal to the prosecutor, and exercises the right of defense (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO7436, decided October 22, 2009, and Supreme Court Decision 2009DO10412, decided April 28, 2011).\\n\\nIn light of these basic principles of the Criminal Procedure Act, where a person whom the prosecutor has requested and examined as a witness on the trial date is, without special circumstances, summoned in advance to the investigative authority and interviewed, and thereafter the witness makes a statement in court unfavorable to the defendant, the witness’s in-court testimony may be relied upon only if it is guaranteed that the prosecutor did not influence the witness’s in-court testimony through persuasion, pressure, leading responses, or suggestion during the pre-examination interview. Even if the prosecutor may interview a witness in advance as needed for the preparation of witness examination, the possibility cannot be ruled out that the witness may be coached or guided through a unilateral advance interview, without the court’s or the defendant’s participation, and thereby make distorted statements in court. The circumstance that there was no persuasion or pressure upon the witness must be proved by the prosecutor through the witness’s testimony or materials recording the witness’s in-court testimony or the interview process, thereby revealing the time, reasons, method, and specific content of the advance interview.\\n\\nB. Summary of the facts charged in this part and the course of the proceedings\\n\\n1) The summary of the amended facts charged in this part is that the defendant, from around October 2000 to around May 2011, in connection with his duties, received bribes totaling at least KRW 51,600,345 from Person 1 in the form of credit card usage payments, gift certificates, borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, charges for drinks, money, and the like, and at the same time, by using his status as a public official, received bribes in the same amount in connection with arranging matters belonging to the duties of another public official.\\n\\n2) The first-instance court held: ① with respect to the portion of the receipt of gift certificates among the receipt of bribes from around June 2009 to around May 2011, which falls within the ten-year statute of limitations counted backward from the date of indictment, the proof of the receipt was insufficient; and with respect to the portion of the receipt of borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, the receipt was recognized, but the credibility of Person 1’s in-court testimony in the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case was rejected, and proof of the connection with official duties and quid pro quo could not be deemed sufficient based on the remaining evidence alone, and therefore acquitted the defendant; and ② with respect to the remaining portions of the receipt of bribes, it held that the statute of limitations had expired and dismissed the case on the merits.\\n\\n3) By contrast, the appellate court held: ① with respect to the parts of the acceptance of bribes in connection with mediation involving credit card usage payments, borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, charges for drinks on May 19, 2009, and money, Person 1’s in-court testimony in the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and Person 1’s appellate in-court testimony regarding the borrowed-name mobile phone were credible, and therefore found the defendant guilty on the ground that he received money or property benefits as consideration for mediation and that criminal intent was established; and with respect to the receipt of gift certificates and the charges for drinks on February 26, 2009 and March 25, 2009, it held that there was no proof of the crime and acquitted the defendant on the merits; and ② with respect to the portion of simple bribery, it held that the connection with official duties could not be recognized and acquitted the defendant on the merits.\\n\\nC. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nHowever, the appellate court’s determination cannot be accepted.\\n\\n1) According to the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na) On July 26, 2019, at the second pretrial preparation hearing in the first instance, the prosecutor requested Person 1 as a witness, and on August 13, 2019, at the first trial date, the first-instance court adopted Person 1 as a witness and conducted the examination of Person 1 in closed session on September 24, 2019, at the fifth trial date.\\n\\nBefore the examination of Person 1 was conducted, however, the prosecutor summoned Person 1 and interviewed Person 1, including by having Person 1 confirm the contents of the prosecutorial statement record.\\n\\nIn the first-instance witness examination, Person 1 testified, unlike his prosecutorial statement, with respect to the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case, which was his bribery-giving case in or around 1998, that “Person 2 discussed the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case by, for example, asking the defendant what would happen to Person 2, and the defendant told him that Person 1 himself also seemed to be a subject of investigation, and shortly thereafter a search and seizure of his office was conducted.”\\n\\nb) On June 17, 2020, at the first trial date in the appellate court, the prosecutor again requested Person 1 as a witness, and on the same day the appellate court adopted Person 1 as a witness and conducted the examination of Person 1 in closed session on August 19, 2020, at the second trial date.\\n\\nAs in the first instance, however, the prosecutor in the appellate court summoned Person 1 before the examination of Person 1 was conducted and interviewed Person 1, including by having Person 1 confirm the contents of the first-instance in-court testimony and the prosecutorial statement record. During the interview, Person 1 even asked the prosecutor about matters he would testify to.\\n\\nThereafter, in the appellate witness examination, Person 1 testified, unlike his prosecutorial statement, with respect to the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case, that “the apartment permitting and licensing process carried out by Person 3 Co., Ltd., where Person 1 worked, was the issue, and at that time Person 2, then head of the relevant division in Yongin City, was a friend of mine, and because he consulted me saying that he was being investigated for bribery, I asked the defendant for help, and later I received a message from the defendant that I too was a subject of investigation, and at that time a search and seizure took place at my office and I was investigated at the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office for about 48 hours.”\\n\\nIn addition, after the prosecutor’s advance interview, Person 1 testified in the appellate witness examination, unlike his first-instance in-court testimony, with respect to the borrowed-name mobile phone, that “distinguishing it from the provision of other money or property benefits, the borrowed-name mobile phone was not provided purely for the reason of helping the defendant or simply lending a mobile phone.”\\n\\n2) These factual circumstances are examined in light of the legal principles stated above. The prosecutor summoned and interviewed Person 1 before the witness examination on two occasions, in the first instance and in the appellate court. During the interview process, Person 1 not only confirmed the contents of his prosecutorial statement record and his first-instance in-court testimony, but even asked the prosecutor about matters he would testify to in court. And in the witness examination that followed immediately thereafter, he changed his prior statements regarding the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and the borrowed-name mobile phone, and with respect to the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case he made increasingly specific statements unfavorable to the defendant. In such circumstances, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that, before Person 1 testified in court in the first instance and in the appellate court, he changed his prior statements to statements consistent with the facts charged under the influence of persuasion, pressure, leading responses, or suggestion by the investigative authority during the process of being summoned and interviewed by the prosecution. Therefore, unless the prosecutor proves through the witness’s testimony or otherwise that he did not influence Person 1’s in-court testimony through persuasion or pressure during the pre-examination interview process, it is difficult to recognize the credibility of Person 1’s in-court testimony regarding the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and Person 1’s appellate in-court testimony regarding the borrowed-name mobile phone, which formed the basis of the appellate court’s guilty finding contrary to the first instance.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the appellate court, without conducting any specific review as to the timing, reasons, method, or content of the prosecutor’s advance interview, recognized the credibility of Person 1’s in-court testimony regarding the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and Person 1’s appellate in-court testimony regarding the borrowed-name mobile phone, and found guilty the portions of the facts charged for acceptance of bribes in connection with mediation involving credit card usage payments, borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, charges for drinks on May 19, 2009, and money.\\n\\nThis appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the determination of the credibility of the in-court testimony of a witness who had undergone an advance interview by the prosecutor, and by failing to conduct the necessary review. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the appellate court held that, with respect to the parts concerning Person 4 and Person 5 among the facts charged in this case, each violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act”) (bribery) had not been proved or the statute of limitations had expired, and therefore found not guilty or dismissed the case on the merits, and held that, with respect to the parts concerning Person 1 among the violations of the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act (bribery) arising from acceptance of bribes in connection with mediation, the receipt of gift certificates and the charges for drinks on February 26, 2009 and March 25, 2009 had not been proved, and therefore acquitted the defendant on the merits. Examining the reasons of the appellate judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the appellate court did not err by violating the rules of logic and experience and going beyond the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, nor by misapprehending the legal principles concerning improper solicitation in the third-party bribery offense, the establishment of the offense of improper action after receipt of a bribe, the connection with official duties in bribery offenses, or the statute of limitations.\\n\\n3. Scope of reversal\\n\\nAmong the appellate judgment, the guilty portion of the part concerning the violation of the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act (bribery) related to Person 1 must be reversed for the reasons stated above, and the portions acquitting on the merits among the part concerning the violation of the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act (bribery) related to Person 1, which stand in comprehensive concurrence and ideal concurrence with that guilty portion, must also be reversed together.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal of the defendant, the guilty portion of the appellate judgment (including the portions acquitted on the merits) is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the appellate court for further trial and determination. The remainder of the Prosecutor’s appeal is dismissed, and accordingly, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2022DO9510]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the charges concerning violation of the restriction on methods of intra-party primary election campaigning in relation to recruiting responsible party members\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, found this part of the indictment not guilty, holding that the acts of recruiting responsible party members committed by Defendants 1, 3, 4, and 5 could not be regarded as intra-party primary election campaigning.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “campaigning in a primary election.”\\n\\n2. As to the charges concerning intra-party primary election campaigning by a person who cannot engage in primary election campaigning\\nThe court below, as noted above, held this part of the indictment not guilty on the ground that, since the acts of recruiting responsible party members could not be regarded as intra-party primary election campaigning, this part of the indictment was also not guilty.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of violation of the Public Official Election Act.\\n\\n3. As to the charges concerning pre-election campaigning\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that the method of pre-election campaigning described in this part of the indictment and made the subject of trial was merely “the method of appealing for support of Defendant 1 orally,” and that the placards, business cards, name tags, etc. were merely statements of the factual circumstances attendant upon the above oral appeal for support; and even if these were regarded as having been stated as separate methods of pre-election campaigning, they did not constitute “election campaigning,” and thus found this part of the indictment not guilty.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of violation of the Public Official Election Act and failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n4. As to the charges concerning the receipt and provision of money and valuables in relation to intra-party primary election campaigning and election campaigning\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that Defendants 1, 5, and 4 could not be deemed to have provided or received benefits in connection with election campaigning, and thus found this part of the indictment not guilty.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “election campaigning” and “primary election campaigning.”\\n\\n5. As to the evidentiary admissibility of the party membership application forms\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n1) Article 18(2) item 7 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act” (before its partial amendment by Act No. 16930 on February 4, 2020; hereinafter the same) provided that where the personal information controller deems it necessary “for the investigation of crimes and the institution and maintenance of public prosecution,” it may use personal information for a purpose other than the original purpose or provide it to a third party, except where there is a risk of unduly infringing the interests of the data subject or a third party. However, this applies only where the “personal information controller” is a “public institution” and does not apply to corporations, organizations, individuals, etc. (proviso to Article 18(2), and Article 2 items 5 and 6, of the former “Personal Information Protection Act”). In addition, the phrase “where there is a special provision in another Act” under Article 18(2) item 2 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act” should be construed, according to its plain meaning, as limited to cases where individual statutes specifically provide that personal information may be disclosed; therefore, a general provision such as Article 199(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, under which an investigative agency may inquire of public offices and other public or private organizations and request a report on necessary matters, does not fall thereunder. If Article 199(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act were included in “where there is a special provision in another Act” under Article 18(2) item 2 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act,” it would not only defeat the legislative intent and purpose of Article 18(2) item 7 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act,” which allows investigative agencies to receive personal information from public institutions only under certain restrictions, but would also likely bypass the constitutional principle of warrant requirement and due process.\\n2) The “person who processes or has processed personal information” who is the subject of the duty under Article 59 item 2 of the Personal Information Protection Act is not limited to the “personal information controller” under Article 2 item 5, but includes a person who “processes” or “has processed” “personal information” under Article 2 item 1, by the means under Article 2 item 2, which he or she learned in the course of business (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO8766, decided March 10, 2016).\\n\\nB. Determination\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that the act by Defendants 5 and 4 of arbitrarily submitting to the investigative agency, without the consent of the author, the party membership application forms they had processed for Defendant 1 constituted an act prohibited by Article 59 item 2 of the Personal Information Protection Act, that Article 18(2) item 2 or item 7 of the former Personal Information Protection Act could not apply, and that although it constituted illegally obtained evidence, it was not a case where evidentiary admissibility should exceptionally be recognized; accordingly, it did not recognize the admissibility of the party membership application forms and the evidence related thereto.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning illegally obtained evidence, Article 59 item 2 of the Personal Information Protection Act, and Article 18(2) item 7.\\n\\n6. As to the evidentiary admissibility of the “written statement”\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\nSince Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that Articles 312(1) through (4) of the Criminal Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to the evidentiary admissibility of a written statement prepared during the investigative process by the defendant or a person other than the defendant, the legal principle that, for the evidentiary admissibility of a protocol in which a prosecutor or judicial police officer recorded the statement of a person other than the defendant, it must have been “prepared in accordance with lawful procedures and methods” also applies to the evidentiary admissibility of a written statement prepared during the investigative process by a person other than the defendant. Meanwhile, when a prosecutor or judicial police officer requests the appearance of a person who is not a suspect and examines him or her, the purport of Articles 221(1) and 244-4(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which require that the process of examination be recorded by entering in the protocol or recording on a separate written document the time of arrival at the place of examination, the time when the examination began and ended, and other matters necessary to confirm the progress of the examination process, and then filing it in the investigative record, as in the case of examining a suspect, is to institutionally guarantee procedural legality in that process by making transparent the process by which the investigative agency obtains testimonial evidence from the person examined during the examination process. Therefore, even where the investigative agency, as necessary for the investigation, has a person other than the suspect prepare and submit a written statement, the procedure must be complied with; accordingly, if a person other than the defendant prepared a written statement during the investigative process but the investigative agency did not take appropriate measures, such as recording in the written statement or on a separate written document the matters necessary to confirm the progress of the examination process and then filing it in the investigative record, thereby violating the procedure prescribed in Articles 244-4(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, then, unless there are special circumstances indicating that the institutional guarantee of procedural legality in the process of obtaining testimonial evidence was not infringed, it cannot be said that the written statement was prepared during the investigative process “in accordance with lawful procedures and methods,” and its evidentiary admissibility cannot be recognized (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013DO3790, decided April 23, 2015).\\nIn light of these provisions and wording of the Criminal Procedure Act and their legislative purpose, the “written statement prepared during the investigative process” subject to Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act means a document prepared after the investigation has begun under the involvement of the investigative agency, or prepared for the purpose of being submitted during the investigative process in relation to an investigation already commenced; so long as its substance falls thereunder in light of various circumstances such as the time and circumstances of preparation, it does not matter what it is called or whether it was prepared at a particular place.\\n\\nB. Determination\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that, insofar as a police officer visited the residence and workplace of the person who prepared the party membership application forms, questioned the circumstances of their preparation, and then required the preparation of a written statement and received it, Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act should apply, and therefore the evidentiary admissibility of the above evidence, which did not comply with the procedure prescribed in Article 244-4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, could not be recognized; and it rejected the prosecutor’s argument that, unlike this, since the written statement was not prepared at a police station but was received by visiting the place desired by the preparer, the provisions concerning the above procedures do not apply.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning whether Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act applies, or whether Articles 221(1) and 244-4(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act apply.\\n\\n7. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the case."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the following case is correct? (In case of dispute, according to precedents) The Chief of the Tax Office imposed a tax disposition on A, who constitutes a secondary taxpayer under the Framework Act on National Taxes, with respect to B Corporation’s delinquent national taxes (hereinafter referred to as “the tax disposition at issue”). The filing period for an administrative lawsuit to assert the illegality of the tax disposition at issue has elapsed. However, one year later, the Constitutional Court, in a constitutional complaint case filed by B, decided that the provision of the Framework Act on National Taxes that served as the basis for the tax disposition at issue was unconstitutional (hereinafter referred to as “the unconstitutional decision at issue”). The Chief of the Tax Office attached the deposit claim in A’s name, on the basis of the National Tax Collection Act, which was validly in force at the time pursuant to the tax disposition at issue, in order to collect the delinquent amount and deficiency amount (including additional tax) that A had been in arrears with.
A: Since the provision of the Framework Act on National Taxes that served as the basis for the tax disposition at issue was declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court, the tax disposition at issue is a disposition lacking legal basis and is therefore void ab initio; accordingly, although the filing period has elapsed, bringing an administrative lawsuit seeking confirmation of its nullity is lawful.
B: The statutory provision that was the subject of the unconstitutional decision is the basis of the tax disposition at issue, and even if the retroactive effect of the unconstitutional decision is recognized, there is no risk of undermining legal stability; therefore, the retroactive effect of the unconstitutional decision also extends to A.
C: If, before the unconstitutional decision at issue, A had brought an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the tax disposition at issue and had already lost with final and conclusive effect, then because the unconstitutional decision at issue constitutes a ground for retrial under Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act, A may petition for retrial.
D: The defect constituting a ground for revocation in the prior disposition, namely the tax disposition at issue, is succeeded to by the subsequent delinquent tax disposition, namely the attachment disposition.
E: If the statutory provision that served as the basis for the imposition of tax is declared unconstitutional, then, because of the binding force of the unconstitutional decision, it is no longer permitted to commence or continue a new delinquent tax collection disposition for the enforcement of the tax claim after the unconstitutional decision. A delinquent tax collection disposition made in violation of the effect of such unconstitutional decision is, by that reason alone, so seriously and objectively manifestly defective as to be void ab initio.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DU10907]": "The grounds of appeal are considered together.\\n\\n1. In order for a defective administrative disposition to become automatically void, the defect must be grave enough to violate an important part of the relevant law and must be objectively clear; in determining whether the defect is grave and obvious, the purpose, meaning, and function of the relevant legal provision must be examined teleologically, and the special features of the specific case itself must also be reasonably considered (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc judgment dated 1995. 7. 11. in 94NU4615, and Supreme Court en banc judgment dated 2006. 3. 16. in 2006DU330).\\nMeanwhile, Article 47(1) of the former Constitutional Court Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 10546 on 2011. 4. 5., hereinafter referred to as the “former Constitutional Court Act”) provides that “a decision that a statute is unconstitutional shall bind the courts, other state agencies, and local governments.” In light of the binding force of such a decision of unconstitutionality and the systemic demand of the legal order that takes the Constitution as the supreme norm, it is reasonable to view that state agencies and local governments may not make a new administrative disposition on the basis of a statutory provision declared unconstitutional, and that even a subsequent disposition based on legal relations already formed before the decision of unconstitutionality may not be permitted if it creates or expands a new unconstitutional legal relationship.\\nAccordingly, where the statutory provision that served as the basis for the imposition of taxes has been declared unconstitutional, even if the tax assessment disposition based thereon was made before the decision of unconstitutionality, and the period for filing a lawsuit against that tax assessment disposition has already elapsed so that the tax claim has become final, and even if no separate decision of unconstitutionality has been rendered with respect to the provision itself that served as the basis for collection dispositions to enforce that tax claim, it is no longer permissible, after such decision of unconstitutionality, to commence or continue a new collection disposition to enforce the tax claim; furthermore, a collection disposition made in violation of the effect of such decision of unconstitutionality must be deemed, for that reason alone, to be grave and objectively obvious in its defect and therefore void ab initio.\\nAccording to the reasons of the first-instance judgment, as partially cited by the court below, the facts are as follows: on 1997. 10. 22., the Defendant made a tax imposition disposition (hereinafter referred to as the “tax assessment disposition at issue”) against the Plaintiff concerning the delinquent national taxes of Kyungsung Co., Ltd., on the ground that the Plaintiff fell under a secondary taxpayer under Article 39(1)2(c) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (prior to amendment by Act No. 5579 on 1998. 12. 28., hereinafter referred to as the “former Framework Act on National Taxes”); the Constitutional Court, by its decision dated 1998. 5. 28. in 97HEONGA13, declared that Article 39(1)2(c) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes was in violation of the Constitution; and thereafter, the Defendant, on the basis of the National Tax Collection Act then validly in force pursuant to the tax assessment disposition at issue, seized a deposit claim in the name of the Plaintiff on 2005. 10. 11. in order to collect the amount in arrears and the amount of deficiency (including additional taxes) then delinquent by the Plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as the “seizure disposition at issue”).\\nOn the premise of these facts, the court below held that, in light of the fact that after a decision of unconstitutionality, from the perspective of the remedy of citizens’ rights, it must not be allowed to leave the state of application of an unconstitutional statute as it is or to permit additional acts by state agencies for the final execution of an unconstitutional statute, the seizure disposition at issue made after the decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision serving as the basis for the tax assessment disposition at issue constituted an additional act by the Defendant for the final execution of the tax assessment disposition at issue and thus fell under an administrative disposition void ab initio.\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the record, although there is an improper point in part of the court below’s reasoning, the conclusion of the court below that the seizure disposition at issue is void ab initio on the premise that, after a decision of unconstitutionality, additional acts by state agencies for the final execution of an unconstitutional statute may not be permitted, is proper. There is no illegality that affected the outcome of the judgment due to misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the grounds for automatic nullity of a seizure disposition made after a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying a tax assessment disposition, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, Shin Young-chul, and Kim Yong-deok, the opinions of the participating Justices were in accord.\\n\\n2. The dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, Shin Young-chul, and Kim Yong-deok are as follows.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, in light of the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality under Article 47(1) of the former Constitutional Court Act and the systemic demand of the legal order that takes the Constitution as the supreme norm, even if there is a decision of unconstitutionality only with respect to the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition and no decision of unconstitutionality with respect to the provision underlying the collection disposition based on that tax assessment disposition, a collection disposition first made after the decision of unconstitutionality pursuant to a tax assessment disposition made before the decision of unconstitutionality is, for that reason alone, grave and objectively obvious in its defect and therefore void ab initio. However, I cannot concur with this majority opinion for the following reasons.\\nFirst, if an administrative agency made an administrative disposition on the basis of a provision of a statute and thereafter the Constitutional Court declared that provision unconstitutional, then the administrative disposition would, as a result, be equivalent to one made without legal basis and thus would have a defect, albeit retroactively; however, as a general rule, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot be said to be objectively obvious before there is a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court, and therefore, absent special circumstances, such a defect constitutes only a ground for revocation of the administrative disposition, not a ground for automatic nullity (see, e.g., Supreme Court judgment dated 1994. 10. 28. in 92NU9463, and Supreme Court judgment dated 2009. 5. 14. in 2007DU16202).\\nAlso, where separate acts for a specific administrative purpose are carried out in stages, it cannot be said that the defect in the prior disposition is automatically succeeded by the subsequent disposition, except where the prior disposition has a defect that makes it void ab initio or nonexistent (see, e.g., Supreme Court judgment dated 1961. 10. 26. in 4292HAENGSANG73, and Supreme Court judgment dated 2001. 11. 27. in 98DU9530).\\nIf the foregoing established Supreme Court precedents are taken as the premise, the tax assessment disposition at issue and the seizure disposition at issue are separate administrative dispositions; thus, except where the prior disposition, namely the tax assessment disposition at issue, is void ab initio, the validity of the seizure disposition at issue, being a subsequent collection disposition, cannot be challenged on the ground of any defect in the tax assessment disposition at issue. Moreover, as stated above, the tax assessment disposition at issue may be regarded as a valid disposition.\\nSecond, under Article 47 of the former Constitutional Court Act concerning the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality, a decision that a statute is unconstitutional binds the courts, other state agencies, and local governments (paragraph (1)); however, a statute or statutory provision declared unconstitutional loses its effect from the date of the decision, but, in the case of a criminal statute or a statutory provision, it is in principle retroactively deprived of effect (paragraph (2)); accordingly, it is reasonable to interpret the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality on state agencies and local governments as having effect only within the scope to which the effect of unconstitutionality extends.\\nHowever, a collection disposition, such as a seizure disposition, is a separate administrative disposition from the tax assessment disposition, and the provisions underlying the tax assessment disposition are not directly applied; only the provisions concerning collection dispositions are applied. Therefore, the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provisions underlying the tax assessment disposition is unrelated to, and does not extend to, the collection disposition.\\nFurthermore, where, with respect to a tax assessment disposition made in the past, the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality is limited and it is viewed that such effect does not extend thereto, the relevant tax assessment disposition should be regarded as valid and not unconstitutional; accordingly, the collection disposition based on that tax assessment disposition is also not unconstitutional and cannot be said to violate the binding force of the decision of unconstitutionality. Therefore, in order to halt the progression of collection proceedings based on a tax assessment disposition, as in the case of criminal statutes, separate legislation is necessary, such as establishing a procedure to exclude the effect of the tax assessment disposition by extending the scope of the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition, or restricting the progress of collection proceedings.\\nNevertheless, if, as the majority opinion does, the scope of binding force is construed to extend to the point of prohibiting the progress of collection proceedings concerning a valid tax assessment disposition, thereby substantially denying the effect of the tax assessment disposition in question and causing it to disappear in fact, then it may be pointed out that this excessively expands the scope of binding force and consequently does not accord with the purport of the main clause of Article 47(2) of the former Constitutional Court Act, which limited the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality.\\nThird, when compared with certain foreign legislative examples, in Germany, retroactive effect is in principle recognized for a decision of unconstitutionality, but it is understood that such retroactive effect does not extend to legal relationships already finally determined at the time of the decision of unconstitutionality; moreover, there is an express statutory provision to the effect that no enforcement act may be taken pursuant to the statutory provision declared unconstitutional. The majority opinion ultimately means that Korea's relevant provisions should be interpreted and applied like those of Germany, which has such an express provision; however, in Korea, where no such express provision exists, it is difficult to accept such an interpretive theory as it stands.\\nAccordingly, so long as the tax assessment disposition, being the prior disposition, has no ground for automatic nullity and the provisions underlying the collection disposition based on the tax assessment disposition remain valid, the collection disposition cannot be deemed unlawful merely because the Constitutional Court has rendered a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition.\\nIn light of this legal principle, the tax assessment disposition at issue has no ground for automatic nullity, and the provisions underlying the seizure disposition at issue, which constitutes a subsequent collection disposition based on that tax assessment disposition, remain valid; absent an express provision, as seen in some foreign legislative examples, excluding the enforceability of an unconstitutional statute, the seizure disposition at issue cannot be regarded as void ab initio.\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the seizure disposition at issue, made after the decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition at issue, was void ab initio, relying only on the reason that, after a decision of unconstitutionality, from the perspective of the remedy of citizens’ rights, it must not be allowed to leave the state of application of an unconstitutional statute as it is or to permit additional acts by state agencies for the final execution of an unconstitutional statute. Accordingly, this judgment of the court below contains illegality that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending, inter alia, the legal principles concerning the grounds for automatic nullity of a seizure disposition made after a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying a tax assessment disposition. Therefore, the judgment of the court below must be reversed."}

{"[4292HAENGSANG73]": "Where independent acts are carried out in stages for a certain administrative purpose, except where there exist grounds that would naturally render the prior act void, it cannot be said that the defect of illegality in the prior act is naturally succeeded to by the subsequent act. In the present case, according to Article 11 of the Education Tax Act before amendment, it provided that Education Tax, being a national tax, could not be levied on the portion falling short of a certain amount as certain income; and according to Article 15(1) of the same Act, it provided that local Education Tax shall be levied on income on which Education Tax, being a national tax, is not levied pursuant to the provisions of Article 11 of the same Act; and, considering in conjunction Article 15(2) and (3) and Article 4 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, since it is provided that, where there is income other than certain income, local Education Tax may be levied by taking, as the tax base, the total income amount or the gross total income amount of that income and the amount based on assets or the standard of living calculated according to certain standards, it is not only a literal interpretation that, even for the same person, both national Education Tax and local Education Tax may be concurrently imposed, but also, if income that had not been subject to taxation is newly discovered, then if such income is an income amount on which national Education Tax may be levied, national Education Tax should be additionally levied thereon, and local Education Tax cannot be levied thereon. However, such an improper measure cannot be said to constitute a ground for voidness ab initio, but is to be construed as merely a ground for revocation; whereas the record clearly shows that the Plaintiff objected to the Defendant’s disposition imposing local Education Tax on the ground that the assessed tax amount was excessive, and that the Defendant rendered a ruling correcting the same, and, on the premise that that ruling had become final and conclusive, made the present disposition for collection of delinquent taxes, the Plaintiff has not raised any defect with respect to the delinquent-tax collection disposition itself, and is contesting the present delinquent-tax collection disposition on the ground of the so-called defect in the already final and conclusive taxation disposition itself, as is clear from the Plaintiff’s claim itself; therefore, the Plaintiff’s claim, which contests the subsequent delinquent-tax collection disposition on the ground of a defect in the prior taxation disposition as aforesaid, is improper, but despite that, the court below, on a contrary premise, upheld the Plaintiff’s claim, and the original judgment is improper, without the need to determine the other grounds of appeal."}

{"[92NU9463]": "We shall determine together the first and second points of the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below duly found that the non-party Korea Light Semiconductor Co., Ltd., in obtaining a loan from the non-party Korea Exchange Bank on 1989.5.17., had provided the machinery involved in this case as security by way of security assignment; that the Defendant, on 1990.4.3., for the collection of the Value-Added Tax, Corporate Tax, and Defense Tax imposed on the said company, attached the machinery in this case pursuant to Article 42(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (prior to its amendment by Act No. 4277 of 1990.12.31.); and that, with respect to the Plaintiff, who paid the company’s debt to the said Korea Exchange Bank and acquired the rights to the said machinery, the proviso to the said provision to the effect that only property subject to security assignment may not be attached one year before the payment deadline for the said national taxes (more precisely, the part of the proviso reading “one year before”) is unconstitutional, and therefore the said attachment disposition is void. As to that argument, the court below held that it lacks merit because, first, no constitutional ruling has been rendered with respect to the said proviso, and second, even if such a constitutional ruling were rendered, the defect in the said disposition cannot be deemed so grave and obvious as to render it void.\\n\\n2. If, after an administrative disposition has been issued on the basis of a statute, the Constitutional Court declares the statute that constituted the basis for the administrative disposition unconstitutional, then, in consequence, the said administrative disposition would be deemed to have been made without any legal basis and thus to be defective. However, in order for a defective administrative disposition to be void as a matter of course, the defect must not only be grave but also obvious. Generally, before a constitutional decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot objectively be said to be obvious. Accordingly, absent special circumstances, the ground that the statute constituting the basis of an administrative disposition violates the Constitution before a constitutional decision by the Constitutional Court may serve only as a premise for an action seeking revocation of that administrative disposition, and is not a ground for automatic nullity. If, contrary to the above, an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute were generally deemed void as a matter of course, this would result in a serious threat to legal stability, and even in light of the principle of the rule of law, it would have to be regarded as improper.\\n\\nFurther, whether an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute is void as a matter of course is a question separate from the retroactive effect of a constitutional decision; even if retroactive effect of a constitutional decision is recognized, it cannot be said that an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute becomes void as a matter of course. Rather, for an administrative disposition whose period for filing an action for revocation has already elapsed and whose finality has thereby arisen, the retroactive effect of a constitutional decision should be deemed not to extend. Therefore, where an action seeking a declaration of nullity is brought against an administrative disposition on the ground that the statute constituting its basis is unconstitutional, the court, absent other special circumstances, should dismiss the said action seeking a declaration of nullity without needing to determine whether the statute is unconstitutional. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that the Defendant’s attachment disposition in this case cannot be deemed void as a matter of course merely because the relevant provision of the said Framework Act on National Taxes is unconstitutional is proper in light of the legal principles stated above, and it cannot be said to contain an illegality such as the alleged misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the retroactive effect of a constitutional decision or the automatic nullity of an administrative disposition. All the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered as follows by unanimous agreement of the Justices involved."}

{"[92NU9463]": "The first and second grounds of appeal are examined together.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below properly found that Non-party Hanguk Gwang Semiconductor Co., Ltd., in obtaining a loan from Non-party Korea Exchange Bank on 1989.5.17., had provided the machinery at issue in this case as transfer security as collateral, and that the Defendant, on 1990.4.3., seized said machinery pursuant to Article 42(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (as amended by Act No. 4277 on 1990.12.31.) for the collection of value-added tax, corporate tax, and defense tax against said company; and, with respect to the Plaintiff, who had discharged the company’s debt to said Korea Exchange Bank and received the rights to said machinery, the court below held that the proviso to the above provision to the effect that only the property subject to transfer security that became the object of security could not be seized within 1 year before the due date for payment of the above national taxes (more precisely, the portion of the above proviso stating “1 year earlier”) was unconstitutional, and therefore the said seizure disposition was void. As to that contention, the court below held that there had been no decision of unconstitutionality with respect to the provision of the above proviso, and further that even if a decision of unconstitutionality were rendered, the defect in the said disposition could not be deemed to be grave and obvious so as to make it void, and accordingly held that the above argument was without merit.\\n\\n2. If, after an administrative disposition has been issued on the basis of a statute, the Constitutional Court declares the statute that formed the basis of that administrative disposition unconstitutional, then, as a result, such administrative disposition would be regarded as having been made without legal basis and thus as defective. However, for a defective administrative disposition to be void as a matter of course, the defect must not only be grave but also obvious; and, generally, before the Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot objectively be said to be obvious. Therefore, it is reasonable to view the ground that the relevant statute forming the basis of an administrative disposition violates the Constitution before the Constitutional Court’s decision of unconstitutionality as, absent special circumstances, merely a premise for an action to revoke that administrative disposition, and not a ground for voidness as a matter of course. If, contrary to the above, an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute were generally deemed void as a matter of course, this would result in a substantial threat to legal stability and, in light of the principle of the rule of law, cannot be said to be proper.\\n\\nIn addition, whether an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute is void as a matter of course is a matter separate from the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality; even if retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality is recognized, it cannot be said that an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute becomes void as a matter of course. Rather, it should be understood that the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality does not extend to an administrative disposition whose finality has arisen after the period for filing an action for revocation has already elapsed. Therefore, in a case where an action seeking confirmation of invalidity is brought against an administrative disposition on the ground that the statute forming the basis of that administrative disposition is unconstitutional, the court should, absent other special circumstances, dismiss the above action seeking confirmation of invalidity without needing to determine whether the statute is unconstitutional. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that the Defendant’s seizure disposition in this case cannot be deemed void as a matter of course merely because the relevant provision of the above Framework Act on National Taxes is unconstitutional is proper in light of the foregoing legal principles, and there is no illegality, such as the alleged misunderstanding of the law concerning the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality or the voidness as a matter of course of an administrative disposition. All arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The participating Justices being in agreement, it is so adjudged as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[99HEONBA66]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nA.
