(97NU12174); after remand, the Seoul High Court rendered, on 1998. 9. 16., a judgment partly in favor of the plaintiff revoking the disposition imposing 1,579,070 won out of the above charge of 189,421,690 won (98NU8768), and that judgment became final around that time. As the former Act on the Ownership Ceiling on Land, which served as the basis for the imposition of the Excess Land Ownership Charge, was declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court on 1999. 4. 29., the Petitioner filed an action for retrial with the Seoul High Court (99JAENU302) and, while asserting that Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act, which grants an opportunity for retrial to a person who has filed a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act while not granting such an opportunity to a person who has not filed such a constitutional complaint, violates the principle of equality and is therefore unconstitutional, applied for a referral of a constitutional review of the said provision (99A324); however, that court, on 1999. 8. 26., dismissed the retrial request and also dismissed the application for referral as without merit. Accordingly, the Petitioner received service of the decision dismissing the application for referral of a constitutional review on 1999. 9. 7. and filed the constitutional complaint for adjudication in this case on 1999. 9. 21. pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act (Act No. 5454, 1997. 12. 13.) (hereinafter referred to as the “provision subject to review”) is unconstitutional. The contents of the provision subject to review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act Article 75 (Ruling of Grant)\\n①～⑤ Omitted\\n⑥ In the cases of paragraph 5 and in the case of granting a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2), Articles 45 and 47 shall apply mutatis mutandis.\\n⑦ Where a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) is granted and the litigation case related to the relevant constitutional complaint has already become final, the party may request a retrial.\\n⑧ In a retrial under paragraph 7, the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to criminal cases, and the provisions of the Civil Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to other cases.\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act Article 68 (Grounds for Complaint)\\n② When an application for referral of a constitutional review of the constitutionality of a law under Article 41(1) is dismissed, the party who made the application may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court. In this case, the party may not again apply for a referral of a constitutional review on the same grounds in the litigation procedure of the relevant case.\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act Article 45 (Decision of Unconstitutionality)\\nThe Constitutional Court shall decide only whether the referred law or provision of law is unconstitutional. Provided, that where it is recognized that the entire law cannot be enforced due to a decision of unconstitutionality of a provision of law, a decision of unconstitutionality may be made as to the entirety thereof.\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act Article 47 (Effect of a Decision of Unconstitutionality)\\n① A decision of unconstitutionality of a law binds the courts and other state agencies and local governments.\\n② A law or provision of law that is declared unconstitutional shall lose effect from the date of the decision. Provided, that a law or provision of law concerning criminal punishment shall lose effect retroactively.\\n③ In the case of the proviso of paragraph 2, a retrial may be requested with respect to a final judgment of conviction based on the law or provision of law declared unconstitutional.\\n④ The provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to a retrial under paragraph 3.\\n\\n2. Petitioner’s Arguments, Reasons for the Court’s Rejection of the Application for Referral, and Opinions of Interested Institutions\\n\\nA. Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nAllowing, under the provision subject to review, only those who happened to file a constitutional complaint to have the path to retrial opened, while blocking the path to retrial for those who did not file a constitutional complaint, directly conflicts with Article 11(1) of the Constitution, which declares the right to equality.\\n\\nThe Act on the Ownership Ceiling on Land is, by the wording of the statute itself, clearly a law that restricts the exercise of property rights, and by declaring that law unconstitutional, the restriction on the exercise of property rights was lifted so that genuine protection of property rights would be ensured. However, under the provision subject to review, allowing only those who filed a constitutional complaint to request retrial while blocking the path to retrial for those who did not file such a complaint ultimately violates Article 23(1) and (3) of the Constitution concerning the protection of property rights.\\n\\nArticle 27(1) of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall have the right to a trial by judges qualified under the Constitution and laws,” and “trial by law” should be understood to mean “a valid law that does not contravene the Constitution”; more specifically in this case, if the Act on the Ownership Ceiling on Land has been declared unconstitutional, it should be interpreted to mean that, on the premise that it has been so declared unconstitutional, the propriety of the disposition imposing the excess charge under that law may be sought by adjudication. If the provision subject to review is applied as written, then persons who did not file a constitutional complaint are blocked from the path to retrial, which ultimately results in the deprivation of the constitutional right to a trial, and thus conflicts with Article 27(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nIf the provision subject to review does not open the path to retrial for persons who did not file a constitutional complaint, this results in the inability to exercise the right to pursue happiness under Article 10 of the Constitution, and further results in violating the duty of the State under the latter part of Article 10, namely, the duty to guarantee the fundamental human rights of individuals.\\n\\nIn addition, even if the Constitution does not contain an express provision that anyone has the right to request retrial when there is a final judgment in relation to the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court, such a right to request retrial should be regarded as one of the fundamental human rights based on the above constitutional provisions; therefore, if retrial is not recognized in a case such as this, it directly results in a violation of Article 37 of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Reasons for the Court’s Rejection of the Application for Referral\\n\\nWhere there is doubt concerning the constitutionality of a statutory provision that is the premise of a trial and the party applies to the court for a referral on its constitutionality, but the court dismisses the application, a constitutional complaint may be filed pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act. However, the trial in the relevant litigation case may not be stayed and may become final; in such a case, even if the Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality on the statutory provision that is the premise of the trial, the retroactive effect of the decision of unconstitutionality does not extend to the judgment already finalized (Article 47(2) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that, except for laws or provisions of law concerning criminal punishment, a decision of unconstitutionality loses effect from the date of the decision. Meanwhile, the so-called erga omnes effect of the decision of unconstitutionality asserted by the applicant is a matter of recognizing the so-called normative effect, namely, that no one may any longer assert the validity of a law or provision of law declared unconstitutional, and is entirely distinct from the issue of whether retroactive effect should be recognized in a decision of unconstitutionality; therefore, even if erga omnes effect is recognized in a decision of unconstitutionality, retroactive effect is not thereby automatically recognized). Accordingly, the party cannot receive relief of rights.\\n\\nTherefore, the provision subject to review provides that, where a constitutional complaint is granted, retrial may be requested even if the litigation case related to the relevant constitutional complaint has already become final; in light of this legislative purpose, the “litigation case related to the relevant constitutional complaint” in the provision subject to review should be understood to refer only to the relevant litigation case that was the premise of the relevant constitutional complaint (see, e.g., Supreme Court 1993. 7. 27. judgment, 92NU13400).\\n\\nAs the retrial under the provision subject to review, as stated above, is an exceptional remedy prepared under certain strict requirements to redress the infringement of a party’s rights caused by the fact that retroactive effect is not, in principle, recognized for a decision of unconstitutionality, if, as the applicant argues, the right to request retrial were recognized even for parties who did not lawfully seek a constitutional review in relation to the relevant litigation case, this would amount to recognizing retroactive effect in practice for a decision of unconstitutionality, which might cause great confusion to the existing legal relations formed pursuant to already finalized judgments. Since the provision subject to review recognizes the right to request retrial under the requirements of filing a lawful constitutional complaint and having it granted in order to avoid this, it cannot be deemed improper; by following the procedures prescribed in the Constitutional Court Act, a party may avoid the disadvantages arising from the fact that retroactive effect is not recognized for a decision of unconstitutionality, and such procedures are not particularly difficult. Accordingly, even if the provision subject to review does not recognize the right to request retrial for parties who have not followed such procedures, despite the fact that the statutory provision that was the premise of the trial has been declared unconstitutional, it cannot be said to violate the Constitution.\\n\\nC. Opinions of Interested Institutions\\n\\n(1) Opinion of the Minister of Justice\\n\\nAlthough this constitutional complaint in this case has the appearance of raising the unconstitutionality of the provision subject to review, as long as the phrase “the litigation case related to the relevant constitutional complaint” is interpreted as “the relevant litigation case that was the premise of the constitutional complaint,” the complaint is in substance an argument that it is unconstitutional. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court has consistently held that the meaning of “related litigation case” in the provision subject to review refers only to the relevant litigation case that was the premise of the relevant constitutional complaint (see Supreme Court 1992. 7. 1. judgment, 92NU13400; Supreme Court 1991. 6. 13. judgment, 91NU7101). Ultimately, the essence of the Petitioner’s argument is that the above Supreme Court judgment is unconstitutional and should be changed.\\n\\nArticle 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act excludes “court judgments” from the subject matter of review, and even according to the decisions of the Constitutional Court, a constitutional complaint is permitted with respect to a court judgment only exceptionally, where a court, by applying a law that the Constitutional Court has declared unconstitutional and thereby has lost its effect in whole or in part, or that has been confirmed unconstitutional, has infringed the fundamental rights of the people. Since this case does not fall within such an exception, it is a case that cannot be the subject of a constitutional complaint. Although in appearance it seems like a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, the true substance of the Petitioners’ argument is a constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the same Act and a constitutional complaint against a court judgment, and thus it lacks the proper requirements for a constitutional complaint and must therefore be dismissed.\\n\\nThe question whether a law or provision of law declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court loses effect retroactively to the time of enactment or loses effect prospectively is, absent special circumstances, not so much a matter of constitutional conformity as it is a matter of legislative policy to be determined by the legislature while comparing and balancing various interests, such as legal stability and individual relief of rights. Our legislature, through the main text of Article 47(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, selected a scheme that gives greater weight to legal stability except in criminal punishment provisions; and such legislation is justified by the principle of legal stability or the principle of protection of trust, which is derived from the constitutional principle of the rule of law, even if concrete reasonableness or the principle of equality is not perfectly realized. However, because of the special nature of a decision of unconstitutionality, which necessarily has varying effects, the Constitutional Court exceptionally recognizes partial retroactive effect.\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that, in this constitutional complaint, the demand for concrete reasonableness for the relief of a party’s rights is remarkable, whereas even if retroactive effect were recognized there would be no concern of infringing legal stability; further, the case is one in which the interests of vested persons formed under the former law would not be harmed, and thus the denial of retroactive effect would rather be seriously contrary to constitutional ideals such as justice and equity, so that retroactive effect should exceptionally be recognized. However, as already noted, the Constitutional Court Act adopted the scheme of, in principle, not recognizing retroactive effect except in criminal punishment provisions, and if retroactive effect were extended even to cases like this, the result would be to recognize retroactive effect generally for decisions of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court. Accordingly, the Petitioners’ argument that their constitutional rights and interests were infringed because they could not request retrial under the provision subject to review is based on the position that retroactive effect should be recognized for a decision of unconstitutionality. The Petitioner also argues that this case is one in which retroactive effect should exceptionally be recognized, but without explaining any concrete reasons, and instead merely argues that the cases subject to retrial under the Constitutional Court Act should be expanded to cases of the same kind other than the relevant case in which the constitutional complaint was filed.\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality is inherently erga omnes, and that opening the path to retrial for persons who filed a constitutional complaint while blocking the path to retrial for persons who did not file such a complaint infringes the latter’s right to request trial, is contrary to the principle of equality, and also infringes the right to pursue happiness. However, the erga omnes effect of a decision of the Constitutional Court is a matter of the so-called normative effect, namely, that no one may any longer assert the validity of a law or provision of law declared unconstitutional, and is a matter distinct from whether retroactive effect is recognized for a decision of unconstitutionality. Also, allowing only persons who filed a constitutional complaint to request retrial is not only an inevitable measure under our legal system, which in principle does not recognize retroactive effect but exceptionally does so, but also the fact of whether a constitutional complaint was filed means whether the party used procedures to contest the important issues in the relevant case; thus there is a rational basis for treating differently persons who exhausted such procedures and persons who did not, and since filing a constitutional complaint is not a particularly cumbersome or difficult procedure, it cannot be said to infringe the right to request trial or to violate the principle of equality.\\n\\nAs examined above, the petition for a constitutional complaint in this case is substantively directed against a court judgment, and therefore is improper and must be dismissed. Even if it were proper, however, the provision subject to review cannot be regarded as having infringed the Petitioner’s right to request trial, the right to pursue happiness, or the right to equality, and thus it should be dismissed.\\n\\n(2) Opinion of the Head of Yeongdeungpo-gu Office\\n\\nThe phrase “the litigation case related to the relevant constitutional complaint” in Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act refers to the relevant litigation case that was the premise of the relevant constitutional complaint. The cases that formed the cause of the Petitioner’s claim do not fall within the relevant litigation case that was the premise of the constitutional complaint here. The fact that the Constitutional Court Act provides that a law declared unconstitutional shall lose effect prospectively, except for criminal punishment provisions, is justified by the principle of legal stability and trust protection, and is consistent with the Constitution.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\nA. Judgment on the Requirements for Admissibility\\n\\nIn a petition for constitutional adjudication under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, the constitutionality of the law to be applied to a specific case pending before a court of general jurisdiction must be a premise of adjudication.\\n\\nAccording to the established precedent of our Constitutional Court (see Constitutional Court 1993. 5. 13. 92HEONGA10 et al., Case Reports 5-1, 226, 238-239), the premise of adjudication means that, first, a specific case must have been pending before a court or must be pending; second, the law whose constitutionality is at issue must be applicable to the adjudication of the relevant litigation case; and third, it means a case in which, depending on whether that law violates the Constitution, the court in charge of the relevant litigation case would render a different judgment. The phrase “different judgment” by the court, in principle, includes not only any effect on the conclusion or main text of the adjudication in the relevant case being tried by the court, but also cases where, even if the constitutionality of the law at issue does not affect the main text of the judgment itself, it is related to rendering different reasons leading to the conclusion of the judgment or where the legal meaning concerning the content and effect of the judgment is entirely changed.\\n\\nThe provision subject to review, pursuant to Article 40(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, in effect establishes an independent ground for retrial in addition to the grounds for retrial under Article 422(1) of the Civil Procedure Act, which are applied mutatis mutandis to the adjudicatory proceedings of the Constitutional Court.\\n\\nIn addition, where the Petitioner’s argument is not merely a dispute over the interpretation of a statutory provision but is understood as a petition concerning the unconstitutionality of the statutory provision itself, such as by disputing it on the ground that the provision is unclear, this Court has accepted as proper under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act even petitions seeking a determination of limited unconstitutionality (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21. 92HEONBA40, Case Reports 7-2, 34, 36-37; Constitutional Court 1997. 2. 20. 95HEONBA27, Case Reports 9-1, 156, 161-162; Constitutional Court 1999. 3. 25. 98HEONBA2, Case Reports 11-1, 200, 208-209; Constitutional Court 1999. 7. 22. 97HEONBA9, Case Reports 11-2, 112, 121; Constitutional Court 1999. 11. 25. 98HEONBA36, Case Reports 11-2, 529, 536; Constitutional Court 2000. 6. 1. 97HEONBA74, Official Gazette 46, 448, 449).\\n\\nIn this case, it is reasonable to view the gist of the Petitioner’s argument not as seeking a simple declaration of unconstitutionality of the provision in this case, but rather as seeking the following determination of limited unconstitutionality. That is, the Petitioner’s argument is that, where a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act is granted, not only the party to the relevant case but also a party to another case who did not file a constitutional complaint but was subject to the provision of law declared unconstitutional may request retrial of the already finalized related case; unless the provision in this case is interpreted accordingly, it violates the constitutional right to equality and the principle of protection of property rights.\\n\\nIf the Petitioner’s constitutional complaint in this case is granted, there will be rendered a determination of limited unconstitutionality to the effect that “the provision in this case is unconstitutional insofar as it is interpreted as allowing retrial to be requested only by the party to the relevant case that was the premise of the constitutional complaint,” and the Petitioner’s retrial would be lawful. Thus, notwithstanding the relief explicitly stated by the Petitioner, this petition for adjudication should be accepted as a petition concerning the unconstitutionality of the provision itself in this case, and therefore it satisfies the premise of adjudication.\\n\\nThe Minister of Justice’s argument that the petition for adjudication in this case is substantively directed against a court judgment and therefore must be dismissed as improper is without merit.\\n\\nB. Judgment on the Merits\\n\\nWhen a court refers the constitutionality of a law to the Constitutional Court, the adjudication of the relevant litigation case is stayed until the Constitutional Court renders a decision on constitutionality (Article 42(1) of the Constitutional Court Act). However, when an application for referral of the constitutionality of a law is dismissed, even if the party who made the application files a constitutional complaint, the adjudication of the relevant litigation case is not stayed (Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act). Accordingly, the relevant litigation case may become final before a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court. The provision subject to review allowed retrial to be requested with respect to a final case when the Constitutional Court has rendered a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the law on which the final judgment was based. Here, the phrase “the litigation case related to the relevant constitutional complaint” in the provision subject to review can, on the face of the text, only be understood as referring to the relevant litigation case that was the premise of the relevant constitutional complaint (see Supreme Court 1993. 7. 27. judgment, 92NU13400).\\n\\nIf the provision subject to review is not interpreted as the Petitioner contends, we further consider whether it infringes the Petitioner’s right to request trial, right to equality, property rights, and right to pursue happiness.\\n\\nA law or provision of law declared unconstitutional by a constitutional complaint adjudication under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act loses effect from the date of the decision, provided that a law or provision of law concerning criminal punishment loses effect retroactively (Article 75(6) and Article 47(2) of the Constitutional Court Act).\\n\\nIn this case, the decision of unconstitutionality concerning the Act on the Ownership Ceiling on Land does not pertain to criminal punishment, and therefore retroactive effect is not recognized for that decision of unconstitutionality.\\n\\nThe question of what grounds should be allowed as grounds for retrial is a matter of legislative policy to be decided by the legislature taking into account legal stability concerning final judgments, the promptness and propriety of trials, and the burden of work on the courts, etc. (see Constitutional Court 1996. 3. 28. 93HEONBA27, Case Reports 8-1, 179, 187), and the right to request retrial is merely a legal right created only through the exercise of legislative discretion, not a fundamental human right directly arising under Article 27(1) and Article 37(1) of the Constitution, as the Petitioner contends.\\n\\nAlso, in light of the essence of adjudication as the ascertainment of facts and the interpretive application of law, the constitutional right to a trial means that at least one opportunity for judicial review of both factual and legal aspects by a judge must be guaranteed (see Constitutional Court 1992. 6. 26. 90HEONBA25, Case Reports 4, 343, 349-350). Furthermore, retrial is a special means of objection against a final judgment, and the demand for legal stability concerning a final judgment is much greater than that concerning a non-final judgment. Therefore, the right to request retrial cannot be naturally included in the right to a trial prescribed in Article 27 of the Constitution. The benefit of requesting retrial under the provision subject to review is generally recognized for anyone who, under certain lawful requirements, has filed a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act and had it granted, and because the opportunity to file a constitutional complaint is normatively equally guaranteed, it cannot be said that the provision subject to review infringes the Petitioner’s right to request trial, right to equality, property rights, or right to pursue happiness merely because it does not grant an opportunity for retrial to persons who did not file a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act and did not receive a grant.\\n\\nIf so, since all of the Petitioner’s arguments are without merit, it cannot be said that the provision subject to review, which allows only the party to the final litigation case that was the premise of the relevant constitutional complaint to request retrial when a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) is granted, violates the Constitution.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the operative part, with the unanimous opinion of all Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the rights and duties of public officials is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: The State Public Officials Act does not prescribe the “principle of statutory determination of working conditions” with respect to public officials’ remuneration, etc., so payment of public officials’ remuneration is possible if it has been included in the national budget.
B: Among the provisions of the State Public Officials Act, the part stating that elementary and secondary school teachers who are education public officials may not participate in the formation of or join “other political organizations” violates the principle of clarity.
C: Unlike military personnel, civilian military employees who are not in the status of State public officials should not be subject to strict restrictions on freedom of political expression, and acts of civilian military employees publicly expressing political opinions also do not need to be strictly restricted.
D: The “collective acts for purposes other than official duties” prohibited by the State Public Officials Act do not refer only to “collective acts that are contrary to the public interest and that have effects such as neglecting the duty of devotion to duty,” but mean all collective acts undertaken by public officials for any purpose other than official duties, based on the mission of public officials as servants of the entire people.
E: Because of a provision of the former Rules on the Payment of Honorary Retirement Allowances, etc. for Judges and Court Officials, which provided that the amount of a judge’s honorary retirement allowance be calculated not only on the basis of the remaining period until mandatory retirement age but also by reflecting the remaining term of office, there is a possibility that a judge may suffer disadvantage as compared with “other career public officials” in whether an honorary retirement allowance is paid and in its amount, etc.; this constitutes arbitrary discrimination.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2013DU14610]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 46(5) of the State Public Officials Act provides, “No money or valuable goods may be paid as remuneration to public officials unless in accordance with the provisions concerning remuneration under this Act or other Acts.” Article 47(1) provides, “The following matters concerning the remuneration of public officials shall be determined by Presidential Decree,” and item 2 thereof lists “matters concerning allowances.” Article 31 of the Regulations on the Remuneration of Public Officials provides, “Public officials may be paid necessary allowances, in addition to salary, within the limits of the budget” (paragraph (1)), and “The types, scope, amount of payment, and other matters necessary for the payment of allowances under paragraph (1) shall be separately determined by Presidential Decree” (paragraph (2)). In addition, the Regulations on Allowances, etc. for Public Officials classify and prescribe the types of allowances, such as bonus allowances, household stabilization allowances, and special area duty allowances, and provide that they are to be calculated and paid in the manner prescribed in the relevant provisions within the limits of the budget.\\n\\nMeanwhile, pursuant to Article 21(4), Articles 29 and 30, etc. of the National Finance Act, with respect to the State’s revenue and expenditure budget, the “specific classification criteria for the budget and the classification of subitems and items according to the nature of each expense” are determined in accordance with the budget formulation guidelines, etc. prepared by the Minister of Economy and Finance.\\n\\nAs such, the State Public Officials Act prescribes the so-called “statutory reservation principle for working conditions” with respect to the remuneration, etc. of public officials. This is because public officials have a special status as servants of the entire people based on the civil service system prescribed in Article 7 of the Constitution, and thus it is appropriate for the National Assembly, which represents the will of the entire people, to determine their working conditions. Moreover, since remuneration, etc. of public officials is paid from the State budget, there is a need for the National Assembly, which has the authority under Article 54 of the Constitution to deliberate on and finalize the budget bill, to determine the working conditions of public officials by law reflecting budgetary considerations as well.\\n\\nIn addition, pursuant to Article 31 of the Regulations on the Remuneration of Public Officials, public officials’ allowances and other remuneration are paid within the limits of the budget, and “within the limits of the budget” here means that the remuneration item in question must be appropriated in the State budget (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA9227, decided September 10, 2009).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing, since working conditions such as remuneration for public officials must be prescribed by law and payment of public officials’ remuneration is impossible if it is not appropriated in the State budget, where a public official seeks payment from the State of money that is, in substance, remuneration, there must be an express provision in the laws concerning public officials’ remuneration, such as the State Public Officials Act and its subordinate statutes, serving as the legal basis for such payment, and furthermore, the relevant remuneration item must also be appropriated in the State budget.\\n\\n2. Article 10 item 3 of the former Infant and Young Child Care Act (as amended by Act No. 10789 on June 7, 2011, the same shall apply hereinafter) defines a workplace child-care facility as “a child-care facility established and operated by an employer for workers at the place of business,” and includes therein “facilities established and operated by the head of a State agency or a local government for affiliated public officials.” Article 14(1) of the same Act provides, “An employer of a place of business of a certain scale or more, as prescribed by Presidential Decree, shall establish a workplace child-care facility. Provided, That where the employer of the place of business cannot independently establish a workplace child-care facility, the employer shall jointly establish and operate a workplace child-care facility with other employers, enter into a consignment contract with a local child-care facility to support child care for workers’ children, or pay a childcare allowance to workers” (hereinafter referred to as “the provision at issue”), and it delegates to Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare the matters necessary for the establishment, consignment contract, and payment of childcare allowances (paragraph (2) of the same Article). Pursuant to that delegation, Article 8 of the former Enforcement Rule of the Infant and Young Child Care Act (as in force before amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare No. 50 on April 7, 2011) provides, “The childcare allowance under the proviso to Article 14(1) of the Act shall be at least 50/100 of the government childcare fee support unit cost” (this provision was partially amended by the April 7, 2011 amendment, so that the amount portion became “at least 50/100 of the age-specific government childcare fee support unit cost,” and was later deleted by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare No. 53 on January 28, 2015).\\n\\nAs such, the former Infant and Young Child Care Act prescribes the employer’s obligation to pay childcare allowances within the framework of the employment relationship between employer and worker, and if the State, as employer, must pay childcare allowances to its affiliated public officials pursuant to the provision at issue, such payment is in substance no different from the “allowances” that constitute public officials’ remuneration, and thus falls within the working conditions of public officials that must be prescribed by law. However, the Regulations on Allowances, etc. for Public Officials, which determine the types, etc. of public officials’ allowances pursuant to the delegation of the State Public Officials Act, do not contain any allowance item corresponding to the childcare allowance under the provision at issue, and even in other allowance items such as the “family allowance,” they do not contemplate any special consideration for infant and young child children under the former Infant and Young Child Care Act.\\n\\nIn addition, whether the provision at issue applies is determined according to the scale of each individual workplace to which the worker belongs (at least 300 regularly employed female workers or at least 500 regularly employed workers), but where the employer is the State, although remuneration is paid on the basis of the same State budget, it cannot be said that the payment of a particular allowance may differ merely according to the scale of the workplace to which the employee belongs, and therefore the provision at issue cannot be regarded as a provision creating a new statutory allowance item not prescribed in the State Public Officials Act and its subordinate statutes only for public officials belonging to workplaces of at least a certain scale.\\n\\nMoreover, according to the budget formulation guidelines, etc. established by the Minister of Economy and Finance pursuant to Article 21(4) of the National Finance Act, it appears that, unlike other allowance items prescribed in the State Public Officials Act and its subordinate statutes, the childcare allowance at issue is not separately appropriated in the State budget.\\n\\nConsidering these various circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, with respect to the childcare allowance at issue, there is not only no legal basis for payment under the State Public Officials Act and its subordinate statutes, but the provision at issue cannot be deemed to fall within the “provisions concerning remuneration of public officials under other Acts” prescribed in Article 46(5) of the State Public Officials Act, and because the childcare allowance at issue is also not separately appropriated in the State budget, the Plaintiffs, who are State public officials, seeking direct payment of the childcare allowance at issue based on the provision at issue cannot be permitted as it would be contrary to the statutory principle regarding public officials’ working conditions and the principle of payment of public officials’ remuneration based on a State budget in which the relevant item has been appropriated.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that the Plaintiffs, as workers, did not acquire a claim for childcare allowances under the provision at issue; although the explanation of the reasons in the judgment of the court below cannot be regarded as appropriate, the conclusion rejecting the Plaintiffs’ claim for payment of the childcare allowance at issue is correct. There is thus no illegality affecting the judgment, such as an error in the legal principles concerning the legal nature of the obligation to pay childcare allowances under the provision at issue, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case.\\n\\n[Appendix] List of Plaintiffs: Omitted"}

{"[2018HEONMA550]": "1. Case Overview\\nPetitioners Shin ○○, Park ○○, Heo ○○, Lee ○○, Hong ○○, and Kim ○○ (hereinafter referred to as “Petitioners Shin ○○, etc.”) were each appointed on March 1, 2018, as public school teachers who are national public officials. Petitioners Lee □□ and Kang ○○ were each appointed on March 1, 1990, as public school teachers who are national public officials. The Petitioners filed this constitutional complaint on May 29, 2018, alleging that the main text of Article 66(1) of the National Civil Service Act infringes their fundamental rights.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\nThe Petitioners take as the subject matter of adjudication the main text of Article 66(1) of the National Civil Service Act; however, since they do not contest the unconstitutionality of the portion concerning “labor movements” among the aforesaid statutory provision, that part is excluded from the subject matter of adjudication. Accordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the portion of the main text of Article 66(1) of the National Civil Service Act (as amended by Act No. 8996 on March 28, 2008) that concerns “collective acts for any purpose other than official duties” infringes the Petitioners’ fundamental rights, and the challenged provision and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Challenged Provision]\\nNational Civil Service Act (as amended by Act No. 8996 on March 28, 2008)\\nArticle 66 (Prohibition of Collective Acts) (1) A public official shall not engage in labor movements or in any collective acts for any purpose other than official duties. Provided, That this shall not apply to public officials who are de facto engaged in manual labor.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nNational Civil Service Act (as amended by Act No. 8996 on March 28, 2008)\\nArticle 65 (Prohibition of Political Activities) (1) A public official shall not participate in the formation of, or join, a political party or any other political organization.\\n(2) A public official shall not engage in any of the following acts to support or oppose a specific political party or specific person in an election:\\n1. Conducting solicitation campaigns to vote or not to vote\\n2. Planning, presiding over, or soliciting signature campaigns\\n3. Posting or causing to be posted documents or books in public facilities, etc.\\n4. Collecting or causing to be collected donations, or using or causing to be used public funds\\n5. Conducting solicitation campaigns to induce another person to join, or not to join, a political party or any other political organization\\n(3) A public official shall not require another public official to engage in acts that violate paragraphs (1) and (2), or promise benefits or disadvantages as a reward or retaliation for political acts.\\nArticle 78 (Grounds for Disciplinary Action) (1) If a public official falls under any subparagraph of the following, a request for a disciplinary resolution shall be made, and a disciplinary disposition shall be taken according to the result of that disciplinary resolution.\\n1. Where this Act or an order issued under this Act is violated\\nNational Civil Service Act (as amended by Act No. 12792 on October 15, 2014)\\nArticle 84-2 (Penal Provisions) A person who violates Article 44, Article 45, or Article 66 shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than one year or by a fine not exceeding 10 million won, unless specially provided otherwise by other Acts.\\n\\n3. The Petitioners’ Arguments\\nA. The Constitutional Court previously held that the challenged provision, as narrowly construed by the courts as “the concerted conduct of a number of public officials that may have effects such as neglecting the duty to devote themselves to their duties for a purpose contrary to the public interest, or that may impair public trust in public affairs,” does not violate the principle of clarity. However, insofar as “purpose contrary to the public interest” and “neglect of the duty to devote oneself to duties” are vague concepts, the challenged provision violates the principle of clarity.\\nB. The challenged provision, which also prohibits collective acts that do not run counter to the public interest, lacks legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means. Since the challenged provision comprehensively restricts collective expression, there is no public interest achieved by the challenged provision, whereas the freedom of political expression infringed thereby is extremely grave; therefore, the minimality of infringement and balance of legal interests are also not satisfied.\\n\\n4. Judgment on the Petition Filed by Petitioners Lee □□ and Kang ○○\\nA constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act must be filed within 90 days from the day on which the petitioner became aware of the cause of infringement of fundamental rights, and within one year from the day on which such cause arose (Article 69(1) of the Constitutional Court Act). Where a constitutional complaint against a statute is brought in a case where fundamental rights are infringed simultaneously with the statute’s enforcement, the complaint must be filed within 90 days from the day on which the fact of the statute’s enforcement became known, and within one year from the day on which the statute was enforced; and where, after the statute’s enforcement, a cause falling within the statute subsequently arises and fundamental rights are thereby infringed, the constitutional complaint must be filed within 90 days from the day on which the petitioner became aware that such cause arose, and within one year from the day on which such cause arose (see Constitutional Court 2007. 7. 26. 2006HEONMA1164).\\n\\nTurning to this case, Petitioners Lee □□ and Kang ○○ were appointed on March 1, 1990, as public school teachers who are national public officials, and thereafter the challenged provision took effect on March 28, 2008, and became applicable to them. Nevertheless, Petitioners Lee □□ and Kang ○○ filed this constitutional complaint on May 29, 2018, more than one year thereafter.\\n\\nAccordingly, the petition filed by Petitioners Lee □□ and Kang ○○ is inadmissible because it failed to comply with the filing period.\\n\\n5. Judgment on the Petition Filed by Petitioners Shin ○○, etc.\\nA. Whether the principle of clarity has been violated\\n(1) In Decision 2011HEONBA32 et al. of August 28, 2014, the Constitutional Court held that the portion of “this Act” in Article 78(1)1 of the National Civil Service Act (as amended by Act No. 8996 on March 28, 2008), which has the same content as the challenged provision, and the portion of “collective acts for any purpose other than official duties” in the main text of Article 66(1) of the National Civil Service Act do not violate the principle of clarity. The gist thereof is as follows.\\n\\n“‘Collective acts for any purpose other than official duties’ does not mean all collective acts performed by public officials for any matter not belonging to official duties, but is construed narrowly as ‘collective acts that have effects such as neglecting the duty to devote oneself to one’s duties for a purpose contrary to the public interest,’ in light of Article 21(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of speech, the legislative purpose of the National Civil Service Act, and the duty of fidelity and duty to devote oneself to one’s duties under the National Civil Service Act, taken together. In addition, in light of the purpose of the National Civil Service Act in prohibiting collective acts by public officials, the collective acts at issue here should be regarded as the concerted conduct of a number of public officials that may impair their devotion to duties or damage public trust in public affairs. Furthermore, the concept of ‘public interest’ derived through the interpretation of the National Civil Service Act refers not to the interests of an individual or a specific organization or group, but to the interests of the general public or the common interests of society. However, in the process of specifying the meaning of the challenged provision, there is a possibility that the use again of an abstract concept such as public interest may not completely eliminate ambiguity as to its meaning, but it is desirable to supplement this through ordinary statutory interpretation or the supplementary function of law.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that the challenged provision violates the principle of clarity.”\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, Petitioners Shin ○○, etc. argue that the meaning of “the duty to devote oneself to duties,” derived through the courts’ interpretation of the challenged provision, is unclear. In ordinary meaning, “duty” refers to affairs assigned and entrusted with responsibility by virtue of one’s position or occupation, and “devotion” means focusing one’s mind exclusively on one thing. And under the Constitution, public officials are servants of the entire people, owe responsibility to the people (Article 7(1) of the Constitution), and are required to maintain political neutrality (Article 7(2) of the Constitution). The National Civil Service Act, which prescribes matters concerning the appointment and service of public officials, provides for the duty of fidelity (Article 56), duty to obey (Article 57), duty not to leave one’s post (Article 58), duty of kindness and fairness (Article 59), duty to maintain secrecy (Article 60), duty of integrity (Article 61), duty to maintain dignity (Article 63), duty to refrain from profit-making business and concurrent office-holding (Article 64), duty of prohibition of political activities (Article 65), and duty of prohibition of collective acts (Article 66).\\n\\nUltimately, the duty of a public official to devote oneself to duties means to faithfully engage in the work one is entrusted with from an impartial standpoint, and therefore it is difficult to regard its meaning as unclear.\\n\\n(3) Taking these circumstances into account, since no change in circumstances or necessity is recognized in this case that would require a different conclusion from the above precedent, the challenged provision does not violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nB. Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction has been violated\\nIn Decision 2011HEONBA32 et al. of August 28, 2014, the Constitutional Court held that the portion of “collective acts for any purpose other than official duties” in the main text of Article 66(1) of the National Civil Service Act (as amended by Act No. 8996 on March 28, 2008), which has the same content as the challenged provision, does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction. The gist thereof is as follows.\\n\\n“The reason the challenged provision prohibits ‘collective acts by public officials for any purpose other than official duties’ is that collective action by public officials may hinder the pursuit of the interests of the entire public by representing the interests of the public official group, and this is understood as prescribing one of the duties arising from the special status of being a public official. The phrase ‘collective acts for any purpose other than official duties’ can be narrowly construed as ‘collective acts that have effects such as neglecting the duty to devote oneself to duties for a purpose contrary to the public interest,’ and thus it cannot be regarded as an excessive restriction on freedom of expression.\\n\\nMass collective action, by its nature, is more likely than individual action as a means of expression to come into conflict with public peace and order or legal peace. In particular, when public officials engage in collective political expression, this may be perceived as representing the interests of the public official group, and may undermine trust in the fairness and objectivity of public administration by impairing political neutrality. Therefore, even if the challenged provision restricts collective acts by public officials, including acts of political expression, this cannot be viewed as an excessive restriction on freedom of expression.\\n\\nFurthermore, the challenged provision prohibits political expression by public officials even when it invokes ‘public interest.’ This derives from the duty of political neutrality owed by public officials. In the political reality of our country, criticism of or opposition to government policy that is carried out collectively, even if it does not take the form of support for or opposition to a specific political party, faction, or specific politician, has a high potential to be misunderstood as an attempt to intervene in actual politics or as factional or partisan, and even if it is undertaken for the purpose of the development of the state and society, it is in fact difficult to eliminate suspicions of political bias therefrom. Therefore, even if a public official’s collective political expression invokes the public interest, it cannot be regarded as falling within acts for ‘public interest’ to which the application of the challenged provision is excluded, unless it satisfies the requirement of political neutrality of public officials.”\\n\\nSince no change in circumstances or necessity is recognized in this case that would require a different conclusion from the above precedent, the challenged provision does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, among the petitions in this case, the petition filed by Petitioners Lee □□ and Kang ○○ is inadmissible and is dismissed in its entirety, and the petitions filed by Petitioners Shin ○○, etc. are without merit and are dismissed in their entirety; thus, the decision is rendered as stated in the order. Except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Seok-tae and Kim Gi-young regarding the challenged provision, as set forth in 7 below, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Seok-tae and Kim Gi-young Regarding the Challenged Provision\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we share the dissenting opinion in Decision 2011HEONBA32 et al. of August 28, 2014, which held that the challenged provision violates the principle of clarity and the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, and we further state our views as follows.\\n\\nA. Whether the principle of clarity has been violated\\n(1) First, the gist of the dissenting opinion in Decision 2011HEONBA32 et al. is as follows.\\n\\n“The majority opinion, with respect to the meaning of ‘collective acts for any purpose other than official duties’ in the challenged provision, narrowly construes it as ‘collective acts that have effects such as neglecting the duty to devote oneself to duties for a purpose contrary to the public interest,’ and then says that it does not violate the principle of clarity. However, this is nothing more than interpreting an abstract concept through an even more unclear concept.\\n\\nA determination whether a particular expressive act is indeed harmful to the ‘public interest’ or not must inevitably vary greatly according to each person’s values and ethical view, and it cannot be denied that there exist interests whose status as public interest may be differently determined depending on the decision-maker; thus, it is difficult to regard this as a concept whose meaning and content can be objectively fixed through the ordinary interpretation of the law-enforcement authority. Under the present pluralistic and value-relative social structure, when a specific act situation is at issue, the public interest in question in most cases does not converge into a single one, and the act at issue may simultaneously promote one public interest while harming another. Moreover, in order to determine whether there is an intent to harm public interest overall, balancing among public interests inevitably becomes necessary, and since the result of such balancing is not always objectively clear, the concept of ‘public interest’ is an unclear concept (Constitutional Court 2010. 12. 28. 2008HEONBA157 et al.).\\n\\nAs such, unless the concept of public interest is clear, even if ‘collective acts for any purpose other than official duties’ are narrowly construed as ‘collective acts that have effects such as neglecting the duty to devote oneself to duties for a purpose contrary to the public interest,’ its meaning remains unclear. Therefore, the challenged provision violates the principle of clarity.”\\n\\n(2) The meaning of public interest in a concrete case becomes clear only by identifying and balancing mutually conflicting general and abstract public interests, and such balancing is completed only when various elements such as objective data relating to the case, evaluation and interpretation of such data, and normative judgment are introduced. Balancing and the elements introduced into balancing may be compared to scales and weights. Just as one cannot know where the scale will tip if one does not know what weights will be placed on it, if the elements introduced into balancing are not clear, the meaning of public interest also cannot be clear.\\n\\nConcepts under the National Civil Service Act, such as the duty of fidelity and the duty to devote oneself to duties, have different ranges of meaning depending on how the statutory interpreter interprets constitutional concepts such as “servants of the entire people” or “political neutrality.” Thus, in cases where the breadth of the scope of application is especially at issue, as in the challenged provision, these statutory concepts do not make clear what elements must be introduced into balancing. Moreover, constitutional concepts such as freedom of speech, servants of the entire people, and political neutrality are also general and abstract concepts whose meaning must be clarified through balancing. Those constitutional concepts can only be identified as being related to balancing; they do not, in and of themselves, clearly indicate what elements must be introduced into balancing in the case at hand.\\n\\nIf, as above, it is not clear what elements must be introduced into balancing, then the concept of public interest is merely an unclear concept that only informs one that balancing is necessary; therefore, the challenged provision violates the principle of clarity.\\n\\nB. Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction has been violated\\n(1) Gist of the dissenting opinion in Decision 2011HEONBA32 et al.\\n“(a) Breadth of the scope of regulation\\nRestrictions on the freedom of political expression of public officials should be limited to acts that may impair political neutrality, but the challenged provision unduly restricts the freedom of political expression of public officials by prohibiting even political expression regarding general policies, which is difficult to evaluate as closely related to political neutrality, such as election campaigns or party activities.\\n\\n(b) Scope of public officials and relevance to duties\\nEven if collective expressive acts are regulated only with respect to public officials who perform duties related to national policy, public officials who possess personnel authority or command and supervisory authority or who have authority to decide important policies, or public officials above a certain rank, or public officials of agencies related to national security, trials, inspection, elections, etc., the purpose sought by the challenged provision could be achieved (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Mok Young-jun and Lee Jung-mi in Constitutional Court 2012. 5. 31. 2009HEONMA705 et al.). Nevertheless, the challenged provision, without distinguishing the public officials whose political expressive acts are restricted according to their duties or rank, prohibits even political expression unrelated to their own duties for all public officials, which is an excessive restriction.\\n\\n(c) During and outside working hours\\nThe challenged provision restricts the collective expressive acts of public officials without distinguishing between during and outside working hours. Since public officials are both public servants and private individuals, when outside working hours or not performing duties, they should be able to enjoy their fundamental rights as private individuals to the fullest extent. In particular, when a public official does not use public facilities or exercise public authority outside working hours, such conduct cannot but be regarded as conduct as a private individual rather than as a public official. Nevertheless, if such conduct is restricted on the ground of establishing work discipline among public officials or ensuring political neutrality, this violates the principle of minimal infringement.\\n\\n(d) Conclusion\\nThe challenged provision does not selectively regulate expressive acts strongly tinged with partisanship, but instead presumes as conduct contrary to the public interest and prohibits in its entirety even political expression undertaken for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, so long as it is carried out collectively; therefore, it violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.”\\n\\n(2) Minimality of infringement\\nEducational public officials such as the Petitioners occupy the status of public officials, but in light of their duties and rank, it is difficult to say that there is a need to comprehensively and uniformly restrict collective political expressive acts.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court has previously stated that “teachers are not subordinate administrative executors or mere appliers of laws and regulations in educational activities, but persons who guide students with respect to value-laden issues so that students may have their own views on matters” (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 22. 89HEONGA106). This view of teachers, unless teachers actively attempt to influence students by inducing them toward their own perspective, calls for an attitude of respecting students as subjects who can face teachers and surrounding persons with different values and worldviews and achieve a balance of opinions through generalization and relativization, even if they are confronted with the teacher’s political expression. Teachers who participate in collective acts outside working hours cannot directly convey their perspective to students, and only indirectly influence students when the students become aware of such acts through some channel. Unlike the perspectives encountered by students in unavoidable time and space such as class hours, even if students come to know that a teacher participated in collective acts outside working hours, they can generalize and relativize the teacher’s perspective through interaction with other teachers, parents, friends, and various media, and this also becomes an opportunity for students to grow as members of a democratic community who have their own views.\\n\\nFurthermore, even if an act performed by a teacher as a private individual creates an external appearance of bias and thereby affects students in some way, such influence is only indirect and factual; therefore, restricting the exercise of fundamental rights by law on that basis is not appropriate. If a comprehensive and uniform restriction of fundamental rights is justified merely because a person simultaneously holds the status of a teacher, the teacher can no longer enjoy the dual status of “servant of the entire people” and “subject enjoying fundamental rights.”\\n\\nTherefore, the challenged provision violates the principle of minimal infringement.\\n\\n(3) Balance of legal interests\\nEven if the need for a comprehensive and uniform restriction of fundamental rights on teachers’ freedom of collective political expression is recognized, the private interests infringed by the challenged provision must not be more serious than the public interest additionally achieved thereby. Also, the more abstract the additionally achieved public interest and the more serious the private interests infringed, the more carefully the balance of legal interests should be assessed.\\n\\nThe Petitioners, who are teachers, already bear duties of neutrality under Article 3 of the Act on the Establishment and Operation of Teachers’ Trade Unions, Article 6(1) of the Framework Act on Education, Article 14(4) of the Framework Act on Education, and so forth. Ultimately, the additional public interest achieved by the challenged provision is the dispelling of abstract concerns about political bias by restricting collective acts by teachers that are difficult to regard as actually impairing or posing a concrete risk of impairing political neutrality.\\n\\nThe modern state has various institutions and regulations fundamentally distinct from the classical structure of separation of powers premised on the antagonistic relationship between the monarch and the bourgeoisie, and one such institution is the separation of powers through the civil service system. The constitutional civil service system intends the separation and checks and balances of power between political forces and career public officials, that is, the division of roles and balance of power between “politically biased forces” and “politically neutral career public officials.” Teachers are most highly accessible to the bias and errors of education policy. The role of teachers, who do not uncritically follow erroneous policies contrary to the Constitution and constitutional values but rather actively criticize and correct them, is extremely important, and to perform such a role effectively, there are cases in which it is necessary to exchange views and unite at the collective level.\\n\\nThe desire to come into contact with others, exchange thoughts with one another, and collectively manifest personality is the most basic human desire as a social animal, and the freedom to express one’s views collectively is an indispensable fundamental element for a democratic community to function. Atomized individuals, who are easily overwhelmed by the state, government, or majority, can develop their identity and thinking through collective action and further amplify their influence on the political community. The freedom to express views collectively, guaranteed by freedom of assembly and freedom of expression, is a constitutional decision for a pluralistic “open society” in which tolerance and diverse opinions coexist (see Constitutional Court 2003. 10. 30. 2000HEONBA67 et al.).\\n\\nThe challenged provision comprehensively restricts teachers’ freedom to express views collectively in order to suppress abstract concerns. However, freedom to express views collectively is a significant fundamental right that should not be disparaged merely because one holds the status of a teacher, and the challenged provision hardly permits the possibility that a person who holds the status of a teacher may form and express opinions and expertise as a citizen or as a teacher who corrects governmental bias.\\n\\nTherefore, the challenged provision violates the balance of legal interests."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding the right to informational self-determination? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law.) (a). The statutory provision that designates a person whose conviction for the offense of indecent assault in a crowded public place has become final as a person subject to registration of personal information, regardless of the gravity of his or her criminal liability, infringes the right to informational self-determination. (b). The statutory provision that requires game business operators to establish a procedure enabling identity verification when a user of a game product registers as a member does not infringe the right to informational self-determination. (c). The statutory provision that requires a person subject to a security surveillance disposition to report the fact of release within 7 days after release from prison, etc., and punishes a violation thereof, does not infringe the right to informational self-determination because the inconvenience to the person subject to the security surveillance disposition is not great and the 7-day reporting period cannot be said to be excessively short. (d). The statutory provision that allows DNA identification information to be entered into and managed in a database until the death of the person subject to collection infringes the right to informational self-determination because it is uniformly applied merely upon the finalization of a conviction for the target offenses, without any consideration of the gravity of the offense, the risk of recidivism, and the like. (e). The statutory provision that requires the public announcement of the violation facts concerning a daycare center that received a suspension of operation, a closure order, or a penalty surcharge because it received subsidies by falsehood or other improper means or misappropriated subsidies does not infringe the right to informational self-determination because it is intended to prevent similar violations by daycare center installers/operators and to ensure the right of guardians of infants and young children to choose a childcare institution.
