supporting_precedents: {"[2014HEONMA45]": "1. Summary of the Case\\n\\na. The Petitioner was sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment for the crime of rape resulting in injury, and that sentence became final and conclusive (Wonju Branch Court of Chuncheon District Court 2011GOHAP38, Chuncheon Division of Seoul High Court 2012NO24).\\n\\nb. The Petitioner, at XX Prison, from 2013. 11. 10. to 2013. 11. 21., was suspected of noncompliance with orders and obstruction of duties, and, as a person subject to disciplinary action, was placed under investigative confinement (hereinafter referred to as “the investigative confinement disposition in this case”), during which he was restricted in outdoor exercise, educational training, and participation in group events.\\n\\nc. On 2013. 11. 22., because the above charges were found to be substantiated, the Petitioner was subjected to a 25-day confinement to a disciplinary cell disposition (hereinafter referred to as “the disciplinary-cell disposition in this case”), and the disciplinary-cell disposition in this case was executed from 2013. 11. 10., with 12 days of the investigative confinement disposition in this case counted toward the period, until 2013. 12. 4.; additionally, from 2013. 11. 22. to 2013. 12. 4., the Petitioner was also subjected to suspension of participation in group events, restriction on reading newspapers, restriction on watching television, restriction on use of self-purchased items, suspension of work, restriction on telephone calls, restriction on writing, restriction on receipt and dispatch of correspondence, restriction on visits, and suspension of outdoor exercise.\\n\\nd. Accordingly, alleging that Article 108 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates, which prescribes the types of disciplinary sanctions, infringes human dignity and value, the right to trial, freedom of expression, and the like, the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2014. 1. 21.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court shall comprehensively determine the gist of the Petitioner’s claims, without being bound by the relief sought as stated in the petition, and may ex officio ascertain the subject matter of review by investigating the fundamental rights alleged to have been infringed and the exercise of public power alleged to be the cause of the infringement (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA90, 2003. 5. 15.).\\n\\nAlthough the Petitioner and state-appointed counsel have designated Article 108 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates, which prescribes the types of disciplinary sanctions, as the subject matter of review, they in substance argue that the statutory provisions prescribing that, during the investigation period, treatment restrictions such as suspension of outdoor exercise, suspension of educational training, and suspension of participation in group events are to be imposed, and that, during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, treatment restrictions such as suspension of participation in group events, restriction on reading newspapers, restriction on watching television, restriction on use of self-purchased items, restriction on telephone calls, restriction on writing, restriction on receipt and dispatch of correspondence, restriction on visits, and suspension of outdoor exercise are to be imposed, infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights and are therefore unconstitutional.\\n\\nArticle 108 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates merely enumerates the types of disciplinary sanctions, whereas Article 110(2) of the same Act provides that, if a person subject to disciplinary action is separately confined during the investigation period, all or part of the treatment allowing contact with other persons, such as visits, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, telephone calls, outdoor exercise, work, educational training, and participation in group events, may be restricted, and the main text of Article 112(3) of the same Act provides that a person who has received a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition shall be subject, during that period, to treatment restrictions, including suspension of participation in group events. Accordingly, taking into account the gist of the Petitioner’s claims, the subject matter of review in this case is changed ex officio to the relevant portions of Article 110(2) and the main text of Article 112(3) of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates (see Constitutional Court 2011HEONMA201, 2013. 2. 28.; Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA623, 2014. 8. 28., et al.).\\n\\nTherefore, the subject matter of review in this case is whether ① Article 110(2) of the former Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates (completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., and before amendment by Act No. 13235 on 2015. 3. 27.) (hereinafter referred to as “the investigation provision at issue in this case”), and ② the portion concerning Article 108 items 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 of the main text of Article 112(3) of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates (completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., hereinafter referred to as “the Sentence Execution Act”) (hereinafter referred to as “the confinement provision at issue in this case”) are in violation of the Constitution by infringing the Petitioner’s fundamental rights. The content of the provisions subject to review and the related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nFormer Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates\\n(completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., and before amendment by Act No. 13235 on 2015. 3. 27.)\\n\\nArticle 110 (Investigation of Persons Subject to Disciplinary Action) (2) The warden may restrict all or part of the treatment allowing contact with other persons, such as visits, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, telephone calls, outdoor exercise, work, educational training, and participation in group events, if the person subject to disciplinary action falls under any of the items of paragraph (1).\\n\\nAct on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates\\n(completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21.)\\n\\nArticle 112 (Execution of Disciplinary Sanctions) (3) A person who has been subjected to the disposition under Article 108, item 14, shall, during that period, also be subject to the treatment restrictions under items 4 through 13 of the same Article. Provided, That if the warden deems it especially necessary for the relief of an inmate’s rights, the reformation of a prisoner, or the prisoner’s sound return to society, the warden may permit writing, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, visits, or outdoor exercise.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nAct on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates\\n(completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21.)\\n\\nArticle 108 (Types of Disciplinary Sanctions) The types of disciplinary sanctions are as follows:\\n4. Suspension of participation in group events for up to 30 days\\n5. Restriction on reading newspapers for up to 30 days\\n6. Restriction on watching television for up to 30 days\\n7. Restriction on use of self-purchased items (excluding medicines prescribed by a doctor for treatment) for up to 30 days\\n9. Restriction on telephone calls for up to 30 days\\n10. Restriction on writing for up to 30 days\\n11. Restriction on receipt and dispatch of correspondence for up to 30 days\\n12. Restriction on visits for up to 30 days\\n13. Suspension of outdoor exercise for up to 30 days\\n14. Confinement to a disciplinary cell for up to 30 days\\n\\nArticle 110 (Investigation of Persons Subject to Disciplinary Action) (1) The warden may confine separately during the investigation period an inmate (hereinafter referred to as “a person subject to disciplinary action”) who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of having committed an act constituting grounds for disciplinary sanction if such inmate falls under any of the following items:\\n1. When there is a risk of destruction of evidence\\n2. When there is a risk of causing harm to other persons or a need to protect the inmate from harm by other inmates\\n3. Petitioner’s Claims\\n\\na. Uniformly suspending or restricting participation in group events, reading newspapers, watching television, use of self-purchased items, telephone calls, writing, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, visits, and outdoor exercise during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period infringes the right to pursue happiness.\\n\\nb. In particular, restricting the use of stationery among self-purchased items and restricting writing during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period creates obstacles to filing administrative litigation to challenge disciplinary dispositions and the treatment of persons subject to disciplinary action, and therefore infringes the right of access to the courts and freedom of expression. In addition, considering the practical custom of allowing items that persons subject to disciplinary action purchased at their own expense before receiving a disciplinary disposition to be used during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, the confinement provision at issue in this case infringes the right to equality by treating without reasonable grounds persons who had already purchased items before the said disposition and persons who are only to purchase items after the said disposition differently.\\n\\n4. Judgment on Procedural Requirements\\n\\na. The Investigation Provision at Issue in This Case\\n\\nIn order for a statute or a statutory provision itself to be the subject of a constitutional complaint, the fundamental rights of the Petitioner must be directly infringed by such statute or statutory provision, without waiting for any specific enforcement act. The “directness” of the infringement of fundamental rights referred to here means a case in which restrictions on freedom, imposition of duties, or deprivation of legal status occur by the statute itself, without any enforcement act; therefore, where the legal effect of infringement of fundamental rights arises only through a specific enforcement act based on the relevant statute, the requirement of directness is lacking (see Constitutional Court 2011HEONMA131, 2013. 5. 30.).\\n\\nHowever, according to the investigation provision at issue in this case, the head of a correctional facility (hereinafter referred to as the “warden”) may restrict all or part of the treatment allowing contact with other persons, such as visits, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, telephone calls, outdoor exercise, work, educational training, participation in group events, and intermediate treatment, when the person subject to disciplinary action is separately confined; thus, the infringement of fundamental rights is realized only through the warden’s specific enforcement act of restricting treatment (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA523, 2014. 9. 25.).\\n\\nTherefore, the petition for review in this part does not satisfy the requirement of direct infringement of fundamental rights.\\n\\nb. The Confinement Provision at Issue in This Case\\n\\n(1) The disciplinary-cell disposition at issue in this case ended on 2013. 12. 4., and the accompanying treatment restrictions also ended simultaneously; therefore, even if the Petitioner were to obtain a ruling of unconstitutionality concerning the confinement provision at issue in this case, it would not assist in the remedy of the Petitioner’s rights.\\n\\n(2) However, because a constitutional complaint serves not only to remedy an individual’s subjective rights but also to guarantee the constitutional order, even if the petition for review concerning the confinement provision at issue in this case would not be of much help in the remedy of the Petitioner’s rights, an interest in review may still be recognized where there is a risk that the infringement of fundamental rights by the confinement provision at issue in this case may be repeated in the future, and where the determination of constitutionality regarding that statutory provision is an important matter for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, such that its constitutional clarification has significant meaning (see Constitutional Court 2011HEONMA267, 2013. 11. 28.).\\n\\nAccordingly, it is examined whether the petition for review concerning the confinement provision at issue in this case falls within such exceptional circumstances where an interest in review may be recognized as above.\\n\\n(a) Article 108 item 5 (restriction on reading newspapers), the portion concerning books under item 7 (restriction on use of self-purchased items), item 9 (restriction on telephone calls), and the portion concerning item 12 (restriction on visits)\\n\\nWith respect to the portion concerning books under Article 108 item 5 and item 7, and the portion concerning item 9 and item 12, which are applicable to pretrial detainees, among the confinement provision at issue in this case, the Constitutional Court found them constitutional on the ground that they do not infringe the right to know or freedom of communication (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA549, 2016. 4. 28., et al.), and since the same reasoning can equally apply to prisoners whose sentence has been imposed and has become final and conclusive, there is no need for constitutional clarification regarding these matters.\\n\\nTherefore, no interest in review is recognized for any of the petitions concerning this part.\\n\\n(b) The portion concerning newspapers under Article 108 item 7 (restriction on use of self-purchased items)\\n\\nThe “self-purchased items” whose use is restricted under Article 108 item 7 of the Sentence Execution Act refer to items that an inmate may purchase at his own expense with the approval of the warden of a prison, detention house, or its branch, and include food, medicines and medical supplies, clothing, bedding and footwear, newspapers, magazines, books and stationery, items necessary for correction and reformation such as prisoner education, and other items deemed necessary for inmate life (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 2 item 1, Article 16(1)). Accordingly, as to restriction on reading newspapers, not only Article 108 item 5 of the Sentence Execution Act but also the portion concerning newspapers under Article 108 item 7 of the same Act may serve as the basis provision.\\n\\nAs noted above, with respect to the portion concerning Article 108 item 5, which restricts reading newspapers during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period and applies to pretrial detainees, the Constitutional Court found it constitutional on the ground that it does not infringe the right to know (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA549, 2016. 4. 28., et al.), and since the same reasoning can equally apply not only to inmates whose sentence has become final and conclusive but also to the portion concerning newspapers under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, there is no need for constitutional clarification regarding this matter.\\n\\nTherefore, no interest in review is recognized also for this part.\\n\\n(c) The portion concerning magazines under Article 108 item 7 (restriction on use of self-purchased items)\\n\\nAn inmate may apply to subscribe to magazines and books at his own expense, and the warden shall permit the subscription unless the applied-for magazine or book is a harmful publication under the Promotion of the Publication and Culture Industry Act; moreover, the number of magazines and books for which an inmate may apply to subscribe is limited to not more than 10 per month (Sentence Execution Act, Article 47(1) and (3); Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 35), and magazines and books are treated identically under the Sentence Execution Act.\\n\\nAs noted above, with respect to the portion concerning books under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, which restricts reading books during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period and applies to pretrial detainees, the Constitutional Court found it constitutional on the ground that it does not infringe the right to know (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA549, 2016. 4. 28., et al.), and since the same reasoning can equally apply not only to inmates whose sentence has become final and conclusive but also to the portion concerning magazines under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, there is no need for constitutional clarification regarding this matter.\\n\\nTherefore, no interest in review is recognized for this part as well.\\n\\n(d) The portion concerning Article 108 item 10 (restriction on writing) and item 11 (restriction on receipt and dispatch of correspondence)\\n\\nWith respect to the portion concerning Article 108 item 10 and item 11 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, which apply to pretrial detainees, the Constitutional Court found them constitutional on the ground that they do not infringe freedom of expression or freedom of communication (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA623, 2014. 8. 28.; Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA549, 2016. 4. 28., et al.), and since the same reasoning can equally apply to prisoners whose sentence has been imposed and has become final and conclusive, there is no need for constitutional clarification regarding these matters.\\n\\nTherefore, no interest in review is recognized for any of the petitions concerning this part either.\\n\\n(e) The portion concerning Article 108 item 4 (suspension of participation in group events), item 6 (restriction on watching television), the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under item 7 (restriction on use of self-purchased items), and the portion concerning item 13 (suspension of outdoor exercise)\\n\\nAs long as the portions concerning Article 108 item 4, item 6, the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under item 7, and item 13 among the confinement provision at issue in this case exist, it is highly likely to recur that inmates, when subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition, will also be subject to treatment restrictions such as suspension of participation in group events, restriction on watching television, restriction on use of self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books, and suspension of outdoor exercise; and because the determination of constitutionality regarding these statutory provisions is an important matter for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, and constitutional clarification is necessary, an interest in review is recognized for all petitions concerning this part.\\n\\nc. Conclusion on Procedural Requirements\\n\\nAccordingly, the petition for review concerning the investigation provision at issue in this case and the portion concerning newspapers, books, and magazines under Article 108 item 5 and item 7, and the portions concerning item 9, item 10, item 11, and item 12, among the confinement provision at issue in this case, are all procedurally defective, and the remaining petitions are all procedurally proper.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. Disciplinary Sanctions and Treatment Restrictions under the Sentence Execution Act\\n\\n(1) Disciplinary sanctions under the Sentence Execution Act\\n\\nThe Sentence Execution Act requires inmates to observe certain rules for the safety and maintenance of order in correctional facilities (prisons, detention houses, juvenile prisons, and their branches) (Article 105(1)), and provides that disciplinary sanctions shall be imposed on those who violate such rules (Article 107). Because correctional facilities are places where inmates are forcibly confined, the need to ensure order and safety within the facility is substantial; and since disciplinary sanctions under the Sentence Execution Act are imposed upon persons who are under disadvantages arising from pretrial detention to secure investigative and trial procedures and from the execution of punishment, it can be anticipated that the disadvantage as a sanction for rule violations will further restrict freedom and rights beyond the disadvantages inherent in ordinary imprisonment and inmate life included in punishment (see Constitutional Court 2003HEONMA289, 2005. 2. 24.; Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA623, 2014. 8. 28.).\\n\\n(2) Confinement to a disciplinary cell and treatment restrictions\\n\\nAmong disciplinary sanctions, confinement to a disciplinary cell is the most severe sanction, meaning punitive confinement aggravated beyond the ordinary state of inmate confinement, by confining the subject in a disciplinary cell (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 231(2)) and imposing certain restrictions on living conditions (Sentence Execution Act, Article 112(3)). If there is a risk that an inmate under confinement to a disciplinary cell may commit suicide or self-harm with daily necessities or the like, or a risk that such items may undermine the safety and order of the correctional facility, those items may be separately stored and used only when necessary (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 232). When executing a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition, the warden must have the medical officer ascertain the inmate’s health in advance; even during execution, the inmate’s health status must be checked at intervals (Sentence Execution Act, Article 112(4)), and upon completion of the execution of the above disposition, the medical officer must be made to ascertain the inmate’s health without delay (Enforcement Decree of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 133(4)).\\n\\nThe confinement provision at issue in this case provides that, for inmates who have been subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition, treatment restrictions such as suspension of participation in group events, reading newspapers, watching television, use of self-purchased items, and telephone calls are uniformly prohibited during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, and that treatment restrictions such as writing, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, visits, and outdoor exercise are, in principle, also imposed.\\n\\nb. The Portion of the Confinement Provision at Issue in This Case Concerning Article 108 Item 4 (Suspension of Participation in Group Events)\\n\\n(1) Related provisions\\n\\nAlthough no definitional provision for “group events” can be found in the Sentence Execution Act, when Article 108 of the same Act, the investigation provision at issue in this case, and the confinement provision at issue in this case are comprehensively considered, group events may be understood as excluding outdoor exercise, work, and educational training among the treatments allowing contact with others within the prison.\\n\\nRepresentative group events under the Sentence Execution Act include religious services and reformation programs. An inmate may attend religious rites or events conducted within the correctional facility; provided, however, that the warden may restrict them if there are grounds corresponding to cases where such restriction is necessary for the reformation of a prisoner, the prisoner’s sound return to society, or for the safety and maintenance of order of the facility (Sentence Execution Act, Article 45(1) and (3)). Meanwhile, the warden shall conduct counseling, psychotherapy, and other reformation programs for the correction and reformation of prisoners (Sentence Execution Act, Article 64).\\n\\nThe portion concerning Article 108 item 4 among the confinement provision at issue in this case uniformly imposes on persons subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition the treatment restriction of suspension of participation in group events during that period.\\n\\n(2) Fundamental rights restricted\\n\\nBy the portion concerning Article 108 item 4 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, the Petitioner is unable to attend group events such as religious services and reformation programs during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period. Although an inmate is already restricted in free intercourse and communication with the outside world by confinement, the above provision further prevents a person subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition not only from intercourse and communication with the outside world but also from intercourse and communication within the facility, and prohibits attendance at religious rites or events that are permitted to ordinary inmates; thus, beyond the restrictions on fundamental rights already contemplated for inmates for the execution of punishment, it additionally restricts the Petitioner’s freedom of communication and freedom of religion (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA523, 2014. 9. 25.).\\n\\n(3) Whether freedom of communication and freedom of religion are infringed\\n\\n(a) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and suitability of the means\\n\\nThe most fundamental premise of the legislative purpose of the Sentence Execution Act is the maintenance of safety and order in detention or confinement facilities. Because correctional facilities involve collective life due to forced confinement, strict discipline in daily life is indispensable not only for the safety of the facility and personnel but also for the safety of the inmates. The portion concerning Article 108 item 4 among the confinement provision at issue in this case is intended to maintain safety and order within the correctional facility by compelling observance of discipline, by imposing the disadvantage of suspension of participation in group events during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, together with execution of the confinement disposition, on persons who have violated discipline and are deemed to have committed a serious violation; thus, its legislative purpose is legitimate.\\n\\nThe above provision can also be a necessary and effective means to induce inmates to observe discipline, by uniformly prohibiting, for persons who have received a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition due to a disciplinary violation, participation in group events that is otherwise actually permitted to ordinary inmates, thereby encouraging reflection in violators and warning ordinary inmates of the disadvantages of disciplinary violations. Accordingly, suitability of the means is also recognized.\\n\\n(b) Minimum impairment\\n\\nIn order to maintain order and safety in prisons, discipline must be observed, and sanctions must inevitably be imposed on those who violate discipline; however, for inmates who must already endure forced confinement for a certain period against their will under a state in which fundamental rights are restricted, and who in most cases are scheduled to leave prison upon completion of their sentence, there are not many sanctions that can exert real deterrent force.\\n\\nAs one such sanction, the Sentence Execution Act prescribes confinement to a disciplinary cell as the heaviest disciplinary sanction for a person who violates discipline, and through the confinement provision at issue in this case, it imposes the disadvantage of treatment restrictions that additionally restrict or deprive part of the freedom otherwise enjoyed by ordinary inmates even in a limited form, in addition to confining the subject to a disciplinary cell (see Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA623, 2014. 8. 28.; Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA549, 2016. 4. 28., et al.).\\n\\nIn order to achieve the purpose of confinement to a disciplinary cell itself—namely, to confine the person who has received such disposition to a disciplinary cell and to exhort reform through strict segregation—it is necessary to restrict that person from participating in group events in which direct contact with other inmates and correctional officers is possible.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to the proviso of Article 112(3) of the Sentence Execution Act, the warden may permit receipt and dispatch of correspondence and visits if deemed especially necessary for the relief of an inmate’s rights, the reformation of a prisoner, or the prisoner’s sound return to society; thus, an inmate may exceptionally communicate with the outside world even during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period. Furthermore, the warden must have experts such as correctional officers, correctional committee members, and volunteers counsel inmates undergoing execution of disciplinary sanctions to endeavor to prevent recurrence of the conduct subject to discipline (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 223), and where religious counseling is needed among them, the warden may have a correctional officer or a participating person in correctional services who follows the relevant religion provide such counseling (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 33); thus, a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell may engage in religious activities through religious counseling.\\n\\nAs stated above, while a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell cannot participate in group events for a period of up to 30 days, the person may communicate with the outside world through receipt and dispatch of correspondence and visits, and may engage in religious activities through religious counseling; accordingly, the portion concerning Article 108 item 4 among the confinement provision at issue in this case does not violate the requirement of minimum impairment.\\n\\n(c) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nA person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell suffers the disadvantage of being unable, during the confinement period, to interact with inmates within the correctional facility or engage in religious activities by participating in group events, but this cannot be regarded as greater than the public interest in maintaining inmate order through observance of discipline; accordingly, the above provision also satisfies the balance of legal interests.\\n\\n(d) Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion concerning Article 108 item 4 among the confinement provision at issue in this case does not infringe the Petitioner’s freedom of communication or freedom of religion.\\n\\nc. The Portion of the Confinement Provision at Issue in This Case Concerning Article 108 Item 6 (Restriction on Watching Television)\\n\\n(1) Related provisions\\n\\nAn inmate may watch television for emotional stability and general education (Sentence Execution Act, Article 48(1)). The warden may temporarily suspend television broadcasting to inmates or prohibit an individual inmate from watching television if there are grounds corresponding to cases where such restriction is necessary for the reformation of a prisoner, the prisoner’s sound return to society, or for the safety and maintenance of order of the facility (Sentence Execution Act, Article 48(2)). The warden shall set the broadcasting schedule within up to 6 hours per day, taking into account the inmate’s health and working hours, and may adjust the broadcasting schedule by considering Saturdays, public holidays, work and educational conditions, and the characteristics of inmates (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 39). Inmates shall watch television through the designated channel at the place designated by the warden; provided, however, that a prisoner classified as open treatment grade or reduced security treatment grade and permitted to live autonomously may watch television in the manner prescribed by the Minister of Justice (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 41(1)). Inmates shall not arbitrarily manipulate or change broadcasting equipment or channels, nor possess unauthorized reception equipment (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 41(2)).\\n\\nThe portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case uniformly imposes on persons subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition the treatment restriction of restriction on watching television during that period.\\n\\n(2) Fundamental rights restricted\\n\\nThe right to know, a fundamental right derived from Article 21 of the Constitution and others, refers to the right to collect and process general information from all sources of information; here, “general” refers to that which may be open to an unspecified and large number of persons such as newspapers, magazines, and broadcasting, and “information” means all materials related to the formation of conscience, thought, opinion, knowledge, and the like (see Constitutional Court 2008HEONMA638, 2010. 10. 28.). Watching television is a basic means by which an inmate may access general information, which serves as a premise for free formation of will, even if only within a limited range; accordingly, the portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, which prohibits watching television during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, restricts the Petitioner’s right to know.\\n\\n(3) Whether the right to know is infringed\\n\\n(a) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and suitability of the means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of establishing inmate order by prohibiting a person who has received the most severe disciplinary sanction, confinement to a disciplinary cell, from contacting the outside world through strict segregation and causing that person to devote himself to reflection is legitimate, and restricting television viewing during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period is a suitable means to achieve that purpose.\\n\\n(b) Minimum impairment\\n\\nOrdinary inmates may watch television for emotional stability and general education; however, the warden may temporarily suspend television broadcasting to inmates or prohibit an individual inmate from watching television if there are grounds corresponding to cases where such restriction is necessary for the reformation of a prisoner, the prisoner’s sound return to society, or for the safety and maintenance of order of the facility (Sentence Execution Act, Article 48). Furthermore, unless permitted autonomous living, ordinary inmates must watch television through the designated channel at the place designated by the warden (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 41(1)). In this manner, the Sentence Execution Act grants the warden certain discretion regarding whether and how ordinary inmates may watch television. However, because a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition itself is executed by confining the person subject to discipline to a disciplinary cell (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 231(2)) and has the purpose of causing such person to devote himself to reflection in segregation, it is difficult in correctional practice to ensure television viewing for a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell at the same level as ordinary inmates.\\n\\nIn addition, because the confinement period is prescribed as up to 30 days (Sentence Execution Act, Article 108 item 14), the period during which the Petitioner is restricted from watching television cannot exceed 30 days.\\n\\nMoreover, while restricting television viewing by a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell, the Sentence Execution Act allows such person to access other sources of information by being provided with a book list and reading books kept in the correctional facility (see Constitutional Court 2009HEONMA99, 2009. 10. 29.; Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA549, 2016. 4. 28., et al.).\\n\\nAs stated above, a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell cannot watch television for a period of up to 30 days; however, because there are difficulties in ensuring television viewing for such person at the same level as ordinary inmates in the process of executing the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition, and because the person may instead read books provided in the correctional facility, the portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case cannot be said to violate the requirement of minimum impairment.\\n\\n(c) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe disadvantage suffered by a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell by the portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case is that the person cannot watch television for a limited period, and the public interest in maintaining safety and order in the correctional facility through observance of discipline is greater than the restriction thereby imposed on the Petitioner’s right to know; accordingly, the above provision also satisfies the balance of legal interests.\\n\\n(d) Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case does not infringe the Petitioner’s right to know.\\n\\nd. The Portion of the Confinement Provision at Issue in This Case Concerning Article 108 Item 7 (Restriction on Use of Self-Purchased Items), Other Than Newspapers, Magazines, and Books\\n\\n(1) Related provisions\\n\\nThe warden shall provide inmates with clothing, bedding, and other daily necessities suitable for maintaining health (Sentence Execution Act, Article 22); clothing and bedding shall be provided one set per person, though two sets may be provided taking into account whether work is performed and heating conditions, and other daily necessities include toothpaste, toothbrushes, toilet soap, laundry soap, towels, toilet paper, and sanitary pads (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 8(1), [Attached Table 1] of Article 8(2)).\\n\\nIn addition to the above items that are compulsorily provided, an inmate may, with the warden’s permission, purchase food, clothing, bedding, and other items necessary for inmate life (hereinafter referred to as “self-purchased items”) at his own expense (Sentence Execution Act, Article 24; Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 2 item 1). Self-purchased items must be suitable for correction and reformation and must not be likely to undermine the safety and order of the correctional facility (Enforcement Decree of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 31). Self-purchased items include food, medicines and medical supplies, clothing, bedding and footwear, newspapers, magazines, books and stationery, items necessary for correction and reformation such as prisoner education, and other items deemed necessary for inmate life (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 16(1)). When an inmate applies to purchase self-purchased items, the warden shall approve within the limits of the use of stored money determined by the Minister of Justice taking into account correctional performance or the security treatment grade, the scope kept in the correctional facility, and the scope of possession by the inmate, and may restrict the purchase application when the use of self-purchased items is suspended due to the execution of disciplinary sanctions against the inmate (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 17(1) and (2)).\\n\\nThe portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case uniformly prohibits a person subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition from using self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books (excluding medicines prescribed by a doctor for treatment) during that period.\\n\\n(2) Fundamental rights restricted\\n\\n(a) The Petitioner is unable to use clothing, bedding, watches, washing supplies, and the like among self-purchased items by the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, and thus his general freedom of action is restricted.\\n\\n(b) The Petitioner argues that the portion concerning Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case also restricts freedom of expression and the right to access the courts, because he cannot use stationery among self-purchased items, which creates obstacles to preparing administrative litigation or the like challenging disciplinary sanctions and the treatment of persons subject to disciplinary action.\\n\\nHowever, the obstacle to preparing administrative litigation or the like challenging disciplinary sanctions and the treatment of persons subject to disciplinary action arises not because the use of stationery among self-purchased items is restricted by the portion concerning Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, but because writing is restricted by the portion concerning Article 108 item 10 among the confinement provision at issue in this case. Accordingly, the Petitioner’s right to access the courts and freedom of expression are not restricted by the portion concerning Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case.\\n\\n(c) The Petitioner also argues that, considering the practical custom of allowing items that persons subject to disciplinary action purchased at their own expense before receiving a disciplinary disposition to be used during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, the portion concerning Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case infringes the right to equality by treating without reasonable grounds persons who already purchased items before the disciplinary disposition and persons who are only to purchase items after the disciplinary disposition differently. However, the above provision itself uniformly prohibits the use of self-purchased items regardless of the time of purchase, and thus it is difficult to say that it treats differently persons who purchased items before the disciplinary disposition and persons who are to purchase items after the disciplinary disposition. Therefore, the Petitioner’s right to equality is not restricted by the portion concerning Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case.\\n\\n(3) Whether general freedom of action is infringed\\n\\n(a) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and suitability of the means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of establishing inmate order by prohibiting a person who has received the most severe disciplinary sanction, confinement to a disciplinary cell, from contacting the outside world through strict segregation and causing that person to devote himself to reflection is legitimate, and prohibiting the use of self-purchased items during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period is a suitable means to achieve that purpose.\\n\\n(b) Minimum impairment\\n\\nItems that an inmate may purchase at his own expense include food, medicines and medical supplies, clothing, bedding and footwear, stationery, items necessary for correction and reformation such as prisoner education, and other items deemed necessary for inmate life (Enforcement Rule of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 16(1)).\\n\\nHowever, the fact that a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell, like ordinary inmates, is provided with food necessary for maintaining health and physical strength (Sentence Execution Act, Article 23), and with clothing, bedding, and other daily necessities suitable for maintaining health (toothpaste, toothbrushes, toilet soap, laundry soap, towels, toilet paper, sanitary pads) is the same (Sentence Execution Act, Article 22); therefore, even during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, the person can lead a life at the minimum necessary level for maintaining health through the items provided by the warden, and medicines prescribed by a doctor for treatment may still be used (the confinement provision at issue in this case; Sentence Execution Act, Article 108 item 7).\\n\\nAs stated above, while a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell is restricted, for a period of up to 30 days, from using self-purchased items excluding medicines prescribed by a doctor for treatment, the person can still lead a life at the minimum necessary level for maintaining health through the items provided by the warden; accordingly, the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case does not violate the requirement of minimum impairment.\\n\\n(c) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe disadvantage suffered by a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell by the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case is that the person cannot use self-purchased items for a limited period of up to 30 days; as the public interest in maintaining order and safety in prisons through observance of discipline and in the correction and reformation of inmates is greater than such disadvantage, it does not violate the balance of legal interests either.\\n\\n(d) Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under Article 108 item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case does not infringe the Petitioner’s general freedom of action.\\n\\ne. The Portion of the Confinement Provision at Issue in This Case Concerning Article 108 Item 13 (Suspension of Outdoor Exercise)\\n\\n(1) Related provisions and Constitutional Court precedents\\n\\nThe warden shall ensure that inmates can regularly exercise as needed to maintain health (Sentence Execution Act, Article 33(1)). The warden shall ensure that inmates can exercise outdoors for up to 1 hour within working hours each day; provided, however, that outdoor exercise may be omitted where it is deemed unnecessary due to the nature of the work, where it is deemed harmful to the inmate’s health due to illness or the like, or where outdoor exercise is difficult because of rain, investigation, trial, or other unavoidable circumstances (Enforcement Decree of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 49).\\n\\nArticle 145(2) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Punishment Execution Act (amended by Presidential Decree No. 16579 on 2000. 3. 28., and before being completely amended by Presidential Decree No. 21095 on 2008. 10. 29.) provided that a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell shall be confined to a disciplinary room and shall be prohibited from exercise during that period; however, the Constitutional Court held that the above provision violated the Constitution by infringing the prisoner’s human dignity and value, physical liberty, and the like (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA478, 2004. 12. 16.).\\n\\nThereafter, the portion concerning Article 108 item 13 of Article 112(3) of the Sentence Execution Act, completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., provides that a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell is, in principle, prohibited from outdoor exercise, but that the warden may exceptionally permit outdoor exercise if deemed especially necessary for the relief of the inmate’s rights, the reformation of a prisoner, or the prisoner’s sound return to society.\\n\\n(2) Whether physical liberty is infringed\\n\\n(a) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and suitability of the means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of establishing inmate order by prohibiting a person who has received the most severe disciplinary sanction, confinement to a disciplinary cell, from contacting the outside world through strict segregation and causing that person to devote himself to reflection is legitimate, and suspending outdoor exercise in principle during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period is a suitable means to achieve that purpose (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA478, 2004. 12. 16.).\\n\\n(b) Minimum impairment\\n\\n1) Outdoor exercise is the minimum basic requirement for maintaining the physical and mental health of a confined inmate. Accordingly, while the Sentence Execution Act grants the warden discretion to decide whether to allow participation in group events, television viewing, purchase of self-purchased items, telephone calls, visits, and receipt and dispatch of correspondence for ordinary inmates, it provides, with respect to outdoor exercise, that “the warden shall ensure that ordinary inmates can regularly exercise as needed to maintain health” (Sentence Execution Act, Article 33(1)). Enforcement Decree of the Sentence Execution Act, Article 49, which specifies the above provision, states that, unless the case falls under situations where outdoor exercise is deemed unnecessary due to the nature of the work, where outdoor exercise is deemed harmful to the inmate’s health due to illness or the like, or where outdoor exercise is difficult because of rain, investigation, trial, or other unavoidable circumstances, the warden shall ensure that inmates can exercise outdoors for up to 1 hour each day within working hours.\\n\\nCompared with ordinary inmates, persons subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell are uniformly prohibited from participation in group events, reading newspapers, watching television, use of self-purchased items, and work, while telephone calls, writing, and visits are exceptionally permitted, and therefore are generally in a state of cut-off communication with the outside world. Moreover, persons subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell are confined to a disciplinary cell measuring 4.6㎡ (1.397 pyeong) with a window measuring 0.46㎡; the prohibition of outdoor exercise means not only that they cannot exercise, but also that they are confined in a narrow disciplinary cell without any opportunity during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period to come out of the disciplinary cell and breathe fresh air outdoors. The confinement period is up to 30 days, and according to the 2013 statistics of the Correction Headquarters of the Ministry of Justice, the proportion of confinement among disciplinary sanctions reached 88.1% (27.8% within 30 days, 45.7% within 20 days, 14.6% within 10 days). Taking these circumstances into account, where an inmate confined to a 4.6㎡ disciplinary cell cut off from the outside world is, in principle, prohibited from exercise for up to 30 days, the risk that the inmate may suffer harm not only to physical health but also to mental health is remarkably high (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA478, 2004. 12. 16.). The Sentence Execution Act requires the warden to have the inmate’s health checked frequently before and after execution and during execution even when the treatment restriction of suspension of outdoor exercise, as well as confinement to a disciplinary cell, is imposed (Sentence Execution Act, Article 112(4); Enforcement Decree of the same Act, Article 133(4)), which indicates that suspension of outdoor exercise itself is a treatment restriction that may have a serious effect on the inmate’s physical and mental health.\\n\\nConsidering that outdoor exercise is indispensable for maintaining the physical and mental health of inmates, and that the inmate’s physical and mental health must underpin the fundamental goals of sentence execution, namely the correction and reformation of inmates and their sound return to society, there is doubt whether the confinement provision at issue in this case, in addition to execution of confinement by confinement in a disciplinary cell, necessarily needs to impose, in principle, the treatment restriction of suspension of outdoor exercise in order to achieve the legislative purpose of maintaining safety and order inside the correctional facility.\\n\\n2) Although Article 112(3) of the Sentence Execution Act has been amended since Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA478, 2004. 12. 16., the portion concerning Article 108 item 13 of the same provision still, in principle, prohibits outdoor exercise for persons subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell and, only by discretion of the warden, permits it exceptionally (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DA24050, rendered on 2009. 6. 25.); thus, the necessity of in principle prohibiting outdoor exercise for all inmates subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell still cannot be found. Since there may be exceptional cases in which allowing outdoor exercise would make it difficult to achieve the purpose of confinement to a disciplinary cell because the inmate is noisy, riotous, or likely to harm others, the necessity of restricting outdoor exercise exceptionally only in such cases would be recognized.\\n\\nIn addition, the proviso to Article 112(3) of the Sentence Execution Act permits outdoor exercise exceptionally, but does not set a minimum standard for the number of days on which an opportunity for outdoor exercise must be afforded.\\n\\n3) Even when examining foreign legislative examples, in cases where a sanction involving isolation of an inmate is imposed, outdoor activity or outdoor exercise is protected more strongly than other treatment restrictions, and even where outdoor exercise is restricted, the minimum standard is expressly stipulated in the legislation.\\n\\nUnder the United States Code of Federal Regulations, an inmate who receives “disciplinary segregation,” one of the disciplinary sanctions, is confined to a Special Housing Unit, in which personal items other than those necessary for writing and reading and religious texts are confiscated, canteen use is restricted, and correspondence, telephone calls, and visits may be restricted; whereas the right to outdoor exercise is, in principle, guaranteed for 5 hours per week. However, if the warden determines that the inmate’s outdoor exercise would harm the safety, security, order, or public safety of the correctional facility, outdoor exercise may be restricted, but in that case only one week’s worth of exercise may be restricted at a time (28 C.F.R. §541.21, 541.22, 541.31).\\n\\nUnder Japan’s Act on Penal Institution and Treatment of Inmates and Detainees, in the case of one of the disciplinary sanctions, confinement in a closed room (heukgeo), acts corresponding to use or consumption of self-purchased items, participation in religious rites or services, receiving religious instruction together with other inmates, reading books and the like, self-contract work, visits, and receipt and dispatch of letters are suspended (Article 152(1)); on the other hand, outdoor exercise is restricted only to the extent that it does not interfere with health maintenance (Article 152(2)), and in such case, the number of days on which the opportunity for outdoor exercise is afforded shall not be less than 1 day per week (Rule on the Treatment of Inmates and Detainees in Penal Institutions, Article 87).\\n\\n4) Taking the foregoing circumstances together, it is desirable, with respect to outdoor exercise for a person subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell, to allow it in principle and restrict it only exceptionally in consideration of the characteristics of the person subject to disciplinary action; and even where the need for restriction is recognized, it is necessary to expressly provide the minimum standard for such restriction in the legislation. Therefore, the portion concerning Article 108 item 13 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, which in principle prohibits outdoor exercise merely because a person has received a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition, constitutes an excessive restriction on physical liberty and violates the requirement of minimum impairment.\\n\\n(c) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe public interest in maintaining safety and order in the correctional facility, which the portion concerning Article 108 item 13 among the confinement provision at issue in this case seeks to achieve, may also be maintained by restricting outdoor exercise for persons subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell who are noisy, riotous, or likely to harm others. On the other hand, the above provision, by exceptionally permitting outdoor exercise at the discretion of the warden, imposes on the inmate’s mental and physical health an excessive disadvantage beyond what is necessary, and since this is greater than the public interest, the above provision also fails to satisfy the requirement of balance of legal interests.\\n\\n(d) Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion concerning Article 108 item 13 among the confinement provision at issue in this case infringes the Petitioner’s physical liberty.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion concerning Article 108 item 13 among the confinement provision at issue in this case infringes the Petitioner’s physical liberty and is unconstitutional; the petition for review concerning the portion concerning self-purchased items other than newspapers, magazines, and books under Article 108 item 4, item 6, and item 7 among the confinement provision at issue in this case is all without merit and is therefore dismissed; and the remaining petitions for review are all procedurally defective and are therefore dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as follows. In this decision, except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim I-su, Justice Lee Jin-seong, and Justice Kang Il-won regarding the portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case as stated in 7 below, the opinions of the remaining Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kim I-su, Justice Lee Jin-seong, and Justice Kang Il-won Regarding the Portion Concerning Article 108 Item 6 Among the Confinement Provision at Issue in This Case\\n\\na. Our view is not different from the majority opinion in that the legislative purpose of the portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case—that is, to cause inmates subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell to devote themselves to reflection and to establish order within prison confinement—is legitimate. However, when enacting legislation that restricts fundamental rights, one must choose, among the various means to achieve the legislative purpose, the means that least restricts fundamental rights. It is clear that, for the safety and order of the prison, the disciplinary effect can be increased by restricting other treatment as well, such as prohibiting receipt and dispatch of correspondence and visits, in addition to confining the inmate subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell. However, completely restricting television viewing cannot be regarded as a necessary or appropriate measure to achieve the legislative purpose.\\n\\nb. For democracy to function properly, free formation of public opinion must be possible. For free formation of public opinion to be possible, anyone must be able to freely express opinions. However, freedom of expression presupposes the right to know, which is the freedom to obtain information without interference from the State. Therefore, the right to know is a very important fundamental right for the realization of democracy.\\n\\nTelevision is an audio-visual medium that is easily accessible even to persons who cannot read, and it transmits information about events occurring in society almost in real time. Meanwhile, even prisoners isolated from society by committing crimes should, to the maximum extent possible, be guaranteed the right to know, so that they may obtain up-to-date information about events occurring in the society to which they belong. If a person confined in prison is subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition, telephone calls and receipt and dispatch of correspondence and visits are restricted, and contact with the outside world, such as listening to radio broadcasts or reading newspapers, is also restricted. If television viewing is additionally restricted, a person subjected to the disciplinary sanction of confinement will be unable, for as long as 30 days, to know at all what is happening in society. Even if a natural disaster occurs in the person’s hometown, the person would not know of it; and if there is an important election during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, the person cannot obtain information regarding the election, so an inmate who has voting rights cannot properly exercise that right. In some cases, the inmate may not even know who has become the President of Korea or who has become the member of the National Assembly or the head of the local government in his constituency of residence.\\n\\nEven an inmate subjected to a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition must be guaranteed at least the minimum opportunity to access news about events occurring in society. If allowing television viewing to an inmate subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell is difficult in correctional administration, then the inmate should be allowed to access new information through reading newspapers or listening to radio broadcasts. The inmate’s access to new news and information from society is an extremely personal act related to the person’s mental activity, and is an act that poses no risk whatsoever to the maintenance of order and safety in prisons. If only entertainment programs that are contrary to the purpose of confinement or punishment are restricted, allowing the acquisition of new information through television viewing would pose no risk of undermining the purpose of the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition or the establishment of inmate order.\\n\\nAllowing inmates subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell, for whom reading newspapers and listening to radio broadcasts are completely prohibited, to obtain information through television viewing can instead contribute to the inmate’s correction and reformation by promoting sound mental activity and enabling preparation for a smooth return to society in the future. Nevertheless, restricting all methods of information access by inmates merely because they violated discipline constitutes an excessive restriction on fundamental rights, even in light of the legislative purpose of establishing order in prison confinement, and is contrary to the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nc. Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights declares that “Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.” Article 39 of the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners also declares that “Prisoners shall be kept informed regularly of the more important items of news by the reading of newspapers, periodicals or special institutional publications, by hearing wireless transmissions, by lectures or by similar means as authorized or controlled by the administration.” The portion concerning Article 108 item 6 among the confinement provision at issue in this case, which restricts television viewing while no other opportunity to know new news, such as newspaper reading, is provided at all to prison inmates subjected to confinement to a disciplinary cell, also violates the minimum standards for the treatment of prisoners declared by the United Nations. Even for prison inmates who are disciplined for violating rules, guaranteeing the right to know at least minimum information conforms to the standards of the United Nations and is a constitutional interpretation in line with the international human rights level."}
