{"[2015HEONBA46]": "1. Case Summary\\n\\na. The Petitioner, as a pastor operating the “○○ Church” in ○○ Township, Hwaseong City, was indicted on the criminal facts that “although the nursing facility operated by the above church fell under an elderly residential welfare facility requiring a report, he did not report it to the Mayor of Hwaseong City, and from around 2012. 7. 3. to around 2012. 11. 29., provided meals and conveniences necessary for daily life to elderly persons including An ○ Sun and 11 others.” He was sentenced to a judgment of suspension of the pronouncement of sentence (Suwon District Court 2013GODAN440).\\n\\nb. The Petitioner appealed this and, while the appellate proceedings were pending (Suwon District Court 2014NO2534), filed a motion for referral of a constitutional review concerning Article 32(1)1 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act and Article 2 item 4 of the Social Welfare Services Act. However, on 2014. 12. 18., when the criminal appeal was dismissed, the portion concerning the Senior Citizens Welfare Act was dismissed and the portion concerning the Social Welfare Services Act was dismissed as inadmissible on the same day (Suwon District Court 2014CHOGI2258), and on 2015. 2. 2., he filed this constitutional complaint.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Petitioner sought a review of Article 32(1)1 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act. However, since the provisions applied to the Petitioner in the underlying criminal case are the provision requiring reports for certain nursing homes for the elderly and the provision punishing a person who establishes or operates a nursing home for the elderly without filing such report, the subject matter of review in this case is whether the part concerning “nursing homes for the elderly” in Article 32(1)1 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (as amended by Act No. 8608 on 2007. 8. 3.) within Article 33(2), and the part concerning “nursing homes for the elderly” in Article 33(2) of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (as amended by Act No. 9964 on 2010. 1. 25.) within Article 57(1), violate the Constitution.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nSenior Citizens Welfare Act (as amended by Act No. 8608 on 2007. 8. 3.)\\n\\nArticle 33 (Establishment of Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities) (2) In cases where a person other than the State or a local government intends to establish elderly residential welfare facilities, he or she shall file a report thereon to the Governor of a Special Self-Governing Province, Mayor, County Governor, or District Head (hereinafter referred to as the “Mayor/County Governor/District Head”).\\n\\nSenior Citizens Welfare Act (as amended by Act No. 9964 on 2010. 1. 25.)\\n\\nArticle 57 (Penal Provisions) A person falling under any of the following items shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 1 year or by a fine not exceeding 3 million won.\\n\\n1. A person who establishes or operates a nursing home for the elderly, a group home for the elderly, housing for the elderly, a nursing facility for the elderly, a group home for elderly care, an elderly leisure welfare facility, or a home care welfare facility for the elderly without filing a report pursuant to Article 33(2), Article 35(2), Article 37(2), or Article 39(2)\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]\\n\\nSenior Citizens Welfare Act (as amended by Act No. 8608 on 2007. 8. 3.)\\n\\nArticle 32 (Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities) (1) Elderly residential welfare facilities shall be the following facilities:\\n\\n1. Nursing home for the elderly: a facility whose purpose is to admit elderly persons and provide meals and other conveniences necessary for daily life\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Assertion\\n\\na. Since the provisions subject to review do not clearly provide whether “religious facilities” are included in “nursing homes for the elderly,” they violate the principle of clarity under the principle of legality.\\n\\nb. If religious facilities are included in the provisions subject to review, religious organizations would be unable to establish elderly residential welfare facilities without filing a report, and this infringes the Petitioner’s freedom of religion, the elderly’s freedom of residence and movement and right to lead a life worthy of human dignity, and infringes a juridical person’s personality rights and freedom of corporate management.\\n\\n4. Overview of the System for Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities\\n\\na. The State’s Duty and Management/Supervision over Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities\\n\\n(1) The State’s Duty Regarding Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities\\n\\nArticle 34(1) of the Constitution provides that all citizens shall have the right to lead a life worthy of human dignity, thereby guaranteeing the right to lead a life worthy of human dignity, and paragraph (4) of the same Article provides that the State has the duty to implement policies for the enhancement of the welfare of the aged and juveniles. Meanwhile, the Constitution provides in Article 35(3) that the State shall endeavor, through the development of housing policy, to enable all citizens to enjoy comfortable housing life. Accordingly, the State bears the duty to endeavor, from the perspective of welfare enhancement, to develop housing policies suitable for the characteristics of the elderly, so that the elderly may engage in comfortable housing activities. In accordance therewith, Article 8 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act provides that the State or a local government shall promote the supply of residential facilities equipped with functions and facilities suitable for the housing of the elderly, and may provide appropriate support to the suppliers of such residential facilities.\\n\\n(2) Necessity of Management/Supervision over Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities\\n\\nThe residential welfare of elderly residential welfare facilities, such as nursing homes for the elderly, aims to secure space for maintaining safe and comfortable daily life while preserving individual independence, and to support this through the construction and supply of housing, and services related thereto.\\n\\nAmong such elderly residential welfare facilities, the persons eligible for admission to a nursing home for the elderly are: ① persons aged 65 or older who are recipients of livelihood benefits or medical benefits under the National Basic Living Security Act; ② persons aged 65 or older who do not receive proper support from their persons obligated to support them; ③ persons aged 65 or older whose own monthly average income amount and the monthly average income amount of the persons obligated to support them who share their livelihood are not more than the per capita monthly average income amount obtained by dividing the previous year’s monthly average income of urban workers’ households by the previous year’s average household size; and ④ persons aged 60 or older who enter at their own expense. In the cases of ① and ② above, the State and local governments bear all admission expenses, and in the case of ③, they bear a part thereof (Articles 14 and 15-2 of the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act).\\n\\nHowever, the above-mentioned nursing homes for the elderly, in which elderly persons enter and live in group settings, are prone to being cut off from or isolated from the outside world, so even if problems arise, they are difficult to detect and highly susceptible to concealment. Moreover, elderly persons residing in nursing homes for the elderly are mostly likely to be pushed into blind spots of protection physically, mentally, emotionally, and sexually, and there is also a risk that they may become targets of violence and exploitation or be exposed to safety accidents. Therefore, the State and local governments responsible for the welfare of the elderly must establish a system to protect elderly persons so that they are not placed in such blind spots of protection in elderly welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly. In other words, the State and local governments have the duty to manage and supervise whether the relevant facilities provide comfortable housing life meeting appropriate facility standards and personnel standards, thereby enabling elderly persons to live safely and comfortably.\\n\\nb. History and Requirements of the Reporting System for the Establishment of Elderly Residential Welfare Facilities\\n\\n(1) History of the Reporting System for Establishment\\n\\nThe Senior Citizens Welfare Act was enacted on 1981. 6. 5. by Act No. 3453. At the time of enactment, elderly welfare facilities were classified into nursing homes for the elderly, nursing facilities for the elderly, paid nursing homes for the elderly, elderly welfare halls, etc. (Article 13), and if a social welfare foundation or other non-profit juridical person other than the State or a local government intended to establish an elderly welfare facility, it had to obtain permission from the Mayor of Seoul Special City, Mayor of a Direct-Controlled City, or Governor of a Province (Article 14). When the types of elderly welfare facilities were wholly amended by Act No. 4178 on 1989. 12. 30., self-pay nursing homes for the elderly, self-pay nursing facilities for the elderly, paid nursing facilities for the elderly, housing for the elderly, etc. were added (Article 18), and if a social welfare foundation or other non-profit juridical person other than the State or a local government intended to establish an elderly welfare facility, permission from the Mayor of Seoul Special City, Mayor of a Direct-Controlled City, or Governor of a Province was required (Article 19).\\n\\nWhen the types of elderly welfare facilities were provided as elderly residential welfare facilities, elderly medical welfare facilities, elderly leisure welfare facilities, and home care welfare facilities for the elderly as the law was wholly amended by Act No. 5359 on 1997. 8. 22., nursing homes for the elderly came to be provided as one type of elderly residential welfare facility under Article 32(1)1 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act. At this time, if the person intending to establish elderly residential welfare facilities was a person other than the State or a local government, he or she was required to file a report with the Mayor/Do Governor (Article 33(2)), and the existing permission requirement was changed to a reporting requirement.\\n\\n(2) Facility Standards for Facilities Subject to Reporting\\n\\nElderly residential welfare facilities must satisfy the standards prescribed in Attached Table 2 pursuant to Article 17(1) of the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act. In the case of nursing homes for the elderly, facilities with a capacity of 10 or more residents become subject to reporting, and a space of at least 15.9㎡ of total floor area per resident capacity must be secured; the bedroom area per resident must be at least 5.0㎡; and the capacity of one dormitory-style bedroom shall be 4 persons or fewer. The structure and equipment of elderly residential welfare facilities must sufficiently take into account the health and sanitation of residents and disaster prevention, including sunlight, lighting, and ventilation; facilities usually used by residents, such as corridors, toilets, and living rooms, must secure space for movement by wheelchairs and the like; and they must be equipped with a structure convenient for elderly persons’ activities, such as removal of thresholds, attachment of handrails, and slip prevention for floors. Firefighting equipment must be installed and emergency exits must be provided, and for the healthy life of residents, ancillary cultural and physical education facilities such as libraries and sports/recreation facilities shall be installed, but they may be operated by opening them to the outside to the extent that it does not hinder residents’ use, in order to enhance ties with the local community. When a person other than the State or a local government intends to establish a nursing home for the elderly, he or she shall secure the above facility standards and file a report with the head of the competent Si/Gun/Gu Office (Articles 33 and the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, Article 16).\\n\\n5. Determination\\n\\na. Restricted Fundamental Rights\\n\\n(1) The provisions subject to review impose a duty to file a report on nursing homes for the elderly subject to reporting, regardless of who operates them. However, for religious persons or religious organizations to establish social welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly for socially vulnerable groups or the poor and to conduct missionary activities is a method of missionary activity established through long tradition, and building facilities for the socially weak and providing assistance is related to the essence of religion. Accordingly, the fact that the provisions subject to review do not exclude nursing homes for the elderly operated by religious organizations from nursing homes for the elderly subject to reporting raises an issue of restriction on the freedom of religion, namely, the freedom of missionary work through the free operation of nursing homes for the elderly.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, the provisions subject to review impose a reporting duty on elderly residential welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly and impose criminal punishment in case of violation, but whether nursing homes for the elderly operated by “religious organizations” are included is not clearly apparent from the text, and thus whether they violate the principle of clarity under the principle of legality is at issue.\\n\\nIn addition, conducting missionary activity by establishing social welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly is a religious act subject to restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution (Constitutional Court, 2001. 9. 27., 2000HEONMA159). However, in imposing such restrictions, the limits on the restriction of fundamental rights must be observed, and thus whether imposing a reporting duty also on nursing homes for the elderly operated by religious organizations violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is also at issue.\\n\\n(3) The Petitioner argues that the provisions subject to review infringe the elderly’s freedom of residence and movement and right to lead a life worthy of human dignity. However, since the provisions subject to review are merely provisions requiring that nursing homes for the elderly operated by religious organizations also be reported if they exceed a certain scale, and cannot be regarded as causing restrictions on the freedom of residence and movement or the right to lead a life worthy of human dignity, these issues shall not be separately determined.\\n\\n(4) The Petitioner argues that the provisions subject to review infringe a juridical person’s personality rights and freedom of corporate management, but, as noted above, the operation of welfare facilities by religious organizations falls within the sphere of the freedom of religion, and thus the issue ultimately comes down to whether the freedom of religion is infringed.\\n\\n(5) Therefore, below we will examine whether the provisions subject to review violate the principle of clarity under the principle of legality and the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nb. Whether the Principle of Clarity under the Principle of Legality Has Been Violated\\n\\n(1) Standard of Review\\n\\nThe principle of legality of crimes and punishment guaranteed through Articles 12 and 13 of the Constitution means that crimes and punishments must be prescribed by law, and the principle of clarity derived from such principle of legality requires that the constituent elements be clearly defined so that anyone can foresee what conduct the law intends to punish and what punishment will be imposed therefor, and accordingly determine his or her conduct. However, even though the constituent elements of punitive provisions must be clear, this does not mean that all constituent elements must be defined by simple descriptive concepts; even if somewhat broad concepts requiring supplementary interpretation by judges are used, if, by ordinary methods of interpretation, the relevant punitive provision is structured so that a person with sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiment can know the protected legal interests of the punitive provision, the prohibited conduct, and the type and degree of punishment, it does not run counter to the clarity of punitive provisions required by the Constitution.\\n\\nWhether a legal norm is clear can be determined based on whether the legal norm provides fair notice to addressees so that they can know its meaning and content, thereby giving predictability, and whether it informs the institutions that interpret and enforce the law of sufficient meaning and content so as to exclude arbitrary legal interpretation or enforcement; in other words, whether predictability and exclusion of arbitrary enforcement are secured. The meaning and content of a legal norm are concretized by an interpretive method that comprehensively considers not only the text, but also the legislative purpose or intent, legislative history, and the systematic structure of the legal norm. Ultimately, whether a legal norm violates the principle of clarity depends on whether a standard of interpretation can be obtained that can reasonably grasp its meaning and content by such interpretive methods (see Constitutional Court, 2011. 6. 30., 2009HEONBA199).\\n\\n(2) Determination\\n\\nAs to nursing homes for the elderly, which the provisions subject to review require to be reported, the Senior Citizens Welfare Act provides that they are “facilities whose purpose is to admit elderly persons and provide meals and other conveniences necessary for daily life” (Article 32(1)1). Since “elderly person” has the dictionary meaning of “a person of advanced age,” “admit” means “to enter and stay in a dormitory or the like,” and “convenience” means “a condition or circumstances being comfortable and favorable,” a nursing home for the elderly may be regarded as a facility that provides various conveniences necessary for daily life, such as meals, housing convenience, life guidance, counseling, and safety management, so that persons over a certain age can pursue a comfortable and stable life.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Senior Citizens Welfare Act provides that the State or a local government shall promote the supply of residential facilities equipped with functions and facilities suitable for the housing of the elderly (Article 8), and that when a person other than the State or a local government intends to establish elderly residential welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly, he or she shall file a report with the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head (Article 33(2)); and it provides that standards for facilities, personnel, and operation of elderly residential welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly, matters to be observed by persons filing reports for establishment and persons establishing and operating such facilities, and the like shall comply with subordinate statutes (Article 33(3)). Thus, if a facility is established to admit elderly persons and provide daily conveniences such as meals, it is a nursing home for the elderly, and whether the person establishing and operating the nursing home for the elderly is a religious organization or whether it was established and operated for the purpose of missionary work is not considered in determining whether it falls under a nursing home for the elderly.\\n\\nUltimately, nursing homes for the elderly that bear the reporting duty under the provisions subject to review are facilities equipped with a certain scale of facilities required by law, regardless of the entity or purpose of establishment, and as they are facilities that provide various conveniences necessary for daily life such as meals and housing so that elderly persons can pursue a comfortable and stable life, it cannot be said that the provisions subject to review are unclear.\\n\\n(3) Conclusion on this Point\\n\\nTherefore, the provisions subject to review do not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of legality.\\n\\nc. Whether the Principle of Prohibition of Excessive Restriction Has Been Violated\\n\\n(1) Content of the Freedom of Religion and Standard of Review\\n\\nThe freedom of religion generally consists of freedom of belief, freedom of religious acts, and freedom of religious assembly and association. Freedom of belief refers to freedom concerning an individual’s internal conviction regarding God, the transcendent, or the afterlife; because such freedom of belief is itself the core of freedom of conscience, it cannot be infringed even by law. Freedom of religious acts includes the freedom to act in accordance with religious conviction and live according to doctrine, such as freely performing religious acts including rites and worship as each individual wishes, the negative freedom not to be compelled to engage in acts contrary to one’s religious conviction, and the freedom of missionary work and freedom of religious education. Freedom of religious assembly and association refers to the freedom of believers to assemble or form religious organizations for religious purposes. Unlike freedom of belief, such freedom of religious acts and freedom of religious assembly and association are not absolute freedoms; however, if they are restricted, the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution must be observed (see Constitutional Court, 2001. 9. 27., 2000HEONMA159; Constitutional Court, 2011. 12. 29., 2009HEONMA527, etc.).\\n\\n(2) Legitimacy of Purpose and Appropriateness of Means\\n\\nThe reason the provisions subject to review require reporting for all nursing homes for the elderly above a certain scale, including facilities operated by religious organizations, is to enable the State or local governments to manage and supervise such facilities so that they provide a comfortable and pleasant housing environment to elderly persons admitted therein. Such legislative purpose is legitimate, and imposing a reporting duty on elderly residential welfare facilities and imposing criminal sanctions in case of violation appear to be effective means of identifying the status of elderly residential welfare facilities and supervising whether nursing homes for the elderly comply with facility standards, personnel standards, and operating standards, so the appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(3) Least Restrictive Means\\n\\n(a) Nursing homes for the elderly are facilities that provide lodging, meals, and other living conveniences to elderly persons, and must be safe and pleasant, so they must be able to function as elderly residential welfare facilities by securing private space of at least a certain area and having an appropriate medical system. In particular, since the elderly who enter such facilities are mostly socially vulnerable persons who are economically difficult to live independently and are at risk of being exposed to various diseases, the provision of facilities that can protect them from such threats and maintain their physical and mental health is essential. Therefore, in the case of elderly residential welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly, the State or local governments need to manage and supervise them so that they have the minimum necessary material and human facilities that can contribute to the above purpose, and for this purpose it is necessary to impose a reporting duty on the relevant facilities.\\n\\nIn particular, in the case of nursing homes for the elderly under the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, since elderly persons enter the facilities and live in group settings, there is a possibility of being cut off from or isolated from the outside world, and under such circumstances, malicious abuse or neglect of elderly persons whose ability to protect themselves has markedly declined may occur. The fact that exploitation or abuse in elderly residential welfare facilities such as nursing homes for the elderly sometimes becomes a social problem also means that such facilities may at any time be exposed to the above risks. Relevant public officials or elderly welfare counselors must also manage and supervise whether the human rights and safety of elderly residents are guaranteed by entering nursing homes for the elderly and other elderly welfare facilities and conducting necessary investigations of the elderly persons or related persons (see Article 39-11(1) of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act). If no report has been filed, such facilities may be omitted from the subject of such management and supervision. Therefore, for the comfortable housing life and the guarantee of safe and healthy life of elderly persons, it is necessary for the State or local governments to manage and supervise such facilities, and this is equally true even where a religious organization operates a nursing home for the elderly as a method of realizing freedom of religion; therefore, it cannot be said that imposing a reporting duty on nursing homes for the elderly above a certain scale is excessive.\\n\\n(b) To establish a nursing home for the elderly, certain facility standards and personnel standards must be met, including securing a space of at least 15.9㎡ of total floor area per resident capacity, and having bedrooms of at least 5.0㎡ per resident, medical and nursing rooms, physical fitness rooms and program rooms, toilets, bathing rooms, dining rooms and kitchens, disaster preparedness facilities, and assigning personnel such as social workers, nurses or nursing assistants, and cooks (see Attached Table 2 of Article 17(1) of the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act). Meanwhile, where the eligible persons for admission to a nursing home for the elderly are persons aged 65 or older who are recipients of livelihood benefits or medical benefits under the National Basic Living Security Act, or who do not receive proper support from their persons obligated to support them, the State and local governments bear all admission expenses, and where they are persons whose monthly average income per person is not more than the monthly average income of urban workers, they bear part of the admission expenses (Article 15-2 of the above Enforcement Rules).\\n\\nHowever, the above facility and personnel standards are set in consideration of the health and sanitation of elderly residents and disaster prevention, and are merely minimum standards for ensuring a safe and pleasant living space for elderly persons. In this way, where a nursing home for the elderly falls under the support target for facility operating expenses, it receives support from the State and local governments for personnel expenses of facility workers, management and operation expenses, program project expenses, and the like, so requiring an excessive burden for the establishment and operation of a nursing home for the elderly is not the case.\\n\\nTherefore, management and supervision by the State and local governments over the establishment and operation of nursing homes for the elderly are necessary, and the imposition of a reporting duty cannot be said to be excessive.\\n\\n(c) Traditionally, the operation by religious organizations, as part of relief activities, of facilities for socially vulnerable persons such as nursing homes for the elderly has been recognized within the sphere of freedom of religion. However, if facilities operated by religious organizations are excluded from facilities subject to reporting merely because they are facilities operated by religious organizations, despite being nursing homes for the elderly above a certain scale, it would be difficult to protect the elderly even if they become targets of exploitation or abuse by organizations masquerading as religious activities, and in some cases it would be difficult to rule out the risk of their being left out of welfare benefits such as health and medical care. Any person who establishes and operates a nursing home for the elderly must provide living conveniences suitable for the elderly, taking into account the safety, convenience, and hygiene of elderly persons living in groups, and the State and local governments have the duty to ensure through management and supervision of the relevant facilities that elderly persons are not placed in blind spots of safety. Moreover, in the case of facilities above a certain scale with a resident capacity of 10 or more, the degree of damage from safety accidents or human rights violations may be greater, and where many persons live in groups, it is necessary to sufficiently establish and manage/supervise health sanitation and disaster prevention measures; therefore, for facilities above a certain scale, it is necessary to uniformly compel reporting without recognizing exceptions. Therefore, even if a religious organization establishes and operates a nursing home for the elderly in the dimension of social relief or missionary work, the reporting duty needs to be imposed as with ordinary nursing homes for the elderly.\\n\\n(d) Furthermore, in Korea there are many social welfare facilities not registered as juridical persons, and in many cases their actual status has not been properly ascertained, while there are quite a number of cases causing social controversy due to some unlawful or inhumane operation. In order to prevent such occurrences, reporting is required as the minimum measure for ascertaining the actual status of the relevant facility and for management and supervision, regardless of who the operating entity is, and the necessity of imposing strong sanctions such as criminal punishment in case of violation of the reporting duty is also recognized in order to compel reporting.\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review prescribe imprisonment and fines alternatively, so if the reporting duty is violated, not only is it possible to impose a fine depending on the gravity of the case, but the content of imprisonment is also prescribed as “not more than 1 year,” making a short-term sentence possible. In this respect, there is no basis to conclude that the punishment for violating the reporting duty imposed by the provisions subject to review is excessively heavy. Therefore, it cannot be said that imposing the reporting duty on nursing homes for the elderly operated by religious organizations without excluding them from nursing homes for the elderly subject to establishment reporting, and imposing criminal sanctions in case of violation, runs contrary to the principle of least restriction.\\n\\n(4) Balance of Legal Interests\\n\\nAs a result of the provisions subject to review, religious organizations bear a reporting duty when establishing and operating nursing homes for the elderly, but since it is possible to establish and operate nursing homes for the elderly simply by filing a report, the restriction on fundamental rights resulting therefrom cannot be said to be very large. On the other hand, the public interest to be achieved through the provisions subject to review is to ensure a comfortable and safe housing environment for the elderly admitted to nursing homes for the elderly, which is highly significant. Therefore, it cannot be said that the balance of legal interests has been lost.\\n\\n(5) Conclusion on this Point\\n\\nTherefore, the provisions subject to review cannot be said to violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since the provisions subject to review do not violate the Constitution, we decide as stated in the disposition. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the remaining participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Han-cheol, Lee Jeong-mi, Ahn Chang-ho, and Cho Yong-ho as set forth below in 7.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Park Han-cheol, Lee Jeong-mi, Ahn Chang-ho, and Cho Yong-ho\\n\\nWe believe that the provisions subject to review, which uniformly criminalize the establishment and operation without reporting of nursing homes for the elderly above a certain scale, violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringe constitutional fundamental rights such as the freedom of religious acts related to social welfare activities, freedom of general action, and freedom of corporate management. Accordingly, we state our dissenting opinion as follows.\\n\\na. The State’s Duty to Promote Welfare for the Elderly and Welfare for the Elderly by Private Entities\\n\\n(1) The Social State Principle and the State’s Duty to Promote Welfare for the Elderly\\n\\nOur Constitution adopts, in Article 34(1) and (2), the social state principle, which makes it the responsibility of the State to ensure a healthy and cultural life by satisfying the basic needs of life for all citizens. In addition, Article 34(4) of the Constitution provides, “The State shall have the duty to implement policies for enhancing the welfare of the elderly and juveniles,” and paragraph (5) provides, “Citizens unable to maintain a livelihood by reason of physical disability, disease, old age, or other causes shall be protected by the State as prescribed by Act,” thereby explicitly providing at the constitutional level the State’s duty to protect elderly persons unable to maintain a livelihood and the State’s duty to promote welfare for the aged and infirm. The Senior Citizens Welfare Act concretizes these constitutional duties and imposes on the State and local governments the duty to devise and promote policies for the health and welfare of the elderly (Article 4(1) of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act).\\n\\nTherefore, the resolution of housing problems for elderly persons who have difficulty securing housing due to reduced social activity and limited economic income is required as one of the State’s duties to promote welfare for the elderly in order to realize the social state principle.\\n\\n(2) Voluntary Welfare for the Elderly by Private Entities\\n\\nHowever, the limited national budget alone has limitations in meeting the welfare needs of the elderly and infirm, and in situations where the overall accommodation capacity of welfare facilities established by the State and local governments is far from sufficient, blind spots in welfare are inevitable. Accordingly, private social welfare activities based on the will of social solidarity founded on humanitarianism have filled the blind spots in the welfare affairs of the State and local governments and have contributed to realizing the policy of social welfare facilities, which is one pillar of the social welfare system. In particular, it cannot be denied that religious persons or religious organizations have played a role in elevating the quality of social welfare in our country by one level through operating nursing homes for the elderly or child care facilities for socially vulnerable groups as a traditional method of missionary activity and by taking the lead in voluntary service activities.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Senior Citizens Welfare Act provides that the State or a local government shall promote the supply of residential facilities for the elderly even by persons other than the State or local governments, and may provide appropriate support to suppliers of such residential facilities (Article 8 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act). This can be seen as an indirect realization of the State’s duty regarding welfare for the elderly by allowing some welfare demand to be met in the private sector.\\n\\nb. Whether the Provisions Subject to Review Are Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of Legislative Purpose\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review are provisions that criminalize the establishment and operation without reporting of nursing homes for the elderly above a certain scale. The requirement to report in establishing nursing homes for the elderly, in order for the State or local governments to manage and supervise so that elderly persons admitted to nursing homes for the elderly are provided with a comfortable and pleasant housing environment, is the same as the majority opinion in that the legitimacy of the legislative purpose is recognized because it is intended to realize the State’s duty to promote welfare for the elderly.\\n\\n(2) Appropriateness of Means and Least Restrictive Means\\n\\nHowever, requiring reporting upon the establishment of a nursing home for the elderly only if it satisfies certain facility standards and imposing criminal punishment for violation of the reporting duty not only hinders the achievement of the original legislative purpose of providing the necessary housing environment for elderly persons by restricting social welfare activities carried out in unreported nursing homes for the elderly, but also constitutes an excessive exercise of penal power for the following reasons.\\n\\n(a) The Senior Citizens Welfare Act and its Enforcement Rules require a person other than the State or a local government who intends to establish elderly residential welfare facilities to equip himself or herself with lawful facilities meeting certain facility establishment standards prescribed by subordinate statutes and to file a report with the competent Mayor/County Governor/District Head (Article 33(2) and (3) of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act; Article 16 of the same Enforcement Rules). Specifically, in the case of a nursing home for the elderly, if the resident capacity is 10 or more, it becomes subject to reporting, and certain facility standards are required, such as securing a space of at least 15.9㎡ of total floor area per resident capacity, having a bedroom area of at least 5.0㎡ per resident, and having a capacity of 4 persons or fewer in one dormitory-style bedroom (see Attached Table 2 of Article 17(1) of the Enforcement Rules).\\n\\nHowever, because economic conditions must support the fulfillment of such facility standards, the facility standards under the statutes function as a kind of barrier to entry into social welfare activities. In particular, in the case of small non-profit organizations or individuals, it is often the case that they cannot fully satisfy the statutory facility standards required for social welfare facilities due to economic circumstances, so expecting them to comply with the reporting duty is virtually difficult.\\n\\nIn this way, the provisions subject to review, in conjunction with the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, require conformity with certain facility standards as a reporting requirement, and criminally punish failure to fulfill the reporting duty for economic reasons, thereby fundamentally blocking opportunities for social welfare activities in religious facilities or other nursing homes for the elderly that do not meet the statutory facility standards.\\n\\n(b) Requiring reporting upon the establishment of a nursing home for the elderly only if it satisfies certain facility standards and imposing criminal punishment for violation of the reporting duty also does not conform to the constitutional intent of the State’s duty to promote welfare for the elderly.\\n\\nIn Korea, the number of social welfare facilities is far from sufficient compared to welfare demand, and the eligibility requirements for admission to nursing homes for the elderly are also strictly limited (Article 14(1)1 of the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act). Accordingly, many elderly persons who do not meet the admission requirements but desperately need help from society are left out of social welfare facilities and pushed into blind spots of welfare; to solve such social problems, small organizations and individuals have played a role in supplementing existing social welfare facilities by providing housing conveniences to the elderly through facilities established with voluntary fund-raising.\\n\\nIf, without considering at all the contribution of such nursing homes for the elderly to the promotion of social welfare and merely on the ground of failure to fulfill the reporting duty, strong sanctions such as criminal punishment are imposed, this will discourage the voluntary participation of the private sector in social welfare and lead to a quantitative reduction of welfare facilities, and moreover may cause situations in which elderly persons who have been receiving stable shelter through such facilities, even if somewhat weak in scale or facility because they do not meet the facility standards required by law, are inevitably pushed out into the streets without any alternative. In addition, by stigmatizing as criminals those who have devoted themselves to welfare activities with a pure purpose of helping others based on humanitarianism merely for non-compliance with the reporting duty, there is also a concern that the general public’s perception of social welfare activities as a whole will be distorted.\\n\\n(c) The provisions subject to review, in conjunction with the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, exclude nursing homes for the elderly with a resident number of fewer than 10 from the scope of reporting for establishment of nursing homes for the elderly, and if the resident number is fewer than 5, they do not even fall under group homes for the elderly, so they do not fall under the reporting subject based on establishment of facilities under the Senior Citizens Welfare Act. This current reporting system, which divides the reporting target according to the number of residents, also needs to be pointed out as contrary to the original purpose of introducing the reporting system to have the State manage and supervise nursing homes for the elderly in order to ensure a comfortable and safe housing environment for the elderly.\\n\\nIf the State or local governments’ grasp of the actual conditions of social welfare facilities is insufficient, there is a possibility that human rights violations occurring within the facilities may be concealed, and therefore management and supervision by the State and local governments are necessary; the necessity of such management and supervision is equally recognized in the case of religious facilities. In addition, through State management and supervision based on the reporting system, elderly persons can be provided with a comfortable and pleasant housing environment, and the possibility of human rights violations can be prevented in advance. In light of this, there is also a need to fully establish a reporting system irrespective of the number of residents in nursing homes for the elderly or the scale of the facilities.\\n\\nHowever, the provisions subject to review, in conjunction with the Enforcement Rules of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, exclude from the reporting requirement as nursing homes for the elderly or group homes for the elderly those with fewer than 5 residents, thereby leaving them in a blind spot from State management and supervision, and even if they voluntarily wish to report, reporting itself is impossible under the current Senior Citizens Welfare Act and Enforcement Rules, so they are also excluded from support by the State. Although there is no reason to distinguish the need to ensure a comfortable and safe housing environment for elderly persons and the necessity of State management and supervision according to the number of residents, it is difficult to find a rational basis for such a limitation on the scope of reporting, and it may result in the inability to prevent in advance the possibility of human rights violations occurring within facilities not subject to reporting, as well as the inability to devise advanced measures or support for improving the operation of these facilities.\\n\\nUltimately, dividing reporting targets according to the number of residents and excluding facilities with fewer than 5 residents from the scope of reporting as nursing homes for the elderly or group homes for the elderly does not conform to the legislative purpose of ensuring a comfortable and safe housing environment for the elderly. Since the current reporting system itself has such irrationality, it is difficult to recognize the legitimacy of criminal punishment provisions based on such a reporting system.\\n\\n(d) Meanwhile, the Senior Citizens Welfare Act already contains penal provisions concerning human rights violations such as assault on the elderly, abandonment, and neglect (see Articles 55-2, 55-3, and 55-4 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act), and these penal provisions do not limit the persons to whom they apply, so they apply equally to acts committed not only in reported facilities but also in unreported facilities. Therefore, since such penal provisions are sufficient to sanction human rights violations within facilities, the practical benefit of separately criminally punishing violation of the reporting duty in establishing nursing homes for the elderly is not significant. Rather, criminal punishment on the sole ground of failure to fulfill the reporting duty, regardless of human rights violations, gives rise to a strong suspicion that the limitations and insufficiency of the State’s management and supervision of social welfare facilities are merely being shifted to the private sector’s failure to report.\\n\\nEven without establishing a strong sanction such as criminal punishment for the act of establishing an unreported nursing home for the elderly, as in the provisions subject to review, there exist less restrictive means that can facilitate the State’s management and supervision of nursing homes for the elderly. For example, the State or local governments may induce voluntary conversion to reported facilities after a certain grace period through fiscal support, etc., following an investigation into the actual condition of unreported nursing homes for the elderly. Also, for small non-profit facilities, the reporting requirements may be eased so that all who wish may file reports, thereby lowering the barrier to entry into social welfare activities, while expanding the scope of management and supervision by providing various support, including operating expenses, so that they may have material and human facilities enabling the protection of the elderly and the maintenance of physical and mental health. Even if it is not difficult to satisfy the facility requirements because the economic conditions are adequate, where the reporting duty is continuously neglected, it is also possible to compel performance of the reporting duty through administrative sanctions rather than criminal punishment.\\n\\n(e) Ultimately, even if a reporting duty is imposed when establishing a nursing home for the elderly for the purpose of providing elderly persons with a comfortable and pleasant housing environment through State management and supervision, as noted above, the reporting system itself, which is operated according to the number of residents without rational basis, is insufficient to achieve the legislative purpose, and imposing criminal punishment uniformly for failure to comply with the reporting duty on the premise of such insufficient and irrational reporting system does not satisfy appropriateness of means or the least restrictive means.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Legal Interests\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review uniformly impose criminal punishment for failure to comply with the reporting duty even in the case of social welfare activities through small-scale facilities that are difficult to meet the reporting requirements. The degree of restriction on freedom of religious activity, freedom of general action, and freedom of corporate management resulting therefrom, as well as the consequence of contraction of social welfare activities, cannot be said to be light in comparison with the public interest of ensuring a comfortable and safe housing environment for the elderly through management and supervision of social welfare facilities above a certain scale, and therefore the principle of balance of legal interests is also violated.\\n\\nc. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the provisions subject to review, which uniformly impose criminal punishment for the establishment and operation of unreported nursing homes for the elderly, violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringe constitutional fundamental rights such as the freedom of religious activity or freedom of general action, and freedom of corporate management, related to social welfare activities, and therefore violate the Constitution."}

{"[2019HEONMA942]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. On 2019. 6. 27., the Respondent rendered, against the Petitioner, a decision to suspend indictment on suspicion of violation of the Medical Service Act (Seoul Central District Prosecutors' Office 2018 HYEONGJE78172 to 78177, hereinafter referred to as “the decision to suspend indictment at issue”), and the gist of the suspected facts is as follows.\\n\\n“The Petitioner is a dentist who operates ○○ Dental Clinic located in ○○, Nam-gu, Pohang City.\\nMedical practitioners, founders of medical institutions, and persons working at medical institutions shall not receive money, goods, labor, entertainment, or other economic benefits provided by medical device sellers for the purpose of sales promotion, such as adoption or inducement of use of medical devices, or cause the medical institution to receive such benefits.\\nOn or around 2014. 6. 11., at the said ○○ Dental Clinic, the Petitioner received, from Cha ○○, an employee of the Pohang office of the Yeongnam Regional Headquarters of ○○ Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “the company at issue”), which is a medical equipment company, an offer to purchase the so-called ‘Implant Insurance Package ○○ Product (hereinafter referred to as ‘the ○○ Product’)’—planned for the purpose of promoting the sale of implants and consisting of providing implants worth 5,000,000 won and dental alloy worth 5,000,000 won upon payment of 6,000,000 won—and purchased it for 6,000,000 won, thereby receiving dental alloy worth 4,000,000 won free of charge; in addition, from that time until around 2017. 4. 13., over a total of 9 occasions, the Petitioner received dental alloy worth 33,267,230 won under the name of a gift.”\\n\\nb. The Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2019. 9. 10. seeking revocation of the decision to suspend indictment at issue, alleging that the said decision infringed his right to equality and his right to pursue happiness.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nThe Petitioner contends that the company product at issue, the ○○ Product, is merely a product that bundles implant materials and dental alloy as package items and grants a price discount, and is not the economic benefit prohibited by Article 23-2 of the Medical Service Act; and that, in fact, because no claim was made to the National Health Insurance Service for the said implant insurance reimbursement, he has never obtained any economic benefit.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\na. Relevant Provisions\\n\\nFormer Medical Service Act (amended by Act No. 13658 on 2015. 12. 29., and before amendment by Act No. 14438 on 2016. 12. 20.)\\nArticle 23-2 (Prohibition on Obtaining Unjust Economic Benefits, etc.) ② Medical practitioners, founders of medical institutions, and persons working at medical institutions shall not receive economic benefits, etc. provided by manufacturers under Article 6 of the Medical Devices Act, importers of medical devices under Article 15 of the same Act, or sellers or lessors of medical devices under Article 17 of the same Act, for the purpose of sales promotion, such as adoption or inducement of use of medical devices. Provided, That this shall not apply where such benefits, etc. are within the scope prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare, such as acts of providing sample goods.\\n\\nFormer Medical Service Act (amended by Act No. 10325 on 2010. 5. 27., and before amendment by Act No. 14438 on 2016. 12. 20.)\\nArticle 88-2 (Punishment) A person who violates Article 23-2 shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine not exceeding 30,000,000 won. In such a case, the economic benefits, etc. acquired shall be confiscated, and if confiscation is impossible, the equivalent value shall be collected.\\n\\nb. Facts Found\\n\\nAccording to the investigation records of this case, etc., the following facts are recognized.\\n\\n(1) The company at issue (Representative Director Lee ○○) set the price of implants, which is ordinarily 77,000 won per unit, at 122,000 won per unit, exceeding the insurance price (112,750 won), and then sold the ○○ Product (“Implant 5,000,000 won + Dental Alloy 1,000,000 won”) to the Petitioner, which provided dental alloy worth 5,000,000 won at 1,000,000 won when purchased in bundles of 5,000,000 won worth (approximately 41 units) each.\\n\\n(2) In the police investigation, the Petitioner stated to the effect that “after hearing an explanation from an employee of the company at issue about the ○○ Product, which is a package product bundling implants and dental alloy, I purchased it because I thought it was a package product at a reasonable price; however, it is merely an ordinary price-discount product, and moreover, I did not directly obtain any benefit because I did not even claim insurance reimbursement to the Corporation for the implants of the company at issue.”\\n\\n(3) On 2019. 6. 27., Lee ○○ and the company at issue were indicted for the offense that, “from around 2014. 7. to around 2017. 9., by selling implant insurance packages, including the ○○ Product, by the method described in item (1) above, a total of 3,222 times, to founders of hospitals and clinics and dentists nationwide, they provided economic benefits in the aggregate amount of approximately 10,298,283,140 won in dental alloy,” on charges of violation of the Medical Devices Act.\\n\\nHowever, at first instance, on 2020. 7. 21., a judgment of acquittal was rendered on the ground that “it is insufficient to evaluate the defendant company’s price-discount advertisements and sales activities as ‘the provision of economic benefits, etc.’ for the purpose of ‘sales promotion’ prohibited by the Medical Devices Act, and there is no material otherwise proving this” (Seoul Central District Court, 2020. 7. 21., Judgment 2019GOJEONG1871). Thereafter, the appeal was dismissed at the appellate stage (Seoul Central District Court, 2020. 12. 3., Judgment 2020NO2386), and the final appeal was dismissed at the Supreme Court (Supreme Court, 2021. 5. 7., Judgment 2020DO18003).\\n\\nc. Issue of the Case\\n\\nIn this case, the issue is whether the Petitioner acquired unjust economic benefits as prescribed in Article 23(2) of the former Medical Service Act, and whether the Petitioner had intent with respect thereto.\\n\\nd. Determination\\n\\n(1) Article 23(2) of the former Medical Service Act prohibits medical practitioners, etc. from receiving economic benefits provided by medical device sellers, etc. for the purpose of sales promotion, such as adoption or inducement of use of medical devices. In light of the wording, the phrase “for the purpose of sales promotion” here is interpreted to mean, rather than the provider’s purpose or intention as a subjective element, that the objective nature of the economic benefit provided carries a quid pro quo character for the adoption of medical devices. Whether the provision falls under this can be objectively determined by comprehensively considering all circumstances, including not only the subjective intent of the person providing the economic benefit but also the relationship between the provider and the recipient, the amount and nature of the economic value received, and the circumstances and timing by which it came to be received (see Constitutional Court 2015. 2. 26. 2013HEONBA374). The economic benefits, etc. prohibited by the above provision mean those provided covertly, and therefore public price discounts made in ordinary business relationships are not prohibited (see Constitutional Court 2019. 9. 26. 2018HEONBA111).\\n\\n(2) According to the records of this case, the company at issue developed and sold an insurance package product to increase the market share of its own products in the implant market, and carried out extensive sales activities targeting dentists nationwide, selling insurance package products to approximately 1,266 locations. However, the manner of such promotional activities does not appear to have been significantly different from the existing methods of product promotion and sales, and no material has been found indicating that dentists who could be targets of promotional activities were specially selected or sought under particular criteria, or that promotional efforts were made through individual contacts under such criteria. Moreover, the company at issue did not appear to have provided economic benefits directly and covertly, such as by individually contacting dentists and, when they chose the package, selling it at a price determined in advance or giving additional discounts or cost reductions.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Petitioner and most dentists who dealt with the company at issue stated to the effect that “in the case of implants, it is often difficult to calculate the actual transaction price per unit. I did not think that I received dental alloy for free while being supplied with the implants related to this case, and I thought that I paid a fair price. Since tax invoices were also issued normally, I did not think this constituted a rebate,” thereby denying that they acquired covert economic benefits as consideration for the adoption of medical devices, etc.\\n\\nAs examined above, the fact that the company at issue set the price of implants higher than both the ordinary retail price and the insurance price, and provided dental alloy in a bundled form at a discounted price, appears to have been intended to offset the loss a doctor may incur due to the implant price exceeding the insurance price. In other words, the dental alloy was provided on the premise that the implant price was set higher than the ordinary retail price and the insurance price. In light of this, there is a persuasive basis for the Petitioner’s having judged whether the total purchase price of the implants and dental alloy was appropriate.\\n\\nFurthermore, the unit price of the implants sold by the company at issue to the Petitioner is confirmed to have been inflated by as much as 160%, and the difference between the price obtained by adding the market retail prices of the implants and dental alloy supplied by the company at issue to the Petitioner and the price of the ○○ Product actually purchased by the Petitioner was approximately 1,500,000 won to 2,300,000 won in total. The company at issue supplied dental alloy at a substantially discounted price on the condition that implants be purchased, and issued transaction statements and tax invoices, etc. for the dental alloy at the discounted price level.\\n\\nTaken together, even if the Petitioner obtained some benefit by purchasing implants and dental alloy from the company at issue, this appears to correspond to the result of price discounts by a supplier in an ordinary competitive market, and cannot otherwise be regarded as consideration for the adoption of medical devices or as covertly provided economic benefits; nor is it easily deemed that the Petitioner recognized this.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the decision to suspend indictment at issue, premised on the assumption that the Petitioner obtained unjust economic benefits prescribed in Article 23(2) of the former Medical Service Act, was the result of insufficient investigation or an error in the interpretation of law, and thereby the Petitioner’s right to equality and right to pursue happiness were infringed.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since the petition in this case is well-founded, the decision to suspend indictment at issue is to be revoked, and it is so decided as follows by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding property rights? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedent.) (a) Article 13(2) of the Constitution provides, “All citizens shall not be deprived of property rights by retroactive legislation ...,” and here retroactive legislation refers only to laws with genuine retroactive effect. (b) An order for culling under the Act on the Prevention of Contagious Animal Diseases should be regarded as exceeding the scope of social restrictions that livestock owners must tolerate, in that it deprives already formed property rights individually and concretely. (c) A provision of the Act on Dam Construction and Assistance to Surrounding Areas, etc. that allows dam use rights to be cancelled or changed cannot be viewed as providing for expropriation, use, or restriction under Article 23(3) of the Constitution, which requires compensation, insofar as it individually and concretely deprives or restricts already formed specific property rights for the public interest; rather, it should be regarded as a provision that both defines the content and limits of dam use rights, which are exclusive rights of use concerning multipurpose dams constructed for public-interest purposes such as adequate water supply and flood prevention, and concretizes the social restrictions on property rights according to public-interest demands. (d) Where the business of a waste recycling processing reporting business operator under the former provisions falls within the category of waste intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions, an existing waste recycling processing reporting business operator who is effectively forced to discontinue business due to the supplementary provisions of the former Waste Management Act, which require obtaining a permit for waste intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions within 1 year from the date of enforcement of the Act in order to continue business, may receive compensation under Article 23(3) of the Constitution on the ground of infringement of property rights.
