supporting_precedents: {"[2012HEONMA770]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\nThe petitioner is a person who produces and sells phonograms by using sound recordings whose neighboring rights have expired, and on September 14, 2012, filed this constitutional complaint, alleging that Article 4 of the Addenda to the Copyright Act, which restores neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 but expired after the 20-year protection period had elapsed, as from March 15, 2012, and causes them to subsist for 50 years including the remaining protection period, infringes the petitioner’s property rights concerning the production and sale of phonograms.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe petitioner challenges the unconstitutionality of the portion in which neighboring rights, which expired as a result of the expiration of the protection period under the former statutory provision, are restored and continue to subsist for the remaining protection period; the relevant content is Article 4(2) of the Addenda to the Copyright Act, and the remaining provisions of Article 4 of the Addenda are excluded from the subject matter of adjudication because they are unrelated to the content alleged by the petitioner to be unconstitutional.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 4(2) of the Addenda to the Copyright Act (Act No. 11110 of Dec. 2, 2011) (hereinafter referred to as the “Provision Subject to Adjudication”) is unconstitutional because it infringes the petitioner’s fundamental rights.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]\\n\\nCopyright Act (Act No. 11110 of Dec. 2, 2011)\\n\\nAddenda Article 4 (Special Provisions on the Protection Period for Neighboring Rights) ② Among the neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 pursuant to Addenda Article 3 of the same Act, those neighboring rights that expired because the 20-year protection period under the former Act (meaning the Copyright Act before amendment by the Copyright Act under Act No. 4717; hereinafter the same in this Article) had elapsed before the enforcement of this Act shall be restored from the date of enforcement of this Act and shall vest in the neighboring rights holder. In this case, such neighboring rights shall subsist for the remaining period of protection that would have been recognized had they been protected as subsisting for 50 years counted from the year following the time when they first arose.\\n\\n[Related Provisions] As attached. \\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nUnder the former Copyright Act, neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 had a protection period of 20 years, so some neighboring rights have now expired after the protection period elapsed. However, because the Provision Subject to Adjudication restores neighboring rights in works already expired and in the public domain and protects them for the remaining period, it infringes the petitioner’s right to freely use the works by retroactive legislation and therefore violates Article 13(2) of the Constitution, which prohibits deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation.\\n\\nIf works are protected permanently like ownership, they instead hinder cultural development; therefore, after a certain period of time anyone should be able to freely use works. However, the Provision Subject to Adjudication, etc. requires payment of neighboring rights royalties to the neighboring rights holders of sound recordings whose neighboring rights have expired after the two-year grace period in order to sell phonograms (sound recording fixations), and thus infringes the petitioner’s property rights in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\na. Legislative History and Legislative Purpose of the Provision Subject to Adjudication\\n\\nAmong neighboring rights, the protection period for neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 was 20 years under the Copyright Act as amended by Act No. 3916 on December 31, 1986, whereas the protection period for neighboring rights that arose on or after July 1, 1994 is 50 years under the Copyright Act as amended by Act No. 4717 on January 7, 1994. The reason the protection period for neighboring rights differs depending on the time of their arising is that, although the Copyright Act amended on January 7, 1994 extended the protection period for neighboring rights from 20 years to 50 years, Addenda Article 3 did not recognize the retroactive effect of the amended Act, and thus a 20-year protection period was still recognized for neighboring rights arising before July 1, 1994, the date of enforcement of the amended Copyright Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, although there was no rational reason to recognize a shorter protection period for neighboring rights arising between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 than for neighboring rights arising thereafter, a problem arose in which the protection period differed merely according to the time at which neighboring rights arose. In order to resolve this problem, the Copyright Act as amended by Act No. 11110 of Dec. 2, 2011 established Addenda Article 4(1) and set the protection period for neighboring rights arising between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 at 50 years, the same period as for neighboring rights arising on or after July 1, 1994. The Provision Subject to Adjudication has the purpose of protecting neighboring rights for the remaining period by restoring neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 but have already expired.\\n\\nb. Whether There Is Infringement of Property Rights by Retroactive Legislation\\n\\n(1) Distinction Between True Retroactive Legislation and Quasi-Retroactive Legislation\\n\\nArticle 13(2) of the Constitution states that “No citizen shall be deprived of property rights by retroactive legislation,” thereby prohibiting deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation. Retroactive legislation includes, first, legislation with so-called true retroactive effect, which governs facts and legal relations that were already completed in the past, and, second, legislation with quasi-retroactive effect, which governs facts and legal relations that began in the past but have not yet been completed and are still in progress. Retroactive legislation prohibited by Article 13(2) of the Constitution means only laws with true retroactive effect, and legislation with quasi-retroactive effect is, in principle, permitted. However, even in legislation with quasi-retroactive effect, in the process of balancing the public interest reasons requiring retroactive effect against the need to protect trust, the perspective of protection of trust imposes limits on the legislature’s power of formation (Constitutional Court 1999. 4. 29. 94HEONBA37 et al., Cases Collection 11-1, 289, 318; Constitutional Court 2002. 7. 18. 99HEONMA574, Cases Collection 14-2, 29, 43 et al. referenced).\\n\\n(2) Whether It Constitutes Retroactive Legislation\\n\\nBecause the protection period for neighboring rights arising between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 is 20 years, if the petitioner is considered on the basis of the sound recordings whose neighboring rights expired earliest, the petitioner could, at most, have produced and sold phonograms using sound recordings whose neighboring rights had expired for approximately four years between January 1, 2008, after 20 years had elapsed from the year following July 1, 1987, and before March 15, 2012, the date of enforcement of the Provision Subject to Adjudication. However, due to the enforcement of the Provision Subject to Adjudication, the petitioner can produce phonograms only after waiting until January 1, 2038, when the neighboring rights in the sound recordings expire after the 30-year remaining protection period has elapsed, and can use them free of charge, and until then must negotiate with the phonogram producer or pay compensation determined by the Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism.\\n\\nIn light of these circumstances, the Provision Subject to Adjudication does not govern past acts of using sound recordings that occurred before its enforcement, but instead corresponds to a provision governing the use of sound recordings after the enforcement of the amended Act. In other words, the Provision Subject to Adjudication is not true retroactive legislation that legally re-evaluates the past by applying the law ex post facto to facts or legal relations that have already been completed, but rather constitutes quasi-retroactive legislation. Therefore, the Provision Subject to Adjudication does not constitute retroactive legislation prohibited by Article 13(2) of the Constitution, and only the issue of protection of trust for the petitioner, who trusted the continuation of the former legal status, arises (see Constitutional Court 2007. 10. 25. 2005HEONBA68, Cases Collection 19-2, 447, 461).\\n\\n(3) Whether Property Rights Are Infringed\\n\\nWe examine whether, due to the Provision Subject to Adjudication, the petitioner is no longer able to produce and sell phonograms free of charge by using sound recordings with neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994, and whether this constitutes an infringement of the property rights guaranteed by Article 23(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nProperty rights protected by Article 23 of the Constitution concerning the guarantee of property rights and Article 13(2) of the Constitution prohibiting deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation are concrete rights having property value that encompass private utility and, in principle, the power of disposition over such utility. Therefore, mere benefits that are not concrete rights, opportunities to obtain goods or to engage in business activities, or the factual and legal conditions of business activities, are not subject to protection as property rights (Constitutional Court 2005. 2. 3. 2003HEONMA930, Cases Collection 17-1, 167, 181-182; Constitutional Court 2008. 11. 27. 2005HEONMA161 et al., Cases Collection 20-2, 290, 319-322). First, the Provision Subject to Adjudication does not deprive the petitioner of ownership of phonograms already produced and sold, does not confiscate the sales proceeds of phonograms, and does not prohibit use and profit from the facilities or equipment invested by the petitioner to produce phonograms, and therefore does not infringe any concrete right. In addition, although the restoration of expired neighboring rights due to the Provision Subject to Adjudication eliminates the petitioner’s ability to use sound recordings free of charge, because the petitioner may produce and sell phonograms only by consulting with the neighboring rights holder or paying compensation to the neighboring rights holder, the benefit derived from free use of sound recordings is merely an incidental benefit obtainable because the neighboring rights holder’s rights have expired, and does not confer upon the user private utility or a power of disposition over the sound recordings; therefore, it does not constitute property rights protected by Article 23(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(4) Subconclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provision Subject to Adjudication does not constitute retroactive legislation prohibited by Article 13(2) of the Constitution, and does not infringe the property rights guaranteed by Article 23(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nc. Whether There Is Infringement of Freedom of Occupation\\n\\n(1) Standard of Review\\n\\nBy restoring neighboring rights that had continued for a certain period and then expired, the Provision Subject to Adjudication prohibits the act of producing and selling phonograms free of charge by using sound recordings with such neighboring rights, and makes such acts possible only by consulting with the neighboring rights holder or paying compensation; thus, in that it is a provision concerning restrictions on the method of business or the subject matter handled, which are elements of the petitioner’s occupational performance, it imposes a restriction on the freedom of occupational performance, one of the freedom of occupation guaranteed by Article 15 of the Constitution.\\n\\nLike other fundamental rights, freedom of occupation is not absolutely protected and may be restricted for public interest reasons; however, it must not be restricted excessively for the realization of the public interest. Therefore, we examine whether the Provision Subject to Adjudication violates the principle against excessive restriction. However, since the petitioner had been conducting business in reliance on existing laws by producing and selling phonograms using sound recordings whose neighboring rights had expired, but became unable to do so because of the Provision Subject to Adjudication, we examine, in determining whether the principle against excessive restriction has been violated, whether, in establishing the Provision Subject to Adjudication and restoring expired neighboring rights, sufficient protection of trust, as required by the principle of the rule of law, was afforded to phonogram producers and sellers like the petitioner.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Principle Against Excessive Restriction Is Violated\\n\\n(a) The Provision Subject to Adjudication restores neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 and have already expired due to the lapse of the protection period, thereby protecting such neighboring rights for the same period as neighboring rights that arose on or after July 1, 1994 and have a 50-year protection period, in order to promote fairness among the holders of those neighboring rights; accordingly, its legislative purpose is legitimate. A substantial number of neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 have already completed their protection period; restoring their effect so that they continue to subsist for the remaining protection period, in order to grant them a 50-year protection period like that of neighboring rights arising on or after July 1, 1994, is an appropriate means to achieve the above legislative purpose. Moreover, considering that there is no alternative means other than restoring neighboring rights to achieve the above legislative purpose, and that adopting a protection period shorter than 50 years would run counter to the legislative purpose and is therefore difficult to adopt, the Provision Subject to Adjudication does not violate the principle of minimum impairment.\\n\\n(b) We examine whether the public interest sought by extending the existing protection period for neighboring rights and restoring neighboring rights that have already expired through the Provision Subject to Adjudication outweighs the disadvantage suffered by the petitioner.\\n\\nBecause the former Copyright Act provided a 20-year protection period for neighboring rights, the petitioner relied on that and invested funds and personnel to equip facilities and equipment, and then engaged in the phonogram production and sale business by utilizing sound recordings whose neighboring rights had expired; such trust cannot be regarded as unreasonable or improper. However, because the legislature must accept new understandings and appropriately respond to changed realities, citizens cannot, as a matter of principle, trust that the current legal status will always continue. Neighboring rights, like the protection provisions for copyright, have seen the need for protection arise, and their protection period has been amended several times, being extended from 30 years after creation to 20 years after creation, then from 20 years to 50 years; moreover, under the amended Copyright Act enforced on August 1, 2013, the protection period for neighboring rights was extended to 70 years after creation. Although the Copyright Act was amended on January 7, 1994 to change the protection period for neighboring rights to 50 years after creation, the Addenda provided that neighboring rights arising before the amendment to the Act would continue to be governed by the former provisions; through such amendments, the protection period for neighboring rights became 50 years in principle, so the petitioner could foresee that the Copyright Act might at any time be amended and the protection period for neighboring rights changed.\\n\\nIn addition, business conducted by utilizing sound recordings free of charge does not fall within private economic activity induced by the State in order to achieve a particular economic policy objective, but is merely a case of utilizing opportunities granted by law at one’s own risk (see Constitutional Court 2000. 7. 20. 99HEONMA452, Cases Collection 12-2, 128, 148). From that perspective as well, the petitioner’s trust interest cannot be regarded as requiring special protection in priority over the benefit of amending the law. By contrast, in light of the trend in which the protection period for neighboring rights has, through repeated amendments, been extended from 20 years after creation to 50 years, and from 50 years to 70 years, the 20-year protection period was excessively short and insufficient to protect neighboring rights holders; also, while neighboring rights arising on or after July 1, 1994 were granted a 50-year protection period, maintaining a 20-year protection period for neighboring rights already arising as of July 1, 1994 and whose protection period was already running amounted to differential treatment of neighboring rights holders according to the time of arising without rational reason. Taking these circumstances into account, the legislature amended the law and restored expired neighboring rights, and the public interest sought through the legal amendment is substantial. Moreover, considering that the petitioner is not wholly prevented from using the sound recordings whose neighboring rights have expired, but may produce and sell phonograms upon payment of neighboring rights royalties, the petitioner’s trust interest protected under the former Act cannot be said to be superior to the public interest sought by the legal amendment.\\n\\n(c) However, in light of the fact that the petitioner had lawfully been conducting such business before the enforcement of the Provision Subject to Adjudication, the question arises whether the petitioner’s trust interest was taken into account by providing an appropriate grace period to adapt to the changed legal situation.\\n\\nAddenda Article 4(3) of the Copyright Act as amended on December 2, 2011 provides that acts of using performances, phonograms, or broadcasts whose neighboring rights have been restored before March 15, 2012 are not deemed acts infringing rights under the Copyright Act, and Addenda Article 4(4) provides a two-year grace period from the date of enforcement of the Act in this case, so for two years after the enforcement of the amended Act the petitioner may freely sell phonograms already produced without the permission of the neighboring rights holder. Such a two-year grace period may be regarded as sufficient time to recover investment, such as by selling phonograms already produced, and therefore the above grace period does not appear to be excessively short to protect the trust interest as a phonogram producer and seller under the former Act.\\n\\n(3) Subconclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provision Subject to Adjudication sufficiently takes into account the petitioner’s trust interest, and cannot be said to violate the principle against excessive restriction and thereby infringe the petitioner’s freedom of occupational performance.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the petitioner’s request for adjudication in this case is without merit, and it is so decided, with the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, to dismiss it as stated in the order.\\n\\nJustices Park Han-cheol (Presiding Justice), Lee Jung-mi, Kim Yi-soo, Lee Jin-seong, Kim Chang-jong, Ahn Chang-ho, Kang Il-won (unable to sign and affix seal due to an overseas business trip), Seo Gi-seok, Jo Yong-ho\\n\\n[Appendix] Related Provisions\\n\\nCopyright Act (Act No. 11110 of Dec. 2, 2011)\\n\\nAddenda Article 3 (Transitional Measures Concerning Scope of Application) With respect to works, etc. for which all or part of copyright or other rights protected under this Act have expired or are not protected under the former provisions before the enforcement of this Act, this Act shall not apply to that part.\\n\\nArticle 4 (Special Provisions on the Protection Period for Neighboring Rights) ① Notwithstanding Article 3, neighboring rights that arose between July 1, 1987 and June 30, 1994 pursuant to the amended provisions of Addenda Article 2(3) of the Act on the All-Revision of the Copyright Act under Act No. 8101 shall subsist for 50 years counted from the year following the year in which they arose, pursuant to the amended provisions of Article 70 of the Copyright Act under Act No. 4717 that came into force on July 1, 1994 (hereinafter referred to as “the same Act” in this Article).\\n\\n② (Omitted: Provision Subject to Adjudication)\\n\\n③ Acts of using performances, phonograms, or broadcasts whose neighboring rights have been restored pursuant to paragraph 2 before the enforcement of this Act shall not be deemed acts infringing rights prescribed by this Act.\\n\\n④ Copies produced before the enforcement of this Act using the relevant performances, phonograms, or broadcasts after the neighboring rights under paragraph 2 had expired under the former Act may continue to be distributed without the permission of the neighboring rights holder for two years after the enforcement of this Act.\\n\\nCopyright Act (Act No. 8101 of Dec. 28, 2006)\\n\\nAddenda Article 2 (Transitional Measures Concerning Scope of Application) ①-② Omitted\\n\\n③ The former addenda provisions shall continue to apply after the enforcement of this Act.\\n\\nCopyright Act (Act No. 4717 of Jan. 7, 1994)\\n\\nAddenda ③ (Transitional Measures Concerning the Protection Period for Neighboring Rights) The protection period for neighboring rights arising before the enforcement of this Act shall be governed by the former provisions.\\n\\nCopyright Act (as amended by Act No. 11110 of Dec. 2, 2011)\\n\\nArticle 86 (Protection Period)\\n\\n① Omitted\\n\\n② Neighboring rights (excluding the moral rights of performers; hereinafter the same) shall subsist for 70 years (50 years in the case of broadcasts) counted from the year following any of the following times:\\n\\n1. Omitted\\n\\n2. In the case of phonograms, the time when the phonogram was published; provided, that if the phonogram was not published until 50 years have elapsed, counted from the year following the time when the sounds were first fixed on the phonogram, the time when the sounds were first fixed on the phonogram\\n\\n3. {"[2013HEONBA110]": "[Appendix] Related Provisions\\n\\nFormer Act on the Prevention of Contagious Animal Diseases (as amended by Act No. 10244 on 2010. 4. 12., and before amendment by Act No. 11690 on 2013. 3. 23.)\\n\\nArticle 20 (Order of Culling) ① If the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head deems it necessary to prevent the spread of a Category 1 contagious animal disease prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry for Food, Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, he or she shall, in accordance with the Ordinance of the Ministry for Food, Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, order the owner of livestock that has contracted, or that has epidemiological investigation results, precise examination results, or clinical symptoms sufficient to believe that it has contracted, a contagious animal disease to cull such livestock. Provided, That where there are epidemiological investigation results, precise examination results, or clinical symptoms sufficient to believe that livestock has contracted or has contracted a disease such as rinderpest, bovine plague, foot-and-mouth disease, swine fever, African swine fever, or highly pathogenic avian influenza, the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head may, without delay, order the culling of livestock in the area centered on the place where such livestock is or was located, which is the area where there is concern that the contagious animal disease will spread or is likely to spread.\\n\\n② In any of the following cases, the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head shall cause a livestock quarantine officer to cull the relevant livestock without delay. {"[2019HEONBA44]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. Seomjingang Dam commenced construction around 1940. 4. and was completed around 1965. 12. The State made an in-kind capital contribution of the dam-use right of Seomjingang Dam to the Korea Water Resources Development Corporation, and the said Corporation later, around 1978, transferred part of the dam-use right (30.84%) to the ○○ Farmland Improvement Association. Thereafter, on 2000. 1. 1., the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation comprehensively succeeded to the rights and obligations of the ○○ Farmland Improvement Association (Article 9 of the Addenda to the Act on Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation and Farmland Management Fund), and the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation was successively changed to the Korea Rural Community Corporation and then to the Korea Rural Community Corporation, the Claimant (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “Claimant”).\\n\\nb. As part of the Seomjingang Dam redevelopment project, the Minister of Construction and Transportation, on 2007. 10. 12., pursuant to Article 31(4)2 of the former Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc., issued a “Notice of Revision to the Basic Plan for Seomjingang Dam,” changing the allocation of stored water by purpose and the dam-use right holder without altering the size, type, storage capacity, etc. of the dam (Notice of the Ministry of Construction and Transportation No. 2007-427).\\n\\nc. Thereafter, the Government held several rounds of consultations with the Claimant regarding compensation, etc. arising from the change in the Seomjingang Dam dam-use right, but upon failing to reach an agreement on the amount of compensation, sent to the Claimant, on 2015. 9. 11., a draft agreement stating that dam construction burden charges of 156,760,000 won and business loss of 692,520,000 won would be paid; the Claimant refused it.\\n\\nd. On 2015. 11. 30., the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, in accordance with the above “Notice of Revision to the Basic Plan for Seomjingang Dam,” effected the registration of a change in the dam-use right in the dam-use right register and notified the Claimant thereof on 2015. 12. 30. (hereinafter referred to as the “Disposition in this Case”). As a result of this change, the dam-use right of the Claimant was reduced as the State and the Korea Water Resources Corporation were added as dam-use right holders.\\n\\ne. The Claimant filed a lawsuit against the Republic of Korea seeking, primarily, payment of agreed compensation for losses pursuant to the settlement, and, in the alternative, payment of compensation for losses by analogical application of the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects, but received a judgment dismissing the claim on 2017. 12. 15. (Seoul Central District Court 2016GAHAP536898); although it appealed, it received a judgment dismissing the appeal on 2018. 12. 12. (Seoul High Court 2018NA2005995).\\n\\nf. During the pendency of the appellate trial above, the Claimant filed an application for a request for constitutional review regarding Article 31(4)2 and Article 34 of the former Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc.; upon being served with a decision dismissing the application on 2018. 12. 21. (Seoul High Court 2018KAGI20038), it filed the constitutional complaint in this case on 2019. 1. 18.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Claimant requested a review of Article 31(4)2 and Article 34 of the former Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc., but the instant case is a lawsuit seeking compensation for losses arising from the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s disposition of changing the dam-use right pursuant to Article 31(4)2 of the former Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc.; therefore, the subject matter of review is limited to the portion related thereto.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 31(4)2 of the former Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc. (amended by Act No. 11690 on 2013. 3. 23. and prior to amendment by Act No. 15624 on 2018. 6. 8.; hereinafter, regardless of the history of amendment, referred to as the “Dam Construction Management Act”) and the portions of Article 34(1) and (2) concerning each Article 31(4)2 (hereinafter referred to as the “Burden Charge Refund Provision,” and together with the Dam-Use Right Change Provision, the “Provisions Subject to Review”) are contrary to the Constitution. The Provisions Subject to Review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nFormer Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc. (amended by Act No. 11690 on 2013. 3. 23. and prior to amendment by Act No. 15624 on 2018. 6. 8.)\\n\\nArticle 31 (Cancellation of Dam-Use Right) (4) Where the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport finds it difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is because any of the following applies, the Minister may issue a disposition of cancellation or change with respect to the dam-use right. In such case, the Minister shall hear in advance the opinions of the dam-use right holder.\\n\\n2. Where the conditions of use of stored water of the dam have changed, etc.\\n\\nArticle 34 (Refund of Burden Charges, etc.) (1) Where the State has issued a disposition of cancellation or change with respect to a dam-use right pursuant to Article 31, it shall refund a part of the burden charges paid pursuant to Article 20(1) or the charges paid pursuant to Article 33.\\n\\n(2) The amount to be refunded under paragraph (1) shall be calculated by the same method as the method of calculating the relevant burden charges or charges, but the amount to be refunded to a person who has obtained the establishment of a dam-use right pursuant to Article 24(4) shall not exceed the amount obtained by subtracting the amortization amount calculated pursuant to the Presidential Decree from the burden charges under Article 20(1).\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nFormer Act on Dam Construction and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc. (amended by Act No. 11690 on 2013. 3. 23. and prior to amendment by Act No. 15624 on 2018. 6. 8.)\\n\\nArticle 20 (Bearing of Costs for Multi-purpose Dam Construction) (1) A prospective holder of the dam-use right shall bear the costs calculated in accordance with the Presidential Decree among the construction costs for a multi-purpose dam.\\n\\n(3) The amount obtained by subtracting the burden charges under paragraph (1) from the construction costs for a multi-purpose dam shall be borne by the National Treasury.\\n\\n(4) If a prospective holder of the dam-use right has not been granted the dam-use right, the State shall refund to the prospective holder of the dam-use right the burden charges paid pursuant to paragraph (1). Provided, That, except where the basic plan is abolished, the refund of the burden charges may be suspended until a new prospective holder of the dam-use right is determined.\\n\\nArticle 24 (Establishment of Dam-Use Right) (1) The Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport shall establish a dam-use right upon application by a person who intends to use the stored water of a multi-purpose dam for a specific purpose.\\n\\n(4) When the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport has issued a public notice of completion of dam construction pursuant to Article 12, the Minister shall, without delay, establish the dam-use right for the relevant prospective holder of the dam-use right.\\n\\nArticle 31 (Cancellation, etc. of Dam-Use Right) (1) Where the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport cancels all or part of the permit for occupation and use of a river under Article 33 of the River Act and the permit for the use of river water under Article 50 of the same Act with respect to a dam-use right holder, and where the use of the same river water as before cannot be recognized for any person other than the relevant dam-use right holder, the Minister shall cause the dam-use right to be cancelled or changed in correspondence with the cancellation of the permit for occupation and use, etc. for the dam-use right holder.\\n\\n(2) Where the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport cancels all or part of the permit for occupation and use of a river under Article 33 of the River Act and the permit for the use of river water under Article 50 of the same Act with respect to a dam-use right holder, and where it is necessary to newly recognize the use of river water for any person other than the relevant dam-use right holder, the Minister may order the relevant dam-use right holder to transfer all or part of the dam-use right to another person within an appropriate period.\\n\\n(3) Where the dam-use right holder does not transfer the dam-use right within the period under paragraph (2), the Minister may cancel all or part of the dam-use right only when any person other than the relevant dam-use right holder can obtain a permit for the use of river water on the same terms as the permit for the use of river water granted to the dam-use right holder.\\n\\n(5) Where the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport issues a disposition of cancellation or change with respect to a dam-use right pursuant to paragraph (4), the Minister shall revise and publicly notify the matters concerning the allocation of stored water by purpose among the matters in the basic plan publicly notified pursuant to Article 7(4).\\n\\nArticle 33 (Charges) Except in cases where a dam-use right has been established pursuant to Article 24(4), the dam-use right holder shall pay to the National Treasury charges calculated in accordance with the Presidential Decree. In such case, when calculating the charges, the estimated investment amount calculated pursuant to Article 20(2)1 shall be taken into consideration.\\n\\n3. The Claimant’s Arguments\\n\\na. If a decision of unconstitutionality or a decision of constitutional non-conformity is rendered with respect to the Dam-Use Right Change Provision, then even if the Disposition in this Case does not become void, there is a possibility that the Claimant’s alternatively added claim in the appellate trial of the instant case, namely, the claim for damages based on tort, may be upheld or the grounds therefor may differ. In addition, the Burden Charge Refund Provision and the Dam-Use Right Change Provision cited therein are provisions concerning the legality of a disposition of cancellation or change of a dam-use right and whether just compensation therefor has been made, and must be constitutionally evaluated as an integrated whole. Therefore, the Dam-Use Right Change Provision also satisfies the prerequisite for trial.\\n\\nb. The dam-use right prescribed by the Dam Construction Management Act is a property right protected by the Constitution, and in order to restrict it, a legal basis for just compensation must necessarily be prepared pursuant to Article 23(3) of the Constitution. However, the Burden Charge Refund Provision merely provides that, in the event of a reduction of a dam-use right, only a “part” of the burden charges for dam construction costs paid by the dam-use right holder at the time of acquisition of the dam-use right or the charges paid at the time of exercising the dam-use right shall be refunded, and thus cannot constitute just compensation for the loss of the dam-use right, thereby violating Article 23(3) of the Constitution. It also infringes property rights in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nc. The Dam-Use Right Change Provision did not exist at the time the Claimant acquired the dam-use right to Seomjingang Dam. The fact that, while depriving a dam-use right holder who acquired and exercised the dam-use right prior to the enforcement of the Provisions Subject to Review of the dam-use right, it provides only for refunding a part of the burden charges or charges, is retroactive deprivation of property rights and also violates the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nd. The Dam-Use Right Change Provision alone does not reveal what cases mean “where the conditions of use of stored water of the dam have changed, etc.,” so the provision violates the principle of clarity; and because it merely provides that “the opinions of the dam-use right holder shall be heard in advance” and does not specifically prescribe any prior consultation procedure, it violates the principle of due process.\\n\\ne. Although the dam-use right is a property right with a character similar to fishery rights or mining rights and there is no reason to treat it differently from them, the failure to establish procedures for claiming compensation for losses and for calculating compensation only with respect to the dam-use right constitutes discriminatory treatment without reasonable grounds and violates the principle of equality.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Dam-Use Right Change Provision\\n\\nThe Dam-Use Right Change Provision is a provision stating that, where the conditions of use of stored water of the dam, etc. have changed and it is difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is, the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport may issue a disposition of cancellation or change with respect to the dam-use right. The instant case does not challenge the Disposition in this Case itself concerning the change of the dam-use right, but is a case in which compensation for losses or damages is being claimed; therefore, the Dam-Use Right Change Provision cannot be said to be a statutory provision applicable to the instant case, and it cannot be said that, depending on whether it is unconstitutional, the content of the judgment and its legal meaning as to the content and effect of the judgment would differ (see Constitutional Court 2006. 5. 25. 2003HEONBA115, etc.; Constitutional Court 2011. 7. 28. 2009HEONBA244).\\n\\nMoreover, even if the claim for state compensation additionally asserted by the Claimant in the appellate trial is based on the proposition that the Dam-Use Right Change Provision is unconstitutional and void, and that the disposition based thereon constitutes a tort, generally speaking the circumstance that a statute is contrary to the Constitution cannot be said to be objectively obvious before the Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality; therefore, in that a public official who has no authority to review whether a statute is contrary to the Constitution has no choice but to follow the law as it stood at the time of the act, even if a decision of unconstitutionality is rendered with respect to the statutory provision that served as the basis for the act, such public official cannot be said to have intent or negligence, and state compensation liability does not arise (Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONBA56). Therefore, whether the Dam-Use Right Change Provision is unconstitutional has no impact whatsoever on whether a tort is established in the instant case.\\n\\nAccordingly, since it cannot be said that the court in charge of the instant case would render a judgment with different content depending on whether the Dam-Use Right Change Provision is contrary to the Constitution, the request for review concerning the Dam-Use Right Change Provision is improper for failure to satisfy the prerequisite for trial, and thus is inadmissible.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Burden Charge Refund Provision\\n\\na. Content and Nature of the Dam-Use Right\\n\\n(1) Meaning of the Dam-Use Right\\n\\n(a) A dam means a structure of 15 meters or more in height that blocks the flow of a river so that its stored water may be used for domestic water supply, industrial water supply, agricultural water supply, environmental improvement water, power generation, flood control, navigation, or other purposes (hereinafter referred to as “specific purposes”), and includes spillways, auxiliary dams, and other facilities or structures that are integrated with the relevant dam and enable it to fully serve its function (Article 2(1) of the Dam Construction Management Act). A multi-purpose dam means a dam constructed by the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport (under the current Dam Construction Management Act, meaning the Minister of Environment; the same applies hereinafter) for use for two or more among the specific purposes (Article 2(2) of the same Act). The dam-use right means the right to secure a certain quantity of stored water by a multi-purpose dam in a certain area and to use it for a specific purpose (Article 2(3) of the same Act).\\n\\nThe construction of a multi-purpose dam is a large-scale project that entails changes in the surrounding ecological environment and relocation measures caused by inundation on a vast scale, and requires enormous construction costs. While dam construction requires enormous financial resources, it takes several decades or more to recover the investment costs, so it is a project in which private companies find it difficult to make direct investment. In such circumstances, the dam-use right is used as a means to promote dam construction by making those who benefit from the construction of the multi-purpose dam bear part of the dam construction costs. The Dam Construction Management Act secures the enormous costs required for dam construction by having the prospective holder of the dam-use right bear part of the construction costs for a multi-purpose dam and having the remaining amount borne by the National Treasury (Article 20(1) and (3)), while enabling the dam-use right holder to appropriately recover the investment costs by using the stored water.\\n\\n(b) When the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport has issued a public notice of completion of dam construction, the Minister shall, without delay, establish the dam-use right for the relevant prospective holder of the dam-use right (Article 24(4)), and if the prospective holder of the dam-use right has not been granted the dam-use right, the State shall refund the burden charges paid (Article 20(4)). A dam-use right holder who has not been granted a dam-use right pursuant to Article 24(4) of the Dam Construction Management Act shall pay charges calculated in accordance with the Presidential Decree to the National Treasury (Article 33). In other words, instead of designating a dam-use right holder to use the stored water, which is a public thing, the holder is made to bear burden charges or charges.\\n\\nThe dam-use right holder has an exclusive right to use stored water or flowing water only within the scope of the established dam-use right. The dam-use right holder may collect usage fees from persons using the stored water of the relevant dam (Article 35). Meanwhile, the dam-use right holder shall bear the costs necessary for the maintenance, repair, or other management of a multi-purpose dam (Article 36).\\n\\n(2) Legal Nature of the Dam-Use Right\\n\\nThe Dam Construction Management Act treats the dam-use right as a real right and applies mutatis mutandis the provisions concerning real property, except where special provisions are provided in the Dam Construction Management Act (Article 29). The dam-use right is made public in the register and is subject to a mortgage right (Article 32), but it cannot be made the object of any other right except in cases of inheritance, merger of a corporation or other comprehensive succession, transfer, disposition for delinquency, compulsory execution, and being the subject of a mortgage right (Article 30(1)).\\n\\nThe dam-use right is distinguished from ownership over stored water, and is a right granted by the State’s concession for the recycling and utilization of dam construction costs and for the rational development and use of water resources (see Article 1 and Article 24 of the same Act). The Dam Construction Management Act does not set any limitation on the duration of the dam-use right.\\n\\nb. Disposition of Cancellation/Change Concerning the Dam-Use Right and Compensation\\n\\n(1) Disposition of Cancellation/Change Concerning the Dam-Use Right (Article 31 of the Dam Construction Management Act)\\n\\nWhere the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport cancels all or part of the permit for occupation and use of a river under Article 33 of the River Act and the permit for the use of river water under Article 50 of the same Act with respect to a dam-use right holder, and where it is impossible to recognize the use of the same river water as before for persons other than the relevant dam-use right holder, the Minister shall cause the dam-use right to be cancelled or changed in correspondence with the cancellation of the permit for occupation and use, etc. for the dam-use right holder (Article 31(1)); and where it is necessary to newly recognize the use of river water for persons other than the relevant dam-use right holder, the Minister may order the relevant dam-use right holder to transfer all or part of the dam-use right to another person within an appropriate period (Article 31(2)).\\n\\nMeanwhile, once a multi-purpose dam is constructed, it is used in fact semi-permanently, so flexible responses are required according to changes in the surrounding environment after construction. The mode of operation of a dam may change depending on the need for water management in response to the conditions of use of stored water and climate change. Accordingly, the Dam Construction Management Act provides that where the storage capacity changes due to expansion, reconstruction, etc. of the dam, or where the conditions of use of stored water of the dam have changed, and the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport recognizes that it is difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is, the Minister may issue a disposition of cancellation or change concerning the dam-use right (Article 31(4)).\\n\\n(2) Compensation for Cancellation/Change of the Dam-Use Right\\n\\nWhere the State has issued a disposition of cancellation or change concerning a dam-use right pursuant to Article 31 of the Dam Construction Management Act, it shall refund a part of the burden charges paid pursuant to Article 20(1) of the same Act or the charges paid pursuant to Article 33 (Article 34(1)). The amount to be refunded shall be calculated by the same method as the method of calculating the relevant burden charges or charges, but the amount to be refunded to a person who has obtained the establishment of a dam-use right pursuant to Article 24(4) of the Dam Construction Management Act shall not exceed the amount obtained by subtracting the amortization amount calculated pursuant to the Presidential Decree from the burden charges under Article 20(1) of the same Act (Article 34(2)).\\n\\nc. Organization of Issues\\n\\n(1) The Claimant argues that the Burden Charge Refund Provision violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution and infringes the Claimant’s property rights because, in the case of a reduction of the dam-use right, it merely provides that the State refund a part of the burden charges for dam construction costs paid by the dam-use right holder at the time of acquisition of the dam-use right or the charges paid at the time of exercising the dam-use right, and thus cannot constitute just compensation.\\n\\nHereinafter, we will first examine whether the dam-use right is subject to the guarantee of property rights under Article 23 of the Constitution, and if so, whether the cancellation/change of the dam-use right is a public expropriation requiring compensation for losses under Article 23(3) of the Constitution, and accordingly determine whether the Burden Charge Refund Provision violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution or the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) Since the Claimant argues that applying the Burden Charge Refund Provision to dam-use right holders who acquired and have been exercising the dam-use right before the Burden Charge Refund Provision entered into force constitutes deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation and violates the principle of protection of trust, we will examine this issue.\\n\\n(3) The Claimant also argues that, although the dam-use right is a property right with a character similar to fishery rights or mining rights, the failure to establish procedures for claiming compensation for losses and for calculating compensation only with respect to the dam-use right in the event of cancellation/change violates the principle of equality. However, in this case, the issue is whether the Burden Charge Refund Provision is insufficient as a method of compensation and thereby infringes the Claimant’s property rights, and in the process of determining this issue, the Claimant’s argument, including the characteristics of the dam-use right distinguished from fishery rights and mining rights, may be examined; therefore, the violation of the principle of equality will not be separately reviewed.\\n\\nd. Whether Property Rights Are Infringed\\n\\n(1) Nature of the Dam-Use Right\\n\\nAs seen above, the Dam Construction Management Act treats the dam-use right as a real right and applies mutatis mutandis the provisions concerning real property, except where special provisions are provided in the Dam Construction Management Act (Article 29). The dam-use right is made public in the register and is subject to a mortgage right (Article 32), and the dam-use right holder has, within the scope of the established dam-use right, an exclusive right to use stored water or flowing water and may collect usage fees from persons using the stored water of the relevant dam (Article 35). As such, the dam-use right is a specific right with property value that entails private utility and the principle of disposition thereof; accordingly, it is subject to the guarantee of property rights under Article 23 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Legal Nature of the Burden Charge Refund Provision\\n\\nThe Dam-Use Right Change Provision is a provision that seeks to generally and abstractly regulate the legal relationship surrounding the dam-use right by allocating stored water by purpose and changing the dam-use right holder where the conditions of use of stored water of the dam have changed due to changes in the surrounding environment after construction of a multi-purpose dam and it is difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is. In other words, the Dam-Use Right Change Provision cannot be regarded as prescribing the taking, use, or restriction under Article 23(3) of the Constitution requiring compensation, as it individually and concretely deprives or restricts a concrete property right already formed for the public interest; rather, it should be regarded as a provision that determines the content and limits of the dam-use right, which is an exclusive right to use a multi-purpose dam constructed for public-interest purposes such as the appropriate supply of water resources and prevention of water damage, and at the same time concretizes social restraints on property rights according to public-interest demands.\\n\\nThe Burden Charge Refund Provision is a clause that adjusts the legal relationship surrounding the change of the dam-use right by requiring, when the dam-use right is changed, the dam-use right holder to have a part of the burden charges, etc. paid for acquiring the dam-use right refunded. Accordingly, the Burden Charge Refund Provision, together with the Dam-Use Right Change Provision, may also be regarded as a provision that determines the content and limits of the property right, the dam-use right, and at the same time concretizes social restraints on property rights according to public-interest demands (Article 23(1) and (2) of the Constitution).\\n\\n(3) Standard of Review\\n\\nThe main clause of Article 23(1) of the Constitution provides that “the property rights of all citizens shall be guaranteed,” thereby guaranteeing property rights as a fundamental right, but the latter sentence clearly states that “their content and limits shall be determined by Act,” thereby making it clear that property rights may be regulated by Act. The permissible extent of such restriction on property rights varies depending on the social interrelation and function of the object concerned; where its use or disposition does not remain within the owner’s personal sphere of life and significantly affects the daily lives of a large number of the general public, the legislator may have broad authority to regulate the individual’s property rights for the benefit of the community. However, even in such cases, legislation restricting property rights, like legislation restricting other fundamental rights, must comply with the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction (the principle of proportionality) and must not infringe the essential content of property rights (see Constitutional Court 2014. 2. 27. 2010HEONBA483).\\n\\nWater is the most essential good in human life, forms the basis of all industries, and has no substitute. Today, with the improvement in living standards and the development of industry, the demand for water for domestic, industrial, and agricultural uses has greatly increased, making the need to develop water resources very significant.\\n\\nBecause of the climatic characteristics of Korea, there are severe regional and seasonal variations in precipitation, so the Government has established plans for the construction of multi-purpose dams to meet water demand during the dry season and minimize flood damage during the rainy season. The construction of a multi-purpose dam is a large-scale project that entails changes in the surrounding ecological environment and relocation measures caused by inundation on a vast scale, and requires enormous tax expenditures. The dam-use right, which is the right to use the stored water created as a result, may be viewed as a right closely connected with the public interest of the rational development and use of water resources through multi-purpose dams. In light of the characteristics of such dam-use right, it must be said that the legislator has broad legislative discretion in determining the content and limits of the dam-use right.\\n\\n(4) Whether the Principle of Prohibition of Excessive Restriction Is Violated\\n\\n(a) Since the dam-use right under the Dam Construction Management Act must take into account public interests such as the environment and safety of the surrounding area over a broad area and the proper supply of water, flexible cancellation/change of the dam-use right is necessary where it is difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is because the conditions of use of stored water, etc. have changed. The dam-use right holder bears part of the dam construction costs through payment of burden charges, etc. in order to obtain the dam-use right (Articles 20 and 33), and may directly use the stored water of the dam for specific purposes or receive usage fees from stored water users (Article 2(3) and Article 35(1)); accordingly, where the dam-use right is cancelled or changed, the dam-use right holder is subject to restrictions on property rights to the extent of the reduction in the dam-use right. The Burden Charge Refund Provision requires a refund of a part of the burden charges paid by the existing dam-use right holder when the dam-use right is cancelled or changed for the efficient use of the dam, thereby reasonably adjusting the economic loss incurred by the dam-use right holder; ultimately, this is for promoting the development of the national economy by rationally developing and using water resources, and the legitimacy of the legislative purpose is recognized. Meanwhile, where all or part of the dam-use right needs to be used for another purpose, if the existing dam-use right is cancelled or changed and a reasonable adjustment is made by partially refunding the burden charges, etc. of the existing dam-use right holder resulting therefrom, the national economy can also be promoted through efficient use of water resources; thus, suitability of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(b) ① In the event that the dam-use right is cancelled or changed, it is true that the stored-water use right and stored-water usage fee income that the dam-use right holder could previously obtain are reduced by the amount of the cancelled/changed dam-use right. However, water resources have a strong character as a public good for the State and the entire nation, and it can be seen that the dam-use right is also a right subject to the strong public-interest demand of efficient use of water resources. In addition, considering that adjustment of the existing dam-use right is required when the conditions of use of stored water, etc. have changed due to changes in the surrounding environment, and that the dam-use right is a right without a fixed duration, it can be said that the possibility of cancellation or change is inherent in the dam-use right. Accordingly, it is difficult to say that the stored-water use right or stored-water usage fee income enjoyed by the dam-use right holder must necessarily be protected even where the dam-use right is cancelled or changed due to a change in the conditions of use of stored water, etc.\\n\\n② The refund of burden charges is premised on the cancellation/change of the dam-use right, and the Dam Construction Management Act does not merely allow the dam-use right to be cancelled or changed without limitation when the conditions of use of stored water, etc. have changed, but provides that cancellation/change is possible only where it is “difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is” as a result, and in such case, the opinions of the dam-use right holder are to be heard in advance (main text of Article 31(4)). In addition, the dam-use right holder may contest through an administrative lawsuit whether grounds for the disposition exist and whether the cancellation/change disposition was made in accordance with the principle of proportionality. In other words, the Dam Construction Management Act very narrowly prescribes the grounds for cancellation/change of the dam-use right, and since ex post remedies through administrative litigation are available, the damage suffered by the dam-use right holder due to cancellation/change of the dam-use right can be minimized.\\n\\n③ The Burden Charge Refund Provision provides that, when the dam-use right is cancelled or changed, a part of the burden charges, etc. paid by the dam-use right holder shall be refunded to the dam-use right holder, thereby compensating only a part, not all, of the loss incurred by the dam-use right holder. Therefore, if the period of exercise of the dam-use right is short, there may theoretically arise a case where the amount of the burden charges to be refunded is less than the amount paid as burden charges for obtaining the dam-use right, minus the benefit obtained from use of the dam up to that point. However, in light of the purpose of the Dam Construction Management Act in limiting the amount refunded to the amount obtained by subtracting the depreciation amount (Article 34(1) and (2), and Article 27 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act), it can sufficiently be understood that, in general, at least the burden charges paid by the dam-use right holder were intended to be refunded. This is because depreciation will be proportional to the use of the dam, and the dam-use right holder will have obtained profits from the use of the dam through direct use of stored water or through stored water usage fees. However, in view of the public-good nature of water resources and the need for efficient use thereof, it cannot be said that losses exceeding that amount, such as anticipated future profits, must necessarily be compensated.\\n\\n④ The Claimant argues that the Burden Charge Refund Provision merely provides for refund of a part of the burden charges, which has the character of a kind of deposit for future use of the dam, and that this should naturally accompany the cancellation/change of the dam-use right. However, if the entire dam construction costs were borne by the State as general fiscal revenue, it would result in the people bearing the dam construction costs; thus, the dam-use right is a system introduced as a means to procure part of the enormous construction costs involved in multi-purpose dam construction and to appropriately recycle the already invested dam construction costs. Accordingly, the burden charges or charges can be viewed not so much as having the character of a kind of deposit for future use of the dam, but rather as costs incurred to obtain the dam-use right.\\n\\n⑤ The Claimant argues that, in comparison with cases where fishery rights or mining rights are cancelled for public-interest reasons and the average annual income amount is taken into account in calculating the amount of compensation for losses (Article 81(1) of the Fisheries Act, Article 69 [Attached Table 4] of the Enforcement Decree of the Fisheries Act), or future profitability is taken into account (Article 34(4) of the Mining Act, Article 30(1)1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Mining Act), the fact that, in the case of cancellation/change of the dam-use right, only a part of the burden charges, etc. is refunded constitutes insufficient compensation. However, as seen above, in light of the fact that the dam-use right is related to the efficient use of water resources, which are public goods; that it has no fixed duration and the possibility of cancellation or change is inherent; and that, unlike fishery rights or mining rights, no market-based price formation occurs for the dam-use right and thus its exchange value is difficult to assess, it cannot be said to be excessive to allow only the refund of the investment costs, such as burden charges, to the dam-use right holder upon cancellation/change of the dam-use right.\\n\\n⑥ Accordingly, the Burden Charge Refund Provision satisfies the minimum-impairment requirement.\\n\\n(c) As seen above, considering the importance and irreplaceability of water resources used for domestic water supply, industrial water supply, agricultural water supply, power generation water, etc.; the importance of multi-purpose dams for stable water supply and responding to natural disasters such as floods; and the fact that the dam-use right is a private property right but at the same time a right with the public-interest purpose of the rational development and use of water resources through multi-purpose dams, and is recognized on the premise that its content may be changed by a disposition of the administrative agency for the higher public interest of water resource management, the public interest to be realized through the Burden Charge Refund Provision is very significant, whereas it cannot be said that the property rights restricted by the Burden Charge Refund Provision of the dam-use right holder are so significant as to outweigh such public interest. Accordingly, the balance of legal interests is also satisfied.\\n\\n(d) Therefore, since the Burden Charge Refund Provision does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, it does not infringe property rights.\\n\\ne. Whether the Principles of Prohibition of Retroactive Legislation and Protection of Trust Are Violated\\n\\n(1) In order to regulate matters concerning the construction and management of multi-purpose dams, the Specific Multi-purpose Dam Act was enacted on 1966. 4. 23. as Act No. 1785, and the Dam Construction Management Act was enacted when the Specific Multi-purpose Dam Act was repealed by Act No. 6021 on 1999. 9. 7. From the time of its enactment, Article 28 of the former Specific Multi-purpose Dam Act provided that, where a dam-use right is cancelled or changed, the State shall repay the burden charges or charges to the dam-use right holder, and that the amount to be repaid shall deduct the amortization amount determined by Presidential Decree, thereby regulating content similar to that of current Article 34 of the Dam Construction Management Act. In other words, the provision requiring the refund of the amount after deducting the depreciation rate from the burden charges or charges when the dam-use right is cancelled or changed had already been stipulated in the former Specific Multi-purpose Dam Act before the Claimant acquired the dam-use right.\\n\\nHowever, when the Dam Construction Management Act was amended by Act No. 7158 on 2004. 1. 29., the grounds for cancellation/change of the dam-use right were expanded to include “where the storage capacity or conditions of use of stored water of the dam have changed, making it difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is” (Article 31(4)1 and 2), and the instant case concerns a case where the dam-use right was changed because the conditions of use of stored water of the dam have changed, making it difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is (Article 31(4)2). The Burden Charge Refund Provision that is the subject matter of review in this case is “the portions of Article 34(1) and (2) of the Dam Construction Management Act concerning each Article 31(4)2”; the wording of the Burden Charge Refund Provision is similar to that of the former Specific Multi-purpose Dam Act, but its substantive content can be seen as having been changed on 2004. 1. 29., when Article 31(4) of the Dam Construction Management Act was newly enacted, into a “provision that adjusts the interests and relations of the dam-use right holder in the case of cancellation/change of the dam-use right because it is difficult to maintain the dam-use right as it is due to changes in the conditions of use of stored water, etc.” Therefore, as alleged by the Claimant, the issue of whether the principles of prohibition of retroactive legislation or protection of trust are violated may arise.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Principle of Prohibition of Retroactive Legislation Is Violated\\n\\nArticle 13(2) of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall not be deprived of their right to participate in politics or of their property rights by retroactive legislation.” “Retroactive legislation” is divided into “true retroactive legislation” and “quasi-retroactive legislation” depending on whether the new law applies to facts or legal relations that have already been completed, or to facts or legal relations currently in progress. The former is, in principle, not permitted under the Constitution and is permitted only exceptionally where special circumstances exist, whereas the latter is, in principle, permitted, but differs in that, in the process of balancing the public-interest reasons requiring retroactive effect and the demand for protection of trust, the perspective of protection of trust imposes certain limitations on the legislator’s legislative discretion (see Constitutional Court 2008. 2. 28. 2005HEONMA872, etc.; Constitutional Court 2013. 11. 28. 2009HEONBA206, etc.).\\n\\nThe Claimant obtained the dam-use right for Seomjingang Dam before the enactment of the Dam Construction Management Act, and the legal relationship arising from the Claimant’s dam-use right continued even after 2004, when the Burden Charge Refund Provision was amended. Thus, the Burden Charge Refund Provision is legislation that regulates matters in progress and does not constitute true retroactive legislation in the genuine sense, in which a new law is retroactively applied to facts or legal relations in the past that have already been completed and thereby newly evaluates the past. Accordingly, the issue of infringement of property rights by retroactive legislation does not arise. The only issue is whether the trust in the existing legal relationship held by the Claimant should be constitutionally protected (see Constitutional Court 2017. 11. 30. 2016HEONBA38).\\n\\n(3) Whether the Principle of Protection of Trust Is Violated\\n\\nThe principle of protection of trust derives from the constitutional principle of a rule-of-law state and means that, when enacting or amending a law, if the party’s trust in the existing legal order is reasonable and justifiable, while the harm suffered by the party caused by the enactment or amendment of the law is so severe that the public-interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new legislation cannot justify the destruction of that trust, such legislation may not be permitted. In determining whether this principle of protection of trust has been violated, one must comprehensively balance, on the one hand, the protected value of the interest infringed, the degree of infringement, the extent of damage to trust, and the manner of infringement of trust, and on the other hand, the public-interest purpose sought to be realized through the new legislation (see Constitutional Court 2015. 10. 21. 2013HEONBA248).\\n\\nAs seen above, in light of the fact that the dam-use right is related to the efficient use of water resources, which are public goods; that it has no fixed duration and the possibility of cancellation or change is inherent; and that the importance and irreplaceability of water resources are significant, it can be said that the public-interest value of the rational development and use of water resources through multi-purpose dams is very great, rather than the Claimant’s trust interest in the continued existence of the dam-use right. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the Burden Charge Refund Provision is contrary to the constitutional principle of protection of trust.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the request for review concerning the Dam-Use Right Change Provision is dismissed as inadmissible, and the Burden Charge Refund Provision does not violate the Constitution; accordingly, the decision is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}
