Among industrial waste, the following wastes excluding designated waste\\n\\na. to ka. Omitted\\n\\nta. Construction waste materials (limited to earth and sand, waste bricks, waste concrete, and waste asphalt concrete)\\n\\npa. to beo. Omitted\\n\\n2. Claims of the Petitioners and Opinions of the Interested Parties\\n\\nA. Claims of the Petitioners\\n\\n(1) Under the former Act, the waste intermediate treatment business category was divided into the intermediate treatment business and recycling business, which were permit businesses, and the recycling-processing notification business, which was a notification business; however, all of these businesses can be said to be essentially the same business category, namely a waste intermediate treatment business for the purpose of reuse and recycling of waste, with facilities for intermediate treatment of waste in place. Nevertheless, by integrating the above three business categories into the intermediate treatment business through the amendment of the Act, the statutory provision at issue required persons engaged in recycling-processing businesses for construction waste materials, among the former Act’s recycling-processing notification business operators, to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act; compared with the case in which persons engaged in the former Act’s recycling-processing business are deemed to have obtained a permit for intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions pursuant to Addenda Article 5(1) of the amended Act, this is an arbitrary and unequal treatment of essentially equal matters, and thus infringes the Petitioners’ right to equality guaranteed by Article 11(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) The statutory provision at issue provides that the Petitioners, who are former Act recycling-processing notification business operators, must obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act.\\n\\nHowever, the waste intermediate treatment facilities that an intermediate treatment business operator must have under Article 26(4)2 of the Amended Act are facilities subject to urban planning, and can be installed only upon obtaining an urban planning decision under the Urban Planning Act; if an urban planning decision is not obtained, a permit for intermediate treatment business cannot be obtained.\\n\\nYet, obtaining an urban planning decision for the installation of waste disposal facilities in large metropolitan areas is practically almost impossible because the areas where installation is possible are limited to certain areas under the Urban Planning Act and its Enforcement Decree and Enforcement Rules, and due to environmental protection issues, opposition from residents, and the like. In addition, in order to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business, one must go through the permit procedures for intermediate treatment business under Article 26 of the Amended Act, in addition to the urban planning decision procedure; it is practically impossible to go through all such procedures within the short period of 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act.\\n\\nOriginally, the reason the State introduced a waste recycling-processing notification system in addition to the former Act’s intermediate treatment business or recycling business, both of which required permits, and designated the recycling of construction waste as fill material, etc. as subject to notification, was as a legislative policy consideration to promote the recycling of construction waste materials, which are easy to recycle into fill material, subbase material, road base material, and the like, and for this purpose, by merely filing a notification with relaxed requirements, such waste could be recycled. The Petitioners, complying with such State policy, invested hundreds of millions to billions of won, equipped the prescribed facilities and equipment, completed the notification, and have lawfully engaged in the recycling-processing business.\\n\\nIn addition, the State enacted the Act on the Promotion of Saving and Recycling of Resources, showing a strong will to foster the recycling industry, and throughout multiple amendments to the Waste Management Act, transitional provisions were adopted to enable waste disposal business operators, etc. to continue their businesses smoothly; accordingly, the Petitioners had trusted that they would be able to continue their business even if the law were amended.\\n\\nTherefore, the statutory provision at issue, which, by presenting such an impossible permit condition, makes it inevitable that they will have to close down their business after 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act, not only violates the principle of protection of trust, but also lacks substantiality in the means of achieving the legislative purpose of resolving the issue of equity through unification of construction waste treatment into intermediate treatment business and preventing environmental pollution, and thus violates the principle of prohibition of excess and infringes the freedom to decide on, or choose, an occupation guaranteed by Article 15 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(3) Recycling-processing notification business operators were conducting business by investing facilities, equipment, and personnel worth hundreds of millions to billions of won, and as they would inevitably suffer property losses, including losses of business rights, because they could not obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act due to the statutory provision at issue, and business closure would become unavoidable, the statutory provision at issue infringes the property rights guaranteed by Article 23(1) of the Constitution; furthermore, it deprives the Petitioners, who had been lawfully conducting business under the former Act, of their property rights by retroactive legislation, and therefore also violates Article 13(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Opinions of the Minister of Environment and the Incorporated Association, National Construction Waste Treatment Mutual Aid Association\\n\\n(1) The intermediate treatment business or recycling business and the recycling-processing notification business under the former Act are clearly different legal statuses in many respects, such as differences in permit requirements and notification requirements, differences in the types of waste subject to business, and differences in penal provisions, administrative dispositions, and penalty surcharges for unlawful acts; therefore, while integrating the recycling business and the recycling-processing notification business that recycles construction waste into fill material, etc. into the intermediate treatment business, it is rational legislation that the statutory provision at issue, unlike in the case of the recycling business, requires persons engaged in the former Act’s recycling-processing notification business to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act.\\n\\n(2) Integrating the recycling-processing notification business into the intermediate treatment business and requiring former Act recycling-processing notification business operators to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act is intended to resolve the equity issue arising from the dual system and to prevent improper recycling so as to achieve the public purpose of environmental preservation, and it takes into account the time required for former Act recycling-processing notification business operators to satisfy the permit requirements under the amended Act and to obtain an urban planning decision under the Urban Planning Act, thereby granting a grace period and accommodating them by allowing them to obtain the permit within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act.\\n\\nMoreover, construction waste intermediate treatment business is not impossible to permit even in large metropolitan areas, and even if the permit for intermediate treatment business is not obtained within 1 year, such permit is not barred thereafter, so the permit may be obtained at any time once the requirements are met.\\n\\nTherefore, the statutory provision at issue cannot be deemed to have infringed the Petitioners’ freedom of occupation.\\n\\n(3) Even if a permit cannot be obtained within 1 year at the present business location because an urban planning decision under the Urban Planning Act cannot be obtained, it would be possible to move to an area where a permit can be granted and obtain the permit; moreover, even in the case of closing down the business, the value of the facilities and equipment themselves, such as crushing facilities, is not lost, so it is difficult to recognize an infringement of property rights.\\n\\nIn addition, the statutory provision at issue does not have effect with respect to business activities conducted before the effective date of the amended Act, and merely requires that a permit for intermediate treatment business be obtained only for business activities after the effective date of the amended Act; furthermore, since it provides a grace period of 1 year from the effective date, it cannot be regarded as retroactive legislation.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\nA. Amendments to the Provisions concerning Waste Disposal Businesses, etc.\\n\\nThe former Act provided five categories of waste disposal business requiring a permit from the Mayor/Do governor or the Minister of Environment: waste collection and transportation business, intermediate treatment business, waste final disposal business, recycling business, and waste integrated treatment business (Article 26(1) and (2) of the former Act), and also recognized a recycling-processing notification business, which could be conducted merely by filing a notification with the Mayor/Do governor (Article 44-2 of the former Act).\\n\\nHowever, the Amended Act retained only four categories of waste disposal business excluding the above recycling business (Article 26(4) of the Amended Act), while amending the former Act’s recycling-processing notification business into a recycling notification business with different contents, excluding some of the wastes subject to notification, such as construction waste materials, from the scope of the notification\\n\\n(Article 44-2 of the Amended Act).\\n\\nIn other words, the broad category of waste intermediate treatment business under the former Act, including recycling processing, had been divided into three types: intermediate treatment business, recycling business, and recycling-processing notification business; however, under the Amended Act, the broad category of waste intermediate treatment business, including recycling, was divided into two types: intermediate treatment business and recycling notification business, while some of the wastes subject to the former Act’s recycling-processing notification business, including construction waste materials, were excluded from the scope of the recycling notification business and treated as subjects of intermediate treatment business, so that the business could be conducted only upon obtaining a permit.\\n\\nAs a transitional measure in relation thereto, Addenda Article 5 provides that a person who obtained a permit for recycling business under the former Act shall be deemed to have obtained a permit for intermediate treatment business under Article 26(3) of the Amended Act (paragraph 1); and, in the case of a person who filed a recycling-processing notification under the former Act, if the business falls under intermediate treatment business under Article 26(4)2 of the Amended Act, such person shall obtain a permit under Article 26(3) of the Amended Act within 1 year from the effective date of the Amended Act (first sentence of paragraph 2, which is the statutory provision at issue), and if it falls under a recycling notification under Article 44-2 of the Amended Act, such person shall be deemed to have filed such notification (latter sentence of paragraph 2).\\n\\nB. Whether the statutory provision at issue is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Whether freedom of occupation is infringed\\n\\n(a) Raising the issue\\n\\nArticle 15 of the Constitution guarantees freedom of occupation by providing that “all citizens shall enjoy freedom of occupation,” and freedom of occupation means freedom of occupation encompassing freedom to choose an occupation, freedom to perform an occupation, and the like.\\n\\nBecause the statutory provision at issue makes it impossible for former Act recycling-processing notification business operators to continue their business unless they obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act, it should be regarded as a provision restricting the freedom to decide on an occupation of former Act recycling-processing notification business operators, including the Petitioners, and in order for such a legal provision restricting fundamental rights of the people not to violate the Constitution, the principle of prohibition of excess, which is the limit on restrictions of fundamental rights set forth in Article 37(2) of the Constitution, must be observed.\\n\\nAnd while the guarantee of freedom of occupation cannot be understood as requiring the legislature to maintain, forever, an already formed occupation category or to continue to keep the requirements for engaging in an occupation unchanged, when the legislature reforms the occupational system by integrating similar occupations or strengthening the requirements for engaging in an occupation for reasons of public interest, the protection of the trust of existing practitioners is demanded by the constitutional principle of the rule of law, and whether such trust protection has been sufficiently afforded will serve as the standard for determining whether the principle of prohibition of excess has been violated (see Constitutional Court 1997. 11. 27. 97HEONBA10, Decisions 9-2, 651, 667-668).\\n\\nAccordingly, the issue is whether the statutory provision at issue, which provides transitional measures for protection of trust in the course of strengthening occupational requirements from a notification system to a permit system through legislative amendment, violates the principle of prohibition of excess according to the same standard.\\n\\n(b) Amendment of the law and protection of trust\\n\\nWhen a law is amended, some degree of conflict of interests with the existing legal order is inevitable. In such a case, if the parties’ trust in the former legal order is reasonable and just, and if the loss caused to the parties by the amendment of the law is so severe that the public interest objective sought to be achieved by the new legislation cannot justify the damage to such trust, then such new legislation cannot be permitted under the principle of protection of trust derived from the constitutional principle of the rule of law. And in determining whether this principle of protection of trust has been violated, one must comprehensively compare and balance the protectable value of the interest infringed, the degree of severity of the infringement, the extent to which trust has been damaged, the method of the trust infringement, and the public interest objective to be realized through the new legislation (see Constitutional Court 1995. 6. 29. 94HEONBA39, Decisions 7-1, 896, 910).\\n\\n(c) Legislative purpose of the Amended Act\\n\\nUnder the former Act, there were two methods for recycling construction waste materials (earth and sand, waste bricks, waste concrete, and waste asphalt concrete) and using them as fill material, subbase material, road base material for construction and civil engineering works, and cover material for landfill sites: obtaining a permit for intermediate treatment business (Article 26(1) and (2)2 of the former Act; Article 17(1) of the former Enforcement Rules), or filing a recycling-processing notification (Article 44-2(1) of the former Act; item ta of Article 46(2) of the former Enforcement Rules; Article 47(2)6). However, because the Amended Act excluded some of the wastes subject to the former Act’s recycling-processing notification business, including construction waste materials, from the scope of the recycling notification business (Article 44-2(1) of the Amended Act; Article 46 of the Enforcement Rules of the Amended Act), under the Amended Act it became possible to conduct the above business only upon obtaining a permit for intermediate treatment business.\\n\\nThe original reason why the former Act designated the recycling processing of construction waste materials as subject to notification was legislative consideration aimed at promoting the recycling of construction waste materials. However, the dual system of permits and notifications for intermediate treatment businesses contained significant problems from the standpoint of equity.\\n\\nThat is, compared with intermediate treatment business operators, recycling-processing notification business operators had much more relaxed requirements (Article 26(1) of the former Act; Article 44-2(1) of the former Act; Article 17(1) and Article 48 of the former Enforcement Rules), were subject only to lighter criminal penalties for unlawful acts (Article 59(1) and (2), Article 61(8) of the former Act), and were not subject to administrative dispositions such as suspension of business or revocation of permit (Article 28 and Article 29(1) of the former Act). Moreover, their waste disposal facilities were excluded from the scope of urban planning decisions under the Urban Planning Act (Articles 16 and 12 of the Urban Planning Act before amendment by Act No. 6243 of 2000. 1. 28.; Article 126 of the Rules on Standards for Urban Planning Facilities), making business within urban planning zones in large metropolitan areas much easier and giving them an advantage in price competition because of lower logistics costs, which account for a large portion of waste transportation and treatment costs.\\n\\nAlso, because the penalties for unlawful acts applicable to recycling-processing notification business operators were light and administrative dispositions such as suspension of business or revocation of permit could not be imposed, strict management was difficult, and there was considerable concern over environmental pollution caused by improper recycling, such as illegal landfill of fill material containing excessive foreign substances.\\n\\nTherefore, the Amended Act’s decision to convert recycling-processing notification business for some wastes, including construction waste materials, where the above problems are particularly serious, into a permit-based intermediate treatment business is intended to resolve such equity and environmental issues, and such legislative purpose is legitimate.\\n\\n(d) Whether the principle of prohibition of excess is violated\\n\\nAs noted above, the original purpose of the State in establishing the recycling-processing notification system under the former Act was based on legislative policy considerations to promote the recycling of construction waste materials and the like, which are easy to recycle, and it is recognized that when the Waste Management Act was amended multiple times, transitional provisions were adopted to accommodate existing business operators.\\n\\nTherefore, in the present case, the fact that former Act recycling-processing notification business operators, including the Petitioners, invested large sums of money to equip facilities and equipment, completed the notification, and thereafter engaged in business, should be understood as having been caused by their trust in the continuation of the notification system or their trust that continued business would remain possible even if the law were amended.\\n\\nHowever, laws may be amended at any time due to changes in actual circumstances or changes in legislative policy, and this should generally be regarded as foreseeable; thus, absent special circumstances, former Act recycling-processing notification business operators should be understood as having merely taken advantage of opportunities granted by law at their own risk.\\n\\nThen, as seen above, the trust interest that former Act recycling-processing notification business operators should be protected does not absolutely take precedence over the benefits of amending the law, and it should be regarded as capable of protection through transitional provisions prescribing an appropriate grace period.\\n\\nAs its transitional provision, the statutory provision at issue grants a grace period of 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act, or 1 year and 6 months from the date of legislative amendment, requiring former Act recycling-processing notification business operators to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within that period (by 2000. 8. 8.).\\n\\nHowever, in order for a former Act recycling-processing notification business operator to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business under the amended Act, an urban planning decision for waste disposal facilities is also required, and obtaining an urban planning decision for the installation of waste disposal facilities in large metropolitan areas can be said to be quite difficult due to environmental preservation issues, opposition from residents, and the like; in particular, the Petitioners argue that obtaining a permit for intermediate treatment business through the urban planning decision procedure within such a short period of 1 year is practically impossible.\\n\\nTaking such problems into account, Article 3 of the Addenda to the Urban Planning Act Enforcement Decree as amended by Presidential Decree No. 16891 of 2000. 7. 1. provides that “waste disposal facilities installed by a person who must obtain a permit for waste intermediate treatment business pursuant to Addenda Article 5(2) of Act No. 5865, the Act Amending the Waste Management Act, may be installed without an urban planning decision notwithstanding Article 32(1) until 2003. 7. 1.” Thus, although waste disposal facilities are not included in the “facilities that need not be installed by urban planning decision” under the proviso to Article 36(1) of the Urban Planning Act, Article 32(1) of the Enforcement Decree, and Article 6 of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act, former Act recycling-processing notification business operators were enabled to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act by satisfying only the other requirements, without obtaining an urban planning decision for waste disposal facilities.\\n\\nAnd if the permit is obtained within the above period, business may be continued without an urban planning decision until 2003. 7. 1.\\n\\nTherefore, the statutory provision at issue provides a substantial grace period so that former Act recycling-processing notification business operators can appropriately respond to changes in circumstances caused by the amendment of the law, and in light of the fact that a new grace period concerning urban planning decisions was additionally provided by Article 3 of the Addenda to the above Urban Planning Act Enforcement Decree, such period cannot be said to be excessively short.\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provision at issue sufficiently protects the trust interest of former Act recycling-processing notification business operators, and cannot be regarded as violating the principle of prohibition of excess and infringing the Petitioners’ freedom to decide on an occupation guaranteed by Article 15 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Whether the right to equality is infringed\\n\\nThe Petitioners argue that, although the former Act’s recycling business and recycling-processing notification business are essentially the same type of business, namely a waste intermediate treatment business for the purpose of reusing and recycling waste, with waste intermediate facilities in place, the former Act’s recycling business operator is deemed in Addenda Article 5(1) of the amended Act to have obtained a permit for intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions, whereas the statutory provision at issue requires the recycling-processing notification business operator to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act; this is an arbitrary and unequal treatment of essentially equal matters, thereby infringing the Petitioners’ right to equality guaranteed by Article 11(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nHowever, unlike the recycling-processing notification business, which requires only a notification upon meeting relaxed requirements, the former Act’s recycling business not only had to satisfy strict requirements and obtain a permit (Article 26(1) and (2)4 of the former Act; Article 17(1) of the former Enforcement Rules), but the types of waste subject to business also differed from those of the recycling-processing notification business (Article 26(2)4 of the former Act; Article 9 of the former Enforcement Decree). Moreover, recycling business, like intermediate treatment business, has heavier penalties than recycling-processing notification business and is subject to administrative dispositions, and its waste disposal facilities are subject to urban planning decisions, making it difficult to regard the former Act’s recycling business as essentially the same type of business as recycling-processing notification business because there are significant differences.\\n\\nAccordingly, the fact that the statutory provision at issue requires former Act recycling-processing notification business operators, unlike recycling business operators, to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business under the amended provisions cannot be viewed as arbitrarily treating essentially the same matters differently; thus, the Petitioners’ right to equality cannot be said to have been infringed thereby.\\n\\n(3) Whether property rights are infringed and whether property rights are deprived by retroactive legislation\\n\\nThe Petitioners argue that former Act recycling-processing notification business operators had been conducting business by investing facilities, equipment, and large numbers of personnel worth hundreds of millions to billions of won, but because the statutory provision at issue makes it practically impossible to obtain a permit for intermediate treatment business within 1 year from the effective date of the amended Act, closure is unavoidable and the property value including business rights will be lost; therefore, they have been deprived of property rights guaranteed by Article 23(1) of the Constitution. Furthermore, they argue that because the Petitioners, who had already lawfully been conducting business, are forced to close their businesses 1 year after the effective date of the amended Act due to the statutory provision at issue, this constitutes deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation prohibited by Article 13(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nHowever, the property rights protected by the above constitutional provisions are concrete rights having property value that entail private utility and, in principle, the power of disposition over them. Therefore, mere interests that are not concrete rights, opportunities to acquire goods, or the factual and legal conditions for business activities are not subject to property-rights protection (see Constitutional Court 1996. 8. 29. 95HEONBA36, Decisions 8-2, 90, 103-104; Constitutional Court 1997. 11. 27. 97HEONBA10, Decisions 9-2, 651, 664).\\n\\nIn the present case, however, the specific facilities, equipment, or rights such as receivables owned by the Petitioners, including former Act recycling-processing notification business operators, are not being infringed by the State.\\n\\nAnd the Petitioners’ business activities, in principle, are merely acts carried out under their own plans and responsibility while taking advantage of opportunities incidentally granted by the legal system; therefore, the business rights asserted by the Petitioners do not fall within the scope of property rights referred to in the above constitutional provisions.\\n\\nAccordingly, it cannot be said that the Petitioners’ property rights have been infringed by the statutory provision at issue, nor that property rights have been deprived by retroactive legislation.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the petition for adjudication in this case is without merit, it is dismissed, and it is so decided unanimously by all participating Justices as follows."}

question: Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding the Warrant Requirement? (In cases of dispute, according to case law) (a) A warrant issued ex officio by a court has the character of a warrant of authorization, but an arrest warrant issued upon the request of an investigative agency has the character of a warrant of command. (b) A statutory provision that permits the relevant administrative authority, when it discovers a game product that has not been subjected to rating classification or a game product with content different from that of a game product that has received rating classification, to have the relevant public official collect and dispose of it, is intended to address an urgent situation; since its inevitability and legitimacy are sufficiently recognized, even if collection without a warrant is permitted, it cannot be regarded as violating the Warrant Requirement. (c) A decision by the Minister of Justice prohibiting the departure from the country of a national whose criminal trial is pending constitutes a compulsory disposition directly involving physical coercive force against the body to which the Warrant Requirement applies. (d) An act by the warden of a prison of requiring an inmate who is a drug offender to provide urine for a drug reaction test constitutes a compulsory disposition against the body and thus violates the Warrant Requirement.

supporting_precedents: {"[2000HEONGA12]": "1. Overview of the Case and the Subject Matter of Review\\n\\na. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) The applicant for referral operated “OO Computer Game Center” at 255-3, OOdong, Jung-gu, Ulsan, and is a person who has installed and is operating a game product called “Trophy.”\\n\\n(2) The Minister of Culture and Tourism received notification from the Eastern Branch of the Seoul District Prosecutors’ Office that a game product manufacturer, after having the above game product inspected on 1998. 4. 8. as “lamp-type,” had unlawfully manufactured and distributed it in a completely different form, namely as a “reel-type” game machine, and on 1999. 12. 21. sent an official document to each City and Do directing that, under the responsibility of the operator of the game-providing business, the “reel-type Trophy” game product be voluntarily discarded by 2000. 1. 15., and that after the above deadline the circuit boards of the above game machine be collected and discarded pursuant to Article 24(3)4 of the former Act on Audio Records, Video Products and Game Products (prior to its amendment by Act No. 6473 on 2001. 5. 24.) (hereinafter the Minister of Culture and Tourism’s above act is referred to as “the instruction in this case”).\\n\\n(3) Thereupon, on 2000. 5. 1., the Jung-gu District Head of Ulsan Metropolitan City had his subordinate public official crack down on the above game center operated by the applicant for referral, and had seven “reel-type Trophy” circuit boards owned by the applicant for referral that were there collected pursuant to the above statutory provision on the ground that they were “game products that have not received a rating classification or game products whose contents differ from those of game products that have received a rating classification” (hereinafter the above act of the Jung-gu District Head of Ulsan Metropolitan City is referred to as “the collection disposition in this case”).\\n\\n(4) Thereupon, on 2000. 5. 18., the applicant for referral filed a merits action with the Seoul Administrative Court, Case No. 2000GU14510, against the Minister of Culture and Tourism and the Jung-gu District Head of Ulsan Metropolitan City, first on the premise that the Minister of Culture and Tourism and the Jung-gu District Head of Ulsan Metropolitan City jointly made the collection disposition in this case, seeking primarily confirmation of the invalidity of the Minister of Culture and Tourism’s instruction in this case and of each of the collection dispositions in this case by the Minister of Culture and Tourism and the Jung-gu District Head of Ulsan Metropolitan City, and secondarily seeking revocation of the collection disposition in this case by the Jung-gu District Head of Ulsan Metropolitan City, and at the same time filed a request for a constitutional review with respect to the portion of the provisions concerning game products in the above statutory provision (Case No. 2000A1105 of the same court), and the same court accepted it and made the constitutional review referral in this case.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of review in this case is whether the portion concerning game products in Article 24(3)4 of the former Act on Audio Records, Video Products and Game Products (prior to its amendment by Act No. 6473 on 2001. 5. 24.; hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provision at issue in this case”) is in violation of the Constitution, and the content of the provision and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Provision Subject to Review\\n\\nArticle 24 of the Act (Closing and Collection Measures, etc.) ① to ② omitted\\n\\n③ When the Minister of Culture and Tourism, the Mayor/Do governor, the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head discovers any phonograph record, video product, or game product falling under any one of the following subparagraphs, he/she may have the relevant public official collect and discard it.\\n\\n1. to 3. omitted\\n\\n4. A video product or game product that has not received the rating classification under the provisions of Article 18(5) or that has content different from that of a video product or game product that has received a rating classification\\n\\n5. omitted\\n\\n④ to ⑥ omitted\\n\\n(2) Related Provisions\\n\\nArticle 18 of the Act (Rating Classification) ① A person who intends to produce a video product or game product for the purpose of distribution, viewing provision, or entertainment provision, or to receive a recommendation for import or bringing in, shall in advance obtain a rating classification from the Video Rating Board with respect to the contents of the relevant video product or game product. Provided, That this shall not apply to any of the following subparagraphs and cases prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n1. to 2. omitted\\n\\n② The classifications under paragraph 1 shall be as follows, and the standards and procedures for classification shall be prescribed by the regulations of the Video Rating Board. Provided, That for game products intended to be used only at game-providing establishments, only the classifications under subparagraphs 1 and 3 may be assigned.\\n\\n1. All-Ages: video products and game products usable by anyone without age restriction\\n\\n2. 12-and-Over: video products and game products unusable by persons under 12 years of age\\n\\n3. 18-and-Over: video products and game products unusable by persons under 18 years of age\\n\\n③ With respect to game products that the Video Rating Board determines cannot be assigned any of the classifications under paragraph 2 subparagraphs 1 through 3 because of excessive speculative character, it may, notwithstanding paragraph 2, decide that they are unusable. In such case, game products decided to be unusable shall not be distributed or provided for entertainment in any manner whatsoever.\\n\\n④ omitted\\n\\n⑤ No one shall produce, distribute, provide for viewing, or provide for entertainment any video product or game product that has not received the rating classification under paragraph 1 or that has content different from that of a video product or game product that has received a rating classification, and video products and game products falling under paragraph 2 subparagraph 3 shall not be distributed, provided for viewing, or provided for entertainment to juveniles.\\n\\n⑥ omitted\\n\\nArticle 24 of the Act (Closing and Collection Measures, etc.) ① to ③ omitted\\n\\n④ When the relevant public official collects the relevant phonograph record, video product, or game product pursuant to paragraph 3, he/she shall issue a collection certificate to the owner or possessor thereof.\\n\\n⑤ omitted\\n\\n⑥ A relevant public official, or an executive officer or employee of an association or organization, who attaches a notice, seals, collects, or otherwise disposes of property pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 3 shall carry credentials indicating his/her authority and present them to the persons concerned.\\n\\n2. Reasons for the Constitutional Review Referral by the Referring Court and Opinions of Relevant Institutions\\n\\na. Reasons for the Constitutional Review Referral by the Referring Court\\n\\n(1) When the relevant administrative authority discovers an unclassified game product, etc. in use at a game-providing establishment by a game-providing business operator, etc., it would be sufficient to achieve the administrative purpose by taking measures such as first ordering the game-providing business operator to stop using the game product or to collect and discard it, and direct measures of collection and discard of the game product may be exercised only supplementarily in cases where there are urgent circumstances (for example, where a game product manufacturer is attempting to mass-produce and distribute illegal game products) or where the game-providing business operator, etc. fails to comply with the above order.\\n\\nHowever, the statutory provision at issue in this case, as a type of administrative immediate compulsion, provides that once the relevant administrative authority determines that a certain game product is an unclassified game product, etc., it may collect and discard it without any limiting requirement such as urgency. If the administrative authority immediately collects and discards the above unclassified game product, etc. pursuant to the above provision, then even if the collection and discard measure later turns out to have been erroneous, restoration to the original state, such as return thereof to the game-providing business operator, etc., becomes impossible, resulting in the complete deprivation of the game product owner’s ownership.\\n\\nAccordingly, although it would be possible for the relevant administrative authority to take a less restrictive measure on fundamental rights in order to achieve the administrative purpose, the statutory provision at issue in this case prescribes the taking of an excessively restrictive measure on fundamental rights, thereby violating the principle of prohibition of excess.\\n\\n(2) If the administrative authority immediately collects and discards an unclassified game product, etc. pursuant to the statutory provision at issue in this case, as noted above, restoration to the original state becomes impossible, so the game-providing business operator, etc. loses the legal interest in seeking revocation of the collection and discard disposition in litigation, and thus the avenue to obtain judicial relief is completely blocked. Therefore, the statutory provision at issue in this case infringes the constitutional right of game-providing business operators, etc. to a trial.\\n\\nb. Opinion of the Minister of Culture and Tourism\\n\\n(1) The statutory provision at issue in this case has the legislative purpose of fostering game centers as wholesome spaces for everyday culture and further promoting the soundness of our society by necessarily collecting illegal game products from the site of illegal distribution so as to block the mass and repeated distribution of illegal game products and the resulting atmosphere of rapid promotion of speculative tendencies in our society.\\n\\n(2) If illegal game products are not collected in a timely manner, there is a high likelihood of destruction of evidence (there is a risk that disputes in court may frequently arise based on photographs and statements alone), and not only would the effect of enforcement not be achieved because illegal game products are rapidly duplicated, altered, and redistributed, but also there would be widespread insensitivity to illegal game products and an abundance of the mentality of “taking a shot” even while bearing fines and penalties arising from crackdowns on illegal game products, thereby promoting speculative tendencies in our society and risking serious damage to sound social morals. Accordingly, the collection measure for illegal game products is an unavoidable measure to instill awareness by imposing disadvantages on those who violate the law and further to prevent the harm of repeated distribution of these illegal game products in the market.\\n\\n(3) A game product that has not received a rating classification or that has content different from that of a game product that has received a rating classification means, given that the Video Rating Board has quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, and executive functions at the same time, a game product that already has a strong speculative character and whose distribution must therefore be restricted with great urgency, so the administration cannot achieve its administrative purpose by any further less restrictive measure on fundamental rights. In other words, the statutory provision at issue in this case has the character of unavoidable administrative immediate compulsion in an urgent situation with a risk of destruction of evidence, and as an unavoidable administrative measure to realize the administrative purpose of promoting the public interest of the entire people, it cannot be seen as infringing property rights in violation of the principle of prohibition of excess.\\n\\n(4) Since game products, due to their characteristics such as the fact that related programs are largely used both domestically and abroad, are easy to restore to the original state, and since there may be not only administrative litigation but also litigation remedies through damages, etc., the statutory provision at issue in this case does not infringe the constitutional right of game-providing business operators, etc. to a trial.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\na. Meaning and Limits of Administrative Immediate Compulsion\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue in this case provides that when the Minister of Culture and Tourism, the Mayor/Do governor, the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head discovers a game product that has not received the rating classification under Article 18(5) or that has content different from that of a game product that has received a rating classification, he/she may have the relevant public official collect and discard it. This is a case in which the administrative authority directly applies force to the object without going through any command, and the above provision is to be understood as prescribing administrative immediate compulsion, specifically compulsion in rem.\\n\\nAdministrative immediate compulsion is a type of administrative compulsion, and when there is a need to eliminate an imminent and urgent administrative obstacle and there is no time to order performance in advance, or where, by its nature, it is difficult to achieve the purpose by ordering performance, it is the function of directly applying force to the body or property of a citizen to realize the state necessary for administration. It is distinguished from administrative enforcement execution, which presupposes the existence of a prior specific obligation imposed by statutes or an administrative disposition and the nonperformance thereof.\\n\\nAdministrative compulsion is, in principle, administrative enforcement execution, and administrative immediate compulsion, as an exercise of power contrary to the predictability and legal stability required by a rule-of-law state and highly likely to infringe fundamental rights, is an exceptional means of compulsion. Such administrative immediate compulsion not only requires a strict basis in positive law, but its invocation must, within the scope of the law, still be limited to cases in which an administrative obstacle is imminent and urgent and no other means can achieve the administrative purpose, and even in such cases, its exercise is bound by the rational limit that it must be restricted to the minimum necessary extent.\\n\\nb. Whether Property Rights Are Infringed\\n\\n(1) The statutory provision at issue in this case is a provision that restricts the property rights of game-providing business operators, etc. by allowing the Minister of Culture and Tourism, the Mayor/Do governor, the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head, when discovering a game product that has not received the rating classification under Article 18(5) or that has content different from that of a game product that has received a rating classification, to have the relevant public official collect and discard it. If so, the principle of prohibition of excess, which is the basic principle that the State must observe when engaging in legislative activity that restricts the fundamental rights of the people pursuant to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, must be observed, and this point will therefore be examined.\\n\\n(2) Article 18 of the Act contains provisions on rating classification for game products, requiring a rating classification by the Video Rating Board with respect to the contents of game products, and prohibiting the production, distribution, or provision for entertainment of game products that have not received a rating classification or that have content different from that of game products that have received a rating classification. The game product rating system is intended to prevent adverse effects on the people’s cultural and emotional life and to promote the qualitative improvement of game products by restricting the usable age according to the contents of the game product.\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the statutory provision at issue in this case may be said to be to establish the game product rating system by preventing the distribution of game products that have not received a rating classification or that have content different from that of game products that have received a rating classification (hereinafter referred to as “illegal game products”), and further to create a sound social atmosphere by suppressing the promotion of speculative tendencies caused by illegal game products.\\n\\nIf so, the legitimacy of the legislative purpose of the statutory provision at issue in this case can readily be accepted, and it is of course true that the provision establishing the basis for administrative immediate compulsion, by which the relevant public official may immediately collect and discard the game product without first ordering the game-providing business operator to stop using or to collect and discard the illegal game product, can be an appropriate means that contributes to the above legislative purpose.\\n\\n(3) Even if the provision concerning collection and discard in the statutory provision at issue in this case can be an effective and appropriate means to achieve the legislative purpose, in order to satisfy the requirement of minimum infringement, it must be examined whether there exists another means, among equally effective methods for achieving the legislative purpose, that infringes fundamental rights to a lesser extent.\\n\\nFirst, with regard to the need for urgent collection of illegal game products, whether the statutory provision at issue in this case satisfies the requirement of minimum infringement will be examined.\\n\\nIn this regard, since the concept of administrative immediate compulsion itself essentially presupposes urgency, and since specifying the requirement of urgency in laying down a positive-law basis for administrative immediate compulsion would be merely redundant, it is clear that even if the statutory provision at issue in this case does not separately set forth a requirement of urgency in providing for immediate collection and discard by the administrative authority, that alone cannot amount to an excessive restriction of fundamental rights.\\n\\nIf so, what is at issue in this case is only whether the statutory provision at issue, which is the basis for administrative immediate compulsion, can be recognized as unavoidable for dealing with an urgent situation.\\n\\nThe reasons why illegal game products must be immediately collected from the illegal site may be summarized as follows.\\n\\nFirst, there is the possibility of destruction of evidence. That is, game products generally have the characteristic that the form or function of the game can be easily altered through simple manipulation of the circuit board, so legal game products can readily be altered into illegal game products, or illegal game products can readily be restored to their original state as legal game products. Thus, even if a person is found operating by altering the game form, etc. into a game product with content different from a game product that has received a rating classification, if it is not immediately collected, it becomes extremely difficult later in litigation to prove the illegal operation.\\n\\nNext is the harm caused by the speculative character of illegal game products. In most cases, game products that have not received a rating classification are game products with a strong speculative character, and even in the case of game products with content different from that of game products that have received a rating classification, there are many cases where the speculative character of the game product is significantly altered by altering, after classification as lamp-type, into reel-type, or by manipulating the fixed amount, payout, and betting functions at the time of obtaining the rating classification, thereby creating a substantial risk that speculative tendencies will be promoted in our society and sound social morals seriously damaged. Since it is difficult to expect voluntary compliance from the game-providing business operator who is providing illegal game products even if the business operator is ordered to stop using or to collect the game product, ordering the game-providing business operator first to stop using or to collect the game product and then waiting for noncompliance before proceeding with direct collection would not only be ineffective, but may also cause the harm of prolonging the game-providing business operator’s illegal business and opportunities for unjust enrichment.\\n\\nThere is also the possibility of duplication of illegal game products. Because game products generally have the characteristic of being easily duplicated, there is a possibility that they may be mass-produced and distributed. In particular, if one assumes a case where alteration of a game product that has received a rating classification is carried out at the stage of the manufacturer or distributor and then supplied to the game-providing business operator, it is easy to see that unless they are immediately collected before the spread of illegal game products, it is difficult to expect the effectiveness of enforcement.\\n\\nFinally, the collection of illegal game products is based on an authoritative determination already made by the Video Rating Board, which has quasi-judicial functions, regarding the rating classification, and since there is no room for the administrative authority’s arbitrariness to intervene in the determination of whether a game product is illegal, it may also be pointed out that even if administrative immediate compulsion is permitted, there is little room for infringement of an individual’s fundamental rights thereby.\\n\\nConsidering the above points, it may be said that under the ordinary method of ordering the parties concerned to collect and discard illegal game products and then proceeding to administrative enforcement such as direct compulsion after waiting for noncompliance, it is difficult to achieve the purpose. Therefore, it is judged that the establishment of the statutory provision at issue in this case, as a measure to cope with such urgent situations, is sufficiently unavoidable and justified.\\n\\nMoreover, as noted above, administrative immediate compulsion is not something that can be invoked at any time merely when the formal requirements prescribed by the basis provision are met; rather, it must comply with the rational limit that it may be invoked only when a concrete administrative obstacle is immediately imminent.\\n\\nAccordingly, in any event, the statutory provision at issue in this case does not appear to excessively restrict fundamental rights in relation to the issue of urgency.\\n\\nSecond, in comparison with provisions such as Article 56(1) of the Food Sanitation Act, which provide that seizure and discard by the relevant public official and the order of necessary measures to the parties concerned are optional, the question may arise whether the statutory provision at issue in this case, which does not provide optionally for collection and discard by the relevant public official, satisfies the requirement of minimum harm.\\n\\nHowever, even where an optional regulatory form is adopted, the form of the provision itself allows immediate collection and discard by the relevant public official. Moreover, even if such an optional provision did not exist, administrative immediate compulsion, pursuant to the rational limit that it must be invoked only supplementarily when the purpose cannot be achieved by other means, must not be employed as a means of immediate collection and discard by the relevant public official in cases where the purpose can be achieved through an order of necessary measures such as collection and discard to the parties concerned. Therefore, whether to adopt the optional regulatory form cannot be regarded as having special significance in relation to the degree of restriction on fundamental rights.\\n\\nAccordingly, it is difficult to view the statutory provision at issue in this case as violating the requirement of minimum harm merely because it does not make the collection and discard by the relevant public official optional.\\n\\nThird, the fact that the statutory provision at issue in this case provides for not only collection but also discard, which appears unrelated to urgency,\\n\\nmay raise the question whether this is an excessive restriction of fundamental rights, given that if illegal game products are collected and discarded, restoration to the original state becomes impossible even if the collection and discard measure later turns out to have been erroneous.\\n\\nIn our view, it cannot be denied that there are cases where the need for discard is recognized in connection with the post-disposition handling of collected illegal game products. The statutory provision at issue in this case has the character of a basis provision prepared for such cases, and in actual discard it is subject to strict restriction by the principle of proportionality. That is, because the invocation of administrative immediate compulsion is restricted by the principle of proportionality, which requires the selection of the means that causes the least infringement among several appropriate means, discarding even though collection alone would sufficiently achieve the administrative purpose would violate the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nFrom the standpoint of administrative practice, even if illegal game products are collected from the illegal site, they are not discarded immediately but are sent to the Video Rating Board, which also has jurisdiction over matters concerning post-classification management in addition to the rating classification of game products, and they are necessarily subjected to a verification procedure as to whether they are game products that have received a rating classification or are different game products from those that have received a rating classification, so it is difficult for lawful game products to be mistakenly discarded.\\n\\nIn addition, distribution or provision for entertainment of illegal game products is subject to administrative dispositions (Article 13(1)9 of the Act) or criminal punishment (Article 29(1)6, Article 30(5) of the Act), and accordingly, where the illegally collected game products become evidence in litigation procedures such as criminal proceedings, they are not discarded until the conclusion of the litigation, and after the conclusion of the litigation they are discarded pursuant to procedures such as receiving direction from a prosecutor.\\n\\nTherefore, the mere fact that the statutory provision at issue in this case provides the basis for discard does not mean that it is an excessive piece of legislation.\\n\\nIn short, even if the statutory provision at issue in this case does not expressly specify a requirement of urgency, does not optionally provide for an order of collection and discard to the parties concerned, and provides not only for collection but also for discard, it cannot be viewed as violating the requirement of minimum harm.\\n\\nIn addition, since the public interest protected by permitting administrative immediate compulsion concerning the collection and discard of illegal game products under the statutory provision at issue in this case can be seen as greater than the disadvantage suffered by game-providing business operators, etc. as a result of permitting it, it cannot be said to violate the principle of balance of legal interests.\\n\\n(4) Ultimately, the permission of administrative immediate compulsion under the statutory provision at issue in this case appears to satisfy all the requirements to be considered in determining whether it violates the principle of prohibition of excess, including legitimacy of purpose, appropriateness of means, minimum harm, and balance of legal interests. Therefore, it cannot be said that the statutory provision at issue in this case infringes the applicant’s property rights in violation of the principle of prohibition of excess.\\n\\nc. Whether the Right to a Trial Is Infringed\\n\\nThe referring court states that if the administrative authority immediately collects and discards illegal game products pursuant to the statutory provision at issue in this case, restoration to the original state becomes impossible, and the game-providing business operator, etc. loses the legal interest in seeking revocation of the collection and discard disposition in litigation, thereby infringing the constitutional right of game-providing business operators, etc. to a trial; this point will therefore be examined.\\n\\nArticle 27(1) of the Constitution provides, “All citizens shall have the right to a trial by judges qualified under the Constitution and laws, in accordance with law,” thereby guaranteeing the right to seek adjudication.\\n\\nThe right to seek adjudication is a procedural-law request concerning the establishment of a rights-protection procedure and the effectiveness of access to the established procedure; it is concretely formed and realized, and also restricted, by procedural laws that prescribe rights-remedy procedures or litigation procedures.\\n\\nHowever, the statutory provision at issue in this case is merely a basis provision concerning administrative immediate compulsion and has no procedural-law character at all prescribing rights-remedy procedures or litigation procedures, and therefore there is no room for it to infringe the right to seek adjudication.\\n\\nEven if one assumes a case where, due to the immediate collection and discard of illegal game products, the game-providing business operator, etc. loses the legal interest in seeking revocation of the immediate compulsion in administrative litigation, it should be understood that, in that case, only whether property rights are infringed as discussed above may be at issue, and the right to seek adjudication cannot be infringed thereby.\\n\\nd. Whether It Violates the Warrant Principle and the Principle of Due Process\\n\\n(1) Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides, “When an arrest, detention, seizure or search is made, a warrant issued by a judge upon the request of a prosecutor, in accordance with due process, shall be presented. Provided, That where a person is caught in flagrante delicto or where there is an apprehension that a person who has committed a crime punishable by imprisonment for a term of three years or more may flee or destroy evidence, a warrant may be requested post facto.” Article 16 of the Constitution provides, “When a seizure or search is made with respect to a residence, a warrant issued by a judge upon the request of a prosecutor shall be presented.”\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue in this case contains no provision whatsoever regarding warrants, while Article 24(4) and (6) of the Act contain provisions concerning “issuance of a collection certificate” and “presentation of credentials.” Since this is to be construed as excluding the warrant system, the question arises whether the statutory provision at issue in this case violates the warrant principle.\\n\\nThere is debate as to whether the warrant principle applies also to administrative immediate compulsion, but administrative immediate compulsion is an act of directly exercising force without command when there is no time to wait for the voluntary performance of the other party, and by its nature it requires urgency such that the purpose cannot be achieved by waiting for a judicial warrant. Therefore, in principle, the warrant principle should be understood not to apply.\\n\\nIf any statutory provision recognizes administrative immediate compulsion even though urgency is not recognized to such an extent that there is no rational reason to exclude the warrant principle, such a statutory provision would already, in itself, violate the principle of prohibition of excess and would therefore be unconstitutional.\\n\\nAs noted above, the statutory provision at issue in this case is a measure to cope with an urgent situation, and its inevitability and justification are sufficiently recognized. Therefore, even if the statutory provision at issue in this case recognizes collection without a warrant, it cannot be said to violate the constitutional warrant principle.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, although the statutory provision at issue in this case does not contain provisions concerning procedural guarantees such as a hearing or submission of opinions before collection, considering that administrative immediate compulsion is an act of directly exercising force in response to an imminent and urgent obstacle, it is not easily compatible with prior procedures, and therefore it cannot be regarded as violating the principle of due process for that reason.\\n\\nHowever, even though in the case of collection prescribed by the statutory provision at issue in this case the exclusion of the warrant principle is tolerated and it is acknowledged that, by its nature, it is not compatible with prior procedures, it cannot be said that all procedural guarantees are excluded; from the viewpoint of due process, certain procedural guarantees are required in order to prevent abuse of state power and protect the rights of citizens.\\n\\nFrom this perspective, Article 24(4) of the Act provides that when the relevant public official collects the relevant game product, etc., a collection certificate shall be issued to the owner or possessor thereof, and paragraph 6 of the same Article provides procedural requirements such as requiring the relevant public official, or the executive officers or employees of an association or organization, who carry out seizure, etc. to carry credentials indicating their authority and present them to the persons concerned. Therefore, it is difficult to view the statutory provision at issue in this case as violating the principle of due process.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, since the statutory provision at issue in this case does not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as set forth in the order, by the unanimous opinion of all the Justices except for the dissenting opinions of Justice Kwon Seong and Justice Joo Seon-hwi below in 5.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kwon Seong and Joo Seon-hwi\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we believe that the portion of the statutory provision at issue in this case, which is the basis for administrative immediate compulsion and which provides that discard is also possible, violates the Constitution.\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue in this case provides that “the Minister of Culture and Tourism, the Mayor/Do governor, the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head may have the relevant public official collect and discard the game product when it is discovered ...,” thereby not merely providing a provision concerning collection but also providing that discard is possible.\\n\\nAdministrative immediate compulsion, in that it directly exercises force without first imposing a specific obligation and waiting for its nonperformance, rather than doing so after imposing a specific obligation in advance, is a power act that runs counter to the predictability and legal stability required by a rule-of-law state and is highly likely to infringe fundamental rights, as even the majority opinion acknowledges. Such administrative immediate compulsion, of course, should be recognized only in extremely exceptional circumstances.\\n\\nAccordingly, even in laying down a positive-law basis for administrative immediate compulsion, the scope of its permission must, if possible, be prescribed to the minimum extent.\\n\\nWhen establishing a basis provision for compulsion in rem among administrative immediate compulsion, expanding its scope beyond collection to discard can be justified only if the necessity of immediately discarding the object, that is, the independent urgency of discard itself, is recognized. Examples would include cases such as “when quarantine items contaminated with the pathogen of an animal infectious disease, or reasonably believed to have been contaminated, are discovered, or when quarantine items likely to pose a danger to public hygiene are discovered,” as provided in Article 31(1) of the Act on the Prevention of Contagious Animal Diseases. In such cases, there is urgency requiring the prevention of the spread of the infectious disease in a race against time, and it is difficult to immediately implement appropriate measures that can reliably prevent the spread of the infectious disease by means other than culling, which can be considered equivalent to discard, and simple quarantine or storage measures require much effort and expense.\\n\\nHowever, with respect to illegal game products subject to regulation under the statutory provision at issue in this case, while the urgency of collection can be recognized given their nature, it is difficult to conceive of cases in which there is an urgent necessity to discard them immediately.\\n\\nAccordingly, we agree with the majority opinion insofar as it recognizes the necessity of immediately collecting illegal game products from the illegal site; however, in this case, even though realization of the administrative purpose requiring the invocation of administrative immediate compulsion would be sufficiently possible through collection of illegal game products alone, it is our view that providing in the basis provision for administrative immediate compulsion that discard is also possible is excessive legislation exceeding the regulatory purpose.\\n\\nThe majority opinion appears to contend that the statutory provision at issue in this case has the character of a basis provision prepared for the need for discard in connection with the post-treatment of illegal game products, and that, in actual discard, it is not only subject to strict limitation by the principle of proportionality but also, in administrative practice, illegal game products are never discarded immediately, thereby arguing that it is not excessive legislation.\\n\\nHowever, even if rational limits such as the principle of proportionality exist and no harm resulting therefrom is found in administrative practice, these facts alone cannot conceal the unconstitutionality of this provision, which opens the way to immediate discard. Therefore, the statutory provision at issue in this case still cannot escape being unconstitutional.\\n\\nIn short, we believe that the portion of the statutory provision at issue in this case that provides that not only collection but also discard is possible violates the Constitution as excessive legislation contrary to the requirement of minimum harm, and for that reason we express our dissent from the majority opinion."}

{"[2005HEONMA277]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject of Review\\n\\nA. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner was arrested and indicted in early June 2004 on suspicion of violation of the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropic substances), was sentenced by the Daegu District Court on 2004. 9. 23. to imprisonment for 10 months, that sentence became final on 2004. 11. 27., and he was released from Daegu Prison after serving the sentence on 2005. 3. 31.\\n\\n(2) The Petitioner underwent narcotics reaction tests [T.B.P.E. test, a test in which urine is collected in a paper cup from the person subject to testing and submitted, and a T.B.P.E. reagent is dropped to observe the reaction (turning red indicates a positive result)] at Daegu Detention Center on 2004. 6. 9., 2004. 10. 26., and 2004. 11. 23., and at Daegu Prison on 2004. 12. 24., respectively, and each was determined to be negative.\\n\\n(3) On 2005. 1. 6., the Petitioner filed an application for appointment of state-appointed counsel, and through the appointed state-appointed counsel, while filing a constitutional complaint on 2005. 3. 16., argued that the act by which the Respondents caused him to submit urine for the narcotics reaction test on 2004. 12. 24. (hereinafter referred to as “the collection of urine in this case”) infringes the dignity of the human being and the right to pursue happiness, and the freedom of the person guaranteed by the Constitution, is contrary to the warrant principle, and because compelled urine collection for narcotics reaction tests will continue every month in the future as well, he seeks a determination of unconstitutionality thereof.\\n\\nB. Subject of Review and Relevant Provision\\n\\n(1) Subject of Review\\n\\nWhether the act of the Respondents “causing the Petitioner to submit urine for the narcotics reaction test on 2004. 12. 24.” is unconstitutional.\\n\\n(2) Relevant Provision\\n\\nArticle 17-2 (Physical Examination, etc.) of the Prison Administration Act ① Correctional officers may inspect the bodies, clothing, personal effects, cells, and workplaces of inmates when necessary for the safety and maintenance of order of prisons, etc.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments and the Respondents’ Answers\\n\\nA. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\n(1) The act of collecting urine in this case is based on internal regulations without delegation by statute, and thus exceeded the limits of delegated legislation, and was carried out without a warrant issued by a judge, contrary to the constitutional warrant principle.\\n\\n(2) Even if the Petitioner is a narcotics offender, since the bringing in of outside items that is permitted for inmates convicted of other offenses is prohibited and the risk of bringing in narcotics is thereby blocked, compelling the regular collection of urine, to which there is no duty, violates the constitutional principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, excessively restricts the freedom of the person, and infringes the essential content of the dignity of the human being and the right to pursue happiness.\\n\\n(3) The act of collecting urine has no dispositive character that would make it subject to an appeal litigation, and the act of collecting urine that is subject to cancellation has already ended; however, because the periodic urine collection will continue to be carried out repeatedly in the future as well, there is an interest in seeking a determination of its unconstitutionality.\\n\\nB. The Respondents’ Answers\\n\\n(1) The act of collecting urine in this case was carried out pursuant to the voluntary cooperation of the person subject to testing, and no sanctioning disposition such as disciplinary punishment is imposed if he does not comply, and thus “the exercise of public power” is not recognized.\\n\\n(2) Article 6(1) of the Prison Administration Act, Articles 6, 7, and 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Prison Administration Act, regulate the right of petition by which inmates may object to their treatment, the right to request an interview with the warden, and the procedures therefor; however, since the Petitioner did not go through procedures such as the right of petition or the right to request an interview, the present constitutional complaint is inadmissible for lack of subsidiarity.\\n\\n(3) The Petitioner was released on 2005. 3. 31., and the interest in protection of rights has likewise been extinguished.\\n\\n(4) The collection of urine from the Petitioner was conducted as one method of physical examination on the basis of Article 17-2(1) of the Prison Administration Act, and thus has a statutory basis; and because it was carried out pursuant to voluntary cooperation, the warrant principle regarding arrest, detention, seizure, and search, which involve physical force and are executed by compulsion, does not apply.\\n\\n(5) Narcotics offenders, by their nature, tend to be addicted to the drugs or to be habitual offenders, so there is always a risk that narcotics will be brought in from outside. In light of the fact that if narcotics are supplied to inmates it may lead to a major correctional accident, there is a need to block this in advance and maintain safety and order within correctional facilities. Regularly conducting the narcotics reaction test once a month is an appropriate method for blocking the bringing in of narcotics in advance and for protecting narcotics offenders from narcotics through the general preventive effect of blocking the bringing in of narcotics in advance, and since a perfect inspection of the body, clothing, cells, etc., or personal effects, etc., within correctional facilities is impossible, and there is no way to determine by visual inspection whether narcotics have been taken, it cannot be said that the narcotics reaction test through urine collection violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Admissibility Requirements\\n\\nA. As to the Respondent, the Minister of Justice\\n\\nThe subject who caused the narcotics reaction test to be conducted on the Petitioner was the Warden of Daegu Prison, and the Minister of Justice was not that subject; therefore, the constitutional complaint filed naming the Minister of Justice as Respondent is inadmissible, without need to proceed to the remaining points.\\n\\nB. As to the Respondent, the Warden of Daegu Prison\\n\\n(1) In general, whether an administrative act constitutes a coercive factual act subject to a constitutional complaint must be determined individually by comprehensively considering the specific circumstances at the time the act was performed, such as the relationship between the administrative subject and the counterparty, the counterparty’s intent, degree of involvement, and attitude toward the factual act, the purpose and circumstances of the factual act, and whether commands or coercive means by law were triggered (Constitutional Court 1994. 5. 6., 89HEONMA35, Court Reports 6-1, 462, 485).\\n\\nThe collection of urine from narcotics inmates can only be carried out through the cooperative act of the person subject to testing, such as the Petitioner, and no disciplinary punishment or other sanction is imposed merely because the person refuses, but the Respondent, the Warden of Daegu Prison, as the managing authority of the correctional facility, is in a superior position over the Petitioner in executing his sentence; the Petitioner and other inmates are in a relationship in which they must, while isolated from the outside, obey the Respondent’s directions and orders concerning the execution of the sentence; the purpose of urine collection is to prevent inmates from taking narcotics and to maintain safety and order in correctional facilities through early detection; and there is also the fact that there exists an aspect of unilaterally compelling them to collect and submit urine; and one may anticipate that psychological pressure exists, in that if they do not comply with urine collection, they may receive some unfavorable treatment, and in light of the fact that the number of cases in which refusal actually occurs is extremely small, it constitutes a coercive factual act subject to constitutional complaint and, as an exercise of public power subject to review under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\n(2) The collection of urine in this case is not clearly subject to administrative litigation as a coercive factual act, and even if it were subject to such litigation, the infringement would be immediately terminated so that the interest in filing suit concerning that infringement would be denied; moreover, the petition right and the right to request an interview with the warden are insufficient and indirect as remedies in terms of the body handling the matter, procedure, and effect, and thus it is difficult to view them as advance remedy procedures that must necessarily be exhausted before filing a constitutional complaint.
