Therefore, there is no other effective remedy available to the Petitioner apart from filing a constitutional complaint (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21., 92HEONMA144, Court Reports 7-2, 94, 102; Constitutional Court 1998. 10. 29., 98HEONMA4, Court Reports 10-2, 637, 644; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29., 2004HEONMA826, Official Gazette 117, 938, etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, since the Petitioner was released on 2005. 3. 31. and the infringing act against the Petitioner has ended, even if a determination of unconstitutionality is made regarding the act of collecting urine, rights relief for the Petitioner is impossible, so the subjective interest in protection of rights has already been extinguished; however, even if a constitutional complaint is of little help to subjective rights relief, if there is a risk that such infringing act may be repeated in the future and the elucidation of the issue has significant constitutional meaning, the interest in adjudication may be recognized (see Constitutional Court 1997. 11. 27., 94HEONMA60, Court Reports 9-2, 675, 688; Constitutional Court 2001. 7. 19., 2000HEONMA546, Court Reports 13-2, 103, 108; Constitutional Court 2001. 8. 30., 99HEONMA496, Court Reports 13-2, 238, 244; Constitutional Court 2002. 7. 18., 2000HEONMA327, Court Reports 14-2, 54, 60; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29., 2004HEONMA826, Official Gazette 117, 938, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the materials in this case, urine collection is carried out regularly and repeatedly at detention centers or prisons for narcotics offenders upon admission and once a month or once per quarter, so it has significant constitutional meaning in its clarification, and therefore the interest in adjudication may be recognized.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Merits\\n\\nA. Overview of the Narcotics Reaction Test\\n\\n(1) Statutory Basis\\n\\n(a) Article 17-2(1) of the Prison Administration Act (Physical Examination, etc.) provides that “correctional officers may inspect the bodies, clothing, personal effects, cells, and workplaces of inmates when necessary for the safety and maintenance of order of prisons, etc.,” thereby allowing physical examinations of inmates, and since collecting urine from inmates for the narcotics reaction test is likewise one form of the above physical examination, that provision constitutes the statutory basis for the collection of urine in this case.\\n\\n(b) Meanwhile, the narcotics reaction test through urine collection in correctional facilities is generally carried out pursuant to the Minister of Justice’s directive dated 1989. 8. 26. (Correction 01250-11529), which ordered the use of the T.B.P.E. reagent test for the management of inmates convicted of psychotropic-substance-related offenses, and the directive dated 1990. 5. 1. (Correction 01250-5623), which ordered that the T.B.P.E. reagent test be conducted at least once a month and that the results of processing be reported.\\n\\n(2) Contents\\n\\nThe persons subject to the narcotics reaction test through urine collection are inmates such as narcotics offenders, persons who, before admission, had worked at entertainment establishments, persons who had frequent overseas travel such as crew members of foreign-going vessels, and persons with other narcotics-related criminal records, for whom narcotics reaction testing is deemed necessary because there is a likelihood of narcotics use; it is generally conducted once when newly admitted to detention centers and prisons and once a month, and, exceptionally, it is also conducted when necessary. The testing method is to have the inmate collect urine in a paper cup in a place where others cannot see and submit it, and then to drop 0.3cc of sodium borate and 0.5㎖ of T.B.P.E. reagent into 3 to 5cc of it and confirm whether it turns red within 1 to 3 minutes (positive reaction); each time the test is conducted, the timing and result are recorded in the health examination register, reported to the Corrections Agency and the Ministry of Justice, and if the result is positive, a request is made to the relevant agency for an in-depth examination such as serum testing or hair testing.\\n\\nB. Constitutional Limits on Urine Collection\\n\\n(1) The Collection of Urine in This Case and the Petitioner’s Fundamental Rights\\n\\nIf, as the Petitioner argues, he was compelled without any statutory basis to undergo urine collection to which he was under no duty, then the issue would be whether there was an infringement of the general right to freedom of action [the freedom not to do what one does not want to do (the act of collecting urine in a paper cup and submitting it), the freedom not to disclose one’s physical condition or information to the outside] guaranteed by the dignity and value of the human being and the right to pursue happiness under Article 10 of the Constitution, and of the freedom of the person guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Relationship with the Warrant Principle\\n\\nArticle 12(3) of the Constitution provides, with respect to arrest, detention, seizure, or search, that a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s request be presented in accordance with lawful procedure, thereby guaranteeing the warrant principle at the constitutional level, and this warrant principle refers to the principle that coercive measures necessary for investigation may not be taken without a warrant issued by a judge (Constitutional Court 1997. 3. 27., 96HEONGA11, Court Reports 9-1, 245, 258).\\n\\nThe collection of urine in this case is conducted for the purpose of maintaining safety and order in correctional facilities and is not a measure necessary for investigation; moreover, it is one that causes the person subject to testing, such as the Petitioner, to collect and submit urine in a paper cup, so the cooperation of the party is unavoidable, and it could not be called a coercive measure (see Constitutional Court 1997. 3. 27., 96HEONGA11, Court Reports 9-1, 245, 258).\\n\\nAccordingly, the collection of urine in this case cannot be said to be a coercive measure requiring a judicial warrant, and therefore the fact that urine was collected in the above manner within detention centers and other correctional facilities without a judicial warrant cannot be said to violate the warrant principle under Article 12(3) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(3) Whether the Principle of Prohibition of Excessive Restriction Was Violated\\n\\nEven if the collection of urine in this case from the Petitioner, a narcotics offender, is inevitable for the safety and maintenance of order within the correctional facility on the basis of Article 17-2 of the Prison Administration Act, it must not infringe the essential content of fundamental rights or violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, which refers to the legitimacy of the purpose, the appropriateness of the means, the minimum necessary infringement, and the balance of legal interests.\\n\\nConsidering that one of the characteristics of narcotics is addictiveness and that most narcotics offenders are repeat offenders or more, there is always a risk that narcotics will be brought into the correctional facility or that narcotics offenders will consume them, and in such case not only would the purpose of correction concerning the relevant inmate be fundamentally undermined, but another accident may occur due to harm to other inmates. Since such possibilities and risks always exist, regular inspections of inmates who may have access to narcotics, such as narcotics offenders, can enable early detection of the bringing in and consumption of narcotics; by making all inmates aware that regular inspections are conducted, attempts to bring in narcotics can be blocked in advance; and from the inmates’ perspective as well, abandoning attempts to bring in narcotics increases the possibility of complying with the original correctional purpose such as rehabilitation education. In this respect, conducting the narcotics reaction test through urine collection on a regular basis is highly contributory to the safety and maintenance of order within correctional facilities and to the correctional purpose, and thus the legitimacy of the purpose is recognized.\\n\\nIn addition, whether narcotics have been brought in can be confirmed through inspection of clothing, personal effects, cells, and workplaces and through visual observation of the outside of the body or body cavities, etc.; however, this also cannot be done perfectly (such inspections may also infringe inmates’ fundamental rights, and inspection of body cavities, etc., rather has a greater likelihood of infringing fundamental rights), and since whether they have been consumed cannot be determined by visual inspection, the appropriateness of the means is also recognized in the narcotics reaction test through urine collection.\\n\\nFurthermore, the collection of urine in this case is carried out through the cooperative acts of the persons subject to testing, such as the Petitioner, and there are no sanctioning means such as disciplinary punishment for failure to comply. It is conducted within a short time (1 to 3 minutes) by a simple method (dropping sodium borate and T.B.P.E. reagent into the paper cup into which urine has been collected), and the result can be known immediately. In this respect, the principle of minimum infringement can also be said to have been observed.\\n\\nLastly, the collection of urine in this case imposes on the Petitioner and other persons subject to testing the disadvantage that they must regularly collect and submit urine excreted from their own bodies, that is, the restriction of self-determination over their bodies and the limitation of private interests such as having to do something they do not want to do; however, as seen above, the increase in the feasibility of realizing the correctional purpose with respect to the persons subject to testing (which also has the aspect of an increase in private interests) and the public interest of safety and maintenance of order within correctional facilities are far greater, and thus the balance of legal interests is also satisfied.\\n\\nAccordingly, the collection of urine in this case from the Petitioner, a narcotics offender, does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the constitutional complaint seeking a determination of unconstitutionality regarding the collection of urine in this case from the Petitioner, a narcotics offender, is dismissed as inadmissible with respect to the Respondent, the Minister of Justice, because the subjectivity of the exercise of public power is not recognized, and with respect to the Respondent, the Warden of Daegu Prison, it is held that the above urine collection was carried out within the scope of restriction on fundamental rights, and thus is dismissed as lacking merit; and it is so decided by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}

{"[2012HEONBA302]": "1. Summary of the Case\\nThe Petitioner left the country on June 9, 2005, while under investigation on suspicion of fraud, reentered the country on November 22, 2011, and was indicted on April 30, 2012, on suspicion of fraud (Seoul Western District Court No. 2012GODAN837). On May 7, 2012, the Minister of Justice prohibited the Petitioner’s departure for a period of 6 months from May 7, 2012 to November 6, 2012, on the ground that the Petitioner was pending criminal trial, pursuant to Article 4(1)1 of the Immigration Control Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, on May 22, 2012, the Petitioner filed a lawsuit against the Minister of Justice in the Seoul Administrative Court seeking revocation of the above departure prohibition disposition (No. 2012GUHAP16466), and at the same time filed an application for a request for a constitutional review of laws concerning Article 4(1)1 of the Immigration Control Act, which provides that departure may be prohibited for a person pending criminal trial (Seoul Administrative Court No. 2012A1748). When this was dismissed on July 27, 2012, the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint in this case on August 21, 2012.\\n\\n2. Subject of Review\\nThe subject of review in this case is whether Article 4(1)1 of the Immigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10863 on July 18, 2011) is contrary to the Constitution, and its content is as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10863 on July 18, 2011)\\nArticle 4 (Prohibition of Departure) (1) The Minister of Justice may prohibit the departure of a national falling under any of the following subparagraphs for a period not exceeding 6 months.\\n1. A person pending criminal trial\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\nAlthough the prohibition of departure against a person pending criminal trial substantially constitutes a coercive measure in criminal procedure, the provision subject to review allows the Minister of Justice to arbitrarily prohibit departure without a warrant issued by a judge, and thus violates the constitutional principle of warrant requirement. While permitting the Minister of Justice to prohibit the departure of a defendant, who is one party to criminal procedure, upon the request of a prosecutor, who is the other party to criminal procedure, the provision subject to review does not provide for prior notice to the defendant or an opportunity for a hearing, and therefore also violates the constitutional principle of due process. Furthermore, the provision subject to review violates the constitutional principle of presumption of innocence by imposing the disadvantage of departure prohibition on a person whose guilt or innocence has not yet been finally determined and who is still pending criminal trial, and because departure is prohibited when there is evidence favorable to the person abroad, the collection and submission of evidence are fundamentally blocked, so that the Petitioner cannot engage in attack and defense on an equal footing with the prosecutor, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial and freedom to leave the country.\\n\\n4. Determination on Admissibility\\nSince the period of departure prohibition against the Petitioner had already expired after this constitutional complaint was filed, even if the Constitutional Court were to render a decision of unconstitutionality with respect to the provision subject to review, the Petitioner would no longer be able to obtain relief in the relevant case, and thus it is difficult to conclude that the Petitioner still has a protected interest in the relief of rights. However, as the essence of a constitutional complaint is not only the relief of individual rights but also the guarantee of the constitutional order, even if a constitutional complaint does not aid subjective relief of rights, the interest in adjudication may be recognized where there is a risk that such an act of infringement will be repeated, or where resolution of the relevant dispute is an essential matter for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order and its constitutional elucidation is of significant importance (see Constitutional Court Decision of Mar. 25, 2004, 2002HEONBA104, etc.).\\n\\nIn this case, whether the provision subject to review is unconstitutional is an important constitutional issue related to the freedom to leave the country among the freedom of residence and movement, and no clarification thereof has yet been made by the Constitutional Court. Furthermore, departure prohibition dispositions based on the provision subject to review are continuing to be made, so the same type of issue may repeatedly arise in the future. Accordingly, since its constitutional elucidation has significant importance for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, the interest in adjudication is exceptionally recognized.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\nA. Whether the warrant requirement is violated\\nArticle 12(3) of the Constitution declares the warrant requirement, and the warrant requirement is a principle derived from the due process principle of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, according to which, in relation to criminal procedure, coercive measures such as arrest, detention, seizure, and search must be based on a warrant issued by a judge whose status is guaranteed (see Constitutional Court Decisions of May 31, 2012, 2010HEONMA672; Dec. 27, 2012, 2010HEONMA153). However, a departure prohibition decision by the Minister of Justice under the provision subject to review is merely an administrative disposition that restricts the freedom to leave the country of a national pending criminal trial, and cannot be regarded as a coercive measure directly involving physical force against the body to which the warrant requirement applies. Therefore, the provision subject to review cannot be deemed to violate the warrant requirement under Article 12(3) of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Whether the due process principle is violated\\nSince the due process principle under Article 12 of the Constitution applies not only to criminal procedure but to all state action in general (see Constitutional Court Decision of July 24, 2003, 2001HEONGA25), even where, as in this case, the Minister of Justice restricts the freedom to leave the country by means of an administrative disposition against a person pending criminal trial, the constitutional due process principle must be observed. Among the important procedural requirements derivable from the due process principle are the giving of appropriate notice to the party and the granting of an opportunity to submit opinions and materials. However, the specific procedures and the extent to which they are required by this principle can only be determined on a case-by-case basis by comparing various factors such as the nature of the matter being regulated, the rights and interests of the relevant parties, the value to be enhanced by implementing the procedure, the efficiency of state action, the costs involved in the procedure, and opportunities for objection (see Constitutional Court Decisions of July 24, 2003, 2001HEONGA25; Oct. 4, 2007, 2006HEONBA91).\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues, in essence, that the provision subject to review violates the due process principle because it permits the prosecutor, who is one party in criminal procedure, to request departure prohibition against the defendant, while it does not even provide a rule on prior notice to a person pending criminal trial and thereby deprives such person of an opportunity for a hearing.\\n\\nThe departure prohibition decision under the provision subject to review is intended to prevent flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby secure the State’s power to punish, and thus requires speed and secrecy by its nature. However, if the Minister of Justice were required, when making a departure prohibition decision, to give prior notice to the person subject to departure prohibition or to conduct a hearing, it would be difficult to exclude the possibility that the person subject to departure prohibition might flee abroad before the decision in order to evade the State’s power to punish, and this would greatly risk hindering the achievement of the purpose of the departure prohibition system, namely securing the State’s power to punish. Furthermore, the Immigration Control Act provides that when the Minister of Justice has prohibited departure, written notice stating the grounds and period thereof shall be given immediately (Article 4-4(1)), thereby guaranteeing the relevant person subject to departure prohibition an opportunity to prepare a defense and to object, and it also guarantees sufficient opportunities for the person subject to departure prohibition to state opinions or submit materials through an objection or administrative litigation.\\n\\nAs such, since the person subject to departure prohibition is afforded an opportunity to later challenge the departure prohibition decision and is thereby guaranteed procedural participation, it is difficult to conclude that the provision subject to review violates the due process principle merely because it does not provide for prior notice to the person subject to departure prohibition or an opportunity for a hearing.\\n\\nC. Whether the presumption of innocence is violated\\nThe presumption of innocence provided in Article 27(4) of the Constitution means that a defendant or suspect must not be treated as a guilty person before a guilty judgment becomes final, thereby being subjected to tangible or intangible disadvantages in legal and factual respects. Here, disadvantages mean disadvantages as the effect of a finding of guilt, that is, disadvantages imposed on the basis of guilt by way of social reproach or other punitive discriminatory treatment (see Constitutional Court Decisions of May 26, 2005, 2002HEONMA699, etc.; Jan. 28, 2014, 2012HEONBA298).\\n\\nThe provision subject to review merely allows the Minister of Justice to prohibit departure when there is a risk that a person pending criminal trial may flee abroad in order to evade the State’s power to punish. Even if a defendant who is at risk of flight abroad suffers the disadvantage of being prohibited from departing for a certain period, it is difficult to regard this as the disadvantage as the effect of a finding of guilt that is prohibited by the presumption of innocence, namely an attempt to impose social reproach or punitive sanctions on a person pending criminal trial on the basis of guilt. Therefore, the provision subject to review cannot be deemed to violate the presumption of innocence.\\n\\nD. Whether the freedom to leave the country is infringed\\n(1) Standard of review\\nThe freedom of residence and movement under Article 14 of the Constitution is the freedom to freely determine one’s place of residence and sojourn without state interference, and it functions to increase the effectiveness of other fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution by promoting the enhancement of personality in all fields of life, such as politics, economy, society, and culture. The freedom of residence and movement includes the freedom of overseas travel and overseas emigration, namely the freedom to determine freely one’s place of sojourn and residence abroad, and this necessarily includes the freedom to leave the country in order to sojourn or reside in a foreign country, as well as the freedom to enter the country, namely the freedom to discontinue residence or sojourn abroad and return to the Republic of Korea (see Constitutional Court Decision of Oct. 28, 2004, 2003HEONGA18).\\n\\nBy providing that the Minister of Justice may prohibit departure for a period not exceeding 6 months against a person pending criminal trial, the provision subject to review restricts the freedom to leave the country, which is part of the freedom of residence and movement, and therefore must comply with the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution (see Constitutional Court Decision of Oct. 28, 2004, 2003HEONGA18).\\n\\n(2) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and appropriateness of means\\nThe provision subject to review, which seeks to realize the discovery of substantive truth and judicial justice by preventing flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby securing the State’s power to punish, has a legitimate legislative purpose, and allowing the departure of a person pending criminal trial to be prohibited for a certain period also contributes to achieving that legislative purpose, so the appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(3) Minimal impairment\\nAs non-detention investigations and trials have increased pursuant to the principle of investigation and trial without detention under the Criminal Procedure Act, the number of defendants who flee abroad while pending criminal trial is increasing every year, and as a result, obstacles to the realization of the State’s power to punish are arising, such as the trial proceedings being practically suspended and remaining as cases pending indefinitely, or enforcement of punishment becoming difficult. In such circumstances, where it is recognized as necessary to prevent flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial who is not in custody, it is necessary to permit departure prohibition for a certain period.\\n\\nThe Enforcement Rule of the Immigration Control Act provides basic principles for departure prohibition, stating that departure prohibition shall be imposed only within the minimum necessary scope, shall not be imposed merely for the convenience of official duties or for the purpose of imposing administrative sanctions on a person who has received criminal punishment or administrative punishment, and shall be imposed only when the person subject to departure prohibition is deemed to possess a valid passport (Article 6). It further requires the Minister of Justice, when deciding whether to prohibit departure for a person pending criminal trial, to consider such basic principles of departure prohibition, the criminal facts, age, family relations, and the possibility of flight abroad of the person subject to departure prohibition (Article 6-5(1)), and thus requires the Minister to determine whether to prohibit departure by examining concrete circumstances such as whether the defendant has ties or a business base abroad, and whether departure is frequent. Meanwhile, in order for the head of a relevant agency to request departure prohibition, the grounds for the request and the intended period of departure prohibition must be specified, and materials substantiating the fact that the person concerned is a person pending criminal trial and the grounds for the necessity of departure prohibition must also be attached (main text of Article 2(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act, Article 6-4(1) of the Enforcement Rule).\\n\\nIn practice as well, departure prohibition under the provision subject to review is operated in a very limited manner. In 2012, the number of non-detention defendants in criminal trial cases was 319,545, while the number of requests for departure prohibition under the provision subject to review was 734, and only 714 of those resulted in a departure prohibition decision.\\n\\nFurthermore, when the Minister of Justice has made a departure prohibition decision, absent special circumstances such as a risk of serious harm to national security or the public interest, the Minister must immediately notify the person concerned in writing of the grounds and period, etc. (Article 4-4(1) of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, a person whose departure has been prohibited may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against the departure prohibition decision within 10 days from the date on which the person was notified of the decision or from the date on which the person learned of the fact (Article 4-5(1)), and if the objection is dismissed, a means of obtaining relief of rights through administrative litigation is also provided. Of course, it is also possible to file administrative litigation directly without going through the objection procedure, and where it is recognized that there is an urgent necessity to prevent irreparable harm that would be caused by departure prohibition, there is also the possibility of departing after filing a revocation suit and obtaining a decision suspending the execution of the departure prohibition disposition.\\n\\nIn addition, the Minister of Justice must immediately lift departure prohibition when the grounds for departure prohibition have ceased to exist or when it is recognized that departure prohibition is no longer necessary (Article 4-3(1) of the Immigration Control Act), and if a citizen suffers damage because the head of the agency that requested departure prohibition does not request the Minister of Justice to lift departure prohibition even though the grounds therefor have ceased to exist, a claim for state compensation may also be made. The provision subject to review limits the period of departure prohibition against a person pending criminal trial so that, in principle, it may not exceed 6 months.\\n\\nSince various measures have been established to minimize the restriction of fundamental rights of a person pending criminal trial in this way, the provision subject to review does not violate the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\n(4) Balance of legal interests\\nThe disadvantage suffered by a person pending criminal trial due to the provision subject to review is the prohibition of departure for a certain period, whereas the public interest obtained through the provision subject to review is significant, namely realizing the discovery of substantive truth and judicial justice by preventing flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby securing the State’s power to punish. Accordingly, the balance of legal interests is also satisfied between the public interest sought to be achieved by the provision subject to review and the private interest being restricted.\\n\\n(5) Conclusion\\nThe provision subject to review does not infringe the Petitioner’s freedom to leave the country in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nE. Whether the right to a fair trial is infringed\\nThe right to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 27(1) of the Constitution includes the right to receive a trial in which the adversarial principle and oral argument principle are guaranteed so that the parties are sufficiently guaranteed the right to attack and defend, such as by responding to the charges and presenting proof and counterproof (see Constitutional Court Decisions of Apr. 28, 1994, 93HEONBA26; Nov. 25, 2010, 2009HEONBA57). The Petitioner argues, in essence, that the provision subject to review infringes the right to a fair trial by restricting the defense rights of the defendant, since it makes it difficult for the defendant to collect and submit evidence abroad where evidence favorable to the defense may exist. However, the provision subject to review merely allows the Minister of Justice to prohibit a defendant’s departure, and cannot be said to be directly related to the exercise of the defendant’s rights of attack and defense, nor can the right to a fair trial be understood as including the right to go abroad to collect evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that the provision subject to review restricts the defendant’s exercise of the rights of attack and defense and thereby infringes the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nSince the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, excluding the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Jung-mi and Justice Lee Jin-sung as set forth in 7. below.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Jung-mi and Justice Lee Jin-sung\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we believe that the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the Petitioner’s freedom to leave the country, and therefore state our opinion as follows.\\n\\nA. Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and appropriateness of means\\nAs stated by the majority opinion, the provision subject to review, which permits the prohibition of departure by a person pending criminal trial for a certain period, seeks to realize the discovery of substantive truth and judicial justice by preventing flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby securing the State’s power to punish, and thus its legislative purpose is legitimate, and the appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\nB. Minimal impairment\\nBecause the Minister of Justice’s departure prohibition decision restricts the freedom to leave the country, which is an important constitutional fundamental right that the people must enjoy for enhancement of personality through observation abroad and occupational activities, exchange of various information, and formation of personality free from cultural prejudice (see the dissenting opinion to Constitutional Court Decision of Oct. 28, 2004, 2003HEONGA18), it is necessary to permit it only for the minimum period in cases where it is unavoidable for securing the State’s power to punish.\\n\\nIn today’s world, where conducting economic activities or daily life across borders has become common, even a person pending criminal trial may have a need to depart, such as where the person has a main base of life or business base in a foreign country or must travel abroad for work, and there is ample room for different determinations as to whether departure should be prohibited depending on concrete circumstances such as the type and nature of the offense, the degree of reproach, the risk of flight abroad, etc. However, the provision subject to review allows departure to be prohibited merely on the ground that the person is pending criminal trial, and thus has the potential to excessively restrict the fundamental rights of a non-detention defendant for whom a strong need to depart is requested. This is even more so in the case of a non-detention defendant who frequently travels abroad for work, insofar as the person may suffer disadvantages that interfere with livelihood. Even in light of the statistics showing that the Minister of Justice’s approval rate for requests for departure prohibition against persons pending criminal trial exceeds 97%, it is difficult to conclude that the Minister of Justice considers the concrete circumstances of persons pending criminal trial when deciding whether to prohibit departure.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Immigration Control Act allows the period to be extended where it is recognized that departure prohibition must continue beyond the 6-month maximum period of departure prohibition (Article 4-2), but it does not impose any special limitation on the number of extensions. As a result, the Minister of Justice may repeatedly extend the period of departure prohibition without limitation on the number of times, thereby causing serious restrictions on the freedom to leave the country of a person pending criminal trial by prohibiting departure for periods ranging from as short as several months to as long as several years until a guilty or not guilty judgment becomes final.\\n\\nThe departure prohibition of a person pending criminal trial must be limited to the minimum necessary for the realization of the State’s power to punish. Specifically, other methods that are less restrictive of fundamental rights while still achieving the legislative purpose appear to be fully conceivable, such as: a measure of strictly prohibiting departure under explicit statutory additional requirements, such as where there is a high risk of flight abroad or where the person fails to appear on the trial date; a measure of prohibiting departure for a period not exceeding 1 month or limiting the number of extensions, as is done for persons whose departure is prohibited for criminal investigation purposes; a measure enabling prior judicial control, such as requiring the competent trial panel, which knows best about the relevant case, to submit its opinion on whether departure should be permitted by considering various circumstances such as the defendant’s charged facts, the possibility of destruction of evidence, the defendant’s attitude, the necessity of departure, and whether entry into the country is guaranteed; or a measure limiting departure prohibition to cases in which the defendant is indicted for a serious offense according to the gravity of the offense.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that relief of rights may be obtained through objection or administrative litigation, but the objection procedure prescribed in Article 4-5 of the Immigration Control Act is a self-remedy procedure by the Minister of Justice, who is the subject of the departure prohibition decision, and thus cannot be regarded as highly effective. In fact, in light of the fact that only 3 out of a total of 86 objections from 2010 through 2012 were granted, it can be seen that the possibility of relief through objection is slight. Furthermore, in the case of filing administrative litigation such as a suit to revoke a departure prohibition disposition, it cannot be excluded that dismissal may occur on the ground that the period of departure prohibition has elapsed during the litigation and that there is no standing to sue, because litigation takes a relatively long time; thus, this also cannot be regarded as an effective remedy.\\n\\nAccording to statistics, although cases of departure prohibition for criminal investigation account for more than half and constitute a high proportion, cases of departure prohibition on the ground that a person is pending criminal trial also account for 5 to 10% of the total number of departure prohibition cases, showing that the number is by no means small. As for foreign legislative examples, apart from methods such as refusal to issue a passport to a person suspected of a serious crime, surrender or invalidation of an issued passport, there are few legislative examples, like ours, in which the Minister of Justice decides departure prohibition for a person pending criminal trial.\\n\\nIf so, even a person pending criminal trial should, in principle, be guaranteed freedom to leave the country where the smooth progress of the trial can be ensured, and therefore the provision subject to review, which allows departure prohibition throughout the trial period, violates the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\nC. Balance of legal interests\\nThe provision subject to review imposes serious disadvantages amounting to interference with livelihood on persons pending criminal trial who must depart for work, and also restricts for a certain period the freedom to leave the country, which is an important constitutional fundamental right, for other persons pending criminal trial; thus, it excessively restricts the fundamental rights of persons pending criminal trial compared with the public interest of preventing flight abroad and ensuring the smooth progress of trials that the provision subject to review seeks to achieve. Accordingly, the provision subject to review also violates the principle of balance of legal interests.\\n\\nD. Conclusion\\nIf so, the provision subject to review violates the Constitution because it infringes the Petitioner’s freedom to leave the country in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction."}

{"[96HEONBA28]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject of Review\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) Case 96HEONBA28\\n\\nPetitioner Jeon ○ Hwan was arrested on 3 Dec. 1995 on charges including rebellion, and was indicted for the crimes of rebellion, insurrection, and violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes; Petitioner Jeong Ho-yong was arrested on 31 Jan. 1996 on suspicion of insurrection, and was indicted for the crimes of insurrection and violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes; and Petitioners Heo ○ Su and Heo ○ Pyeong were each arrested on 31 Jan. 1996 on suspicion of insurrection, and were indicted for the crimes of insurrection and rebellion, and the above cases were pending before the 30th Criminal Division of the Seoul District Court. In view of the progress of the proceedings in the above cases, the Petitioners filed a motion for a declaration of unconstitutionality as to whether Articles 70(1) and 73 of the former Criminal Procedure Act (as in force before amendment by Act No. 5054 of 29 Dec. 1995, hereinafter referred to as the “Act”), which are the provisions serving as the basis for the court’s ex officio issuance of warrants, violate Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which provides that “... when ... arresting or detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented,” on the ground that it was impossible to conclude the trial by the expiration dates of their respective detention periods (Petitioner Jeon Du-hwan: 2 June 1996; Petitioners Jeong Ho-yong, Heo Sam-su, and Heo Hwa-pyeong: 30 July 1996), and that, since the said court had already issued, on 15 May 1996, separate detention warrants against Petitioners I ○ Woo and No ○ Woo regarding criminal facts among the facts charged that were not stated in the detention warrant, it was expected that it would also issue, ex officio, detention warrants against them regarding the criminal facts among the facts charged that were not stated in the detention warrant. However, when the said court on 16 May 1996 dismissed each of the Petitioners’ motions for referral for a constitutional review, they filed this constitutional complaint adjudication on 27 May of the same month pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\n(2) Cases 96HEONBA31 and 96HEONBA32\\n\\nPetitioner I ○ Woo was arrested on 17 Nov. 1995, and Petitioner No ○ Woo on 16 Nov. of the same month, each on suspicion of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (acceptance of bribery), and each was indicted on 5 Dec. 1995 for the said crimes, etc. When the detention periods for the above Petitioners expired on 16 May 1996 and 15 May of the same month, respectively, after two renewals, the Presiding Judge of the 30th Criminal Division of the Seoul District Court issued, on 10 May 1996, detention warrants pursuant to Articles 70 and 73 of the Act with respect to the criminal facts among the facts charged against the above Petitioners other than those stated in the detention warrant. Accordingly, the above Petitioners filed a quasi-appeal against each detention warrant issued on 10 May 1996, and filed a motion for referral for a constitutional review with the 23rd Criminal Division of the Seoul District Court (96CHO1852, 1830) on the ground that Articles 70(1) and 73 of the Act, which served as the basis for the issuance of the above warrants, violate Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which provides that “when arresting, detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented,” but when the said court on 18 May 1996 dismissed each of the above Petitioners’ motions, they filed this constitutional complaint adjudication on 29 May of the same month pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nb. Subject of Review\\n\\nThe subject of review in this case is whether the phrase in Articles 70(1) and 73 of the Act, “a detention warrant shall be issued when ... arresting or detaining a defendant,” is in violation of the Constitution. The content of each of the above provisions is as follows [Although the Petitioners stated in the petitum of the petition for review that they sought a constitutional review of the entirety of Article 73 of the Act, in substance they are seeking review on the ground that the portion of the above provision relating to the detention (arrest, detention) of a defendant is unconstitutional, and thus the subject of review is determined as above].\\n\\nAct Article 70 (Grounds for Detention) ① The court may detain a defendant if there is a reasonable ground to suspect that the defendant has committed a crime and if any one of the following grounds exists.\\n\\n1. Where the defendant has no fixed residence\\n2. Where there is a risk that the defendant may destroy evidence\\n3. Where the defendant may flee or there is a risk that the defendant may flee\\n\\nAct Article 73 (Issuance of Warrant) A summons shall be issued when summoning a defendant, and a detention warrant shall be issued when arresting or detaining a defendant.\\n\\n2. The Petitioners’ Arguments and the Opinions of Interested Institutions\\n\\na. The Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\nThe main text of Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “when arresting, detaining, searching, or seizing, a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented in accordance with due process of law.” This is a provision intended to guarantee the fundamental rights of the people against unjust infringement of human rights by all public authority, including judges, and it therefore means not only that the warrant-issuing authority must be a judge and that no person may be subjected to arrest, detention, seizure, or search without a warrant, but also that a judge may issue a warrant only upon the prosecutor’s application. Our Constitution has provided the same purport since the Fifth Amendment Constitution of 26 Dec. 1962.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions subject to review in this case, which permit a court to issue a warrant even without the prosecutor’s application, are provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act enacted under the Constitution that had merely provided for “a judge’s warrant” with respect to the issuance of warrants, and have remained in force without being amended to conform to the above Fifth Amendment Constitution; they are therefore unconstitutional statutory provisions.\\n\\nb. Grounds for Dismissal of the Motion for Referral for Constitutional Review and Summary of the Opinion of the Chief Prosecutor of the Seoul District Prosecutors’ Office\\n\\nThe phrase in the main text of Article 12(3) of the Constitution, “... upon the prosecutor’s application ...,” clearly provides that, in order for arrest, detention, etc. to be carried out by an investigative agency, the procedure of an application by a prosecutor must be followed, and that no investigative agency other than a prosecutor may apply for the issuance of a detention warrant; it does not provide that the prosecutor’s application is required even in cases where a judge, at the trial stage, issues a warrant ex officio and detains a person. This is clear from the very nature of the warrant principle.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the provisions subject to review in this case are intended to ensure the defendant’s appearance in court, eliminate obstruction of the proceedings caused by flight and destruction of evidence, thereby making possible the collection and preservation of evidence for the discovery of the substantive truth, and realize the State’s punitive power specifically determined through the trial procedure, and thus do not violate the constitutional principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\na. Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “... when ... detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented ...,” and the above provision may literally be interpreted, as the Petitioners argue, as providing that the issuance of a detention warrant must always be preceded by an application by a prosecutor, regardless of whether it is the pretrial investigative stage or the trial stage. On the other hand, it may also be interpreted as providing that, in detaining a suspect at the investigative stage, a warrant must be obtained from a judge, and that at that time only a prosecutor among the investigative agencies may apply for the warrant. Which of the above interpretations accords with the purport of the Constitution will ultimately be determined in light of the essence of the warrant principle and the history of the adoption of the above constitutional provision.\\n\\nb. Article 12(1) of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall enjoy freedom of the person. No person shall be arrested, detained, searched, or interrogated except as provided by law, and no person shall be punished, subjected to security measures, or forced labor except as provided by law and through due process of law.” The first sentence of the above provision declares freedom of the person, and the second sentence provides that, where freedom of the person is infringed, the principle of due process must be observed.\\n\\nAlthough freedom of the person, together with freedom of thought, is the basis of all fundamental rights, it has historically often been infringed upon by the State, especially in the form of the exercise of punitive power. Therefore, after declaring the principle of due process in Article 12(1), the Constitution lists in Article 12(2) through (7) several principles of particular importance among those that may be derived from the principle of due process. Among them, Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which is the provision relevant to this case, declares the warrant principle by providing that “when arresting, detaining, searching, or seizing, a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented in accordance with due process of law....”\\n\\nThe warrant principle is the principle that, in relation to criminal procedure, coercive measures such as arrest, detention, and seizure may not be taken unless pursuant to a warrant issued by a judge whose status is guaranteed by judicial independence; therefore, the essence of the warrant principle lies in the fact that coercive measures infringing freedom of the person must be based only on a warrant issued, after concrete review, by a neutral judge.\\n\\nWhether at the investigative stage or at the trial stage, there will inevitably be cases where coercive measures such as detention cannot be avoided for the needs of investigation or trial. However, from the standpoint of the suspect or defendant subject to such coercive measures, a serious infringement of fundamental rights will occur. Therefore, the Constitution declares the warrant principle as a means of protecting the fundamental rights of the people from abuse of coercive measures. In particular, among coercive measures, in the case of coercive measures by investigative agencies, as opposed to those by the court, which has the status of a neutral adjudicator (the structure of criminal procedure in our country is, in principle, an adversarial structure; see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONMA44, decided on 30 Nov. 1995), the more public power is exercised overtly for the purpose of finding the offender and securing evidence, the greater the possibility of infringing the fundamental rights of the people. Thus, the significance of the warrant principle is great in that it prevents abuse of coercive measures by investigative agencies and promotes the protection of human rights through prior and judicial restraint by judges over rights infringements by investigative agencies (in this respect, the legal character of warrants issued ex officio by a court and detention warrants issued upon application by an investigative agency does not differ. That is, the former is understood to have the character of a command order, while the latter has the character of an authorization).\\n\\nc. However, Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “... when ... detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application ...,” as though the prosecutor’s application were required for the issuance of every detention warrant. Such a provision, with respect to the issuance of detention warrants, was not present in the original Constitution, which merely provided that “an arrest, detention, or search shall require a judge’s warrant” (Article 9), but was first introduced in the Fifth Amendment Constitution of 26 Dec. 1962 through the provision that “... when detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented” (main text of Article 10(3)). Although there are some differences in wording, the same content has continued through the current Constitution.\\n\\nThe reason why the Fifth Amendment Constitution added the requirement of a “prosecutor’s application” with respect to the issuance of detention warrants can be understood in connection with the amendment of the Criminal Procedure Act of 1 Sept. 1961.\\n\\nAt the time the Criminal Procedure Act was first enacted (Act No. 341 of 23 Sept. 1954), the provision concerning applications for warrants by investigative agencies stated that “where there is a reasonable ground to suspect that a suspect has committed a crime and there exists one of the grounds set forth in subparagraphs of Article 70(1), a prosecutor or judicial police officer may obtain a detention warrant from the competent district court judge and detain the suspect” (main text of Article 201(1)), thereby granting the power to apply for warrants not only to prosecutors but also to judicial police officers. However, by the amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act of 1 Sept. 1961 (Act No. 705), this was amended to provide that “where there is a reasonable ground to suspect that a suspect has committed a crime and there exists one of the grounds set forth in subparagraphs of Article 70(1), a prosecutor may obtain a detention warrant from the competent district court judge and detain the suspect” (main text of Article 201(1)), thereby limiting the person who may apply for a warrant to a prosecutor. This amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act was reflected in the constitutional amendment of 1962.\\n\\nAccordingly, the purport of the Fifth Amendment Constitution in adding the requirement of a “prosecutor’s application” with respect to the issuance of warrants was to establish the prosecutor’s power to direct investigations over other investigative agencies, and thereby to prevent the harmful effects of human rights violations arising from warrant applications by investigative agencies other than prosecutors, which had frequently occurred in the past. Therefore, it is reasonable to interpret the phrase “prosecutor’s application” in Article 12(3) of the current Constitution not as meaning that a prosecutor’s application is required for the issuance of every warrant, but as limiting the person who may apply for a warrant at the investigative stage to a prosecutor. In other words, the purport is to prevent indiscriminate applications for warrants by other investigative agencies and reduce the possibility of infringing the fundamental rights of the people by requiring that warrant applications at the investigative stage pass through a prosecutor, who is a legal expert.\\n\\nd. Taking a comprehensive view of the essence of the warrant principle and the history of Article 12(3) of the Constitution as discussed above, the warrant principle is derived from the provisions of Article 12(1) and (3) of the Constitution, and among them, the purport of Article 12(3) of the Constitution in providing that “... when ... detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application ...” is understood to lie in especially emphasizing the warrant principle at the investigative stage and at the same time limiting the person who may apply for a warrant at the investigative stage to a prosecutor (the constitutional basis for the issuance of warrants at the trial stage lies in Article 12(1) of the Constitution).\\n\\nOtherwise, interpreting the purport of Article 12(3) of the Constitution as requiring the prosecutor’s application even for the issuance of warrants at the trial stage would lead to the result that the investigative agency, which is the object of judicial restraint intended to protect freedom of the person, would control the judge, who is the subject of judicial restraint, and would rather run counter to the essence of the warrant principle.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court’s holding in Decision 96HEONMA256, decided on 28 Nov. 1996, that “after a prosecution is instituted in court, ... under the Criminal Procedure Act, the authority concerning the defendant’s detention belongs solely to the judge, and the prosecutor has no authority even similar to the prosecutor’s right to request a detention warrant in order to detain a suspect ...” was also to the same effect.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions subject to review in this case do not violate Article 12(3) of the Constitution, and they also do not appear to violate any other part of the Constitution.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since the portion of Articles 70(1) and 73 of the Act stating that “a detention warrant shall be issued when ... arresting or detaining a defendant” does not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as stated in the disposition, except for the separate opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyeong regarding the wording of the disposition in 5. below, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyeong Regarding the Wording of the Disposition\\n\\nI think that in the wording of the disposition, the phrase “The portion of Article 70(1) and 73 of the former Criminal Procedure Act (...) stating that ‘a detention warrant shall be issued when ... arresting or detaining a defendant’ does not violate the Constitution” should properly be replaced with “the petition is dismissed.”\\n\\nThe reason is that, as explained in detail in the separate opinions regarding the wording of the disposition in each of the cases of a constitutional complaint concerning Article 75(1)1 of the Military Criminal Act in 92HEONBA45, a constitutional complaint concerning Article 52(1)3 of the former Housing Construction Promotion Act in 93HEONBA62, a constitutional complaint concerning Article 62(3) of the former Tax Reduction and Exemption Regulation Act in 94HEONBA7·8 (consolidated), a constitutional complaint concerning Article 20(1) of the Special Measures Act on the Arrangement of Requisitioned Property in 95HEONBA22, and a constitutional complaint concerning Article 3 of the Small Claims Trial Act in 94HEONBA28, decided by our Court on 26 Oct. 1995, there is no need to issue, despite the absence of binding force under Article 75(7) and Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act, a decision of constitutionality. In this case, since the people have filed the petition alleging unconstitutionality, there is no need to state in the disposition the word “constitutional,” which was not even sought by the people, merely because the conclusion cannot be accepted, that is, because it is constitutional and thus has no practical effect.\\n\\n27 Mar. 1997."}

question: Bar Examination, 13th Session, Public Law Multiple-Choice Question 8. Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding the pardon system? (In case of dispute, according to precedents) (a) The President may grant amnesty, commutation of sentence, or restoration of rights as provided by law, and under the Act on the Pardon, etc., when general amnesty, general commutation of sentence, or general restoration of rights is granted, the consent of the National Assembly must be obtained. (b) Under the Act on the Pardon, etc., when the Minister of Justice submits to the President a recommendation for special amnesty, commutation of sentence for a specified person, and restoration of rights, it must undergo review by the Pardon Review Committee, and when the President grants special amnesty, commutation of sentence for a specified person, and restoration of rights, the consent of the National Assembly is not required. (c) Restoration of rights shall not be granted to a person whose execution of sentence has not yet been completed or who has not been exempted from execution. (d) Because an individual convict has no subjective right to demand special amnesty or commutation of sentence, there is no constitutional duty to act or statutory duty on the President, the Minister of Justice, etc. to grant special amnesty to, or commute the sentence of, a convict.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2005HEONMA111]": "1. Summary of the Case  \\nThe Petitioner, who is confined in Gwangju Prison, was sentenced by the Gwangju High Court on 1997. 9. 10. to imprisonment for 10 months, suspended for 2 years, for violation of the Act on the Regulation of Illegal Checks, etc., and the said sentence became final on 11. 25. of the same year. However, because there was a prior fact that a sentence of a fine of 2,000,000 won had been imposed on the Petitioner and had become final, on 1997. 9. 10. the Gwangju High Court separately sentenced the Petitioner to imprisonment for 6 years for the crime of forging an official document, etc.  \\nThe Petitioner, alleging that, according to Criminal Act Article 37 as amended by Act No. 7077 on 2004. 1. 20., even among several offenses for which judgments have not become final, if there is an offense for which a judgment imposing a fine has become final, one sentence is to be imposed, and thus it is a provision favorable to the defendant because it results in a lighter sentence than when separate sentences are imposed, but that it is not being applied to the Petitioner, whose judgment has already become final and who is serving a term of imprisonment, and asserting that the inaction of not taking measures such as legislation or special amnesty and commutation to relieve cases like the Petitioner violates Articles 11 and 13, etc. of the Constitution, filed the constitutional complaint in this case.\\n\\n2. Decision  \\na. Part of the petition concerning legislative inaction  \\nThe Constitutional Court’s jurisdiction over constitutional complaints concerning legislative inaction is, as established precedent of our Court, recognized only in a limited manner in cases where, although the Constitution expressly delegates legislation for the guarantee of fundamental rights, the legislature has failed to implement it, or in cases where, by constitutional interpretation, a specific person acquires a concrete fundamental right and thereby the State’s duty to act or duty to protect arises, yet the legislature has taken no legislative measures at all (Constitutional Court, 1998. 5. 28., 96HEONMA44, Reports 10-1, 687, 692, etc.).  \\nHowever, the status of a prisoner against whom a judgment imposing imprisonment, etc. has become final and that of a defendant whose sentence has not become final are different, and under Criminal Act Article 37 prior to its amendment by Act No. 7077 on 2004. 1. 20., there is no express constitutional legislative delegation requiring legislation to establish a system to relieve the Petitioner, who received separate sentences rather than one sentence because among several offenses for which judgments had not become final there was an offense for which a judgment imposing a fine had become final, nor can it be said, by constitutional interpretation, that the legislature’s duty to act or duty to protect the Petitioner’s fundamental rights through such legislation arose.  \\nTherefore, this part of the petition, premised on the existence of the legislature’s legislative duty, does not satisfy the requirements for a constitutional complaint concerning legislative inaction and is inadmissible.\\n\\nb. Constitutional complaint concerning inaction in special amnesty or commutation  \\nIn the case of a constitutional complaint against inaction by administrative power, it is permissible only where the subject of public power is specifically and concretely prescribed with a duty to act deriving from the Constitution, and on that basis the holder of a fundamental right may demand an administrative act, yet the subject of public power neglects that duty; therefore, a mere general allegation that one suffered harm because of inaction in violation of a duty would be an inadmissible constitutional complaint (Constitutional Court, 1991. 9. 16., 89HEONMA163, Reports 3, 505, 513; 2002. 12. 18., 2002HEONMA52, Reports 14-2, 904, 908; 2003. 6. 26., 2002HEONMA484, Reports 15-1, 802, 807, etc.).  \\nHowever, according to the Act on Amnesty, special amnesty and commutation for a specific person are effected only when the prosecutor who directed the execution of the sentence and the superintendent of the prison where the prisoner is confined report to the Prosecutor General, the Prosecutor General applies to the Minister of Justice for submission, the Minister of Justice submits it to the President, and the President acts thereon; thus, since an individual prisoner does not have a subjective right to demand special amnesty or commutation, there exists no duty to act or legal duty derived from the Constitution requiring the President, the Minister of Justice, etc. to grant the Petitioner special amnesty or commutation (see Constitutional Court, 1995. 3. 23., 93HEONMA12, Reports 7-1, 416, 422).  \\nAccordingly, the mere fact that the Petitioner was not granted special amnesty or commutation cannot be regarded as non-exercise of public power subject to constitutional adjudication; thus, this part of the petition fails to satisfy the requirements for a constitutional complaint concerning inaction by administrative power and is inadmissible.\\n\\n3. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, as the constitutional complaint in this case is entirely inadmissible and falls within a case where the defects cannot be cured, it is decided, pursuant to Article 72(3)4 of the Constitutional Court Act, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, to dismiss it, and the decision is rendered as follows.  \\n2005. 2. 22."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning the requirements for admissibility of an adjudication on a dispute over authority is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: The chairperson of the Agenda Adjustment Committee under the National Assembly Act does not fall under a state organ that may file an adjudication on a dispute over authority as prescribed by the Constitution and the Constitutional Court Act, and therefore legal capacity as a party in an adjudication on a dispute over authority is not recognized.
B: Under the current legal system, which contains no statutory provision permitting “third-party litigation standing” in an adjudication on a dispute over authority, a petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority filed by National Assembly members alleging that their right of consent was infringed in the conclusion of a contract that would become a burden on the State in addition to the budget is improper for lack of standing as petitioner.
C: A petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority may be filed only when the respondent’s disposition or omission has infringed, or presents a significant risk of infringing, the petitioner’s authority conferred by the Constitution or by law, and here “disposition” means only something of legal significance and must be an act that may specifically affect the petitioner’s legal status.
D: As a requirement for admissibility of a petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority, “omission” does not mean a mere de facto omission, but means failure to perform despite the existence of a constitutional or statutory duty to act.
E: Regardless of whether an act of a state organ constitutes the exercise of its independent power conferred on that state organ by the Constitution and laws, if such act of a state organ is subject to restrictions by another state organ, the possibility that the authority referred to in an adjudication on a dispute over authority is infringed may be recognized.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2004HEONRA3]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) On 2004. 11. 12., the Respondent Government submitted the Draft Act Amending the Act on Local Education Autonomy (hereinafter referred to as the “Autonomy Bill”) and the Draft Act Amending the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Grant Bill”), and these bills were referred to the National Assembly Education Committee on the 15th of the same month.\\n\\nThe stated purpose of the Autonomy Bill was to amend Article 39(1) of the then Act on Local Education Autonomy (hereinafter referred to as the “former Autonomy Act”), which provided that the State bear the expenses related to compulsory education and merely allowed local governments to bear part of the expenses for compulsory middle school education, so as to change the entities bearing the expenses related to compulsory education to the State and local governments.\\n\\nThe stated purpose of the Grant Bill was to re-adjust the support structure for local education finance in accordance with the full implementation of compulsory education for middle schools; specifically, ① to amend Article 11(1) of the then Local Education Subsidy Grant Act (hereinafter referred to as the “former Grant Act”), which provided that compulsory education expenses be covered by grant funds and transfers from local education grants and, with respect to teachers’ salaries at public schools other than compulsory education institutions, that local governments cover part thereof (provided that the Seoul Metropolitan Government cover the full amount) from transfers from the general account of the relevant local government, so as to cover compulsory education expenses with grant funds and transfers from the general account of local governments; and ② to amend Article 11(2) of the former Grant Act, which uniformly provided that an amount equivalent to 36/1,000 of the total local tax of the relevant city/province be appropriated as a transfer to the Special Account for Educational Expenses for the purpose of raising financial resources for education expenses, so as to distinguish between the Seoul Metropolitan Government and other local governments and, in the case of the former, to appropriate an amount equivalent to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax in the general account budget and transfer it to the Special Account for Educational Expenses.\\n\\n(2) On 2004. 11. 22., the Petitioner filed with the Constitutional Court a petition for an adjudication on a competence dispute, against the Respondent Government, seeking confirmation that ① the Respondent Government’s submission of the above amended bills (Article 39 of the Autonomy Bill, Articles 11(1) and 11(2) of the Grant Bill) and ② the laws amended thereby all infringe the Petitioner’s authority and are furthermore void, on the ground that the above amended bills violated Article 31(3) of the Constitution, which provides for the State’s bearing of expenses for compulsory education, Article 117(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees local autonomy, and Article 113(2) of the Local Autonomy Act, which guarantees sound management of local finances, thereby infringing or threatening to infringe the Petitioner’s autonomous fiscal authority.\\n\\n(3) The above amended bills submitted by the Respondent Government were each referred to the National Assembly Education Committee, placed on the agenda of the 7th Education Committee meeting of the 250th National Assembly (regular session), and underwent review reports and substitute debate; however, on 2004. 11. 25., at the 9th Education Committee meeting of the same National Assembly, it was resolved not to submit the above amended bills to the plenary session, but to adopt the corresponding amended bills (alternative bills) as committee bills, and on 2004. 12. 8., each was resolved in the plenary session of the National Assembly as committee bills, and on 2004. 12. 30., the partially amended Act on Local Education Autonomy (amended by Act No. 7252, hereinafter referred to as the “Act on Local Education Autonomy”) and the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act (amended by Act No. 7251, hereinafter referred to as the “Grant Act”) were promulgated, respectively.\\n\\n(4) Accordingly, on 2005. 4. 4., the Petitioner applied to amend the subject of the instant petition so that the “Respondent Government” be corrected to “the Respondent Government and the National Assembly,” stating that the subject of the instant adjudication petition includes not only the Respondent Government’s submission of the above amended bills but also the above amended laws resulting therefrom, and the Constitutional Court granted this on the 11th of the same month.\\n\\nB. Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject of adjudication in this case is whether ① the Respondent Government’s act of submitting the Autonomy Bill and the Grant Bill to the 250th National Assembly (regular session) on 2004. 11. 12. infringes the Petitioner’s authority and, furthermore, is void; and whether ② the Respondent National Assembly’s provision in Article 39(1) of the Act on Local Education Autonomy (Act No. 7252) that the State and local governments shall bear the expenses related to compulsory education, the provision in Article 11(1) of the Grant Act (Act No. 7251) that compulsory education expenses shall be covered by grant funds and transfers from the general account of local governments, and the provision in Article 11(2) 3 that, distinguishing between the Seoul Metropolitan Government and other local governments, in the case of the Seoul Metropolitan Government, an amount equivalent to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax shall be appropriated in the general account budget and transferred to the Special Account for Educational Expenses, infringes the Petitioner’s authority and, furthermore, is void.\\n\\nThe contents of the relevant provisions and related provisions of the Act on Local Education Autonomy and the Grant Act are as follows.\\n\\nAct on Local Education Autonomy, Article 39 (Expenses for Compulsory Education, etc.) ① Salaries of teachers engaged in compulsory education and other expenses related to compulsory education shall be borne by the State and local governments in accordance with the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act.\\n② Expenses related to education other than compulsory education under paragraph (1) shall be borne by the State, local governments, and parents, etc. in accordance with the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act.\\n\\nSupplementary Provisions\\nThis Act shall enter into force on January 1, 2005.\\n\\nGrant Act, Article 11 (Burden of Local Governments) ① Expenses required for education and academic affairs in cities and provinces shall be borne by the Special Account for Educational Expenses of the relevant local government; provided, however, that expenses related to compulsory education shall be covered by grant funds and transfers from the general account under paragraph (2) among the financial resources of the Special Account for Educational Expenses, and expenses related to education other than compulsory education shall be covered by grant funds, transfers from the general account under paragraph (2), tuition fees, admission fees, etc. among the financial resources of the Special Account for Educational Expenses.\\n② For the establishment, operation, and improvement of the educational environment of public schools, each city/province shall appropriate the following amounts in the general account budget for each fiscal year and transfer them to the Special Account for Educational Expenses. The same shall apply where there is an increase or decrease by means of a supplementary budget.\\n1. An amount corresponding to the local education tax under Article 260-3 of the Local Tax Act\\n2. An amount corresponding to 45/100 of the tobacco consumption tax (excluding provinces)\\n3. The Seoul Metropolitan Government: an amount corresponding to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax (excluding the amount corresponding to a purpose tax under Article 6(1) 2 of the Local Tax Act), metropolitan cities and Gyeonggi Province: an amount corresponding to 5/100 of the total metropolitan city tax or provincial tax (excluding the amount corresponding to a purpose tax under Article 6(2) 2 of the Local Tax Act), and other provinces: an amount corresponding to 36/1,000 of the total provincial tax\\n\\nSupplementary Provisions\\n① (Effective Date) This Act shall enter into force on January 1, 2005.\\n② (Term of Validity) The amended provisions of Articles 3 and 11 shall remain effective until December 31, 2006.\\n\\n2. The Grounds for the Petitioner’s Petition and the Respondents’ Answers\\n\\nA. Grounds for the Petition\\n\\n(1) Although our Constitution does not expressly state so, the entity that bears the cost of compulsory education is, of course, the State, and since the establishment of the Republic of Korea, educational finance policy has been consistently maintained on that premise. The former Autonomy Act and the former Grant Act, amended on 2001. 12. 19., also, under the principle that the State bears the salaries of teachers engaged in compulsory education institutions (main text of Article 39(1) of the former Autonomy Act), merely provided that, until December 31, 2004, part of the expenses related to compulsory middle school education would temporarily be borne by local governments (proviso to Article 39(1) of the former Autonomy Act, Supplementary Provisions 2 and 3).\\n\\nAccordingly, even though the State should naturally bear the salaries of middle school teachers from 2005. 1. 1., when compulsory middle school education is fully implemented, the Respondents, through the Act on Local Education Autonomy and the Grant Act, are causing local governments continuously to bear all or part of the salaries of middle school teachers, which are expenses for compulsory education; this violates Article 31(3) of the Constitution concerning the compulsory education system, Article 117(1) of the Constitution concerning the guarantee of local autonomy, and the provisions and spirit of the education-related statutes.\\n\\nIn addition, the Grant Act distinguishes between the Seoul Metropolitan Government and other local governments and, only in the case of the former, requires that an amount equivalent to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax be appropriated in the general account budget and transferred to the Special Account for Educational Expenses; this violates the principle of equality.\\n\\nIf the salaries of teachers at middle schools, which are compulsory education institutions, are forcibly borne by transfers from the general account, the Petitioner will, to that extent, be constrained in autonomously budgeting for the welfare of residents.\\n\\n(2) As the主体 of education, the State not only exercises substantive plenary authority over major educational policies such as the establishment of secondary schools and the curriculum and content of education, but also, since the legal status of teachers at national and public schools is that of national public officials, the State should naturally bear the salaries of such teachers.\\n\\nEven in the 1960s, when national finances were poor, the State adhered to the principle that teachers at compulsory education institutions should be salaried by the State and also bore one-half of the salaries of teachers at non-compulsory education institutions. The fact that, even after the national budget has increased beyond comparison and after secondary schools were completely converted to compulsory education after 2005, the State will not bear the salaries of teachers at compulsory education institutions is contrary to the spirit of the Constitution and to the consistent educational policy of the past 50 years.\\n\\n(3) The Respondent Government’s act of submitting the bills and the laws amended thereby infringe the Petitioner’s autonomous fiscal authority granted by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act, and are void.\\n\\nB.
