{"[2020HEONMA1614]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. The Petitioner held the office of Prosecutor General from 2019. 7. 25. to 2021. 3. 4. The Minister of Justice, while the Petitioner was serving as Prosecutor General, filed a disciplinary request against the Petitioner with the Prosecutors Disciplinary Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Disciplinary Committee”) on 2020. 11. 24.\\n\\nb. Accordingly, the Petitioner filed the present constitutional complaint on 2020. 12. 4., alleging that Article 5(2) items 2 and 3 of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act, which provide that the Minister of Justice shall designate and appoint, respectively, two prosecutors, one attorney-at-law, one law professor, and one person with abundant learning and experience from among the members of the Disciplinary Committee, infringe the right to hold public office, etc. insofar as they apply to the discipline of a prosecutor who is the Prosecutor General.\\n\\nc. Thereafter, the Disciplinary Committee resolved on 2020. 12. 16. to suspend the Petitioner for 2 months, and the President, upon the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, imposed a 2-month suspension on the Petitioner on 2020. 12. 17. (hereinafter referred to as the “disciplinary disposition at issue”). On 2020. 12. 17., the Petitioner instituted an action for revocation against the disciplinary disposition at issue (Seoul Administrative Court 2020GUHAP88541) and at the same time filed an application for a stay of execution (Seoul Administrative Court 2020A13601). On 2020. 12. 24., there was an order staying the effect of the disciplinary disposition at issue until the date 30 days after the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment in the above revocation action, and the above order became final and conclusive. The Petitioner resigned from the office of Prosecutor General on 2021. 3. 4.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe Petitioner seeks a decision that “Article 5(2) items 2 and 3 of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act are unconstitutional insofar as they apply to the discipline of a prosecutor who is the Prosecutor General.” The rank of prosecutors is divided into the Prosecutor General and prosecutors (see Article 6 of the Prosecutors’ Office Act), and disciplinary deliberation begins when, with respect to a prosecutor other than the Prosecutor General, the Prosecutor General, and with respect to the Prosecutor General, the Minister of Justice, respectively, files a disciplinary request with the Disciplinary Committee (see Article 7(1) and (3) of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act). In light of the above system, Article 5(2) items 2 and 3 of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act concerning the composition of the Disciplinary Committee can also be divided into “the part concerning the case where the person subject to disciplinary suspicion is the Prosecutor General” and “the part concerning the case where the person subject to disciplinary suspicion is a prosecutor other than the Prosecutor General.” Since the Petitioner challenges the constitutionality of the former part, the relevant parts of Article 5(2) items 2 and 3 of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act are designated as the subject matter of adjudication.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 5(2) of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act was amended by Act No. 17500 on 2020. 10. 20., but since the amended provision came into force on 2021. 1. 21. (see Article 1 of the Addenda to the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act [Act No. 17500 of 2020. 10. 20.]), the provision applied to the disciplinary procedure against the Petitioner conducted before that date is the pre-amendment provision. Accordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the relevant parts concerning the case where the person subject to disciplinary suspicion is the Prosecutor General among Article 5(2) items 2 and 3 of the former Prosecutors Disciplinary Act (amended by Act No. 9817 of 2009. 11. 2. and before amendment by Act No. 17500 of 2020. 10. 20.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Prosecutors Disciplinary Act”) infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights. The provisions subject to adjudication and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Adjudication]\\nFormer Prosecutors Disciplinary Act (amended by Act No. 9817 of 2009. 11. 2. and before amendment by Act No. 17500 of 2020. 10. 20.)\\nArticle 5 (Duties of the Chairperson and Term of Office of Members, etc.) ② Members shall be the following persons:\\n2. Two prosecutors designated by the Minister of Justice\\n3. One person each commissioned by the Minister of Justice from among attorneys-at-law, law professors, and persons with abundant learning and experience\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nFormer Prosecutors Disciplinary Act (amended by Act No. 9817 of 2009. 11. 2. and before amendment by Act No. 17500 of 2020. 10. 20.)\\nArticle 4 (Prosecutors Disciplinary Committee) ① A Prosecutors Disciplinary Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Committee”) shall be established in the Ministry of Justice to deliberate disciplinary cases.\\n② The Committee shall consist of 7 members, including 1 chairperson, and 3 alternate members shall be appointed.\\nArticle 5 (Duties of the Chairperson and Term of Office of Members, etc.) ① The Minister of Justice shall serve as the chairperson.\\n② Members shall be the following persons:\\n1. Vice Minister of Justice\\n④ The term of office of the member under paragraph (2) item 3 shall be 3 years.\\n\\nProsecutors Disciplinary Act (as amended by Act No. 12585 of 2014. 5. 20.)\\nArticle 7 (Request for and Commencement of Discipline) ① The Committee’s disciplinary deliberation shall begin upon a request by the Prosecutor General.\\n③ Discipline against a prosecutor who is the Prosecutor General and the imposition of an additional disciplinary charge under Article 7-2 (hereinafter referred to as “discipline, etc.”) shall be requested by the Minister of Justice.\\n\\nProsecutors Disciplinary Act (as amended by Act No. 16312 of 2019. 4. 16.)\\nArticle 18 (Decision on Discipline) ① Upon completion of deliberation on the case, the Committee shall decide on discipline by a majority vote of the members present.\\n③ Where the Committee deems that there is a ground for discipline but that it is appropriate not to impose a disciplinary disposition, it may render a decision of taking no action (non-mention).\\n\\nProsecutors Disciplinary Act (amended by Act No. 9817 of 2009. 11. 2.)\\nArticle 21 (Decision of No Grounds for Discipline) When the Committee decides that there is no ground for discipline, it shall conclude the case and notify the person subject to disciplinary suspicion and the requester of discipline thereof.\\nArticle 23 (Execution of Discipline) ① Execution of discipline shall be carried out, in the case of a reprimand, by the Prosecutor General, Chief of the High Prosecutors’ Office, or Chief of the District Prosecutors’ Office to which the prosecutor who received the disciplinary disposition belongs, and, in the case of dismissal, removal, suspension, or salary reduction, by the President upon the recommendation of the Minister of Justice.\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nThe provisions subject to adjudication, by providing that the Minister of Justice, who requested discipline against the Prosecutor General, may designate and appoint a majority of the members of the Disciplinary Committee, enable the Prosecutor General to be unfairly deprived of his office under a state in which the fairness and appropriateness of the disciplinary procedure are not ensured; accordingly, they infringe the right to hold public office, etc. in violation of the principle of due process.\\n\\n4. Judgment\\n\\na. Requirement of Directness and Exception\\n\\nFor a statutory provision itself to be the subject of a constitutional complaint, the Petitioner’s fundamental rights must be infringed directly, presently, and personally by that statutory provision without awaiting any concrete act of execution. The directness of the infringement of fundamental rights referred to here means a case in which restriction of freedom, imposition of duties, or deprivation of rights or legal status occurs by the statutory provision itself, without any act of execution; thus, where the legal effect of infringement of fundamental rights arises only through a concrete act of execution based on the statutory provision in question, there is no directness (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2002HEONMA563; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29. 2005HEONMA165 et al.).\\n\\nHowever, where the content of the statutory provision is univocal and clear so that it directly alters the legal relations of the people even before any act of execution, or the legal status is already fixed to the extent that it cannot be affected by the existence or content of the act of execution, or where there is no remedy procedure targeting the act of execution, or even if such a remedy procedure exists, there is no reasonable prospect of relief and it would amount only to imposing an unnecessary detour on the Petitioner who has suffered an infringement of fundamental rights, the statutory provision itself may be made the subject of a constitutional complaint even if a concrete act of execution is contemplated (see Constitutional Court 2010. 7. 29. 2009HEONMA51; Constitutional Court 2014. 3. 27. 2012HEONMA606).\\n\\nb. Existence of a Concrete Act of Execution\\n\\nThe provisions subject to adjudication regulate matters concerning the composition of the Disciplinary Committee, which is a state organ. However, organizational norms that prescribe the basic structure and scope of duties of a state organ or body, in principle, do not designate the general public as addressees other than the members of that organization or persons who are to become members thereof; therefore, it cannot be said that the fundamental rights of the general public are directly infringed by such organizational norms (see Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29. 2005HEONMA165 et al.; Constitutional Court 2013. 11. 28. 2007HEONMA1189 et al.).\\n\\nEven in the case of the provisions subject to adjudication, the fundamental rights infringement alleged by the Petitioner does not arise directly from the provisions themselves, but arises only when the Disciplinary Committee constituted by the provisions subject to adjudication actually renders a disciplinary decision against the Petitioner (see Article 18(1) of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act) and, subsequently, when a concrete act of execution, namely a disciplinary disposition such as dismissal, removal, suspension, etc. effected by the President upon the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, occurs (see Article 23(1) of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act). Thus, directness is lacking.\\n\\nc. Whether the Case Falls within an Exception to Directness\\n\\n(1) Among the members of the Disciplinary Committee, the 3 members commissioned by the Minister of Justice have a term of office of 3 years (see Article 5(4) of the former Prosecutors Disciplinary Act), so members of the Disciplinary Committee are not newly designated and commissioned for each disciplinary case. Therefore, there may be cases where the Minister of Justice, who requested discipline against a specific Prosecutor General, does not designate and commission a majority of the members of the Disciplinary Committee that renders the disciplinary decision against that Prosecutor General. In addition, the Disciplinary Committee may render a decision of no grounds for discipline or a decision of taking no action against the Prosecutor General in question (see Articles 21 and 18(3) of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act).\\n\\nAccordingly, it cannot be said that the provisions subject to adjudication correspond to a case in which the legal relationship of the Petitioner is directly altered or the legal status is fixed already before any disciplinary disposition such as dismissal, removal, or suspension is imposed.\\n\\n(2) Disciplinary dispositions such as dismissal, removal, or suspension are subject to an administrative litigation for revocation, and the Petitioner instituted an action for revocation against the disciplinary disposition at issue on 2020. 12. 17., which remains pending as of the date of the pronouncement of this decision.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that there is no remedy procedure against the act of execution or that such remedy procedure affords no reasonable prospect of relief, thereby forcing an unnecessary detour upon the Petitioner.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the instant constitutional complaint is improper and is thus decided as ordered. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae set forth in section 6 below.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, I believe that the instant constitutional complaint satisfies the procedural requirements, including legal relevance for infringement of fundamental rights, and should proceed to a decision on the merits; thus, I set forth the following dissenting opinion.\\n\\na. Premise for Determining Legal Relevance of Infringement of Fundamental Rights\\n\\nA constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act is a procedure for relieving “a person whose constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power.” The legal relevance of the infringement of fundamental rights, namely self-relatedness, presentness, and directness, which are procedural requirements for a constitutional complaint, is a legal evaluation of the causal connection between the “exercise or non-exercise of public power” subject to adjudication and the “infringement of constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights” alleged by the Petitioner. Accordingly, it must be determined by considering the nature of the exercise or non-exercise of public power at issue in the case, the protective scope of the constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights, and the characteristics of the situation in which the infringement is alleged.\\n\\nb. Exercise of Public Power and Situation of Infringement of Constitutionally Guaranteed Fundamental Rights in This Case\\n\\nIn this case, the “exercise of public power” is the statutory provision that provides that the Minister of Justice shall designate or commission the members of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Committee that deliberates disciplinary cases against the Prosecutor General. The provisions subject to adjudication bear the character of an “organizational norm” in that they prescribe the composition of the body called the Disciplinary Committee.\\n\\nOrganizational norms that prescribe the basic structure and scope of duties of a state organ or body, in principle, do not designate the general public as addressees other than the members of that organization or persons who are to become members thereof; and they do not, by themselves, restrict the fundamental rights of the people, but whether the fundamental rights of the general public are infringed is determined when the organization or body established pursuant thereto concretely exercises its authority. Accordingly, the Constitutional Court has often held that constitutional complaint petitions targeting organizational norms are improper for lack of directness of infringement of fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 1994. 6. 30. 91HEONMA162; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29. 2005HEONMA165 et al.; Constitutional Court 2013. 11. 28. 2007HEONMA1189 et al.; Constitutional Court 2019. 11. 28. 2017HEONMA1356 et al.).\\n\\nHowever, this is merely the result of determining, in a concrete constitutional complaint case, the causal connection between the provisions subject to adjudication, which are evaluated as organizational norms, and the situation of infringement of fundamental rights alleged by the Petitioner, under the requirement of directness of infringement of fundamental rights. The mere fact that a certain norm appears to have the character of an organizational norm does not mean that directness of the resultant infringement of fundamental rights can be denied without examining the nature of the act by the body established pursuant thereto exercising its authority, the existence and effectiveness of remedies against it, and the situation of infringement of fundamental rights arising from such exercise of authority.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court has recognized directness of infringement of fundamental rights even with respect to a provision concerning the appointment procedure of a special prosecutor, in constitutional complaint cases filed by reference persons or accused persons in an investigation-targeted case under the special prosecutor system, which is limited to a specific case against a specific person. This was because, under the requirement of directness, it was determined that there was no remedy procedure against the concrete acts of execution, namely designation as a reference person or suspect of the special prosecutor and an order to accompany, or that there was no reasonable prospect of relief through such procedure. On the merits, the Court examined whether requiring the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court to recommend two candidates for special prosecutor violated the principle of due process, and whether allowing the National Assembly to decide on the introduction of the special prosecutor system and allowing the President to appoint one of the persons recommended by the Chief Justice during the appointment process violated the principle of separation of powers, thereby determining whether the petitioners’ fundamental rights were infringed (see Constitutional Court 2008. 1. 10. 2007HEONMA1468).\\n\\nUnder the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act, the Disciplinary Committee exists and acts solely for deliberating disciplinary cases against prosecutors, and the subject matter of adjudication in this case is further limited to the case of the Disciplinary Committee for discipline against the Prosecutor General. In addition, the purpose of the formation of the Disciplinary Committee is to secure fairness in the disciplinary procedure, and the content regulated by the provisions subject to adjudication also concerns the procedure for composing the Disciplinary Committee. Thus, although the provisions subject to adjudication in this case have, at first glance, the character of an “organizational norm,” in substantive terms they have a strong character as a “procedural norm” concerning discipline of a Prosecutor General. The exercise of public power subject to adjudication in this case has the character of a “norm that determines the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure for public officials.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the “situation of infringement of constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights” alleged by the Petitioner concerns, within the protective scope of the “right to hold public office” under Article 25 of the Constitution, the prohibition of “unfair deprivation of public official status or unfair suspension of authority (duties).” Such protective scope is closely related to the guarantee of the status and political neutrality of public officials under Article 7(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nAccordingly, whether the petition for adjudication in this case satisfies the requirement of legal relevance for infringement of fundamental rights should be determined on the basis of the characteristics of the norm that determines the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure for public officials and the characteristics of the protective scope of the right to hold public office, understood in relation to Article 7(2) of the Constitution, which guarantees the status and political neutrality of public officials.\\n\\nc. Characteristics of the Norm Determining the Subjects Involved in the Disciplinary Procedure\\n\\n(1) Constitutional Provisions Concerning the Disciplinary Procedure\\n\\nThe constitutional provisions that prescribe status-related disadvantages of public officials in connection with discipline include Article 64 of the Constitution concerning members of the National Assembly and Article 106 concerning judges. Article 64(2) provides that “The National Assembly shall examine the qualifications of its members and may discipline its members.” Paragraph (3) provides that “To expel a member, the approval of at least two-thirds of the members of the National Assembly shall be required,” and paragraph (4) provides that “No action may be brought before a court with respect to the disposition under paragraphs (2) and (3).” Article 106(1) provides that “Judges shall not be removed from office except by impeachment or a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, and shall not be subject to suspension, reduction in salary, or any other unfavorable disposition except by disciplinary action.”\\n\\n(2) Character of a Self-Correcting Mechanism within Separated Powers\\n\\nThe disciplinary procedure that holds a public official accountable through a status-related disadvantage for misconduct within or outside of duty is envisaged, under the Constitution, as a “self-correcting mechanism within separated powers.” The discipline of members of the legislative branch, namely members of the National Assembly, is handled by the National Assembly, and the discipline of judges, who are members of the judiciary, is handled by the courts. With respect to disciplinary dispositions against members of the National Assembly, recourse to court is barred, thereby clarifying its character as an internal procedure of the legislative branch. As to judges, the Constitution provides that, unless there is a removal from office that deprives them of their status itself, no unfavorable disposition may be imposed except by disciplinary action. Since this is intended to guarantee the independence of judges in terms of status, it must be taken as a premise that disciplinary dispositions against judges are likewise internal procedures of the judiciary.\\n\\nSince disciplinary procedures are procedures within separated powers, the subjects participating in them, in principle, are also members inside the institution to which the public officials subject to discipline belong. Discipline of members of the National Assembly is effected by resolution of the National Assembly, and discipline of judges also follows procedures internal to the court organization. The reason why disciplinary procedures under statutes are closely related to the exercise of personnel authority within an institution is also that disciplinary procedures are internal procedures of an institution and, at the same time, concern disadvantages in status for its members.\\n\\nOn the other hand, where the Constitution requires that an action imposing a status-related disadvantage on a public official function as “checks among separated powers” beyond a “self-correcting mechanism within separated powers,” it strictly limits the requirements and procedures for its application. For qualification review and discipline of members of the National Assembly, recourse to court is barred, thereby excluding even post hoc judicial review. Removal from office that results in loss of the status of a judge is limited to impeachment requiring a resolution of the National Assembly and adjudication by the Constitutional Court, or to a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment to which the principle of nulla poena sine lege and criminal procedure apply.\\n\\nThis projects the constitutional principle of separation of powers onto the status relations of public officials constituting state organs. If, while aiming at checks among separated powers, one follows a disciplinary procedure that departs from the strict requirements and procedural limits prescribed by the Constitution and instead resembles an internal self-correcting mechanism whose grounds and dispositions allow relatively broad discretion, one cannot exclude the possibility that one power may arbitrarily intrude into the internal affairs of another power separated by the Constitution, thereby undermining the principle of separation of powers.\\n\\n(3) Mechanisms for Preventing Arbitrary Exercise of Disciplinary Power and Their Limits\\n\\nBecause a disciplinary procedure, by its nature as an internal procedure, necessarily involves a superior in office exercising authority over a subordinate and imposes a status-related disadvantage on the public official concerned, it exerts a kind of coercive influence over the methods and content of the public official’s performance of duties.\\n\\nTherefore, since disciplinary procedures entail the risk that the subject participating in the procedure may arbitrarily exercise authority, mechanisms to prevent such risk must be established. The principle of due process applies as a premise for disadvantageous dispositions against public officials subject to discipline, judicial relief must be available after the fact in the case of public officials other than members of the National Assembly, and, as in the provisions subject to adjudication, involving external members to a certain extent in disciplinary procedures can be regarded as a mechanism for preventing arbitrary exercise of disciplinary authority.\\n\\nHowever, involving persons from outside the institution in the disciplinary procedure must not go so far as to change the very character of the procedure as an internal institutional procedure, beyond merely preventing arbitrariness in the exercise of disciplinary authority. If the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure belong to another power separated by the Constitution from the institution in question, or are placed under its substantial influence, and such involvement determines the disciplinary deliberation and decision, then the resulting discipline may function as a means of checks among separated powers beyond the limits of an internal self-correcting mechanism, and the risk may arise that the constitutional requirements and procedural limits envisaged for that means are exceeded.\\n\\n(4) Problems with the Provisions Subject to Adjudication in This Case\\n\\nThe disciplinary procedure concerning the Prosecutor General at issue in this case also bears the character of a self-correcting mechanism within the executive branch for public officials belonging to the executive branch, and the authority for the final disciplinary disposition belongs to the President, who has the personnel authority over the Prosecutor General. The Minister of Justice’s involvement in the disciplinary procedure, such as requesting discipline against the Prosecutor General and designating or commissioning disciplinary members in accordance with the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act, also means that, as the head of an administrative ministry under Article 94 of the Constitution and in accordance with Article 66(4), he assists the President by carrying out the affairs under his jurisdiction, and its basis lies in the supervisory function over prosecution affairs, which are among the matters under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice.\\n\\nThe point that requires constitutional examination with respect to the provisions subject to adjudication in this case, which determine the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure, is whether, in that the Minister of Justice thus designated has the authority to designate or commission internal or external members of the institution who are also subjects participating in the procedure, there exists a risk that such “position of the Minister of Justice” may not be limited to merely carrying out the affairs under his jurisdiction as the head of an administrative ministry.\\n\\nd. Guarantee of Political Neutrality of Public Officials and the Protective Scope of the Right to Hold Public Office\\n\\n(1) Purpose of Guaranteeing the Status and Political Neutrality of Public Officials\\n\\n(A) The process of express constitutional codification\\n\\nArticle 25 of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall have the right to hold public office under the conditions as prescribed by Act.” The right to hold public office and the guarantee of public officials’ responsibility and their status and political neutrality under Article 7 of the Constitution are closely related to each other in light of the history of constitutional enactment and amendment and the constitutional system.\\n\\nThe Constitution as enacted in 1948 provided in Article 26 of Chapter II, Rights and Duties of Citizens, that “All citizens shall have the right to hold public office under the conditions as prescribed by Act.” It then provided in Article 27 that “Public officials are agents of the sovereign people and shall at all times be responsible to the people. The people shall have the right to petition for the removal of public officials who commit illegal acts. A person who suffers damage due to illegal acts committed by a public official in the performance of official duties may claim compensation from the State or a public entity. Provided, that this shall not exempt the public official from his or her own civil or criminal liability.” In other words, at the time of the establishment of the Constitution, the right to hold public office and the responsibility relating to official duties were provided by placing them on both sides of rights and responsibilities.\\n\\nOn the premise of such a structure, the Constitution as amended for the third time in 1960 newly inserted into Article 27(2), which concerned public officials’ responsibility, the provision that “The political neutrality and status of public officials shall be guaranteed as prescribed by law.” The “Statement of Reasons for the Proposed Amendment to the Constitution” at that time stated that “This amendment proposal contains, in addition to thorough guarantees of the people’s fundamental rights, a parliamentary cabinet system as the structure of power.” It then explained “recognition of the Cabinet’s power to dissolve the National Assembly in response to a vote of no confidence by the National Assembly’s lower house against the Government” and “placing provisions concerning political parties in the Constitution,” and as principal contents of the “guarantee of the people’s fundamental rights” listed, among others, “lowering the voting age to 20,” “making the political neutrality and status of public officials guaranteed by law,” “deleting the provisions in Chapter II of the Constitution concerning the ‘reservation by law’ that could be abused by the executive and regulating them exceptionally by Article 28,” “prohibiting, even by statute, censorship and licensing of speech and publication and licensing of assembly and association,” “prohibiting the limitation of the essential content of rights even where the people’s rights are restricted by statute,” and “establishing provisions concerning political parties and, regardless of whether a party is in government or opposition, ensuring their constitutional guarantee, while providing that even if the purpose or activities of a political party violate the democratic basic order of the Constitution, its dissolution shall not be by unilateral disposition of the Government but shall be effected by judgment of the Constitutional Court upon prosecution by the Government with the President’s approval.”\\n\\n(B) Guarantee of the career civil service system\\n\\nThe constitutional provision guaranteeing the political neutrality and status of public officials is explained as codifying the core guarantee of the career civil service system. The career civil service system functions to realize stability and continuity in national life by enabling the State’s day-to-day exercise of power to proceed continuously and consistently without being greatly affected by changes in political power, notwithstanding changes of government or the phenomenon of power consolidation by political parties.\\n\\nThis function is particularly important in the parliamentary cabinet system, where separation of powers between the legislative and executive branches is relatively relaxed and the phenomenon of power consolidation through political parties appears relatively strong, and it is widely known that in the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and other countries, the career civil service system greatly contributed to the development of the parliamentary cabinet system.\\n\\nIt has also been evaluated that the reason why the Constitution as amended for the third time in 1960 prescribed the core content of the career civil service system was that, by adopting a parliamentary cabinet system in which public opinion is reflected through the National Assembly, there was a strong need to establish the career civil service system in preparation for frequent changes of government that may occur in a parliamentary cabinet system. This evaluation is consistent with the fact that the Statement of Reasons for the Proposed Amendment to the Constitution at that time, while explaining the introduction of the parliamentary cabinet system and the expansion of political fundamental rights such as the right to vote, freedom of speech, publication, assembly and association, and freedom of political party activities, included the guarantee of the political neutrality and status of public officials as one of its major contents.\\n\\n(C) Guarantee as a right of citizens who are public officials\\n\\nArticle 27(2) of the Constitution as amended for the third time in 1960 provided that “The political neutrality and status of public officials shall be guaranteed as prescribed by law,” and, in terms of structure, placed it immediately after Article 26, which had prescribed the right to hold public office, in the section concerning public officials’ responsibility. The Statement of Reasons for the Proposed Amendment to the Constitution at that time expressly identified this as one of the major contents of the constitutional amendment expanding the people’s fundamental rights.\\n\\nAccordingly, when the political neutrality and status of public officials were codified in the Constitution, they were understood to have the character of a “right of citizens who are public officials” together with the right to hold public office, while also being closely related to “public officials’ responsibility.”\\n\\n(2) Status and Political Neutrality of Public Officials Guaranteed by the Right to Hold Public Office\\n\\n(A) Issue of position in the constitutional structure\\n\\nThe constitutional provision guaranteeing the political neutrality and status of public officials was moved, in the Constitution as amended for the fifth time in 1962, to Chapter I, General Provisions, and Article 6(2) provided that “The status and political neutrality of public officials shall be guaranteed as prescribed by law.” Article 6(1) also moved the provision concerning public officials’ responsibility to the General Provisions, revised the wording, and deleted the petition for removal from office of public officials who committed unlawful acts, stating that “Public officials shall be servants of the entire people and shall be responsible to the people.” The provision concerning political parties was also moved to Article 7 of the General Provisions. This structure has continued to the current Constitution, which was amended for the ninth time in 1987, and the wording of Article 7 of the Constitution concerning public officials’ responsibility, status, and guarantee of political neutrality is the same as that of the Constitution as amended for the fifth time in 1962.\\n\\nThe fact that, after the Constitution as amended for the fifth time in 1962, the provision guaranteeing the status and political neutrality of public officials was moved from the chapter on “Rights and Duties of Citizens” to the chapter on “General Provisions” does not exclude its content from the “protective scope of fundamental rights.” Our Constitution, unlike the German Basic Law, does not adopt a structure that distinguishes between “fundamental rights” and “rights analogous to fundamental rights,” and considering that, under Article 37(1) of the Constitution, freedoms and rights of the people are not disregarded on the grounds that they are not enumerated in the Constitution, whether they fall within the protective scope of the “fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution” relieved through constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act has no relation to the position of the relevant constitutional basis provision in the constitutional structure. Among political fundamental rights, the “freedom to establish and engage in political parties” has its basis in Article 8, which has been located in Chapter I, General Provisions, since the fifth constitutional amendment in 1962, and the “freedom of election campaign” has its basis in Article 116(1) of Chapter VII, Election Management, of the Constitution.\\n\\nIn particular, Article 7(1) of the Constitution, while prescribing the responsibility of public officials to the people, emphasizes, unlike Article 27(1) of the Constitution before the fifth amendment in 1962, the status of being servants of “the entire people,” and by deleting the contents that they are responsible “at all times” to the people and the “people’s right to petition for the removal of public officials,” makes clear that public officials’ responsibility to the people does not mean following the will of the governing power at each moment and temporary public opinion. Therefore, the status and political neutrality of public officials are, since the fifth amendment in 1962, guaranteed in a more elevated form from the perspective of representative democracy.\\n\\n(B) Relation to guarantee of the career civil service system\\n\\nThe fact that Article 7(2) of the Constitution prescribes the core content of the career civil service system and that institutional guarantees are conceptually distinguished from guarantees of fundamental rights cannot serve as a basis for concluding that the guarantee of the status and political neutrality of public officials under Article 7(2) does not fall within the protective scope of the right to hold public office under Article 25 of the Constitution.\\n\\nInstitutional guarantee means that the purpose of the guarantee is not to reduce fundamental rights, and that the content of the guarantee is that the core content of the traditional institution must not be abolished. However, the guarantee of the political neutrality and status of public officials was recognized, when first codified in the Constitution, as one of the expansions of the people’s fundamental rights, and as the core content of the career civil service system, it is increasingly emphasized that it functions to realize stability and continuity in state life in parallel with the development of party politics. Article 7(1) of the Constitution, which prescribes public officials’ status as servants of the entire people and their responsibility to the people, also reflects this point in a more elevated form.\\n\\nIn Germany, where the theory of institutional guarantee was established, Article 33(5) of the Basic Law provides that “The law governing the public service shall be regulated and developed with due regard to the traditional principles of the career civil service.” This codifies its character as an institutional guarantee, and Article 93(1) item 4a of the Basic Law also codifies that a constitutional complaint may be filed with the Federal Constitutional Court on the ground that the rights prescribed in Article 33 have been infringed, which should be understood as consistent with this context. It must also be considered that both the period of the Weimar Constitution in Germany, where the theory of institutional guarantee was established, and the time of the fifth constitutional amendment in 1962, when the guarantee of the status and political neutrality of public officials began to be prescribed in the General Provisions of the Constitution, were periods when the constitutional complaint procedure as a remedy for fundamental rights had not yet been known.\\n\\nTaken together, if the right to hold public office under Article 25 of the Constitution, which includes the right to be elected to become an elected public official and the right to become a career public official, is organically connected with the content of Article 7 of the Constitution, then the fact that the guarantee under Article 7(2) has the character of guaranteeing the career civil service system does not by itself mean that it should be excluded from the “protective scope of the right to hold public office” that may be relieved through constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act. The only issue is what the core content is of the “guarantee as prescribed by law” commonly stipulated in Article 7(2) and Article 25 of the Constitution, in terms of the level of protection.\\n\\n(C) Fundamental-rights content of the guarantee of the status and political neutrality of public officials\\n\\nCompared with the period before the fifth constitutional amendment in 1962, Article 7(1) of the Constitution deleted the people’s petition for removal from office of public officials, and paragraph (2) prescribed the guarantee of the “status” of public officials before the guarantee of “political neutrality”; thus, formally, the guarantee of “status” of public officials appears to be emphasized more. This does not mean that the privileges of public officials are guaranteed, but rather that the emphasis lies on realizing stable and continuous state administration through the guarantee of public officials’ status and on strengthening representative responsibility that prioritizes the interests of the entire people and the State.\\n\\nThe political neutrality of public officials under Article 7(2) of the Constitution, unlike the political neutrality of the armed forces under Article 5(2) of the Constitution, must not merely be “observed” but must be “guaranteed,” though the specific content of that guarantee is only “as prescribed by law.”\\n\\nFor career public officials whose political neutrality must be guaranteed, the guarantee of their status should contribute to the guarantee of political neutrality, and guaranteeing only the status of public officials while undermining the political neutrality that must be maintained in the performance of duties of career public officials, or using such undermining as a means, cannot be said to be what the Constitution envisages. Even for elected public officials, for whom the meaning of political neutrality is relatively weaker, it is necessary, in relation to Article 7(1) of the Constitution, which prescribes public officials as servants of “the entire people,” to guarantee that they perform their duties stably and prioritize the national interest during their democratically legitimized term of office.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court takes the view that the protective scope of the right to hold public office includes not only arbitrary exclusion from the opportunity to assume public office, but also the “prohibition of unfair deprivation of public official status or unfair suspension of authority (duties)” (see Constitutional Court 2011. 12. 29. 2009HEONBA282 et al.). The purpose of guaranteeing, within the protective scope of the right to hold public office, the status and official authority of citizens who have already become public officials is to make the realization of such responsibility and the guarantee of political neutrality effective, in relation to the status and responsibility of public officials as servants of the entire people under Article 7(1) of the Constitution and the guarantee of political neutrality under Article 7(2) of the Constitution, rather than to guarantee privileges for public officials. In particular, in the case of career public officials, political neutrality in the performance of their duties must be guaranteed as expressly provided in Article 7(2) of the Constitution, and the guarantee of their status must also be made on the premise of guaranteeing political neutrality.\\n\\n(3) Problems in the Situation of Fundamental Rights Infringement in This Case\\n\\nIn this case, if the subject matter of adjudication is limited to the disciplinary procedure against the “Prosecutor General,” then the regulation of the provisions subject to adjudication should be examined for its impact on the protective scope of the Prosecutor General’s right to hold public office as a citizen, based on the meaning of the “status of the Prosecutor General” from the perspective of the guarantee of the status and political neutrality of public officials under Article 7(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\ne. Constitutional Status of the Minister of Justice and the Prosecutor General\\n\\n(1) Official relationship between the Minister of Justice and the Prosecutor General\\n\\nThe Minister of Justice supervises the Prosecutor General in the course of duties and becomes involved in the disciplinary procedure because this falls within the function of assisting the President by carrying out the affairs under his jurisdiction as the “head of an administrative ministry” under Article 94 of the Constitution. That prosecution affairs are within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice is based on the Government Organization Act and the Prosecutors’ Office Act pursuant to Article 96 of the Constitution, which provides that “The organization, authority, and scope of duties of administrative ministries shall be determined by Act.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Prosecutor General is a “constitutional organ belonging to the executive branch” whose “appointment” is subject to deliberation by the State Council pursuant to Article 89 item 16 of the Constitution, and as a quasi-judicial organ based on the Prosecutors’ Office Act, his duties are to supervise and direct and oversee prosecutors’ affairs, such as criminal investigation and the institution and maintenance of public prosecution, and to direct and supervise public officials of the Prosecutors’ Office.\\n\\n(2) Democratic legitimacy conferred on the Minister of Justice and the Prosecutor General\\n\\n(A) As can be seen from Article 1(2) of the Constitution, which states that “The sovereignty of the Republic of Korea shall reside in the people, and all state authority shall emanate from the people,” the existence and function of all state organs must possess “democratic legitimacy,” meaning that they ultimately derive from the political consent and approval of the people.\\n\\nAll state organs directly or indirectly receive, ultimately, legitimacy for the exercise of their authority from the people. Democratic legitimacy of state organs is not conferred only on elected public officials such as the President or members of the National Assembly; the National Assembly’s involvement, in the form of consent, in the composition of major constitutional organs belonging to the executive branch or judiciary is also a mechanism for indirectly conferring democratic legitimacy, and so is the appointment by the President, who is directly elected by the people, of major constitutional organs and public officials.\\n\\nThe degree of democratic legitimacy conferred on a state organ depends on the method of election or composition of that organ, and the degree of the organ’s constitutional authority will, in principle, correspond to such degree of democratic legitimacy. Accordingly, organs directly endowed with democratic legitimacy by the people are, in principle, more powerful than organs indirectly endowed with democratic legitimacy. The channels through which the people confer democratic legitimacy on state organs may include elections, referenda, and public opinion expressed through freedom of expression, and the “term of office,” which is set differently for each state organ, has the meaning of a “channel through which democratic legitimacy is conferred periodically.”\\n\\nFrom this perspective, the channels through which democratic legitimacy is conferred and the magnitude of that legitimacy for the Minister of Justice, who is a “head of an administrative ministry as a State Council member,” and the Prosecutor General, who is a “constitutional organ belonging to the executive branch,” are as follows.\\n\\n(B) Under the Constitution, the Minister of Justice is appointed by the President from among the State Council members upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister as the head of an administrative ministry pursuant to Article 94. Article 86(1) provides that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the National Assembly, and Article 87(1) provides that State Council members shall be appointed by the President upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister. Meanwhile, the Prosecutor General belongs to the executive branch headed by the President and is appointed, pursuant to Article 89 item 16, after deliberation by the State Council. Accordingly, the channel through which the Minister of Justice receives democratic legitimacy under the Constitution can be said to be indirect, namely through the “appointment by the President” and the “recommendation by the Prime Minister appointed by the President with the consent of the National Assembly.” The channel through which the Prosecutor General receives democratic legitimacy is the “appointment by the President” and the “deliberation by the State Council,” and since the State Council is composed of “the President, the Prime Minister appointed by the President with the consent of the National Assembly, and State Council members appointed upon the recommendation of that Prime Minister,” democratic legitimacy is likewise indirectly conferred.\\n\\nLegally speaking, both the Minister of Justice and the Prosecutor General undergo a parliamentary hearing by the National Assembly under Article 65-2(2) item 1 of the National Assembly Act during the appointment process, but the President’s appointment does not require the consent of the National Assembly. The Prosecutor General is appointed by the President through the National Assembly hearing process after the Minister of Justice recommends a candidate, respecting the recommendations of the Prosecutor General Candidate Recommendation Committee pursuant to Articles 34 and 34-2 of the Prosecutors’ Office Act. As noted above, the President’s appointment of the Prosecutor General must undergo deliberation by the State Council in which State Council members other than the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice under the Constitution participate.\\n\\nWith respect to the Minister of Justice, who is a State Council member, the National Assembly may, pursuant to Article 63 of the Constitution, propose dismissal to the President by the initiative of at least one-third of the total members and the approval of a majority of the total members of the National Assembly; and the Prime Minister may, pursuant to Article 87(3) of the Constitution, recommend dismissal to the President. By contrast, there is no such recommendation-for-dismissal system for the Prosecutor General. The Minister of Justice, as a State Council member and head of an administrative ministry, is subject to impeachment under Article 65(1) of the Constitution, whereas the Prosecutor General is subject to impeachment pursuant to Article 37 of the Prosecutors’ Office Act. In addition, Article 12(3) of the Prosecutors’ Office Act provides that the term of office of the Prosecutor General shall be 2 years and that reappointment is not permitted.\\n\\nAs seen above, the democratic legitimacy conferred on both the Minister of Justice and the Prosecutor General is mainly through appointment by the President, who is directly elected by the people, and no clear difference in the degree of legitimacy can be found. Even when comparing the degree to which the National Assembly, composed of members directly elected by the people, is involved in appointment, it cannot be said that the Minister of Justice’s case involves a greater degree of involvement than the Prosecutor General’s case. Rather, with respect to status deprivation procedures such as dismissal or impeachment, the National Assembly has less room to be involved in the case of the Prosecutor General than in the case of the Minister of Justice, and this is intended to guarantee political neutrality and independence in light of the nature of the Prosecutor General’s duties as a quasi-judicial organ.\\n\\n(C) Therefore, the Minister of Justice’s nomination of the candidate to the President in the appointment procedure of the Prosecutor General and involvement in the disciplinary procedure of the Prosecutor General have significance only as the carrying out of affairs under his jurisdiction as the head of an administrative ministry and as assistance to the President as a State Council member, and have no special relation to the degree of democratic legitimacy.\\n\\n(3) Problems Where the Minister of Justice, Who Concurrently Holds a National Assembly Member’s Office, Becomes Involved in the Prosecutor General’s Disciplinary Procedure\\n\\nArticle 43 of the Constitution provides that “Members of the National Assembly shall not concurrently hold other offices as prescribed by Act,” and Article 29(1) of the National Assembly Act provides that the office of Prime Minister and State Council member may be held concurrently, which is regarded as an element of parliamentary cabinet government.\\n\\nSince the Minister of Justice, as a State Council member, may also concurrently hold the office of National Assembly member, the degree of his involvement may become an issue when the Minister of Justice who concurrently holds the office of National Assembly member becomes involved in the disciplinary procedure of the Prosecutor General. If the Minister of Justice’s involvement in the Prosecutor General’s disciplinary procedure has not only the character of an act of assisting the President by carrying out affairs under his jurisdiction within the executive branch but also the character of an act as a National Assembly member, then it may function as a means of advancing the will of a specific political force, because it goes beyond being a self-correcting mechanism within the executive branch and involves itself in personnel matters within the executive branch without going through a resolution of the National Assembly.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Prosecutor General is a constitutional organ belonging to the executive branch but is, in principle, a highly independent organ with guaranteed term of office, owing to the functional nature of being a quasi-judicial organ that exercises authority related to criminal justice acts such as criminal investigation and the institution and maintenance of public prosecution. Accordingly, the need to guarantee political neutrality in the performance of the Prosecutor General’s duties is greater than that for ordinary career public officials.\\n\\nAs noted above, from the legislative history of Article 7(2) of the Constitution and the function of the career civil service system, the guarantee of the status and political neutrality of public officials is more important in a governmental form that has elements of parliamentary cabinet government, and the guarantee of the status of career public officials presupposes the guarantee of their political neutrality in the performance of duties. In light of this, where the Minister of Justice, who concurrently holds the office of National Assembly member as a State Council member, becomes involved in a disciplinary procedure imposing a status-related disadvantage on the Prosecutor General, who is a constitutional organ and quasi-judicial organ, it can be derived that guaranteeing political neutrality in the performance of duties of the Prosecutor General, within the protective scope of the right to hold public office that he enjoys as a citizen, has greater significance.\\n\\nThe legal relevance of the infringement of fundamental rights resulting from the provisions subject to adjudication in this case should be examined in light of these characteristics of the matter, and in particular the presentness and directness of the infringement of fundamental rights are at issue.\\n\\nf. Determination of Presentness and Directness of Infringement of Fundamental Rights\\n\\n(1) Presentness\\n\\n(A) A petitioner in a constitutional complaint must be presently related to the exercise of public power; the mere possibility that he or she may become related at some future time is not enough to file a constitutional complaint. However, even if the infringement of fundamental rights is to occur in the future, if it is now certainly foreseeable that the infringement will definitely occur, presentness of the infringement may be recognized for the effectiveness of fundamental-rights relief (see Constitutional Court 1992. 10. 1. 92HEONMA68 et al.; Constitutional Court 2002. 7. 18. 2001HEONMA605 et al.).\\n\\n(B) The situation of infringement of fundamental rights alleged by the Petitioner corresponds to the “unfair deprivation of public official status” or “unfair suspension of authority (duties)” prohibited within the protective scope of the right to hold public office, and the core element of the problematic “unfairness” is the undermining of the “political neutrality of public officials” guaranteed by Article 7(2) of the Constitution. Since guaranteeing the status of public officials is aimed at and premised upon guaranteeing political neutrality in the performance of duties, it cannot be said that there is no infringement of the right to hold public office merely because the coercive influence arising from the commencement of disciplinary proceedings has already undermined political neutrality and only the status-related disadvantage is removed ex post facto. Moreover, from the perspective of the coercive influence exerted on the performance of duties by a public official who is a servant of the entire people, it is difficult to say that a restriction on the right to hold public office through discipline is confined only to cases resulting in deprivation of status; thus, it is appropriate to view disciplinary proceedings, regardless of the final type of discipline, as imposing disadvantages on the status of public officials and as having the character of a restriction on the right to hold public office.\\n\\nAt the time the present constitutional complaint was filed, the Minister of Justice had requested discipline against the Petitioner, and thereby the disciplinary procedure had commenced. Under the Prosecutors’ Office Act, the disciplinary procedure against the Prosecutor General goes through the Minister of Justice’s request for discipline, the Disciplinary Committee’s disciplinary deliberation and decision, and, thereafter, the Minister of Justice’s recommendation and the President’s execution, with the effect of a status-related disadvantage arising upon execution by the President’s “disciplinary disposition” in the end. However, such “disciplinary disposition” signifies that the status-related disadvantage of public officials takes legal effect, and the “political neutrality in the performance of duties,” which must be guaranteed as a premise that such disadvantage should not be unfairly imposed, should be deemed already exposed to a risk of undermining upon commencement of the procedure before the final disciplinary disposition.\\n\\nAt the time the present constitutional complaint was filed, at least the alleged ground for infringement of fundamental rights, namely the “situation in which the majority of members of the Disciplinary Committee are designated and commissioned by the Minister of Justice,” was already clear by the provisions subject to adjudication themselves, and this ground was closely related to whether the political neutrality of the Prosecutor General, a quasi-judicial organ, in the performance of his duties was undermined, since the Minister of Justice who requested discipline concurrently held the office of National Assembly member. In addition, in this case, the Minister of Justice directly restricted the Petitioner’s performance of duties by requesting discipline against the Petitioner and, at the same time, ordering the suspension of the Petitioner’s performance of duties (see Seoul Administrative Court Order 2020A13354 dated 2020. 12. 1.), and did not inform the Petitioner of the identity of the members of the Disciplinary Committee before the date of the disciplinary deliberation (see Seoul Administrative Court Order 2020A13601 dated 2020. 12. 24.).\\n\\nTaking these circumstances together, the grounds for infringement of the Petitioner’s right to hold public office should be deemed to have already arisen at the time of filing the petition, when viewed in relation to the guarantee of political neutrality of public officials under Article 7(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(C) Even if the infringement of the Petitioner’s right to hold public office is understood to be concretized and actualized by the President’s disciplinary disposition, which gives legal effect to the status-related disadvantage, and to have still been in the future at the time of filing the petition, then, taking the above circumstances together, it was already foreseeable at the time of filing the present petition that a disciplinary disposition would definitely be imposed on the Petitioner; and if the reason why the effectiveness of the disciplinary disposition against the Petitioner is denied is that it infringed the guarantee of political neutrality, it is also difficult to effectively remedy the already undermined sphere of the guarantee of political neutrality through a remedy that later denies the effect of that disposition.\\n\\n(D) Accordingly, the present constitutional complaint satisfied the presentness of the infringement of fundamental rights already at the time of filing, and given that a disciplinary disposition of suspension for 2 months was later imposed on the Petitioner, such grounds for infringement may be viewed as having actually continued.\\n\\n(2) Directness\\n\\n(A) To file a constitutional complaint on the ground of infringement of fundamental rights by a statute or regulation, the case must be one in which restriction of freedom, imposition of duties, or deprivation of rights or legal status occurs by the law or regulation itself without waiting for a concrete act of execution; where the legal effect of infringement of fundamental rights by the law or statutory provision in question arises only through a concrete act of execution, the requirement of directness is lacking. However, even if a concrete act of execution is contemplated, directness of the infringement of fundamental rights by the relevant law or regulation may be recognized where the content of the legal norm is univocal and clear so that it directly changes the legal relations of the people even before execution, or the legal status is fixed to the extent that it cannot be affected by the existence or content of the act of execution, or where there is no remedy procedure targeting the act of execution, or even if such a remedy procedure exists, there is no reasonable prospect of relief and it would amount only to imposing an unnecessary detour on the Petitioner who has suffered an infringement of fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 2011. 10. 25. 2010HEONMA661; Constitutional Court 2015. 6. 25. 2013HEONMA128 et al.).\\n\\n(B) The infringement of the Petitioner’s right to hold public office alleged due to the provisions subject to adjudication materializes and actualizes through the “act by which the Minister of Justice designates and commissions the members of the Disciplinary Committee” and the final “disciplinary disposition” made by the President after a series of procedures.\\n\\nThe “act by which the Minister of Justice designates and commissions the members of the Disciplinary Committee,” in light of the organizational-norm character of the provisions subject to adjudication in this case, is directed at the members of the Disciplinary Committee who are designated or commissioned, not at the Petitioner, and in light of the procedural-norm character, it is an act of involvement in an internal institutional procedure leading to the final disciplinary disposition, and thus cannot be viewed as an act of execution constituting an exercise of public power against the Petitioner.\\n\\nThe provisions subject to adjudication are “a norm that determines the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure,” and if the President’s “disciplinary disposition,” which gives legal effect to the status-related disadvantage of the Petitioner, is viewed as the act of execution, then the fact that the subject who designates and commissions members of the Disciplinary Committee is the Minister of Justice does not change depending on whether the final disciplinary disposition is made.\\n\\nIn addition, although the Petitioner may challenge the final disciplinary disposition through an administrative litigation for revocation, during the course of the series of procedures leading up to that disposition, he cannot resort to the remedy of revocation litigation, nor can the political neutrality already undermined at the stage before the disciplinary disposition be restored through revocation litigation.\\n\\nSince the President who executes the discipline upon the Minister of Justice’s recommendation based on the Disciplinary Committee’s decision has no room for any review or discretion as to “whether the person with the authority to compose the Disciplinary Committee is the Minister of Justice,” even if administrative litigation against the President’s disciplinary disposition is possible, there is no reasonable prospect through which the rights of the Petitioner who suffered the infringement of fundamental rights would be remedied thereby, and compelling him to undergo such procedure would amount only to imposing an unnecessary detour.\\n\\n(C) Accordingly, directness of the infringement of fundamental rights resulting from the provisions subject to adjudication in this case is also recognized. Meanwhile, the Petitioner received a disciplinary disposition of suspension for 2 months and sought revocation thereof, with the lawsuit remaining pending (Seoul Administrative Court 2020GUHAP88541), and this will be examined in relation to the interest in adjudication.\\n\\ng. Relevance to the Revocation Action Against the Disciplinary Disposition and Interest in Adjudication\\n\\n(1) In this case, an action for revocation against the disciplinary disposition against the Petitioner is currently pending. If, before the Constitutional Court’s decision, a judgment applying the provisions subject to adjudication becomes final and conclusive, then even if a constitutional complaint directly targeting the law is granted without going through constitutional review of statutes or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act premised on that judgment, there arises the problem that the effect of the final and conclusive judgment cannot be denied.\\n\\nHowever, this is a problem common not only to this case but also to other cases in which the presentness and directness of infringement of fundamental rights are recognized for a constitutional complaint directly targeting a law, even though the law in question is not a penal statute and an act of execution and a remedy procedure against it are contemplated. Thus, the fact that constitutional complaint adjudication has, in principle, a supplementary character as a remedy for infringement of fundamental rights is also a reason why more careful reasoning is required when recognizing the presentness and directness of infringement of fundamental rights in a constitutional complaint against a law.\\n\\nNevertheless, if, in light of the nature of the exercise of public power, the protective scope of the fundamental rights infringed thereby, and the characteristics of the infringement situation, there is a need to view a constitutional complaint against the underlying law as lawful despite the contemplation of an act of execution, the issue of securing the binding force of a constitutional decision on a court judgment should not be a reason to deny the lawfulness of the constitutional complaint against the law, but should be a reason to recognize the need for interpretation or procedure that secures binding force.\\n\\n(2) The reason why, despite the contemplated act of execution in the form of a disciplinary disposition, presentness and directness of infringement of fundamental rights are recognized with respect to the instant complaint directly targeting the law is attributable to the characteristics of the exercise of public power, namely “a norm that determines the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure,” and to the “protective scope of the right to hold public office, including the guarantee of political neutrality in the performance of duties of public officials,” as well as to the characteristics of the infringement situation.\\n\\nHowever, to say that the directness of the instant complaint, which has been recognized according to legal principle despite the contemplated act of execution, is to be denied retroactively on the ground that the contemplated act of execution later occurred as a disciplinary disposition and an administrative litigation was filed against it and is pending before the court, is not only unnatural in its logic but also creates blind spots in the guarantee of fundamental rights. To deny the directness of the instant complaint on the ground that an action for revocation against the act of execution has been filed, and therefore constitutional review of statutes or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act can be pursued, is also inconsistent with the accumulated doctrine of directness in relation to the constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act against laws and regulations.\\n\\nRecognizing the directness of infringement of fundamental rights in a constitutional complaint directly targeting a law for which an act of execution and a remedy procedure by suit in court against it exist, and proceeding to a decision on the merits, has the same significance as preempting such norm-control procedure with a constitutional complaint by the Petitioner before the court, in subsequent litigation challenging the validity of the act of execution, makes a request for constitutional review of statutes. The reason why such a determination of procedural admissibility is necessary lies in the nature of the exercise of public power at issue and the nature of the protective scope of the fundamental rights allegedly infringed thereby, and it is particularly necessary in cases where an infringement of, or a significant risk to, the protective scope of fundamental rights has typically already occurred before the act of execution.\\n\\n(3) The Petitioner has now resigned from and retired from the office of Prosecutor General, but Article 5 item 7 of the Attorneys-at-Law Act, which provides that a person who has been suspended by disciplinary disposition while in office and is in the period of suspension is disqualified as an attorney, states that “even if the person retires during the suspension period, the person shall be deemed to remain in suspension until the end of the suspension period under the relevant disciplinary disposition.” Since the application for stay of execution concerning the Petitioner’s 2-month disciplinary disposition of suspension was partially granted and the suspension period has not yet commenced (see Seoul Administrative Court Order 2020A13601 dated 2020. 12. 24.), the interest in the lawsuit for revocation of that disposition still exists.\\n\\nAs such, unless a lawsuit challenging the validity of the disciplinary disposition is lawfully pending and no judgment has yet been rendered thereon, if a decision granting the present constitutional complaint were pronounced, the court too, as one of all state organs, would have to be bound by that decision (Article 75(1) of the Constitutional Court Act), and in this respect the interest in adjudication in this case cannot be denied.\\n\\nh. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the present constitutional complaint is lawful, as legal relevance such as the presentness and directness of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized, and the interest in adjudication cannot be denied in relation to the action for revocation of the disciplinary disposition. Therefore, the matter should proceed to a decision on the merits and determine whether the right to hold public office, including the guarantee of political neutrality in the performance of duties of the Petitioner, was infringed by the provisions subject to adjudication, which determine the subjects involved in the disciplinary procedure."}

question: Among the explanations concerning personal liberty, which of the following are all incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents) (a) A statutory provision that allows the reduction or exemption of a sentence for a person who has served all or part of the sentence in a foreign country does not infringe personal liberty because it falls within the scope of the legislator's legislative discretion. (b) Unlike punishment, a security measure is based on the actor's future risk of recidivism, and since whether to pronounce a security measure is determined by assessing the risk of recidivism at the time of trial rather than at the time of the act, even if a certain security measure has a strong penal character and restricts personal liberty to a degree equivalent to deprivation of personal liberty, the principle of non-retroactivity of punishment does not apply. (c) Excluding foreigners detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act from the scope of detainees who may file a petition for relief under the Habeas Corpus Act deprives them of the opportunity to contest the legality of their detention under the Habeas Corpus Act and thus infringes personal liberty. (d) A statutory provision that states that a person who has received a deportation order may be detained in a detention facility until deportation becomes possible if the person cannot be immediately deported outside the Republic of Korea infringes personal liberty because it emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity. (e) The right to meet and communicate with counsel, in light of the constitutional provisions, is a fundamental right concerning personal liberty limited only to suspects or accused persons who have been arrested or detained, and it cannot be said that those provisions derive a right of counsel to meet and communicate with an arrested or detained suspect or accused person.
