Furthermore, ex post control by the Minister of Justice, who is merely a supervisory authority rather than a neutral and objective institution, or other procedures prescribed by the Immigration Control Act, such as prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention, presentation of the detention order to the person concerned, and detention notices, cannot be regarded as supplementing the system of judicial review of arrest or detention.\\n\\nAs noted above, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power in shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, but considering the purpose of Article 12(6) of the Constitution in guaranteeing that right, a procedure must be secured whereby the legality of the state of detention itself under the provision subject to review may be requested to a court for review; and this is equally true even if detention under the provision subject to review is carried out as part of immigration control administration, because the detention causes a serious restriction on freedom of the person.\\n\\nTaken together, the provision subject to review, which does not establish a procedure for requesting judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention from a court in the event of detention under the provision subject to review, violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution."}

question: Among the explanations concerning the Executive Branch, which is correct? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: The Prime Minister, upon the President’s order, directs and supervises the heads of each central administrative agency, and when an order or disposition by the head of a central administrative agency is recognized as unlawful, he may suspend or revoke it without obtaining the President’s approval.
B: If the Prime Minister is unable to perform his duties due to an accident, the Deputy Prime Minister who concurrently serves as Minister of Education, and then the Deputy Prime Minister who concurrently serves as Minister of Economy and Finance, shall act in his stead in that order; and if both the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Ministers are unable to perform their duties due to an accident, then, if the President makes a designation, the State Council member so designated shall act in his stead, and if there is no designation, the State Council member according to the order prescribed in Article 26(1) of the Government Organization Act shall act in his stead.
C: Even if the President did not undergo deliberation by the State Council in the process of deciding to suspend operations of the Kaesong Industrial Complex, it cannot be said that the decision had a defect of violating the procedures prescribed by the Constitution and laws, or that it had a defect of not undergoing procedures necessarily required under the principle of due process.
D: The Constitution establishes the Board of Audit and Inspection under the President in order to conduct audit and inspection of public officials’ duties, etc. The scope of the Board of Audit and Inspection’s authority to inspect duties includes the authority to request disciplinary action from the appointing authority, and illegality is the standard for audit, while impropriety is not the standard.
E: When the President’s term expires or the office becomes vacant, or when the President-elect dies or loses his qualification by judgment or other reasons, a successor shall be elected within a certain period, and the same applies when the President is unable to perform his duties due to an accident.
label: C

XX Co., Ltd., Representative Jung ○○, et al.  \\nCounsel for the Petitioners: Law Firm Suryoon Asia, Attorney Song Gi-ho  \\nCounsel for Petitioners 4, 5, 8, 18, 35, 42, 47, 53, 56, 57, 59, 80, 95, 97, 99, and 107  \\nLaw Firm (Limited Liability) Ace  \\nAttorneys-in-charge: Kim Jeong-hak, Lee Hyeon-seop  \\n\\n[Appendix 2] Government Statement on the Complete Suspension of the Kaesong Industrial Complex  \\n• North Korea, turning a blind eye to repeated warnings from the international community and the lives of its suffering residents, committed an extreme provocation by launching a long-range missile following its fourth nuclear test.  \\n• Such provocation by North Korea is a direct challenge to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and in the international community, and is an act that can never be tolerated.  \\nDespite the efforts of the international community thus far to prevent North Korea’s development of nuclear weapons and long-range missiles, North Korea has shown no intention whatsoever of abandoning the development of nuclear weapons and missiles, openly declaring, following its recent provocation, that it will conduct additional nuclear tests and missile launches in the future.  \\nIf this situation continues without change, it is not the maintenance of the status quo; rather, as North Korea’s nuclear capability is advanced, it can only lead to a catastrophic disaster. question: Which of the following statements regarding legal interest under the Administrative Litigation Act are correct? (In cases of dispute, according to case law) (a) The competent administrative agency granted A a permit to alter the structure of the lodging business so that guest rooms could be installed on the 4th and 5th floors of a building owned by A, and A person who operates an inn at a distance of about 700 m from there filed an action seeking a declaration of invalidity of the disposition granting A the permit to alter the structure of the lodging business, on the ground of infringement of residential peace and the living environment; in such case, there is a benefit in seeking a declaration of invalidity. (b) B's term of office expired while an action seeking revocation of the dismissal disposition was pending; however, if the dismissal disposition is revoked, and B can claim payment of remuneration for the period from the date of the dismissal disposition until the date of expiration of the term of office, B has legal interest in seeking revocation of the dismissal disposition. (c) Under the statutes concerning the Act on Promotion of Installation of Waste Disposal Facilities and Support for Nearby Areas, etc., where residents living within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility and within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility are required to form a residents' support consultative body and consult on the determination of the surrounding influence area, if C, a local resident within that area, files an action seeking revocation of the disposition determining the surrounding influence area, standing to sue is recognized. (d) D received a business suspension disposition, and although the suspension period has elapsed, the disposition criteria prescribed in the form of Enforcement Rules provide that a punitive administrative disposition previously imposed shall be treated as an aggravating factor and that a future punitive administrative disposition shall be imposed; where such Enforcement Rules have a statutory basis and there is a risk of receiving an aggravated punitive disposition, if an action seeking revocation is filed against the business suspension disposition whose suspension period has already elapsed, there is legal interest in seeking revocation.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DU1684]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. The latter sentence of Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that an action for revocation may be filed “in the case of a person who has a legal interest that would be restored by revocation of the disposition, etc., even after the effects of the disposition, etc. have been extinguished due to the lapse of time, execution of the disposition, etc., or other reasons,” and thus permits a revocation action even for an administrative disposition whose effects have already ceased, where the necessity for protection of rights is recognized.\\n\\nHowever, where a sanctioning administrative disposition has lost its effect due to the expiration of the sanction period prescribed in the disposition, but the disposition criteria prescribed in the form of the Enforcement Rule, which is a Ministerial Ordinance, or the rules of a local government (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “Rules”), provide that having received a sanctioning administrative disposition (hereinafter referred to as the “prior disposition”) is to be treated as an aggravating circumstance or prerequisite for imposing a future sanctioning administrative disposition (hereinafter referred to as the “subsequent disposition”), views have been divided as to whether there is a legal interest, under the above provision of the Administrative Litigation Act, to seek revocation of the prior disposition; and the view denying such legal interest reasons that such Rules merely have the character of an administrative order within the administrative organization and have no binding force externally against the people or the courts, so that even if there is concern that an aggravated subsequent disposition may be imposed in the future pursuant to the Rules, this is no more than a de facto disadvantage, and that facts or illegality relating to the prior disposition can be contested at the stage of examining and determining whether the aggravated subsequent disposition is lawful.\\n\\nHowever, even if the provisions concerning aggravating circumstances or prerequisites for a sanctioning administrative disposition are in the form of Rules rather than statutes, insofar as such Rules are based on statutes, the competent administrative agency and the official in charge are under a duty to comply with them, regardless of whether their legal nature is that of a normative regulation having external and general binding force; accordingly, it is naturally foreseeable that they will carry out administrative action in accordance with the Rules, and as a result, the people who are the addressees of administrative action cannot help but be affected by those Rules. Therefore, for the addressee who has received the prior disposition in accordance with such Rules, the disadvantage to be suffered in the future by reason of the existence of that disposition, namely the risk of the subsequent disposition, is concrete and real; thus, it should be said that the addressee has a need for protection of rights to eliminate such disadvantage through a revocation action against the prior disposition.\\n\\nMoreover, even if there remains room to contest the facts or illegality of the prior disposition in a later revocation action against the subsequent disposition, such circumstance does not negate the necessity of filing a revocation action directly challenging the illegality of the prior disposition in order to prevent it before the subsequent disposition is made. This is because blocking such a method of litigation may impair the effectiveness of rights relief by causing the following unreasonable results. First, if the method of litigation directly challenging the illegality of the prior disposition is not allowed merely because the sanction period of the prior disposition has elapsed, the person challenging the illegality of the prior disposition will be placed in an unstable position in which he or she cannot timely eliminate the disadvantage expected to be definitively suffered in the future with respect to the relevant business or qualification due to the existence of that disposition, and may consequently suffer considerable difficulty in relation to the relevant business, etc. because of anxiety about it. Further, even if a revocation action is filed to challenge the illegality of the prior disposition itself, if the sanction period expires during the pendency of the lawsuit, the suit will end without any determination on whether the prior disposition was unlawful, even if there has been sufficient trial; as a result, the litigation conducted and the trial results thus far will be rendered vain, and the party will have no choice but to bear the inconvenience and burden of expending effort and costs twice by filing a revocation action against the subsequent disposition later in order to contest again the same issue, namely the illegality of the prior disposition. In addition, where a considerable period has elapsed between the prior disposition and the subsequent disposition, trial regarding the facts, etc. of the prior disposition may become difficult because of the loss of evidence relating to whether the prior disposition was unlawful. In any event, no reason can be found that would justify delaying rights relief until the subsequent disposition, while compelling the person challenging the illegality of the prior disposition to bear the above-mentioned difficulties and burdens.\\n\\nRather, as noted above, since it is naturally foreseeable from the standpoint of the administrative agency that the subsequent disposition will be made on the premise that the prior disposition is lawful, allowing the disadvantage arising from such prior disposition to be removed in advance through litigation against the prior disposition itself is the most effective and appropriate means of dispelling anxiety concerning the other party’s legal status; moreover, through such litigation, the facts and illegality of the prior disposition will be promptly established, thereby ensuring the lawfulness of future administrative action related thereto while at the same time promoting stability in the lives of the people.\\n\\nTherefore, in light of the foregoing circumstances, together with the purport of Article 27(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to a trial, and the purpose of the Administrative Litigation Act, which seeks to effectively remedy infringements of rights and interests caused by administrative dispositions, if there is a realistic concern that a subsequent disposition will be imposed, with the prior disposition serving as an aggravating circumstance or prerequisite pursuant to the Rules, then, even if the sanction period prescribed in the prior disposition has expired, the addressee of the prior disposition should be deemed to have a sufficient need for protection of rights to eliminate such disadvantage through an action for revocation of that disposition; accordingly, it should be regarded as having a legal interest in seeking revocation of the prior disposition.\\n\\nAccordingly, to the extent that the decisions in Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on Oct. 17, 1995, 94NU14148, and Supreme Court Decisions rendered on May 24, 1988, 87NU944; July 10, 1992, 92NU3625; Sept. 30, 1997, 97NU7790; Oct. 10, 2003, 2003DU6443; and other decisions to the same effect, which held contrary to the foregoing and to the effect that even if the Rules provide that a sanctioning administrative disposition constitutes an aggravating circumstance where the same person is subjected again to a future sanctioning administrative disposition, and even if there is concern that an aggravated sanctioning administrative disposition may be imposed pursuant to such provision, there is no legal interest in seeking revocation of the sanctioning administrative disposition whose sanction period has elapsed, they are all modified.\\n\\n2. In the present case, according to the record, the Defendant imposed on the Plaintiff a disposition of one-month suspension of environmental impact assessment agency services (hereinafter referred to as the “disposition at issue”) pursuant to Article 13(1)6 and other provisions of the former Environmental Impact Assessment Act (before its repeal pursuant to Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Act on Assessment of Impacts of Works on Environment, Traffic, and Disasters, etc., which entered into force on January 1, 2001) on the ground that the Plaintiff had prepared an environmental impact statement in an unsound manner. The period of business suspension began on February 2, 2001, was interrupted on February 8, 2001 by the first-instance court’s decision to stay execution, and resumed on March 23, 2002, the day after the first-instance court rendered judgment, and it is clear that the entire period had elapsed by around April 13, 2002; however, Article 12(1)8 of the Act on Assessment of Impacts of Works on Environment, Traffic, and Disasters, etc. provides that where an assessment agency “violates this Act or any order under this Act,” its registration may be revoked or the suspension of all or part of its business may be ordered for a period not exceeding six months, and Article 12(2) provides that the standards for administrative dispositions under paragraph (1) and other necessary matters shall be prescribed by a joint Ministerial Ordinance of the Ministry of Government Administration and Home Affairs, the Ministry of Environment, and the Ministry of Construction and Transportation; and pursuant to that delegation, Article 10 [Attached Table 2] 2. Individual Standards (11) of the Enforcement Rule of the same Act, which sets forth the standards for administrative dispositions against assessment agencies, provides that where an assessment agency performs environmental impact assessment agency services by a new contract during the period of a business suspension disposition, a first violation shall result in a six-month business suspension and a second violation shall result in revocation of registration. According to the materials submitted by the Plaintiff after filing the appeal, the Plaintiff appears to have newly entered into an environmental impact assessment agency contract during the above business suspension period and to have performed such agency services.\\n\\nIf so, in light of the legal principles discussed above, the Plaintiff faces a risk of receiving a subsequent disposition of business suspension or revocation of registration under the above Enforcement Rule on the ground that the Plaintiff performed environmental impact assessment agency services by a new contract during the business suspension period due to the disposition at issue, and this is a direct and concrete disadvantage to the legal status of being able to perform business as an assessment agency; accordingly, even after the business suspension period prescribed in the disposition at issue has elapsed, the Plaintiff should be deemed to have a legal interest in seeking revocation of the disposition at issue in order to avoid the subsequent disposition under the above Enforcement Rule.\\n\\nNevertheless, the judgment of the court below, which held this action inadmissible on the sole ground that the business suspension period prescribed in the disposition at issue had entirely elapsed and that, therefore, no infringement of any legal interest of the Plaintiff could be found merely because the disposition at issue still remained outwardly extant, contains an error of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning legal interest under the latter sentence of Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act or in failing to conduct the necessary trial.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination. It is so decided as stated in the operative part. In this decision, all participating Justices concurred except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Kang-guk.\\n\\n4. The separate opinion of Justice Lee Kang-guk is as follows.\\n\\nA. The majority opinion does not specifically discuss the legal nature of the Enforcement Rule, a Ministerial Ordinance that sets forth the standards for a sanctioning administrative disposition (hereinafter referred to as a “sanctioning disposition”), but, in a case where the Enforcement Rule provides that a future subsequent disposition shall be made on the basis of having received a prior disposition as an aggravating circumstance or prerequisite, it deems that there is a legal interest in seeking revocation of the prior disposition even after the sanction period prescribed in the prior disposition has elapsed, on the ground that the disadvantage to be suffered in the future by the addressee of the prior disposition due to the existence of that disposition is concrete and real. While I agree with the majority opinion’s conclusion that, in such a case, legal interest in seeking revocation of the prior disposition exists, I think that, as to the reason, it would be more legally appropriate to affirm such legal interest on the theoretical basis that recognizes the norm-setting character of the Ministerial Ordinance prescribing the standards for sanctioning dispositions, as follows.\\n\\nB. As to the criteria for distinguishing between normative regulations and administrative rules, there has traditionally been continuing disagreement among views such as the formal theory and the substantive theory; however, in this case, the legal nature of the standards for sanctioning dispositions prescribed in a Ministerial Ordinance should first be examined.\\n\\nThe traditional Supreme Court precedents, including Supreme Court Decision rendered on Dec. 26, 1997, 97NU15418, recognized the norm-setting character of sanctioning disposition standards where the form of their enactment was a Presidential Decree (Supreme Court Decisions rendered on Dec. 8, 1998, 98DU14174, and Mar. 9, 2001, 99DU5207, among others), but where the form of their enactment was a Ministerial Ordinance, it has steadfastly maintained the position that such disposition standards merely prescribe internal office-handling guidelines of the administrative agency and therefore have no external binding force, cannot become judicial norms, and need not bind the courts (Supreme Court Decisions rendered on Jan. 25, 1990, 89NU3564; May 30, 1997, 96NU5773; Mar. 27, 1998, 97NU20236; and others). However, the position of the prior precedents denying the norm-setting character of sanctioning disposition standards prescribed in the form of a Ministerial Ordinance is not appropriate for the following reasons.\\n\\nFirst, the traditional precedents are premised on the notion that certain matters are inherently the proper subject of administrative rules, but whether to enact sanctioning disposition standards in the form of normative regulations or in the form of administrative rules is merely a matter of legislative policy.\\n\\nSecond, Presidential Decrees and Ministerial Ordinances are both delegated orders provided for in Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution; the only difference is that Presidential Decrees undergo deliberation by the State Council in the process of enactment, and this is insufficient as a basis for treating their legal effect differently. Accordingly, if sanctioning disposition standards in the form of Presidential Decrees are regarded as normative regulations, then disposition standards prescribed by Ministerial Ordinance should also, for the sake of logical consistency, be regarded as normative regulations.\\n\\nThird, because sanctioning disposition standards directly affect the rights and duties of the people, they cannot simply be regarded as mere internal office-handling standards of an administrative agency.\\n\\nFourth, the traditional sanctioning disposition standards were mostly unclear or uniformly prescribed and thus lacked concrete validity; accordingly, there was a practical necessity to deny them norm-setting character, because recognizing such character would bind the courts as well and thus make it difficult to protect the rights and interests of the people. However, it is also worth noting that most current sanctioning disposition standards, in order to secure concrete validity, specify in detail the types and degree of the violation, and moreover provide mitigating provisions, thereby making it possible to impose sanctions with concrete validity.\\n\\nFifth, even if the court denies the norm-setting character of sanctioning disposition standards prescribed in a Ministerial Ordinance in a concrete case, the Ministerial Ordinance does not thereby immediately become invalid; the relevant administrative officials will, notwithstanding the judgment, have no choice but, under their duty to comply with the law, to continue making the same dispositions as before based on the standards set forth in the applicable Ministerial Ordinance, and the court will, after repeatedly confirming that the Ministerial Ordinance is merely an administrative rule, cancel the administrative disposition. This will ultimately seriously undermine legal stability and predictability. Therefore, where concrete and appropriate disposition standards cannot be derived even through constitution-conforming or statute-conforming interpretation of the sanctioning disposition standards prescribed in a Ministerial Ordinance, it would be more desirable to exclude their effect by declaring them void on the ground of exceeding the scope of delegation or excessive legislation.\\n\\nIn the end, taking these points together, the Enforcement Rule, a Ministerial Ordinance that sets forth sanctioning disposition standards pursuant to delegation from the superior statute, falls under the delegated orders provided for in Article 95 of the Constitution, and because its content in substance concerns matters that directly affect the rights and duties of the people, it should be regarded not merely as an internal office-handling guideline of the administrative agency, but as a normative regulation that externally binds the people and the courts.\\n\\nC. Next, as to the legal interest in seeking revocation of a sanctioning disposition after the sanction period has elapsed, where an administrative disposition has a fixed period of effectiveness, its effect ceases upon the expiration of that period, and after that period has elapsed, there is no legal interest in seeking revocation of the disposition unless there are other circumstances from which it can be found that some legal interest is infringed merely because the disposition still remains outwardly extant (Supreme Court Decisions rendered on Oct. 23, 1990, 90NU3119; Nov. 25, 2004, 2004DU9012; and others).\\n\\nHowever, in relation to the so-called aggravating sanctioning grounds, whereby a prior sanctioning disposition becomes a prerequisite or aggravating requirement for a future sanctioning disposition, the traditional Supreme Court precedents, including Supreme Court Decision rendered on Oct. 23, 1990, 90NU3119, held that where the aggravating sanctioning grounds are prescribed by statute or Presidential Decree, there is a risk of receiving a future aggravated sanctioning disposition pursuant thereto, and therefore, even if the sanction period prescribed in the sanctioning disposition has elapsed, there is a legal interest in seeking revocation of the disposition in order to eliminate the risk or anxiety concerning one’s legal status arising therefrom (Supreme Court Decisions rendered on Aug. 27, 1991, 91NU3512; Feb. 5, 1999, 98DU13997; Mar. 25, 2005, 2004DU14106; and others). But where the aggravating sanctioning grounds are prescribed by a Ministerial Ordinance, the position has been maintained that, since they are merely internal office-handling guidelines of the administrative agency, even if the administrative agency imposes an aggravated sanctioning disposition pursuant thereto, the court may examine and determine whether the aggravated sanctioning disposition is lawful in accordance with the provisions and purport of the underlying statute without being bound thereby; and therefore, even if a prior sanctioning disposition is prescribed as an aggravating ground, the disadvantage arising therefrom is merely a de facto disadvantage, so if the sanction period has elapsed, there is no legal interest in seeking revocation (Supreme Court Decisions rendered on July 10, 1992, 92NU3625; Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on Oct. 17, 1995, 94NU14148; Supreme Court Decisions rendered on Sept. 30, 1997, 97NU7790; Mar. 15, 2002, 2001DU10622; Oct. 10, 2003, 2003DU6443; and others).\\n\\nHowever, as noted above, if one takes the position that the sanctioning disposition standards prescribed in a Ministerial Ordinance should be recognized as normative regulations with external binding force, then even where the aggravating sanctioning grounds are prescribed in a Ministerial Ordinance, they should likewise be regarded as normative regulations that externally bind the people and the courts; accordingly, just as where the aggravating sanctioning grounds are prescribed by statute or Presidential Decree, there should be deemed to be a legal interest in seeking revocation of the prior disposition even after the sanction period has elapsed.\\n\\nAnd even from a practical standpoint, from the perspective of the people, who are the addressees of the disposition, it is the same whether the aggravating sanctioning grounds are prescribed in a Presidential Decree or in a Ministerial Ordinance in that there is a risk of suffering disadvantage therefrom; nevertheless, it would not be easy to accept that the existence or absence of legal interest in seeking revocation after the sanction period has elapsed differs depending on the form of the statute, etc. prescribing the aggravating sanctioning grounds.\\n\\nD. Turning to this case, Article 10 [Attached Table 2] of the Enforcement Rule of the Act on Assessment of Impacts of Works on Environment, Traffic, and Disasters, etc. is a Ministerial Ordinance that sets forth the standards for sanctioning dispositions pursuant to the delegation under Article 12(2) of the same Act; it is not merely an internal office-handling guideline of an administrative agency, but a normative regulation that has external effect and binds the people and the courts. Since the Plaintiff entered into a new environmental impact assessment agency contract and performed the agency services during the business suspension period as found by the court below, the Plaintiff faces a risk of receiving an aggravated sanctioning disposition under [Attached Table 2] 2. Individual Standards (11) above; therefore, even though the business suspension period has elapsed, the Plaintiff should be deemed to have a legal interest in seeking revocation of the disposition at issue in order to eliminate the risk or anxiety concerning the legal status of being able to perform business as an assessment agency.\\n\\nBy contrast, the judgment of the court below, which held the action at issue inadmissible on the grounds that the Plaintiff’s business suspension period had elapsed and that, otherwise, no infringement of any legal interest of the Plaintiff could be found merely because the disposition at issue still remains outwardly extant, cannot escape reversal.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state a separate opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2011DU5001]": "We decide on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Defendant’s Ground of Appeal No. 1\\nEven if it is impossible to restore the status by a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the dismissal disposition while a lawsuit for a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the dismissal disposition is pending and the term of office has expired, if salary for the period from the date of the dismissal disposition to the expiration of the term of office can be claimed as a result of such declaration of invalidity or revocation, there is a legal interest in seeking a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the dismissal disposition (see Supreme Court Decisions 2002DU10483, Apr. 22, 2003; 2008DU22662, Mar. 12, 2009, etc.). The same applies even where the person with the authority to dismiss and the person obligated to pay remuneration are different.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that the Plaintiff, whose term of office expired while the fact-finding trial was pending, had a legal interest in seeking a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the dismissal disposition at issue is proper, and there is no illegality arising from an error of law concerning legal interest, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Plaintiff’s Ground of Appeal No. 1\\nThe Broadcasting Act, which provides for matters concerning the establishment and operation of the Korean Broadcasting System, stipulates in Article 50(2) that “the President shall be appointed by the President upon the recommendation of the board of directors,” but it does not contain an express provision regarding the dismissal of the President of the Korean Broadcasting System. However, the Board of Audit and Inspection conducts external audits of the Korean Broadcasting System (Article 63(3) of the Broadcasting Act) and may request the appointing authority or the authority recommending appointment to dismiss executives, etc. (Article 32(9) of the Board of Audit and Inspection Act), which may be viewed as presupposing that the President has the authority to dismiss the President of the Korean Broadcasting System. In addition, Article 15(1) of the former Korean Broadcasting System Act, which was repealed by the enactment of the Broadcasting Act, provided that the President shall “appoint and dismiss” the President of the Korean Broadcasting System; and if the term “appointment” was used in the Broadcasting Act in order to limit the President’s authority to dismiss, the legislature could have separately provided a rule on the restriction of dismissal to make this clear, yet the Broadcasting Act contains no provision concerning security of status, such as restriction on the dismissal of the President of the Korean Broadcasting System. In light of these points, including the legislative process and history of the Broadcasting Act, the relationship with other statutes, and the legislative form, it is reasonable to view the legislative intent behind using the term “appointment” instead of “appoint and dismiss” in the Broadcasting Act as not intended to exclude the President’s authority to dismiss.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality arising from an error of law concerning the President’s authority to dismiss the President of the Korean Broadcasting System, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Plaintiff’s Ground of Appeal No. 2\\nArticle 32(8) of the Board of Audit and Inspection Act provides that “the Board of Audit and Inspection may request the head of the supervisory agency or the head of the relevant agency to take disciplinary action against a person who is not subject to the application of disciplinary provisions prescribed by statutes and who falls under the grounds for accountability prescribed by statutes or by the organization to which the person belongs, or a person who, without justifiable cause, refuses an audit under this Act or neglects to submit materials.” Meanwhile, Paragraph 9 of the same Article provides that “in the case referred to in Paragraph 8, if the Board of Audit and Inspection recognizes that the misconduct of an executive or employee of an organization, etc. who is not subject to the application of provisions concerning accountability prescribed by statutes or by the organization to which the person belongs is clear, it may request the appointing authority or the authority recommending appointment to dismiss such person.”\\nIn addition, Article 44 of the Broadcasting Act provides, on the one hand, that the Korean Broadcasting System shall fulfill the public responsibility of the corporation, including the purpose of broadcasting and its public responsibility, fairness, and public interest of broadcasting; and Article 51(1) of the Broadcasting Act provides, on the other hand, that the President of the Korean Broadcasting System, as the representative of the corporation and the person who supervises the overall business of the corporation, bears responsibility for management performance.\\n\\nIn this case, the Board of Audit and Inspection, as a result of its audit of the Korean Broadcasting System, applied Article 32(9) of the Board of Audit and Inspection Act and requested a dismissal recommendation against the Plaintiff; and the President of the Korean Broadcasting System, as the representative of the corporation, is in a position to fulfill the public responsibility of the corporation, including realizing the purpose of broadcasting and its public responsibility, fairness, and public interest of broadcasting, and if he or she has poorly managed finances as one element of performance of duties, such conduct may be treated as grounds for dismissal. Accordingly, Article 32(9) of the Board of Audit and Inspection Act, Article 44 of the Broadcasting Act, Article 51(1) of the Broadcasting Act, etc. may be viewed as the statutory basis for the grounds of dismissal.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that the foregoing statutory provisions constitute the statutes forming the basis of the grounds for dismissal at issue is proper. However, the Act on the Management of Public Institutions (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Institutions Management Act”) applies to public institutions designated and publicly notified in accordance with the procedures prescribed by law (Article 2(1)), and the Korean Broadcasting System cannot be designated as a public institution (Article 4(2)3); therefore, the Public Institutions Management Act cannot be applied to the Korean Broadcasting System. Thus, it was not appropriate for the lower court to rely on Articles 22 and 35 of the Public Institutions Management Act as one of the statutes forming the basis of the grounds for dismissal at issue. However, such error did not affect the judgment result, insofar as the grounds for dismissal cited by the lower court fall under Article 51(1) of the Broadcasting Act, as stated above.\\n\\nTherefore, the argument in this part of the grounds of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. As to Plaintiff’s Grounds of Appeal Nos. 3 and 4\\nAccording to the reasoning of the first-instance judgment as cited by the lower court, the lower court, based on evidence duly admitted, found the facts as stated in the judgment and then determined, in substance, that the Plaintiff, while serving as President of the Korean Broadcasting System and supervising its overall business for more than five years, (1) in light of the budget structure of the Korean Broadcasting System, which formulates expenditure budgets within the scope of revenues, the over-allocation of the advertising revenue budget without relying on objective data was one cause of business losses; the Board of Audit and Inspection had, on May 21, 2004, notified the Plaintiff to promote management efficiency, including curbing unreasonable personnel-expense-like expenditures; and, in particular, as the Plaintiff himself asserted, if the Korean Broadcasting System was structurally in financial difficulty, the Plaintiff should have induced agreement from employees to reduce costs, including personnel expenses, for the long-term rationalization of the corporation’s management, yet the Plaintiff increased wages to a high level by means such as raising various allowances and maintained the progressive severance pay system (from the standpoint of management administration); (2) in reorganizing the personnel system, the Plaintiff failed to take measures that could limit the increase of higher-level positions, such as integrated management of the authorized personnel complement and improvement of the seniority-based promotion system, and even though staffing-reduction factors arose, such as the closure of local broadcasting stations and the automation of transmission and relay stations, the Plaintiff made no efforts toward restructuring, etc. (from the standpoint of organizational and personnel management); (3) although the Suwon Center, into which KRW 124.7 billion in project costs had been invested, was being operated inefficiently while losing its original function of “transferring the headquarters’ drama production function and concentrating production facilities,” the Plaintiff failed for several years to devise appropriate measures therefor and thus failed to generate utility commensurate with the investment; and, in promoting the construction project for the Gamaksan relay station, the Plaintiff sufficiently failed in advance to review the feasibility of the project, such as whether 50,000 households with poor reception could be resolved, whether five relay stations including Dongducheon could be closed, and whether a wireless station license could be obtained, and went ahead with the project in an unreasonable manner, such as by entering into construction contracts while uncertainty remained as to whether the project could proceed, thereby resulting in waste of project costs, etc. (from the standpoint of installation and operation of broadcasting facilities), and by failing to properly perform duties in this way, the accumulated business loss from 2004 to 2007, during which the Plaintiff served as President of the Korean Broadcasting System, amounted to at least approximately KRW 80 billion, and a net loss of approximately KRW 20.7 billion occurred in the first half of 2008 alone, thereby contributing to the chronic deficit structure of the Korean Broadcasting System; therefore, such reasons, etc. may constitute grounds for dismissal under Article 51(1) of the Broadcasting Act. However, the lower court further held that the grounds for dismissal as above mainly arose from the Plaintiff’s misjudgment in management while operating the Korean Broadcasting System; that in light of the circumstances as found in the judgment, such as the stagnation of subscription fee revenues due to the freezing of the receiving fee since 1981, and the decrease in advertising revenues of terrestrial broadcasting and the increase in expenditure due to the corporation’s fulfillment of public responsibilities, which were also major causes of the deterioration of the Korean Broadcasting System’s financial condition, there may be room to view the dismissal disposition as unlawful due to deviation from or abuse of the discretion granted to the Defendant regarding the dismissal of the President of the Korean Broadcasting System; but given that the Plaintiff bears managerial responsibility for the chronic deficit structure of the Korean Broadcasting System, and that the Defendant took the dismissal disposition at issue pursuant to the Board of Audit and Inspection’s request for a dismissal recommendation following its audit of the Korean Broadcasting System and the board of directors’ resolution recommending dismissal, even if there exists a defect of deviation from or abuse of discretion, such defect is not so serious and clear as to render the dismissal disposition at issue void.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s fact-finding and determination are reasonable and can be accepted, and there is no illegality, such as a violation of the rules of logic and experience beyond the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence by violating the rule of logic and experience, or a failure to conduct sufficient examination of relevant matters affecting the judgment result, or an error of law concerning the degree of deviation from or abuse of discretion, inconsistency in reasons, etc., as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. As to Plaintiff’s Ground of Appeal No. 5 and Defendant’s Ground of Appeal No. 2\\nIf an administrative agency, when taking an infringing administrative disposition, fails to give prior notice under the Administrative Procedures Act or an opportunity to submit opinions to the party concerned, and fails to present the basis and reasons for the disposition, such disposition is unlawful unless it falls within an exceptional case where such procedures need not be followed (see Supreme Court Decisions 90NU1786, Sept. 11, 1990; 2000DU8912, May 17, 2002; 2006DU20631, Sept. 21, 2007, etc.).\\nThe Administrative Procedures Act, which aims to secure fairness, transparency, and reliability in administration and to protect the rights and interests of the people, applies to dispositions, notifications, advance notice of administrative legislation, administrative notice, and administrative guidance, except where other statutes contain specific provisions or where the matters fall under the items of Article 3(2). As a ground for exclusion from the application of the Administrative Procedures Act, Article 3(2)9 of the Administrative Procedures Act provides for “matters that are recognized as difficult or unnecessary to undergo administrative procedures in light of the nature of the relevant administrative act, such as conscription and call-up under the Military Service Act, entry into and departure from the Republic of Korea, recognition of refugee status, naturalization of foreigners, disciplinary action or other dispositions under statutes governing public officials’ personnel matters, or matters prescribed by Presidential Decree as matters concerning mediation, coordination, arbitration, adjudication, or other dispositions under statutes for the purpose of adjusting interests, and matters for which procedures comparable to administrative procedures have been followed.” Pursuant to the above delegation provision, Article 2 of the Enforcement Decree of the Administrative Procedures Act enumerates as “matters prescribed by Presidential Decree” under Article 3(2)9 of the Administrative Procedures Act the following: matters concerning conscription, etc. under the Military Service Act, etc. (No. 1); matters concerning entry into and departure from the Republic of Korea by foreigners, etc. (No. 2); matters concerning disciplinary action or other dispositions under statutes governing public officials’ personnel matters (No. 3); matters concerning dispositions such as mediation under statutes for the purpose of adjusting interests (No. 4); matters concerning the imposition and collection of taxes (No. 5); matters handled following resolutions or decisions of the Fair Trade Commission (No. 6); matters concerning adjudications or decisions under the State Compensation Act, etc. (No. 7); matters handled with respect to students, trainees, etc. in order to achieve educational or training purposes (No. 8); matters handled according to the results of examinations or tests (No. 9); matters concerning the exercise of sovereign rights over foreign fishing, etc. in the Exclusive Economic Zone (No. 10); and matters concerning dispositions such as determination and decision under the Patent Act, etc. (No. 11).\\n\\nNeither the Broadcasting Act nor related statutes contain separate provisions regarding the procedure for the President’s dismissal of the President of the Korean Broadcasting System, and in light of the legislative purpose of the Administrative Procedures Act and the content of Article 3(2)9 of the Administrative Procedures Act and the related Enforcement Decree provisions, the dismissal disposition at issue cannot be regarded as falling within the exception grounds exhaustively prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act and its Enforcement Decree; thus, the Administrative Procedures Act applies to the dismissal disposition at issue as well.\\n\\nMeanwhile, to deem an administrative disposition null and void ab initio, it is not enough merely that there exists a ground of illegality in the disposition; the defect must be a serious one violating an important part of the applicable legal rule and must be objectively apparent. In determining whether a defect is serious and apparent, one must teleologically examine the purpose, meaning, and function of the relevant legal rule, and at the same time reasonably consider the special characteristics of the specific case itself (see Supreme Court Decisions 2004DU10968, June 24, 2005; 2005DU11937, Sept. 21, 2007, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the first-instance judgment as cited by the lower court, the lower court determined that, in the course of the dismissal disposition at issue, the Plaintiff was not given prior notice of the contents of the disposition or an opportunity to submit opinions thereon, and was not given the legal basis and specific grounds for dismissal at the time of the dismissal disposition, so the dismissal disposition at issue was unlawful, but the procedural or formal defect of the disposition cannot be deemed serious and obvious, and therefore constitutes a ground for revocation.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles and the record discussed above, the lower court’s determination is proper, and there is no illegality, such as an error of law concerning the scope of application of the Administrative Procedures Act, as alleged in Defendant’s grounds of appeal, or an error of law concerning the degree of illegality arising from violation of the Administrative Procedures Act, as alleged in Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by each party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision as follows."}

{"[2014DU42520]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the statements in the supplementary brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal has elapsed, to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Concerning the procedure for determining the surrounding impact area of a waste disposal facility\\n\\na. The 「Act on the Promotion of Installation of Waste Disposal Facilities and Support for Surrounding Areas, etc.」 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) and its Enforcement Decree (hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Decree”) provide as follows with respect to the determination of the surrounding impact area of a waste disposal facility.\\n\\n(1) The installing agency of a waste disposal facility shall, within 2 years from the date on which the waste disposal facility installation plan is publicly notified, determine and publicly notify the surrounding area expected to be affected environmentally by the installation and operation of the waste disposal facility as the surrounding impact area of the waste disposal facility. If, after determining and publicly notifying the surrounding impact area, the installing agency of the waste disposal facility deems that there has been a change in environmental impact, it may adjust and publicly notify the surrounding impact area (Article 17(1) and (3) of the Act, Article 17(1) of the Enforcement Decree).\\n\\n(2) The installing agency of a waste disposal facility shall organize a Residents’ Support Consultative Body (hereinafter referred to as the “Support Consultative Body”) in order to consult on matters concerning the determination of the surrounding impact area. The Support Consultative Body shall, taking into account the distance from the waste disposal facility, the degree of environmental impact, and the number of residents, and in consultation with the Governor of the competent Special Self-Governing Province, Mayor, County Head, or District Head, and the Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council, be composed of ㉮ members of the Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council of the area where the relevant waste disposal facility is located, ㉯ resident representatives, and ㉰ two experts recommended by the resident representatives; provided, in principle, that resident representatives shall constitute at least half of the members of the Support Consultative Body. In this context, resident representatives shall be, ① where the surrounding impact area has not been determined and publicly notified, resident representatives for each eup, myeon, and dong recommended by the relevant Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council among local residents residing within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility or within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility, and ② where the surrounding impact area has been determined and publicly notified, resident representatives for each eup, myeon, and dong recommended by the relevant Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council among local residents residing in the surrounding impact area [Article 18(1) [Attached Table 2] Item 2 (b) of the Enforcement Decree].\\n\\n(3) Within 90 days from the date on which the waste disposal facility installation plan is publicly notified, the Support Consultative Body shall select a research institution to conduct a survey of environmental impact caused by the installation and operation of the waste disposal facility. The installing agency of the waste disposal facility shall have the selected specialized research institution conduct a survey of environmental impact, and, on the basis of the results of such survey, shall consult with the Support Consultative Body on matters concerning the determination of the surrounding impact area. Provided, where the Support Consultative Body deems that a survey of environmental impact in the surrounding area is unnecessary, such survey may be omitted or substituted by a written review opinion of a relevant expert (Article 17(2) of the Act, Article 18(6) and (7) of the Enforcement Decree).\\n\\n(4) After the surrounding impact area has been determined and publicly notified, the installing agency of the waste disposal facility shall install convenience facilities for local residents on the site of, or in the vicinity of, the relevant waste disposal facility, and, in order to support residents in the surrounding impact area, shall establish a Residents’ Support Fund and implement projects to support improvement of residents’ income and promotion of welfare. At this time, the specific details shall be determined through consultation with the Support Consultative Body (Articles 20, 21(1), and 22(4) of the Act, Article 27(1) and (3) of the Enforcement Decree).\\n\\nb. When the following circumstances, ascertainable from the contents of these provisions, are comprehensively considered, where the effective period of a surrounding impact area determination previously publicly notified has expired and, due to a change in environmental impact, it becomes necessary to determine the scope of the surrounding impact area again, the installing agency of a waste disposal facility must, pursuant to Article 18(1) [Attached Table 2] Item 2 (b) of the Enforcement Decree, reorganize the Support Consultative Body in the same manner as in the case of “where the surrounding impact area has not been determined and publicly notified,” namely, with “local residents residing within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility or within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility, who are resident representatives for each eup, myeon, and dong recommended by the relevant Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council,” and consult on the determination of the surrounding impact area. Furthermore, it must be deemed that a Support Consultative Body composed of “resident representatives for each eup, myeon, and dong recommended by the relevant Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council among local residents residing in the surrounding impact area previously determined and publicly notified” has neither the authority nor the qualification to participate in redetermining the scope of the surrounding impact area.\\n\\n(1) In a series of administrative processes, the role of the Support Consultative Body differs in nature before and after the determination of the surrounding impact area of a waste disposal facility. ① Until the surrounding impact area of the waste disposal facility is determined, the Support Consultative Body participates in whether to conduct a survey of environmental impact, the selection of a specialized research institution for such survey, and the determination of the scope of the surrounding impact area. This is intended to ensure that the “scope of the recipients of resident support projects” is appropriately determined. ② On the other hand, after the surrounding impact area has been determined and publicly notified, the Support Consultative Body participates in determining the installation of convenience facilities for local residents or the specific contents of resident support projects for residents in the surrounding impact area. This is intended to ensure that resident support projects, etc., which consist of direct or indirect support and allocation of the limited resource called the Residents’ Support Fund to residents residing in the surrounding impact area, are properly implemented.\\n\\n(2) Article 18(1) [Attached Table 2] Item 2 (b) of the Enforcement Decree provides, with respect to the qualifications of resident representative members constituting the Support Consultative Body, ① that where “the surrounding impact area has not been determined and publicly notified,” resident representatives shall be selected from among “local residents residing within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility or within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility.” On the other hand, ② where “the surrounding impact area has been determined and publicly notified,” it provides that resident representatives shall be selected from among “local residents residing in the surrounding impact area,” thus distinguishing between the two. This may be understood as reflecting that the issue of determining the scope of the surrounding impact area and the issue of supporting and allocating limited resources to residents within an already determined surrounding impact area differ in nature.\\n\\n(3) After the surrounding impact area has been determined and publicly notified, “resident representatives selected from among residents residing in the surrounding impact area” will constitute more than half of the members of the Support Consultative Body. However, since the Residents’ Support Fund, which finances resident support projects, is limited, such resident representatives are highly likely not to wish for changes unfavorable to themselves caused by expansion or reduction of the “scope of the recipients of resident support projects.” Accordingly, it is difficult to expect that they will play an objective and fair role with respect to the issue of adjusting the scope of the surrounding impact area.\\n\\n(4) Article 17(1) of the Enforcement Decree provides that, after the installing agency of a waste disposal facility has determined and publicly notified the surrounding impact area, if it deems that there has been a change in environmental impact, it may adjust and publicly notify the surrounding impact area. As such, the Enforcement Decree itself presupposes that the effect of the surrounding impact area once determined and publicly notified need not necessarily remain unchanged throughout the entire period during which the waste disposal facility is installed and operated. Therefore, apart from the question of how long an effective period may be set, it is appropriate to view that the very act of the installing agency of a waste disposal facility designating an effective period when determining and publicly notifying the surrounding impact area is permitted under the law. Where the effective period set by the installing agency of a waste disposal facility when determining and publicly notifying the surrounding impact area expires, unless there are special circumstances such as a lawful extension of that effective period, the effect of the determination and public notification of the surrounding impact area must be deemed to extinguish. Accordingly, the installing agency of the waste disposal facility must again investigate the environmental impact caused by the installation and operation of the waste disposal facility and newly determine and publicly notify the surrounding impact area.\\n\\nc. According to the reasons for the first-instance judgment as cited by the lower court, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) The Defendant is the agency that installed and operates a waste disposal facility (hereinafter referred to as the “facility at issue”) in Chuncheon-si (address omitted), with a total project area of 179,390㎡ and a landfill area of 121,901㎡. The Plaintiffs are residents living in Chuncheon-si (part omitted) near the facility at issue, and the places where the Plaintiffs reside exist within 2 km from the boundary line of the facility at issue.\\n\\n(2) On May 2, 1997, the Defendant determined the surrounding impact area following the installation of the facility at issue and publicly notified it by designating its effective period as “1998 - 2011” (hereinafter referred to as the “First Determination”). Accordingly, the surrounding impact area so determined did not include the area at issue where the Plaintiffs reside.\\n\\n(3) When the effective period designated in the First Determination expired, the Defendant, on January 1, 2012, made and publicly notified a determination stating that “in consideration of the fact that, as the facility at issue is expanded to a landfill area of 143,040㎡, a reimplementation of the environmental impact survey is necessary but a certain period of time is required therefor, the effective period of the designation of the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue is extended to December 31, 2012, while the scope of the surrounding impact area is maintained the same as before” (hereinafter referred to as the “Second Determination”).\\n\\n(4) When the effective period designated in the Second Determination expired, the Defendant, without going through the procedure of newly organizing a Support Consultative Body and consulting therewith, and without conducting a separate environmental impact survey in accordance with the intent of the Support Consultative Body organized in connection with the First Determination, on January 3, 2013, made and publicly notified a determination stating that “the scope of the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue shall remain the same as in the Second Determination, while the effective period of the surrounding impact area is extended until the date of termination of use of the facility at issue” (hereinafter referred to as the “Determination at Issue”).\\n\\nd. When the above circumstances are examined in light of the relevant statutes and legal principles discussed above, the following conclusion follows.\\n\\n(1) In the original First Determination, the Defendant designated the effective period of the determination of the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue as until 2011, and, when that effective period expired and the scale of the facility at issue was also expanded, made the Second Determination on January 1, 2012. This may be understood as acknowledging the need to conduct the environmental impact survey again and newly determine the scope of the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue, while intending to temporarily maintain the scope of the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue as before until the end of that year, taking into account that the environmental impact survey would take a certain period of time.\\n\\n(2) Even according to the contents of such Second Determination, the Defendant acknowledges that it was necessary to conduct the environmental impact survey again in 2012 and newly determine the scope of the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue. Moreover, the Determination at Issue, which again extended the effective period on the basis of the Second Determination, was made ex post facto after the effective period of the Second Determination had expired. In addition, according to Article 18(1) [Attached Table 2] of the Enforcement Decree, which was newly established after the First Determination and applies to the Determination at Issue, the Defendant should, at least when making the Determination at Issue, have reorganized the Support Consultative Body in accordance with the method of organizing the Support Consultative Body in the case of “where the surrounding impact area has not been determined and publicly notified,” namely, as “local residents residing within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility or within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility, who are resident representatives for each eup, myeon, and dong recommended by the relevant Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council,” and then, after consulting with the new Support Consultative Body regarding the conduct of the environmental impact survey and the scope of the surrounding impact area, should have determined and publicly notified the surrounding impact area of the facility at issue.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the Determination at Issue cannot be viewed as an administrative disposition merely extending only its effective period while maintaining its identity with the prior Second Determination, and the Determination at Issue made by the Defendant after the effective period of the Second Determination had expired contains the error of having failed to go through the procedure of reorganizing a new Support Consultative Body and consulting therewith.\\n\\ne. On the same grounds, the lower court held that the Defendant’s making of the Determination at Issue without going through the procedure of reorganizing a new Support Consultative Body and consulting therewith was unlawful because it violated the procedure for determining the surrounding impact area prescribed in Article 17(2) and Article 17-2(3) of the Act, and Article 18(1), (6), and (7) of the Enforcement Decree. The lower court’s determination is based on the legal principles discussed above, and there is no error of law, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the procedure for determining the surrounding impact area of a waste disposal facility.\\n\\n2. Concerning standing to sue\\n\\na. (1) A third party who is not the direct addressee of an administrative disposition and seeks cancellation or confirmation of invalidity on the ground that his or her environmental interest is infringed or likely to be infringed by such disposition must establish that his or her environmental interest is an interest individually, directly, and concretely protected by the statutes forming the basis of the disposition or by related statutes, that is, a legally protected interest, in order for standing to sue to be recognized. However, where the statutes forming the basis of the disposition or related statutes specifically provide for the range of the zone of influence expected to suffer environmental infringement due to the act, etc., business carried out by the disposition, it can be expected that residents within such zone will suffer direct and substantial environmental damage from the relevant disposition. Such environmental interest, as a direct and concrete interest individually protected for each resident, is, unless there are special circumstances, de facto presumed to be infringed or likely to be infringed, and standing to sue is recognized by recognizing it as a legally protected interest (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on Sept. 24, 2009, 2009DU2825).\\n\\n(2) Article 18(1) [Attached Table 2] Item 2 (b) of the Enforcement Decree provides that, “where the surrounding impact area has not been determined and publicly notified,” the Support Consultative Body shall be organized with “resident representatives for each eup, myeon, and dong recommended by the relevant Special Self-Governing Province, City, County, or District Council, among local residents residing within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility or within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility.”\\n\\n(3) The purport of the above provision is that, because there is a possibility that waste disposal facilities’ installation and operation may cause environmental impact within 2 km from the site boundary line of a waste landfill facility or within 300 m from the site boundary line of a waste incineration facility, resident representatives selected from among residents living within such range are to become members of the Support Consultative Body and participate in the survey of environmental impact, determination of the surrounding impact area, and determination of resident support projects, thereby enabling such residents to be compensated for environmental disadvantages arising from the installation and operation of waste disposal facilities. The interest that residents living within the above range have in connection with the determination of the surrounding impact area of a waste disposal facility is a direct and concrete interest individually protected for each resident, and, unless there are special circumstances, it is de facto presumed that such residents’ environmental interest has been infringed or is likely to be infringed, thereby giving rise to standing to sue (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on Mar. 11, 2005, 2003DU13489).\\n\\nb. The lower court determined that, since the Plaintiffs reside within 2 km from the site boundary line of the facility at issue, they have a legally protected interest in seeking cancellation of the Determination at Issue. The lower court’s determination is based on the legal principles discussed above and is proper, and there is no error of law, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning standing to sue.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating.\\n\\n[[Appendix] List of Plaintiffs: Omitted]"}

{"[89NU7900]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. The gist of the Plaintiffs’ assertion is that the Defendant, by granting permission for alteration of the structure of a lodging business so that guest rooms could be installed on part of the 4th and 5th floors of the building at issue, as stated by the court below, located at a distance of approximately 50 meters to 700 meters from the inn operated by the Plaintiffs, caused the Plaintiffs serious harm; accordingly, they seek a confirmation of nullity or revocation of the above disposition granting permission for alteration of the structure of a lodging business. However, the disadvantage the Plaintiffs will suffer from the above permission is merely an indirect, factual, or economic disadvantage, and that alone cannot be said to give the Plaintiffs a legal interest in seeking a confirmation of nullity or revocation of the above disposition granting permission for alteration of the structure of a lodging business.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality arising from an error of law, as alleged, therein.\\n\\n2. According to the record of this case, the inn building at issue, operated by the Defendant-intervenor, is located in an area designated under the city plan as a general residential area; however, its front faces a 25-meter road and its right side faces an 8-meter road, and around it, along the main road, are inns, bars, a car wash, and various shops, while at its rear, across a 6-meter road, various shops such as a beauty salon, restaurant, stationery store, and supermarket face it, so that the area in question has in fact been formed as a commercial district, and it is found only that Plaintiff Lee Eun-suk is operating a lodging business and residing there in that commercial district, while the remaining Plaintiffs are operating a lodging business and residing in a de facto residential district at the distances stated in the judgment below; there is no material to find that, as a result of the disposition granting permission for alteration of the structure of the lodging business in this case, the Defendant-intervenor’s operating a lodging business on part of the 4th and 5th floors of the building at issue infringed the Plaintiffs’ residential peace and living environment. Therefore, by issuing the above permission, the Plaintiffs cannot be said to have a legal interest in seeking confirmation of nullity or revocation of the above disposition on the ground that their residential peace and living environment were infringed. The court of first instance’s dismissal of this action on the above ground is proper, and there is no illegality arising from an error of law, as alleged, therein; accordingly, this argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, the costs of the final appeal are assessed against the losing parties, and it is so adjudicated in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: A private individual, A, while serving in the military suffered a fall accident and received treatment from military physician B, but after being medically discharged from the military, while receiving veterans’ compensation benefits pursuant to statutes, alleged that A suffered a disability due to B’s intentional act or gross negligence and filed a claim for damages against the Republic of Korea and B. During the pendency of the above proceedings, A applied for a motion to refer the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act, which limits the right of soldiers, etc. to claim state compensation, for constitutional review. Among the following explanations, which correctly combines what is correct (○) and what is incorrect (×)? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents) (a) A’s application for a motion to refer for constitutional review is subject to mandatory attorney representation because the party is a private person. (b) The judge in charge of the damages claim lawsuit filed by A must refer the provision of the State Compensation Act to the Constitutional Court for constitutional review even where the judge merely has a simple doubt as to its unconstitutionality. (c) If the motion to refer for constitutional review is dismissed, A cannot file an appeal or re-appeal by way of civil proceedings against the dismissal decision, and cannot file a special appeal either. (d) When the motion to refer for constitutional review is dismissed and A intends to file a constitutional complaint, if A lacks the financial ability to retain an attorney as representative, A may apply to the Constitutional Court for the appointment of court-appointed counsel.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2014GEU247]": "Although the Special Appellant, in respect of the appellate court’s order dismissing the Special Appellant’s application for a referral for adjudication on whether a statute is unconstitutional, filed a “petition for immediate appeal” and thereby challenged it, Article 41(4) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that no appeal may be taken from a decision concerning a referral for adjudication on whether a statute is unconstitutional, and Article 68(2) of the same Act provides only that, when an application for such a referral is dismissed, the party who made the application may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court; therefore, no appeal or re-appeal under civil procedure may be taken from an order dismissing an application for referral on the question of unconstitutionality.\\n\\nMeanwhile, whether a statute that serves as a premise for a judgment is unconstitutional is a matter that the court in charge of the case must examine ex officio, and when a party files an appeal against the principal case, the appellate court must independently examine and determine the prematurity of the statute as a premise of the judgment and whether it is unconstitutional; accordingly, an order dismissing an application for referral on the question of unconstitutionality has the nature of an intermediate judicial decision subject to appellate review together with the final judgment on the merits, and thus does not constitute a decision from which no appeal may be taken and therefore is not subject to a special appeal (see Supreme Court Order dated August 25, 1993, 93GEU34, Supreme Court Order dated January 19, 2009, 2008BU4, etc.). Therefore, the instant special appeal is improper because it is directed against a judicial decision that cannot be the subject of a special appeal.\\n\\nAccordingly, the special appeal is dismissed, and the decision is rendered as set forth in the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[93HEONGA2]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\na. Overview of the Case  \\nThe Yeoju Branch Court of the Suwon District Court, while hearing the case under Case No. 92GOHAP107,131 (consolidated), involving 17 defendants, including Defendant Gu○seo, who had been arrested and indicted on charges of bribery, etc., issued by order dated January 9, 1993, a decision granting bail to the said Defendant Gu○seo, upon the defendant’s counsel filing a motion for bail under Case No. 92CHO452.  \\nOn the 11th of the same month, the Prosecutor filed an immediate appeal against the said decision granting bail pursuant to Article 97(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act. Accordingly, the said court, finding that there was a suspicion of unconstitutionality with respect to Article 97(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides for the Prosecutor’s right to take an immediate appeal against a decision granting bail, made an ex officio referral for this constitutional review on the 15th of the same month.  \\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\nAccordingly, the subject matter of this adjudication is whether the portion of Article 97(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act (Law No. 341, September 23, 1954; amended by Law No. 2450, January 25, 1973) that provides that the Prosecutor may take an immediate appeal against a decision granting bail (hereinafter abbreviated as the “provision at issue”) is in violation of the Constitution, and the content of the said provision is as follows.  \\nArticle 97 [Revocation of Bail and Detention, and Prosecutor’s Opinion]  \\n①② Omitted  \\n③ The Prosecutor may take an immediate appeal against a decision granting bail and a decision revoking detention.  \\n\\nc. Status of Proceedings After the Referral for Constitutional Review in This Case  \\nMeanwhile, after the referring court made the referral for constitutional review in this case, it transmitted the record of the immediate appeal case concerning the said decision granting bail in Case No. 92CHO452 to the appellate court, the Seoul High Court, and, with respect to the merits case on bribery, etc. in Case No. 92GOHAP107,131 (consolidated), it rendered, on the 18th of the same month, a judgment sentencing Defendant Gu○seo to imprisonment for 2 years, suspended for 3 years.  \\nThe appellate court, by order dated February 9 of the same year, dismissed the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal.  \\n\\n2. Grounds for the Referral for Constitutional Review and the Opinions of Interested Parties  \\na.
