Grounds for the Referral for Constitutional Review by the Referring Court  \\nThe provision at issue in Article 97(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which recognizes the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right, having suspensive effect, against a court’s decision granting bail, may, by unduly restricting the defendant’s right to apply for bail, which is guaranteed as an embodiment of the constitutional principle of the presumption of innocence, violate Article 27(1) of the Constitution, which provides for the people’s right to receive a trial in accordance with law, and Article 103 of the Constitution, which provides for the independence of the judiciary, by allowing room for the Prosecutor to intervene in judicial proceedings.  \\n\\nb. Opinion of Counsel for Defendant Gu○seo  \\nThe provision at issue is improper in that, first, it causes the undue result that whether the detention of a defendant who has received a decision granting bail is maintained is determined by whether the Prosecutor, the opposing party to the defendant in criminal procedure, takes an immediate appeal; second, by suspending the execution of a decision granting bail through the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal, it runs counter to the original purpose of the bail system and unduly restricts the defendant’s application for bail; and third, although no Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right is recognized against a detention review decision for a suspect, it is unbalanced in that it allows suspension of the execution of a decision granting bail to a defendant whose detention period is longer than that of a suspect.  \\nAccordingly, the provision at issue is in violation not only of substantive justification but also of Article 12(1) and (3) of the Constitution, which provide for the principle of due process, and Article 27(4) of the Constitution, which provides for the principle of presumption of innocence.  \\n\\nc. Opinion of the Minister of Justice and the Chief of the Yeoju Branch Office of the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office  \\n(1) Impropriety of the Referral for Constitutional Review  \\nUnder our constitutional adjudication system, which adopts a concrete norm-control procedure, for a court to refer a statute for review of constitutionality, there must, at the time of referral, be a concrete dispute case pending before that court, and the constitutionality of the law applicable to that case must be a premise of the adjudication. However, the referring court in this case has no authority to make any determination regarding the appeal case itself, since, in the appeal case regarding the decision granting bail, it can only determine whether the immediate appeal is defective in formal requirements, such as whether it violates the statutory form, and therefore is not in a position to make a referral concerning the constitutionality of the provision at issue. Thus, the referral for constitutional review in this case is improper, having been made by a court lacking standing to make such a referral.  \\nIn addition, because the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal was filed only after the court’s decision granting bail, the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal could not have had any effect whatsoever on the referring court’s decision to grant bail. Moreover, even if the fact that the defendant was not immediately released despite the decision granting bail had affected the trial, that would be merely due to the suspensive effect accompanying the immediate appeal. Accordingly, the constitutionality of the said provision, which is the subject of the referral for constitutional review in this case, does not become a premise or preliminary issue in deriving the dispositive part when the referring court adjudicates matters concerning bail; therefore, this referral for constitutional review in this case is improper for lack of necessity of adjudication.  \\nFurthermore, a court may refer a question of constitutionality only where it is manifest beyond reasonable doubt, from an objectively reasonable perspective, that the law violates the Constitution. However, the referring court made this referral for constitutional review in this case merely on the ground that it had “doubts” as to the proposition that the provision at issue violates the Constitution, and in this respect as well it is improper.  \\n\\n(2) Constitutionality of the Provision at Issue  \\n(a) So long as a law admits of interpretation in conformity with the spirit of the Constitution, it must not be hastily held unconstitutional. The Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right against a decision granting bail was discussed only as a matter of legislative policy with respect to whether to introduce it, and there was no dispute as to its constitutionality. This is because it was judged to conform not only to the constitutional spirit of checks and balances of powers, but also to the principle of equality of parties adopted by the current Criminal Procedure Act, and because it was deemed necessary as an immediate remedy system for securing the defendant’s appearance, which is indispensable for securing custody. Therefore, the provision at issue, which admits of interpretation consistent with the Constitution as above, cannot be said to be in violation of the Constitution.  \\n(b) In criminal procedure, physical detention is an indispensable system within the minimum scope necessary to discover the substantive truth. Recognizing the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right against a court’s decision granting bail is intended to ensure caution in the court’s judgment on bail decisions and to check that judicial decisions are not made at a judge’s discretion. Therefore, it does not violate the principle of presumption of innocence.  \\n(c) In criminal procedure, the Prosecutor has not only the position of the opposing party to the defendant but also the authority, as representative of the public interest, to seek the lawful application of statutes and regulations. Therefore, it cannot be said that recognizing the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right to seek correction of a court’s arbitrary decision granting bail infringes the people’s right to a trial.  \\nIn addition, the detention review system and the bail system are fundamentally different in history and purpose, although they are the same only in that they release a detained suspect or defendant. Therefore, it cannot be said to be inconsistent with equity to recognize an immediate appeal with respect to bail on the ground that no objection is permitted against a detention review decision, and whether to recognize the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right against a decision granting bail is a matter of legislative policy.  \\nMoreover, the provision at issue, which allows the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right against a decision granting bail, was newly established when the Criminal Procedure Act was amended in 1973. In light of the fact that, before the immediate appeal right was allowed, the bail application rate among detained defendants from 1970 to 1972 was only 7.8%, whereas the bail application rate from 1982 to 1991, after the immediate appeal right was allowed, reached 20.9%, it cannot be said that the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right restricts the defendant’s or defense counsel’s right to apply for bail.  \\n(d) The independence of the judiciary means only that a judge exercising judicial power, when adjudicating a concrete case, is not bound by instructions or orders from outside, thereby securing fair and proper adjudication; it does not mean that adjudication by a judge’s arbitrariness or self-will is permitted. The appellate system is intended to correct errors in fact-finding or application of law in the original trial, and it may be said to be a system that faithfully supplements the independence of the judiciary. Therefore, where a decision granting bail contains an error, recognizing in the Prosecutor, who is both a party on one side of the criminal proceedings and a representative of the public interest, the right to take an immediate appeal, which is a form of appeal, cannot be said to infringe the independence of the judiciary.  \\nAnd because the suspensive effect arising from the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal comes into existence after the court’s judgment, that is, after the decision granting bail, the exercise of that immediate appeal right cannot be said to intervene in the trial.  \\n\\n3. Decision  \\na. Whether the Referral for Constitutional Review Is Lawful  \\n(1) First, we examine whether the constitutionality of the provision at issue constitutes a proper subject of adjudication in relation to the premise of adjudication.  \\n(a) According to Article 107(1) of the Constitution and Article 41(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, where the constitutionality of a law becomes a premise of adjudication, the court is to refer the question of constitutionality to the Constitutional Court. Therefore, for a referral for constitutional review of a law to be lawful, it must satisfy the premise of adjudication, namely that the constitutionality of the law at issue be a premise of adjudication.  \\nHere, the premise of adjudication ordinarily means that ① a concrete case must be pending before the court, ② the law whose constitutionality is at issue must be applicable to the case in question, and ③ depending on whether that law violates the Constitution, the court handling the case in question will render a different judgment. The phrase “render a different judgment” ordinarily includes not only cases where the constitutionality of the law at issue affects the conclusion or dispositive part of the adjudication of the case being heard by the court, but also cases where, even if the constitutionality of the law at issue does not affect the dispositive part itself at all, it is related to giving different reasons leading to the conclusion of the adjudication, or where the legal meaning concerning the content and effect of the adjudication differs (see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONGA8, rendered December 24, 1992; Decision 92HEONGA10, 91HEONBA7, 92HEONBA24, 50 (consolidated), rendered May 13, 1993; Decision 89HEONGA98 through 101 (consolidated), rendered June 25, 1990, etc.). And, in principle, the above premise of adjudication must be satisfied not only at the time of referral for review of constitutionality of a law, but also at the time of adjudication.  \\n(b) Bail is a pre-judgment procedural matter, but under Article 403(2) and Article 402 of the Criminal Procedure Act, if there is an objection to a decision concerning bail, an appeal may be taken. And the provision at issue provides that the Prosecutor may take an immediate appeal against a decision granting bail. Meanwhile, according to Article 409 of the same Act, an ordinary appeal other than an immediate appeal does not, in principle, have the effect of staying execution of the judgment, and only where the court of original jurisdiction or the appellate court has rendered a decision to stay execution does it have the effect of staying execution until a decision on the appeal is rendered. According to Articles 404 and 405 of the same Act, the filing period for an ordinary appeal, which in principle does not have the effect of staying execution, may be filed at any time so long as there is a practical interest in revoking the decision concerning bail, whereas the filing period for an immediate appeal is 3 days. However, whether it is an ordinary appeal or an immediate appeal, where an appeal is filed, the court of original jurisdiction shall dismiss it pursuant to Article 407(1) of the same Act if the appeal was filed in violation of statutory form or if it is manifest that the right of appeal has lapsed; if it recognizes that the appeal is meritorious, it shall amend the decision pursuant to Article 408(1) of the same Act; and if it recognizes that all or part of the appeal is without merit, it shall, pursuant to paragraph (2) of the same Article, transmit the record to the appellate court with a statement of reasons attached within 3 days from the date on which it received the petition of appeal. Here, even when the court of original jurisdiction recognizes under Article 408(2) of the same Act that all or part of the appeal is without merit, it is in substance a judgment of the court of original jurisdiction in the sense that it involves a judge’s adjudicative function, and the statement of reasons shall in substance be the statement of the reasons therefor. And in the event this provision is adjudged unconstitutional, the court of original jurisdiction will process the immediate appeal in this case by converting it into an ordinary appeal under Article 404 of the same Act. If the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional, compared with the period before it was so adjudged, the procedural legal relationship will be different and the court will render a different judgment. That is, (a) as to the standard for adjudicating whether there is grounds for dismissal under Article 407 of the same Act, there will necessarily be a difference in the requirements for filing an appeal or immediate appeal, such as the appeal period, between the case where the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional and the case where it is not. Therefore, when the court of original jurisdiction applies that Article, depending on whether the provision at issue is confirmed unconstitutional, the dispositive part of the judgment may differ. (b) On the other hand, when the court of original jurisdiction applies Article 408(1) of the same Act, formally there would be no difference whether the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional or not, so there would be no difference in the dispositive part itself, and the dispositive part at such time would be to revoke the decision granting bail or to alter the conditions for granting bail. However, in the case of an immediate appeal, there is the effect of staying execution of the judgment, whereas in the case of an ordinary appeal there is not, so whether in the former case or the latter case, the basic reasons would differ between the case where the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional and the case where it is not, in the statement of reasons leading to that decision, and the direct content and effect of the judgment would also differ. Therefore, when the court of original jurisdiction applies Article 408(1) of the same Act, in all such cases, depending on whether the provision at issue is confirmed unconstitutional, although the dispositive part of the judgment itself is not affected, there will be a difference in the statement of reasons leading to the conclusion of the judgment and in the legal meaning of the content and effect of the correction decision. (c) Also, when the court of original jurisdiction transmits the record under Article 408(2) of the same Act upon recognizing that all or part of the appeal is without merit, formally there is no difference in the action of the court of original jurisdiction depending on whether the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional, but depending on whether the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional, there will likewise be a difference in the reasons leading to the conclusion of that action and in the legal meaning of the effect of that action.  \\nAccordingly, it is clear that the constitutionality of the provision at issue is a premise of the adjudication and other measures to be taken by the referring court as the court of original jurisdiction with respect to the immediate appeal in this case.  \\nTherefore, it may be said that the constitutionality of the provision at issue had the premise of adjudication at the time of referral, and that it was referred by a court having proper referral authority.  \\n(c) However, as noted above, after the referring court made the referral for constitutional review in this case, it transmitted the record of the immediate appeal case to the appellate court, and the appellate court, by decision dismissing the appeal, rendered the immediate appeal case in this matter concluded before the Constitutional Court adjudicated the constitutionality of the provision at issue. Therefore, it may be said that, at the time of adjudication, the premise of adjudication had disappeared, and we examine the lawfulness of this adjudication in relation thereto.  \\n(d) The Court has previously held, in a constitutional complaint against a law, that “even where the infringing act has already ended and there is no room to revoke it, so that the constitutional complaint would not be of much help in providing subjective relief of rights, if there is a risk that such infringing act will be repeated in the future or if resolution of the dispute in question is a matter of urgency for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, so that the elucidation thereof has constitutionally significant meaning, the interest in a constitutional complaint should be recognized” (see Constitutional Court Decision 90HEONMA82, rendered April 14, 1992, etc.). This legal doctrine should likewise be respected in the procedure of reviewing the constitutionality of laws by referral from a court as a concrete norm-control. Therefore, if the fundamental right infringed by the statutory provision referred for constitutional review is important and the elucidation of the constitutionality of that statutory provision is constitutionally significant, yet no elucidation is provided, or if there is a risk that the infringement of the fundamental right caused by that statutory provision will be repeated but opportunities to review the constitutionality of that statutory provision are difficult to obtain, then even if the case in question has concluded during the period of deliberation due to subsequent developments, as long as the premise of adjudication was recognized at the time of referral, the Constitutional Court should, exceptionally, recognize the necessity of adjudication for the sake of protecting and maintaining the objective constitutional order and actively determine the constitutionality thereof. This also accords with the very reason for the existence of the Constitutional Court and constitutes the faithful performance of its duty.  \\n(e) The provision at issue concerns a matter related to the people’s physical restraint, namely the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right, having suspensive effect, against a court’s decision granting bail. The question of its constitutionality cannot but be an important constitutional issue concerning the people’s freedom of the person, which may be called the most fundamental of fundamental rights, and no elucidation on that issue has been provided by the Constitutional Court. Moreover, unless the provision at issue is adjudged unconstitutional, it is clear from the text of the law that, whenever a court grants bail, the infringement of the freedom of the person, an important fundamental right, will be repeated by operation of the provision at issue.  \\nIn addition, since the period during which a party receives a decision from the court of original jurisdiction or appellate court without undergoing the procedure of constitutional review on the provision at issue is ordinarily shorter than the period during which the party undergoes the procedure of constitutional review and waits for the adjudication, it is difficult to expect that the court or the defendant will make or request a referral for constitutional review of the provision at issue in a situation where bail has been granted but the defendant remains detained due to the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal, so this is a case in which opportunities to seek review of the constitutionality of the provision at issue are unlikely to arise again. And the provision at issue is a procedural rule concerning whether a defendant is detained under the Criminal Procedure Act. The court regarded it as having no effect on the final judgment itself and therefore the concrete merits judgment itself proceeded as it was and has already concluded; however, as noted above, at the time of the referral for constitutional review, the constitutionality of the provision at issue was a premise of the court of original jurisdiction’s judgment in the immediate appeal case concerning the decision granting bail, which was pending before the referring court. Therefore, the Constitutional Court, which has as one of its duties the protection and maintenance of the objective constitutional order, should recognize that there is a necessity to adjudicate the constitutionality of the referred provision, and adjudicating it accordingly fulfills that duty and is lawful.  \\n(2) Furthermore, the purport of Article 107(1) of the Constitution and Articles 41 (Referral for Review of Constitutionality), 43 (Matters to Be Stated in the Referral) of the Constitutional Court Act, etc., is that where the statutory provision in question gives rise to a reasonable suspicion of unconstitutionality beyond mere doubt based on the judge’s own legal view, the court is to refer the question of constitutionality. And the Constitutional Court, to the extent possible, respects this autonomous judgment of the referring court, accepts the referral application, and renders a constitutional determination. Therefore, this referral in this case cannot be said to be improper.  \\n\\nb. Whether the Provision at Issue Violates the Constitution  \\n(1) First, we examine the outline of the provision at issue.  \\nArticle 402 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “if there is an objection to a decision of a court, an appeal may be taken, except where the Act otherwise provides.” Article 403(1) of the same Act provides that appeals may not be taken against pre-judgment proceedings, but paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that appeals may be taken against decisions concerning bail, even though they are pre-judgment proceedings. Moreover, Article 97(3) of the same Act, which is the provision at issue, provides that the Prosecutor may take an immediate appeal against a decision granting bail. And according to Article 405 of the same Act, the filing period for an immediate appeal is 3 days, and according to Article 410 of the same Act, during the filing period for this immediate appeal and when it is filed, execution is stayed until the appellate review decision on the immediate appeal becomes final. Therefore, by recognizing in the Prosecutor, pursuant to the provision at issue, the right to take an immediate appeal against a decision granting bail, execution of the decision granting bail is unconditionally stayed not only during the filing period for the immediate appeal but also, if an immediate appeal is filed, until the appellate review decision on that appeal becomes final. As a result, even if a decision granting bail has been rendered, the defendant cannot be released and remains continuously detained, with the freedom of the person continually restricted. Such provision at issue was newly enacted when the so-called Yushin Constitution was proclaimed in 1972 and the Criminal Procedure Act was amended on January 25, 1973 by the Emergency State Council, not by the National Assembly, and it is a provision unprecedented in any of the so-called developed countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, or Japan.  \\n\\n(2) We next examine the freedom of the person and the constitutional provisions guaranteeing it, as well as the purpose of the bail system.  \\n(a) The first sentence of Article 12(1) of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall enjoy freedom of the person,” thereby constituting it as a constitutional fundamental right so as to respect to the greatest extent the freedom of the person, which is the premise of the freedom of movement of all citizens. This freedom of the person is the most basic freedom and an important fundamental right that forms the root of all social, economic, and spiritual freedoms. When freedom of the person is restricted, the right to pursue happiness in the family and society is lost, economic life including employment relationships and business relationships is destroyed, as are all social and spiritual aspects of life, and there may be cases where a presumption of guilt is cast by others, leaving an indelible stigma on one’s personal honor and future employment; in relation to criminal prosecution, one may become unable to sufficiently prepare a defense, such as collecting evidence favorable to oneself; the court may be led to have prejudice in determining guilt or innocence; in the investigation or trial process, one may impede a fair trial by making an involuntary confession in order to quickly regain freedom of the person; and the family’s livelihood may also fall into hardship. Thus, the constitutional spirit declaring in Article 12(1) that all citizens’ freedom of the person shall be guaranteed is to ensure the maximum protection of the freedom of person of suspects and defendants. As an embodiment of this constitutional spirit, the principle is that suspects or defendants should proceed, as far as possible, without restriction of freedom of the person in criminal procedure during the investigation or trial stage, and there are various institutional safeguards to ensure the greatest possible protection of freedom of the person in the procedures leading to detention and after detention. (In light of this constitutional spirit, it is also required that, in interpreting and applying statutes concerning physical restraint, interpretation and application conform to the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of freedom of the person.)  \\n(b) Accordingly, even in cases where, for unavoidable reasons in the realization of the state’s punitive power, a suspect or defendant must be detained to prevent flight, to collect and secure evidence for maintaining the prosecution, and to prevent destruction of evidence, Article 12(1), second sentence, of the Constitution provides that “No citizen shall be arrested, detained, seized, searched, or subjected to interrogation except as provided by law, nor shall anyone be punished, placed under security measures, or subjected to forced labor except pursuant to due process of law,” and Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “When arresting, detaining, seizing, or searching, a warrant issued by a judge upon application by a prosecutor in accordance with due process of law shall be presented. However, in case of flagrante delicto or where there is concern that a person who has committed a crime punishable by imprisonment for more than 3 years will flee or destroy evidence, a warrant may be requested afterward.” Thus, it clearly states that due process of law and the warrant principle must be observed when restricting freedom of the person by detention, etc. This principle of due process is one that developed in the common-law countries as one of the basic principles for guaranteeing human rights, and historically it has been codified through the Magna Carta of England (1215), the Statute of Edward III (1335), the Petition of Right (1628), etc., and established as a basic principle of the United States Constitution through the Fifth Amendment (1791) and the Fourteenth Amendment (1868). Today, correspondingly, it has been established in civil-law countries as the principle of the rule of law or the principle of legal reservation in restrictions on fundamental rights. We first codified it in the current Constitution, revised for the ninth time on October 29, 1987, and its content is that, in matters such as physical restraint, the provisions of law must be observed, and such laws must be appropriate laws with rationality and justification in both procedural and substantive respects (see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONGA8, rendered December 24, 1992). Therefore, by legal provisions that lack rationality and justification both procedurally and substantively, the freedom of the person of a suspect or defendant cannot be restricted. And whether this law is rational and justified procedurally and substantively must be strictly examined. The warrant principle derives from this principle of due process and means that arrest, detention, and even seizure and search must, under Article 103 of the Constitution, be decided only by judges who adjudicate in accordance with the Constitution and laws and in conscience, and whose status is guaranteed by the principle of independence of the judiciary. It also means that not only the deprivation of freedom of the person at the point when detention begins, but also the decision whether to continue, suspend, or extinguish the validity of that detention warrant, must be made solely by such judicial determination (see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONGA8, rendered December 24, 1992). Therefore, if the effect of a court composed of judges having plenary authority over detention, or of a judge, in respect of whether to detain a suspect or defendant and whether to maintain detention, were to be controlled or restricted merely because there is disagreement or objection from the Prosecutor or any other institution, that would violate the warrant principle and thus also the principle of due process. And even after arrest or detention pursuant to a detention warrant issued by a judge, in order to embody the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of freedom of the person, although bail at the investigation stage like that in foreign countries is not recognized, the Constitution itself has provisions to maximize the guarantee of freedom of the person, such as Article 12(4) and (6), which provide the right to assistance of counsel and the right to request a detention review from the court.  \\nAs to post-indictment matters as well, Article 27(1) of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall have the right to receive a trial in accordance with law by judges established by the Constitution and laws,” thereby guaranteeing to defendants the right to receive a fair trial in accordance with due process of law, while Article 27(4) of the same Article provides that “A criminal defendant shall be presumed innocent until a judgment of guilt has become final and conclusive,” thereby proclaiming the principle of presumption of innocence.  \\n(c) Nevertheless, for a defendant who is detained, it is extremely difficult to prepare a defense, so the right to a fair trial is easily infringed, and, as noted above, one may be presumed guilty by others, and suffer great loss in many respects, such as loss of the pursuit of happiness through family and social activities. Therefore, for the realization of the principle of trial without detention based on the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of the freedom of the person, the warrant principle, the right to a fair trial, and the principle of presumption of innocence, the Criminal Procedure Act establishes a bail system by which a court composed of one or three judges may release the defendant from detention under conditions such as payment of bail, thereby allowing the defendant to prepare sufficiently for trial while pursuing happiness in all family, social, and other aspects through free bodily activity. That is, Article 95 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides for compulsory bail, under which, where there is a motion for bail, the court composed of the above-mentioned judges, who have plenary authority over detention, must grant bail unless the case falls under the exclusion grounds listed in that Article (① where the defendant has committed an offense punishable by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or imprisonment without prison labor for more than 10 years; ② where the defendant has committed a repeat offense or habitual offense; ③ where there are sufficient grounds to believe that the defendant has destroyed or may destroy evidence; ④ where there are sufficient grounds to believe that the defendant has fled or may flee; and ⑤ where the defendant’s residence is not clear), by considering the nature of the offense, the circumstances of the offense, the probative value of the evidence, the defendant’s prior convictions, character, environment, and assets, as prescribed in Articles 98 and 99 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and by setting an amount of bail that the defendant can pay and even adding appropriate conditions, such as restricting the defendant’s residence, so as to ensure the defendant’s appearance in subsequent criminal proceedings. And, on the premise that this compulsory bail is the rule, even where it does not apply, Article 96 of the same Act provides that when the court composed of the above-mentioned judges itself determines that, in light of reasonable grounds—namely, in light of the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of the freedom of the person, the guarantee of the defendant’s right to a fair trial based on the principle of equality of parties, and the principle of presumption of innocence—it is proper to grant bail and try the case without detention, it may, upon the motion of the person entitled to request it under Article 94 of the Criminal Procedure Act or ex officio, grant bail under certain conditions such as bail money and release the defendant.  \\n\\n(3) Here, we examine whether the provision at issue violates the warrant principle and other principles of due process of law.  \\n(a) As noted above, the bail system is a system that implements the warrant principle based on the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of the freedom of the person, which is the most basic of fundamental rights, by allowing a court composed of independent judges, having plenary authority over detention and whether it continues, to determine for itself whether a case falls under compulsory bail prescribed in Article 95 of the Criminal Procedure Act, whether there are reasonable grounds for bail under Article 96 of the same Act, and the amount of bail and other conditions sufficient to ensure the defendant’s appearance, thereby releasing the defendant from detention and allowing the defendant to be tried without detention. The warrant principle realized by the bail system, as already noted above, is the principle that arrest, detention, and even seizure and search may be made only by decision of judges who, under Article 103 of the Constitution, adjudicate in accordance with the Constitution and laws and in conscience, and whose status is guaranteed by the principle of independence of the judiciary. It is the principle that only such judges may decide the deprivation, permission, continuation, or release of freedom. Therefore, if the effect of a decision granting bail, in which such a court composed of judges having plenary authority over detention has itself determined and decided whether there is necessity to maintain detention under this warrant principle, is controlled, restricted, or infringed merely because the Prosecutor or some other state institution disagrees or objects, that would violate this warrant principle and the principle of due process, as noted above. Nevertheless, the provision at issue provides that execution of a decision granting bail made by such a court as an embodiment of this warrant principle is unconditionally stayed for the 3-day period for filing an immediate appeal and, where the Prosecutor has filed an immediate appeal, until the judgment on that immediate appeal becomes final, so that the defendant cannot be released and must remain detained, with freedom of the person continually deprived. As a result, the provision at issue gives priority to the Prosecutor’s objection that the decision granting bail for the defendant in question is improper over the court’s judgment that there is no need to continue detention of that defendant, and it violates the warrant principle noted above, which seeks, on the basis of the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of the freedom of the person, to entrust the question whether to detain and whether to continue detention only to the decision of a judge whose independence is guaranteed under Article 103 of the Constitution.  \\n(b) As noted above, the bail system has the purpose of implementing the principle of trial without detention, based on the constitutional spirit of maximizing the guarantee of the freedom of the person, by staying execution of the detention warrant under conditions such as payment of bail sufficient to ensure the defendant’s appearance in each subsequent proceeding, and of guaranteeing the right to a fair trial under Article 27(1) of the Constitution while realizing, under the principle of equality of parties, the defendant’s right to pursue happiness under Article 10 of the Constitution in all family, social, and other aspects through free bodily activity and while preparing sufficiently for trial, such as by collecting evidence, and of realizing the principle of presumption of innocence under Article 27(4) of the Constitution. Yet, under the provision at issue, execution of every decision granting bail made for such purposes is uniformly and unconditionally stayed under Article 410 of the same Act during the 3-day immediate appeal period prescribed in Article 405 of the Criminal Procedure Act for the Prosecutor’s objection, which may be regarded as the position of one party in criminal proceedings, and, where the Prosecutor has taken an immediate appeal, until the appellate review decision on that immediate appeal becomes final. Therefore, the content of the provision at issue uniformly impedes the realization of the constitutionally significant purpose of guaranteeing or implementing the important fundamental rights and constitutional principles noted above, which are to be achieved through bail, at the sacrifice of the defendant, the opposing party in criminal proceedings, for the objection of the one party. Moreover, as noted in (a) above, the provision at issue also contravenes the warrant principle concerning physical restraint. Therefore, this provision cannot but be a legal provision that restricts the defendant’s freedom of the person while lacking rationality and justification in its content. As noted above, the principle of due process is that the defendant’s freedom of the person cannot be restricted by legal provisions lacking rationality and justification both procedurally and substantively. Accordingly, the provision at issue is a legal provision contrary to the principle of due process.  \\n(4) Finally, we examine whether the provision at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction.  \\nArticle 37(2) of the Constitution proclaims the principle against excessive restriction in legislation by providing that “All freedoms and rights of citizens may be restricted by law only where necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even where they are restricted, the essential content of freedom and rights may not be infringed.” This principle against excessive restriction means the basic principle or limit of legislative activity that must be observed when the state engages in legislative activity restricting fundamental rights of citizens, and it requires securing the legitimacy of the legislative purpose, the appropriateness of the means to achieve that purpose, the minimum necessary infringement resulting from legislation, and the balance between the legal interests sought to be protected by the legislation and the interests infringed thereby; it is one of the constitutional basic principles derived from the principle of the rule of law (see Constitutional Court Decision 88HEONGA13, rendered December 22, 1989; Decision 89HEONGA95, rendered September 3, 1990, etc.). Therefore, in exercising legislative power concerning the detention system, which restricts the especially important freedom of the person among the fundamental rights of citizens guaranteed by the Constitution, this principle must be observed, and any violation thereof would be a violation of the Constitution.  \\nHowever, recognizing in the Prosecutor the immediate appeal right prescribed in the provision at issue is said to constitute a restriction on the defendant’s constitutionally guaranteed freedom of the person, in order to prevent the defendant, after unlawful bail, from fleeing or destroying evidence, thereby causing obstruction to the progress of the trial and a fair trial, or causing disruption in the execution of the sentence.  \\nAccording to Article 402 of the Criminal Procedure Act, if there is an objection to a decision of a court, an appeal may be taken except where the same Act specially provides otherwise. Pursuant to Article 403(2) of the same Act, an objection may also be taken to a decision on a motion for bail, which is a pre-judgment procedural matter. Such an appeal (hereinafter called an ordinary appeal) does not automatically have the effect of staying execution of the judgment, and the effect of staying execution arises only when a decision to stay execution is specially rendered pursuant to the proviso of Article 409 of the same Act. However, permitting only such an ordinary appeal against a bail decision as to the defendant, while recognizing against the Prosecutor, who is the opposing party to the defendant, an immediate appeal having the effect of staying execution by operation of law, violates the principle of equality of parties and the principle of fairness. And the need to secure the defendant’s custody can be achieved by payment of bail sufficient to ensure appearance, restriction of residence, and the addition of other conditions. If the Prosecutor deems that there remains a risk of destruction of evidence or flight, the Prosecutor may assert and substantiate this in expressing an opinion under Article 97(1) of the same Act, thereby preventing improper bail or inducing the court to set a more appropriate bail amount or other conditions for securing the defendant’s custody. If correction of or stay of execution for a decision granting bail is truly necessary, the purpose could also be achieved by taking an ordinary appeal and requesting a stay of execution pursuant to the proviso of Article 409 of the same Act. Therefore, recognizing in the Prosecutor an immediate appeal right under the guise of securing the defendant’s custody or correcting an improper bail decision cannot be said to have appropriateness of means. And even though the purpose could be achieved by an ordinary appeal by the Prosecutor, permitting the Prosecutor an immediate appeal right cannot be said to have appropriateness of means. Moreover, recognizing the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right even though the purpose could be achieved by an ordinary appeal by the Prosecutor is a method that imposes a severe burden on the defendant unnecessary for achieving the purpose, so the provision at issue cannot be said to satisfy the minimum necessary infringement and balance of legal interests either. Therefore, the provision at issue also violates the principle against excessive restriction and thus violates Article 37(2) of the Constitution.  \\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nIn the end, the provision at issue violates the principle of due process and the warrant principle concerning physical restraint as provided in Article 12(1) and (3) of the Constitution, and also violates the principle against excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution; therefore, by the unanimous opinion of all the participating Justices, it is decided as stated in the order. However, Justice Byun Jeong-su has a concurring opinion as set forth in section “5.”  \\n\\n5. Concurring Opinion of Justice Byun Jeong-su  \\na. There is no doubt that the provision of Article 97(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right against a decision granting bail, is an unconstitutional law that violates the constitutional principle of due process, the warrant principle concerning physical restraint, and the principle against excessive restriction on the limitation of fundamental rights, as explained in the constitutional analysis above. Moreover, the said statutory provision contains anti-human rights elements highly likely to be abused for the purpose of delaying the execution of a lawful decision granting bail, and thus it also violates the principle of presumption of innocence, which is the constitutional binding principle securing the maximum protection of human dignity and value (Article 10 of the Constitution) and freedom of the person (Article 12 of the Constitution), which form the basis of the bail system, as well as the principle of trial without detention, which is the embodiment of this principle in criminal procedure (Article 27(4) of the Constitution).  \\nb. However, such constitutional reasoning presupposes that the bail system is thoroughly observed and operated in accordance with its original legislative intent and explicit provisions. The bail system is an institutional mechanism for the protection of human rights, and, unless a case falls under the exceptions prescribed in Article 95 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is a kind of binding act in which the court has an obligation to grant bail when bail is requested. Although, under the Criminal Procedure Act, bail, especially compulsory bail, is at once the defendant’s right and the court’s duty, it cannot be denied that in practice the question of whether to grant bail has been operated, in some respects, as though it were a great prerogative of the court, and as though granting bail were conferring some form of grace or favor, in an arbitrary or self-righteous manner. By abusing the court’s discretion prescribed as an exception to compulsory bail and granting bail in cases inappropriate for bail, the judiciary fostered public distrust in justice (and it was for this reason that the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal system came into being). Such arbitrary exercise of discretion by the court in the operation of the bail system not only renders the purpose of compulsory bail under Article 95 of the Criminal Procedure Act meaningless, but also undermines predictability in the legal life of the people, resulting in consequences contrary to the constitutional principles of equality and presumption of innocence.  \\nAccordingly, in order for the constitutional reasoning concerning the Prosecutor’s immediate appeal right against a decision granting bail under Article 97(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act to be persuasive, I emphasize as a premise that the court must humbly accept the legislative purpose of the bail system and, indeed, operate it fairly according to law.  \\n\\n1993. 11. 23."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning impeachment trials is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: To recognize the interest in impeachment adjudication, it is necessary for the respondent to retain the relevant public office until the time the impeachment decision is pronounced.
B: Even if the respondent was lawfully impeached while holding public office at the time of the impeachment motion, if the respondent retires from that office during the pendency of the impeachment trial, this constitutes a ground that bars the continuation of the adjudicative proceedings, and therefore a declaration of termination of the adjudicative proceedings must be made in the operative part.
C: The Constitution expressly states the grounds for impeachment as “violation of the Constitution or laws,” and by assigning jurisdiction over impeachment trials to the Constitutional Court, it defines the impeachment procedure not as a political adjudicative procedure but as a normative adjudicative procedure; accordingly, it reveals that the purpose of the impeachment trial procedure is removal “based on legal violations rather than political reasons.”
D: A decision of removal under the impeachment trial procedure deprives a high-ranking public official of the executive branch or the judiciary who is the respondent of public office, and this constitutes a restriction on the right to hold public office.
E: Removal by the Constitutional Court’s impeachment decision does not amount to an unjust deprivation of public office, provided that its requirements and procedures are observed, and it does not undermine the balance under the principle of separation of powers.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2004HEONNA1]": "[Appendix 1] List of agents of the Impeachment Prosecutor: Omitted  \\n[Appendix 2] List of agents of the Respondent: Omitted  \\n[Appendix 3] Full text of the National Assembly’s Impeachment Resolution\\n\\nImpeachment Resolution Against President (Roh Moo-hyun)\\n\\nOrder\\n\\nAt the 2nd plenary session of the 246th National Assembly (extraordinary session) (2004. 3. 12), with the approval pursuant to Article 65, paragraph 2, of the Constitution, the impeachment of President (Roh Moo-hyun) is proposed.\\n\\nPerson subject to impeachment\\n\\nName: Roh Moo-hyun (盧武鉉)  \\nPosition: President\\n\\nGrounds for Impeachment\\n\\nPresident Roh Moo-hyun has forgotten his duty as Head of State to uphold the Constitution and laws, and has continued illegal election campaigns for a specific political party. As a result, on 2004. 3. 3., for the first time in constitutional history, he received a determination and warning from the National Election Commission, a constitutional body, that an incumbent President had violated the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act. Nevertheless, instead of reflecting, he ignored this warning and stated that he would continue to openly support a specific political party regardless of the election law, thereby displaying an extra-constitutional and extra-legal dictator-like attitude that directly denies the rule of law, the foundation of democratic constitutional government. The National Assembly cannot leave such a situation denying the rule of law unaddressed. In addition, President Roh Moo-hyun brought about a national crisis in which the State could not be normally administered due to the severe power-related corruption of himself and his close aides, and political instability caused by President Roh Moo-hyun’s insincere performance of duty and reckless administration has brought State affairs to the brink of collapse, plunging the people into extreme misfortune. Thus, it has become manifest that President Roh Moo-hyun no longer has the qualifications or ability to govern the country, and therefore this impeachment motion has been introduced to uphold the Constitution and for the happiness of the people and the future of the nation; the three specific grounds are as follows.\\n\\nFirst, President Roh Moo-hyun has continuously violated the Constitution and laws, thereby disturbing the national legal order.\\n\\n(a) As the National Election Commission determined on 2004. 3. 3. that President Roh Moo-hyun’s recent remarks violated the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act, President Roh Moo-hyun, at a joint press conference held at the Blue House on 2004. 2. 18. with six media outlets from the Gyeongin region, stated, “If even the minimum line to block constitutional amendment collapses, I really cannot tell you what will happen afterward,” thereby intimidating the people and inducing support for a specific political party. At the presidential press conference invited by the Broadcast Journalists Club, which was broadcast live nationwide on 2004. 2. 24., President Roh Moo-hyun said, “It is for the people to make it clear whether [I] should be allowed to do this properly for the next 4 years, or whether [I] should be forced to step down because they cannot bear it,” and also stated, “I expect the people to support the Uri Party overwhelmingly in the general election,” and further, “If the President does well so that our party can obtain votes, I would like to do everything that is lawful.” This constitutes an illegal advance election campaign, which, at the same time, violates Article 9, paragraph 1 (duty of political neutrality of public officials), Article 60, paragraph 1 (persons who may not conduct election campaigning), Article 85 (prohibition on election campaigning by abuse of status), and Article 86 (prohibition on acts by public officials, etc. influencing elections) of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act, and must be punished under Article 255, paragraph 1, item 1 (crime of unlawful election campaigning) of the same Act.\\n\\n(b) On 2003. 12. 19., President Roh Moo-hyun attended the “Remember 1219” event hosted by Nosamo and incited illegal election campaigning by urging, “The citizens’ revolution is continuing; please step forward once again.” Also, at the Gwangwon region media luncheon meeting on 2004. 2. 5., he stated, “The political participation of people like Gukcham 0415 should be legally and politically permitted and encouraged,” thereby engaging in an act disturbing the State by fomenting a law-disobedience movement, despite having taken an oath to uphold the Constitution and bearing responsibility to protect the national legal order as President. Further, as held by the Constitutional Court decision of 2001. 8. 30., which confirmed that any form of campaign for election or defeat by a third party other than an election campaign worker is illegal election campaigning, he encouraged unlawful election campaigning in violation of Article 87 (prohibition on election campaigning by organizations) of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act, and thereby simultaneously violated Article 9, paragraph 1 (duty of political neutrality of public officials) and Article 59 (election campaigning period) of the same Act.\\n\\n(c) In the expressions reported in the 2004. 2. 27. issue of the JoongAng Ilbo from the Uri Party’s general election strategy document, such as “formation of a joint command structure of the party, government, and the Blue House” and “deployment of a strategy of both hard and soft persuasion for targets of the joint command structure,” Blue House-organized intervention in the election was confirmed; this is a clear illegal election by abuse of official power, and President Roh Moo-hyun, as the head of the Blue House, bears responsibility for directing it, and thereby violated Article 9, paragraph 1 (duty of political neutrality of public officials) and Article 86, paragraph 1, item 2 (prohibition on acts by public officials, etc. influencing elections, including participating in the planning of election campaigning or being involved in the implementation of such planning) of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act.\\n\\n(d) At the New Year press conference on 2004. 1. 14., he stated, “Those who supported reform and those who did not support it because reform became unstable were divided, and the people who supported me in the presidential election are doing Uri Party work, so I want to be together with them,” thereby designating the Democratic Party as an anti-reform party; moreover, at a meeting with close aides on 2003. 12. 24., by skillfully using a private setting, he disseminated to the media the remark that “voting for the Democratic Party helps the Grand National Party,” and received, from the National Election Commission on 2003. 12. 30., an official sanction in the form of a “request for cooperation in fair elections” on the ground that it was likely to harm the freedom and fairness of elections. In this way, as the President representing the State, he repeatedly used words and conduct to reject and eliminate a specific political party, thereby violating Article 8, paragraph 3 (the State’s duty to protect political parties) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(e) By repeatedly engaging in acts and remarks that intimidate the people into supporting a specific political party and influence public sentiment in the general election, President Roh Moo-hyun has obstructed the people’s free elections; this is an unlawful act falling under Article 237, paragraph 1, item 3 (crime of obstructing the freedom of election) of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act, and is an act violating Article 24 (right to vote as a basic right of the people), Article 19 (freedom of conscience), and Article 10 (the State’s duty to guarantee basic rights) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(f) As stated above, President Roh Moo-hyun, as head of the Executive, unlawfully intervened in the National Assembly election for members of the National Assembly to form the Legislature, thereby destroying the constitutional principle of separation of powers. Also, on 2004. 3. 4., President Roh, through Senior Secretary for Public Relations Lee Byung-wan of the Blue House, protested against and expressed regret at the National Election Commission’s decision warning against election interference by saying that it was “incomprehensible,” and stated that he would continue to openly support a specific political party, thereby engaging in constitutional-destroying conduct that flatly disregards the lawful decisions of other constitutional bodies. President Roh’s such disregard for other constitutional bodies extends back to his disregard of the unanimous determination at the National Assembly confirmation hearing on 2003. 4. 25. that Ko Young-koo was unqualified to be Director of the National Intelligence Service, his internet letter to the people on 2003. 5. 8. branding incumbent members of the National Assembly as “weeds that must be pulled out,” his failure to act regarding the adoption on 2003. 9. 3. of the resolution to dismiss Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs Kim Du-kwan, and countless other instances, including on 2004. 3. 8., when President Roh disparaged the National Assembly’s lawful push for impeachment as an “unjust oppression.” Furthermore, on 2004. 3. 4., President Roh, through Senior Secretary Lee Byung-wan of the Blue House, revealed that, as President of the Republic of Korea, he lauded foreign laws while denigrating the Republic of Korea’s election law as a “relic of the era of elections by abuse of official power,” thus exposing that he had no will at all to uphold and protect his own constitutional order and national law, and he denied the constitution and the national law itself. Also, on 2004. 3. 8., President Roh reduced the unlawful act that the National Election Commission had ruled to be in violation of Article 9, the duty of neutrality of public officials, a core provision of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act, to something “minor,” “slight and ambiguous.” President Roh’s series of extra-legal acts, such as denials of and disregard for the National Election Commission, the National Assembly, and other constitutional bodies, and disregard for the Constitution and laws, is a violation of the rule of law itself, which is the basic spirit of the constitutional system of the Republic of Korea. In this manner, President Roh’s series of extra-constitutional actions, which deny the authority of the constitutional bodies of the Republic of Korea, the rule of law, and the principle of separation of powers, the foundation of democratic constitutional government, amount to the conduct of a dictator who stands above the law and a dangerous constitutional-destroying act shaking the very existence of democracy and democratic constitutional government, and thereby simultaneously violate Article 66, paragraph 2 (duty to protect the Constitution) and Article 69 (duty to observe the Constitution) of the Constitution.\\n\\nSecond, President Roh Moo-hyun has lost the minimum moral and legal legitimacy required to carry out State affairs normally due to power-related corruption involving himself, his close aides, and his staff. President Roh and his close aides and staff are those who, immediately after winning the primary to select the presidential candidate of the Millennium Democratic Party, and especially after winning the 16th presidential election, openly collected and received illegal funds, and some of them personally misappropriated the money. As is made clear by these criminal acts, they lack even the minimum moral consciousness and respect for the law required to exercise State power.\\n\\n(a) As revealed by the testimony of witnesses at the hearings of the Legislation and Judiciary Committee held from 2004. 2. 11. to 13., President Roh Moo-hyun, during his time as a presidential candidate, accepted a request for a tax reduction from Sun & Moon and directly exerted tax-reduction pressure on the National Tax Service, thereby committing the crime of reducing Sun & Moon’s taxes from 17.1 billion won to 2.3 billion won.\\n\\n(b) Jeong Dae-cheol, who was co-chairman of the election campaign committee and was responsible for President Roh Moo-hyun’s presidential campaign, received a total of 900 million won in illegal political funds, used part of it as presidential campaign funds, and personally misappropriated some of it; Lee Sang-soo, the general affairs committee chair, received more than 700 million won in illegal political funds in total; and Lee Jae-jeong, head of the campaign headquarters, received a total of 1 billion won in illegal political funds and delivered it to President Roh Moo-hyun’s presidential campaign, and all were arrested.\\n\\n(c) Choi Do-sul, Ahn Hee-jung, Lee Kwang-jae, Yang Kil-seung, and Yeo Taek-soo, among President Roh’s close aides, were successively confirmed to have received illegal political funds and to have received various bribes and entertainment, and during the prosecutor’s investigation it was confirmed that President Roh Moo-hyun was in a co-principal relationship with respect to these corrupt acts, directly or indirectly involving him in the crimes.\\n\\n① Choi Do-sul, who has so far been found to have received a total of 1.9 billion won in illegal political funds, was President Roh Moo-hyun’s closest aide from his high school days and, in May 2002, to clear President Roh Moo-hyun’s debt related to Jangsucheon, embezzled 250 million won from the leftover balance of local election funds remaining in the account of the Millennium Democratic Party’s Busan regional election campaign committee and delivered it to Sun Bong-sul, the representative of Jangsucheon. This embezzlement was confirmed during the prosecutor’s investigation to have been instigated by President Roh Moo-hyun. In addition, Choi Do-sul gathered illegal funds to repay the remaining Jangsucheon debt and delivered a total of 500 million won to Sun Bong-sul between 2002. 12. and 2003. 2. 6.; he testified in court that he reported these results to President Roh Moo-hyun just before the presidential inauguration, and that President Roh replied, “Understood.” Special counsel investigations confirmed that Choi Do-sul, from March to April 2002, during the Democratic Party’s primary to select a presidential candidate, received a total of 100 million won in illegal political funds through a borrowed-name account to prepare President Roh Moo-hyun’s primary campaign funds.\\n\\nChoi Do-sul, who was in a co-principal relationship with President Roh Moo-hyun, received 47 million won from Samsung and others while serving as Senior Secretary for General Affairs at the Blue House after the presidential inauguration, and it was confirmed that he committed the shameless criminal act of laundering illegal funds through the Blue House’s official account. When the prosecution got hold of the trail of these corrupt acts by Choi Do-sul, President Roh Moo-hyun was shocked enough to say that his “vision went black” during his 3-day official visit to Indonesia from 2003. 10. 7. to 9., and, in order to conceal this crime in which he himself was implicated, he attempted an unconstitutional referendum on a vote of public confidence, shaking the country and intimidating the people; even after the Constitutional Court effectively declared this referendum unconstitutional, he has continued, whenever possible, to threaten the people again and again with the card of a renewed vote of confidence. This is President Roh Moo-hyun’s own confession that the scale of the power-related corruption involving Choi Do-sul was far greater than what had been revealed and that he himself was deeply involved in the corruption. In this way, President Roh Moo-hyun instigated Choi Do-sul to embezzle a political party’s election funds, knew that illegal political funds had been raised for the repayment of his own debt, and, by appointing Choi Do-sul, who was in such a co-principal relationship, as Senior Secretary for General Affairs at the Blue House and keeping him in that post, he aided and abetted the receipt of illegal political funds and the laundering of illegal funds through the Blue House’s official account.\\n\\n② Ahn Hee-jung, President Roh Moo-hyun’s “business partner” and closest aide like a second self, has been found to have received a total of 7.9 billion won in illegal political funds; in order to pay President Roh’s Jangsucheon debt, he, together with Kang Keum-won, Chairman of the Changsin Group, devised a plan to disguise the sale of Lee Gi-myeong’s Yongin land, and pursuant to this plan Kang Keum-won provided Lee Gi-myeong with a total of 1.9 billion won from 2002. 8. 29. to 2003. 2. Subsequently, Kang Keum-won canceled the contract, but cleared President Roh Moo-hyun’s personal debt by not reclaiming the money that had been provided from Lee Gi-myeong. It was confirmed that President Roh Moo-hyun received prior reports from Ahn Hee-jung and Kang Keum-won regarding this illegal disguised-sale transaction plan. Also, when Sun Bong-sul and Oh Cheol-ju, who had provided collateral in relation to Jangsucheon in July 2002 only to lose Jinyang Shopping Center through a forced auction, demanded compensation for their losses, President Roh Moo-hyun instructed Ahn Hee-jung and Choi Do-sul to “compensate the losses,” and accordingly Ahn Hee-jung is confirmed to have collected a total of 790 million won in illegal political funds from 2002. 9. through 12. of the same year and delivered them to Sun Bong-sul and others. Investigations by the prosecutor’s office confirmed that Ahn Hee-jung also received a total of 50 million won in illegal political funds during the 2002 Democratic Party primary to select a presidential candidate and used it as President Roh Moo-hyun’s primary campaign funds. The prosecution also confirmed that Ahn Hee-jung received a total of 3 billion won in illegal presidential campaign funds from Samsung during the presidential election. In addition, it was confirmed that between 2003. 3. and 8., after President Roh Moo-hyun took office, Ahn Hee-jung received 600 million won into a borrowed-name account under the name of Kang Keum-won’s nephew, and that in 2003. 3. and 8. he received a total of 400 million won from two companies in the Busan area. Ahn Hee-jung also personally misappropriated some of the illegal funds received, such as buying an apartment with 200 million won. In other words, President Roh Moo-hyun, during his candidacy and after being elected, instigated crimes in a co-principal relationship with Ahn Hee-jung, and after assuming the duties of the presidency, he openly introduced Ahn Hee-jung to the public as his “business partner” and thereby aided and abetted Ahn Hee-jung’s collection of illegal funds.\\n\\n③ Lee Kwang-jae, who has been found to have received a total of approximately 100 million won in illegal political funds, is President Roh Moo-hyun’s closest aide like a second self, and on 2002. 11. 9., immediately after President Roh Moo-hyun finished a breakfast at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Seoul together with Moon Byung-wook, chairman of Sun & Moon, Lee Kwang-jae received 100 million won in illegal political funds from Moon Byung-wook after President Roh left the room.\\n\\n④ Yang Kil-seung, Chief of the Blue House Annex Office, in June 2003 received entertainment from Lee Won-ho, the president of the Kiss Tourism Night establishment, who was under investigation for tax evasion, extortion, and instigation of murder, and was arrested on charges including solicitation to suppress the investigation.\\n\\n⑤ Yeo Taek-soo, who has been found to have received a total of 330 million won in illegal political funds, is President Roh Moo-hyun’s aide-de-camp-like personal secretary, and on 2002. 12. 7., while together with President Roh Moo-hyun, received 30 million won in illegal political funds from Moon Byung-wook. Also, after taking office, President Roh Moo-hyun, by keeping Yeo Taek-soo, who was in such a co-principal relationship, on as a Blue House administrative officer, aided and abetted him in receiving 300 million won in illegal funds from Lotte.\\n\\n⑥ Even more shocking is that, with President Roh Moo-hyun’s complicity, Blue House administrative officer Yeo Taek-soo provided 200 million won out of this 300 million won in black money to the Uri Party as its founding funds. Because Yeo Taek-soo is an entity like a second self directly under President Roh Moo-hyun’s direction and supervision, it cannot be said that he provided the founding funds on his own. President Roh Moo-hyun functioned as an indirect perpetrator in the process of providing these illegal founding funds. It is presumed that this 200 million won is only “the tip of the iceberg” among the illegal founding funds raised through President Roh’s involvement as a co-principal.\\n\\n(d) On 2003. 12. 14., at a meeting with party leaders at the Blue House, President Roh Moo-hyun declared that he would retire from politics if the amount of his illegal funds exceeded one-tenth of the amount of the Grand National Party. However, the amount of illegal political funds received by President Roh’s side has reached 11.3 billion won, already exceeding one-tenth of Lee Hoi-chang’s side’s illegal funds of 82.3 billion won and reaching one-seventh. This is the result produced in a situation where the investigation has been focused only on the illegal presidential campaign funds the Grand National Party received from the five major conglomerates. As it has recently come to light that Ahn Hee-jung received illegal presidential campaign funds such as 600 million won from Lotte and 3 billion won from Samsung, if investigations into the five major conglomerates proceed fairly from this point on, the scale of President Roh’s side’s illegal presidential campaign funds will increase even further. Therefore, before President Roh Moo-hyun suffers more political damage, it would be proper for him to resign from office in accordance with his pledge to withdraw from politics. President Roh is already in danger of completely losing the people’s trust as Head of State because the illegal presidential campaign funds are nearing one-seventh. However, far from feeling responsible for this situation, President Roh has been merely desperate to conceal the fact of his involvement in corruption, and has recklessly repeated threats of a renewed vote of confidence and boasts of retiring from politics, as if he would discard even the weighty duties of the presidency like a used rag, and he is now playing a numbers game through strange manipulation of illegal fund amounts. However, now that the scale of the illegal presidential campaign funds is beginning to be revealed as at least greater than the “one-tenth” line that President Roh himself set, there is no choice left but resignation. The President’s loss of public trust means that the minimum authority and leadership necessary to perform presidential duties have collapsed. The people cannot endlessly wait for the President’s confession. The National Assembly also cannot leave this situation unaddressed any longer. After much debate, anguish, and distress, the National Assembly first urged the President to apologize and waited for President Roh’s declaration to the people and his pledge that he would respect the Constitution and laws. However, the President has continued anti-rule-of-law remarks saying that the election-law violations found by the National Election Commission are “minor,” “slight and ambiguous,” and has ultimately refused to apologize and promise to prevent recurrence, while refusing to yield to the National Assembly’s impeachment discussions. Accordingly, because President Roh, in this way, denies the rule of law, the foundation of democratic constitutional government, and also ignores even his own pledge to withdraw from politics, and remains in office without resigning, the National Assembly has been confronted with a situation in which, with a sense of urgency, it cannot but impeach him according to legal procedure.\\n\\n(e) Furthermore, in order to mislead the corruption cases in which he himself is implicated, President Roh Moo-hyun has been threatening the prosecution and the people by saying that he would hold a referendum on renewed public confidence or find another way to secure renewed confidence, and has been setting investigative guidelines by saying things such as “retire from politics if the one-tenth line is exceeded,” “Tico level,” and “several million won, tens of millions of won.” In this way, President Roh has directly and indirectly interfered with and obstructed the investigation of the four major categories of illegal funds: presidential primary funds, presidential campaign funds, congratulatory money for winning the election, and founding funds for the Uri Party. As shown by the investigative results concerning the illegal presidential campaign funds provided by the five major conglomerates, namely, 73.2 billion won received by Lee Hoi-chang’s presidential campaign team versus 3.6 billion won received by Roh Moo-hyun’s presidential campaign team, or the interim investigative result for all illegal presidential campaign funds, namely, 82.3 billion won versus 11.3 billion won, the investigation into the four major categories of illegal funds has proceeded in a grossly biased manner, and it has also been utterly insufficient; in the case of the founding funds, which revealed only “the tip of the iceberg,” the matter is being brushed aside as merely Yeo Taek-soo’s personal corruption, and in the case of primary funds, the investigation is only at a rudimentary stage. Also, whereas opposition lawmakers are arrested even for minor reasons, the investigations consistently serve merely to provide cover in cases such as those of Kim Won-gi, Presidential Political Affairs Special Adviser of the Uri Party; Shin Kye-ryun, former Chief Secretary to the President-elect; and Lee Ho-ung, former head of the organization bureau of the Roh Moo-hyun campaign team, all of whom are close aides to the President, by either clearing them of suspicion or filing non-custodial indictments. All of this is due to President Roh Moo-hyun’s obstruction of the investigation. President Roh’s interference with and obstruction of the prosecutor’s investigation has reached a level that is politically intolerable.\\n\\n(f) President Roh Moo-hyun cannot avoid moral and political responsibility regarding corruption by close aides and obstruction of the corruption investigation, and, in particular, with respect to criminal acts committed through close aides in a co-principal relationship after 2003. 2. 25., the commencement date of the exercise of his official duties, he cannot evade legal responsibility and therefore has “violated the law in the exercise of official duties.” This is because, even after 2003. 2. 25., when he began exercising presidential duties, President Roh Moo-hyun has directly and indirectly been involved in the corruption crimes of his co-principals, as accomplice conduct specified in Articles 30, 31, 32, and 33 of the Criminal Act and as an indirect perpetrator under Article 34 of the same Act, by aiding and abetting the corrupt crimes of Ahn Hee-jung, Choi Do-sul, Yeo Taek-soo, and Yang Kil-seung. On 2003. 12. 29., the prosecution also publicly disclosed that it had recognized and confirmed the co-principal relationship between President Roh Moo-hyun and his close aides. However, the prosecution stated, “We have our own conclusions, but in light of the President’s privilege against criminal prosecution under the Constitution, the continuity of official duties, and the spirit of the Constitution, it is not appropriate to disclose their contents,” and inevitably postponed direct investigation and indictment of President Roh Moo-hyun. Whenever a corruption case involving him as a co-principal was uncovered, President Roh Moo-hyun directly and indirectly influenced the investigation by giving the prosecution directions and policies, and in order to cover up his own involvement, he has threatened the people with the card of renewed confidence and shaken the country amid economic hardship. It goes without saying that, in a situation where President Roh, a co-principal in corruption involving close aides, is obstructing the investigation, the prosecution cannot possibly uncover power-related corruption cases of so-called “living power.” For this reason, the National Assembly must now step forward and impeach President Roh Moo-hyun in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Constitution and laws.\\n\\nThird, as shown by the fact that our economy is, even amid a global economic boom, unusually remaining at a growth rate far lower than that of the United States, President Roh Moo-hyun has devastated the national economy and State administration, plunging people’s livelihoods into ruin and inflicting upon the people more severe pain and misfortune than during the IMF crisis.\\n\\n(a) Economists have characterized the first year of Roh’s administration as “failure in State administration, a lost year,” and even the people who voted for President Roh in the last presidential election have turned their backs on President Roh Moo-hyun, resulting in the shocking situation of a lame duck just one year into his administration.\\n\\n(b) The fundamental cause of this collapse in State administration cannot be denied: President Roh Moo-hyun’s repeated verbal blunders and reversals, including the reckless remark, “I cannot go on being President,” his declaration, after announcing the dispatch of troops to Iraq, of an anti-war stance toward the Iraq War, his unconstitutional proposal for a referendum on renewed public confidence and his pledge to retire from politics, all of which show no seriousness or consistency whatsoever; his insincere exercise of duties and reckless governance; and so-called “all-in strategy” illegal advance election campaigning, in which, while neglecting the duties of the presidency, he poured all efforts only into the general election.\\n\\n(c) Therefore, President Roh Moo-hyun is now violating Article 10 of the Constitution, which stipulates the people’s “right to pursue happiness” and the “State’s duty to guarantee fundamental rights,” and has abandoned the duty of “faithful performance of the office as President” set forth in Article 69 of the Constitution.\\n\\nOur country is now faced with a crisis of constitutional destruction in which the President, in an extra-constitutional and extra-legal manner, denies the rule of law and disregards the warnings of the National Election Commission, a constitutional body, as well as the National Assembly’s inherent authority. The National Assembly, entrusted under Article 65 with the sacred power to impeach, bears the duty to protect the Constitution and the rule of law from President Roh’s arbitrary exercise of power.
