supporting_precedents: {"[2012HEONMA374]": "1. Outline of the Case  \\nThe petitioner is a voter whose constituency is Yongsan District. In the election of the 19th National Assembly members held on 2012. 4. 11., the petitioner voted for candidate Jo ○-yong of the ○○ Party in the constituency National Assembly election, and voted for the □□ Party in the proportional representation National Assembly election; however, in the constituency, the candidate of the △△ Party who received the highest number of votes was determined to be the elected person, and the □□ Party failed to obtain at least 3/100 of the total valid votes and thus did not receive an allocation of seats.  \\nAccordingly, the petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2012. 4. 12., arguing that Article 188(1) of the Public Official Election Act, by “determining as the elected person the person who obtained the majority of valid votes in the constituency National Assembly election,” causes the votes of the people who voted for candidates other than the top vote-getter to become wasted votes, and therefore infringes the petitioner’s right to vote and other rights.  \\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review  \\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the main text of Article 188(1) of the Public Official Election Act (enacted by Act No. 4739 on 16. 3. 1994) (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provision at issue”) infringes the petitioner’s fundamental rights, and the provision subject to review (the underlined portion) and the relevant provisions are as follows.  \\n[Provision Subject to Review]  \\nPublic Official Election Act (enacted by Act No. 4739 on 16. 3. 1994)  \\nArticle 188 (Determination, Announcement, and Notification of Elected Constituency National Assembly Members) ① In a constituency National Assembly election, the electoral district election commission shall determine as the elected person the person who obtained the majority of valid votes in the relevant National Assembly constituency. Provided, That where there are two or more top vote-getters, the eldest shall be determined as the elected person.  \\n[Relevant Provision]  \\nPublic Official Election Act (amended by Act No. 14073 on 3. 3. 2016)  \\nArticle 21 (Number of National Assembly Members) ② The number of National Assembly members to be elected in one National Assembly electoral district (hereinafter referred to as “National Assembly constituency”) shall be one.  \\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments  \\nThe statutory provision at issue infringes the petitioner’s right to vote and right to equality by determining the person who obtained the majority of valid votes in the constituency National Assembly election as the elected person, thereby rendering the petitioner’s vote for the candidate who received the next highest number of votes a wasted vote.  \\n\\n4. Decision  \\nA. The current National Assembly election system and Constitutional Court precedents  \\n(1) The current National Assembly election system  \\nAccording to the Public Official Election Act, in constituency National Assembly elections, one person who obtains the majority of valid votes in each electoral district is elected (Article 21(2)), and in proportional representation National Assembly elections, it adopts a system under which proportional representation seats are allocated according to each vote ratio to each political party that has obtained at least 3/100 of the total valid votes or has secured 5 or more seats in the general election of constituency National Assembly members (Article 189(1)). In other words, the current National Assembly election system may be said to be a form that combines a single-member district plurality system for constituencies with a party-list proportional representation system.  \\nThe number of National Assembly members is 300 in total, combining constituency National Assembly members and proportional representation National Assembly members, and the number of National Assembly members to be elected in one National Assembly electoral district is one (Article 21(1) and (2)). Since there are 253 National Assembly electoral districts (Appendix Table 1), 253 seats are allocated to constituency members and the remaining 47 seats are proportional representation seats. However, in the election of the 19th National Assembly members held on 2012. 4. 11., 246 seats were allocated to constituency members and the remaining 54 seats were allocated to proportional representation members [Supplementary Provisions Article 3 of the Public Official Election Act (Act No. 11374, enacted on 29. 2. 2012), Appendix Table 1 of the former Public Official Election Act (amended by Act No. 11374 on 29. 2. 2012 and before amendment by Act No. 14073 on 3. 3. 2016)].  \\n(2) Relevant precedents  \\nThe Constitutional Court has held that all constitutional principles of elections are realized by guaranteeing universal, equal, direct, secret, and free elections, and that even if the statutory provision at issue did not adopt a minimum voting-rate system, it does not infringe the representativeness of elections or the principle of popular sovereignty (Constitutional Court 2003. 11. 27. 2003HEONMA259 et al.).  \\n\\nB. Whether the statutory provision at issue is unconstitutional  \\n(1) Article 41(3) of the Constitution provides, “The electoral districts for National Assembly members, the proportional representation system, and other matters concerning elections shall be determined by Act,” thereby entrusting specific decisions concerning the content of the electoral system to legislative enactment by the National Assembly. There are no specific constitutional standards regarding whether the legislature should adopt one of the large-, medium-, or small-district systems; whether it should choose a plurality system, a proportional representation system, or a mixed electoral system as the method of determining elected persons; in the case of a plurality system, whether it should provide by statute that a candidate must obtain at least a certain percentage of the votes of all eligible voters, or, when introducing such a system, to what extent that percentage should be specified; in the case of a proportional representation system, its form and whether a threshold clause should be established, or, if a threshold clause is established, how the percentage should be determined; and in the case of a mixed electoral system, how the ratio between constituency National Assembly members and proportional representation National Assembly members should be determined (see Constitutional Court 2001. 7. 19. 2000HEONMA91 et al.; Constitutional Court 2003. 11. 27. 2003HEONMA259 et al.).  \\nAs the National Assembly election system is concretely determined according to statute, the legislature, which possesses legislative discretion, may rationally enact election systems such as electoral districts for National Assembly member elections by comprehensively considering the historical background of Korea’s election system and political parties, the particularity of Korea’s electoral and political culture, the political, economic, and social environment, and the degree of public consciousness and legal sentiment regarding elections. So long as the legislature, in shaping the National Assembly election system, does not unjustly restrict the principles of universal, equal, direct, and secret elections expressly set forth in Article 41(1) of the Constitution and the people’s right to vote, including free elections, it cannot be said to violate the Constitution (see Constitutional Court 2002. 3. 28. 2000HEONMA283 et al.; Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONMA411).  \\n(2) Elections are acts of selecting representatives according to certain procedures and are a means of realizing democracy by constituting representative organs; therefore, an electoral system must possess accuracy in the formation of representation. As noted above, the current National Assembly election system may be said to combine a single-member district plurality system and a party-list proportional representation system for the formation of representation.  \\nThe single-member district plurality system elects one National Assembly member in one constituency, enabling voters to directly scrutinize and choose candidates; it concentrates votes around the two major parties, so that in a parliamentary cabinet system the executive branch can be formed by a single party, and in a presidential system the party can support policy, which is advantageous to political accountability and stability. In addition, because the single-member district plurality system can form an integrated opposition within the legislature, it may also be efficient in checking the executive branch.  \\nAnd although it is pointed out that under the single-member district plurality system, votes cast for the runner-up candidate become wasted votes, creating a discrepancy with the rate of support for political parties, a constituency National Assembly election also carries the meaning of evaluating not only whether one supports a political party but also the candidate as a person, and thus such a result cannot necessarily be said to be unreasonable. Moreover, a medium-district or large-district system, which could be alternative systems, may rather run counter to voters’ intent by bringing about the result that all lower-ranked vote-getters are also elected, contrary to the will of the majority that wishes to elect a particular candidate.  \\nThus, although the single-member district plurality system raises the problem that it may generate a large number of wasted votes, it has advantages such as strengthening political accountability and stability and electing winners through evaluation of candidates as persons, and even from the perspective of representativeness in elections or the principle of equal elections, it cannot be concluded that it is necessarily inferior when compared with other alternative electoral systems.  \\n(3) The Public Official Election Act, in constituting the National Assembly, provides not only for the constituency National Assembly election system but also for the election of National Assembly members through the proportional representation election system. This enables the proportional reflection of the public will regarding political parties through the proportional representation election system, thereby supplementing the discrepancy between the vote ratio and the seat ratio of political parties that arises from adopting a single-member district plurality system in constituency National Assembly elections. In light of this point, although under the statutory provision at issue only candidates who obtain the majority of votes in constituency National Assembly elections are elected, and a wasted vote arises when voting for a candidate who does not obtain the majority of votes, this cannot be said to have originated from an intent to deprive voters whose votes became wasted votes of opportunities to participate in the political process or to discriminate against them.  \\nMoreover, while all voters freely cast their votes and the different support that voters give to candidates is natural, and since it is impossible within the electoral system to elect all candidates, the occurrence of wasted votes in the electoral system has an inevitable aspect.  \\n(4) In representative democracy, an electoral system is to be determined so as to suit the conditions of each country, taking into account the demand for political stability and the political, social, and historical circumstances of each country, and there is no form that is logically and necessarily required. Comparative law also shows that in the election of legislative members, about 50 countries including the United States and the United Kingdom have adopted the single-member district plurality system; about 60 countries including Greece, the Netherlands, and Spain have adopted the party-list proportional representation system; Japan, Italy, and New Zealand have adopted mixed electoral systems; and Germany, although it is a mixed electoral system, has adopted an electoral system under which the total number of legislative seats for each party is determined through the vote ratio of party votes.  \\n(5) Taking these points together, all constitutional election principles are realized by granting all voters in National Assembly elections opportunities to participate in voting without restrictions based on sex, property, social status, educational background, or the like (universal suffrage); by giving no weight distinction to the value of their votes and counting each vote of one voter as one vote of equal value (equal suffrage); by having election results directly determined by voters rather than intermediate electors or political parties (direct election); by guaranteeing the secrecy of the vote (secret ballot); and by guaranteeing free voting rather than compulsory voting (free election). Accordingly, one cannot additionally require that the single-member district plurality system be excluded and another electoral system adopted in order to reduce wasted votes in National Assembly elections. The representativeness of elections can be realized by the current method, under which all voters are granted opportunities to participate in voting without differentiation, the votes of the voters who participate in the vote are assessed as having equal value, and the person who obtains the majority of valid votes is determined as the elected person (see Constitutional Court 2003. 11. 27. 2003HEONMA259 et al.).  \\nTherefore, even if the statutory provision at issue prescribes a single-member district plurality system and a large number of wasted votes arise, this alone does not mean that it infringes the essence of the representativeness of elections required by the Constitution, or that it thereby infringes the principle of popular sovereignty, and it cannot be said to infringe the petitioner’s right to equality or right to vote.  \\n\\n5. Conclusion  \\nAs this petition for review is without merit, it is dismissed, and a decision is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices. This decision includes the supplementary opinion of Justice Ahn Chang-ho as set forth in 6 below.  \\n\\n6. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Ahn Chang-ho  \\nAlthough I do not consider that the statutory provision at issue violates the Constitution, the petitioner raises the issue that, because the statutory provision at issue adopts a single-member district plurality system, the petitioner’s vote for the candidate receiving the next highest number of votes became a wasted vote; accordingly, I state the following opinion regarding the proportional representation system in this connection.  \\nA. As noted in the majority opinion, the legislature may determine, by comprehensively considering the historical background of Korea’s election system and political parties, the particularity of Korea’s electoral and political culture, the political, economic, and social environment, and the degree of public consciousness and legal sentiment regarding elections, which among the plurality system, the proportional representation system, and the mixed electoral system to adopt as the method for determining the elected person among National Assembly candidates; in the case of a proportional representation system, its form and whether to establish a threshold clause; or, if a threshold clause is established, how to determine the percentage; and in the case of a mixed electoral system, how to determine the ratio between constituency National Assembly members and proportional representation National Assembly members.  \\nAnd so long as this does not unjustly restrict the people’s right to vote, including the principles of universal, equal, direct, and secret elections expressly set forth in Article 41(1) of the Constitution and free elections, it cannot be said to violate the Constitution.  \\nB. The proportional representation system means an electoral system that allocates seats of a political party in proportion to voters’ support for that party. Under the proportional representation system, what is directly determined by voters’ political expression is not so much which proportional representation National Assembly candidate is elected as a proportional representation National Assembly member, but rather the number of proportional representation National Assembly seats allocated to the party that is to be assigned proportional representation National Assembly members; and the proportional representation member election has the character not of an election for a person but of an election for a political party (see Constitutional Court 2006. 7. 26. 2004HEONMA217; Constitutional Court 2009. 6. 25. 2008HEONMA413 et al.).  \\nAccordingly, for the proportional representation system to properly reflect the true will of the people, a party’s identity, such as its platform or policies, must be established, and fairness and transparency in the process of selecting proportional representation National Assembly candidates must be secured as a premise. If these prerequisite conditions are not met in political reality, the proportional representation system may instead seriously distort the true will of the people and cause harm through adverse functions such as running counter to the democratization of political parties.  \\nAnd the proportional representation system has the positive function of preventing wasted votes, reflecting various views regarding support for political parties, publicizing them, and excluding political monopoly by large parties; on the other hand, it also carries the risk of causing instability in the political situation. In particular, unlike a parliamentary cabinet system in which the majority party forms the executive branch, in a presidential system, strengthening proportional representation may make it difficult to form a stable majority necessary for smooth policy implementation, so it must also be noted, in the operation of the proportional representation system, that in a political soil where a culture of dialogue and compromise has not matured, it may undermine political stability and reduce the efficiency of state administration.  \\nC. Political parties perform the function of political conduits as intermediaries between the people and the state, and by subjectively and actively inducing and integrating the people’s pluralistic political opinions, they form political will that can directly influence the determination of national policy. Today, in representative democracy, political parties are emphasized even more in importance as the bearers and mediators of the people’s political will formation and as an indispensable element of democracy (Constitutional Court 2014. 1. 28. 2012HEONMA431 et al.).  \\nThe proportional representation system was devised and implemented as a corrective to the defects of the (single-member district) plurality system, namely, that it is favorable to large parties, fails properly to represent the diversified voices of the people, and generates wasted votes, on the basis of party-based democracy. When properly operated, the proportional representation system can form representation corresponding to social forces, invigorate party politics, promote competition among parties, and exclude political monopoly (see Constitutional Court 2009. 6. 25. 2007HEONMA40; Constitutional Court 2013. 10. 24. 2012HEONMA311 et al.).  \\nAs such, while the importance of political parties is emphasized in representative democracy, the proportional representation system, grounded in party-based democracy, has the advantage of strengthening the proportionality of election results, which is the starting point of popular sovereignty, and faithfully reflecting the pluralistic political ideologies of society in accordance with the voters’ will. In addition, considering that Article 41(3) of the Constitution delegates the election system concerning National Assembly members to statute while particularly providing for the proportional representation system, even if an electoral system including a single-member district plurality system does not violate constitutional election principles, it is desirable to gradually expand the party-list proportional representation system, and the reduction of the proportional representation system currently in force should be strictly limited unless it is verified that political instability has been caused by the proportional representation system in particular.  \\nD. Proportional representation by region has been continuously discussed on the ground of alleviating regionalism. If effectively operated, regional proportional representation appears to be a measure well worth considering for introduction, in that it can alleviate the regional bias of political parties and faithfully reflect the political will of voters.  \\nHowever, the current party-list proportional representation system (fixed system), which makes the entire nation one electoral district, has the advantage of weakening the connection between elections and locality and thereby blocking regional antagonism in elections, whereas regional proportional representation may weaken this advantage of the proportional representation system, and, in particular, because regionalism is deeply entrenched in Korea, regional proportional representation may further intensify regionalism depending on the political situation.  \\nMoreover, depending on its method, regional proportional representation may generate a large number of wasted votes due to threshold clauses and the like; and if, in particular, the introduction of regional proportional representation fails to secure an appropriate number of proportional representation National Assembly members capable of reflecting diverse factors beyond the region, it may restrict opportunities for minority political forces to enter the legislature and hinder the formation of diverse public opinion among the people, while also undermining the advantages of the proportional representation system by negatively affecting the recruitment of socially vulnerable persons such as women and persons with disabilities, and experts, into political parties.  \\nReform of the electoral system must consider not only the resolution of regionalism, but also the strengthening of proportionality in election results, the securing of diversity in democracy, consideration for socially vulnerable persons, the development of party politics, and political stability. Therefore, in the current National Assembly election system, which adopts a form combining a single-member district plurality system for constituencies and a nationwide party-list proportional representation system (fixed system), one may first consider a measure to alleviate regionalism while minimizing harm to the advantages of the current electoral system by requiring each political party to prepare its party list so that proportional representation National Assembly members may be elected in light of regional population.  \\nWhether to introduce regional proportional representation and the method thereof should be carefully reviewed together with the expansion of the proportional representation system, on the premise that the identity of political parties is established and fairness and transparency in the candidate selection process are secured, taking into account the particularity of Korea’s electoral and political culture, the political, economic, and social environment, and the like. However, as seen in the process of German reunification, in Korea as well, during the reunification process, the introduction of proportional representation by the North and South Korean regions, in relation to threshold clauses and the like, should be positively considered on a temporary basis."}

{"[2017HEONMA867]": "1. Case Summary\\nThe Petitioner is a person with a level 1 brain lesion disability and receives assistance from an activity support worker. The Petitioner sought to vote with the assistance of the activity support worker at the ○○ polling place in ○○-dong, Gyeyang-gu, Incheon on 2017. 5. 9., which was the election day for the 19th Presidential Election. The latter part of Article 157(6) of the Public Official Election Act provides that “an elector who, due to visual or physical disability, is unable to mark the ballot himself or herself may be assisted in voting by accompanying his or her family members or two persons designated by the elector,” and, accordingly, the voting management manual prepared by the National Election Commission guided that, where an elector with visual or physical disability has no designated person or has one person who is not a family member, two persons shall be selected from among the voting clerks in the presence of a poll watcher to assist in voting. The Petitioner attempted to enter the voting booth accompanied by only one activity support worker, but was stopped by the voting manager at the above polling place for the above reason.\\nAccordingly, the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2017. 8. 5., alleging that the latter part of Article 157(6) of the Public Official Election Act and the acts of the Respondents in stopping the Petitioner, who attempted to enter the voting booth accompanied by only one activity support worker, infringed the Petitioner’s right to vote, the freedom and secrecy of private life, and the right to equality.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\nThe Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint against the entire latter part of Article 157(6) of the Public Official Election Act, but since the Petitioner, as an elector with a physical disability, sought to have voting assistance by accompanying one activity support worker who was not a family member, the subject matter is limited to the portion related thereto.\\nTherefore, the subject matter of this case is whether the act of the Respondents in preventing the Petitioner from attempting to enter the voting booth accompanied by one activity support worker who was not a family member, designated by the Petitioner as a voting assistant, in the 19th Presidential Election on 2017. 5. 9. (hereinafter referred to as “the act of prevention at issue”), and the portion of Article 157(6) of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7189 on 2004. 3. 12.) that provides that “an elector who, due to physical disability, is unable to mark the ballot himself or herself may be assisted in voting by accompanying two persons designated by the elector” (hereinafter referred to as “the provision at issue”), infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights and are unconstitutional. The provision at issue and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision at Issue]\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7189 on 2004. 3. 12.)\\nArticle 157 (Receiving a Ballot and Marking Procedure) (6) An elector may, within the extent that does not disturb the order of the polling station, enter and leave the polling station (excluding the voting booth in the case of children of elementary school age or younger) together with children of elementary school age or younger, and an elector who, due to visual or physical disability, is unable to mark the ballot himself or herself may be assisted in voting by accompanying his or her family members or two persons designated by the elector.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 13617 on 2015. 12. 24.)\\nArticle 157 (Receiving a Ballot and Marking Procedure) (7) Except in the case under paragraph (6), no more than two persons may enter the same voting booth at the same time.\\nArticle 167 (Guarantee of Secrecy of Voting) (1) The secrecy of voting shall be guaranteed.\\n(2) An elector shall not be obligated to disclose to anyone, under any circumstances, the name of the candidate or the name of the political party for whom he or she voted, and no one may ask or require such disclosure from the elector until the closing time of voting on election day. Provided, That this shall not apply where a television broadcasting station, a radio broadcasting station, or a daily newspaper company under subparagraph 1(a) and (b) of Article 2 of the Act on the Promotion of Newspapers, etc. asks questions from a point 50 meters away from the polling station on election day in a manner that does not infringe the secrecy of voting in order to predict the result of the election; in this case, the circumstances and result thereof may not be made public until the closing time of voting.\\n(3) An elector may not disclose the ballot he or she marked, and any disclosed ballot shall be invalid.\\nArticle 241 (Crime of Infringement of Secrecy of Voting) (1) A person who, in violation of Article 167 (including cases where it is applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 218-17(9)), infringes the secrecy of voting, or who, before the expiration of the closing time of voting on election day, asks an elector from within 50 meters of the polling station in order to predict the voting result, with respect to the political party or candidate he or she intends to vote for or has voted for, or who publicly announces the circumstances and result thereof before the closing time of voting, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 6,000,000 won.\\n(2) If a member or employee of an election commission, a public official related to election affairs, a prosecutor, a police official (including judicial police officers), or a military person (including military civil servants belonging to military investigation agencies) commits or causes the acts prescribed in paragraph (1), he or she shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years.\\nArticle 248 (Crime of Fraudulent Voting) (1) A person who votes or causes another to vote, or who attempts to vote, by impersonating a name, forging or altering and using an identification card, or by any other fraudulent means, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 10,000,000 won.\\n(2) If a member or employee of an election commission or a public official related to election affairs (including voting clerks, advance voting clerks, and ballot counting clerks) commits or causes the acts prescribed in paragraph (1), he or she shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 7 years.\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\na. The provision at issue requires an elector who, due to physical disability, is unable to mark the ballot himself or herself to be accompanied by two persons if the voting assistant is not a family member, but the Respondents, where an elector is accompanied by one voting assistant who is not a family member, select an additional voting assistant from among the voting clerks so that the ballot contents of the Petitioner are disclosed to a third party with whom no relationship of trust whatsoever exists. Therefore, the act of prevention at issue and the provision at issue infringe the Petitioner’s right to vote, the right to a secret ballot, and the freedom and secrecy of private life.\\nb. The act of prevention at issue and the provision at issue treat differently electors who vote with assistance from family members and electors who vote with assistance from persons other than family members, in order to promote the fairness of elections. However, determining the number of voting assistants based on whether the assistant is a family member is an unjustified discrimination without any basis. Therefore, the act of prevention at issue and the provision at issue infringe the Petitioner’s right to equality.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Act of Prevention at Issue\\nBecause all procedures for the 19th Presidential Election have been completed and the state of fundamental-rights infringement caused by the act of prevention at issue alleged by the Petitioner has already ended, even if the petition for adjudication on the act of prevention at issue is granted, it will not help remedy the Petitioner’s rights.\\nWhat the Petitioner ultimately contests is that, even where an elector who, due to physical disability, is unable to mark the ballot himself or herself designates a person other than a family member as a voting assistant, the elector should be able to vote accompanied by one person; however, even if the Constitutional Court grants the petition for adjudication on the act of prevention at issue, as long as the provision at issue and related provisions such as Article 157(7) of the Public Official Election Act remain unchanged, it cannot prevent the recurrence of a similar infringement of fundamental rights as the act of prevention at issue. The Petitioner also filed a constitutional complaint not only against the act of prevention at issue but also against the provision at issue in order to resolve the ultimate dispute.\\nTherefore, the petition for adjudication on the act of prevention at issue has no protectable interest in rights and no interest in filing the petition, without further review (see Constitutional Court 2018. 8. 30. 2016HEONMA263).\\n\\n5. Determination on the Provision at Issue\\na. Organization of the Issues\\nArticle 24 of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall have the right to vote as prescribed by Act.”\\nThe right to vote means the right of citizens to elect public officials by universal, equal, direct, and secret election (see Constitutional Court 2016. 3. 31. 2015HEONMA1056 et al.). The provision at issue was primarily enacted to realize the principle of universal suffrage with respect to electors who, due to physical disability, are unable to mark the ballot themselves. However, because the provision at issue stipulates that, where the voting assistant is not a family member, an elector may be assisted in voting only by accompanying two persons, it establishes an exception to the principle of secret ballot. Therefore, the issue is whether the provision at issue infringes the Petitioner’s right to vote by creating an exception to the principle of secret ballot.\\nMeanwhile, the Petitioner’s argument that the provision at issue infringes the freedom and secrecy of private life is because the provision at issue prescribes disclosure of the ballot contents to the voting assistant; thus, determination on this part is included in the determination on whether the right to vote was infringed, as discussed above.\\nAlso, the issue of infringement of the right to equality asserted by the Petitioner may be determined together when deciding whether the provision at issue excessively restricts the Petitioner’s right to vote, because the provision at issue, unlike the case where the voting assistant is a family member, compels the elector to be accompanied by two persons and thus makes it impossible to assist in voting by being accompanied by one person.\\nTherefore, the issue in this case is whether the provision at issue infringes the Petitioner’s right to vote by establishing an exception to the principle of secret ballot.\\n\\nb. The Principle of Secret Ballot and the Limits of Restricting the Right to Vote\\n(1) The Principle of Secret Ballot\\nThe Constitution explicitly provides the principle of secret ballot in elections for members of the National Assembly and the President (Article 41(1), Article 67(1)). Secret ballot means an election in which the elector’s decision is not known to others. The reason for guaranteeing secret ballot is to prevent electors from suffering disadvantages due to the exercise of the right to vote by guaranteeing the secrecy of the ballot contents. Secret ballot is an essential and effective means of protecting voters’ political decision-making from state coercion and social pressure, and a prerequisite for substantially guaranteeing the principle of free elections.\\nSince the principle of secret ballot is an election principle under the Constitution, the legislature must observe and realize it when shaping the right to vote by statute. Accordingly, the Public Official Election Act guarantees the secrecy of voting (Article 167(1)), and provides that an elector is not obligated to disclose to anyone, under any circumstances, the name of the candidate or the political party for whom he or she voted, and that no one may ask or require such disclosure until the closing time of voting on election day (Article 167(2)). And a person who infringes the secrecy of voting in violation thereof is subject to criminal punishment (Article 241).\\n(2) Limits on Restricting the Right to Vote\\nThe principle of popular sovereignty proclaimed in Article 1 of the Constitution means that state power is organized by the consent of the people. For this purpose, broad opportunities must be guaranteed so that the people, as sovereign, can participate in the political process. Under today’s democratic politics based on representative democracy, people’s participation occurs basically through elections, so elections can be said to be the channel through which the sovereign people exercise sovereignty.\\nFor the principle of popular sovereignty and the people’s participation through elections, Article 24 of the Constitution guarantees the right to vote to all citizens as prescribed by Act, Article 11 of the Constitution prescribes the right to equality in the political sphere, and Article 41(1) and Article 67(1) of the Constitution guarantee the principles of universal, equal, direct, and secret elections in elections for members of the National Assembly and the President. The Constitution’s explicit guarantee of the right to vote and election principles in this manner is because, under popular sovereignty and representative democracy, state power is created and constituted through the exercise of the people’s right to vote, and democratic legitimacy is thereby conferred.\\nMeanwhile, although Article 24 of the Constitution takes the form of statutory reservation by providing that all citizens shall have the right to vote “as prescribed by Act,” this is not for restricting the right to vote, but rather for realizing and guaranteeing it. Therefore, even when the content and procedures of the right to vote are prescribed by statute, they must conform to the purport of Article 1 of the Constitution, which declares popular sovereignty, Article 11 of the Constitution on equality rights, and Articles 41 and 67 of the Constitution, which guarantee universal, equal, direct, and secret elections in elections for members of the National Assembly and the President. And because the right to vote has important significance as a means of realizing popular sovereignty and representative democracy in a democratic state, the legislature must enact laws in a direction that guarantees the right to vote to the maximum extent, and when reviewing the constitutionality of laws restricting the right to vote, the intensity of review must also be strict.\\nTherefore, legislation restricting the right to vote may be justified only in necessary and unavoidable exceptional cases pursuant to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, so even when determining whether the provision at issue, which establishes an exception to the principle of secret ballot, infringes the Petitioner’s right to vote, strict review under Article 37(2) of the Constitution is required (see Constitutional Court 2018. 1. 25. 2015HEONMA821 et al.).\\n\\nc. Whether the Provision at Issue Infringes the Petitioner’s Right to Vote\\n(1) Legitimate Aim and Appropriateness of Means\\nThe provision at issue contributes to substantially guaranteeing the right to vote of electors with physical disabilities of such degree that they cannot mark the ballot themselves by allowing them to be assisted in voting by accompanying two persons designated by them even if they are not family members. In particular, the provision at issue is meaningful in that it enables persons with disabilities who live apart from their family and thus cannot receive assistance from family members, such as those residing in welfare facilities for persons with disabilities, to exercise the right to vote.\\nIn addition, by requiring, where the voting assistant is not a family member, that two persons be accompanied so that voting assistance is performed under mutual checks and balances, the provision at issue prevents the voting assistant from marking the ballot contrary to the elector’s will or exerting undue influence on the elector.\\nTherefore, the provision at issue has a legitimate aim because it seeks to substantially guarantee the right to vote of electors who, due to physical disability, cannot mark the ballot themselves and to secure fairness in elections by preventing voting assistants from exerting undue influence on the exercise of the right to vote by persons with disabilities. Also, because requiring two persons to be accompanied where the voting assistant is not a family member is an appropriate means to achieve the above purpose, appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n(2) Least Restrictive Means\\n(a) Fairness in elections is a constitutional value no less important than freedom of elections, and especially in view of our political culture and election climate, securing fairness in elections is the most important task above all else.\\nIn Korea, the majority of persons with severe disabilities whose mobility is inconvenient still live in residential facilities for persons with disabilities. Persons in charge of such facilities can greatly influence the persons with disabilities living there, and may use that influence to exert undue influence on the exercise of those persons’ right to vote. Also, severely disabled persons who do not reside in facilities also need someone’s assistance in order to exercise their right to vote, and depending on the case, cannot avoid being affected by the voting assistants. In other words, because severely disabled persons find it very difficult to vote on their own, the people assisting them in voting can use that opportunity to render the exercise of their right to vote nominal and abuse it as a means of proxy voting. In fact, even recently election crimes such as abuse of the exercise of severely disabled persons’ right to vote as proxy voting have been discovered.\\nAccordingly, the provision at issue requires that, for fair voting assistance to be provided and to secure the fairness of elections and substantially guarantee the exercise of the right to vote by severely disabled persons, two persons must accompany the voting assistant where the assistant is not a family member.\\n(b) However, because the provision at issue permits voting assistance, an elector inevitably cannot maintain the secrecy of the ballot. Nonetheless, as the principle of secret ballot is an important constitutional value to be guaranteed in the exercise of the people’s right to vote, even if the result of voting must inevitably be disclosed in part, the scope should be minimized. For this purpose, instead of compelling two voting assistants to accompany the elector as under the provision at issue, one may consider a method of allowing only one voting assistant to accompany the elector while strictly regulating the requirements and procedures for voting assistance. For example, one may restrict the qualifications of voting assistants by not allowing persons in positions that may influence the elector, such as the head or staff of a residential facility for persons with disabilities, to serve as voting assistants, or by allowing them to assist voting only when it is confirmed that the elector expressly trusts the voting assistant. Alternatively, specific procedures for voting assistance may be prepared, such as imposing on the voting assistant the duty to swear to mark the ballot according to the elector’s will, or having the polling manager, etc. confirm from the elector after voting that the voting assistant marked the ballot in accordance with the elector’s will.\\nHowever, even if the above methods are used, it is not possible to completely block the possibility that the voting assistance system may be abused to undermine fairness in elections. Rather, the above methods may become an obstacle that makes it difficult for electors to utilize the voting assistance system and causes them to give up exercising the right to vote. Also, if use of the voting assistance system becomes difficult, severely disabled persons living in residential facilities for persons with disabilities may use absentee voting at their place of residence (Public Official Election Act Article 38(4) subparagraph 3), but in the case of absentee voting at one’s place of residence, there is a greater concern that election irregularities such as proxy voting may occur or that the secrecy of voting may be infringed, so it cannot be said to produce a better result than the provision at issue.\\nTherefore, the above methods cannot be regarded as alternatives capable of achieving the legislative purpose at the same level as the provision at issue.\\n(c) Also, in order to fundamentally resolve the problem that the provision at issue establishes an exception to the principle of secret ballot, an election aid device should be prepared so that even electors who, due to physical disability, are unable to mark the ballot themselves can mark the ballot on their own without the assistance of a voting assistant.\\nCurrently, the National Election Commission provides two kinds of special ballot-marking devices, mouthpiece-type and wrist-type ballot markers, at all polling stations for electors with physical disabilities. However, because the special ballot-marking devices can only be used in a limited manner depending on the type and degree of the elector’s disability, the provision at issue is being used to support the exercise of the right to vote by severely disabled persons who cannot use special ballot-marking devices.\\nHowever, for severely disabled persons who cannot use the above special ballot-marking devices, the motions or possible physical movements for marking the ballot may vary widely depending on the type or degree of the disability, so it is not easy to prepare all election aids that such persons can use according to the type of disability. Also, even if such aids are prepared, because comprehensive consideration is required to secure fairness in the use of such supplementary devices, including special ballot papers, related apparatus and facilities, separate election management personnel, and the like, it cannot be definitively said that they can be introduced without difficulty. Furthermore, even if election aid devices are introduced, a person to assist the elector in using the device may still be necessary, and among severely disabled persons there are those who find it difficult even to use such assistive devices, so it is not easy to fully guarantee the secrecy of voting by severely disabled persons. Ultimately, if related technology is developed in the future and measures to secure fairness for new election aid devices are established, it would be desirable to introduce such election aid devices so that the range in which electors with physical disabilities can mark the ballot on their own may expand, but voting with the assistance of a voting assistant is, for the present, the more realistic method.\\n(d) Although various means can be adopted to check the voting assistant in order to secure fairness in elections, the provision at issue limits the number of voting assistants to the minimum number, two, who can mutually check each other, so that electors can easily utilize the voting assistance system while the secrecy of voting is better maintained. The Public Official Election Act also provides that, when a family member is accompanied as the voting assistant, one person may assist in voting by deeming that the marking is guaranteed according to the person’s own will by reason of the family relationship (see Supreme Court judgment 99U48 dated 1999. 7. 13.). This is in the same purport.\\nHowever, requiring an elector with physical disabilities to be accompanied by two voting assistants who are not family members may impose an excessive burden on the elector. Accordingly, the National Election Commission in practice supports the exercise of the right to vote by allowing, where an elector is not accompanied by two voting assistants who are not family members, one or two persons from among the voting clerks to be selected as voting assistants in the presence of a poll watcher to assist voting. Even where the elector is accompanied by only one voting assistant or by no voting assistant at all, support is provided by voting assistants to reduce the burden.\\nIn addition, the Public Official Election Act guarantees the secrecy of voting (Article 167(1)); a person who infringes the secrecy of voting is punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 6,000,000 won (Article 241(1)); and where a voting assistant votes for a candidate other than the elector’s will or casts an invalid vote, thereby voting in a manner different from the elector’s will, the person is punished for fraudulent voting by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 10,000,000 won (Article 248(1)). Furthermore, the Public Official Election Act provides for aggravated punishment where a member or employee of an election commission or a public official related to election affairs commits the above acts (Article 241(2), Article 248(2)). Although the provision at issue establishes an exception to the principle of secret ballot, the above penal provisions compel voting assistants to comply with the duty of confidentiality and prevent the elector’s harm caused by the provision at issue from expanding.\\n(e) Therefore, the provision at issue does not violate the principle of least restriction.\\n(3) Balance of Interests\\nThe public interest the provision at issue seeks to achieve is to substantially guarantee the right to vote of electors who, due to physical disability, cannot mark the ballot themselves and to secure fairness in elections by preventing voting assistants from exerting undue influence on the exercise of the right to vote by persons with disabilities. Such substantial guarantee of the right to vote of severely disabled persons and the securing of fairness in elections are very important public interests.\\nOn the other hand, the disadvantage suffered by the Petitioner due to the provision at issue is that, where the voting assistant is not a family member, two persons must accompany the elector, so compared with the case where there is one voting assistant, it is more difficult to maintain the secrecy of the ballot, and there is the inconvenience of having to additionally secure a voting assistant.\\nHowever, as seen above, the National Election Commission in practice eases the inconvenience that the elector must secure voting assistants by allowing, where an elector is not accompanied by two voting assistants who are not family members, one or two persons from among the voting clerks to be selected as voting assistants in the presence of a poll watcher so that two voting assistants can assist the voting, and these two voting assistants cannot be said to be a great disadvantage in that they are the minimum number necessary to substantially guarantee the exercise of the right to vote by severely disabled persons and to secure fairness in elections. Furthermore, the Public Official Election Act prevents voting assistants from infringing the secrecy of the elector’s vote through criminal punishment so that the secrecy of voting is maintained.\\nTherefore, because the public interest sought to be achieved by the provision at issue is greater than the disadvantage suffered by the Petitioner, the provision at issue does not violate the principle of balance of interests.\\n(4) Subconclusion\\nTherefore, although the provision at issue establishes an exception to the principle of secret ballot, it is limited to necessary and unavoidable exceptional cases, and thus does not infringe the Petitioner’s right to vote in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the petition for adjudication on the provision at issue is without merit and is dismissed, and the Petitioner’s remaining petition for adjudication is inadmissible and is therefore dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the disposition. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinion on the provision at issue by Justice Lee Seon-ae, Justice Lee Seok-tae, and Justice Moon Hyung-bae as set forth in Section 7 below.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae, Justice Lee Seok-tae, and Justice Moon Hyung-bae on the Provision at Issue\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we determine that the provision at issue is unconstitutional because it infringes the Petitioner’s right to vote in violation of the principle against excessive restriction, and therefore we set forth the following dissenting opinion.\\n\\na. Legitimate Aim and Appropriateness of Means\\nThe provision at issue is for substantially guaranteeing the right to vote of electors who, due to physical disability, are unable to mark the ballot themselves and for securing fairness in elections by preventing voting assistants from exerting undue influence on the exercise of the right to vote by persons with disabilities. Therefore, the legitimacy of the legislative purpose is recognized, and because the provision at issue requires that two persons be accompanied where the voting assistant is not a family member as an appropriate means to achieve the above purpose, appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\nb. Least Restrictive Means\\n(1) The Principle of Secret Ballot and the Principle of Free Elections\\nThe people realize self-government by expressing their political will and participating in political decision-making through elections. In order for the people’s political will not to be distorted and to be expressed through elections, the principle of free elections, which guarantees freedom in forming the elector’s will and freedom in realizing that will throughout the election process, must be observed (see Constitutional Court 1994. 7. 29. 93HEONGA4 et al.; Constitutional Court 2018. 4. 26. 2016HEONMA611). The principle of free elections basically guarantees deciding the content of the vote freely by oneself and expressing it in the vote.\\nThe principle of secret ballot ensures that the above principle of free elections is observed by guaranteeing the secrecy of voting. The legislature must establish voting procedures, methods, and equipment that can technically maintain the secrecy of voting. Through this, the principles of secret ballot and free elections are realized in that the elector expresses the political will he or she decided on through the vote, and only he or she can know its contents. Since even the possibility that the contents of the vote may be disclosed can infringe the elector’s freedom to vote, secret ballot has special significance in relation to free elections.\\nThe principle of secret ballot must be guaranteed not only by the state but also between private persons. In particular, when a particular person is in a relationship that may be subordinate to another, more careful consideration is needed to ensure that the principle of secret ballot is observed.\\nTherefore, considering the importance of such secret ballot, the legislature’s establishment of an exception to the principle of secret ballot may be allowed only where it is confirmed that the elector can freely determine the contents of the vote by himself or herself and express it in the vote.\\n(2) Whether the Provision at Issue Minimizes the Restriction on the Petitioner’s Right to Vote\\nThe voting assistance system was established to ensure that electors who, due to physical disability, are unable to mark the ballot themselves can substantially exercise the right to vote. The most important role of the voting assistant is to assist so that the elector’s political will can be accurately expressed in the vote.\\nAs seen above, the Constitution and the Public Official Election Act guarantee the secrecy of voting. Also, the Public Official Election Act punishes acts that infringe the secrecy of voting, and does not take issue with an act of voluntarily disclosing the content of the vote unless it is for disclosing the ballot or influencing the election (Public Official Election Act Articles 167 and 241). This is because political expression through voting belongs to the most intimate sphere, and therefore the elector’s intention regarding disclosure is regarded as important. The elector discloses his or her most intimate political will to the voting assistant and has the assistant aid the voting. Therefore, for the elector’s political will to be accurately expressed through the vote and for the elector to vote free from undue influence by the voting assistant, above all else the elector must be able to independently select a person whom he or she can trust as the voting assistant.\\nHowever, the provision at issue, in order to prevent the voting assistant from marking the ballot contrary to the elector’s will or exerting undue influence on the elector, requires that where the voting assistant is not a family member, two persons must be accompanied so that voting assistance is provided under mutual checks and balances. As a result, the elector cannot himself or herself determine the number of voting assistants he or she needs.\\nAlso, when two voting assistants are accompanied, the secrecy of the ballot is less maintained than when there is one. The more intimate the sphere is, such as the contents of the vote, the more the mere disclosure to others becomes a serious restriction on individual freedom. Therefore, even if fairness in elections is secured by requiring two voting assistants to be accompanied, the elector is inevitably constrained in exercising the right to vote by having to disclose the contents of the vote to two voting assistants.\\nFurthermore, the National Election Commission’s practice of allowing, where an elector is not accompanied by two voting assistants who are not family members, one or two persons from among the voting clerks to be selected as voting assistants in the presence of a poll watcher may also excessively restrict the elector’s secret ballot. The particularly problematic case is when, as in the Petitioner’s case, only one voting assistant selected by the elector is accompanied. Even though the elector expressly accompanies a voting assistant selected by himself or herself, he or she can vote only by additionally accompanying one person from among the voting clerks regardless of his or her will. This causes the relevant elector to suffer the disadvantage of having to disclose his or her most intimate political will even to an unfamiliar third party with whom no relationship of trust has been formed, in order to vote.\\nThe Public Official Election Act provides penal provisions that can compel voting assistants to observe the secrecy of voting, thereby preventing the elector’s harm from expanding (Article 167(1), Article 241, Article 248). However, such penal provisions can prevent voting assistants from disclosing the contents of the vote externally, but cannot prevent the freedom of the elector from being constrained by disclosing the contents of the vote to the added voting assistant itself.\\nTherefore, because the provision at issue focuses on securing fairness in elections and overlooks the importance of secret ballot, it is difficult to say that it minimizes the restriction on the Petitioner’s right to vote.\\n(3) Whether There Exists an Alternative to the Provision at Issue\\nAs seen above, what is most important in the voting assistance system is ensuring and confirming that the elector independently selects a person whom he or she trusts to be suitable as a voting assistant. Since the voting assistance system establishes an exception to the principle of secret ballot and thus may undermine freedom of elections, it must ensure that voting is carried out according to the elector’s will by confirming whether the voting assistant was selected according to the elector’s will and whether the voting assistant marked the ballot contrary to the elector’s will or exerted undue influence on the elector. It must not be overlooked that when the elector can freely exercise the right to vote, the fairness in elections sought by the provision at issue is also secured.\\nHowever, the provision at issue does not provide a procedure for confirming whether the elector’s freedom of election has been secured, but simply adopts a method whereby two voting assistants mutually check each other. Yet even if two voting assistants are compelled to accompany the elector where the assistant is not a family member, if both voting assistants are in a special relationship that can influence the elector, or if the voting assistants share interests with each other and plan to vote contrary to the elector’s will, it is difficult to secure fairness in elections.\\nOn the other hand, if more explicit procedures are established regarding the specific method of voting assistance, fairness in elections can be secured while reducing the extent to which the contents of the vote are disclosed even if only one voting assistant accompanies the elector. For example, procedures may be adopted whereby voting may be assisted only when it is confirmed from the elector that there is special trust in the voting assistant, the voting assistant is subjected to a duty of oath to mark the ballot according to the elector’s will, and after voting, the polling manager, etc. confirms from the elector that the voting assistant marked the ballot in the same way as the elector’s will. Furthermore, the qualifications of voting assistants may be restricted so that persons in positions that may influence the elector, such as the head or staff of a residential facility for persons with disabilities, cannot become voting assistants.\\nThe majority opinion points out that such alternatives would make the voting assistance system less readily usable. However, fairness in elections can be secured only when the people’s political will is not distorted and is correctly reflected in elections, so an election in which freedom of elections is not guaranteed cannot be said to have secured fairness. Therefore, even if effort and cost are required to establish specific procedures for voting assistance, if through them the elector can freely vote according to his or her will, the fairness in elections is ultimately also secured, so such alternatives can be said to produce a better result than the provision at issue.\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that there is no alternative to the provision at issue that can better maintain the secrecy of the Petitioner’s vote.\\n(4) Need to Establish a Means for Disabled Voters to Vote on Their Own\\nThe current Public Official Election Act provides that voting shall be conducted by marking the ballot with a ballot-marking device (Public Official Election Act Articles 146(1) and 159). As a result, electors who cannot vote in the above manner because of physical disability have difficulties in exercising the right to vote. Although the relevant statutes provide that the State shall develop and disseminate election aid devices such as ballot-marking methods suitable for the type and degree of disability in order to guarantee the political participation rights of persons with disabilities (Welfare of Persons with Disabilities Act Article 26; Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities, Remedy against Infringement of their Rights, etc. Article 27(2)), the election aid devices currently provided are merely two kinds of special ballot-marking devices, mouthpiece-type and wrist-type ballot markers.\\nEven if a person is not a person with severe disability, an elector with a physical disability has no choice but to vote using a special ballot-marking device, even at the risk of producing an invalid ballot, or to use the voting assistance system pursuant to the provision at issue. Therefore, the provision at issue is not merely a system to substantially guarantee the right to vote of persons with severe disabilities; rather, it is a realistic means by which a large number of persons with disabilities who have difficulty voting accurately by the current voting method due to physical disability can directly and substantially exercise the right to vote themselves. As a result, a large number of persons with disabilities have no choice but to accept the situation in which secret ballot is restricted by the provision at issue, and the resulting harm can by no means be said to be small.\\nTo fundamentally solve this problem, in addition to special ballot-marking devices, it is necessary to prepare election aid devices or ballot methods using new technology that allow electors with physical disabilities to mark the ballot on their own without the assistance of a voting assistant, according to the type and degree of disability, thereby minimizing the cases in which voting assistance is received through the provision at issue. For example, if election aid devices are prepared whereby marking is accomplished through simple physical movements such as pressing a button or blowing air, a significant number of electors with physical disabilities would be able to mark the ballot on their own without the assistance of a voting assistant.\\nOf course, there may be practical constraints such as cost in introducing new election aid devices as above, and new election aid devices may not satisfy all persons with disabilities at once, but improvements to election aid devices or ballot methods can be an alternative that reduces the situation in which secret ballot is restricted for many electors with physical disabilities.\\n(5) Subconclusion\\nTherefore, the provision at issue contravenes the principle of least restriction.\\n\\nc. Balance of Interests\\nThe public interest the provision at issue seeks to achieve is to substantially guarantee the right to vote of electors who, due to physical disability, cannot mark the ballot themselves and to secure fairness in elections by preventing voting assistants from exerting undue influence on the exercise of the right to vote by persons with disabilities. However, as seen above, because the provision at issue does not establish clear procedures for the specific method of voting assistance, it cannot fundamentally prevent two voting assistants from exerting undue influence on the exercise of the right to vote. Also, because the provision at issue compels two voting assistants to disclose the elector’s most intimate political will, there is a greater concern that freedom of elections will be chilled. Therefore, the public interest achieved by the provision at issue is limited.\\nOn the other hand, the disadvantage suffered by the Petitioner due to the provision at issue is that, where the voting assistant is not a family member, two persons must accompany the elector, so compared with the case where there is one voting assistant, it is more difficult to maintain the secrecy of the ballot, and there is the restriction that one additional voting assistant must be secured on voting day in order to vote.\\nBecause ballot contents are the most intimate political will, even if the object of additional disclosure is only one person, it may amount to a serious restriction on the exercise of an individual’s right to vote. Also, the National Election Commission’s practice of allowing, where an elector is accompanied by only one voting assistant who is not a family member, voting only when one person from among the voting clerks is additionally added as a voting assistant in the presence of a poll watcher regardless of the elector’s will, is a serious restriction because the elector must disclose his or her most intimate political will even to an unfamiliar third party with whom no relationship of trust has been formed. And because the provision at issue applies even to many persons with disabilities who have difficulty voting accurately by the current voting method due to physical disability, the above disadvantage cannot be said to be small.\\nBecause the right to vote is the exercise of political self-determination, the voter must be able to complete it under his or her own responsibility, from the formation of political will through realization of that will by voting. Therefore, although the voting assistance system is a means of support for disabled voters, even in this case it should be operated in a manner that assigns the disabled voter who uses it responsibility to confirm whether the voting was accurately carried out according to his or her will and, if not, to raise an objection. However, the provision at issue disregards the point that a disabled voter can complete the exercise of political self-determination by personally bearing such responsibility, and instead assumes that fairness in elections can be secured only through mutual checks between two voting assistants from a merely benevolent perspective. A disabled voter using the provision at issue not only cannot maintain the secrecy of the ballot, but also cannot receive procedural guarantees to complete the exercise of political self-determination, and is forced to exercise the right to vote in a completely different manner from voters without disabilities, such as by having three persons including the voter enter the voting booth together.\\nTherefore, because the disadvantage the Petitioner suffers due to the provision at issue is greater than the public interest to be achieved by the provision at issue, the provision at issue contravenes the principle of balance of interests.\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\nBecause the provision at issue cannot be regarded as establishing an exception to the principle of secret ballot only in necessary and unavoidable exceptional cases, it infringes the Petitioner’s right to vote in violation of the principle against excessive restriction. However, if the provision at issue were declared simply unconstitutional and immediately lose effect, the legal basis for the voting assistance system would disappear, resulting in a legal vacuum. Also, what content should be used to eliminate the unconstitutional elements of the provision at issue and adjust it constitutionally is, in principle, within the legislative discretion of the legislature. Therefore, it is appropriate to render a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution with respect to the provision at issue, while provisionally continuing to apply the provision at issue until new legislation replacing it is enacted."}

{"[2018HEONMA146]": "The Applicant alleges that the suspension of indictment disposition that the Respondent decided on 2017. 10. 17. with respect to the Jeonju District Prosecutors’ Office 2017 year HYEONGJE17338 case concerning residential intrusion infringed the Applicant’s fundamental rights, including the constitutional right to equality and the right to pursue happiness.\\n\\nEven upon a detailed examination of the record of this case, it does not appear that the Respondent conducted an investigation markedly contrary to justice and equity, or that there was any serious error in the interpretation of the Constitution, the application of the law, or the assessment of evidence that affected the decision to suspend indictment; nor is there any material to find that the suspension of indictment disposition was otherwise arbitrary to the extent that it would warrant the intervention of the Constitutional Court. question: Which of the following statements regarding the nationality of the Republic of Korea is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to case law)
A: A person who becomes a dual national before reaching 20 years of age shall choose one nationality pursuant to the procedures prescribed by the Nationality Act by the time he or she reaches 22 years of age, and a person who becomes a dual national after reaching 20 years of age shall choose one nationality within 2 years from that time. However, this shall not include a dual national who, pursuant to the same Act, has pledged to the Minister of Justice that he or she will not exercise a foreign nationality in the Republic of Korea.
B: A national of the Republic of Korea who acquires the nationality of the spouse by marriage to a foreigner shall, within 6 months from the time of acquiring such foreign nationality, notify the Minister of Justice that he or she does not intend to retain Korean nationality, and if the Minister of Justice recognizes this, he or she shall lose Korean nationality from the time of such notification.
C: The provision of the Nationality Act stating, “The Minister of Justice may revoke the permission or determination granted to a person who has obtained permission for naturalization, permission for restoration of nationality, permission to renounce nationality, or a determination of retention of nationality by false or other wrongful means,” does not infringe the freedom of residence and movement or the right to pursue happiness insofar as it concerns revocation of permission for restoration of nationality.
D: A dual national shall choose one nationality within 3 months from the time he or she is incorporated into the military service preparatory status pursuant to Article 8 of the Military Service Act, and a provision of the Nationality Act that prohibits filing a report of loss of nationality after that period and before the military service obligation has been extinguished infringes the freedom to renounce nationality.
E: In a provision of the Nationality Act, the requirement that a person be “of upright conduct” means being endowed with character and conduct such that there is no impediment to accepting a naturalization applicant as a new member of the Republic of Korea, and thus does not violate the principle of clarity.
label: B
