{"[2015HEONBA239]": "1. Case Summary\\n\\na. Case 2015HEONBA239\\n\\nThe Petitioner was indicted on June 26, 2014, on the criminal facts that “in filing final VAT returns on July 25, 2012 and around January 25, 2013, he submitted a false aggregate statement of tax invoices totaling KRW 19.7 billion.”\\nThe court of first instance, on December 19, 2014, rendered a judgment sentencing the Petitioner to imprisonment for 1 year and 6 months and a fine of KRW 2 billion, and ordering that, if the fine is not paid, he shall be confined in a workhouse for a period calculated by converting KRW 4 million into one day [Seoul Northern District Court 2014GOHAP218·320 (consolidated)]; the appeal (Seoul High Court 2015NO148) and the final appeal (Supreme Court 2015DO4677) therefrom were all dismissed.\\nWhile the above final appeal was pending, the Petitioner filed a motion for a referral for constitutional review, arguing that Article 70(2) of the Criminal Act, which provides that, where a fine of not less than KRW 500 million but less than KRW 5 billion is imposed, the period of confinement in a workhouse shall be at least 500 days, and Supplementary Provision Article 2(1) of the Criminal Act, which applies the above provision only to cases in which an indictment is first filed after the effective date of that provision, namely May 14, 2014, violate the principle of nulla poena sine lege and the principle against retroactive punishment. However, when that motion was dismissed on June 11, 2015 (Supreme Court 2015CHOGI301), the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on July 14, 2015.\\n\\nb. Case 2016HEONBA177\\n\\nThe Petitioner was indicted on June 11, 2015, on the criminal facts that “in conspiracy with non-parties Cheon○Yun, Lee○Chan, and Choi○Su, for profit, he evaded approximately KRW 800 million in taxes by preparing and submitting to the government, on three occasions, on October 25, 2006, January 25, 2007, and April 25, 2007, false aggregate statements of tax invoices by purchase counterparties totaling approximately KRW 62.4 billion, and on two occasions, on January 25, 2007 and April 25, 2007, false aggregate statements of tax invoices by sales counterparties totaling approximately KRW 41 billion.”\\nThe court of first instance, on September 11, 2015, rendered a judgment sentencing the Petitioner to imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months and a fine of KRW 12 billion, and ordering that, if the fine is not paid, he shall be confined in a workhouse for a period calculated by converting KRW 12 million into one day (Uijeongbu District Court, Goyang Branch 2015GOHAP118). The Petitioner appealed, but on April 7, 2016, only the term of imprisonment was reduced to 2 years, and the fine and workhouse confinement portions were adjudged in the same content as in the first-instance judgment (Seoul High Court 2015NO2707). The final appeal against that judgment was dismissed on June 10, 2016 (Supreme Court 2016DO5582).\\nWhile the above appellate proceedings were pending, the Petitioner filed a motion for a referral for constitutional review regarding Article 70(2) of the Criminal Act, which provides that, where a fine of not less than KRW 5 billion is imposed, the period of confinement in a workhouse shall be at least 1,000 days, and Supplementary Provision Article 2(1) of the Criminal Act, which applies the above provision only to cases in which an indictment is first filed after the effective date. When that motion was dismissed on April 7, 2016 (Seoul High Court 2015CHOGI475), the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on May 2, 2016.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of this review is whether Article 70(2) of the Criminal Act (as amended by Act No. 12575 of May 14, 2014) (hereinafter referred to as the “workhouse confinement provision”) and Supplementary Provision Article 2(1) of the Criminal Act (Act No. 12575 of May 14, 2014) (hereinafter referred to as the “supplementary provision”) are unconstitutional.\\nThe provisions subject to review and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nCriminal Act (as amended by Act No. 12575 of May 14, 2014)\\n\\nArticle 70 (Workhouse Confinement) (2) Where the fine imposed is not less than KRW 100 million but less than KRW 500 million, the period of confinement shall be at least 300 days; where it is not less than KRW 500 million but less than KRW 5 billion, at least 500 days; and where it is not less than KRW 5 billion, at least 1,000 days.\\n\\nSupplementary Provisions to the Criminal Act (Act No. 12575 of May 14, 2014)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Application and Transitional Measures) (1) The amended provisions of Article 70(2) shall apply from the first case in which an indictment is filed after the enforcement of this Act.\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]\\n\\nCriminal Act (as amended by Act No. 12575 of May 14, 2014)\\n\\nArticle 70 (Workhouse Confinement) (1) When a fine or minor fine is imposed, the period of confinement in the event of nonpayment shall be determined and pronounced at the same time.\\n\\nCriminal Act (enacted by Act No. 293 of September 18, 1953)\\n\\nArticle 69 (Fine and Minor Fine) (1) A fine and a minor fine shall be paid within 30 days from the date on which the judgment becomes final and conclusive. Provided, That when a fine is imposed, it may simultaneously be ordered that the offender be confined in a workhouse until the amount is paid in full.\\n(2) A person who has not paid a fine shall be confined in a workhouse and made to perform labor service for a period of not less than 1 day and not more than 3 years, and a person who has not paid a minor fine shall be confined in a workhouse and made to perform labor service for a period of not less than 1 day and less than 30 days.\\n\\n3. The Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\na. The workhouse confinement provision uniformly fixes the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period, thereby making it impossible to determine a reasonable workhouse confinement period according to the specific degree of responsibility; thus, it violates the principle of culpability under the principle of nulla poena sine lege, and because it discriminates between persons who have the financial capacity to pay a fine and those who do not, it violates the principle of equality. In addition, the workhouse confinement provision is mainly applied to offenses under special statutes prescribing fines of not less than KRW 100 million, but because the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period for offenses under special statutes is prescribed in the Criminal Act, it violates systemic consistency.\\n\\nb. The workhouse confinement provision allows for longer workhouse confinement than before and can thus be viewed as a rule that effectively aggravates punishment; however, the supplementary provision retroactively applies the workhouse confinement provision even to persons who committed offenses before that provision entered into force, and therefore it violates the principle of nulla poena sine lege and the principle against retroactive punishment. Moreover, it discriminates by punishing differently, on the basis of the accidental circumstance of whether an indictment was filed, persons who committed the same offense on the same day, and therefore it violates the principle of equality.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\na. Legislative purpose of the workhouse confinement system and the workhouse confinement provision\\n\\n(1) Meaning and content of workhouse confinement\\n\\nWorkhouse confinement refers to a conversion disposition in connection with the execution of a fine or minor fine, under which the offender is confined in a workhouse and made to perform labor service until the fine is paid in full. Workhouse confinement is distinct from penal labor, that is, punishment consisting of compulsory labor itself, in that it is a conversion disposition for a fine, etc. (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2010HEONBA188, etc.). Workhouse confinement, in principle, functions as a substitute means of paying a fine, etc., because when a person who has not paid a fine, etc. is confined in a workhouse, the amount of the fine, etc. is reduced by the number of days of confinement; however, it also functions to compel payment in that it exerts strong psychological pressure on the person who has not paid the fine, etc.\\n\\nWhen imposing a fine, the period of confinement in the event of nonpayment shall be determined and pronounced at the same time (Article 70(1) of the Criminal Act), and a person who has not paid a fine shall be confined in a workhouse and made to perform labor service for a period of not less than 1 day and not more than 3 years (Article 69(2) of the Criminal Act). The Criminal Act prescribes the amount of the fine and the period of confinement, but does not prescribe the amount to be converted per day of confinement; ordinarily, however, the amount of the fine is divided by the period of confinement to ascertain the daily conversion amount. Since the provisions concerning the execution of punishment apply mutatis mutandis to the execution of workhouse confinement (Article 492 of the Criminal Procedure Act), a person ordered to be confined in a workhouse is incarcerated in a prison together with inmates sentenced to imprisonment and performs prison labor (Article 67 of the Criminal Act; Article 2 subparagraph 2 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates). When a person sentenced to a fine pays a part thereof, the number of days corresponding to the amount paid shall be deducted in proportion to the amount of the fine and the number of days of confinement (Article 71 of the Criminal Act). The number of days of detention before pronouncement of judgment is credited in full toward the period of confinement for the fine, and one day of detention is counted as one day of the period of confinement (Article 57 of the Criminal Act).\\n\\n(2) Legislative background and purpose of the workhouse confinement provision\\n\\nPreviously, there were instances in which a defendant sentenced to a large fine was able to be exempted from the entire fine through only a short period of workhouse confinement because the daily conversion amount was set high. In particular, when even persons of wealth were found to be exempted from large fines through short periods of workhouse confinement despite having sufficient financial means, this came to be criticized by the public as so-called “imperial workhouse labor.” In addition, it was pointed out that the excessive imbalance in the daily conversion amount depending on the amount of the fine is contrary to justice in criminal justice and causes public distrust in the entire judicial system. The workhouse confinement provision was enacted under the legislative judgment that improvement of these problems was urgent. The workhouse confinement provision is intended to prevent large fines from being rendered ineffective through short periods of workhouse confinement by setting the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period for fines of not less than KRW 100 million, and to enhance fairness in the daily conversion amount by establishing standards for the workhouse confinement period.\\n\\nb. Whether the workhouse confinement provision is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Issue\\n\\nThe workhouse confinement provision requires Petitioners whose fines are not less than KRW 100 million to be confined in a workhouse for at least a certain period if they do not pay the fine, and therefore the issue is whether it infringes the Petitioners’ freedom of the person in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\nThe Petitioners argue that the workhouse confinement provision violates the principle of culpability, but this argument is no different from an argument that it violates the principle of proportionality; and they argue that placing the workhouse confinement provision in the Criminal Act rather than in a special statute violates systemic consistency, but even if systemic consistency is violated, that does not automatically render it unconstitutional, and the Constitution must be violated in a manner contrary to its provisions or principles such as proportionality (see Constitutional Court 2010. 6. 24. 2007HEONBA101, etc.; Constitutional Court 2015. 7. 30. 2013HEONBA120, etc.). Accordingly, it is sufficient to determine this part of the argument by examining whether the principle of proportionality has been violated.\\nThe Petitioners argue that the workhouse confinement provision discriminates between persons who have the financial capacity to pay a fine and those who do not. However, this provision applies to all persons who have not paid a fine regardless of the presence or absence of economic capacity, and the difference in the possibility of workhouse confinement depending on the ability to pay the fine is not a discrimination contemplated by this provision, but merely stems from the essential nature of the fine as a property punishment. Therefore, the workhouse confinement provision cannot be said to discriminate between persons with economic capacity and those without it (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2010HEONBA188, etc.).\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of proportionality is violated\\n\\n(a) Legitimate purpose and suitability of means\\n\\nThe workhouse confinement provision is intended to prevent workhouse confinement from being used as a means of evading payment of large fines and to enhance fairness in the daily conversion amount, and such legislative purpose is legitimate. If the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period is prescribed by law when a fine of not less than KRW 100 million is imposed, payment of the fine can be psychologically compelled and excessive discrepancies among daily conversion amounts can be narrowed, thereby promoting fairness; thus, the workhouse confinement provision is a suitable means to achieve the legislative purpose.\\n\\n(b) Minimal impairment\\n\\n1) Workhouse confinement functions to compel payment of a fine by warning that failure to pay the fine will result in the sanction of deprivation of liberty. If the workhouse confinement period is set excessively short in relation to the fine, there may be persons who serve the term with the purpose of avoiding payment of a large fine despite having sufficient financial means; therefore, it is necessary to set a minimum workhouse confinement period capable of psychologically compelling payment of a large fine. In addition, even if the problem that the daily conversion amount inevitably becomes larger as the fine is larger cannot be avoided because the upper limit of the workhouse confinement period is set at 3 years under current law, prescribing the lower limit of the confinement period by law for large fines can minimize imbalances that arise among daily conversion amounts.\\nIn this respect, setting the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period can be said to be an unavoidable means for securing the effectiveness of fine payment and promoting fairness among daily conversion amounts.\\n\\n2) The workhouse confinement provision sets the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period only where the fine is “not less than KRW 100 million.” The workhouse confinement provision mainly targets economic crimes, food, health, and environmental offenses under special criminal statutes that prescribe “not less than a multiple of the proceeds of the crime” as the lower limit of the fine. For example, there are bribery offenses under the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (Article 2), violations of the Customs Act (Article 6), tax evasion (Article 8), violations of the duty to issue tax invoices (Article 8-2), offenses of bribery, etc. under the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Article 5), the manufacture of illicit food, illicit pharmaceuticals, and illicit toxic substances under the Special Measures Act on the Control of Health Crimes (Articles 2 to 4), capture of endangered wildlife under the Act on the Control and Aggravated Punishment of Environmental Offenses, etc. (Article 6), illegal waste disposal (Article 7), sale of food using prohibited ingredients under the Food Sanitation Act, manufacture and sale of harmful food, use of toxic utensils, unlicensed business operations, and false and exaggerated advertising (Article 94), and unlicensed business operations, manufacture and sale of harmful health functional foods, and false and exaggerated advertising under the Act on Health Functional Foods (Article 43).\\n\\nThese offenses are generally crimes committed for economic gain, and are characterized by the fact that the harm they cause is great and the illegality is serious, such as disturbing the economic order or causing serious harm to human life or bodily integrity. Without imposing enormous economic loss together with deprivation of criminal proceeds through strict enforcement of payment of the fine on those sentenced to a fine, it is difficult to prevent the commission of such offenses. Therefore, setting the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period in cases where a fine of not less than KRW 100 million is imposed does not go beyond the bounds of legislation, as it is a legislative judgment aimed at effectively securing payment of the fine and preventing such offenses.\\n\\n3) The workhouse confinement provision promotes fairness according to the gravity of the offense and the quality of the offense by increasing the lower limit of the confinement period step by step according to the amount of the fine. The workhouse confinement provision states that “where the fine imposed is not less than KRW 100 million but less than KRW 500 million, the confinement period shall be at least 300 days; where it is not less than KRW 500 million but less than KRW 5 billion, at least 500 days; and where it is not less than KRW 5 billion, at least 1,000 days,” but considering the fact that the upper limit of the workhouse confinement period has long been set at 3 years and the amount of the fine imposed, it is difficult to view the lower limit as excessively long. In addition, although the daily conversion amount under the workhouse confinement provision differs depending on the amount of the fine—KRW 333,000 to KRW 1.66 million where the fine is not less than KRW 100 million but less than KRW 500 million; KRW 1 million to KRW 10 million where the fine is not less than KRW 500 million but less than KRW 5 billion; and not less than KRW 5 million where the fine is not less than KRW 5 billion—this is an unavoidable result of setting the upper limit of the workhouse confinement period at 3 years.\\n\\n4) Since the workhouse confinement provision merely sets the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period according to the amount of the fine imposed, the judge may determine the daily conversion amount and the workhouse confinement period within that range by considering various sentencing factors. In addition, if there are sentencing factors such as the confiscation or collection of proceeds from the criminal act or the defendant’s efforts to recover the damage, the judge may reduce the fine and may also suspend the pronouncement of the fine sentence alone separately from the imprisonment sentence (Article 59(2) of the Criminal Act). Furthermore, because most offenses subject to the workhouse confinement provision are prescribed as mandatory cumulative imposition of a fine together with imprisonment, the judge may, if necessary, achieve concrete equity by taking into account the lower limit of the confinement period prescribed by the workhouse confinement provision in the process of sentencing imprisonment.\\n\\n5) Taking these points together, the workhouse confinement provision satisfies the requirement of minimal impairment.\\n\\n(c) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe workhouse confinement provision is intended to enhance the fairness and equity of the workhouse confinement system by preventing large fines from being rendered ineffective through short periods of workhouse confinement and by preventing excessive discrepancies among daily conversion amounts; such public interest is highly important.\\n\\nOn the other hand, the disadvantage suffered by the Petitioners as a result is that, if they do not pay the fine imposed, they will be confined in a workhouse for at least a certain period and thus have their freedom of the person restricted. Workhouse confinement is contemplated in preparation for the case where a fine is not paid, and if the fine is paid there is no possibility of enforcement; considering also the fact that workhouse confinement substitutes for the fine sentence, the disadvantage suffered by the Petitioners cannot be said to be greater than the public interest sought to be achieved by the workhouse confinement provision.\\n\\nTherefore, the workhouse confinement provision satisfies the requirement of balance of legal interests.\\n\\n(3) Conclusion on this point\\n\\nAccordingly, the workhouse confinement provision cannot be deemed to infringe the Petitioners’ freedom of the person in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nc. Whether the supplementary provision is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Issue\\n\\nThe supplementary provision makes the workhouse confinement provision applicable even when an offense was committed before the workhouse confinement provision was amended and entered into force, provided that the indictment was filed after the entry into force of the workhouse confinement provision. This constitutes retroactive legislation in that it applies a law amended after completion of the criminal act. Therefore, if workhouse confinement has the character of punishment, and if setting the lower limit of its confinement period is an unfavorable change, it may violate the principle against retroactive punishment in Article 13(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Meaning and standard of application of the principle against retroactive punishment\\n\\nThe second sentence of Article 12(1) of the Constitution provides that “... No person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to compulsory labor except as provided by law and through due process of law,” and the first sentence of Article 13(1) of the Constitution provides that “No citizen shall be prosecuted for an act that does not constitute a crime under the law in force at the time of the act ...,” thereby prescribing the principle of nulla poena sine lege and the principle against retroactive punishment. The fundamental purpose of these provisions is to clearly draw the boundary between permitted acts and prohibited acts, to inform citizens in advance of what acts are prohibited and what punishment is prescribed for violations thereof, so that they may conform their conduct accordingly, and to protect legal stability, predictability, and public trust by prohibiting punishment or aggravated punishment through ex post facto legislation (see Constitutional Court 1996. 2. 16. 96HEONGA2, etc.).\\n\\nHowever, if the scope of “punishment” to which the principle against retroactive punishment applies were viewed as limited only to the types of punishment prescribed by the Criminal Act, the result would be that criminal sanctions or disadvantages that can be imposed in forms other than the punishments prescribed by the Criminal Act would be allowed to be applied retroactively, thereby nullifying the purpose of the principle against retroactive punishment, which is to secure legal stability and predictability and to protect citizens from arbitrary punishment. The “punishment” contemplated by the principle against retroactive punishment is not limited merely to the formal types of punishment prescribed in the Criminal Act.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court, long ago, regarding “protective custody” under the former Social Protection Act, a preventive measure, held that “protective custody, which as one of the preventive measures against habitual offenders, etc. consists in depriving a person of liberty, can be imposed only pursuant to due process at the same level as punishment and in accordance with the principle of nulla poena sine lege set forth in Article 13(1) of the Constitution; therefore, as to crimes that are the basis for its requirements, protective custody by retroactive legislation cannot be allowed.” It thus made clear that the principle against retroactive punishment can apply even to sanctions other than the “punishments prescribed by the Criminal Act” (see Constitutional Court 1989. 7. 14. 88HEONGA5, etc.). Thereafter, the Constitutional Court has also held that “even if it is a preventive measure, if it has a strong punitive character and deprives a person of liberty or restricts liberty to a degree equivalent thereto, the principle against retroactive punishment applies” (see Constitutional Court 2012. 12. 27. 2010HEONGA82, etc.; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2011HEONMA28, etc.).\\n\\nThe Supreme Court also held, with respect to “protective custody” under the former Social Protection Act, that only offenses committed after the enforcement of the Social Protection Act are subject to a request for protective custody (see Supreme Court Judgment of February 9, 1982, 81DO2897); and with respect to “community service order,” one of the protective dispositions prescribed by the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Domestic Violence Crimes, it likewise ruled to the effect that, although it has the character of a preventive measure, since in substance it restricts personal liberty, the law in force at the time of the act must be applied pursuant to the principle against retroactive punishment (see Supreme Court Judgment of July 24, 2008, 2008EO4).\\n\\nAs such, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court determine whether the principle against retroactive punishment applies, when imposing sanctions for criminal acts, not by the formal classification of the sanction, but by the degree of punitive disadvantage brought about by the substance of the sanction.\\n\\nTaking these points together, where the content or practical effect of a sanction for a criminal act is aggravated, or an incidental effect is changed disadvantageously, it is desirable to apply the law in force at the time of the act (see Article 2(1) of the German Criminal Code). In particular, where the content or practical effect of a sanction for a criminal act has a strong punitive character and deprives a person of liberty or restricts liberty to a degree equivalent thereto, the principle against retroactive punishment must apply in order to protect legal stability, predictability, and public trust.\\n\\n(3) The workhouse confinement provision and the principle against retroactive punishment\\n\\n(a) The Criminal Act provides that “a person who has not paid a fine shall be confined in a workhouse and made to perform labor service for a period of not less than 1 day and not more than 3 years” (Article 69(2)), and provides that “when a fine is imposed, the period of confinement in the event of nonpayment shall be determined and pronounced at the same time” (Article 70(1)). As such, workhouse confinement is a method of execution for a fine sentence and is not itself an independent punishment, but a conversion disposition additionally imposed in connection with a fine sentence.\\n\\nIn addition, the provisions concerning the execution of punishment apply mutatis mutandis to the execution of workhouse confinement (Article 492 of the Criminal Procedure Act), and a person ordered to be confined in a workhouse is incarcerated in a prison together with inmates sentenced to imprisonment and performs prison labor, etc. (Article 67 of the Criminal Act; Article 2 subparagraph 2 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates); thus, the method of execution of workhouse confinement is identical to that of imprisonment. Moreover, the Criminal Act provides that all days of detention before pronouncement of judgment are credited toward the period of confinement, and that one day of detention is counted as one day of the period of confinement (Article 57), thereby prescribing the substance of workhouse confinement as the same as imprisonment.\\n\\nTherefore, workhouse confinement is a conversion disposition additionally imposed in connection with a fine sentence, and its substance has a punitive character similar to imprisonment because it deprives a person of liberty; accordingly, it is subject to the principle against retroactive punishment.\\n\\n(b) The principle against retroactive punishment applies not only where an act did not constitute a crime under the law at the time of the criminal act, but also where the punishment is aggravated compared to the law at the time of the criminal act. The principle against retroactive punishment applies even where the upper or lower limit of punishment is raised compared to the law at the time of the criminal act, and applies not only where the principal punishment is aggravated but also where ancillary or cumulative punishment is aggravated.\\n\\nAs noted above, since workhouse confinement is a conversion disposition additionally imposed in connection with a fine sentence and, in substance, has a punitive character similar to imprisonment by depriving a person of liberty, where the amendment of the law relating to workhouse confinement makes the disadvantage heavier, such as by prolonging the period for persons sentenced to the same fine, the period of confinement in the event of nonpayment must be determined and pronounced in accordance with the law in force at the time of the criminal act.\\n\\nPreviously, apart from the rule that workhouse confinement could be imposed for a period of not less than 1 day and not more than 3 years, there was no lower limit prescribed for the workhouse confinement period, and even if the fine was large, the workhouse confinement period was not necessarily prolonged proportionally. However, the workhouse confinement provision states that “where the fine imposed is not less than KRW 100 million but less than KRW 500 million, the confinement period shall be at least 300 days; where it is not less than KRW 500 million but less than KRW 5 billion, at least 500 days; and where it is not less than KRW 5 billion, at least 1,000 days,” thereby setting the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period at 300 days or more where a fine of not less than KRW 100 million is imposed. As a result, the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period for persons sentenced to a fine of not less than KRW 100 million became longer than before. In this case as well, the Petitioners subject to the workhouse confinement provision were sentenced to workhouse confinement periods nearly 3 to 17 times longer than their accomplices against whom indictments had been filed before this provision entered into force.\\n\\nTherefore, because the workhouse confinement provision has materially aggravated the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period for persons sentenced to a fine of not less than KRW 100 million, offenses committed before this provision entered into force must be governed by the law that existed at the time of the offense.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion on this point\\n\\nSince the supplementary provision applies the workhouse confinement provision even to offenses committed before the workhouse confinement provision entered into force, so long as the indictment is filed after the entry into force of the workhouse confinement provision, the supplementary provision can be said to require retroactive application of a law more disadvantageous than the law at the time of the criminal act, and therefore it violates the constitutional principle against retroactive punishment.\\n\\nSince, as above, we determine that the supplementary provision violates the Constitution by contravening the principle against retroactive punishment, we do not further determine the Petitioners’ remaining arguments.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nThe workhouse confinement provision does not violate the Constitution, whereas the supplementary provision does violate the Constitution; accordingly, the decision is rendered as stated in the order. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, except for the separate opinions on the supplementary provision by Justice Kang Il-won and Justice Jo Yong-ho as set forth in 6. below, and the concurring opinion on the workhouse confinement provision by Justice Ahn Chang-ho as set forth in 7. below.\\n\\n6. Separate Opinion of Justices Kang Il-won and Jo Yong-ho on the Supplementary Provision\\n\\nWe agree with the conclusion of the majority opinion regarding the workhouse confinement provision and the supplementary provision, but we differ from the majority opinion as to the reasons why the supplementary provision is unconstitutional, and therefore state our opinion as follows.\\n\\na. Whether the principle of workhouse confinement and the principle against retroactive punishment apply\\n\\nThe first sentence of Article 13(1) of the Constitution provides that “No citizen shall be prosecuted for an act that does not constitute a crime under the law in force at the time of the act ...,” thereby prescribing the principle against retroactive punishment. The area in which retroactive legislation is prohibited under the principle against retroactive punishment is the constituent elements of a crime and the punishment that follows therefrom.\\n\\nThe principle against retroactive punishment means prohibiting ex post facto changes to the conditions of punishability, in other words, prohibiting retroactive enactment of constituent elements of a crime and retroactive aggravation of punishment. The reason the Constitution expressly sets forth the principle against retroactive punishment is, as the majority opinion also explains, to clearly establish the boundary between permitted acts and prohibited acts, to inform citizens in advance which acts are prohibited and what punishment is prescribed for violations thereof, and thereby to prohibit punishment or aggravated punishment by ex post facto legislation and secure legal stability, predictability, and trust in the legal order.\\n\\nThe supplementary provision applies the workhouse confinement provision even where an offense was committed before the workhouse confinement provision entered into force, provided that the indictment was filed after the entry into force of the workhouse confinement provision, and thus constitutes retroactive legislation in that it allows the amended law to be applied even to acts completed before the workhouse confinement provision entered into force.\\n\\nThe question is whether the principle of non-retroactivity in criminal law can be applied to the fact that, unlike before, the workhouse confinement provision, which sets the lower limit of the confinement period according to the amount of the fine imposed, is applied from the first case in which an indictment is filed after its entry into force.\\n\\nWorkhouse confinement may be evaluated as heavier than merely paying money in that it has an outward form similar to a custodial sentence restricting liberty. However, in order for workhouse confinement, as a substitute for a fine, to function as a means of compelling payment of the fine, it must be able to inflict pain equivalent to that of the principal punishment, and a large fine sentence must not be rendered ineffective through a short period of workhouse confinement. Therefore, because workhouse confinement merely restricts liberty, it is difficult to view it as an independent punishment or a separate disadvantageous sanction that can be evaluated on the same level as punishment.\\n\\nOf course, considering that the workhouse confinement provision fixed a minimum period for fines of a certain amount in order to improve the so-called “imperial workhouse labor” problem that arose under the previous legal system, which had no lower-limit provision for the workhouse confinement period, there is room to view it as an ex post aggravation of sanctions in that it increases the possibility that the confinement period will be longer than before for the same fine sentence. However, whether such ex post legislation can be constitutionally tolerated and whether it falls within the area to which the principle against retroactive punishment applies are entirely different questions. It is difficult to view it as a heavier change in punishment to which the principle against retroactive punishment applies merely because it increases the possibility that the confinement period will become longer than before.\\n\\nAs the majority opinion also explains, workhouse confinement is a method of execution for a fine sentence and, in connection with the execution of a fine or minor fine, consists in confining the offender in a workhouse and making him perform labor service until the fine is paid in full; it is a method of execution of a fine sentence and has the function of substituting for payment and compelling payment. It is distinct from penal labor, that is, punishment consisting of compulsory labor itself, in that it is a conversion disposition for a fine sentence (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2010HEONBA188, etc.). Workhouse confinement for a fine sentence is not imposing punishment again upon a case already punished, but merely changing the method of execution of punishment (see Constitutional Court 2005. 7. 21. 2003HEONBA98; Constitutional Court 2009. 3. 26. 2008HEONBA52; Constitutional Court 2010. 7. 29. 2008HEONBA88, etc.). Therefore, even if the amended Criminal Act set the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period by amount and made it applicable from cases in which an indictment is filed after the enforcement of the Act, rather than from cases arising after the enforcement of the Act, this merely strengthens the method of execution substituting for the fine sentence, and it is difficult to see a problem of retroactive punishment arising therefrom.\\n\\nThe majority opinion cites the Constitutional Court’s precedents and Supreme Court precedents concerning “protective custody” under the former Social Protection Act and “community service orders” under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Domestic Violence Crimes, and says that, because the substance of workhouse confinement deprives a person of liberty and thus has a punitive character similar to imprisonment, it is subject to the principle against retroactive punishment. However, workhouse confinement is nothing more than a method of execution substituting for a fine sentence, and the supplementary provision is a transitional provision concerning the enforcement of the workhouse confinement provision, whereas the above-mentioned “protective custody” and “community service orders” are prescribed in the main text of the respective special statutes as independent sanctions and have the character of preventive measures restricting liberty. Since the two differ in legislative purpose, form of prescription, and legal nature, the above precedents and Supreme Court decisions are not to be cited here. In addition, the majority opinion expands the concept of “punishment” by using the expression “punitive character similar to imprisonment,” focusing only on the content or practical effect of the sanction, and there is a contradiction in arguing unconstitutionality not from the inherent unconstitutionality of the supplementary provision but rather centered on the workhouse confinement provision, which it itself earlier argued to be constitutional (see 4(b) above).\\n\\nb. Whether the supplementary provision violates the prohibition of retroactive legislation\\n\\nBecause the supplementary provision makes the workhouse confinement provision applicable from the first case in which an indictment is filed after its entry into force, it constitutes retroactive legislation in that it allows the amended provision to be applied even to completed criminal acts; therefore, it is necessary to examine whether such retroactive legislation can be constitutionally permitted.\\n\\nPure retroactive legislation, which affects facts or legal relations already completed by new legislation, is not constitutionally permitted under the principle of the rule of law, which embodies the protection of individual trust and legal stability, absent special circumstances. However, it may be exceptionally permitted where the public need to change the existing law is extremely grave, while the need to protect the individual’s trust in his or her legal position is relatively unjustifiable, and there are special circumstances (Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29. 2005HEONMA165, etc.).\\n\\nWorkhouse confinement is only a method of execution of a fine sentence and not the punishment itself, but because its substance is no different from a custodial sentence, if the period of workhouse confinement is longer than before for the same amount of fine, it may result in a serious infringement of fundamental rights. Therefore, the trust in the existing legal order regarding, for example, how long one may be confined in a workhouse if one is sentenced to a fine and does not pay it, or whether there exists an upper or lower limit for the confinement period, is highly deserving of protection.\\n\\nIn the case of the Petitioners, even under the previous legal order, it was entirely possible that, for a fine sentence, they could be confined in a workhouse for a period longer than the period prescribed in the workhouse confinement provision, within the range of not less than 1 day and not more than 3 years; however, because no lower limit for the workhouse confinement period was prescribed, even if the fine amount was large, the workhouse confinement period did not necessarily become longer in proportion to the fine amount. In addition, at the time the Petitioners committed the offenses, there was an established trust that, regardless of the amount of the fine, they could be sentenced to workhouse confinement for a period shorter than that prescribed in the workhouse confinement provision, and the practical practice of the courts was also such (specifically, a trust that even where a fine sentence of not less than KRW 100 million was imposed, workhouse confinement of less than 300 days could be imposed; even where a fine sentence of not less than KRW 500 million was imposed, less than 500 days; and even where a fine sentence of not less than KRW 5 billion was imposed, less than 1,000 days). Therefore, such trust in the workhouse confinement period deserves protection just like a legal interest.\\n\\nHowever, although the workhouse confinement provision, by setting intervals according to the amount of the fine and requiring that a minimum period of confinement be prescribed for each amount, has in effect made the workhouse confinement period longer than before, the supplementary provision applies the amended workhouse confinement provision disadvantageously to the Petitioners, who acted in reliance on the old legal order and formed their legal status, thereby infringing the above-mentioned trust interest of the Petitioners.\\n\\nNevertheless, even if, as above, the Petitioners’ trust in the old legal order merits protection and the supplementary provision infringes that trust interest, such retroactive legislation may still be constitutionally permissible if there exist public-interest reasons that make retroactive legislation such as the supplementary provision unavoidable.\\n\\nAlthough the legislative purpose of the workhouse confinement provision—to strengthen payment enforcement for large fines and promote fairness regarding the amount converted into workhouse confinement—is important, the public interest that can be achieved by retroactively applying such legislative purpose even to offenses committed before the workhouse confinement provision entered into force cannot be said to be very large. This is because the purpose of preventing large fines from being rendered ineffective through short periods of workhouse confinement and inducing sincere payment of fines becomes effective only through enhanced legislation such as the workhouse confinement provision; in the earlier situation where such legislation did not exist, it is difficult to expect such effect. Imposing heavier responsibility ex post facto for conduct committed when the warning function of the enhanced sanction had not operated does not accord with the spirit of prohibiting retroactive legislation in order to protect trust in the existing legal order and legal stability. Regulating past events through law enacted after the fact is not justified merely by public necessity; rather, such retroactive legislation runs the risk of merely increasing distrust in the legal order as a whole.\\n\\nMoreover, by applying from the first case in which an indictment is filed after the enforcement of this Act, the supplementary provision raises even concerns about arbitrary law enforcement. This is because even similar forms of criminal conduct committed at the same time can lead to markedly unreasonable results in the workhouse confinement period depending on when the prosecutor files the indictment.\\n\\nAs seen above, the supplementary provision in this case violates the prohibition of retroactive legislation.\\n\\n7. Concurring Opinion of Justice Ahn Chang-ho on the Workhouse Confinement Provision\\n\\nAlthough I do not find the workhouse confinement provision to be unconstitutional, I believe that special criminal statute provisions mandatorily imposing a fine of a large amount in combination with imprisonment may, when combined with the workhouse confinement provision, become an excessive sanction for the offender, and that legislative improvement to reorganize the relevant laws is necessary. I therefore state the following concurring opinion.\\n\\na. The workhouse confinement provision sets the lower limit of the workhouse confinement period from cases in which the fine imposed is “not less than KRW 100 million.” The workhouse confinement provision mainly targets economic crimes and food, health, and environmental offenses under special criminal statutes that prescribe “not less than a multiple of the proceeds of the crime” as the lower limit of the fine.\\n\\nThese include, for example, Article 2 (bribery offenses), Article 6 (false declarations, smuggling import/export, etc. under the Customs Act), Article 8 (tax evasion, etc. under the Punishment of Tax Offenses Act), Article 8-2 (receipt or issuance of sham tax invoices, etc. under the Punishment of Tax Offenses Act), Article 5 (bribery by officers and employees of financial institutions, etc.), and Article 11 (unauthorized short-term financial business) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes; Article 2 (manufacture of illicit food, etc.), Article 3 (manufacture of illicit pharmaceuticals, etc.), Article 4 (manufacture of illicit toxic substances, etc.), and Article 5 (unauthorized medical practitioners) of the Special Measures Act on the Control of Health Crimes; Article 6 (export, import, manufacture, sale, etc. of narcotics as a business) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Prevention of Illegal Trafficking in Narcotics, etc.; Article 6 (capture of endangered wildlife), Article 7 (illegal waste disposal), and Article 8 (aggravated punishment for repeat offenses under Article 7) of the Act on the Control and Aggravated Punishment of Environmental Offenses, etc.; and Article 43(3) (unlicensed business operations, etc.) of the Act on Health Functional Foods.\\n\\nb. The question of which acts are to be defined as crimes and how they are to be punished is, in principle, a matter of national legislative policy to be determined by the legislature by comprehensively considering our history and culture, the circumstances of the times at the time of legislation, the general values and legal sentiments of the people, the actual state and quality of the offense, the protected legal interests, and the effect of crime prevention, and is an area in which broad legislative discretion or freedom of formation should be recognized (Constitutional Court 1995. 11. 30. 94HEONGA3; Constitutional Court 2010. 5. 27. 2009HEONGA28).\\n\\nEconomic crimes and food, health, and environmental offenses for which a fine subject to the workhouse confinement provision may be imposed are generally crimes committed for economic gain and are characterized by large harm and serious illegality, such as disturbing the economic order or causing serious harm to human life or bodily integrity. In order to prevent the commission of such offenses, it may be difficult to do so without imposing enormous economic loss together with deprivation of criminal proceeds, and therefore it is necessary to impose large fines to prevent such offenses. On the other hand, if there are sentencing factors, the judge may reduce the amount of the fine and may suspend the pronouncement of the fine sentence alone separately from the imprisonment sentence (Article 59(2) of the Criminal Act). And because most of these offenses are prescribed as mandatory cumulative imposition of a fine together with imprisonment, the judge may, if necessary, achieve concrete equity by taking the fine sentence into account in the course of sentencing imprisonment.\\n\\nTaking these points into consideration, the Constitutional Court has rendered decisions upholding special criminal statute provisions prescribing fines to which the workhouse confinement provision may apply, on the ground that such provisions are legislative judgments to prevent the commission of offenses and cannot be said to go beyond legislative discretion (Constitutional Court 2013. 12. 26. 2012HEONBA217, etc.; Constitutional Court 2015. 12. 23. 2015HEONBA244; Constitutional Court 2015. 12. 23. 2015HEONBA249; Constitutional Court 2016. 5. 26. 2016HEONBA81; Constitutional Court 2017. 7. 27. 2017HEONBA226, etc.).\\n\\nc. Economic crimes and food, health, and environmental offenses, etc., which prescribe “not less than a multiple of the proceeds of the crime” as the lower limit of the fine, often provide for the mandatory cumulative imposition of a fine.\\n\\nSuch mandatory cumulative imposition of a large fine is intended to exert not only deprivation of criminal proceeds but also general deterrence through loss of property. However, where deprivation of the monetary gains obtained through the criminal act is already contemplated by mandatory confiscation or collection, the mandatory addition of a large fine may inflict double economic suffering on the offender.\\n\\nIn particular, among accomplices, there may be cases where some have no economic gain or only slight gain, and in such cases, the mandatory cumulative imposition of a large fine on all accomplices may be an excessive punishment. In the case of economic crimes, etc. that prescribe “not less than a multiple of the proceeds of the crime” as the lower limit of the fine, where there are multiple accomplices, all accomplices are sentenced to large fines under the relevant statute, and they must each pay the fine sentenced to them; unlike confiscation and collection, even if a particular accomplice pays the fine, the other accomplices are not exempted from execution of the fine sentence they were individually sentenced to and must pay the full amount.\\n\\nd. The workhouse confinement provision requires that, where the fine imposed is not less than KRW 100 million, the period of confinement in a workhouse shall be at least a certain period (Article 70(2)).\\n\\nThis workhouse confinement provision, when combined with special criminal statute provisions mandatorily imposing a large fine, may in substance become an excessive custodial punishment for the offender. As examined in the majority opinion, workhouse confinement has, in substance, the punitive character of deprivation of liberty similar to imprisonment because it deprives a person of liberty, and the period of workhouse confinement may be prolonged for a considerable time due to the workhouse confinement provision. In particular, for economically disadvantaged persons, paying a fine of not less than KRW 100 million is not easy; therefore, large fines imposed on them create a high likelihood of conversion into workhouse confinement. As a result, the workhouse confinement provision may cause economically vulnerable persons sentenced to large fines to be additionally incarcerated in prison and made to perform prison labor for a considerable period beyond the imprisonment sentence imposed, and this may be criticized as contrary to the principle of culpability.\\n\\ne. The workhouse confinement provision also allows, even where the execution of an imprisonment sentence is suspended, that if the fine cannot be paid, the workhouse confinement period may be set at at least 300 days, 500 days, or 1,000 days depending on the amount of the fine.\\n\\nHowever, there is criticism that, while suspending the execution of imprisonment in light of the offender’s age, character and conduct, intelligence and environment, relationship to the victim, motive, means and result of the offense, and circumstances after the offense, it is not appropriate to allow the offender to be confined in a workhouse and made to perform labor service for such a considerable period merely because the fine jointly imposed could not be paid due to economic reasons, etc. In addition, there is also criticism that even where a short term of imprisonment is imposed, imprisonment is a heavier punishment than a fine (Article 50 of the Criminal Act), and therefore it is not appropriate for the period of workhouse confinement, a conversion disposition additionally imposed on a fine sentence, to become longer than imprisonment.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 59(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “Even where punishments are cumulatively imposed, the pronouncement of the whole or part of the punishment may be suspended,” thus allowing, where a fine is imposed together with imprisonment, the pronouncement of the fine sentence alone to be suspended separately from the imprisonment sentence. In such a case of suspension of pronouncement for a fine sentence, there is no limitation on the amount of the fine that is subject to the suspension. However, with the introduction of the suspended execution system for fines through the amendment of the Criminal Act on January 6, 2016, the scope of that system is limited to fines of KRW 5 million or less (Article 62(1) of the Criminal Act). Generally, because suspension of pronouncement is used where the punishment is lighter than suspended execution, there may be criticism that, unlike suspended execution of a fine sentence, the ability to suspend the pronouncement of all fine sentences without limitation on the amount of the fine is not justified in the criminal punishment system.\\n\\nf. Taking the foregoing together, even if the workhouse confinement provision is not contrary to the principle of proportionality as held in the majority opinion, this provision may, when the fine imposed is not less than KRW 100 million, cause the workhouse confinement period to be prolonged to at least a certain period, and there are various grounds for controversy, including criticism that special criminal statute provisions mandatorily imposing a large fine may, when combined with the workhouse confinement provision, contravene the principle of responsibility.\\n\\nTherefore, new special criminal statute provisions mandatorily imposing a fine should be enacted with caution, and efforts should also be made to improve legislation by reexamining the purpose of existing special criminal statute provisions that provide for the mandatory cumulative imposition of fines and by rationally and systematically reorganizing them.\\n\\nJustice Kim Yi-soo, Justice Lee Jin-seong, Justice Kim Chang-jong, Justice Ahn Chang-ho, Justice Kang Il-won, Justice Seo Gi-seok, Justice Jo Yong-ho (unable to sign electronically for administrative reasons due to overseas travel), Justice Lee Seon-ae"}
