{"[2018HEONBA88]": "1. Case Summary\\n\\na. The Petitioners are persons who, on 2016. 11. 24., acquired ownership by winning at auction 688㎡ of a watercourse located in ○○-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan, and 231㎡ of a road in □□ in the same dong (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the land at issue”). On 2017. 4. 3., the Petitioners filed an action for return of unjust enrichment against Jung-gu, Ulsan Metropolitan City, alleging that Jung-gu, Ulsan Metropolitan City was occupying and using the land at issue by means such as road paving without any legal title and therefore had an obligation to pay the amount of unjust enrichment arising therefrom (Ulsan District Court 2017GASO205205).\\n\\nb. In response, Jung-gu, Ulsan Metropolitan City argued that: the father of Kim △△, the former owner of the land at issue, namely Kim ▽▽ (Japanese-style name ☓☓), purchased the land at issue from ◇◇, a Japanese national in Korea (hereinafter referred to as “Japanese”), on 1945. 8. 10. and completed registration of transfer of ownership on 1945. 9. 7.; Ordinance No. 2 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (hereinafter referred to as the “Military Government Ordinance”) promulgated on 1945. 9. 25. prohibited all acts of transfer of property rights by Japanese nationals (Article 1) and at the same time rendered void legal acts concluded after 1945. 8. 9. for the purpose of transferring property rights (Article 4); Article 2 of Ordinance No. 33 of the Military Government, promulgated on 1945. 12. 6., provided that all property of Japanese nationals after 1945. 8. 9. shall be acquired by the Military Government in Korea; under Article 5 of the “First Agreement concerning Finance and Property between the Government of the Republic of Korea and the Government of the United States of America” concluded around 1948. 9. 11. (hereinafter referred to as the “First Korea-U.S. Agreement”), among the property of Japanese nationals that had vested in the Military Government, vested property not yet disposed of at that time was transferred to the Government of the Republic of Korea; and under Article 2, Item 1 of the former “Act on Special Measures concerning the Disposal of Vested Property” and Article 5 of the Addenda to the same Act, property for which a sales contract had not been concluded by the end of December 1964 was nationalized without compensation. Accordingly, since no sales contract had been concluded for the land at issue by the end of December 1964, it was state-owned property, and the Petitioners had succeeded to it from persons without ownership rights. Therefore, the Petitioners’ claim for return of unjust enrichment premised on the validity of the registration of transfer of ownership in the Petitioners’ names should be dismissed.\\n\\nc. While the above action was pending, on 2017. 6. 19., the Petitioners applied for a motion for referral of a constitutional review regarding Article 4 of Ordinance No. 2 of the Military Government, Article 2 of Ordinance No. 33 of the Military Government, Article 2 of the former Act on the Disposal of Vested Property, Item 1 of Article 2 of the former “Act on Special Measures concerning the Disposal of Vested Property,” and Article 5(1) of the Addenda to the same Act, but when this was dismissed on 2018. 1. 2. (Ulsan District Court 2017KAGI10033), they filed the constitutional complaint at issue on 2018. 1. 23., seeking a declaration of unconstitutionality of the above provisions.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Petitioners seek a declaration of unconstitutionality with respect to the entirety of Article 4 of Ordinance No. 2 of the Military Government and the entirety of Article 2 of Ordinance No. 33 of the Military Government; however, the part of those provisions that the Petitioners seek to challenge as unconstitutional is the part that renders all transactions concerning the property of “Japanese nationals” after 1945. 8. 9. void and causes ownership of such property to vest in the Military Government as of 1945. 9. 25. Accordingly, the subject matter of review is limited to that part.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since the Petitioners do not assert the inherent unconstitutionality of the provisions concerning the disposal of vested property after the establishment of the Government of the Republic of Korea, Article 2 of the former Act on the Disposal of Vested Property and Item 1 of Article 2 and Article 5(1) of the Addenda to the former Act on Special Measures concerning the Disposal of Vested Property are excluded from the subject matter of review.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of review in this case is whether the main text of Article 4 of Ordinance No. 2 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (promulgated on 1945. 9. 25.) (hereinafter referred to as “the voiding provision at issue”) and the part concerning “Japanese nationals” in the first sentence of Article 2 of Ordinance No. 33 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (promulgated on 1945. 12. 6.; hereinafter, Ordinance No. 2 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea and Ordinance No. 33 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea are collectively referred to as “the Ordinances at issue”) (hereinafter referred to as “the vesting provision at issue”; the voiding provision at issue and the vesting provision at issue are hereinafter collectively referred to as “the provisions subject to review”) are unconstitutional.\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nOrdinance No. 2 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (promulgated on 1945. 9. 25.)\\n\\nArticle 4 Any transaction of the kind described in this Ordinance that was concluded after 9 August 1945 shall be void in its entirety as of this date. (Proviso omitted)\\n\\nOrdinance No. 33 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (promulgated on 1945. 12. 6.)\\n\\nArticle 2 With respect to gold, silver, platinum, currency, securities, bank accounts, claims, negotiable securities, or any and all other property and the income therefrom existing within the jurisdiction of this Military Government, which after 9 August 1945 was directly or indirectly owned or administered in whole or in part by the Japanese Government, its agencies, or its nationals, companies, organizations, associations, or other entities organized or administered by that Government, ownership thereof shall be acquired by the Korean Military Government as of 25 September 1945, and the Korean Military Government shall own all such property. (Latter part omitted)\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nOrdinance No. 2 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (promulgated on 1945. 9. 25.)\\n\\nArticle 4 (main text omitted) However, if there is submitted to the Government of Korea a statement regarding the details of the transaction, valid application, the compensation paid, and the persons, property, and other relevant facts, the transaction concerned may become valid.\\n\\nOrdinance No. 33 of the United States Army Military Government in Korea (promulgated on 1945. 12. 6.)\\n\\nArticle 2 (first sentence omitted) No person shall, without the permission of the Military Government, trespass upon or occupy such property, or transfer such property, or impair the value or utility of such property.\\n\\nFormer Act on the Disposal of Vested Property (as enacted by Act No. 74 on 1949. 12. 19. and prior to amendment by Act No. 427 on 1956. 12. 31.)\\n\\nArticle 2 Vested property under this Act means all property transferred to the Government of the Republic of Korea pursuant to the provisions of Article 5 of the First Agreement concerning Finance and Property concluded between the Government of the Republic of Korea and the Government of the United States of America on 11 September 1948. Provided, agricultural land shall be separately disposed of pursuant to the Agricultural Land Reform Act. With respect to a profit-making corporation or association established in Korea before 9 August 1945, the stock or equity interests of which belonged to a Japanese agency, its nationals, or such entity, such stock or equity interests shall be deemed vested (hereinafter referred to as vested stock or equity interests). With respect to a foundation or incorporated association established in Korea before 9 August 1945, the right to exercise directors’ powers or membership rights of which belonged to a Japanese agency, its nationals, or such entity, such right to exercise directors’ powers or membership rights shall also be deemed vested (hereinafter referred to as vested right to exercise directors’ powers or vested membership rights).\\n\\nFormer Act on Special Measures concerning the Disposal of Vested Property (as enacted by Act No. 1346 on 1963. 5. 29. and extinguished on 1964. 12. 31.)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definition of Terms) The definitions of the terms used in this Act are as follows.\\n1. “Vested property” means property prescribed in Article 2 of the Act on the Disposal of Vested Property.\\n\\nAddenda to the former Act on Special Measures concerning the Disposal of Vested Property (Act No. 1346 of 1963. 5. 29.)\\n\\nArticle 5 (Nationalization Measures) ① Vested property for which a sales contract has not been concluded by the end of December 1964 shall be nationalized without compensation. The same shall also apply to vested property for which a sales contract was concluded by the end of December 1964 but the sales contract was rescinded after 1 January 1965.\\n\\n[The contents of the above provisions subject to review and related provisions are based on those contained in the volume published by the National Court Library, Ordinances of the United States Army Military Government in Korea, Judicial Materials, Vol. 42 (1988), but the old terms “取引”, “取締”, and “銀行勘定” are rendered respectively as “transaction,” “administration,” and “bank account,” and the]\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\na. Although the provisions subject to review were promulgated on 1945. 9. 25. and 1945. 12. 6., respectively, they render void all transactions concluded after 1945. 8. 9. and provide that all property owned or administered by Japanese nationals after 1945. 8. 9. shall vest in the Military Government in Korea as of 1945. 9. 25., thereby violating the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation.\\n\\nb. Although the provisions subject to review were intended to hold the Japanese Government responsible for war by confiscating the property of the enemy state, they provide for confiscation even of private property of ordinary Japanese nationals unrelated to the war of aggression, and by retroactively fixing the relevant date, they provide for the confiscation without exception of all property, including property of Koreans who lawfully acquired property from Japanese nationals; therefore, they violate the principle of proportionality.\\n\\n4. Judgment on the Procedural Requirements\\n\\na. The legal system during the Military Government period\\n\\nAfter Japan’s defeat, MacArthur, the Supreme Commander of the United States Army Forces in the Pacific, established the United States Army Military Government in Korea as the administrative organ for military government in the Korean region south of the 38th parallel north latitude, and, through Article 6 of Proclamation No. 1 of the United States Army Forces in the Pacific (hereinafter referred to as “Proclamation No. 1”) on 1945. 9. 7., declared that the authority to enact proclamations, ordinances, regulations, notices, or ordinances belonged to the Military Government in Korea.\\n\\nA Proclamation is issued in the name of MacArthur, the Supreme Commander of the United States Army Forces in the Pacific, and, based on international law concerning military occupation, has the force of a basic law in Korea. Ordinances of the United States Army Military Government in Korea were issued by the Military Government in Korea in the name of the Military Governor, and were promulgated in the form of identifying the rank and name of the person in charge at the end of the document and affixing a signature.\\n\\nAs to the method of promulgation of ordinances and other regulations enacted by the Military Governor at the time, there was no legal provision governing this, and as a result, many matters that today would have to be enacted by statute were enacted in the form of “ordinances and other regulations,” while, as to the method of public announcement, some were published in the Official Gazette and others were announced by methods other than publication in the Official Gazette. The mere fact that something took the form of an “ordinance or other regulation” did not necessarily mean that it was subordinate to a “statute”; rather, if its content concerned legislative matters, it was understood to have the same force as a statute (see Constitutional Committee 1954. 2. 27. 1953HEONWI1; Constitutional Court 2001. 4. 26. 98HEONBA79, etc.).\\n\\nb. Susceptibility to constitutional complaint review and premise for adjudication\\n\\n(1) The Ordinances at issue were promulgated on 1945. 9. 25. and 1945. 12. 6. in the name of the respective Military Governors, and thus took the form of ordinances; however, since they regulate legislative matters that today would have to be enacted by statute, such as “matters concerning the prohibition of the exercise of property rights, etc. by the government of the defeated state” and “matters concerning measures for the transfer of property rights,” they may be deemed to have the force of statutes.\\n\\nThe Ordinances at issue lost their force as of 1948. 8. 15., when the Military Government was officially abolished and the Government of the Republic of Korea was established, but were incorporated into the legal order of the Republic of Korea when Article 100 of the Constitution enacted on 1948. 7. 12. provided that “existing laws and regulations shall remain in force insofar as they do not conflict with this Constitution.”\\n\\nThereafter, the “Special Measures Act concerning the Disposal of Former Laws and Regulations,” enacted on 1961. 7. 15., required former laws and regulations that had been in force before 1948. 7. 16. and whose force continued pursuant to Article 100 of the Constitution to be organized by 1961. 12. 31. and replaced by statutes or decrees (Articles 1 and 2), and deemed former laws and regulations that were not so organized to have been repealed as of 1962. 1. 20. (Article 3). Accordingly, the Ordinances at issue were repealed as of 1962. 1. 20.\\n\\n(2) A constitutional complaint against a repealed statute is, as a rule, unlawful; however, if the constitutionality of the repealed statute is a premise for adjudication in the related litigation case, it is subject to constitutional review (see Constitutional Court 1994. 6. 30. 92HEONGA18).\\n\\nIn the underlying case, the issue is whether the land at issue, which the Korean person purchased from a Japanese national on 1945. 8. 10. and for which registration of transfer of ownership was completed on 1945. 9. 7., falls under vested property pursuant to the provisions subject to review.\\n\\nWith respect to whether the disputed land constitutes vested property, the Supreme Court has held: “Property registered in the name of a Japanese national as of 1945. 8. 9. became vested property acquired by the Military Government in Korea pursuant to Article 2 of Ordinance No. 33 of the Military Government and transferred to the Government of the Republic of Korea pursuant to Article 5 of the First Korea-U.S. Agreement; therefore, even if a Korean person had already acquired ownership thereof from a Japanese national by purchase or otherwise prior thereto, such person cannot assert ownership unless, within the prescribed period, the person obtained a release from vesting from the Property Appeals Committee through the Military Government Ordinance No. 103 and the directives of the Military Governor dated 1948. 4. 17. and 1948. 7. 28. by submitting the fact constituting the cause of acquisition, or obtained a release from vesting through the simplified appeals procedure and confirmation under Act No. 102 and Act No. 230, or obtained a release from vesting by a final and conclusive judgment from the court, and ownership thereof vests in the State” (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA32812, decided 1996. 11. 15., etc.).\\n\\nAccordingly, although the provisions subject to review are provisions that were in force as statutes and were later repealed, they continue to be applied as effective adjudicative norms even now with respect to whether the disputed land constitutes vested property; and in the adjudication of the underlying case as well, whether the land at issue falls under vested property pursuant to the provisions subject to review decisively affects the conclusion of the case. Therefore, the provisions subject to review satisfy both the requirements for constitutional complaint review and the premise for adjudication.\\n\\n5. Judgment on the Merits\\n\\na. Content of the provisions subject to review\\n\\nThe voiding provision at issue provides that “any transaction of the kind described in this Ordinance that was concluded after 9 August 1945 shall be void in its entirety as of this date,” and the vesting provision at issue provides that “ownership of gold, silver, platinum, currency, securities, bank accounts, claims, negotiable securities, or any and all other property and the income therefrom existing within the jurisdiction of this Military Government, which after 9 August 1945 was directly or indirectly owned or administered in whole or in part by Japanese ... nationals ..., shall be acquired by the Korean Military Government as of 25 September 1945, and the Korean Military Government shall own all such property.”\\n\\nThe purpose of the voiding provision at issue and the vesting provision at issue, in regulating property owned by Japanese nationals after 1945. 8. 9., is, on the basis of the method of public notice concerning changes in real rights, to vest ownership of Japanese property in the Military Government in Korea as of the state existing on 1945. 8. 9.; therefore, “after 9 August 1945” means that, based on “00:00 on 9 August 1945,” even if a Korean person had purchased property from a Japanese national before that time, if registration still existed after 00:00 on 9 August 1945 indicating ownership in the name of the Japanese national, the relevant property became property of the Military Government in Korea as of 1945. 9. 25. (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 87DAKA2176, decided 1989. 12. 26.).\\n\\nThe acquisition of ownership by the Military Government in Korea under the vesting provision at issue is an original acquisition and, as an acquisition by operation of law, does not require registration or other requirements for opposition to third parties (see Supreme Court Decision 68DA1754, decided 1969. 1. 21.; Supreme Court en banc Decision 87DAKA2176, decided 1989. 12. 26., etc.).\\n\\nb. Judgment\\n\\n(1) Organization of the issues\\n\\n(a) Although the Ordinances at issue were promulgated on 1945. 9. 25. and 1945. 12. 6., respectively, the voiding provision at issue renders void all transactions concerning property owned by Japanese nationals as of 1945. 8. 9., and the vesting provision at issue provides that Japanese property to which the voiding provision at issue applies shall, retroactively as of 1945. 9. 25., vest in the ownership of the Military Government in Korea, and thus has the nature of true retroactive legislation.\\n\\nArticle 13(2) of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall not be deprived of ... property rights by retroactive legislation,” thereby prohibiting retroactive legislation. Although no constitutional provision like the above existed at the time the Ordinances at issue were enacted and promulgated, as noted above, the Ordinances at issue were incorporated into the legal order of the Republic of Korea by Article 100 of the Constitution, and although repealed on 1962. 1. 20. pursuant to Articles 1 through 3 of the Special Measures Act concerning the Disposal of Former Laws and Regulations, they still possess substantive normative force as effective adjudicative norms with respect to the disposal of vested property; accordingly, it is necessary to examine whether they violate the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation under the current Constitution.\\n\\n(b) Meanwhile, the Petitioners argue that the provisions subject to review violate the principle of proportionality because, merely because the property had once belonged to Japanese nationals in the past, they confiscate even property lawfully acquired by Koreans from Japanese nationals. However, the provisions subject to review are provisions that prohibited all transactions and caused such property to vest in the Military Government in Korea in order to prevent dispersal and deterioration of property owned or administered by Japanese nationals, and they do not contain a provision confiscating property acquired by Koreans from Japanese nationals; in some cases, even property acquired by Koreans from Japanese nationals may be recognized as vested property pursuant to the provisions subject to review and thereby have property rights restricted, but this is merely an incidental consequence of retroactive legislation. Ultimately, the above argument of the Petitioners is nothing more than an argument that property rights were deprived by retroactive legislation, and therefore it will not be separately addressed.\\n\\n(2) Whether the provisions subject to review violate the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation\\n\\n(a) Retroactive legislation may be divided into true retroactive legislation, which applies a new law to facts or legal relationships that have already been completed, and quasi-retroactive legislation, which applies to facts or legal relationships currently in progress. Quasi-retroactive legislation is, in principle, permissible; however, while in the process of balancing the public interest requiring retroactive effect against the request for protection of reliance, the aspect of reliance protection restricts the legislature’s power to form the law. By contrast, true retroactive legislation is, in principle, constitutionally impermissible under the rule-of-law principle, which protects individual reliance and legal stability, unless special circumstances exist; however, exceptionally, it may be permitted where the legal status was uncertain and confusing, so that there was little reliance interest worthy of protection, or where highly compelling public-interest reasons that outweigh the request for protection of reliance justify retroactive legislation (see Constitutional Court 1996. 2. 16. 96HEONGA2, etc.; Constitutional Court 2011. 3. 31. 2008HEONBA141, etc.).\\n\\n(b) The provisions subject to review are provisions that, on the basis of the method of public notice concerning changes in real rights, froze the property owned and administered by Japanese nationals as of 1945. 8. 9. and caused ownership thereof to vest in the Military Government in Korea as of 1945. 9. 25. The purpose of setting the date of freezing of property owned and administered by Japanese nationals not as the dates of promulgation of the respective Ordinances but as 1945. 8. 9. is not clearly stated; however, according to relevant records, 1945. 8. 9. is the date on which the Pacific War was effectively brought to an end by the dropping of the second atomic bomb on Nagasaki by the United States Army Air Forces, and at the same time the date on which acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration, by which the Allied powers demanded Japan’s unconditional surrender, was de facto determined at the Supreme Council for the Direction of the War in Japan.\\n\\nOn 1945. 8. 15., the Second World War came to an end and the Korean Peninsula was separated from the Japanese Empire by Japan’s declaration of unconditional surrender, but at that time there was no independent government or legislative body on the Korean Peninsula. Only after the Military Government in Korea was established south of the 38th parallel north latitude by Proclamation No. 1 on 1945. 9. 7., and the Military Government in Korea was formally established on 1945. 9. 20., was Ordinance No. 2 of the Military Government in Korea finally issued on 1945. 9. 25., thereby freezing the property in the Korean Peninsula owned by defeated Japan, based on 1945. 8. 9., when Japan’s defeat had become a fait accompli, and restricting transactions prior to that date.\\n\\nHowever, with respect to the disposal and vesting of the private property of Japanese nationals in Korea frozen as of 1945. 8. 9., there were no clear international legal rules at the time. Article 46 of the Regulations concerning the Laws and Customs of War on Land (signed on 1907. 10. 18. and effective on 1910. 1. 26.), which is an international rule concerning an occupying power, provided that “Family honor and rights, the lives of persons, and private property, as well as religious convictions and practice, must be respected. Private property cannot be confiscated,” but unlike the Japanese mainland, the Korean Peninsula was a region separated and made independent from Japan, the occupying power, and thus it was difficult to view the provisions concerning an occupying power in international law as directly applicable to Japanese nationals remaining in the Korean Peninsula. Above all, the private property of Japanese nationals remaining in the Korean Peninsula was property accumulated by Japanese people who advanced into Korea in the course of Japan’s encroachment upon Korea pursuant to the illegal Japan-Korea Annexation Treaty, and thus was a legacy of Japan’s aggression against Korea and its colonial rule; accordingly, measures by the Military Government to preserve and vest property owned and administered by Japanese nationals were unavoidable. In response, the Military Government in Korea promulgated Ordinance No. 33 of the Military Government on 1945. 12. 6., thereby causing all Japanese property frozen under Ordinance No. 2 of the Military Government to vest in the Military Government in Korea as of 1945. 9. 25.\\n\\nConsidering these circumstances, after 1945. 8. 9. the Military Government was established in the southern part of Korea and the Ordinances at issue were enacted and promulgated, and until the freezing and vesting measures were taken for property owned and administered by Japanese nationals, the legal situation was highly uncertain and confusing; thus, even if Japanese nationals in Korea and Koreans at the time relied on the belief that, despite Japan’s defeat and the establishment of the Military Government, free disposal or transactions of property owned and administered by Japanese nationals would remain possible, such reliance cannot be regarded as reliance worthy of constitutional protection.\\n\\n(c) Proclamation No. 1 expressly states that “in considering the fact that Koreans had been in a state of slavery for a long period and the decision to liberate and make Korea independent at the appropriate time, the purpose of the occupation of Korea is to carry out the provisions of the instrument of surrender and to protect the human rights and religious rights of Koreans,” thereby confirming that the purpose of the occupation of the Korean Peninsula by the Military Government was limited to helping the independence and self-determination of the Korean Peninsula and the reconstruction of the state by temporarily managing and preserving the territory that had been occupied by Japan.\\n\\nThe public interest sought to be achieved by the provisions subject to review through retroactive legislation must be interpreted consistently with the purpose of the occupation of the Korean Peninsula by the Military Government stated in Proclamation No. 1. Thus, although the provisions subject to review were measures to prevent unlawful occupation or arbitrary disposal of Japanese property by Japanese nationals as well as Koreans, it is reasonable to view them as intended to cut off immediately Japan’s influence, after Japan lost governing authority over the Korean Peninsula as of 1945. 8. 9. by accepting the Potsdam Declaration; to freeze in bulk, as of the state of 1945. 8. 9. when Japan’s defeat had become a fait accompli, the property accumulated by Japanese people who advanced into Korea in the course of Japan’s encroachment upon Korea through the illegal Japan-Korea Annexation Treaty; to prevent its dispersion and deterioration; and to transfer it to the Government of the Republic of Korea to be established in the future.\\n\\nThe public interest in preserving and transferring the property accumulated by Japanese people who advanced into Korea in the course of Japan’s encroachment upon Korea through the illegal Japan-Korea Annexation Treaty is far more serious than the request for protection of reliance of Japanese nationals in Korea who wished to freely dispose of property within the Korean Peninsula and withdraw to the Japanese mainland, or of those who purchased property from Japanese nationals immediately after Japan’s defeat.\\n\\n(d) Meanwhile, because the freezing and vesting by the Military Government in Korea of property owned and administered by Japanese nationals within the Korean Peninsula immediately after the end of the Second World War was a historically highly special and exceptional measure, even if the constitutionality of retroactive legislation is recognized, concern that true retroactive legislation will frequently occur and its attendant harms will become widespread can sufficiently be dispelled.\\n\\n(e) Taking all of the above circumstances into comprehensive consideration, the provisions subject to review do not violate Article 13(2) of the Constitution as an exception to the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since none of the provisions subject to review violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}

Overview of the Case\\n\\na. 2019HEONMA106  \\nPetitioner Jeong ○○, as the owner of a unit of a condominium building located at Seoul ○○-gu ○○-ro (lot number omitted), leased part of the exclusive portion of the above building to ○○ Co., Ltd. on April 1, 2017, setting the security deposit at KRW 15,000,000 and the lease term from April 1, 2017 to November 30, 2018.\\n\\nAt the time Petitioner Jeong ○○ entered into the above lease agreement, under Article 10(2) of the former “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” (as amended by Act No. 9361 on January 30, 2009, and before amendment by Act No. 15791 on October 16, 2018) (hereinafter the “former provision”), the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease could be exercised only within the scope in which the total lease term did not exceed 5 years; however, Article 10(2) of the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” amended by Act No. 15791 on October 16, 2018 (hereinafter the “amended provision”) extended the period so that the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease may be exercised within the scope not exceeding 10 years, and Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” (Act No. 15791 of October 16, 2018) provided that the amended provision shall also apply to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act.\\n\\nPetitioner Jeong ○○, after his above lease agreement was renewed on December 1, 2018 and thereby became subject, pursuant to the above supplementary provision, to the 10-year period prescribed by the amended provision, filed the present constitutional complaint seeking a determination of unconstitutionality of the above supplementary provision on January 25, 2019.\\n\\nb. 2019HEONMA1049  \\nPetitioner Kim ○○ purchased commercial unit No. ○ of building No. ○ located at Seoul ○○-gu ○○-ro (lot number omitted) from Cha ○○ on April 10, 2016 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership on April 29, 2016, and prior thereto, on March 18, 2016, Cha ○○ had entered into a lease agreement with Jeong ○○ concerning the above apartment commercial space, setting the security deposit at KRW 10,000,000, the monthly rent at KRW 650,000, and the lease term from March 21, 2016 to March 20, 2017; Petitioner Kim ○○ succeeded to Cha ○○’s status as lessor by purchasing the commercial space as above.\\n\\nAt the time Petitioner Kim ○○ succeeded to the status of lessor as above, under the former provision, the tenant’s right to request renewal could be exercised only within the scope in which the total lease term did not exceed 5 years; however, the amended provision extended the period so that the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease may be exercised within the scope not exceeding 10 years, and Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the above “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” provided that the above amended provision shall also apply to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act.\\n\\nPetitioner Kim ○○, after his above lease agreement was renewed on March 21, 2019 and thereby became subject, pursuant to the above supplementary provision, to the 10-year period prescribed by the amended provision, filed the present constitutional complaint seeking a determination of unconstitutionality of the above supplementary provision on September 18, 2019.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\nPetitioner Jeong ○○ sought adjudication with respect to the phrase “newly concluded or renewed” among Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases,” and Petitioner Kim ○○ sought adjudication with respect to the phrase “renewed” among the same Article 2; however, as the petitioners’ argument is in substance that applying the amended provision also to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act infringes their fundamental rights, the subject matter of this adjudication is whether the part concerning “renewed leases” in Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” (Act No. 15791 of October 16, 2018) (hereinafter the “Supplementary Provision at Issue”) infringes the petitioners’ fundamental rights. The adjudicated provision and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Adjudicated Provision]  \\nSupplementary Provisions of the Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases (Act No. 15791 of October 16, 2018)  \\nArticle 2 (Application to the period for requesting renewal of lease agreement) The amended provision of Article 10(2) shall apply from leases first concluded or renewed after the enforcement of this Act.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]  \\nFormer Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases (as amended by Act No. 9361 on January 30, 2009, and before amendment by Act No. 15791 on October 16, 2018)  \\nArticle 10 (Request for renewal of lease agreement, etc.) ② The tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease may be exercised only within the scope in which the total lease term, including the initial lease term, does not exceed 5 years.\\n\\nAct on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases (as amended by Act No. 15791 on October 16, 2018)  \\nArticle 10 (Request for renewal of lease agreement, etc.) ② The tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease may be exercised only within the scope in which the total lease term, including the initial lease term, does not exceed 10 years.\\n\\n3. Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\na. 2019HEONMA106  \\nThe Supplementary Provision at Issue applies the amended provision, which extended the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease from 5 years to 10 years, also to lease agreements already concluded before the enforcement of the amended Act, thereby infringing the lessor’s trust that once the lease agreement was renewed within the scope of 5 years after the conclusion of the lease agreement, the lease agreement would terminate, and this constitutes a restriction on property rights by public necessity yet does not provide just compensation, and thus violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution, and infringes the lessor’s dignity and worth as a human being, equality right, and property right by violating the principle against retroactive legislation and the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nb. 2019HEONMA1049  \\nThe Supplementary Provision at Issue minimizes the limitation on the lessor’s fundamental rights by excluding from its application leases that, before the enforcement of the amended Act, were already subject to the 5-year period, even though the amended provision extends the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease from 5 years to 10 years; however, by providing that the amended provision also applies even when such lease agreements are renewed, it imposes unilateral sacrifice on the lessor, and therefore the Supplementary Provision at Issue violates the principle of proportionality and infringes the lessor’s property right.\\n\\nAlthough leases first concluded after the enforcement of the amended provision and lease agreements that had already been concluded before that and are renewed thereafter are inherently different, the Supplementary Provision at Issue treats the two alike without rational basis; therefore, the Supplementary Provision at Issue infringes the equality right.\\n\\nThe lessor trusted, pursuant to the former provision, that the tenant would be able to exercise the right to request renewal of the lease only within the 5-year scope after the conclusion of the lease agreement; however, because the Supplementary Provision at Issue applies the amended provision to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act without any urgent circumstances, for the sake of achieving the unclear public interest of stabilizing legal relations concerning commercial building leases, it violates the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\na. Significance and legislative purpose of the Supplementary Provision at Issue  \\n(1) From the time of its enactment on December 29, 2001, the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” had granted commercial tenants the “right to request renewal of the lease agreement” (Article 10(1) through (3)), allowing them to renew the lease agreement within the scope in which the total lease term did not exceed 5 years. This was intended to enable tenants to indirectly recover premium money or facility investment costs, etc., by guaranteeing them a certain period of the lease term (see Constitutional Court Decision 2013HEONBA76 of August 28, 2014).\\n\\nAnd when the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” was amended by Act No. 15791 on October 16, 2018, the 5-year period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease was extended to 10 years. Under the former provision, the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease could be exercised only within the scope in which the total lease term, including the initial lease term, does not exceed 5 years, whereas the amended provision extended that period by providing that it may be exercised only within the scope in which the total lease term does not exceed 10 years.\\n\\nThe reason is not substantially different from the background to the initial introduction of the right to request renewal. In other words, in circumstances where the security deposit and monthly rent continuously rise, it was considered that the tenant cannot conduct stable business merely through a 5-year lease renewal, and that the period of 5 years is insufficient to recover the amounts invested by a commercial building tenant, such as interior design costs and premium money. In particular, practical considerations were also taken into account: if the tenant’s business makes the area gain attention as a distinctive neighborhood, the rent soars and the tenants who contributed to the development of the commercial district end up having to leave the area due to the phenomenon of gentrification, whereby the existing merchants, craftsmen, and artists who contributed to the formation of the commercial district lose their living base, and by the entry of standardized large corporation stores and large-scale franchise businesses in their place, the unique characteristics of the existing commercial district disappear and, rather, the commercial district contracts, causing unfavorable results for lessors, lessees, and business operators alike.\\n\\n(2) Article 1 of the Supplementary Provisions of the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” (Act No. 15791 of October 16, 2018) sets the enforcement date of the amended Act as the date of promulgation, namely October 16, 2018, and Article 2 of the same Supplementary Provisions provides that “the amended provision of Article 10(2) shall apply from leases first concluded or renewed after the enforcement of this Act.” As seen above, the amended provision aims to faithfully secure the period during which a tenant of a commercial building can recover expenses such as facility investment costs and premium money by extending the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease. However, if the amended provision were applied only to leases newly concluded after the enforcement of the amended Act, lessors might reflect the resulting losses or disadvantages in advance in new lease agreements to avoid them, causing rents to rise sharply all at once, which would ultimately run counter to the legislative purpose of the amended provision. Therefore, in order to prevent such side effects and secure the effectiveness of the amended provision, the Supplementary Provision at Issue provides that the extended period under the amended provision shall apply not only to leases concluded after the enforcement of the amended provision but also to leases concluded before that time if they are renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act.\\n\\nb. Issues in this case  \\nThe issues in this case are whether the Supplementary Provision at Issue constitutes deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation prohibited by Article 13(2) of the Constitution, and whether it violates the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nThe petitioners also argue that it violates the principle of proportionality; however, it is clear that they have made only the transitional provision of the Supplementary Provisions the subject matter of adjudication, and the essence of their argument is that the Supplementary Provision at Issue, by applying the amended provision, which extended the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease from 5 years to 10 years, even to lease agreements already concluded before the enforcement of the amended Act, has caused lessors to be unable to use and derive benefits from commercial buildings in the manner they desire for the extended period; this is ultimately nothing different from an argument that the principle of protection of trust has been violated, and therefore we do not separately determine this issue.\\n\\nIn addition, Petitioner Jeong ○○ argues that, because the Supplementary Provision at Issue constitutes a restriction on property rights by public necessity yet does not provide just compensation, it violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution and infringes the lessor’s property right. However, the Supplementary Provision at Issue is a transitional provision that determines the scope of application of the amended provision, which sets the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease in commercial building leases, and is thus a provision by which the legislature generally and abstractly defines the content and limitations of property rights concerning commercial building leases and concretizes the social restrictions on property rights (Article 23(1) and (2) of the Constitution); accordingly, just compensation under Article 23(3) of the Constitution is not at issue.\\n\\nAlso, Petitioner Jeong ○○ argues that the Supplementary Provision at Issue infringes the dignity and worth of the lessor as a human being; however, because the dignity and worth of a human being have the character of a supplementary fundamental right to other fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court Decision 2009HEONMA286 of March 31, 2011), insofar as we determine whether the Supplementary Provision at Issue infringes the primary fundamental right, namely the property right, we do not separately determine whether the dignity and worth of a human being have been infringed.\\n\\nThe petitioners also argue that, although leases first concluded after the enforcement of the amended provision and leases that had already been concluded before that and are renewed after the enforcement of the amended provision are inherently different, the Supplementary Provision at Issue treats the two alike, thereby treating things that are essentially different as if they were the same and infringing the equality right. It is true that if the amended provision is applied to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended provision, a difference arises in that, unlike the case where it is applied to leases first concluded after the enforcement of the amended provision, the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease is extended during the term of that lease. However, whether this is constitutionally justified can ultimately be examined together when determining whether the Supplementary Provision at Issue violates the principle of protection of trust and the principle against retroactive legislation, and therefore we do not separately determine whether the equality right has been infringed.\\n\\nAccordingly, below we examine whether the Supplementary Provision at Issue violates the principle against retroactive legislation and the principle of protection of trust so as to infringe the property rights of lessors of commercial buildings.\\n\\nc. Whether it constitutes infringement of property rights by retroactive legislation  \\nArticle 13(2) of the Constitution provides, “All citizens shall not be restricted in their political rights or deprived of their property rights by retroactive legislation.” “Retroactive legislation” is divided, depending on whether the new law applies to facts or legal relations that have already ended or to facts or legal relations that are currently ongoing, into “true retroactive legislation” and “quasi-retroactive legislation.” The former is, in principle, not permitted under the Constitution and is exceptionally permitted only where special circumstances exist, whereas the latter is, in principle, permitted, but in the process of balancing the public interest requiring retroactive effect against the demand for protection of trust, the perspective of trust protection imposes certain limitations on the legislature’s power to form legislation (see Constitutional Court Decision 2008HEONMA581 et al. of July 29, 2010).\\n\\nHowever, the amended provision extended the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease, which had been set at 5 years under the former provision, to 10 years, and the Supplementary Provision at Issue provides that the amended provision also applies to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act; and among “leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act,” cases in which, under the former provision, the mandatory lease period has elapsed and the lease ends without renewal but by expiration of the term, etc., are excluded, and only cases in which renewal is still possible even under the former provision are included (see Supreme Court Decision 2020DA241017 of November 5, 2020); therefore, the Supplementary Provision at Issue constitutes quasi-retroactive legislation, which regulates matters still in progress.\\n\\nAccordingly, in this case there is no room for the issue of infringement of property rights by retroactive legislation as referred to in Article 13(2) of the Constitution; rather, the only issue is whether the trust in the existing legal status held by the petitioners should be constitutionally protected from the standpoint of the rule of law.\\n\\nd. Whether it infringes property rights by violating the principle of protection of trust  \\n(1) Significance of the principle of protection of trust  \\nWhen a statute is amended, if the party’s trust in the former legal order is reasonable and justified, and the loss suffered by the party caused by the amendment of the statute is so severe that the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new legislation cannot justify the destruction of that trust, then the new legislation cannot be permitted under the principle of protection of trust. However, because statutes inevitably must change flexibly in response to changes in the social environment or economic conditions, and because conflicts of interest between the changed new legal order and the existing legal order are unavoidable, not every expectation or trust held by the people is protected as a constitutional right; whether it is protected should be determined by balancing the necessity of protecting the trust of those who relied on the existing system against the public interest sought to be achieved through the new system (see Constitutional Court Decision 2008HEONMA581 et al. of July 29, 2010).\\n\\nTherefore, whether the principle of protection of trust has been violated should be determined by comprehensively balancing, on the one hand, the protected value of the trust interest infringed, the degree of severity of the infringement, and the method of the trust infringement, and, on the other hand, the public interest purpose sought to be realized through the new legislation (see Constitutional Court Decision 97HEONBA58 of November 26, 1998).\\n\\n(2) Judgment  \\n(a) Protected value of the trust interest  \\nIn the case of statutes regulating economic activities such as commercial building leases, it is common to impose new legal regulations according to social and economic circumstances, and the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease in commercial building leases is likewise not immutable but may be changed according to social and economic policies, etc. (see Constitutional Court Decision 2018HEONBA205 et al. of March 26, 2020).\\n\\nSince the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” maintained the 5-year period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease for about 17 years, from its enactment on December 29, 2001 until it was amended by Act No. 15791 on October 16, 2018, it can be said that the petitioners had an expectation or trust that the period was 5 years; however, it is also true that the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” has consistently been amended in the direction of strengthening the protection of tenants since its enactment, and in particular, while social criticism continued that the period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease prescribed in the former provision was too short to protect tenants who were suffering due to the continuous rise in security deposits and monthly rents for commercial buildings, bills seeking to extend that period were repeatedly proposed and discussed over a long period. The amended provision and the Supplementary Provision at Issue are the result of such social and economic discussions being reflected in legislation.\\n\\nMoreover, because in previous amendments to the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” there had been multiple instances where, in accordance with the practical necessity of achieving the legislative purpose of the amended Act, supplementary provisions were enacted in the form that “the amended provision shall apply from leases first concluded or renewed after the enforcement of this Act,” as in the Supplementary Provision at Issue, it cannot be said that adopting such a transitional provision in the Supplementary Provision at Issue was unusual or entirely unforeseeable.\\n\\nIn light of these points, even if there existed a lessor’s expectation or trust that the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease would continue to remain 5 years in the future, it cannot be regarded as a definitive or absolute expectation or trust; therefore, the extent to which it can be protected may vary depending on the degree of infringement of trust and the seriousness of the public interest sought to be achieved through changing the period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease.\\n\\n(b) Degree of infringement  \\nBecause the Supplementary Provision at Issue does not provide that the amended provision applies to all leases existing at the time of the enforcement of the amended Act, but only to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act, if after the enforcement of the amended provision the period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease under the former provision elapses and the lease agreement is not renewed but ends by expiration of the term, etc., the amended provision will not apply (see Supreme Court Decision 2020DA241017 of November 5, 2020); accordingly, the scope of application of the Supplementary Provision at Issue is appropriately limited.\\n\\nEven when the amended provision is applied pursuant to the Supplementary Provision at Issue, the tenant may not exercise the right to request renewal of the lease without limitation, but only within the scope not exceeding 10 years; and even if the tenant exercises the right to request renewal of the lease, the lessor may refuse renewal if there is just cause pursuant to the main clause of Article 10(1) of the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases,” and may also refuse renewal if any of the following grounds stipulated in each item of the proviso to the same paragraph exists. That is, the lessor may refuse renewal where the tenant has defaulted on rent in an amount equivalent to three installments of rent or more (item 1), where the tenant leased the property by fraud or other wrongful means (item 2), where the tenant subleased all or part of the leased building without the lessor’s consent (item 4), where the tenant has intentionally or grossly negligently damaged all or part of the leased building (item 5), or where the tenant has substantially violated obligations as a tenant or there exists a serious reason making it difficult to continue the lease (item 8). Even if there is no such fault attributable to the tenant, the lessor may also escape the constraints of the lease agreement where the lessor has provided the tenant with reasonable compensation by mutual agreement (item 3), where all or part of the leased building is destroyed so that the purpose of the lease cannot be achieved (item 6), or where the lessor needs to recover possession of the leased building in order to demolish or reconstruct all or most of the leased building for certain reasons (item 7). Therefore, it is also difficult to view the Supplementary Provision at Issue as overly protecting the tenant’s stable business while imposing one-sided and harsh burdens only on the lessor.\\n\\nIn light of these points, the degree to which the lessor’s trust is infringed cannot be regarded as severe.\\n\\n(c) Seriousness of the public interest  \\nAs noted above, the amended provision is intended to faithfully secure the period during which a tenant of a commercial building can recover expenses such as facility investment costs and premium money by extending the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease; however, if the amended provision were applied only to leases newly concluded after the enforcement of the amended Act, lessors might reflect the resulting losses or disadvantages in advance in new lease agreements to avoid them, causing rents to rise sharply all at once, which would ultimately be contrary to the legislative purpose of the amended provision. Accordingly, in order to prevent such side effects and secure the effectiveness of the amended provision, the Supplementary Provision at Issue provides that the extended period under the amended provision shall apply not only to leases concluded after the enforcement of the amended provision but also to leases concluded before that time if they are renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act. In other words, the Supplementary Provision at Issue aims to apply the amended provision not only to leases first concluded after the enforcement of the amended provision but also to renewed leases, thereby protecting the stable business of tenants, who are placed in a relatively disadvantaged position in commercial building leases, and securing opportunities for tenants to recover the amounts they invested, such as facility investment costs and premium money, thereby promoting the stability of tenants’ economic life and achieving a fair economic order.\\n\\nOur Constitution provides that the State may regulate and coordinate the economy in order to prevent domination of the market and abuse of economic power and to harmonize economic agents (Article 119(2)); around the time of the introduction of the Supplementary Provision at Issue, and thereafter, real estate prices overall and continuously rose, and the security deposits and monthly rents in commercial building leases also rapidly increased, thereby intensifying the phenomenon that tenants, who contributed greatly to developing the relevant commercial district, could not endure the burden of rent, etc., and had to leave the area. Under such circumstances, the public interest of protecting the tenant’s stable business and providing an opportunity to recover the costs invested by the tenant is a more urgent and serious public interest than the lessors’ expectations or trust discussed above.\\n\\n(d) Sub-conclusion  \\nTherefore, the Supplementary Provision at Issue cannot be deemed to infringe the property rights of the petitioners, who are lessors, by violating the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\n5. Conclusion  \\nAll of the petitions in this case are without merit, and the Court decides as stated in the order. Aside from the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Young-jin as set forth in 6. below, the opinions of the Justices participating in this decision were unanimous.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Young-jin  \\nUnlike the majority opinion, I think that the Supplementary Provision at Issue violates the principle of protection of trust and infringes the property rights of the lessor, and therefore I state my view as follows.\\n\\na. Protected value of the trust interest  \\nThe “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases,” from the time of its enactment on December 29, 2001, had granted commercial tenants the “right to request renewal of the lease agreement” (Article 10(1) through (3)), allowing them to renew the lease agreement within the scope in which the total lease term does not exceed 5 years, and the 5-year period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease has been maintained for about 17 years thereafter; thus, it is difficult to say that there were circumstances from which it could be expected that the period would be extended to 10 years merely because there had been social discussion that the period should be extended or because numerous bills to that effect had been proposed. And the trust in the 5-year period prescribed by the former provision was granted by statute, so its protected value cannot be regarded as small by any means.\\n\\nb. Degree of infringement  \\nEven if there is a need to extend the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease, the amended provision could have extended it gradually from 5 years to 7-8 years and then to 10 years thereafter, yet it doubled it all at once. The Supplementary Provision at Issue, although it could have mitigated the extent to which the lessor’s trust interest is infringed by not applying such amended provision to leases that were already subject to the 5-year period before the enforcement of the amended Act, or by applying it with a certain grace period and limiting the scope of leases renewed, nonetheless, without such transitional measures, provides that the amended provision shall also apply to leases first concluded after the enforcement of the amended Act as well as to leases renewed thereafter.\\n\\nIn particular, unlike Article 6-3(1)8 of the Housing Lease Protection Act, the “Act on the Protection of Commercial Building Leases” does not include as a ground for refusal of renewal the case where the lessor intends to use the commercial building directly; accordingly, if, under the former provision, the 5-year period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease expires, a lessor who planned to use the commercial building personally cannot use the building owned by him or her for another 5 years. If such legislative amendments are repeatedly permitted, the 10-year period for exercising the right to request renewal of the lease may be extended again to 15 years before the 10-year period expires, so that the lessor will be placed in a state of instability, unable to predict at all when he or she will be able to use the building.\\n\\nTherefore, the degree to which the lessor’s trust is infringed pursuant to the Supplementary Provision at Issue is severe.\\n\\nc. Balancing the public interest and the trust interest  \\nAs the majority opinion states, the amended provision is intended to protect the business of tenants, who are in a relatively disadvantaged position in commercial building leases, and to secure opportunities for them to recover the amounts they invested, while the Supplementary Provision at Issue is intended to prevent side effects that may arise from the enforcement of the amended provision, such as sharp increases in rents, and to secure the effectiveness of the amended provision.\\n\\nHowever, because the above public interest conflicts with the lessor’s trust interest, in order to determine whether the Supplementary Provision at Issue violates the principle of protection of trust, the two must be balanced; furthermore, if there is a possibility of harmonizing the interests of the tenant and the lessor without sacrificing either one, such a method should be sought (see Constitutional Court Decision 2005HEONBA20 et al. of May 28, 2009).\\n\\nHowever, even in the case of the same commercial lease, the positions of the tenant and the lessor may differ depending on various circumstances such as the amount of the lease deposit or the size of the commercial space, the location of the leased facilities, the status of the office, and whether premium money has been formed; yet, without examining these matters, to conclude that only one side is socially disadvantaged and to preferentially protect only that side is often lacking in concrete appropriateness. For example, in areas where commercial districts are not developed, or in small commercial spaces, or in commercial spaces where the rent is not high, there may be cases where the tenant’s facility investment costs or premium money in relation to the commercial building are not excessively invested, as stated in the majority opinion, and there may also be cases where rents did not rise sharply all at once. In particular, with the development of various promising franchise industries, tenants are not always in a more disadvantaged position than lessors, and even if they were socially and economically vulnerable tenants at the beginning, if they have conducted business stably for 5 years, it is difficult to categorically conclude that they are in a more disadvantaged position than lessors. In such cases, it is difficult to say that tenant protection is always correct and a serious public interest.\\n\\nMeanwhile, if the period for exercising the tenant’s right to request renewal of the lease is extended in order to prevent tenants from leaving because they cannot endure the burden of security deposits and monthly rents in commercial building leases, then that burden ultimately has to be borne by the lessor who can no longer use the commercial building, and because the lessor will try in one way or another to recoup the resulting costs and losses in a new lease agreement, rents will ultimately rise and tenants will also inevitably suffer. The Supplementary Provision at Issue, without closely examining these economic principles and market responses, merely puts forward the pretext of protecting tenants, so the public interest it seeks to achieve is uncertain, and it is also highly questionable how much the Supplementary Provision at Issue will realistically contribute to achieving such public interest.\\n\\nTherefore, the Supplementary Provision at Issue prioritizes only the interests of the tenant on the basis of the lessor’s unilateral sacrifice, and the public interest sought to be achieved through it cannot always be regarded as serious or urgent; accordingly, it is difficult to justify the infringement of the lessor’s trust interest solely on the basis of such public interest."}

question: Which of the following cases should all be contested as an action between parties under the Administrative Litigation Act? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) A person who has applied for the payment of compensation under the Act on the Restoration of Honor and Compensation for Persons Related to the Democratization Movement disputes the Deliberation Committee’s decision regarding the payment of compensation. (b) Under the former Fire Service Officers Act, a local fire official claims, against the local government to which he or she belongs, payment of overtime allowance whose existence and scope are directly determined by the provisions of statutes and regulations. (c) A member of an association who seeks to dispute the validity of an association general meeting resolution on a proposed management and disposition plan under the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents files a lawsuit against a housing reconstruction and improvement project association before approval of the management and disposition plan. (d) A business operator liable for value-added tax claims, against the State, payment of the amount of value-added tax refund. (e) On the premise that a tax assessment disposition is null and void ab initio, a claim is made for the return of taxes already paid.
label: C
